================================================================================
  ABOUT THIS DOCUMENT
================================================================================
  This is the GOLD-STANDARD CKA learning guide — a single source of truth for
  content, structure, visual language and quality bar. It takes a complete
  beginner from zero → CKA-certified → confident, working administrator,
  WITHOUT ever needing official docs, blogs, books or videos again.

  MISSION — every concept is taught once, in depth, and demonstrated on ONE real
  application (easypj/jobpost) so knowledge compounds instead of resetting each
  chapter. Each topic carries an "Exam lens" (what's tested) AND a "Day-2 lens"
  (real operations), with internals included so you never have to leave.

  INTENDED AUDIENCE
  -----------------
    • Primary ... newcomers preparing for the CKA exam (no prior Kubernetes assumed).
    • Secondary . practitioners wanting one deep, exam-AND-production reference for
                  day-to-day Kubernetes administration.

  SCOPE
  -----
    IN  ... 100% of the official 2025 CKA exam domains, PLUS production "Day-2"
            administration (HA, cloud, GitOps, hardening, policy, observability, SRE).
    OUT ... application-developer patterns (CKAD) and deep security specialism
            (CKS) are referenced where useful but are not the focus.

  CONVENTIONS
  -----------
    Difficulty, exam-relevance and content types use a fixed symbol system — see
    SECTION 1 (Symbol & Icon Legend) and SECTION 2 (Visual Component Catalog).
    Reading guidance is in SECTION 0. The running project is SECTION 5; the exam
    audit is SECTION 6; the roadmap is SECTION 7; the master TOC closes the front
    matter.


================================================================================
  SECTION 0 — HOW TO READ THIS GUIDE  (the design philosophy)
================================================================================

    THE 5 PROMISES OF THIS GUIDE
    ────────────────────────────
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  1. ZERO-ASSUMPTION       Every term is defined the first time it      │
    │                           appears. No "you should already know X."     │
    │  2. SHOW, DON'T TELL       Never 3 paragraphs in a row without a        │
    │                           diagram, table, card, or code block.         │
    │  3. ONE REAL PROJECT       Every concept is demonstrated on easypj/     │
    │                           jobpost — the SAME app, start to finish.     │
    │  4. EXAM + BEYOND          Each topic has an "Exam lens" (what's        │
    │                           tested) AND a "Day-2 lens" (real ops use).   │
    │  5. SELF-CONTAINED         Internals included ("Under the Hood") so you │
    │                           never need to leave this document.           │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    THE LEARNER'S LADDER  (how difficulty is signposted)
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🟢 BEGINNER      Concepts, vocabulary, "what & why"
       🟡 INTERMEDIATE  Hands-on, YAML, kubectl, "how"
       🔴 ADVANCED      Internals, HA, failure modes, "what if it breaks"
       🎯 EXAM TOPIC    Directly graded on the CKA performance exam
       🏢 DAY-2 / BEYOND Real-world administration the exam doesn't test
       🧪 LAB           A hands-on, timed, exam-style task

    HOW TO USE THIS GUIDE
    ─────────────────────
      • Each chapter builds on the previous one — read in order the first pass.
      • Every concept includes easypj/jobpost real examples.
      • 🟢 = Beginner | 🟡 = Intermediate | 🔴 = Advanced.
      • 🎯 = CKA Exam Topic (directly tested) — drill these hardest.
      • Do the 🧪 Lab Q&A at the end of every chapter; hands-on > reading.
      • Returning practitioner? Jump to a Part by its TOC anchor; each chapter
        is self-contained behind its SECTION MAP diagram.

    PREREQUISITES & YOUR TOOLKIT  (what you need before Chapter 1)
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  💻 Linux CLI comfort: bash, systemctl, journalctl, vi/nano, ssh      │
    │  🐳 Docker basics — Ch 2 teaches exactly what you need                │
    │  🐍 Any programming literacy (examples use Python/Django — easypj)    │
    │  💾 A machine with 8GB+ RAM (16GB for multi-node kubeadm practice)    │
    │  🧰 Tools (installed in Ch 5): minikube/kind, kubectl, helm,          │
    │     kustomize (built into kubectl), + a kubeadm lab (VMs or cloud)    │
    │  🌐 Internet — to pull images and, on the OPEN-BOOK exam, kubernetes.io│
    │  ⏱️ Budget ~50-70 hours; Appendix G has a 12-week plan (8-12h/week).  │
    │  🐍 The example app lives in Dem/easypj (Django 5.2.5 / Python 3.13). │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

================================================================================
  SECTION 2 — THE VISUAL COMPONENT CATALOG  (the art direction)
================================================================================
    These are the building blocks used to render content. The rule:
    "NEVER a wall of text." Every subsection must contain >=1 of these.
    Each entry = [WHAT it is] + [WHEN to use it] + an ASCII mock to follow.

    2.1  CONCEPT CARD GRID          — 2-4 cards, icon + title + 1-line idea.
         WHEN: introduce a set of sibling concepts (e.g. 4 Service types).
         [ 📦 Pod ][ 🔄 Deploy ][ 🔌 Service ][ 🌍 Ingress ]

    2.2  ANATOMY CALLOUT            — label every field of a YAML/command.
         WHEN: first time a manifest or command is shown.
         kubectl  get   pods   easypj-web   -n easypj
         └cmd──┘ └verb┘ └kind┘ └──name───┘ └namespace┘

    2.3  COMPARISON TABLE          — side-by-side feature matrix.
         WHEN: "X vs Y" decisions (VM vs container, RWO vs RWX).

    2.4  DECISION TREE 🧭          — branching "which one do I use?" guide.
         WHEN: choosing among options (Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet).

    2.5  SEQUENCE / FLOW DIAGRAM   — numbered steps with arrows (left->right
         or top->down). WHEN: a process over time (pod creation, TLS handshake).

    2.6  ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM      — boxed components + connections + legend.
         WHEN: showing how parts of the system relate spatially.

    2.7  MENTAL-MODEL / ANALOGY 🧠 — relate K8s to everyday life.
         WHEN: a concept is abstract (etcd = the cluster's memory/brain).

    2.8  COMMAND CHEAT-CARD 🔑     — grouped, copy-paste commands with notes.
         WHEN: end of every chapter ("most-used commands to remember").

    2.9  YAML SKELETON (annotated) — minimal manifest, every line commented.
         WHEN: teaching the shape of a resource; also used inside lab answers.

    2.10 UNDER THE HOOD 🔧         — deep-dive (internals, etcd keys, controller
         loops, packet paths). WHEN: once per chapter.

    2.11 GOTCHA BOX ⚠️            — the trap + why it happens + the fix.
         WHEN: a place learners reliably fail (indent, wrong ns, deprecated API).

    2.12 SPEED TIP ⚡             — exam time-saver (dry-run, aliases, $do).
         WHEN: an imperative shortcut beats writing YAML.

    2.13 DAILY-LIFE OPS 🏢        — "in a real job you would..." scenario.
         WHEN: connecting a tested skill to actual administration.

    2.14 TROUBLESHOOTING FLOW 🩺  — symptom -> checks -> cause -> fix tree.
         WHEN: any failure mode (CrashLoopBackOff, NotReady, Pending).

    2.15 BEFORE / AFTER SPLIT     — "without K8s" vs "with K8s" two-panel.
         WHEN: motivating why a feature exists.

    2.16 LIFECYCLE PILLS          — state badges joined by arrows
         (Pending -> Running -> Succeeded/Failed). WHEN: object states.

    2.17 STAT / PROGRESS BARS     — weights, adoption %, exam-domain %.
         WHEN: quantitative emphasis.

    2.18 RELATIONSHIP / MIND MAP  — central node with labeled spokes.
         WHEN: "how everything connects" (object relationship map).

    2.19 KEY TAKEAWAYS BANNER     — ✅ bullet recap + 🎯 exam relevance +
         🔑 commands. WHEN: end of every chapter AND every part.

    2.20 VISUAL SUMMARY           — one big picture that re-tells the whole
         chapter/part in a single diagram. WHEN: closing every chapter/part.
         (RULE: every diagram-only block also carries a short prose summary —
         we never give a diagram without its text recap.)

    2.21 PRACTICE DRILL 🧪        — short timed checklist task (do-it-now).
         WHEN: mid/after a chapter, before the formal lab questions.

    2.22 LAB Q&A CARD 🧪          — exam-style question + Answer + Explanation
         (with YAML/diagram). WHEN: 10+ per chapter, end.

    2.23 EXAM-TOPIC BADGE 🎯      — inline tag marking graded competencies.

    2.24 KEY TERM / GLOSSARY POP 📖 — bold term + tight definition box.


================================================================================
  SECTION 3 — THE PER-CHAPTER SCAFFOLD  (fixed anatomy of EVERY chapter)
================================================================================
    Every chapter is assembled from these blocks IN THIS ORDER:

      [A] CHAPTER HEADER      Title + difficulty meta (🟢/🟡/🔴, ⏱️ est time,
                              🎯 domain %, tags) — the META line.
      [B] WHY THIS MATTERS    1-paragraph hook framed on easypj + a Before/
                              After or analogy visual.
      [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES "🎯 What you'll be able to DO" — action bullets.
      [D] CKA RELEVANCE       Which exact official competencies this maps to.
      [E] SECTION-MAP DIAGRAM A single diagram showing how all sections of
                              THIS chapter relate (the "you are here" map).
      [F] CONCEPT SECTIONS    The numbered sections (x.1, x.2, ...). Each one:
                                · 📖 key terms · 🧠 analogy where useful
                                · core explanation broken by visuals
                                · annotated YAML / kubectl as relevant
                                · ⚠️ gotcha · ⚡ speed tip · 🏢 Day-2 note
      [G] UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 / DEEPER   One internals deep-dive for the chapter.
      [H] KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑   ✅ recap + 🎯 exam relevance.
      [I] EXAM GOTCHAS ⚠️    The top traps for this chapter, listed.
      [J] SPEED TIPS ⚡      Imperative shortcuts / dry-run patterns.
      [K] COMMANDS TO REMEMBER 🔑  Cheat-card of must-know commands.
      [L] PRACTICE DRILL 🧪  A short, timed do-it-now checklist.
      [M] LAB QUESTIONS 🧪   >=10 exam-style Q&A. EACH has: Question, Answer
                              (commands/steps), Explanation (the WHY) + at
                              least one YAML/diagram/table.
      [N] VISUAL SUMMARY      One closing big-picture diagram + prose recap.


================================================================================
  SECTION 4 — THE PER-PART SCAFFOLD  (fixed anatomy of EVERY part)
================================================================================
      [A] PART COVER          Title, difficulty band, exam-domain weight,
                              chapter range, "what you'll build" line.
      [B] PART INTRO          What this part is, why it exists, what it
                              unlocks — framed on the easypj journey.
      [C] "HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT" DIAGRAM   A map showing each chapter in the
                              part and the dependency/flow between them.
      [D] SECTION SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION  (placed BEFORE the chapters) — a
                              concise summary of the whole part and HOW it is
                              implemented end-to-end on easypj.
      [E] CHAPTERS            (each following the Section 3 scaffold)
      [F] PART KEY TAKEAWAYS  ✅ + 🎯 + 🔑 across the whole part.
      [G] PART VISUAL SUMMARY One diagram tying the whole part together.


================================================================================
  SECTION 5 — THE RUNNING PROJECT: easypj / jobpost
================================================================================
    Everything in this guide is taught on ONE real application so concepts
    compound instead of resetting each chapter.

    5.1  WHAT IT IS
         📖 easypj   = the Django PROJECT (the deployable unit / repo root).
         📖 jobpost  = the Django APP inside it (a job-board: post & browse
                       jobs, skills, employers, locations).
         Real code (Dem/easypj): Python 3.13, Django 5.2.5.

    5.2  THE DATA MODEL  (real models from jobpost/models.py)
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  User (django.contrib.auth)                                    │
         │     │ 1─1                                                       │
         │     ▼                                                          │
         │  Author(company, designation)                                  │
         │     │ 1─many (jobpost)                                          │
         │     ▼                                                          │
         │  JobPost(title, description, salary, type, slug, expiry, date) │
         │     ▲ 1─1            ▲ many─many                                │
         │     │                │                                         │
         │  Location(...)     Skills(name)                                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         API surface (jobpost/urls.py + views.py):
           GET /jobs/             -> jobpost_list   (JSON list of jobs)
           GET /jobs/<int:id>/    -> jobpost_detail (one job, 404 if missing)
           GET /skills/           -> skills_list    (JSON list of skills)

    5.3  THE CONTAINERIZATION STORY  (the through-line)
         🐳 Dev:    runserver + SQLite (db.sqlite3) — what the repo ships.
         🐳 Build:  multi-stage Dockerfile -> small gunicorn image easypj:vN.
         ☸️ Deploy: Pods (Deployment) + Service + Ingress/Gateway, config via
                    ConfigMap/Secret, data via PostgreSQL (StatefulSet + PVC).
         📖 Why swap SQLite -> PostgreSQL? SQLite is a single file on local
            disk — it cannot be shared by multiple replicas across nodes.
            Kubernetes scales easypj horizontally, so the database must be a
            networked, concurrent server: PostgreSQL (🐘). This swap is the
            single most important "why" that motivates Services, PV/PVC,
            StatefulSets, Secrets, and NetworkPolicy later in the guide.

    5.4  TARGET ARCHITECTURE  (what we build by the end)
         ┌─────────────────────── NAMESPACE: easypj ───────────────────────┐
         │  🌍 Ingress / 🚪 Gateway  (easypj.example.com)                    │
         │              │                                                    │
         │       🔌 Service: easypj-web (ClusterIP)                          │
         │        ┌─────┼───────────────┐                                   │
         │     📦 web-0  📦 web-1  📦 web-2   (Deployment, replicas=3, 📈HPA) │
         │        │  envFrom ⚙️ ConfigMap + 🔒 Secret                        │
         │        ▼                                                          │
         │       🔌 Service: easypj-db (headless)                            │
         │        │                                                         │
         │     🐘 postgres-0  (StatefulSet) ── 💾 PVC ── 🧱 StorageClass     │
         │                                                                   │
         │  🛡️ RBAC(SA+Role)  🧯 NetworkPolicy  PDB  CronJob(db-backup)      │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    5.5  WHERE THE PROJECT APPEARS (mapping)  — every part advances easypj:
         P1 understand it · P2 deploy it · P3 run it on a real cluster ·
         P4 scale/schedule it · P5 connect/expose it · P6 give it storage ·
         P7 secure it · P8 maintain it · P9 troubleshoot it · P10 make it HA ·
         P11 ship it (CI/CD) · P12 harden/policy it · P13 observe it (SRE) ·
         P14 prove it (exam).

    RESULT: 24/24 graded competencies covered (concept + hands-on + labs).

    │                                                              │
    │  Quick deletion:                                             │
    │  k delete pod nginx $now                                    │
    │                                                              │
    │  ⏱️ These aliases save 15-20 minutes during the exam!       │

    PREREQUISITES:
      • Basic Python / Django understanding
      • Familiarity with terminal / command line (Linux basics)
      • A computer with 8 GB+ RAM (16 GB recommended for multi-node clusters)
      • Basic understanding of Linux (systemd, systemctl, journalctl)

    BUILD ORDER NOTE: chapters numbered 1..45, grouped into 14 parts;
    appendices A..L are reference material. Parts 1-9 plus Ch 37 (Helm/
    Kustomize) and Ch 38 (CRDs/operators) cover the graded 2025 exam; Parts
    10-13 are the "and beyond" production depth; Part 14 is exam mastery.
    The detailed chapter/section breakdown follows below, part by part.

    PROSE RECAP — The journey is three arcs. Arc 1 (Parts 1-2, 🟢) builds the
    vocabulary and gets easypj running locally on Kubernetes. Arc 2 (Parts 3-9,
    🟡→🔴) is the graded exam: you install a real cluster with kubeadm, run and
    schedule workloads, wire up Services/DNS/Ingress, attach storage, secure it
    with RBAC and TLS, keep it alive through upgrades and node maintenance, and
    troubleshoot every failure mode. Arc 3 (Parts 10-14, 🔴) is "and beyond":
    HA, cloud K8s, Helm/CRDs/GitOps, hardening and policy, observability and
    day-2 SRE, then a full exam-strategy chapter with a 20-task simulator.

PART 1: FOUNDATIONS — THINK LIKE KUBERNETES                              🟢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapters 1-4  ·  Difficulty: Beginner  ·  "What is all this, and why?"
  What you'll build by the end: a clear mental model of a cluster and the
  ability to read any easypj manifest and say what each object does.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [PART 1 INTRO]
  Before you can administer a cluster you must be able to SEE it in your head.
  Part 1 builds that picture from nothing: why Kubernetes exists, what a
  container actually is, the machines and brains that make up a cluster, and
  the handful of objects you'll use every single day. We anchor it all on
  easypj so the abstractions have a face.

  This is the "foundation" in the truest sense — everything in Parts 2 through
  the end (scheduling, networking, storage, security, troubleshooting) assumes
  you already think in the vocabulary built here. Do not skim it because it
  looks easy. The candidates who fail the CKA on the clock are almost never
  beaten by an obscure feature; they are beaten because their mental model is
  fuzzy, so they waste minutes re-deriving what a Deployment owns or where a
  Pod actually runs. Part 1 makes that model automatic.

  🧠 ANALOGY. Think of a Kubernetes cluster as a shipping port. Containers
  (the literal cargo kind) arrive, and a control tower decides which dock
  (node) each one goes to, restarts the cranes when they jam, and keeps a
  manifest of what SHOULD be on the dock versus what IS. Part 1 is you
  learning to read that manifest and to point at every crane, dock and tower
  by name — before anyone hands you the keys to the tower.

  🐍 OUR RUNNING EXAMPLE — easypj. Throughout the guide we deploy ONE real
  application so the abstractions never float free. easypj is a Django 5.2.5
  job board (Python 3.13). Its single Django app, jobpost, exposes job
  listings backed by a small data model:

      ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  easypj  (Django PROJECT)                                        │
      │  └─ jobpost  (Django APP)                                        │
      │       ├─ JobPost   ── the central record (title, body, salary)  │
      │       ├─ Author    ── FK, who posted it                         │
      │       ├─ Location   ── FK, where the job is                      │
      │       ├─ Skills     ── M2M, tags the post requires              │
      │       └─ auth.User ── Django's built-in user (login / admin)    │
      │                                                                 │
      │  Stack: Python 3.13 · Django 5.2.5 · Docker image               │
      │  DB:   SQLite (laptop / dev)  ──▶  PostgreSQL (in Kubernetes)    │
      └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Every Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap and Secret you meet from here on
  carries a piece of easypj. By the final part you will have taken it from "an
  app that runs on my laptop" all the way to "an app described as desired state
  that a self-healing cluster keeps alive."

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 1 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Ch1 WHY ───────▶ Ch2 HOW (containers) ───────▶ Ch3 WHERE (architecture)│
  │   the problem        the unit K8s runs            the machines & brains  │
  │      │                                                   │               │
  │      └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘               │
  │                              ▼                                            │
  │                 Ch4 WHAT (the core objects you declare)                   │
  │            Pod · ReplicaSet · Deployment · Service · Namespace            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read the map as a sentence: we ask WHY clusters exist, learn HOW the thing
  they run (a container) is built, see WHERE that container lands (the node and
  control-plane split), and finally name WHAT objects you declare to make it
  all happen. Each chapter is a prerequisite for the next — do them in order.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — where do I start?
  ┌───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ If you...                      │ Then...                               │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ have never touched containers  │ start at Ch1 and do not skip Ch2      │
  │ know Docker but not K8s        │ skim Ch2, study Ch3 (architecture)    │
  │ used kubectl but it's "magic"  │ go straight to Ch4 (core objects)     │
  │ are revising for the exam      │ read every chapter's 🔑 + 🧪 blocks   │
  └───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITHOUT vs WITH KUBERNETES — why any of this exists
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WITHOUT Kubernetes               │  WITH Kubernetes                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  🐍 easypj runs on ONE server     │  🐍 easypj runs as N pods across     │
  │     — that server dies, app dies  │     nodes — a node dies, pods move   │
  │  You SSH in and restart by hand   │  Controllers restart it for you      │
  │  Scaling = buy + wire a new box   │  Scaling = change one number (3→6)   │
  │  "Works on my machine" drift      │  Same image, declared desired state  │
  │  Rollback = pray you kept a copy  │  Rollback = one rollout undo command │
  │  Config baked into the box        │  Config in ConfigMaps / Secrets      │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
  CAPTION: Kubernetes does not make easypj fancier — it makes easypj SURVIVE.
  You stop telling a server what to DO and start telling a cluster what you
  WANT; the cluster's controllers spend every second closing the gap between
  desired and actual state. That single shift — imperative "do this" to
  declarative "keep it like this" — is the whole idea behind every page ahead.

  [PART 1 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION  — read before the chapters]
  By the end you will have: installed nothing yet, but you can explain the
  control-plane/worker split, draw how "kubectl apply" turns YAML into a
  running easypj pod, and identify every object in the target architecture
  (Section 5.4). Implementation thread: we take easypj from "an app that runs
  on my laptop" to "an app described as desired state that a cluster keeps
  alive."

      kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml
              │
              ▼
      ┌─────────────────┐   validates &    ┌─────────────────────────┐
      │   API SERVER    │ ───persists───▶  │   etcd (desired state)  │
      └─────────────────┘                  └─────────────────────────┘
              │  "a Pod is wanted but unscheduled"
              ▼
      ┌─────────────────┐   picks a node   ┌─────────────────────────┐
      │   SCHEDULER     │ ──────────────▶  │   kubelet on node-2     │
      └─────────────────┘                  └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                                       │ start container
                                                       ▼
                                            🐍 easypj pod RUNNING
  CAPTION: this is the loop you will narrate in your sleep by the end of the
  guide. Nothing "runs" until the API server has written your wish to etcd, a
  controller has noticed the gap, and the scheduler + kubelet have closed it.

  🔑 PART 1 — MUST-REMEMBER
   • Kubernetes is a DESIRED-STATE engine: you declare, controllers reconcile.
   • The atomic unit Kubernetes schedules is the POD, not the container.
   • The cluster splits into a CONTROL PLANE (the brains) and WORKER NODES
     (where pods actually run) — know which component lives where.
   • You rarely create bare Pods; you declare a Deployment and let it own the
     ReplicaSet that owns the Pods.
   • A Service gives the moving pods one stable name + IP to be reached at.
   • Namespaces slice one cluster into logical tenants (e.g. easypj-prod).

  ⚠️ PART 1 — GOTCHAS
   • "Pod = container" is WRONG: a Pod can hold several containers sharing one
     network + storage. Most easypj pods hold one, but never assume it.
   • Editing a live object by hand drifts from your YAML — the controller may
     overwrite you, or your YAML re-applies stale config later.
   • A Pod is mortal and has NO stable identity or IP; that is the whole reason
     Services and controllers exist.

  ⚡ PART 1 — SPEED TIPS
   • kubectl explain <kind> teaches you any field's schema — no internet needed
     in the exam.
   • Generate, don't type: kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:1
     --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml, then edit.
   • Set up aliases early: alias k=kubectl ; export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'

================================================================================
  Chapter 1: What Is Kubernetes & Why Administrators Need It           🟢 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟢 Beginner · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture (foundation)

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      easypj runs fine on your laptop with `python manage.py runserver`. The
      moment real users arrive it must survive a 3 AM crash, a traffic spike, a
      bad deploy and a dead server — AUTOMATICALLY, without you waking up. That
      automation IS Kubernetes, and building & operating the platform that
      provides it is the CKA's job. This chapter installs the mental model the
      rest of the guide is built on.  VISUAL: Before/After split (below).

  [C] OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
      ✅ define "container orchestration" in one sentence;
      ✅ give the one-line definition of Kubernetes + the desired/actual model;
      ✅ distinguish CKA (administrator) from CKAD (developer) work;
      ✅ name & place the 5 core concepts (cluster, control plane, nodes, pod,
         desired state);
      ✅ identify the major ecosystem tools (CNCF, runtimes, CNI, Helm, GitOps);
      ✅ describe what a Kubernetes administrator actually does day to day;
      ✅ explain the Kubernetes object model (the 4 required fields, spec vs
         status, API groups, object management).

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE: not a graded task by itself, but every Architecture (25%)
      and Troubleshooting (30%) question assumes this model — get it wrong and
      nothing else lands.

  [E] SECTION MAP (you are here):
      1.1 the problem → 1.2 the definition → 1.3 admin vs dev → 1.4 the 5 core
      concepts → 1.5 the ecosystem → 1.6 real-world usage → 1.7 the object model
      & the Kubernetes API.


  ── 1.1  The Problem Before Kubernetes ──────────────────────────────  🟢
     Before orchestration: one app, one server. To run easypj for real you'd
     hand-install Python, Django, gunicorn, nginx and PostgreSQL on a box and
     pray. Picture your easypj job board the night it gets popular.
       • 💀 Single point of failure — the box dies, easypj is down, full stop.
       • 😱 3 AM pager — a crashed process restarts only when YOU ssh in.
       • 📈 Scaling = capex — more traffic means buying & configuring another
         server by hand.
       • 🚀 Risky deploys — copy files, restart, hope; no safe rollback.

     [THE SCALING PROBLEM — before vs after]
     ┌────────────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────────┐
     │  ❌ WITHOUT KUBERNETES      │    │  ✅ WITH KUBERNETES         │
     │                             │    │                             │
     │  ┌──────────┐               │    │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │
     │  │ 🖥️ SERVER │               │    │  │ 📦 │ │ 📦 │ │ 📦 │     │
     │  │          │               │    │  │app │ │app │ │app │     │
     │  │ easypj   │ ← everything  │    │  └────┘ └────┘ └────┘     │
     │  │ postgres │   on ONE box  │    │    ↑ auto-heal, auto-scale │
     │  │ nginx    │               │    │                             │
     │  │          │               │    │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │
     │  │ 💀 crash │ = total       │    │  │Node│ │Node│ │Node│     │
     │  │   = down │   downtime    │    │  │ 1  │ │ 2  │ │ 3  │     │
     │  └──────────┘               │    │  └────┘ └────┘ └────┘     │
     │  Manual restart at 3AM 😱   │    │  Self-healing 24/7 🎉      │
     └────────────────────────────┘    └────────────────────────────┘

     📖 KEY TERM — Container orchestration: automated management of containerized
        apps across many machines (placement, scaling, healing, networking,
        rollout) done by software, not humans.
     🧠 ANALOGY: a lone server is a solo musician; Kubernetes is the conductor of
        an orchestra — it decides who plays what and covers anyone who drops out.


  ── 1.2  What Is Kubernetes? (the simple answer) ────────────────────  🟢
     "Kubernetes is a container orchestrator." More precisely:
     📖 DEFINITION: "an open-source system for automating deployment, scaling and
        management of containerized applications."
     It manages WHERE your containers run, WHEN they restart, HOW they scale, and
     WHO can access them. You tell Kubernetes "I want 3 copies of easypj running"
     → Kubernetes makes it happen and KEEPS it happening.

     The heart is DECLARATIVE control: you describe the END STATE you want
     ("3 copies of easypj:v2, always up") and Kubernetes continuously makes
     reality match it — restarting, rescheduling and scaling on its own.
        💡 Desired State  →  [control loops]  →  Actual State  (reconciliation)

     [THE KUBERNETES ELEVATOR PITCH]
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  You DECLARE what you want:                           │
     │    "Run 3 copies of easypj, always"                  │
     │                                                       │
     │  Kubernetes DELIVERS:                                  │
     │    ✅ Starts 3 containers across available servers    │
     │    ✅ Restarts any that crash                         │
     │    ✅ Replaces any on a failed server                 │
     │    ✅ Scales up/down based on traffic                 │
     │    ✅ Routes network traffic to healthy instances     │
     │    ✅ Rolls out new versions with zero downtime       │
     │                                                       │
     │  🎯 "Desired State" → Kubernetes → "Actual State"    │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🧠 ANALOGY: Kubernetes = Air Traffic Controller for containers — it knows
        every "flight" (pod), every "runway" (node), reroutes around failures and
        keeps the whole airspace safely moving.
     📖 Sticky trivia: name = Greek κυβερνήτης ("helmsman") — steers the ship;
        descends from Google's internal "Borg"; open-sourced 2014; donated to the
        CNCF; written in Go. K8s = K + 8 letters + s.


  ── 1.3  The CKA Perspective: Administrator vs Developer ────────────  🟢 🎯
     Two Linux Foundation certs, two jobs:
       👩‍💻 CKAD (Developer) — "I deploy & configure APPS on a cluster someone
          else runs" (Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, probes).
       🔧 CKA (Administrator) — "I BUILD, OPERATE & TROUBLESHOOT the CLUSTER
          ITSELF" ← this guide. As a CKA admin you are responsible for:
            • Installing Kubernetes clusters from scratch (kubeadm)
            • Upgrading cluster versions safely
            • Backing up and restoring the cluster database (etcd)
            • Managing certificates and security (PKI)
            • Troubleshooting broken nodes and failed components
            • Ensuring high availability and disaster recovery

     [CKA ADMIN RESPONSIBILITIES MAP]
     ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  THE K8s ADMINISTRATOR OWNS EVERYTHING BELOW THE APP  │
     │                                                        │
     │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
     │  │  👨‍💻 Developer's World (CKAD)                   │    │
     │  │  Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps       │    │
     │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤    │
     │  │  🔧 Administrator's World (CKA) ← YOU          │    │
     │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐  │    │
     │  │  │ Cluster Installation (kubeadm)          │  │    │
     │  │  │ Certificate Management (PKI)            │  │    │
     │  │  │ etcd Backup & Restore                   │  │    │
     │  │  │ Cluster Upgrades (version management)   │  │    │
     │  │  │ Node Management (drain, cordon, uncordon)│  │    │
     │  │  │ RBAC & Security Policies                │  │    │
     │  │  │ Networking (CNI, DNS, kube-proxy)       │  │    │
     │  │  │ Storage (PV, PVC, StorageClasses)       │  │    │
     │  │  │ Troubleshooting (nodes, pods, cluster)  │  │    │
     │  │  │ High Availability & Disaster Recovery   │  │    │
     │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────┘  │    │
     │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
     └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🧠 ANALOGY: CKAD furnishes the rooms; CKA builds & maintains the house —
        foundations, plumbing and wiring included.


  ── 1.4  The 5 Core Concepts — the big picture ──────────────────────  🟢
     - Cluster: a set of machines (nodes) managed by Kubernetes
     - Control Plane: the "brain" that makes decisions
     - Worker Nodes: the "muscles" that run your containers
     - Pod: smallest deployable unit (one or more containers)
     - Desired State vs Actual State: declarative magic

     Everything else is built from five ideas:
       1. 🗂️ CLUSTER — a set of machines K8s manages as one.
       2. 🧠 CONTROL PLANE — the "brain": API, state, scheduling, reconciliation.
       3. 💪 WORKER NODES — the "muscle": actually run your containers.
       4. 📦 POD — smallest deployable unit (1+ containers sharing IP & storage).
       5. 🔄 DESIRED vs ACTUAL STATE — you declare desired; controllers drive
          actual toward it, forever.

     [KUBERNETES BIG PICTURE — 5 core concepts]
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                    CLUSTER                              │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
     │  │        🧠 CONTROL PLANE ("The Brain")            │   │
     │  │   ┌─────────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌────────┐ │   │
     │  │   │API Server│ │ etcd │ │Scheduler │ │Ctrl Mgr│ │   │
     │  │   └─────────┘ └──────┘ └──────────┘ └────────┘ │   │
     │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
     │                        │                                │
     │              "Desired State" vs "Actual State"          │
     │                        │                                │
     │  ┌─────────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐   │
     │  │        💪 WORKER NODES ("The Muscles")           │   │
     │  │                                                   │   │
     │  │  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐        │   │
     │  │  │  Worker Node │        │  Worker Node │        │   │
     │  │  │  ┌────────┐  │        │  ┌────────┐  │        │   │
     │  │  │  │📦 POD   │  │        │  │📦 POD   │  │        │   │
     │  │  │  │ easypj │  │        │  │ easypj │  │        │   │
     │  │  │  │ :8000  │  │        │  │ :8000  │  │        │   │
     │  │  │  └────────┘  │        │  └────────┘  │        │   │
     │  │  └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘        │   │
     │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
     │                                                         │
     │  You say: "I want 3 easypj pods" (Desired State)       │
     │  K8s ensures: 3 pods are ALWAYS running (Actual State) │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     [DESIRED STATE vs ACTUAL STATE — the declarative magic]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                                                        │
     │  📝 YOU DECLARE (YAML):        ⚙️ KUBERNETES ENSURES:   │
     │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐    │
     │  │ replicas: 3      │  ──▶    │ 📦 📦 📦 running  │    │
     │  │ image: easypj:v2 │         │ all v2 images     │    │
     │  │ memory: 256Mi    │         │ each ≤ 256Mi      │    │
     │  └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘    │
     │                                                        │
     │  Pod crashes?     K8s restarts it automatically  🔄    │
     │  Node dies?       K8s moves pods to other nodes  🔀    │
     │  Traffic spikes?  K8s can auto-scale up          📈    │
     │  New version?     K8s rolls out with 0 downtime  🚀    │
     │                                                        │
     │  💡 You never say "start a container on node 2"        │
     │     You say "I want 3 copies" — K8s figures out the how│
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  ── 1.5  The Kubernetes Ecosystem ──────────────────────────────────  🟢 🏢
     A core that everything plugs into (all governed by the CNCF, the Cloud
     Native Computing Foundation):
       • 🐋 Runtimes — containerd, CRI-O (via the CRI).
       • 🌐 CNI plugins — Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave (pod networking).
       • 💾 CSI drivers — cloud / Ceph / NFS storage.
       • 📦 Packaging — Helm (charts), Kustomize (overlays).
       • 🔄 GitOps — ArgoCD, FluxCD (git as source of truth).
       • 🕸️ Service mesh — Istio, Linkerd.
       • 📊 Observability — Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry.

     [KUBERNETES ECOSYSTEM ORBIT]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                                                    │
     │               Helm 📦                               │
     │          ╱                  ╲                       │
     │    ArgoCD 🔄          Calico 🌐                     │
     │       ╲                 ╱                           │
     │         ┌─────────────┐                             │
     │    ─────│ KUBERNETES  │─────  Prometheus 📊        │
     │         │   ⚙️ Core    │                             │
     │         └─────────────┘                             │
     │       ╱                 ╲                           │
     │   containerd 🐋      Istio 🕸️                      │
     │          ╲                  ╱                       │
     │            Grafana 📈                               │
     │                                                    │
     │  All governed by CNCF (Cloud Native Foundation)    │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  ── 1.6  How Companies Use Kubernetes (a day in an admin's life) ────  🟢 🏢
     Scale changes the job, not the fundamentals:
       🏠 Startup (5–20) — 1 small cluster (minikube → managed cloud EKS/AKS);
          one admin deploys easypj, monitors, basic troubleshooting.
       🏢 Mid-size (50–200) — dev/staging/prod; CI/CD, RBAC, upgrades, cost
          control; 2–4 admins.
       🏙️ Enterprise (500+) — many HA, multi-region clusters; DR, compliance,
          GitOps, service mesh; a dedicated platform team.

     [COMPANY SIZE → K8s USAGE → ADMIN TASKS]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  Company    │ K8s Setup          │ Admin Tasks             │
     │  Size       │                    │                         │
     │ ────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────────────────── │
     │             │                    │                         │
     │  🏠 Startup │ 1 cluster, 3 nodes │ Deploy apps, monitor    │
     │  (5-20 ppl) │ Minikube → managed │ basic troubleshooting   │
     │  easypj ✅  │ cloud (EKS/AKS)    │ 1 admin does it all    │
     │             │                    │                         │
     │ ────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────────────────── │
     │             │                    │                         │
     │  🏢 Mid-size│ 2-5 clusters       │ CI/CD pipelines, RBAC,  │
     │  (50-200)   │ dev/staging/prod   │ upgrades, monitoring,   │
     │             │ multi-team access   │ cost optimization       │
     │             │                    │ 2-4 admins              │
     │             │                    │                         │
     │ ────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────────────────── │
     │             │                    │                         │
     │  🏙️ Enter-  │ 10-100+ clusters   │ HA, disaster recovery,  │
     │  prise      │ multi-region, HA   │ security policies,      │
     │  (500+)     │ custom networking  │ compliance, GitOps,     │
     │             │ service mesh       │ multi-cluster mgmt      │
     │             │                    │ Dedicated platform team │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🏢 A CKA admin's day: check cluster/node health → read events & logs →
        ship changes via GitOps/PRs → drain-patch-uncordon a node → verify etcd
        backups → handle an incident → capacity-plan.


  ── 1.7  The Object Model & the Kubernetes API ──────────────────────  🟢 🎯
     Everything you create is a Kubernetes OBJECT — a persisted record of intent.
     Four ideas make the whole API click:

     • THE 4 REQUIRED FIELDS (every manifest, no exceptions):
         apiVersion — which API group+version defines it (e.g. apps/v1)
         kind       — the object type (e.g. Deployment); immutable
         metadata   — identity: name (required), namespace, labels, annotations,
                      and the server-set uid
         spec       — your DESIRED state (shape varies per kind)
       Omit one (or mis-case `kind`) → the apiserver rejects it before etcd.

       [THE 4 REQUIRED FIELDS — an easypj Deployment manifest]
       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ apiVersion: apps/v1          ← group + version            │
       │ kind: Deployment             ← object type (immutable)    │
       │ metadata:                    ← identity                   │
       │   name: easypj-web           ← required, DNS-subdomain    │
       │   namespace: default                                      │
       │   labels: { app: easypj }                                 │
       │ spec:                        ← DESIRED state              │
       │   replicas: 3                                             │
       │   template:                                               │
       │     spec:                                                 │
       │       containers:                                         │
       │       - name: web                                         │
       │         image: easypj:v2                                  │
       │ # status: {...}              ← cluster writes this back   │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     • SPEC vs STATUS: spec = what YOU declared; status = what the cluster
       observes & writes (read-only). The reconcile loop just keeps status → spec.

     • NAMING RULES (validation, not taste):
         DNS Subdomain (most objects): ≤253 chars, lowercase a–z 0–9 - . ;
            start/end alphanumeric (may start with a digit).   e.g. easypj-web
         DNS Label (namespaces, nodes): ≤63 chars, lowercase a–z 0–9 - (NO dots);
            MUST START WITH A LETTER, end alphanumeric.  ❌ easypj_web · EasyPJ · 9web
         Service names also follow RFC 1035 (must start with a letter).
         UID — cluster-unique, auto-generated, never user-set.

     • API GROUPS, VERSIONS & STABILITY:
         core group  → /api/v1            (Pod, Service, ConfigMap, Namespace, Node)
         named groups → /apis/<grp>/<ver> (apps/v1, batch/v1, rbac.../v1 …)
         alpha (v1alpha1, off by default, may vanish) → beta (v1beta1, may change)
            → stable/GA (v1, backward-compatible).
         Deprecation policy: a GA API is NOT removed within a major version; a
            deprecated BETA is dropped after 9 months or 3 releases (whichever is
            longer); alpha can change any release. No LTS — each minor release is
            maintained ~14 months (≈12 months + a ~2-month maintenance window).
         `kubectl api-resources` lists every kind → its group, version, namespaced?

     • OBJECT MANAGEMENT — 3 approaches (the exam loves `apply`):
         imperative cmd  → kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v2
         imperative cfg  → kubectl create -f f.yaml / replace -f  (NOT idempotent)
         declarative     → kubectl apply -f f.yaml  (idempotent — the default)
         Server-Side Apply (`--server-side`) tracks field ownership in
            managedFields so several controllers co-own one object cleanly.

     • ADD-ONS a fresh cluster still needs: CoreDNS (in-cluster DNS, usually
       installed) · metrics-server (powers `kubectl top` + HPA, NOT default) ·
       an Ingress controller (you pick & install) · Dashboard (optional UI).

     📖 KEY TERM — Object: a persisted etcd entry expressing intent (spec) and
        observed reality (status), reconciled by a controller.
     🧠 ANALOGY: a manifest is a work order — apiVersion/kind name the shop, the
        metadata is the label, the spec is the instructions; status is the shop's
        progress note you read back.

   ┌────────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
   │ 🏠 Startup  │ 1 cluster, few nodes  │ deploy + monitor; 1 admin  │
   │ 🏢 Mid-size │ dev / staging / prod  │ CI/CD, RBAC, upgrades; 2–4 │
   │ 🏙️ Enterprise│ many HA, multi-region │ DR, compliance, GitOps;   │
   │            │                       │ a platform team            │
   └────────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — the reconciliation loop
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     At the core of Kubernetes is one repeating pattern: the control loop.
        observe  →  diff  →  act   (then repeat, forever)
     A controller continually OBSERVES actual state, DIFFS it against desired
     state, and ACTS to close the gap. This is why easypj self-heals: nobody
     pushes an event saying "a pod died" — the controller simply notices, on its
     next pass, that actual (2 pods) ≠ desired (3 pods) and recreates one.

     LEVEL-TRIGGERED vs EDGE-TRIGGERED:
       • Edge-triggered = react to the change event; miss the event, miss the fix.
       • Level-triggered = react to the CURRENT STATE; even a missed event is
         caught on the next observe pass. Kubernetes is level-triggered → it
         self-heals reliably even after the controller itself restarts.

     🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
       • The closed-loop control model is idempotent and eventually consistent —
         re-running `kubectl apply` with the same YAML changes nothing; converging
         to desired state may take several passes but it converges.
       • EVERYTHING is an API object reconciled by a controller — that uniformity
         is what makes Kubernetes a universal control plane (CRDs let you teach it
         new object types and write your own controllers).

       • API-SERVER WRITE PIPELINE (the only path to etcd):
           authN → authZ (RBAC) → mutating admission → schema validation →
           validating admission → persist to etcd.
         No client ever talks to etcd directly; the apiserver is the front door.

       • Controllers scale via SHARED INFORMERS: one LIST+WATCH per resource type,
         cached in memory and shared by all controllers → load is O(resource
         types), not O(controllers). Failed reconciles re-queue with exponential
         backoff (≈5ms, doubling, capped ~1000s), deduped, reset on success.

       • WATCH machinery: resourceVersion is an optimistic-concurrency cursor —
         write with a stale rv → 409 Conflict → re-read & retry; periodic BOOKMARK
         events prove a watch is alive; a too-old rv → 410 Gone → client re-LISTs.

     [THE WRITE PATH — your YAML to etcd]
       kubectl apply ─► API server ─► authN ─► authZ(RBAC) ─► mutating admission
            ─► schema validation ─► validating admission ─► etcd (persisted)
                                                              │
       controller WATCHes ◄──────────────────────────────────┘
            └─► diff vs actual ─► act ─► kubelet runs the easypj pod


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     🔑 Orchestration AUTOMATES operations (placement, healing, scaling, rollout)
        that a human used to do by hand.
     🔑 Kubernetes is DECLARATIVE, not imperative — you declare desired state and
        control loops reconcile actual toward it, continuously, forever.
     🔑 The administrator (CKA) owns EVERYTHING BELOW the app: install, certs,
        etcd, upgrades, nodes, RBAC, networking, storage, HA/DR, troubleshooting.
     🔑 The API server is the ONLY path to etcd — every change flows through its
        authN → authZ → admission → validation → persist pipeline.
     🔑 The 5 core concepts — cluster, control plane, worker nodes, pod, desired
        vs actual state — frame the entire rest of the guide.
     🔑 Every object carries the 4 required fields (apiVersion, kind, metadata,
        spec); spec is intent, status is observed reality.
     🔑 Level-triggered reconciliation (react to current state, not events) is why
        K8s self-heals even after a controller restart.


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     ⚠️ "Kubernetes replaces Docker." No — it ORCHESTRATES containers; it runs
        them through a runtime (containerd/CRI-O) via the CRI.
     ⚠️ Thinking imperatively ("start a container on node 2") instead of
        declaratively ("I want 3 copies"). Declare the END state; let K8s place it.
     ⚠️ Confusing CKA with CKAD — CKAD deploys apps; CKA builds & operates the
        cluster. The exam tests the cluster, not your app code.
     ⚠️ Editing `status` in a manifest does nothing — it's read-only, written by
        the cluster. Only `spec` is yours.
     ⚠️ Naming: DNS Labels (namespaces, nodes) must START WITH A LETTER and allow
        NO dots/underscores — `easypj_web`, `EasyPJ`, `9web` are all invalid.


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     ⚡ Think in DESIRED STATE — most exam tasks are "make the cluster look like
        X," not "run these steps."
     ⚡ `kubectl explain <kind>` (and `--recursive`) is your in-exam field manual —
        no need to memorize every spec field.
     ⚡ Learn to READ EVENTS FIRST — `kubectl get events` and `kubectl describe`
        explain WHY before you start guessing.
     ⚡ Prefer `kubectl apply -f` over `create`/`replace` — it's idempotent and
        re-runnable, the safe default under exam time pressure.


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     kubectl cluster-info                 # control-plane & core add-on endpoints
     kubectl get nodes -o wide            # nodes, roles, IPs, versions, runtime
     kubectl get componentstatuses       # (legacy) control-plane health summary
     kubectl api-resources               # every kind → group, version, namespaced?
     kubectl api-versions                # all served group/versions
     kubectl version                     # client & server versions
     kubectl explain deployment.spec     # field-level docs for any kind
     kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml        # declarative, idempotent create/update


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     🧪 In 5 minutes, sketch the cluster from memory and label every box: cluster,
        control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager), worker
        nodes, an easypj pod, and the desired→actual arrow.


  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 1)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Q1. Define "container orchestration" in one sentence.
         → The automated deploy / scale / heal / connect of containers across many
           machines, performed by software rather than humans.

     Q2. easypj's pod crashes at 3 AM — what does Kubernetes do, and why?
         → A controller sees actual (2 pods) ≠ desired (3 pods) on its next
           observe pass and recreates the pod. This is level-triggered
           reconciliation — no human and no "crash event" is required.
              desired: 3  │  actual: 2  →  controller acts  →  actual: 3

     Q3. Give the one-line definition of Kubernetes.
         → An open-source system for automating the deployment, scaling and
           management of containerized applications (declarative, self-healing).

     Q4. Explain desired-vs-actual state using a `replicas: 3` example.
         → You DECLARE replicas: 3 (desired). The controller continuously checks
           how many easypj pods actually run (actual). If actual < 3 it creates
           pods; if actual > 3 it deletes pods — converging actual → desired.

     Q5. List three tasks that belong to CKA but NOT CKAD.
         → etcd backup & restore · cluster upgrades · certificate/PKI management
           (also valid: kubeadm install, node drain/cordon, CNI install, HA/DR).

     Q6. Name the four control-plane components and the one that stores state.
         → API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd — and etcd stores all
           cluster state.

     Q7. What is a Pod, and what do containers inside it share?
         → The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a
           network namespace (one IP/port space) and can share storage volumes.

     Q8. Why is `kubectl apply` idempotent?
         → It is declarative: it sends desired state, and reconciliation converges
           actual → desired. Re-applying the same YAML changes nothing because
           actual already equals desired.

     Q9. Match each tool to its job: Calico · Helm · ArgoCD · Prometheus ·
         containerd.
         → Calico = CNI / pod networking · Helm = packaging (charts) ·
           ArgoCD = GitOps continuous delivery · Prometheus = metrics/monitoring ·
           containerd = container runtime.

     Q10. Sort "admin-owns vs dev-owns": etcd backup · a Deployment · RBAC ·
          a ConfigMap · a node upgrade.
         → 🔧 ADMIN (CKA): etcd backup · RBAC · node upgrade.
           👩‍💻 DEV (CKAD): a Deployment · a ConfigMap.


  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — "From your YAML to a running easypj pod"
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  📝 easypj.yaml          📡 API server           🗄️ etcd                 │
  │  (desired state)  ──►  authN→authZ→admission ──►  (state persisted)      │
  │   replicas: 3                                          │                 │
  │   image: easypj:v2                                     ▼                 │
  │                       🔄 controller WATCHes ──► diff actual vs desired   │
  │                                                       │                  │
  │                                                       ▼                  │
  │   📋 scheduler picks a node ──► 💪 kubelet ──► 🐋 runtime runs the pod   │
  │                                                       │                  │
  │                                                       ▼                  │
  │                                          📦 easypj pod RUNNING (:8000)   │
  │  💡 You declared the END state; the loop made reality match it.          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  .vs-prose — In words: you write easypj.yaml describing the END STATE (3 pods of
  easypj:v2). kubectl sends it to the API server, which authenticates, authorizes
  (RBAC), runs admission and validation, then persists the object to etcd. A
  controller watching that object diffs desired (3) against actual, and asks the
  scheduler to place each missing pod on a node. On that node the kubelet tells
  the container runtime (containerd) to start the pod, which comes up listening on
  :8000. Nothing pushed an "event" — the level-triggered loop simply drove actual
  state toward your declared desired state, and it keeps doing so forever.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 2: Containers & Docker — The Unit Kubernetes Runs           🟢 🎯
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  [A] META: 🟢 Beginner · ⏱️ ~2h · Foundation for Cluster Architecture (CRI).
      The container is the atom Kubernetes schedules; this chapter is the floor
      everything else is built on.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ────────────────
  Kubernetes does not schedule "your code" — it schedules CONTAINERS. When a pod
  refuses to start, sits in ImagePullBackOff, or dies with exit 137, the truth
  lives one layer below the pod: in the image, its layers, and the container
  runtime. To debug a pod that won't start you must understand images, layers,
  and runtimes. easypj works perfectly on your laptop and explodes in production
  because of a different Python, a missing psycopg2, or absent env vars — a
  container is the fix. See the "works on my machine" panel below, grounded on
  easypj (missing psycopg2, wrong Python).

  OBJECTIVES
  ──────────
  • Explain why containers exist and how they differ from virtual machines.
  • Read and write a Dockerfile (single-stage and production multi-stage).
  • Build the easypj image and run it.
  • Use the core docker AND crictl/ctr commands for node-level debugging.
  • Explain the CRI and why the Docker "dockershim" was removed in v1.24.
  • Understand how the CLUSTER names, pulls, authenticates and garbage-collects
    images, and the pull-failure states you will debug.

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
  ────────────────
  • CRI is an "extension interface" of the node → Cluster Architecture (25%).
  • Runtime-level debugging (crictl, exit codes, ImagePullBackOff) appears in
    Troubleshooting (30%). When the apiserver/kubectl is down, crictl is the
    only window you have into a node.

  ───────────
   2.1  Why Containers? The "Works on My Machine" Problem ............ 🟢
