  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.1  Why Containers? The "Works on My Machine" Problem               🟢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Without containers: "it works on my laptop but not in production"
     - Containers package EVERYTHING: code + dependencies + config
     - Like a shipping container: same box works on any ship/truck/train

     easypj works on your laptop and explodes in production: a different Python,
     a missing psycopg2, no env vars. A CONTAINER fixes this by packaging the app
     WITH everything it needs — code + Python 3.13 + Django 5.2.5 + gunicorn +
     psycopg2 + config — into one immutable image that runs IDENTICALLY anywhere.

     🧠 ANALOGY: a shipping container — the same sealed box rides any ship, truck
        or crane. The dockworkers never open it; they just move the standard box.
        Docker did the same for software: standardize the BOX, not the cargo.

     [THE "WORKS ON MY MACHINE" PROBLEM]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  👩‍💻 Developer laptop:  "easypj works perfectly!"       │
     │  🖥️ Production server:  "ModuleNotFoundError" 💀        │
     │                                                         │
     │  WHY? Different Python version, missing packages,       │
     │  different OS, missing environment variables...          │
     │                                                         │
     │  SOLUTION: Pack EVERYTHING into a container 📦           │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                        │
     │  │ 📦 Docker Container          │                        │
     │  │ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │                        │
     │  │ │ Python 3.13             │ │                        │
     │  │ │ Django 5.2.5            │ │                        │
     │  │ │ gunicorn, psycopg2      │ │                        │
     │  │ │ easypj source code      │ │                        │
     │  │ │ settings & config       │ │                        │
     │  │ └─────────────────────────┘ │                        │
     │  │ Runs IDENTICALLY everywhere │                        │
     │  └─────────────────────────────┘                        │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     .vs-prose — The panel above is the whole reason containers exist: the SAME
     easypj source behaves differently on two machines because the ENVIRONMENT
     differs (Python build, installed packages, OS libraries, env vars). A
     container removes that variable by sealing the environment INTO the artifact.
     Build once, run the byte-identical image on laptop, CI, staging and the
     Kubernetes cluster — the failure surface collapses to "is the image right?"

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.2  Containers vs Virtual Machines                                  🟢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     A VM virtualizes HARDWARE: a hypervisor gives each VM a full guest OS, so a
     VM is measured in GIGABYTES and boots in MINUTES. A container virtualizes
     the OS — every container SHARES the host kernel, so it is measured in
     MEGABYTES and starts in milliseconds. That single difference (own kernel vs
     shared kernel) drives every other row in the tables below.

     [SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON DIAGRAM]
     ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐
     │  VIRTUAL MACHINES   │    │  CONTAINERS          │
     │                     │    │                      │
     │ ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐   │    │ ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐    │
     │ │App A│  │App B│   │    │ │App A│  │App B│    │
     │ ├─────┤  ├─────┤   │    │ ├─────┤  ├─────┤    │
     │ │Libs │  │Libs │   │    │ │Libs │  │Libs │    │
     │ ├─────┤  ├─────┤   │    │ └──┬──┘  └──┬──┘    │
     │ │Guest│  │Guest│   │    │    │ Shared  │       │
     │ │ OS  │  │ OS  │   │    │ ┌──▼────────▼──┐    │
     │ └─────┘  └─────┘   │    │ │Container Eng.│    │
     │ ┌─────────────────┐│    │ └──────────────┘    │
     │ │   Hypervisor    ││    │ ┌──────────────────┐ │
     │ └─────────────────┘│    │ │   Host OS        │ │
     │ ┌─────────────────┐│    │ └──────────────────┘ │
     │ │   Host OS       ││    │ ┌──────────────────┐ │
     │ └─────────────────┘│    │ │   Hardware       │ │
     │                     │    │ └──────────────────┘ │
     │ Heavy: GB, minutes  │    │ Light: MB, seconds   │
     └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘

     [COMPARISON TABLE]
     | Feature       | Virtual Machine          | Container             |
     | Size          | Gigabytes                | Megabytes             |
     | Startup       | Minutes                  | Seconds               |
     | OS            | Full guest OS per VM     | Shares host kernel    |
     | Isolation     | Strong (hardware-level)  | Process-level         |
     | Performance   | Near-native              | Native                |
     | Use case      | Different OS needed      | Same OS, many apps    |

     [CONTAINERS vs VMs — shared kernel = light & fast]
      VIRTUAL MACHINES                CONTAINERS
      ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐                 ┌──────┐ ┌─────┐
      │App A│ │App B│                 │easypj│ │nginx│
      │Libs │ │Libs │                 │Libs  │ │Libs │
      │Guest│ │Guest│                 └──┬───┘ └──┬──┘
      │ OS  │ │ OS  │                 ┌──▼────────▼──┐
      ├─────┴─┴─────┤                 │ container rt  │ (containerd)
      │ Hypervisor  │                 ├───────────────┤
      ├─────────────┤                 │  Host kernel  │ (SHARED)
      │   Host OS   │                 ├───────────────┤
      └─────────────┘                 │   Hardware    │
      GB · minutes                    MB · seconds   └───────────────┘

     .vs-prose — Both diagrams say the same thing from two angles. The VM stack
     repeats a Guest OS for EVERY app — that duplication is the gigabytes and the
     minutes. The container stack draws the kernel exactly ONCE, shared by all
     containers through the container runtime; each container adds only its app
     and libs on top. Strong hardware isolation is the VM's trade for that weight;
     a container's isolation is process-level (namespaces + cgroups), which is why
     a hostile workload that needs a hard boundary may still want a VM-class
     sandbox (gVisor/Kata — see RuntimeClass in 2.7).

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.3  Docker Basics for Kubernetes Admins                             🟢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Dockerfile: recipe for building an image
     - Image: the built package (read-only template)
     - Container: a running instance of an image
     - Registry: image storage (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR)

     📖 Dockerfile (recipe) → `docker build` → IMAGE (read-only template) →
        `docker run` → CONTAINER (running instance) → `docker push` → REGISTRY
        (Docker Hub / ECR / GCR). An image is built from stacked, cached LAYERS:
        each instruction in the Dockerfile produces one read-only layer, and
        Docker caches a layer until the instruction or its inputs change.

     [DOCKER WORKFLOW]
     ┌──────────────┐  build   ┌──────────────┐  run    ┌──────────────┐
     │ 📝 Dockerfile │ ───────▶ │ 📀 Image      │ ──────▶ │ 📦 Container  │
     │ (recipe)      │          │ (template)    │         │ (running app)│
     └──────────────┘          └──────┬───────┘         └──────────────┘
                                      │ push
                                      ▼
                               ┌──────────────┐
                               │ 🏪 Registry   │
                               │ (Docker Hub)  │
                               └──────────────┘

     [IMAGE LAYERS — easypj built in stages, cached]
      FROM python:3.13-slim        ◄ base layer (shared / cached)
      COPY requirements + pip install ◄ deps layer (reused until reqs change)
      COPY . (easypj source)       ◄ app layer (changes most -> put it LAST)
      CMD gunicorn ...             ► image easypj:v1 ─► a running 📦 container
      💡 multi-stage build discards the builder -> small, fewer-CVE final image.

     .vs-prose — A Dockerfile is a deterministic recipe; `docker build` runs it
     once to produce a read-only IMAGE made of stacked layers; `docker run`
     instantiates that image into a live CONTAINER (image + a thin writable top
     layer); `docker push` ships the image to a REGISTRY so the cluster can pull
     it. The layer model is the performance secret: identical lower layers are
     shared and cached across images and across pulls, so only what changed moves.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.4  Building an easypj Docker Image                                 🟡 🧪
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     a) Base image: python:3.13-slim
     b) Install dependencies: requirements.txt
     c) Copy source code
     d) Set environment variables
     e) Run with gunicorn

     A simple single-stage Dockerfile is fine for learning:
       # Dockerfile (single-stage, dev)
       FROM python:3.13-slim
       ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
       WORKDIR /app
       COPY requirements.txt .
       RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
       COPY . .
       EXPOSE 8000
       CMD ["gunicorn","easypj.wsgi:application","-b","0.0.0.0:8000"]

     A production MULTI-STAGE Dockerfile keeps the final image small & safe by
     discarding all the build-only tooling:
       # Dockerfile.production
       # ── stage 1: builder ──
       FROM python:3.13-slim AS builder
       WORKDIR /app
       COPY requirements.txt .
       RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt
       # ── stage 2: slim runtime ──
       FROM python:3.13-slim
       RUN useradd -m app                       # run as non-root
       WORKDIR /app
       COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
       COPY . .
       RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
       USER app
       EXPOSE 8000
       CMD ["gunicorn","easypj.wsgi:application","-b","0.0.0.0:8000"]

     .dockerignore (keeps junk and secrets out of the build context & image):
       .git
       __pycache__
       *.pyc
       db.sqlite3
       .env
       venv/

     🏢 DAY-2: Multi-stage = smaller image, fewer CVEs, faster pulls (the builder
        stage, with its compilers and headers, is thrown away — the runtime image
        ships only the installed packages + your code). Smaller surface = less to
        patch and less to exploit.

     🧪 LAB: from the easypj repo root, build and run it:
        docker build -t easypj:v1 .
        docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
        curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/        # the jobpost app's list view

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.5  Essential Docker (and crictl) Commands for Admins               🟡
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     [COMMAND TABLE]
     | Command                          | What it does                    |
     | docker build -t easypj:v1 .     | Build image from Dockerfile     |
     | docker run -p 8000:8000 easypj  | Run container, expose port      |
     | docker ps                        | List running containers         |
     | docker logs <id>                 | View container logs             |
     | docker exec -it <id> bash        | Shell into container            |
     | docker images                    | List local images               |
     | docker push <registry>/easypj   | Push to registry                |
     | docker pull <image>              | Pull from registry              |
     | docker stop <id>                 | Stop a container                |
     | docker system prune              | Clean up unused resources       |

     Build and run with Docker on your build host. But on a NODE — where kubectl
     and Docker may be ABSENT and only containerd is running — you reach for
     crictl (the CRI debug CLI) or ctr (containerd's own CLI):

     ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
     │ Docker (build host)      │ crictl / ctr (on the node)  │
     │ docker ps                │ crictl ps                   │
     │ docker logs <id>         │ crictl logs <id>            │
     │ docker exec -it <id> sh  │ crictl exec -it <id> sh     │
     │ docker inspect <id>      │ crictl inspect <id>         │
     │ docker images            │ crictl images / ctr images  │
     └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
     ⚡ crictl is your LIFELINE when the kubelet/apiserver is down — it talks
        straight to the runtime socket (e.g. /run/containerd/containerd.sock),
        so it answers even when nothing above the node is responding.

     .vs-prose — Two CLIs, two altitudes. Docker is the developer/build-host tool
     for making and pushing images. crictl/ctr are the node-administrator tools
     for inspecting the containers a kubelet has ALREADY created on a node. In the
     exam, "the node is broken and kubectl returns nothing" is the cue to SSH to
     the node and switch from kubectl/docker to crictl ps / crictl logs.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.6  Container Runtimes: Beyond Docker (the CRI)                     🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Kubernetes doesn't use Docker directly anymore (since v1.24)
     - containerd: industry standard runtime (extracted from Docker)
     - CRI-O: lightweight, Kubernetes-native runtime
     - As a CKA admin: you configure the container runtime on nodes

     📖 KEY TERM — CRI (Container Runtime Interface): the gRPC socket the kubelet
        talks to in order to create, start, stop and inspect containers. Since
        v1.24 the "dockershim" shim is GONE — nodes RUN containers via containerd
        or CRI-O directly. You still BUILD images with Docker/buildkit; the node
        just doesn't need the Docker daemon in the data path.

     [CONTAINER RUNTIME EVOLUTION]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  HOW KUBERNETES RUNS CONTAINERS                     │
     │                                                     │
     │  Before v1.24:        After v1.24:                  │
     │  kubelet               kubelet                      │
     │     │                     │                          │
     │     ▼                     ▼                          │
     │  dockershim (removed)  CRI interface                │
     │     │                     │                          │
     │     ▼                  ┌──┴──┐                      │
     │  Docker daemon        ▼     ▼                       │
     │     │              containerd  CRI-O                │
     │     ▼                  │        │                    │
     │  containerd            ▼        ▼                    │
     │     │               containers  containers           │
     │     ▼                                                │
     │  containers        (direct, no Docker overhead)     │
     │                                                     │
     │  💡 Docker images still work! Just the runtime      │
     │     changed. You still USE Docker to BUILD images.  │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     [CONTAINER RUNTIME EVOLUTION — Docker out of the data path (v1.24)]
      BEFORE v1.24             AFTER v1.24
      🤖 kubelet               🤖 kubelet
         │                        │  CRI
      dockershim (removed)     ┌──┴───┐
         │                     ▼      ▼
      Docker daemon         containerd  CRI-O
         │                     │        │
      containerd              📦        📦   containers (no Docker daemon)
      💡 You still BUILD images with Docker; nodes RUN them via containerd.

     .vs-prose — Both runtime diagrams tell the migration story. BEFORE v1.24 the
     kubelet spoke to a Docker daemon through a translation shim ("dockershim"),
     and Docker in turn drove containerd — three hops with Docker in the middle.
     AFTER v1.24 the shim was deleted: the kubelet speaks the CRI directly to
     containerd or CRI-O, removing the Docker daemon from the data path. The
     headline for nervous engineers: your Docker-built images are OCI-standard and
     still run unchanged — only the node's RUNTIME plumbing changed, not the image
     format and not how you build. As the admin, your job is to ensure each node
     has a CRI runtime installed and the kubelet pointed at its socket.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2.7  Images in Kubernetes — Pull Policy, Registries & Failures      🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Building easypj:v1 was the laptop side; here's how the CLUSTER names, pulls,
     authenticates and garbage-collects images — and the pull errors you'll debug.

     • IMAGE REFERENCE: [REGISTRY[:PORT]/]NAME[:TAG][@DIGEST].
         bare `easypj` → docker.io/library/easypj:latest (default registry + tag!)
         `easypj@sha256:…` → pinned by immutable digest (exact bytes, ignores tags)
     • TAG vs DIGEST: a tag is MUTABLE (someone can re-push :v1) → two nodes may
        run different builds; a DIGEST is immutable & tamper-evident — pin prod.
     • imagePullPolicy DEFAULTS (inferred from the tag — exam favourite):
         :latest or no tag → Always (pull every start)
         a fixed tag (:v1) → IfNotPresent (use the node cache)
         @sha256:… digest  → IfNotPresent
         Override: Always | IfNotPresent | Never  (Never = must already be on node)
     • PRIVATE REGISTRIES: `kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred …`, then
        spec.imagePullSecrets (or attach it to the ServiceAccount so every pod
        inherits it). Missing/bad secret → ImagePullBackOff with "unauthorized".
     • PULL FAILURE STATES: ErrImagePull (a pull just failed) → ImagePullBackOff
        (retried, backing off ≤ ~5min) · InvalidImageName (malformed ref).
        Diagnose: `kubectl describe pod` → Events names the exact error.
     • SERIAL PULLS: the kubelet pulls one image at a time per node by default
        (serializeImagePulls / maxParallelImagePulls) → big images leave pods in
        ContainerCreating for a while.
     • IMAGE GARBAGE COLLECTION: the kubelet deletes unused images when node disk
        crosses imageGCHighThresholdPercent (default 85%), down to Low (80%);
        images in use are never removed; staying high → DiskPressure → eviction.
     • RuntimeClass: maps a name → a runtime handler the node supports; a pod opts
        in via spec.runtimeClassName to run in a stronger sandbox (gVisor / Kata).

     📖 KEY TERM — imagePullPolicy: when the kubelet (re)pulls an image; its
        DEFAULT is inferred from the tag, not fixed.
     🧠 ANALOGY: a tag is a sticky note on a box (can be moved to another box); a
        digest is the box's tamper-proof serial number.

     [IMAGE PULL DECISION — kubelet, per container start]
      ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ image ref has…                  → effective default      │
      │   :latest / no tag              → Always   (pull again)  │
      │   fixed tag :v1                 → IfNotPresent (cache ok) │
      │   @sha256:… digest              → IfNotPresent (cache ok) │
      │                                                          │
      │ pull attempt → fails → ErrImagePull                      │
      │            └→ retried w/ backoff → ImagePullBackOff       │
      │ bad name/ref          → InvalidImageName                 │
      │ kubectl describe pod  → Events line names the cause      │
      └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     .vs-prose — In the cluster, an image is named by a full reference; anything
     you leave out gets a hidden default (docker.io, :latest), which is exactly
     how "it pulled the wrong thing" happens. Pin production by DIGEST so every
     node runs the identical bytes. The kubelet's imagePullPolicy decides WHEN to
     re-pull, and its default is read off the tag — :latest pulls every start,
     fixed tags and digests trust the cache. Pull failures form a small,
     diagnosable family (ErrImagePull → ImagePullBackOff → InvalidImageName), and
     `kubectl describe pod` always names the real cause in its Events. Behind the
     scenes the kubelet also serializes pulls and garbage-collects images under
     disk pressure — both explain "why is my pod stuck in ContainerCreating?".

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER  (exam + beyond)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The 3 pillars of container isolation: namespaces (what a process can SEE) +
     cgroups (what a process can USE) + union FS (how layers become one rootfs).
     Together they turn a process on the shared host kernel into something that
     looks and feels like its own machine.

     • THE 8 LINUX NAMESPACES — pid · net · mnt · uts · ipc · user · cgroup ·
       time. Each container gets its own slice. CRUCIAL for Kubernetes: inside a
       POD the NET and IPC namespaces are SHARED across containers (which is why
       containers in a pod reach each other on localhost and share the pod IP).
       Those shared namespaces are held open by the pause / sandbox container —
       a tiny do-nothing container that exists only to OWN the network namespace
       so app containers can come and go without losing the pod's IP. PID sharing
       is optional (spec.shareProcessNamespace: true).

     • cgroups v1 vs v2 — cgroups enforce CPU/memory limits. v2 is a single
       unified hierarchy (enables PSI pressure metrics, MemoryQoS); v1 is the old
       split-controller tree and is DEPRECATED as of v1.35 (the kubelet won't
       start on a v1-only node by default). The kubelet and the container runtime
       MUST agree on the same cgroup DRIVER (use systemd on both) — a mismatch is
       a classic "kubelet won't start" failure.

     • UNION / OVERLAY FILESYSTEM (copy-on-write) — reads fall THROUGH the stacked
       read-only layers to the first one that has the file; a WRITE copies that
       file UP into the container's thin ephemeral upper layer; a DELETE writes a
       "whiteout" marker that hides the lower file. This is why the image stays
       read-only and shareable while each container still appears writable, and
       why anything written to that upper layer is LOST when the container dies
       (you need a Volume to persist — Chapter on Storage).

     • OCI SPECS — the image format and runtime behavior are standardized by the
       Open Container Initiative (image-spec + runtime-spec), which is why a
       Docker-built image runs under containerd, CRI-O, runc, etc. unchanged.

     • CONTENT-ADDRESSABLE DIGESTS — @sha256:… names an image by the hash of its
       content, making it immutable and tamper-evident (the basis of "pin by
       digest" in 2.7).

     • ROOTLESS & USER NAMESPACES — mapping container UID 0 to an unprivileged
       host UID so "root in the container" is NOT root on the host — a major
       hardening win.

     • BUILD TOOLS — you don't need the Docker daemon to build: buildkit, kaniko
       (in-cluster, daemonless) and buildah all produce OCI images, handy in CI
       running on Kubernetes itself.

     • NODE IMAGE GC & imagePullSecrets — covered operationally in 2.7; under the
       hood the kubelet runs GC on a timer against the disk thresholds, and
       imagePullSecrets are just docker config JSON stored in a Secret.

     • EXIT CODES (read these off `kubectl describe pod` / crictl):
         0   clean exit
         1–128 application error
         137 = 128+9  → SIGKILL, almost always OOMKilled (hit memory limit)
         143 = 128+15 → SIGTERM (graceful stop / shutdown)
         139 = 128+11 → SIGSEGV (segfault)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • Containers share the HOST KERNEL → light and fast (MB/seconds); VMs ship a
     full guest OS → heavy (GB/minutes).
   • An image is a stack of cached, read-only LAYERS; a container = image + a thin
     writable upper layer.
   • Containers package code + deps + config so the app runs IDENTICALLY
     everywhere — the cure for "works on my machine."
   • Kubernetes runs containers via the CRI (containerd / CRI-O), NOT Docker —
     dockershim was removed in v1.24, but Docker-built OCI images still run.
   • Docker is for building/pushing; crictl/ctr are for debugging containers on a
     node when kubectl is unavailable.
   • Isolation = namespaces (visibility) + cgroups (resources) + union FS (layers).
   • Image refs default to docker.io/library/...:latest; pin PROD by digest;
     imagePullPolicy's default is inferred from the tag.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • `:latest` (or no tag) → non-reproducible deploys AND imagePullPolicy=Always;
     two nodes can silently run different builds. Pin tags/digests.
   • Running the container as ROOT — add a non-root USER in the Dockerfile and/or
     a securityContext.runAsNonRoot.
   • Forgetting / mis-setting the CRI socket path so the kubelet can't reach the
     runtime.
   • cgroup-driver MISMATCH between kubelet and runtime (must both be systemd) →
     kubelet won't start. On v1.35+, a cgroups-v1-only node also won't start.
   • Writing data to the container's ephemeral upper layer — it vanishes on
     restart; use a Volume.
   • Missing/wrong imagePullSecret on a private image → ImagePullBackOff
     "unauthorized."
   • Fat single-stage images ship compilers and CVEs you never run.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • Order Dockerfile layers CHEAP→EXPENSIVE / stable→changing: copy
     requirements.txt and `pip install` BEFORE copying source, so editing code
     doesn't bust the deps cache.
   • Pin image DIGESTS (@sha256:…) for reproducible, tamper-evident prod.
   • Use a MULTI-STAGE build to discard the builder → small, fewer-CVE image.
   • Add a tight .dockerignore (.git, __pycache__, *.pyc, db.sqlite3, .env, venv/)
     to shrink the build context and keep secrets out.
   • When kubectl/apiserver is DEAD, jump straight to `crictl ps` / `crictl logs`
     against the runtime socket.
   • Read the EXIT CODE first: 137 ⇒ OOMKilled, 143 ⇒ SIGTERM — it tells you the
     bug class instantly.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   docker build -t easypj:v1 .            build image from Dockerfile
   docker run -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1      run, expose port 8000
   docker ps                              list running containers
   docker logs <id>                       view container logs
   docker exec -it <id> bash              shell into a container
   docker images                          list local images
   docker push <registry>/easypj:v1       push to a registry
   docker pull <image>                    pull from a registry
   docker stop <id>                       stop a container
   docker system prune                    clean up unused resources
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   crictl ps                              list containers on the node (CRI)
   crictl logs <id>                       container logs via the runtime
   crictl inspect <id>                    inspect a container
   crictl images                          list images known to the runtime
   ctr images ls                          containerd-native image list
   nerdctl ...                            docker-compatible CLI for containerd
   kubectl describe pod <p>               Events line = real pull/exit cause

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 2  (full answer + explanation each)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Q1. State two differences between a VM and a container.
       A. (1) A VM runs a FULL guest OS on a hypervisor (GB, boots in minutes);
          a container SHARES the host kernel (MB, starts in seconds/ms). (2) A VM
          isolates at the hardware level (stronger); a container isolates at the
          process level via namespaces + cgroups. Trade-off: weight vs isolation
          strength.

   Q2. A pod is ImagePullBackOff — give 3 likely causes and how to confirm.
       A. (1) Wrong image name/tag → registry returns not-found; (2) Private
          registry with missing/bad imagePullSecret → "unauthorized"; (3)
          Registry/network unreachable or rate-limited. CONFIRM with
          `kubectl describe pod <p>` and read the Events line — it names the exact
          error (ErrImagePull/unauthorized/not found). ImagePullBackOff just means
          "a failed pull is being retried with backoff."

   Q3. Why does a multi-stage build produce a smaller, safer image?
       A. The builder stage (compilers, headers, build deps) is DISCARDED; only
          the installed packages + your source are copied into a fresh slim
          runtime stage. Result: fewer megabytes, fewer CVEs, faster pulls.

   Q4. kubectl is down on a node — how do you list and log containers?
       A. SSH to the node and use crictl against the runtime socket:
          `crictl ps`, `crictl logs <id>`, `crictl inspect <id>`. crictl talks
          straight to containerd (/run/containerd/containerd.sock), so it works
          even when the kubelet/apiserver doesn't respond.

   Q5. What is the CRI, and what replaced dockershim in v1.24?
       A. The CRI (Container Runtime Interface) is the gRPC contract the kubelet
          uses to drive a runtime. In v1.24 the in-tree dockershim was REMOVED;
          the kubelet now speaks CRI directly to containerd or CRI-O. Docker-built
          OCI images still run unchanged.

   Q6. Reorder a Dockerfile so `pip install` stays cached across code edits.
       A. COPY requirements.txt and RUN pip install BEFORE `COPY . .`. Layers are
          cached top-down until an input changes; putting deps above the
          frequently-changing source means editing code doesn't invalidate the
          (expensive) install layer.

   Q7. Name three ways to shrink the easypj image.
       A. (1) Use a multi-stage build (drop the builder). (2) Start from a slim
          base (python:3.13-slim, or distroless). (3) Use a tight .dockerignore
          and `pip --no-cache-dir` so junk and caches never enter the image.
          (Bonus: combine RUN steps to reduce layers.)

   Q8. Why run as non-root, and how?
       A. So a container breakout doesn't hand the attacker host root and so the
          process can't tamper with files it shouldn't. HOW: add `RUN useradd -m
          app` + `USER app` in the Dockerfile, and/or set
          securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true (with runAsUser) on the pod/container.

   Q9. Why is `:latest` dangerous, and what should you use instead?
       A. `:latest` is MUTABLE — someone can re-push it, so two nodes may run
          different builds; it also forces imagePullPolicy=Always. Use a pinned,
          immutable tag (:v1.4.2) or, best, a content digest (@sha256:…) for
          reproducible, tamper-evident deploys.

   Q10. A node's kubelet won't start citing cgroups — what's the fix?
       A. The kubelet and the runtime disagree on the cgroup driver. Make them
          match by setting the runtime to systemd — for containerd, set
          `SystemdCgroup = true` under the runc options in
          /etc/containerd/config.toml (and ensure the kubelet uses
          cgroupDriver: systemd), then restart containerd and the kubelet. On
          v1.35+, also ensure the node is on cgroups v2 (v1 is deprecated).

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🖼️ VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 2: "easypj source → image → pod"
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   📝 Dockerfile ─build─▶ 📀 easypj:v1 (layers) ─push─▶ 🏪 Registry
                                                          │ pull (kubelet, CRI)
                                                          ▼
                                                 🤖 kubelet ─CRI─▶ containerd
                                                          │
                                                          ▼
                                                 📦 container in a Pod
                                                   (shares host kernel;
                                                    pause owns net/ipc ns)

   .vs-prose — The whole chapter in one line: your easypj SOURCE is baked by a
   Dockerfile into a layered IMAGE, pushed to a REGISTRY, then PULLED by a node's
   kubelet through the CRI to containerd, which starts it as a CONTAINER inside a
   Pod. Every debugging skill here maps to one arrow: build problems live in the
   Dockerfile/layers; pull problems (ImagePullBackOff) live on the registry/CRI
   arrow; runtime problems (exit 137, cgroups) live in the container/Pod box.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.1  Cluster Architecture Overview                                        🟡
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A cluster = CONTROL-PLANE node(s) + WORKER nodes.
       • Control Plane: makes ALL decisions — scheduling, state, the API.
       • Worker Nodes: run the actual application containers.
       • As a CKA admin you install, configure and MAINTAIN both halves, and
         when something breaks you repair both halves too.

     🧠 ANALOGY: the control plane is the brain (it decides) and the worker
        nodes are the muscle (they do the work). The brain never lifts a box;
        the muscle never plans the route.

     [KUBERNETES CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE — COMPLETE VIEW]
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  KUBERNETES CLUSTER                                          │
     │                                                              │
     │  ┌────────────────── CONTROL PLANE ──────────────────┐     │
     │  │                                                    │     │
     │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌──────────────┐   │     │
     │  │  │ API      │  │ etcd      │  │ Scheduler    │   │     │
     │  │  │ Server   │  │ (database)│  │ (placement)  │   │     │
     │  │  │ 🚪 Front │  │ 🧠 Brain  │  │ 📋 Assigns   │   │     │
     │  │  │ door for │  │ stores    │  │ pods to      │   │     │
     │  │  │ ALL req  │  │ all state │  │ nodes        │   │     │
     │  │  └──────────┘  └───────────┘  └──────────────┘   │     │
     │  │                                                    │     │
     │  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐   │     │
     │  │  │ Controller       │  │ Cloud Controller    │   │     │
     │  │  │ Manager          │  │ Manager (optional)  │   │     │
     │  │  │ 🔄 Watches state │  │ ☁️ Cloud integration│   │     │
     │  │  │ & corrects drift │  │ LB, routes, disks  │   │     │
     │  │  └──────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘   │     │
     │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
     │                          │ API                               │
     │  ┌───────────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐     │
     │  │                   WORKER NODES                      │     │
     │  │                                                      │     │
     │  │  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐         │     │
     │  │  │ Worker Node 1   │    │ Worker Node 2   │         │     │
     │  │  │                 │    │                 │         │     │
     │  │  │ kubelet    🤖   │    │ kubelet    🤖   │         │     │
     │  │  │ kube-proxy 🌐   │    │ kube-proxy 🌐   │         │     │
     │  │  │ containerd 🐋   │    │ containerd 🐋   │         │     │
     │  │  │                 │    │                 │         │     │
     │  │  │ ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │    │ ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │         │     │
     │  │  │ │ 📦 │ │ 📦 │  │    │ │ 📦 │ │ 📦 │  │         │     │
     │  │  │ │pod │ │pod │  │    │ │pod │ │pod │  │         │     │
     │  │  │ └────┘ └────┘  │    │ └────┘ └────┘  │         │     │
     │  │  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘         │     │
     │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.2  Control Plane Components — Deep Dive for Admins                  🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

     a) 📡 kube-apiserver
        - The ONLY entry point to the cluster — the front door.
        - Every kubectl command, every component and every controller talks to
          it. All requests and watches flow through it.
        - Validates and processes REST requests; pipeline is
          authN (who are you?) → authZ/RBAC (can you do this?) →
          admission (validate/mutate) → then reads/writes etcd.
        - Stateless and horizontally scalable — it is the only component that
          reads/writes etcd.
        - Listens on :6443.
        - As admin: you configure its flags, certificates and RBAC.

        [ALL PATHS LEAD TO THE API SERVER]
        ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────┐
        │ kubectl  │   │ controllers  │   │ kubelet    │
        └────┬─────┘   └──────┬───────┘   └─────┬──────┘
             │                │                 │
             └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                              ▼
                     ┌─────────────────┐
                     │ 📡 kube-apiserver│
                     │  :6443           │
                     └────────┬─────────┘
                              ▼
                     ┌─────────────────┐
                     │ 🗄️ etcd          │  (ONLY apiserver writes here)
                     └─────────────────┘

     b) 🗄️ etcd
        - Distributed key-value store — THE cluster database.
        - Stores ALL cluster state under /registry/...: pods, services,
          secrets, config, everything.
        - Uses the Raft consensus protocol for consistency.
        - Default ports: 2379 (client), 2380 (peer).
        - As a CKA admin you MUST know backup and restore cold — it is the #1
          admin task.
        ⚠️ [WARNING] If etcd is lost without a backup, the cluster is GONE.

        [etcd REPLICATION ACROSS 3 NODES — Raft quorum]
        ┌─────────┐  peer :2380  ┌─────────┐  peer :2380  ┌─────────┐
        │ etcd-1  │◄────────────►│ etcd-2  │◄────────────►│ etcd-3  │
        │ LEADER  │              │ FOLLOWER│              │ FOLLOWER│
        └────┬────┘              └─────────┘              └─────────┘
             │ writes replicated to a MAJORITY (quorum = 2 of 3)
             ▼
        A write is committed only once a quorum acknowledges it.
        Lose 1 of 3 → still healthy. Lose 2 of 3 → no quorum → read-only/down.

     c) 📋 kube-scheduler
        - Decides WHICH node a new (unbound) pod should run on.
        - Considers: resource availability, affinity rules, taints/tolerations,
          node conditions.
        - Algorithm: FILTER nodes (which CAN run it?) → SCORE them
          (which is BEST?) → BIND the pod to the chosen node.
        - As admin: you configure scheduler policies and priority classes.

        [SCHEDULER FLOW — new pod → filter → score → bind]
        ┌──────────────┐
        │ unbound Pod  │
        └──────┬───────┘
               ▼
        ┌──────────────┐   removes nodes that CANNOT run the pod
        │ 1. FILTER    │   (taints, insufficient Allocatable, affinity)
        └──────┬───────┘
               ▼
        ┌──────────────┐   ranks the survivors (LeastAllocated,
        │ 2. SCORE     │   BalancedAllocation, ImageLocality, NodeAffinity)
        └──────┬───────┘
               ▼
        ┌──────────────┐   writes the Binding → Pod is assigned to best node
        │ 3. BIND      │
        └──────────────┘

     d) 🔄 kube-controller-manager
        - Runs multiple reconciliation controllers in a SINGLE process.
        - Each controller watches one thing and corrects drift.
        - Key controllers:
          • Node Controller: detects when nodes go down.
          • ReplicaSet Controller: maintains the correct pod count.
          • Endpoint / EndpointSlice Controller: connects Services to Pods.
          • ServiceAccount Controller: creates default accounts.
          • Job Controller and many more.

        [THE CONTROLLER LOOP — heart of Kubernetes]
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  CONTROLLER LOOP (runs continuously)        │
        │                                              │
        │  ┌──────────┐                               │
        │  │ OBSERVE  │ ← Watch actual state           │
        │  │ (watch)  │   "3 pods running"             │
        │  └────┬─────┘                               │
        │       │                                      │
        │       ▼                                      │
        │  ┌──────────┐                               │
        │  │ COMPARE  │ ← Compare to desired state     │
        │  │ (diff)   │   "spec says 5 replicas"       │
        │  └────┬─────┘                               │
        │       │                                      │
        │       ▼                                      │
        │  ┌──────────┐                               │
        │  │   ACT    │ ← Take corrective action       │
        │  │ (reconcile)│  "create 2 more pods"        │
        │  └────┬─────┘                               │
        │       │                                      │
        │       └───────────── loop forever ──────────┘│
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     e) ☁️ cloud-controller-manager (optional)
        - Integrates with cloud provider APIs (AWS, GCP, Azure).
        - Manages: LoadBalancers, Routes, Node lifecycle.
        - Only present in cloud-hosted clusters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.3  Worker Node Components — Deep Dive for Admins                    🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

     a) 🤖 kubelet
        - The agent running on EVERY worker node.
        - Registers the node, then watches for Pods assigned to it.
        - Receives pod specifications from the API server and drives the
          runtime to start/stop containers.
        - Ensures containers are running and healthy; runs probes; manages
          container lifecycle and volume mounts.
        - Reports node status back to the control plane.
        - Config: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
        - As admin: you configure kubelet flags and troubleshoot it.
        📖 [NOTE] kubelet is NOT a pod — it is a SYSTEMD service on the node.
           That is why you debug it with `journalctl -u kubelet`, not kubectl.

     b) 🌐 kube-proxy
        - Network proxy running on every node.
        - Implements Service networking rules (programs Service → Pod routing).
        - Modes: iptables (default), IPVS (high performance), nftables.
        - Routes traffic to the correct pod endpoints.
        - As admin: you choose the mode and troubleshoot connectivity.

     c) 🐋 Container Runtime
        - Runs the actual containers.
        - containerd (default for most K8s installations).
        - CRI-O (used by OpenShift).
        - Must implement the Kubernetes CRI (Container Runtime Interface).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.4  How a Pod Gets Created — The Full Journey                       🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — understand every step]
     This is the single most important sequence to know cold; it is assumed in
     virtually every troubleshooting task.

     [POD CREATION JOURNEY — admin must understand every step]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  "kubectl apply -f easypj-deployment.yaml"             │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 1: kubectl → API Server                            │
     │          (HTTPS + certificate authentication)            │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 2: API Server → Authentication (who are you?)      │
     │          → Authorization/RBAC (can you do this?)         │
     │          → Admission Controllers (validate/mutate)       │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 3: API Server → etcd                               │
     │          (stores Deployment object in database)           │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 4: Controller Manager sees new Deployment          │
     │          → creates ReplicaSet → creates Pod objects      │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 5: Scheduler sees unassigned Pods                  │
     │          → evaluates nodes → assigns to best node        │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 6: kubelet on chosen node sees assigned Pod        │
     │          → pulls container image                          │
     │          → starts container via containerd                │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 7: kube-proxy updates network rules                │
     │          → Service can now route traffic to new Pod      │
     │                                                          │
     │  Step 8: Pod is Running ✅                                │
     │          kubelet reports status → API Server → etcd      │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     [HOW A POD IS BORN — kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml]
      1  kubectl ─►📡 apiserver         (HTTPS + client cert)
      2  apiserver ─► authN ─► authZ(RBAC) ─► admission   (who? allowed? valid?)
      3  apiserver ─►🗄️ etcd            (Deployment object persisted)
      4  🔄 controller-mgr sees Deployment ─► creates ReplicaSet ─► creates Pod(s)
      5  📋 scheduler sees an unbound Pod ─► filter ─► score ─► binds to Node 2
      6  🤖 kubelet(Node 2) sees its Pod ─►🐋 containerd pulls easypj:v2 ─► starts
      7  🌐 kube-proxy programs Service routing to the new Pod IP
      8  ✅ Pod Running ─► kubelet reports status ─► apiserver ─► etcd
      💡 INSIGHT: each actor only reconciles its OWN slice — there is no central
         script. The Pod's creation is the emergent result of many independent
         loops each doing one job and writing back to the apiserver.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.5  Cluster Networking Overview (Admin Perspective)                 🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     Three foundational rules:
       • Every Pod gets its own unique IP address.
       • All Pods can talk to all other Pods WITHOUT NAT — a flat network.
       • A CNI plugin implements the networking: Calico, Cilium, Flannel.
     As admin you choose, install and troubleshoot the CNI.

     Three layers to keep straight:
       • Pod-to-Pod (POD network): direct IP communication, pod ↔ pod.
       • Pod-to-Service (SERVICE network): stable VIPs routed via kube-proxy.
       • External-to-Service (EXTERNAL): via NodePort / LoadBalancer / Ingress /
         Gateway.
     (Full detail in Part 5.)

     [3-LAYER NETWORK — pod / service / external]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ EXTERNAL    client ─► NodePort / LoadBalancer / Ingress     │
     │                              │                              │
     │ SERVICE     stable VIP (ClusterIP) ◄─ kube-proxy programs ─►│
     │                              │  iptables/IPVS rules         │
     │ POD         Pod-IP ◄──────► Pod-IP   (flat, no NAT, via CNI)│
     │             10.244.x.x      10.244.y.y                       │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.6  Static Pods — Admin-Only Concept                                🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     📖 KEY TERM — Static Pods are managed DIRECTLY by the kubelet (not by the
        scheduler/apiserver).
        - Defined as YAML files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
        - The control plane components are usually static pods themselves!
        - The kubelet watches the directory and manages their lifecycle: drop a
          file in → the pod appears; remove the file → the pod is gone.
        - The kubelet creates a read-only "mirror pod" in the API so you can SEE
          a static pod with kubectl, but you cannot manage it through the API.
        - Use case: deploying the control plane before any cluster is running
          (the bootstrap paradox — see Under the Hood).
        📖 [NOTE] Static pods have a "-<nodename>" suffix in their name (e.g.
           kube-apiserver-cka-master), which is how you spot a mirror pod.

     [CODE: Example static pod manifest]
     [PATH: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml]
     ----------------------------------------------------------------
     apiVersion: v1
     kind: Pod
     metadata:
       name: static-web
       labels:
         role: static
     spec:
       containers:
       - name: web
         image: nginx:1.27
         ports:
         - containerPort: 80
     ----------------------------------------------------------------
     # Save the file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ on a node and the kubelet
     # starts it within seconds; the API shows it as "static-web-<nodename>".
     # Delete the file and the kubelet stops and removes the pod.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  3.7  Node Health & Control-Plane ↔ Node Communication                🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     How the control plane KNOWS a node is alive, how much it can schedule onto
     it, and how the two halves talk — the backbone of "node NotReady" debugging.

     • NODE CONDITIONS (kubectl describe node): Ready (True / False / Unknown)
       plus the pressure flags MemoryPressure · DiskPressure · PIDPressure ·
       NetworkUnavailable.

     • HEARTBEATS: the kubelet renews a lightweight Lease in the
       kube-node-lease namespace (~every 10s) AND posts a fuller .status on
       change. If heartbeats stop:
         ~50s (node-monitor-grace-period) → Ready=Unknown + taint
           node.kubernetes.io/unreachable (or …/not-ready):NoExecute;
         ~5min → pods without a matching toleration are evicted (rate-limited).

     • CAPACITY vs ALLOCATABLE:
         Allocatable = Capacity − kube-reserved − system-reserved
                       − eviction-threshold.
       The scheduler only fills Allocatable, so a pod can sit Pending though the
       node "looks" half-empty.

     • NODE REGISTRATION: the kubelet self-registers by default
       (--register-node). `kubectl cordon` marks a node unschedulable WITHOUT
       evicting its existing pods; `kubectl drain` cordons AND evicts.

     • CP ↔ NODE COMMS (trust asymmetry):
         node → apiserver :6443 is TLS + RBAC by default (secure);
         apiserver → kubelet :10250 is HTTPS but does NOT verify the kubelet
           cert unless --kubelet-certificate-authority is set;
         apiserver → nodes/pods/services is plain HTTP by default → use the
           Konnectivity service for a secured tunnel.
       Mental model: everything DIALS the apiserver.

     📖 KEY TERM — Allocatable: the slice of a node's resources the scheduler may
        actually place pods into (Capacity minus reservations).
     🧠 ANALOGY: the node Lease is a heartbeat monitor — miss a few beeps and the
        controller calls a code (Ready=Unknown), then moves the patients
        (eviction).

  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 3

  [THE COMPLETE CLUSTER — brain (control plane) + muscle (workers)]
  ┌───────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ────────────────────────────┐
  │  🧠 CONTROL PLANE                                                     │
  │   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐   │
  │   │📡 apiserver│ │🗄️ etcd │ │📋 scheduler│ │🔄 controller-mgr   │   │
  │   │ front door │ │ ALL    │ │ place pods │ │ reconcile loops    │   │
  │   │ :6443      │ │ state  │ │            │ │ (node/RS/endpoint) │   │
  │   └─────┬──────┘ └────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────────────┘   │
  │         │  every request & watch flows through the apiserver         │
  │  ───────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  💪 WORKER NODES                                                      │
  │   ┌─────▼────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐          │
  │   │ Node 1               │        │ Node 2               │          │
  │   │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 proxy │        │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 proxy │          │
  │   │ 🐋 containerd        │        │ 🐋 containerd        │          │
  │   │ ┌────┐ ┌────┐        │        │ ┌────┐ ┌────┐        │          │
  │   │ │📦  │ │📦  │ easypj  │        │ │📦  │ │🐘  │        │          │
  │   │ │web │ │web │ pods    │        │ │web │ │ db │        │          │
  │   │ └────┘ └────┘        │        │ └────┘ └────┘        │          │
  │   └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [KUBERNETES IS PLUGGABLE — the 3 extension interfaces]
        🤖 kubelet ──CRI──► 🐋 containerd / CRI-O        (RUN containers)
        pod network ──CNI──► 🌐 Calico / Cilium / Flannel (WIRE pods)
        volumes ──CSI──► 🧱 CSI driver (EBS/PD/Ceph/NFS)   (ATTACH storage)
   📖 CRI=runtime · CNI=network · CSI=storage — the three "sockets" of K8s.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 The watch/list mechanism: components don't poll, they open long-lived
     WATCH connections to the apiserver. Informers cache objects locally and a
     reconcile workqueue keeps actual==desired. Leader election (for scheduler
     and controller-manager) is done via a Lease object so only one replica is
     active at a time.

  🔬 API machinery: REST + watch + resourceVersion gives every client a
     consistent, resumable event stream. The Binding subresource is how the
     scheduler assigns a Pod to a node. API Priority & Fairness (APF) protects
     the apiserver under load; the aggregation layer lets extension API servers
     plug in; controller-runtime provides the informers & workqueues most
     operators are built on.

  • Full pod-creation trace (internals beneath §3.4): admission chain
    (Mutating → schema validation → Validating: LimitRanger / PodSecurity /
    webhooks) → scheduler plugins (NodeResourcesFit[LeastAllocated],
    NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, ImageLocality, NodeAffinity) → kubelet
    CRI calls RunPodSandbox → PullImage → CreateContainer → StartContainer →
    containerd → runc.

  • Static-pod BOOTSTRAP paradox: the kubelet runs the apiserver itself from a
    manifest BEFORE any apiserver exists, then registers a read-only mirror pod;
    restart one by moving its manifest out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and
    back.

  • Lease fields: holderIdentity · leaseDurationSeconds (~15s for sched/c-m) ·
    renewTime. APF rejects with 429 (queued / over-limit, retry) vs 503 (no
    queue / overloaded). Admission failurePolicy Fail (default) vs Ignore;
    mutating webhooks run BEFORE validating ones, so validators always judge the
    FINAL object.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • The control plane DECIDES; the worker nodes RUN. As admin you maintain both.
  • Only the apiserver talks to etcd — it is the single source-of-truth gateway.
  • The apiserver is the single choke point: authN → authZ(RBAC) → admission →
    etcd; if it's down, kubectl is useless.
  • The kubelet is a SYSTEMD service, not a pod (debug with journalctl/crictl).
  • The control plane itself runs AS static pods from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  • CRI (runtime) / CNI (network) / CSI (storage) are the 3 plug points.
  • etcd uses Raft; ports 2379 (client) / 2380 (peer); back it up or lose the
    cluster.
  • Scheduler = FILTER → SCORE → BIND; it only fills Allocatable, not Capacity.
  • Everything DIALS the apiserver; node health is tracked by Leases in
    kube-node-lease.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • kubelet is a systemd service, NOT a pod — kubectl can't restart it.
  • Editing a static-pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ AUTO-restarts
    that pod; a stray edit can take down the apiserver on that node.
  • The apiserver is the single choke point — if it's down, kubectl is useless;
    drop to the node and use crictl/journalctl.
  • A node can look half-empty yet a pod stays Pending — the scheduler only
    counts Allocatable, not Capacity.
  • componentstatuses (`kubectl get cs`) is DEPRECATED — use the readyz/healthz
    endpoints instead.
  • apiserver → kubelet (:10250) does NOT verify the kubelet cert unless
    --kubelet-certificate-authority is set.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • apiserver down? Debug from the node: `crictl ps -a`, `crictl logs <id>`,
    `journalctl -u kubelet -f`.
  • Node NotReady? Check the kubelet first (systemd), then the CNI, then the
    runtime — in that order.
  • To restart a control-plane static pod, move its manifest out of
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and back.
  • `kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'` gives a per-check health breakdown of
    the apiserver.
  • Pod stuck Pending? `kubectl describe pod` → look at the scheduler Events for
    the filter that rejected every node.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'        # apiserver health (cs is deprecated)
  kubectl get pods -n kube-system            # see control-plane static pods
  kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease       # node heartbeats
  kubectl describe node <node>               # conditions, Capacity vs Allocatable
  kubectl cordon <node> / kubectl drain <node>
  crictl ps -a                               # containers (run on the node)
  crictl logs <container-id>
  journalctl -u kubelet -f                   # kubelet logs (it's systemd)
  ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests               # the static-pod manifests

  🧪 DRILL: list the control-plane static pods; tail the apiserver logs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 3) — union of both sources, deduplicated
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Q1. Which component is the ONLY one that reads/writes etcd?
      A: The kube-apiserver. Every other component (scheduler, controller-
         manager, kubelet) reaches state ONLY by talking to the apiserver, which
         in turn is the sole gateway to etcd. This is why etcd backups are taken
         via the apiserver's etcd client and why a down apiserver blinds the
         whole cluster.

  Q2. A node shows NotReady — which agent do you check first, and how?
      A: The kubelet, because it is the node agent that posts the Ready
         condition. SSH to the node and run `systemctl status kubelet` and
         `journalctl -u kubelet -f`. Then check the CNI plugin and the container
         runtime (`crictl ps -a`). Remember kubelet is systemd, not a pod.

  Q3. Trace what happens after `kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml`.
      A: kubectl → apiserver (authN → authZ/RBAC → admission) → etcd persists
         the Deployment → controller-manager creates a ReplicaSet then Pod
         objects → scheduler filters/scores/binds each Pod to a node → the
         kubelet on that node tells containerd to pull easypj:v2 and start it →
         kube-proxy programs Service routing → Pod Running, status flows back to
         the apiserver and etcd. (See the 8-step "how a pod is born" diagram.)

  Q4. The scheduler is down — what symptom appears, and on which objects?
      A: Newly created Pods stay in status Pending with no node assigned
         (.spec.nodeName empty) because nothing performs the Bind. Existing
         running Pods are unaffected. `kubectl get pods` shows Pending; `describe`
         shows no scheduling Events.

  Q5. Create a static pod on a worker, then delete it. Which files/commands?
      A: Write a Pod manifest to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml on
         the node; the kubelet starts it within seconds and the API shows
         "static-web-<nodename>" (a read-only mirror pod). To delete it, remove
         the file from that directory — `rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
         static-web.yaml`; the kubelet stops and deletes the pod. You cannot
         delete it via `kubectl delete` (it will be recreated).

  Q6. Name the 3 network layers and what routes each.
      A: POD network — pod ↔ pod, flat, no NAT, implemented by the CNI plugin.
         SERVICE network — stable ClusterIP VIPs, routed by kube-proxy
         (iptables/IPVS/nftables). EXTERNAL — client → cluster via NodePort,
         LoadBalancer, Ingress or Gateway.

  Q7. Which ports does etcd listen on, and for what?
      A: 2379 for client traffic (the apiserver connects here) and 2380 for
         peer/replication traffic between etcd members.

  Q8. Why is the apiserver the cluster's single choke point?
      A: It is the ONLY component that talks to etcd and the ONLY entry point
         for every request and watch. All authN, authZ/RBAC and admission happen
         there. If it's down, kubectl and all controllers are blind, so you must
         debug from the node with crictl/journalctl.

  Q9. Explain a controller's reconcile loop with the ReplicaSet example.
      A: OBSERVE (watch actual state — "3 pods running") → COMPARE (to desired —
         "spec says 5 replicas") → ACT (reconcile — "create 2 more pods") →
         loop forever. The ReplicaSet controller continuously drives the actual
         pod count toward the desired replica count, recreating any pod that
         dies.

  Q10. What is a "mirror pod" and why does its name end in -<nodename>?
      A: A mirror pod is the read-only API representation the kubelet creates for
         each static pod so you can SEE it with kubectl. The kubelet appends
         "-<nodename>" so the names are unique per node and so it's obvious the
         pod is kubelet-managed (static), not scheduler-managed; you cannot edit
         or delete it through the API.

  📌 VISUAL SUMMARY: the full annotated cluster in one picture — a brain
     (control plane: apiserver front door, etcd state, scheduler placement,
     controller-manager reconcile loops) wired to muscle (worker nodes running
     kubelet + kube-proxy + containerd + pods), with everything DIALING the
     apiserver and only the apiserver touching etcd.

================================================================================

    4.2  ReplicaSets — maintaining the count
