────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.1  Pods — The Smallest Unit                                          🟡
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - One or more containers sharing network and storage
     - Every container in a pod shares the same IP address
     - Pods are ephemeral: they die and are replaced, never "repaired"
     - As admin: you debug pods, not typically create them directly

     A Pod is one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP,
     reachable over localhost) and storage volumes. Pods are EPHEMERAL — when one
     dies it is replaced, never repaired, so never rely on a pod's identity or
     IP. Multi-container pods follow patterns like the SIDECAR (e.g. easypj +
     an nginx static-file sidecar), the ADAPTER and the AMBASSADOR. Containers in
     the same pod reach each other over localhost on their own ports.

     [POD ANATOMY — containers share one network + storage]
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  POD (shared network namespace)                │
     │  IP: 10.244.1.5                                │
     │                                                │
     │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐         │
     │  │ 📦 Container 1│    │ 📦 Container 2│         │
     │  │ easypj Django │    │ nginx sidecar │         │
     │  │ port: 8000    │    │ port: 80      │         │
     │  └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬───────┘         │
     │         │    shared         │                   │
     │         └────────┬──────────┘                   │
     │              ┌───▼────┐                         │
     │              │ Volume │  (shared storage)       │
     │              └────────┘                         │
     │                                                │
     │  localhost:8000 = Django                        │
     │  localhost:80   = Nginx                         │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🧠 ANALOGY: a Pod is an apartment; its containers are roommates sharing one
        front door (IP) and a shared closet (volume), but each runs its own
        appliance (process/port).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.2  ReplicaSets — Maintaining Pod Count                               🟡
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Ensures a specified number of pod replicas are running
     - If a pod dies, ReplicaSet creates a replacement
     - Rarely created directly — Deployments manage them for you
     - Uses label selectors to track which pods belong to it

     A ReplicaSet keeps a desired number of identical Pods running, using a label
     SELECTOR to know which pods are "its". If a pod dies it creates a
     replacement (self-healing reconciliation). You rarely create one directly —
     a Deployment manages it for you and adds rollout/rollback on top.

     [REPLICASET SELF-HEALING — maintaining 3 pods]
     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  ReplicaSet: easypj-rs (replicas: 3)                   │
     │  Selector: app=easypj                                   │
     │                                                         │
     │  HEALTHY STATE:                                         │
     │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                         │
     │  │ 📦 1  │  │ 📦 2  │  │ 📦 3  │   3/3 Running ✅     │
     │  │easypj│  │easypj│  │easypj│                         │
     │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                         │
     │                                                         │
     │  POD 2 CRASHES:                                         │
     │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                         │
     │  │ 📦 1  │  │ 💀 2  │  │ 📦 3  │   2/3 Running ⚠️     │
     │  │easypj│  │ DEAD │  │easypj│                         │
     │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                         │
     │                 │                                       │
     │                 │ ReplicaSet detects: "I need 3,        │
     │                 │ but only 2 are running!"               │
     │                 ▼                                       │
     │  SELF-HEALED:                                           │
     │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                         │
     │  │ 📦 1  │  │ 📦 4  │  │ 📦 3  │   3/3 Running ✅     │
     │  │easypj│  │ NEW! │  │easypj│   (new pod created)    │
     │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                         │
     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     ⚠️ The ReplicaSet's .spec.selector must match the pod template's labels, or
        it will adopt/strand the wrong pods — or none at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.3  Deployments — Managing Application Lifecycle                      🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - The standard way to run stateless applications
     - Manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods
     - Supports rolling updates, rollbacks, scaling
     - You declare what you want → Deployment controller makes it happen

     A Deployment is the standard way to run a stateless app. It manages
     ReplicaSets, which manage Pods, and adds rolling updates, rollbacks and
     revision history: Deployment → ReplicaSet(v_current) → Pods, with old
     ReplicaSets kept at 0 replicas for instant rollback.

     [DEPLOYMENT OWNERSHIP CHAIN]
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  Deployment: easypj                            │
     │  ├── manages ──▶ ReplicaSet (current: v3)     │
     │  │              ├── owns ──▶ Pod easypj-abc1  │
     │  │              ├── owns ──▶ Pod easypj-abc2  │
     │  │              └── owns ──▶ Pod easypj-abc3  │
     │  │                                             │
     │  ├── keeps ──▶ ReplicaSet (old: v2, 0 replicas)│
     │  └── keeps ──▶ ReplicaSet (old: v1, 0 replicas)│
     │                                                │
     │  Old ReplicaSets kept for rollback history!    │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🧩 easypj-web Deployment (skeleton — generate with --dry-run, then edit):
       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: Deployment
       metadata:
         name: easypj-web
         namespace: easypj-prod
         labels: { app: easypj, tier: web }
       spec:
         replicas: 3
         selector:
           matchLabels: { app: easypj, tier: web }   # IMMUTABLE
         strategy:
           type: RollingUpdate
           rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25% }
         revisionHistoryLimit: 10
         template:
           metadata:
             labels: { app: easypj, tier: web, version: v2 }
           spec:
             containers:
             - name: easypj
               image: easypj:v2
               ports: [ { containerPort: 8000 } ]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.4  Services — Stable Network Endpoints                              🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Pods get random IPs that change on restart
     - Services provide a STABLE IP and DNS name
     - Types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName
     - Label selectors match Services to Pods

     Pods get random IPs that change on restart; a Service gives a STABLE virtual
     IP + DNS name and load-balances across the Pods its selector matches (its
     Endpoints / EndpointSlices). Four types: ClusterIP (internal, default),
     NodePort (node IP:port), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), ExternalName (DNS alias).

     [SERVICE TYPES — 4 ways to expose]
     | Type          | Access from        | Use case                    | Port range    |
     | ClusterIP     | Inside cluster only| Internal services (default) | Any           |
     | NodePort      | External via node  | Dev/testing                 | 30000-32767   |
     | LoadBalancer  | External via LB    | Production (cloud)          | Any           |
     | ExternalName  | DNS alias          | External services           | N/A           |

     [SERVICE → POD WIRING (easypj-web)]
        client ──▶ Service easypj-web (ClusterIP 10.96.0.50)
                       │  selector: app=easypj,tier=web
                       │  port 80  ──▶ targetPort 8000
                       ▼
        ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐  (Endpoints, only Ready pods)
        │ 📦 pod-1 │ 📦 pod-2 │ 📦 pod-3 │  each :8000
        └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

     ⚠️ A wrong targetPort = "connection refused"; an empty selector or
        mismatched labels = 0 endpoints (the #1 "Service not working" cause).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.5  Namespaces — Virtual Clusters                                    🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     - Logical partitions within a cluster
     - Isolate teams, environments, or applications
     - Default namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease
     - As admin: you create namespaces, apply quotas, and set RBAC per namespace

     Logical partitions of one cluster, used to isolate teams/environments. The
     built-ins: default, kube-system (control-plane add-ons like CoreDNS &
     kube-proxy), kube-public (world-readable cluster info), kube-node-lease
     (node heartbeats). Each namespace can carry its own ResourceQuota, RBAC and
     NetworkPolicy (e.g. easypj-dev vs easypj-prod).
     ⚠️ Namespaces do NOT isolate nodes or cluster-scoped objects (PV, Node,
        StorageClass, ClusterRole) — those live cluster-wide.

     [NAMESPACE ISOLATION — easypj example]
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  CLUSTER                                             │
     │                                                      │
     │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐         │
     │  │ NS: easypj-dev   │  │ NS: easypj-prod   │         │
     │  │ 🟢 1 replica     │  │ 🔴 3 replicas     │         │
     │  │ DEBUG=True       │  │ DEBUG=False       │         │
     │  │ limits: low      │  │ limits: high      │         │
     │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘         │
     │                                                      │
     │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐         │
     │  │ NS: kube-system  │  │ NS: monitoring    │         │
     │  │ 🔧 System pods   │  │ 📊 Prometheus     │         │
     │  │ CoreDNS, proxy   │  │ Grafana           │         │
     │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘         │
     │                                                      │
     │  Each namespace can have its own:                     │
     │  • ResourceQuotas  • RBAC Roles  • NetworkPolicies  │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.6  Labels, Selectors, and Annotations                              🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     - Labels: key-value pairs for organizing and selecting objects
     - Selectors: filter objects by labels (matchLabels)
     - Annotations: metadata for tools and humans (not used for selection)
     - As admin: labels are CRITICAL for Services, RBAC, NetworkPolicies

     📖 Labels — key/value tags used to SELECT objects (matchLabels). They wire
        Services→Pods, Deployments→Pods, NetworkPolicies and RBAC. 📖 Annotations
        — non-identifying metadata for tools/humans; NEVER used for selection
        (e.g. kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration, change-cause).
     easypj convention: app=easypj · tier=web|db · version=v2.

     [LABELS WIRE A SERVICE TO A DEPLOYMENT — easypj]
       # Deployment pod template
       template:
         metadata:
           labels:
             app: easypj
             tier: web
             version: v2
       ---
       # Service selector — MUST match the labels above
       apiVersion: v1
       kind: Service
       metadata: { name: easypj-web }
       spec:
         selector:
           app: easypj
           tier: web        # matches → endpoints populated
         ports:
         - port: 80
           targetPort: 8000

     LABEL GRAMMAR: key = [prefix/]name; name ≤63 chars of [a-z A-Z 0-9 - _ .],
     must start/end alphanumeric; value same rules, ≤63 chars (or empty).
     SELECTORS: equality-based (app=easypj,tier=web means AND) and set-based
     (in, notin, exists / !key).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.7  Kubernetes Object Relationship Map                               🟡
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     How it all connects: Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pods; Service finds Pods by
     label; ConfigMap/Secret feed env via envFrom; Ingress/Gateway routes to a
     Service; PVC→PV→StorageClass for storage; a Namespace contains it all and
     RBAC governs access. THIS is the picture to memorise.

     [HOW KUBERNETES OBJECTS CONNECT]
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                                                         │
     │  Deployment ──manages──▶ ReplicaSet ──owns──▶ Pods     │
     │       │                                         │       │
     │       │ references                     labels   │       │
     │       ▼                                         ▼       │
     │  ConfigMap ◀──────── envFrom ──────── Pod spec  │       │
     │  Secret    ◀──────── envFrom ──────── Pod spec  │       │
     │                                         │       │       │
     │  Service ────selector────matches────────┘       │       │
     │       │                                                 │
     │       ▼                                                 │
     │  Ingress ──routes traffic──▶ Service                    │
     │                                                         │
     │  PVC ◀──────── volumeMount ──────── Pod spec            │
     │   │                                                     │
     │   ▼                                                     │
     │  PV / StorageClass                                      │
     │                                                         │
     │  Namespace ──contains all above──                       │
     │  RBAC ──controls access to all above──                  │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     [OBJECT RELATIONSHIP MAP — how easypj wires together]
      🌍 Ingress / 🚪 Gateway
           │ routes host/path
           ▼
      🔌 Service ──selector(app=easypj)──► 📦 Pods
           ▲                                  ▲ owned by
      🔄 Deployment ──manages──► ReplicaSet ──┘ creates
           │ pod template references
           ├─ ⚙️ ConfigMap (envFrom)   ┌─ 💾 PVC ──► PV ──► 🧱 StorageClass
           ├─ 🔒 Secret   (envFrom)    │
           └─ 🛡️ ServiceAccount ◄─ RBAC (Role+Binding) controls access
      🗂️ Namespace contains ALL of the above   ·   🧯 NetworkPolicy firewalls it
      💡 Labels are the glue: a Service finds Pods only by matching labels.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.8  Pod Lifecycle & Health Probes                                    🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     A pod isn't just up/down — it has phases, per-container states, conditions,
     and probes that gate traffic. This is the heart of the Troubleshooting
     domain.

     • PHASES (.status.phase): Pending → Running → Succeeded / Failed / Unknown.
     • CONTAINER STATES (.status.containerStatuses[].state):
         Waiting  — reason: ContainerCreating / ImagePullBackOff / CrashLoopBackOff
         Running  — startedAt timestamp
         Terminated — exitCode: 137 = OOM/SIGKILL · 143 = SIGTERM · 0 = clean
     • restartPolicy: Always (default; Deployments) · OnFailure (Jobs) · Never.
       Restarts back off exponentially (10s, 20s, 40s … capped at 5 min) →
       CrashLoopBackOff.
     • POD CONDITIONS flip in order: PodScheduled → Initialized → ContainersReady
       → Ready. Only a Ready pod joins its Service endpoints — this is the answer
       to "the pod is Running but gets no traffic."
     • TERMINATION: delete → deletionTimestamp set (Terminating) → removed from
       endpoints → SIGTERM → grace window (terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default
       30s) → SIGKILL.
     • PROBES (concept here; full config in Part 4):
         startup   — gate slow boots; disables liveness/readiness until it passes
         liveness  — fail → RESTART the container
         readiness — fail → REMOVE the pod from Service endpoints (no restart)
       Each via httpGet / tcpSocket / exec / grpc.

     📖 KEY TERM — readiness probe: decides if a pod can serve traffic right now;
        failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it.
     🧠 ANALOGY: liveness = "are you alive?" (if not, restart); readiness = "are
        you open for business?" (if not, stop sending customers).

     [POD LIFECYCLE — phases & conditions]
       kubectl apply
            │
            ▼
       Pending ──scheduled──▶ Initialized ──▶ ContainersReady ──▶ Ready ✅
         │ (image pull,                                            │
         │  scheduling)                                            ▼
         │                                              joins Service endpoints
         └──fail──▶ Failed / CrashLoopBackOff (back-off 10→20→40s…5m)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  4.9  Rollouts, Service Ports, Label Rules & Resource Scope           🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     The exam-critical details that make §4.3–4.6 actually behave.

     • DEPLOYMENT ROLLOUT: strategy RollingUpdate (default) vs Recreate (causes
       downtime). maxSurge 25% (extra pods above desired during the roll) ·
       maxUnavailable 25% (how many may be down during the roll) ·
       revisionHistoryLimit 10 (old ReplicaSets kept at 0 for rollback). The
       .spec.selector is IMMUTABLE.
       Commands:
         kubectl rollout status   deploy/easypj-web
         kubectl rollout history  deploy/easypj-web
         kubectl rollout undo      deploy/easypj-web [--to-revision=N]
         kubectl rollout pause|resume deploy/easypj-web
         kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v2

     • SERVICE PORTS: port (the Service's own) → targetPort (the container's,
       8000 for easypj); NodePort adds <nodeIP>:nodePort, range 30000–32767.
       Wrong targetPort = "connection refused"; port defaults to targetPort if
       omitted.

     • CROSS-NAMESPACE DNS: same namespace → short name (easypj-db); across
       namespaces → FQDN service.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

     • LABEL GRAMMAR: key = [prefix/]name, name ≤63 chars of [a-z A-Z 0-9 - _ .],
       start/end alphanumeric; value same ≤63 (or empty). Selectors: equality
       (app=easypj,tier=web = AND) and set-based (in, notin, exists / !key).

     • RESOURCE SCOPE:
         namespaced — Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, Role,
                      RoleBinding, Ingress, NetworkPolicy
         cluster-scoped — Node, PersistentVolume, StorageClass, Namespace,
                      ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, CRD
       List with: kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true|false. Deleting a
       namespace deletes everything namespaced in it; cluster-scoped objects
       survive.

     📖 KEY TERM — maxSurge / maxUnavailable: the two knobs that pace a rolling
        update (both default 25%).
     🧠 ANALOGY: a rolling update is changing tires while driving — maxSurge bolts
        on a spare first, maxUnavailable is how many you'll briefly take off.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER                                          🔴
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     🔧 ownerReferences & cascading deletion are how a Deployment "owns" its
        ReplicaSet and a ReplicaSet "owns" its Pods. The endpoints /
        EndpointSlice controller is what wires a Service to its live, Ready pods.

     🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
       • GVK / GVR & the RESTMapper — every object is a Group/Version/Kind, and
         the apiserver maps it to a Group/Version/Resource path.
       • The spec/status split & subresources — you write .spec; controllers
         write .status; /status and /scale are separate subresources (which is
         why `kubectl scale` and HPA work without touching the whole object).
       • Server-side apply & managedFields — field ownership tracking that lets
         multiple controllers co-own one object.
       • Garbage-collection modes via:
           kubectl delete --cascade=background(default) | foreground | orphan
       • ownerReferences CANNOT cross namespaces (only a cluster-scoped owner may
         own across them). EndpointSlices shard endpoints ≤100/slice (the legacy
         Endpoints API is deprecated); only Ready pods land in a slice.
       • finalizers + deletionTimestamp pause deletion until the finalizer is
         cleared — the classic "stuck Terminating" namespace/pod.
       • generateName — server-side unique name suffixing (e.g. easypj-web-7d4-).

║  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 4                                       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  ✅ Pod < ReplicaSet < Deployment — each layer adds a capability:    ║
║     Pod = run, ReplicaSet = keep N alive, Deployment = roll/rollback ║
║  ✅ Pods are EPHEMERAL — never rely on a pod's name or IP            ║
║  ✅ Services give STABLE networking (virtual IP + DNS) and load-     ║
║     balance only across Ready pods their selector matches           ║
║  ✅ Namespaces ISOLATE namespaced objects; they do NOT isolate      ║
║     nodes, PVs, StorageClasses or other cluster-scoped objects      ║
║  ✅ LABELS are the glue — Services, Deployments, NetworkPolicies     ║
║     and RBAC all find objects by matching labels (annotations don't)║
║  ✅ Only a Ready pod (PodScheduled→Initialized→ContainersReady→     ║
║     Ready) joins Service endpoints                                  ║
║  ✅ rollout undo restores a previous ReplicaSet kept at 0 replicas  ║
║  🎯 CKA: powers Workloads (15%) + Services/Networking (20%) and a   ║
║     large slice of the 30% Troubleshooting domain                   ║
║  🔑 Must-Remember Commands:                                         ║
║     kubectl get all -n easypj                                        ║
║     kubectl get po -l app=easypj                                     ║
║     kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web                         ║
║     kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true|false                   ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
     • A Service/Deployment selector MUST match the pod-template labels — else
       you get empty endpoints (Service) or orphaned/adopted pods (controller).
     • Deleting a Pod under a Deployment just respawns it — edit the Deployment.
     • Annotations ≠ labels — annotations are NOT selectable.
     • .spec.selector on a Deployment/ReplicaSet is IMMUTABLE — you cannot edit
       it; you must recreate the object.
     • Wrong targetPort = "connection refused" even with a healthy pod.
     • "Running but no traffic" usually means the readiness probe is failing, so
       the pod was removed from the Service endpoints.
     • A namespace stuck in Terminating is almost always a finalizer holding it.
     • NodePort must be in 30000–32767, or the apiserver rejects it.

  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
     • Generate every object with --dry-run=client -o yaml, then edit:
         kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v2 --dry-run=client -o yaml
     • Change live objects in place: kubectl label / kubectl annotate.
     • Filter fast with -l: kubectl get po -l app=easypj,tier=web.
     • kubectl explain <kind>.<field> for any schema field, offline.
     • kubectl rollout undo for an instant rollback; --to-revision=N for a
       specific revision (check kubectl rollout history first).
     • kubectl get ep <svc> (or get endpointslices) to confirm a Service has
       backends.

  🔑 COMMANDS
     kubectl get all -n easypj
     kubectl get po -l app=easypj
     kubectl label pod <pod> tier=web        # add/change a label
     kubectl annotate deploy easypj-web note="..."
     kubectl get ep easypj-web               # Service backends
     kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy
     kubectl rollout status|history|undo deploy/easypj-web
     kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v2
     kubectl scale deploy/easypj-web --replicas=5
     kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true|false
     kubectl delete <obj> --cascade=foreground|background|orphan

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 4 (full answer + explanation each)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Pod vs Deployment — when would you create each?
      A. Create a bare Pod only for a throwaway/debug task (e.g. a temporary
         curl/netshoot pod). For anything real — especially a stateless app like
         easypj-web — create a Deployment, because it gives self-healing,
         scaling, rolling updates and rollback. A bare Pod, once dead, stays
         dead; a Deployment respawns it.

  Q2. A Service has 0 endpoints — give the two most common causes.
      A. (1) The Service selector does not match the pods' labels (typo or wrong
         tier). (2) The pods exist and match, but none is Ready (readiness probe
         failing or still starting), so they aren't added to endpoints. Check:
         kubectl get ep <svc>  and  kubectl get po -l <selector> -o wide.

  Q3. How do Namespaces isolate, and what do they NOT isolate?
      A. They isolate NAMESPACED objects (Pods, Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps,
         Secrets, Roles, etc.) and give scope for ResourceQuota, RBAC and
         NetworkPolicy. They do NOT isolate cluster-scoped objects — Nodes,
         PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles — and do NOT provide
         network isolation by themselves (that needs NetworkPolicy).

  Q4. Add the label tier=web to a running Deployment (command).
      A. kubectl label deployment easypj-web tier=web
         (use --overwrite to change an existing value). Note: this labels the
         Deployment object; to change pod labels you edit the pod template.

  Q5. Difference between a label and an annotation; give a use for each.
      A. A LABEL is identifying metadata used for SELECTION (app=easypj wires a
         Service to its pods). An ANNOTATION is non-identifying metadata for
         tools/humans and is NEVER selectable (e.g. a change-cause, an Ingress
         controller config hint, last-applied-configuration).

  Q6. Name the ownership chain for a pod named easypj-web-7d4-x9k2.
      A. Deployment easypj-web ──manages──▶ ReplicaSet easypj-web-7d4 ──owns──▶
         Pod easypj-web-7d4-x9k2. The middle hash is the pod-template hash; the
         last segment is the pod's random suffix. ownerReferences encode this
         chain and drive cascading deletion.

  Q7. Why are Pods "ephemeral", and what's the implication for IPs?
      A. Pods are disposable units that are replaced (not repaired) on failure,
         node drain or rollout. Each replacement gets a NEW IP, so you must never
         hard-code or rely on a pod IP — always reach pods through a Service's
         stable virtual IP / DNS name.

  Q8. List the 4 Service types and who can reach each.
      A. ClusterIP — reachable only inside the cluster (default). NodePort —
         reachable externally via <anyNodeIP>:<30000-32767>. LoadBalancer —
         reachable externally via a cloud load balancer. ExternalName — no proxy;
         returns a CNAME/DNS alias to an external hostname.

  Q9. You delete a Pod managed by a Deployment — what happens and why?
      A. The Deployment's ReplicaSet observes desired=N > actual=N-1 and
         immediately creates a replacement pod (new name, new IP). The
         reconciliation loop enforces desired state, so deleting the pod doesn't
         remove it permanently — to truly remove it, scale/delete the Deployment.

  Q10. From the relationship map: how does a ConfigMap reach a container?
      A. The pod template references the ConfigMap via envFrom (or individual
         env valueFrom.configMapKeyRef, or a mounted volume). At pod start the
         kubelet injects those keys as environment variables (or files), so
         easypj's settings (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, DB host) come from the ConfigMap
         without rebuilding the image.

  Q11. Default RollingUpdate values, and what each controls?
      A. maxSurge=25% (how many EXTRA pods above desired may exist during the
         roll) and maxUnavailable=25% (how many of the desired pods may be
         unavailable during the roll). Together they pace a zero-downtime update;
         Recreate strategy skips this but causes downtime.

  Q12. A namespace is stuck in Terminating — likely cause and check?
      A. A finalizer on a resource (or on the namespace) is blocking deletion.
         Inspect with kubectl get namespace <ns> -o yaml and look at
         .spec.finalizers / .metadata.finalizers and any leftover resources;
         deletion completes once the finalizer is cleared by its controller.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: the object relationship map (above) is THE picture to
      memorise — Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pods, a Service finding those Pods by
      label, ConfigMap/Secret feeding env, Ingress routing in, PVC→PV→
      StorageClass for storage, all inside one Namespace, all governed by RBAC.
      .vs-prose: Read the map as a sentence — "A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet
      that owns Pods; a Service routes traffic to those Pods by matching their
      labels; the pods pull configuration from ConfigMaps and Secrets and storage
      from a PVC; an Ingress brings outside traffic to the Service; and the whole
      assembly lives in a Namespace whose access is controlled by RBAC and whose
      traffic is fenced by NetworkPolicy." Labels are the glue holding it together.

  ╔════════════════════════════ PART 1 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ═════════════════════╗
  ║ ✅ K8s automates deploy/scale/heal via desired-state reconciliation.     ║
  ║ ✅ Containers share the host kernel; K8s runs them via the CRI.          ║
  ║ ✅ Control plane = apiserver+etcd+scheduler+controller-manager; nodes =  ║
  ║    kubelet+kube-proxy+runtime. Only the apiserver talks to etcd.         ║
  ║ ✅ Core objects: Pod < ReplicaSet < Deployment; Service for networking;  ║
  ║    Namespace for isolation; labels wire everything together.             ║
  ║ ✅ Everything is declarative — you tell K8s WHAT you want, not HOW.       ║
  ║ 🎯 EXAM: architecture + "which component?" thinking powers the whole     ║
  ║    25% Cluster-Architecture and 30% Troubleshooting domains.             ║
  ║ 🔑 cluster-info · get nodes -o wide · api-resources · explain · crictl   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
  [PART 1 VISUAL SUMMARY]: one diagram from "easypj source" through image,
  YAML, apiserver, etcd, scheduler, kubelet, to 3 running pods behind a Service.
  .vs-prose: Trace the full path — your easypj source is built into an image,
  described by YAML, submitted to the apiserver, persisted in etcd, placed onto
  a node by the scheduler, started by that node's kubelet, and finally served to
  users as three running pods behind one stable Service.

  PART INTRO
  ──────────
  Part 1 gave you the map; Part 2 puts your hands on the wheel. Where Part 1
  explained WHAT Kubernetes is and WHY it exists, Part 2 is where you stop
  reading about the cluster and start driving it. You'll set up a real (local)
  cluster, master kubectl as your "remote control," learn the YAML language
  Kubernetes speaks, and deploy easypj for the first time — watching every
  concept from Part 1 (Pods, Deployments, Services, the control plane) become
  a real, running object you can query, describe, and break.

  This is the most tactile part of the guide. By the end you will have typed
  the commands that 90% of the CKA exam is built on, generated your first
  manifests, and stood up the easypj Django job board (project: easypj, app:
  jobpost) as a live workload — namespace, ConfigMap, Secret, Deployment and
  Service — reachable in your browser via port-forward. Everything that comes
  later (scaling, storage, networking, security, troubleshooting) assumes you
  are fluent in exactly these four chapters.

  🎯 EXAM NOTE: The muscle memory you build here — kubectl run, kubectl
     create, --dry-run=client -o yaml, kubectl apply -f, kubectl get/describe
     — is the single highest-leverage skill set on the CKA. You will use these
     commands in nearly every task on exam day, so practice them until they
     are reflexive.

  up). This is the picture every later part refers back to:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            DEPLOYING easypj — "WHAT JUST HAPPENED" FLOW                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │   You (kubectl)                                                           │
  │       │  kubectl apply -f easypj/                                         │
  │       ▼                                                                   │
  │   ┌──────────────┐   validates & stores desired state                    │
  │   │ API SERVER   │◀──────────────────────────────┐                       │
  │   └──────┬───────┘                                │                       │
  │          │ writes objects                         │ watches              │
  │          ▼                                         │                      │
  │   ┌──────────────┐    Namespace: easypj            │                      │
  │   │     etcd     │    ConfigMap: easypj-config      │                      │
  │   │ (desired     │    Secret:    easypj-secret      │                      │
  │   │  state DB)   │    Deployment: easypj (3 repl.)  │                      │
  │   └──────────────┘    Service:   easypj-svc         │                      │
  │          │                                         │                      │
  │          ▼                                         │                      │
  │   ┌──────────────────┐  Deployment ─▶ ReplicaSet ─▶ Pods                  │
  │   │  CONTROLLERS     │──────────────────────────────┘                     │
  │   │ (deployment,     │  "current ≠ desired → reconcile"                   │
  │   │  replicaset)     │                                                    │
  │   └────────┬─────────┘                                                    │
  │            │ creates Pod objects (unscheduled)                            │
  │            ▼                                                              │
  │   ┌──────────────┐   picks a node for each Pod                            │
  │   │  SCHEDULER   │                                                        │
  │   └──────┬───────┘                                                        │
  │          │ binds Pod ─▶ Node                                              │
  │          ▼                                                                │
  │   ┌──────────────┐   kubelet pulls image (easypj:latest),                 │
  │   │   KUBELET    │   mounts ConfigMap/Secret as env/volume,               │
  │   │  (on node)   │   starts the jobpost container via the                 │
  │   └──────┬───────┘   container runtime (containerd)                       │
  │          │                                                                │
  │          ▼                                                                │
  │   ┌──────────────┐   easypj Pods RUNNING  ◀── readiness probe passes      │
  │   │  easypj POD  │   Service easypj-svc gets Endpoints                    │
  │   │  jobpost     │                                                        │
  │   └──────┬───────┘                                                        │
  │          │  kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-svc 8000:80                   │
  │          ▼                                                                │
  │   http://localhost:8000/jobs/   ◀── you see the job board in a browser    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧠 ANALOGY: Part 1 was reading the car's manual and looking under the hood.
     Part 2 is turning the key, finding the gear stick, learning the dashboard,
     and actually driving easypj around the block. Stalls and wrong turns here
     are expected — that is how the controls become automatic.

  📖 KEY TERMS YOU'LL MEET IN PART 2:
     • Minikube / kind — single-machine Kubernetes clusters for learning/dev.
     • kubeconfig — the file (~/.kube/config) that tells kubectl which cluster,
       user, and namespace to talk to.
     • context — a named (cluster + user + namespace) tuple you switch between.
     • imperative vs declarative — typing a command that does a thing, vs
       writing a YAML file that describes a desired end state and applying it.
     • --dry-run=client -o yaml — generate a manifest from a command without
       creating anything; the exam's #1 time-saver.
     • manifest — a YAML (or JSON) file describing one or more API objects.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP (carry this through all of Part 2): never hand-type YAML from a
     blank file under exam pressure. Generate a skeleton with an imperative
     command + --dry-run=client -o yaml, redirect to a file, then edit. This
     single habit saves minutes per task.

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: by the end of Part 2 you should be able to, from memory,
     spin up a cluster, switch context, generate and apply a ConfigMap, Secret,
     Deployment and Service for easypj, and reach the running app — without
     looking anything up. If you can do that, you own the foundation the whole
     exam is built on.

  Chapter 5: Setting Up Your Environment                              🟢 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟢 Beginner · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Foundation for everything hands-on.
  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS: you need a sandbox to practice in; the CKA exam is a
      live terminal, so muscle memory starts here. Every later chapter assumes
      a working cluster, a working kubectl, and a kubeconfig you can read and
      switch. If you cannot reliably point kubectl at the RIGHT cluster and the
      RIGHT namespace, you will silently apply changes to the wrong place — in
      the exam that is an instant zero on the task. VISUAL: a tool-choice
      decision tree 🧭 plus an annotated kubeconfig map.
  [C] OBJECTIVES:
        • pick a local Kubernetes tool that fits your goal
        • install Minikube + kubectl per-OS and start a (multi-node) cluster
        • read and understand a kubeconfig (clusters / users / contexts)
        • switch contexts and set a default namespace
        • verify cluster health before deploying anything
        • enable the essential addons (metrics-server, ingress, dashboard)
  [D] CKA RELEVANCE: 🎯 kubeconfig and context switching are used in EVERY
      exam question. The exam gives you several clusters and tells you which
      context each task uses — getting that first move right is worth points
      on its own.

  SECTION MAP
     5.1  Choosing a Local Kubernetes Tool        🧭
     5.2  Installing Minikube (Quick Start)
     5.3  Installing kubectl
     5.4  Understanding kubeconfig                🎯

  ── 5.1  Choosing a Local Kubernetes Tool 🧭 ──────────────────────────  🟢

     Before you install anything, decide WHAT you are optimizing for: learning
     speed, low resource use, CI automation, or a real production-shaped
     control plane. The five common choices:

     [COMPARISON TABLE — which tool to use]
     | Tool          | Best for          | Nodes      | Resources    | Install      |
     | Minikube      | Learning, single  | 1-multi    | Medium       | Easy         |
     | Kind          | CI/CD, testing    | Multi      | Low          | Easy         |
     | k3s           | Edge, lightweight | Multi      | Very low     | Easy         |
     | kubeadm       | Real clusters     | Multi      | High         | Manual ⚠️    |
     | Docker Desktop| Windows/Mac dev   | 1          | Medium       | Very easy    |

     ┌─────────────┬───────────────┬─────────┬──────────────────────────┐
     │ Tool        │ Best for      │ Nodes   │ Notes                    │
     │ Minikube    │ learning      │ 1–multi │ easiest single-node start│
     │ Kind        │ CI / testing  │ multi   │ K8s in Docker, fast      │
     │ k3s         │ edge / light  │ multi   │ tiny footprint           │
     │ kubeadm     │ REAL clusters │ multi   │ you MUST learn this (CKA)│
     │ Docker Desk │ Win/Mac dev   │ 1       │ one-click                │
     └─────────────┴───────────────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────┘

     🧭 DECISION GUIDE — pick a tool
     ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  What is your goal?                                                │
     │                                                                    │
     │  "I want to learn fast on my laptop" ───────────────▶  Minikube    │
     │  "I need throwaway clusters in CI pipelines" ───────▶  Kind        │
     │  "Tiny box / edge / Raspberry Pi" ──────────────────▶  k3s         │
     │  "I must understand how a real cluster is built" ───▶  kubeadm     │
     │  "Just give me one-click on Win/Mac" ───────────────▶  Docker Desk │
     └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     For CKA exam prep: Minikube (start) → kubeadm (must learn).
     💡 CKA path: Minikube to learn fast → kubeadm because the exam tests it.
     Minikube gets you a cluster in two minutes so you can practice kubectl;
     kubeadm teaches you the control-plane components, certificates and the
     join flow that the exam actually grades (see the cluster-setup chapters).


  ── 5.2  Installing Minikube (Quick Start) ────────────────────────────  🟢

     Install per-OS:
        a) Windows: choco install minikube   OR   winget install minikube
        b) macOS:   brew install minikube
        c) Linux:   curl + install the binary, e.g.
             curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
             sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

     d) Starting your first cluster:
        $ minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096
        $ minikube status

     [STEP-BY-STEP with expected output]
        $ minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096 --nodes=3
        😄  minikube v1.33 on Darwin/Windows/Linux
        ✨  Using the docker driver based on user configuration
        👍  Starting control-plane node minikube in cluster minikube
        🔥  Creating docker container (CPUs=2, Memory=4096MB) ...
        🌟  Enabled addons: storage-provisioner, default-storageclass
        🏄  Done! kubectl is now configured to use "minikube" cluster

        $ minikube status
        minikube
        type: Control Plane
        host: Running
        kubelet: Running
        apiserver: Running
        kubeconfig: Configured

     Lifecycle commands:
        minikube stop          # pause the cluster, keep state
        minikube delete        # destroy the cluster entirely
        minikube start         # bring it back up

     💡 [TIP] Use --nodes=3 for multi-node practice. A 3-node sandbox lets you
        practice scheduling, taints/tolerations, cordon and drain — none of
        which you can rehearse on a single node.


  ── 5.3  Installing kubectl ───────────────────────────────────────────  🟢

     📖 kubectl = the CLI tool to interact with ANY Kubernetes cluster. It is
     independent of Minikube — the same binary talks to your laptop cluster,
     a cloud cluster, or the exam cluster. It connects using ~/.kube/config
     (the very next section).

     [CODE: Installation commands per OS]
        # Windows
        choco install kubernetes-cli
        # macOS
        brew install kubectl
        # Linux
        curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
        sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

     Verify:
        $ kubectl version --client
        Client Version: v1.31.x


  ── 5.4  Understanding kubeconfig ─────────────────────────────────────  🟢 🎯

     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     📖 ~/.kube/config (or whatever $KUBECONFIG points at) is THE file that
     tells kubectl how to connect. It has three sections:
        • CLUSTERS  — WHERE to connect (API server URL + CA certificate)
        • USERS     — WHO you are (client certificate or token)
        • CONTEXTS  — a cluster + user + namespace combination
     current-context is the active one — the combo kubectl uses right now.

     [CODE: kubeconfig file structure annotated]
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Config
        clusters:                              # WHERE
        - name: minikube
          cluster:
            server: https://192.168.49.2:8443
            certificate-authority: /home/you/.minikube/ca.crt
        users:                                 # WHO
        - name: minikube-user
          user:
            client-certificate: /home/you/.minikube/profiles/minikube/client.crt
            client-key:         /home/you/.minikube/profiles/minikube/client.key
        contexts:                              # WHICH combo
        - name: minikube
          context:
            cluster: minikube
            user: minikube-user
            namespace: default
        current-context: minikube              # ACTIVE

     [KUBECONFIG STRUCTURE]
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  ~/.kube/config                                   │
     │                                                    │
     │  clusters:     ← WHERE to connect                 │
     │  ├── minikube  (https://192.168.49.2:8443)       │
     │  ├── staging   (https://staging.k8s.example.com)  │
     │  └── prod      (https://prod.k8s.example.com)     │
     │                                                    │
     │  users:        ← WHO you are                      │
     │  ├── minikube-user (client certificate)           │
     │  ├── dev-user      (token)                        │
     │  └── admin-user    (client certificate)           │
     │                                                    │
     │  contexts:     ← cluster + user + namespace       │
     │  ├── minikube  (minikube + minikube-user)         │
     │  ├── dev       (staging + dev-user + easypj-dev)  │
     │  └── prod      (prod + admin-user + easypj-prod)  │
     │                                                    │
     │  current-context: minikube  ← active connection   │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  ── 5.5  Managing Multiple Clusters and Contexts ──────────────────────  🟢 🎯

     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     [COMMANDS: context management with examples]
        kubectl config get-contexts                              # list all
        kubectl config use-context prod                          # switch
        kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj  # default ns
        kubectl config current-context                           # print active

     • kubectl config get-contexts → list all contexts (a * marks current)
     • kubectl config use-context prod → switch to prod
     • kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj → set default NS
     • KUBECONFIG env var: merge multiple config files
          KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/staging.yaml:~/work/prod.yaml kubectl get-contexts
       The merge is in-memory for that session; the first file that defines a
       key wins, and writes go to the first file unless you say otherwise.

     ⚠️ [WARNING] Always verify context AND namespace before running commands
        in production! Acting on the wrong context/cluster is the #1 way to
        lose exam points (and to break prod for real). Make
        `kubectl config use-context <task-context>` the FIRST line you type
        for every exam question.


  ── 5.6  Verifying Your Cluster ───────────────────────────────────────  🟢 🩺

     🩺 Before deploying anything, confirm the cluster is actually healthy:
        $ kubectl cluster-info               # is the API server reachable?
        $ kubectl get nodes                  # are all nodes Ready?
        $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system    # CoreDNS / kube-proxy Running?
        $ kubectl get componentstatuses      # (deprecated but still useful)

     [EXPECTED OUTPUT]
        $ kubectl cluster-info
        Kubernetes control plane is running at https://192.168.49.2:8443
        CoreDNS is running at https://192.168.49.2:8443/api/v1/.../kube-dns:dns/proxy

        $ kubectl get nodes
        NAME           STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
        minikube       Ready    control-plane   5m    v1.31.0
        minikube-m02   Ready    <none>          4m    v1.31.0
        minikube-m03   Ready    <none>          4m    v1.31.0

        $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system
        NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
        coredns-xxxx               1/1     Running   0          5m
        etcd-minikube              1/1     Running   0          5m
        kube-apiserver-minikube    1/1     Running   0          5m
        kube-proxy-xxxx            1/1     Running   0          5m

     DNS smoke test from a throwaway pod (proves cluster networking works):
        $ kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
            nslookup kubernetes.default

     🩺 Any node NotReady, or a kube-system pod in CrashLoopBackOff, must be
     fixed BEFORE you deploy workloads — otherwise you will chase phantom
     application bugs that are really a broken control plane.


  ── 5.7  Enabling Essential Addons ────────────────────────────────────  🟢

        $ minikube addons enable metrics-server
        $ minikube addons enable ingress
        $ minikube addons enable dashboard
        $ minikube addons list                 # see what is on/off

     [TABLE: Key addons and what they enable]
     ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ Addon                │ What it unlocks                              │
     │ metrics-server       │ kubectl top nodes/pods · HPA autoscaling     │
     │ ingress (nginx)      │ Ingress resources / host+path HTTP routing   │
     │ storage-provisioner  │ dynamic PersistentVolumeClaims (auto PVs)    │
     │ dashboard            │ web UI: `minikube dashboard`                 │
     │ default-storageclass │ a default StorageClass for PVCs              │
     └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     💡 metrics-server is the one most labs forget — without it
     `kubectl top` and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler simply will not work.


  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 5

  [KUBECONFIG — one file, many clusters; a CONTEXT picks the combo]
   ~/.kube/config
   ┌─ clusters: WHERE  minikube · easypj-dev · easypj-prod   (server + CA)
   ├─ users:    WHO    admin (cert) · dev (token)
   └─ contexts: combo  dev  = easypj-dev  + dev   + ns:easypj
                       prod = easypj-prod + admin + ns:easypj
   current-context: dev   ◄ kubectl acts HERE
   🔀 switch: kubectl config use-context prod
   📌 set default ns: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
   ⚠️ ALWAYS verify context + namespace before acting — wrong cluster = 0 points.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — laptop → kubeconfig → many clusters
   ┌──────────┐    reads     ┌───────────────┐   current-context picks
   │  kubectl │ ───────────▶ │ ~/.kube/config│ ──────────────┐
   │ (laptop) │              └───────────────┘                │
   └──────────┘                                               ▼
        │                                       ┌──────────────────────────┐
        │   one binary, many targets            │ context "dev"            │
        ├──────────────────────────────────────▶│  → easypj-dev cluster    │
        │                                       │  → user dev · ns:easypj  │
        │                                       └──────────────────────────┘
        │                                       ┌──────────────────────────┐
        └──────────────────────────────────────▶│ context "prod"           │
                                                │  → easypj-prod cluster   │
                                                │  → user admin · ns:easypj│
                                                └──────────────────────────┘
   .vs-prose: kubectl is a single CLI on your laptop. It reads one kubeconfig
   file; current-context selects which cluster + user + namespace combination
   it talks to. Switching context re-points the SAME kubectl at a different
   cluster — so the first thing to check, every time, is which context and
   namespace are active.


  [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — how kubectl finds & merges kubeconfig
      Loading order (highest precedence first):
        1. the --kubeconfig flag (explicit path on the command line)
        2. the $KUBECONFIG environment variable (colon/`;`-separated list,
           merged in order — first definition of a key wins)
        3. the default ~/.kube/config
      A flag beats the env var, which beats the default file. Within a merged
      $KUBECONFIG list, writes (e.g. set-context) land in the FIRST file that
      can hold the key.

      🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
        • exec credential plugins — clusters can call an external binary
          (e.g. `aws eks get-token`, `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`) to fetch a
          short-lived token at request time, instead of a static cert/token.
        • client-go loading order — kubectl, controllers and operators all use
          the same client-go ClientConfig rules described above.
        • insecure-skip-tls-verify: true disables CA validation — convenient
          in a lab, a security hole anywhere real (man-in-the-middle risk).
        • impersonation flags --as / --as-group let an admin run a command AS
          another user/group to test RBAC ("can dev-user list pods?").
        • KUBECONFIG in CI: point it at a generated file so pipeline steps
          target the right ephemeral cluster without touching ~/.kube.
        • kubectx / kubens: tiny helpers to switch context/namespace fast;
          worth muscle-memory for daily ops (not installable in the exam, so
          also drill the raw `kubectl config` commands).


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 5
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • kubeconfig = three sections: clusters (WHERE) + users (WHO) + contexts
     (the combo); current-context is the active one.
   • A CONTEXT binds cluster + user + namespace into one named selection.
   • Confirm context AND namespace FIRST — before every action.
   • Minikube to learn fast; kubeadm because the exam tests real cluster build.
   • Addons unlock real features: metrics-server → top/HPA, ingress → routing.
   • kubectl is one binary that talks to any cluster; the kubeconfig decides
     which one.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 5
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • Acting on the WRONG context/cluster = 0 points (and broken prod for real).
   • A stale default namespace silently sends objects to the wrong place —
     `get pods` looks "empty" because you are in the wrong namespace.
   • metrics-server not enabled → `kubectl top` and HPA fail with no obvious
     reason ("error: metrics not available yet").
   • insecure-skip-tls-verify hides cert problems in dev that bite in prod.
   • Single-node Minikube can't reproduce scheduling/drain — use --nodes=3.
   • `kubectl get componentstatuses` is deprecated; don't rely on it as the
     sole health check.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 5
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   • alias k=kubectl                         (then `k get po`, `k config …`)
   • A `kns` helper / kubens to flip namespaces fast.
   • Make `kubectl config use-context <task>` the FIRST move of EVERY question.
   • `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj` once, then drop
     the repetitive `-n easypj` for the rest of the task.
   • `kubectl config current-context` to sanity-check in one line.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 5
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096 --nodes=3
   minikube status | stop | delete
   minikube addons enable metrics-server | ingress | dashboard
   minikube addons list
   kubectl version --client
   kubectl config get-contexts
   kubectl config current-context
   kubectl config use-context <name>
   kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
   KUBECONFIG=a.yaml:b.yaml kubectl config get-contexts
   kubectl cluster-info
   kubectl get nodes
   kubectl get pods -n kube-system

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL — Chapter 5
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Create 2 contexts, switch between them, and set the default namespace of the
   current context to easypj. Prove each step with a `get-contexts` listing.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 5 (10 questions — full answer + explanation)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Q1. Name the 3 sections of a kubeconfig and what each holds.
       A. clusters (WHERE — API server URL + CA cert), users (WHO — client
          cert or token), contexts (a named cluster+user+namespace combo).
          current-context names the active context. kubectl resolves the
          current context to know which cluster to hit, as whom, in which ns.

   Q2. Switch to context "prod".
       A. kubectl config use-context prod
          This only rewrites current-context in the kubeconfig; it does not
          contact the cluster. Verify with `kubectl config current-context`.

   Q3. Set the current context's default namespace to easypj.
       A. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
          Afterwards kubectl commands without -n target easypj. Confirm with
          `kubectl config get-contexts` (the NAMESPACE column shows easypj).

   Q4. Merge two kubeconfig files for one kubectl session.
       A. KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/prod.yaml kubectl config get-contexts
          The list is merged in memory for that process; first definition of a
          given key wins. Useful to combine a personal config with a cluster
          config without editing files.

   Q5. Verify a freshly-built cluster is healthy (3 commands).
       A. kubectl cluster-info        (API server + CoreDNS reachable)
          kubectl get nodes           (all nodes STATUS=Ready)
          kubectl get pods -n kube-system   (CoreDNS/etcd/apiserver Running)
          Optionally a DNS smoke test with a busybox pod nslookup.

   Q6. What exactly is a "context"?
       A. A named pointer that ties together one cluster, one user and one
          (optional) namespace. Selecting a context tells kubectl which
          cluster to talk to, with which identity, in which default namespace.
          It is metadata in the kubeconfig — switching contexts does not
          touch any cluster.

   Q7. Enable metrics-server and prove `kubectl top` works.
       A. minikube addons enable metrics-server
          # wait ~30–60s for it to scrape
          kubectl top nodes        (shows CPU/MEM)
          kubectl top pods -A      (per-pod usage)
          Without metrics-server, top/HPA return "metrics not available".

   Q8. Start a 3-node local cluster.
       A. minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096 --nodes=3
          Multi-node lets you practice scheduling, taints, cordon and drain.

   Q9. Print the current context in one command.
       A. kubectl config current-context

   Q10. KUBECONFIG precedence: flag vs env vs ~/.kube/config — which wins?
       A. The --kubeconfig flag wins; if absent, $KUBECONFIG (a merged list);
          if that is unset too, the default ~/.kube/config is used. So:
          flag  >  $KUBECONFIG  >  ~/.kube/config.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
