  Chapter 6: kubectl — The Administrator's Command Center              🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2h · Used in 100% of exam tasks. This is the
      SPEED CHAPTER — every task you face on the CKA runs through kubectl, so
      fluency here is the single biggest multiplier on your final score.

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      kubectl is the steering wheel of the cluster. Every other chapter — Pods,
      Deployments, Services, storage, RBAC, troubleshooting — is ultimately
      "drive kubectl at the apiserver." On the exam you are graded on RESULTS
      under a clock, and the candidates who pass are the ones who generate
      manifests instead of typing them, who know the short names, and who reach
      for `kubectl explain` instead of guessing a field. The command anatomy
      callout below is the mental model that makes all of this click.

  [C] OBJECTIVES
      • Master the verb + resource + name + flags pattern and the short names.
      • Drill the daily admin command set (get / describe / create / edit /
        delete / debug), grouped for muscle memory.
      • Use `kubectl explain` as your in-exam API manual.
      • Choose between imperative and declarative — and use THE HYBRID to win.
      • Format and filter output: -o wide/yaml/json, jsonpath, custom-columns,
        sort-by, label selectors (-l), field selectors (--field-selector).
      • Debug pods with logs, exec, port-forward, and ephemeral containers
        (`kubectl debug`) — including crashed and distroless images.

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE
      🎯 Directly exercised in essentially every domain. Cluster Architecture
      (15%), Workloads & Scheduling (15%), Services & Networking (20%), Storage
      (10%), and Troubleshooting (30%) are all performed THROUGH kubectl. The
      exam never asks "what does kubectl do?" — it asks you to DO things, fast.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      6.1  The kubectl Syntax Pattern
      6.2  Essential Admin Commands — Daily Use
      6.3  kubectl explain — Built-in API Documentation
      6.4  Imperative vs Declarative — When to Use Each
      6.5  Output Formatting and Filtering
      6.6  Debugging Pods — logs, exec & ephemeral containers

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.1  The kubectl Syntax Pattern                                          🟡
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       $ kubectl [VERB] [RESOURCE] [NAME] [FLAGS]

       Examples:
       $ kubectl get pods
       $ kubectl describe node worker-1
       $ kubectl delete deployment easypj
       $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

       Every command is the same four parts. Once the pattern is automatic you
       stop thinking about syntax and start thinking about the task.

       [KUBECTL COMMAND ANATOMY]
       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │  kubectl    get      pods     easypj-xyz   -n prod   │
       │  ───────   ─────   ───────   ───────────  ─────────  │
       │  command   verb    resource    name        namespace  │
       │                                                       │
       │  Verbs: get, describe, create, apply, delete,        │
       │         edit, logs, exec, top, patch, label,         │
       │         annotate, scale, rollout, auth, drain...     │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

       [kubectl COMMAND ANATOMY — exam form]
        kubectl   get    pods   easypj-web-x9k   -n easypj   -o wide
        └binary─┘ └verb┘ └kind┘ └────name─────┘ └namespace┘ └output┘
        verbs: get·describe·logs·exec·apply·create·delete·edit·scale·rollout·top
        short names: po svc deploy ns cm rs sts ds pvc sa netpol ing

       💡 INSIGHT — Learn the short names. They save real seconds under the
       clock, and seconds are the currency of the CKA. The most common:
         po  = pods            svc    = services         deploy = deployments
         ns  = namespaces      cm     = configmaps       rs     = replicasets
         sts = statefulsets    ds     = daemonsets        pvc   = persistent-
         sa  = serviceaccounts netpol = networkpolicies   ing   = ingresses
                                                          pv    = persistent-
                                                                  volumes

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.2  Essential Admin Commands — Daily Use                                🟡
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       Grouped by category so they live in muscle memory, not in a cheat sheet:

         GET    : get all -n easypj · get po -o wide · get events --sort-by=…
         INSPECT: describe <kind> <name> · explain <path>
         CREATE : create / apply / run / expose / scale  (imperative = fastest)
         MODIFY : edit · set image · label · annotate · patch
         DELETE : delete <kind> <name> [$now]
         DEBUG  : logs [-p][-c] · exec -it · port-forward · debug · cp · top

       a) Get Information
          $ kubectl get nodes -o wide
          $ kubectl get pods -A                    # all namespaces
          $ kubectl get pods -o yaml               # full YAML output
          $ kubectl get pods --sort-by=.status.startTime
          $ kubectl get all -n easypj              # everything in namespace
          $ kubectl top nodes                      # resource usage
          $ kubectl top pods                       # pod resource usage

       b) Inspect Details
          $ kubectl describe pod easypj-xyz
          $ kubectl describe node worker-1
          $ kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
          $ kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy   # API docs in CLI

       c) Create and Modify
          $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
          $ kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
          $ kubectl edit deployment easypj         # open in editor
          $ kubectl patch deployment easypj -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'
          $ kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd
          $ kubectl taint node worker-1 key=value:NoSchedule

       d) Delete and Clean Up
          $ kubectl delete pod easypj-xyz
          $ kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
          $ kubectl delete pods --field-selector status.phase=Failed

       e) Debug and Troubleshoot
          $ kubectl logs easypj-xyz
          $ kubectl logs easypj-xyz --previous     # crashed container
          $ kubectl exec -it easypj-xyz -- /bin/sh
          $ kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-xyz 8000:8000
          $ kubectl debug node/worker-1 --image=busybox

       ⚡ SPEED TIP — `$now` is the alias `--force --grace-period 0` for deleting
       a stuck pod instantly. Pair it with delete when a pod is wedged:
          $ kubectl delete pod easypj-xyz --force --grace-period 0

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.3  kubectl explain — Built-in API Documentation                     🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC — use this DURING the exam!

       💡 This is your in-exam manual. The API reference website may be allowed,
       but `kubectl explain` is faster: it lives in the terminal and gives you
       the EXACT YAML structure with no scrolling.

         $ kubectl explain pod
         $ kubectl explain pod.spec
         $ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers
         $ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources
         $ kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy --recursive

       `kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources` prints the precise nested
       fields you need; add `--recursive` to dump the whole subtree at once.

       🔑 MUST-REMEMBER — Forgot a field name? Don't guess. `explain` it. This
       single habit prevents the most common cause of failed exam tasks:
       a manifest that the apiserver rejects because of a typo'd field.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.4  Imperative vs Declarative — When to Use Each                     🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

       [IMPERATIVE vs DECLARATIVE — visual comparison]
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │                                                        │
       │  🏃 IMPERATIVE: "Do this NOW"                          │
       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
       │  │ $ kubectl run easypj --image=easypj:v1       │     │
       │  │ $ kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5│     │
       │  │ $ kubectl expose deployment easypj --port=80  │     │
       │  │                                                │     │
       │  │  Like giving step-by-step cooking instructions │     │
       │  │  "chop onions, then fry them, then add salt"   │     │
       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
       │  ✅ Faster for one-off tasks & CKA exam speed         │
       │  ❌ No record of what you did, hard to reproduce      │
       │                                                        │
       │  📝 DECLARATIVE: "Make it look like THIS"              │
       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
       │  │ $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml            │     │
       │  │                                                │     │
       │  │  deployment.yaml defines the desired state:    │     │
       │  │  replicas: 5, image: easypj:v1, port: 80      │     │
       │  │                                                │     │
       │  │  Like ordering from a menu:                    │     │
       │  │  "I want pasta" — the kitchen figures it out   │     │
       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
       │  ✅ Repeatable, version-controlled, auditable         │
       │  ✅ Production standard, GitOps friendly               │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

       Imperative (quick, one-off):
       $ kubectl run easypj --image=easypj:v1 --port=8000
       $ kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3
       $ kubectl expose deployment easypj --port=80 --target-port=8000

       Declarative (production, repeatable):
       $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

       [COMPARISON TABLE]
       ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
       │ Approach     │ When to use             │ CKA exam   │ Production  │
       ├──────────────┼─────────────────────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
       │ Imperative   │ Quick tasks, exam speed │ ✅ Faster   │ ❌ Avoid   │
       │ Declarative  │ Real environments       │ ✅ Required │ ✅ Always  │
       └──────────────┴─────────────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

       💡 THE HYBRID (exam gold): generate imperatively, then apply
       declaratively. Use imperative to GENERATE YAML quickly, edit it to add
       what the imperative form can't express (volumes, probes, resources),
       then apply the file:

       [THE FAST PATH — generate, don't hand-write]
        k run nginx --image=nginx $do > pod.yaml   ($do = --dry-run=client -o yaml)
             ▼ edit (add volumes / probes / resources)
        k apply -f pod.yaml ─► validated by the apiserver ─► created
        🔍 forgot a field? kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe

       Pro tip for CKA exam — generate manifests this way and never hand-write:
       $ kubectl run easypj --image=easypj:v1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
       $ kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

       🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — client vs server dry-run:
       • `--dry-run=client` renders the object locally WITHOUT contacting the
         apiserver. Perfect for generating YAML; does NOT validate against
         admission controllers or defaulting.
       • `--dry-run=server` sends the object to the apiserver, which runs
         validation, defaulting and (most) admission, then DISCARDS it. Use this
         to ask "would this actually be accepted?" without persisting anything.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.5  Output Formatting and Filtering                                  🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

       The output flags let you extract ANY field from ANY object — the
       difference between scrolling through pages of describe output and getting
       the one value you need in one line.

       [TABLE: output & filter flags]
       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ Flag                                     │ What it does / example                       │
       ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
       │ -o wide                                  │ Extra columns (node, IP) on the table        │
       │ -o yaml  /  -o json                      │ Full object definition                       │
       │ -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'   │ Extract specific fields (single quotes!)     │
       │ -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,   │ Build your own table from any paths          │
       │    IP:.status.podIP                      │                                              │
       │ --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp    │ Order rows by any field                      │
       │ -l app=easypj                            │ Filter by LABEL                              │
       │ --field-selector status.phase=Running    │ Filter by FIELD (server-side)                │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

       Worked examples:
       $ kubectl get pods -o wide
       $ kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'
       $ kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,IP:.status.podIP
       $ kubectl get pods --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
       $ kubectl get pods -l app=easypj
       $ kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running

       ⚠️ GOTCHA — jsonpath expressions MUST be in single quotes in bash, or the
       shell will try to expand the `{...}` and `*` characters and the command
       silently does the wrong thing.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  6.6  Debugging Pods — logs, exec & ephemeral containers              🟡 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC — Troubleshooting is 30% of the exam; this is its core.

       • logs — read what the container already printed:
         $ kubectl logs <pod> [-c <ctr>] [-p|--previous] [-f] [--since=1h]
         The `--previous` flag shows the LAST crashed container's logs — vital
         for CrashLoopBackOff, where the running container is brand new and its
         logs are empty but the crashed one holds the error.

       • exec — get a shell or run a command inside a RUNNING container:
         $ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
         Requires that the image actually ships a shell.

       • port-forward — tunnel a local port to a pod or service:
         $ kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-xyz 8000:8000
         $ kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:80

       • EPHEMERAL CONTAINERS via `kubectl debug` — the only way to "get a shell"
         into a CRASHED pod or a DISTROLESS image (one with no shell at all).
         They share the target pod (optionally its PID namespace), CANNOT be
         removed or restarted, and take no ports / probes / resources:
         $ kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>   # attach to running pod
         $ kubectl debug <pod> -it --image=busybox --copy-to=dbg --share-processes
         $ kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox            # node (host fs at /host)

       • wait — block until a condition is met (great in scripts and timed tasks):
         $ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/<x> --timeout=60s

       📖 KEY TERM — ephemeral container: a temporary debug container injected
       into a running pod. It is NOT part of pod.spec, is never restarted, and
       cannot be removed once added. It exists purely to give you tools (sh,
       curl, ps) next to a container that lacks them.

       🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING DECISION GUIDE
        Container won't even start?           → describe pod (Events) + logs -p
        Running but image has no shell?       → kubectl debug --image=busybox
        Need to see another container's procs?→ debug --share-processes / --target
        Need to inspect the NODE itself?      → kubectl debug node/<node>
        App reachable from inside but not out?→ port-forward to bypass Service/Ingress

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER (exam + beyond)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🔧 kubectl is simply a REST client for the Kubernetes API. There is no
       magic — every command becomes one or more HTTP calls to the apiserver.
       You can SEE them:
         $ kubectl get po -v=8        # show the raw API requests & responses
       Verbosity `-v=6` through `-v=9` peels back successive layers (URLs,
       headers, full request/response bodies). When a command behaves
       unexpectedly, `-v=8` tells you exactly what was sent.

       🔬 DEEPER topics worth knowing:
       • Server-side apply (`kubectl apply --server-side`) — the apiserver, not
         the client, computes the merge and tracks field ownership ("managed
         fields"), which avoids the last-applied-configuration annotation drift.
       • go-template output (`-o go-template='...'`) — more powerful than
         jsonpath for conditional/formatted output.
       • `kubectl wait` and `kubectl get --raw /healthz` — scripting primitives.
       • krew — the kubectl plugin manager (`kubectl krew install ...`).
       • `explain --recursive` — dump an entire spec subtree in one shot.
       • custom-columns and label/field selectors compose: filter THEN format.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       • Every command is verb + resource + name + flags — internalize it.
       • Learn the short names (po svc deploy ns cm rs sts ds pvc sa netpol ing).
       • GENERATE YAML with `--dry-run=client -o yaml`; never hand-write a manifest.
       • THE HYBRID wins the exam: generate imperatively → edit → apply -f.
       • `kubectl explain` is your in-terminal API manual — explain, don't guess.
       • Output flags (jsonpath / custom-columns / sort-by / -l / --field-selector)
         extract or reshape anything fast.
       • `--previous` recovers the logs of a crashed (CrashLoopBackOff) container.
       • `kubectl debug` (ephemeral containers) is the ONLY shell into a crashed
         or distroless pod.
       • kubectl is just a REST client — `-v=8` reveals the raw API calls.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       • Forgetting `-n <namespace>` — you operate on `default` and "see nothing."
       • Confusing client vs server dry-run (local render vs apiserver validation).
       • jsonpath quoting — must be SINGLE quotes in bash, or the shell mangles it.
       • Editing a LIVE object with `kubectl edit` instead of the manifest in git —
         the change is lost on the next `apply`.
       • `kubectl logs` (without -p) on a CrashLoopBackOff pod shows the empty new
         container; you needed `--previous`.
       • Ephemeral containers can't be removed or restarted — don't expect cleanup.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS / SPEED CARD
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       Put these in your shell at the START of the exam:
         alias k=kubectl
         alias kgp='k get po'
         export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'      # k run x --image=nginx $do
         export now='--force --grace-period 0'      # k delete po x $now
         source <(kubectl completion bash)          # TAB completion
         complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k   # completion for the alias
       Then: generate with $do, delete stuck pods with $now, TAB-complete names.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS — Quick Reference
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       kubectl get / describe / logs / exec / apply / create / run / expose
       kubectl scale / rollout / edit / patch / label / annotate / delete
       kubectl explain <path> [--recursive]
       kubectl get ... -o jsonpath='{...}'  |  -o custom-columns=...  |  -o wide
       kubectl get ... -l <key>=<val>  |  --field-selector <field>=<val>  |  --sort-by=...
       kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>
       kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox
       kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/<x> --timeout=60s
       kubectl apply --server-side -f <file>
       kubectl ... -v=8        # show raw API calls

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       Generate a Deployment YAML with $do, edit it to add a liveness probe and
       resource requests, then apply it — all without ever hand-writing the
       boilerplate.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Q1  Generate a Pod manifest WITHOUT creating it.
       A:  kubectl run easypj --image=easypj:v1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
       WHY: --dry-run=client renders the object locally and never contacts the
            apiserver; `-o yaml` prints it; redirect to a file to edit and apply.
            This is the fast path — generate, never hand-write.

   Q2  Show the YAML path for a container's liveness probe via explain.
       A:  kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe
       WHY: explain walks the API schema; this prints the exact nested fields
            (httpGet, initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds…) so you don't guess.
            Add --recursive to dump the whole subtree at once.

   Q3  Extract every pod's IP with jsonpath.
       A:  kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'
       WHY: a get of a list returns an object with .items[]; [*] iterates them;
            single quotes stop bash from expanding {} and *.

   Q4  List pods sorted by start time.
       A:  kubectl get pods --sort-by=.status.startTime
            (or --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp)
       WHY: --sort-by takes a jsonpath into each item and orders the table by it.

   Q5  Show only pods labelled app=easypj.
       A:  kubectl get pods -l app=easypj
       WHY: -l is the LABEL selector — filtering on metadata.labels, the same
            mechanism Deployments and Services use to find their pods.

   Q6  Show only Running pods (field selector).
       A:  kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running
       WHY: --field-selector filters on object FIELDS server-side (here
            status.phase), distinct from label selectors.

   Q7  Get logs from a container that already crashed.
       A:  kubectl logs easypj-xyz --previous
       WHY: a CrashLoopBackOff pod's CURRENT container is a fresh restart with
            empty logs; --previous (-p) reads the LAST terminated container's
            logs, which hold the actual error.

   Q8  Open a shell inside a running easypj pod.
       A:  kubectl exec -it easypj-xyz -- /bin/sh
       WHY: -it gives an interactive TTY; everything after -- is run inside the
            container. Requires the image to ship a shell — if it doesn't, use
            kubectl debug --image=busybox instead.

   Q9  Port-forward the easypj Service to localhost:8000.
       A:  kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:80
            (or: kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-xyz 8000:8000)
       WHY: port-forward tunnels a LOCAL port to a pod/service port through the
            apiserver, letting you reach an app without an Ingress or NodePort.

   Q10 Print NAME + node + IP as custom columns.
       A:  kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=\
             NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,IP:.status.podIP
       WHY: custom-columns builds a table from arbitrary jsonpath fields —
            cleaner than -o wide when you want exactly those three values.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │   kubectl   <verb>   <resource>   <name>  <flags> │
            │      │         │          │          │       │    │
            │   binary    action     kind       target  options │
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       .vs-prose — One command, four parts, infinite power. Master the
       verb/resource/name/flags pattern and the rest of kubectl is just
       vocabulary: pick a verb, name a resource, point at a target, shape it
       with flags. Generate manifests with --dry-run, look fields up with
       explain, extract anything with jsonpath, and debug the un-shellable with
       `kubectl debug`. Fluency here is the score multiplier that carries the
       entire exam.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 7: YAML & Kubernetes Manifests                                  🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~1.5h · The language of every manifest & every
        exam answer. Get this wrong by one space and the whole task breaks.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  YAML is the lingua franca of Kubernetes. Every object you create, edit, or
  debug in the CKA exam is described in YAML. One wrong indent, one tab, one
  missing space after a colon, and a perfectly good idea becomes a broken task
  and lost points. The good news: the grammar is tiny, the structure is
  predictable, and once you internalise the 4 required fields and the
  "spaces-not-tabs" rule, YAML stops fighting you. This chapter makes YAML
  muscle-memory so you can spend exam minutes on Kubernetes, not on syntax.
  💡 INSIGHT: in the exam you almost never hand-write YAML from scratch — you
     GENERATE it imperatively (`--dry-run=client -o yaml`) and edit. But you
     MUST be able to read, fix, and validate it fast. That is what this chapter
     drills.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  ▸ Write valid YAML: key/value, lists, nested maps, multi-document files.
  ▸ Know the 4 required fields present in EVERY manifest.
  ▸ Find the right apiVersion for any object (api-resources / api-versions).
  ▸ Combine multiple resources in one file and apply whole directories.
  ▸ Validate before you apply: --dry-run=client vs server, kubectl diff.
  ▸ Understand object management: imperative vs declarative, 3-way merge, and
    server-side apply with field ownership (managedFields).

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
  🎯 EXAM: YAML is not a stand-alone domain on the syllabus — it is the
     substrate of ALL of them. Workloads, Services, Storage, RBAC,
     Scheduling: every single task is graded on the YAML you produce.
     Generating manifests fast and validating them with --dry-run=server /
     diff is one of the highest-leverage exam skills.
  🏢 DAY-2 & BEYOND: in real life YAML lives in Git (GitOps), is templated
     (Helm) or overlaid (Kustomize), and is reconciled by controllers using
     server-side apply. The same grammar scales from a one-pod demo to a
     fleet of production clusters.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
    7.1  YAML Basics for Kubernetes
    7.2  The 4 Required Fields — Every Manifest
    7.3  Finding the Right apiVersion
    7.4  Multi-Resource YAML Files
    7.5  YAML Validation and Dry Run
    7.6  Object Management & Server-Side Apply
    🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.1  YAML Basics for Kubernetes                                          🟡
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     📖 KEY TERM — YAML = "YAML Ain't Markup Language", a human-friendly data
        serialisation format. In Kubernetes it is built from just three things:
        key/value PAIRS, LISTS (each item begins with `- `), and nested MAPS
        whose hierarchy is shown by INDENTATION (2 spaces per level).

     - Indentation matters (spaces only, NO tabs!).
     - Key-value pairs, lists, nested objects.
     - A space is required after every colon: `key: value`.
     - Strings are usually unquoted; quote them only when needed.
     - Use `---` to separate multiple documents in one file.
     - Every K8s manifest has 4 required fields:
       apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec.

     [YAML SYNTAX — visual cheat sheet]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  YAML BUILDING BLOCKS                                   │
         │                                                         │
         │  1️⃣ KEY-VALUE PAIR:                                     │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                       │
         │  │ name: easypj               │  key: value            │
         │  │ replicas: 3                │  key: number           │
         │  │ debug: true                │  key: boolean          │
         │  └─────────────────────────────┘                       │
         │                                                         │
         │  2️⃣ LIST (array):                                       │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                       │
         │  │ ports:                      │  each "- " is an item │
         │  │ - 8000           ◄── item 1 │                       │
         │  │ - 8080           ◄── item 2 │                       │
         │  │ - 443            ◄── item 3 │                       │
         │  └─────────────────────────────┘                       │
         │                                                         │
         │  3️⃣ NESTED OBJECT:                                      │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                       │
         │  │ metadata:        ◄── parent │  indent = nesting     │
         │  │   name: easypj   ◄── child  │  2 spaces per level   │
         │  │   labels:        ◄── child  │                       │
         │  │     app: easypj  ◄── grandchild                     │
         │  └─────────────────────────────┘                       │
         │                                                         │
         │  ⚠️ RULES:                                              │
         │  ✅ Spaces only (2 per indent level)                   │
         │  ❌ NO tabs (YAML breaks with tabs!)                   │
         │  ✅ Colons need a space after them: key: value         │
         │  ❌ NOT key:value (missing space!)                     │
         │  ✅ Strings can be unquoted: name: easypj              │
         │  ✅ Use --- to separate multiple documents              │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     [CODE: Basic YAML syntax examples]
       # --- scalars (single values) ---
       name: easypj            # a string (unquoted is fine)
       replicas: 3             # an integer
       enabled: true           # a boolean
       ratio: 0.75             # a float
       note: "true"            # FORCED string — quotes stop it parsing as bool
       empty: null             # explicit null (also written ~ or just blank)

       # --- a list of scalars ---
       ports:
       - 8000
       - 8080
       - 443

       # --- a list of maps (most common shape in K8s) ---
       containers:
       - name: django
         image: easypj:v1
         ports:
         - containerPort: 8000

       # --- a nested map ---
       metadata:
         name: easypj
         labels:
           app: easypj
           tier: web

       # --- multi-line strings ---
       script: |                # block scalar: keeps newlines
         python manage.py migrate
         python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
       greeting: >              # folded scalar: newlines become spaces
         this becomes one
         long single line

     🧠 ANALOGY: YAML indentation is like an org chart drawn sideways. Each
        extra two spaces means "reports to the line above". Mixing tabs and
        spaces is like two managers swearing the same employee reports to them
        — the parser refuses to guess and throws.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.2  The 4 Required Fields — Every Manifest                            🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC] EVERY Kubernetes manifest, no matter the object, has
     the SAME four top-level keys:

         apiVersion  ← which API group/version describes this object?
         kind        ← what TYPE of object is this?
         metadata    ← identity: name, namespace, labels, annotations
         spec        ← the DESIRED STATE (the meat — the part you write most)

     [ANNOTATED EXAMPLE — minimal Pod, every field explained]
       apiVersion: v1            # Pod lives in the core ("") group → just "v1"
       kind: Pod                 # the object type
       metadata:                 # identity block
         name: easypj-pod        # must be unique within the namespace
         namespace: default      # optional; defaults to "default"
         labels:                 # arbitrary key/values for selecting/grouping
           app: easypj
       spec:                     # DESIRED STATE
         containers:             # a list — a Pod can hold one or more
         - name: web             # container name (unique within the Pod)
           image: easypj:v1      # which image to run
           ports:
           - containerPort: 8000 # informational; the port the app listens on

     [KUBERNETES MANIFEST STRUCTURE]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: apps/v1    ← Which API group?       │
         │  kind: Deployment       ← What type of object?   │
         │  metadata:              ← Identity (name, labels)│
         │    name: easypj                                   │
         │    namespace: default                             │
         │    labels:                                        │
         │      app: easypj                                  │
         │  spec:                  ← Desired state (THE MEAT)│
         │    replicas: 3                                    │
         │    selector:                                      │
         │      matchLabels:                                 │
         │        app: easypj                                │
         │    template:                                      │
         │      metadata:                                    │
         │        labels:                                    │
         │          app: easypj                              │
         │      spec:                                        │
         │        containers:                                │
         │        - name: django                             │
         │          image: easypj:v1                         │
         │          ports:                                   │
         │          - containerPort: 8000                    │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     🔑 MUST-REMEMBER — for any object with a Pod template (Deployment,
        ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job), the spec.selector.matchLabels
        MUST EQUAL the spec.template.metadata.labels. If they disagree, the API
        rejects the Deployment (selector is immutable and must select its own
        template). This single rule is the most common self-inflicted exam bug.

         spec.selector.matchLabels:    {app: easypj}  ── MUST ──┐
                                                        match    │
         spec.template.metadata.labels:{app: easypj} ◄──────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.3  Finding the Right apiVersion                                      🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     - kubectl api-resources → every resource: kind, short name, API group,
       namespaced? — the fastest way to discover the apiVersion.
     - kubectl api-versions → every API group/version enabled on the cluster.
     - kubectl explain <kind> → shows the apiVersion line plus the field tree.

     [TABLE: Common resources and their apiVersion]
     ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
     │ Resource         │ apiVersion                   │ Kind             │
     ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
     │ Pod              │ v1                           │ Pod              │
     │ Service          │ v1                           │ Service          │
     │ ConfigMap        │ v1                           │ ConfigMap        │
     │ Secret           │ v1                           │ Secret           │
     │ PersistentVolume │ v1                           │ PersistentVolume │
     │ ServiceAccount   │ v1                           │ ServiceAccount   │
     │ Deployment       │ apps/v1                      │ Deployment       │
     │ ReplicaSet       │ apps/v1                      │ ReplicaSet       │
     │ StatefulSet      │ apps/v1                      │ StatefulSet      │
     │ DaemonSet        │ apps/v1                      │ DaemonSet        │
     │ Job              │ batch/v1                     │ Job              │
     │ CronJob          │ batch/v1                     │ CronJob          │
     │ Ingress          │ networking.k8s.io/v1        │ Ingress          │
     │ NetworkPolicy    │ networking.k8s.io/v1        │ NetworkPolicy    │
     │ Role             │ rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1│ Role             │
     │ RoleBinding      │ rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1│ RoleBinding      │
     │ ClusterRole      │ rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1│ ClusterRole      │
     └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

     💡 INSIGHT: the rule of thumb — the OLDEST, most fundamental objects (Pod,
        Service, ConfigMap, Secret, PV) live in the CORE group and use a bare
        `v1` with no slash. Everything newer is in a NAMED group and uses
        `group/version`, e.g. `apps/v1`, `batch/v1`, `networking.k8s.io/v1`.

     ⚠️ GOTCHA — deprecated apiVersions. `extensions/v1beta1` (old home of
        Deployment, Ingress, DaemonSet, NetworkPolicy) is GONE in modern
        clusters. If a manifest fails with "no matches for kind … in version
        …", check the apiVersion first — it is almost always stale.

       # Find the apiVersion for an object you are unsure about:
       kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
       # NAME       SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION             NAMESPACED   KIND
       # ingresses  ing          networking.k8s.io/v1   true         Ingress
       kubectl explain ingress | head -2
       # KIND:     Ingress
       # VERSION:  networking.k8s.io/v1

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.4  Multi-Resource YAML Files                                          🟡
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     - Separate multiple objects in ONE file with a `---` line.
     - Apply entire directories: kubectl apply -f k8s/
     - Overlay-customise with Kustomize: kubectl apply -k overlays/prod/
       (Kustomize in depth: see Chapter 37.)

     [CODE: Combined Deployment + Service in one YAML file]
       # k8s/easypj.yaml — Deployment + Service, applied together
       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: Deployment
       metadata:
         name: easypj-web
         labels:
           app: easypj
       spec:
         replicas: 3
         selector:
           matchLabels:
             app: easypj
         template:
           metadata:
             labels:
               app: easypj          # ◄── matches selector above
           spec:
             containers:
             - name: jobpost
               image: easypj:v1
               ports:
               - containerPort: 8000
       ---                            # ◄── document separator
       apiVersion: v1
       kind: Service
       metadata:
         name: easypj-web
       spec:
         selector:
           app: easypj              # ◄── routes to Pods with app: easypj
         ports:
         - port: 80
           targetPort: 8000
         type: ClusterIP

       # apply the whole thing in one shot:
       kubectl apply -f k8s/easypj.yaml
       # or apply every manifest in a directory:
       kubectl apply -f k8s/

     🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: a file with `---` separators is a YAML "document
        stream". kubectl splits on the separators and submits each document as
        an independent API request, IN FILE ORDER. Order matters when a later
        object references an earlier one (e.g. put a Namespace or ConfigMap
        ahead of the Deployment that consumes it). An empty document (nothing
        but whitespace between two `---`) is harmless and simply skipped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.5  YAML Validation and Dry Run                                       🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
     - kubectl apply -f file.yaml --dry-run=client → validate locally (shape
       only; the object is NOT sent to the apiserver).
     - kubectl apply -f file.yaml --dry-run=server → validate against the API
       (runs schema validation, defaulting, AND admission — catches far more),
       but still does NOT persist the object.
     - kubectl diff -f file.yaml → preview EXACTLY what would change before you
       apply (shows a unified diff of live vs proposed state).

       client vs server dry-run — what each one actually does:
       ┌──────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
       │ Step             │ --dry-run=    │ --dry-run=server                 │
       │                  │ client        │                                  │
       ├──────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
       │ YAML/struct check│ ✅ yes        │ ✅ yes                           │
       │ Talks to apiserver│ ❌ no        │ ✅ yes                           │
       │ Schema validation│ partial       │ ✅ full (real OpenAPI schema)    │
       │ Defaulting       │ ❌ no         │ ✅ yes (shows server-filled vals)│
       │ Admission webhooks│ ❌ no        │ ✅ yes (policies actually run)   │
       │ Persists object? │ ❌ no         │ ❌ no                            │
       └──────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

     [TIP] Always dry-run before applying in production! And use `kubectl diff`
        to SEE the change first — it is the closest thing to a "git diff" for
        live cluster state.

       # Validate a manifest WITHOUT creating it (server-side = strongest):
       kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --dry-run=server
       # Preview the change against the live object:
       kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml
       # Generate a manifest skeleton then validate it (the exam workflow):
       kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:v1 \
         --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

     ⚡ SPEED TIP: client dry-run is instant and great for "does this YAML even
        parse?". Server dry-run is the real validator — reach for it whenever a
        cluster is available and the object is non-trivial.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  7.6  Object Management & Server-Side Apply                             🟡 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     THREE ways to manage objects — pick one per object, DON'T mix them:

       ┌───────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
       │ Style             │ Commands                     │ Use when         │
       ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
       │ Imperative cmd    │ kubectl create/run/expose/   │ fast, throwaway, │
       │                   │ scale/label/expose           │ exam speed; no   │
       │                   │                              │ file kept        │
       │ Imperative config │ kubectl create -f /          │ whole-object     │
       │                   │ replace -f                   │ from a file      │
       │ Declarative       │ kubectl apply -f / -k        │ the DEFAULT;     │
       │                   │                              │ GitOps, prod     │
       └───────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

     HOW `apply` KNOWS WHAT CHANGED — the client-side 3-WAY MERGE
     ------------------------------------------------------------
     `kubectl apply` reconciles THREE versions of the object:
       (1) the last-applied-configuration annotation
           (kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration) — what you applied
           last time,
       (2) the LIVE object on the server,
       (3) your NEW file.
     From these it computes a patch that:
       ▸ SETS the fields you set,
       ▸ CLEARS the fields you REMOVED since last time, and
       ▸ LEAVES fields ANOTHER actor wrote (e.g. a replica count set by
         `kubectl scale`, or a status field set by a controller).

         ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
         │ last-applied │   │  LIVE object │   │  your NEW    │
         │  annotation  │   │  on server   │   │  file        │
         └──────┬───────┘   └──────┬───────┘   └──────┬───────┘
                └─────────┬────────┴────────┬─────────┘
                          ▼ 3-WAY MERGE ▼
                ┌────────────────────────────────┐
                │ patch: set yours · clear removed│
                │       · keep others' fields     │
                └────────────────────────────────┘

     SERVER-SIDE APPLY  (kubectl apply --server-side)
     ------------------------------------------------
     The APISERVER does the merge (not the client) and records FIELD OWNERSHIP
     in metadata.managedFields. Each manager (you, a controller, a GitOps
     agent) "owns" the fields it writes. If two managers try to write the SAME
     field with different values → a CONFLICT, which you resolve explicitly
     with --force-conflicts (taking ownership). Preferred for controllers,
     GitOps, and any object with several writers — there is no hidden
     last-applied annotation, so the truth lives on the server.

     📖 KEY TERM — managedFields: the server-side record of WHICH manager owns
        each field of an object, so multiple actors can co-own one object
        without silently clobbering each other.

     ⚠️ GOTCHA: Don't `kubectl edit` or `kubectl scale` an object you ALSO
        manage with `apply`. Because client-side apply diffs against the
        last-applied annotation (which your imperative edit did not update), the
        NEXT `apply` may quietly REVERT your imperative change. Either go
        all-declarative, or move to server-side apply where ownership is
        tracked.

     🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which management style?
        ▸ One-off / exam time pressure ............ imperative cmd (+ -o yaml to
          capture it).
        ▸ Hand-maintained manifests in Git ........ declarative `apply -f`.
        ▸ Several writers / controllers / GitOps .. server-side apply.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 7
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [EVERY MANIFEST = 4 REQUIRED FIELDS]
   apiVersion: apps/v1     ◄ which API group/version? (api-resources to find)
   kind: Deployment        ◄ what TYPE of object?
   metadata:               ◄ identity: name, namespace, labels
     name: easypj-web
   spec:                   ◄ DESIRED STATE (the meat)
     selector.matchLabels:   {app: easypj}  ── MUST match ──┐
     template.metadata.labels:{app: easypj} ◄───────────────┘
     template.spec.containers:[{name, image: easypj:v1, ports}]
   ⚠️ spaces not tabs · a space after every colon · selector == template labels.
   ✅ validate: kubectl apply -f x.yaml --dry-run=server  ·  kubectl diff -f x.yaml

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UTH — HOW THE APISERVER VALIDATES A MANIFEST
     When you POST a manifest, the apiserver runs a fixed pipeline:
       1. DECODE — parse YAML/JSON into an internal object for the kind+version.
       2. SCHEMA VALIDATION — check fields against the OpenAPI/structural schema
          (unknown or mistyped fields are rejected).
       3. DEFAULTING — fill in omitted fields with their defaults (e.g. a
          Service's clusterIP, a Deployment's strategy).
       4. ADMISSION — run mutating then validating admission controllers and
          webhooks (quotas, PodSecurity, policy engines like Kyverno/OPA).
       5. PERSIST — write the final object to etcd.
     This is exactly WHY `--dry-run=server` catches more than `--dry-run=client`:
     client-side stops at step 1's local shape check, while server-side runs
     steps 1–4 (decode, schema, defaulting, admission) and only skips the final
     persist. A manifest that passes client dry-run can still be rejected by a
     webhook the client never sees.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
     ▸ MULTI-DOC STREAMS: `---` splits one file into independent documents
       submitted in order; a blank doc is skipped. Useful for shipping a
       Namespace + ConfigMap + Deployment + Service as one unit.
     ▸ ANCHORS & ALIASES: `&name` defines, `*name` reuses, `<<: *name` merges a
       map — handy in hand-written YAML to avoid repetition. (kubectl resolves
       them client-side; the server never sees the anchor.)
         defaults: &res {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}
         resources:
           requests: *res
     ▸ PATCH STRATEGIES: strategic-merge patch (Kubernetes-aware, merges list
       items by key like container name) vs JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386,
       whole-field replace) vs JSON Patch / RFC 6902 (ordered op list:
       add/replace/remove by path). `kubectl patch --type=` selects which.
     ▸ NULL / EMPTY PITFALLS: `null`, `~`, and an empty value all mean null;
       `field: ""` is an empty STRING, not null — they behave differently in
       merges (null can DELETE a field, empty string sets it to "").
     ▸ PRUNING & DEFAULTING: declarative apply with `--prune` deletes objects
       that vanished from your config set — powerful and dangerous; scope it
       with a label selector. Server defaulting means the live object will have
       MORE fields than your file — don't be surprised by `diff` output.
     ▸ OFFLINE VALIDATION: tools like `kubeconform` and `kubectl-validate`
       check manifests against published CRD/OpenAPI schemas in CI, without a
       live cluster — great for GitOps pre-merge checks.
     ▸ managedFields: inspect with `kubectl get <obj> -o yaml
       --show-managed-fields` to see exactly which manager owns which field
       under server-side apply.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 Every manifest has 4 required top-level fields: apiVersion, kind,
     metadata, spec.
  🔑 Spaces, never tabs; one space after every colon; 2 spaces per indent level.
  🔑 selector.matchLabels MUST equal template.metadata.labels for any
     Pod-template object — mismatch = rejected Deployment / empty Service.
  🔑 Core, fundamental objects use bare `v1`; newer objects use `group/version`
     (apps/v1, batch/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1, rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1).
  🔑 Don't hand-write — GENERATE with `--dry-run=client -o yaml`, then edit and
     validate with `--dry-run=server` and `kubectl diff`.
  🔑 Find any apiVersion with `kubectl api-resources` (and `kubectl explain`).
  🔑 Separate multiple objects in one file with `---`; apply whole directories
     with `-f k8s/`; overlay with Kustomize (`-k`).
  🔑 `apply` reconciles via a 3-way merge; server-side apply tracks ownership
     in managedFields. Pick ONE management style per object.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ TABS anywhere — YAML refuses to parse. Configure your editor to insert
     spaces.
  ⚠️ Missing space after a colon (`key:value`) — parsed as one bare string,
     not a key/value pair.
  ⚠️ selector ≠ template labels — the API rejects the Deployment outright.
  ⚠️ A LABEL TYPO on a Service selector vs Pod labels — the Service has NO
     endpoints and silently routes nowhere (see Lab Q8).
  ⚠️ Deprecated apiVersion (extensions/v1beta1 is gone) — "no matches for kind".
  ⚠️ Unquoted "yes"/"no"/"on"/"off" become booleans; unquoted version numbers
     like 1.10 may parse as floats. Quote them when you mean a string.
  ⚠️ "expected map, got list" (and vice versa) — usually a missing or extra
     `- ` or a wrong indent level (see Lab Q9).
  ⚠️ Mixing imperative edits (`kubectl edit`/`scale`) with `apply` — the next
     apply can silently revert your change.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ Never hand-write a manifest. Set up the generate alias and edit the output:
       alias do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'
       kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml
  ⚡ `kubectl diff -f x.yaml` BEFORE every `apply` — see the change first.
  ⚡ `kubectl explain <kind>.<field> --recursive` to discover unfamiliar fields
     without leaving the terminal (e.g. `kubectl explain deploy.spec.template`).
  ⚡ `kubectl apply -f x.yaml --dry-run=server` is your strongest validator —
     it runs admission, not just a shape check.
  ⚡ `kubectl api-resources | grep -i <thing>` to find an apiVersion in seconds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  kubectl api-resources                         # all kinds: group, short name
  kubectl api-versions                          # all enabled group/versions
  kubectl explain <kind>[.field] [--recursive]  # apiVersion + field tree
  kubectl create <obj> ... --dry-run=client -o yaml > f.yaml   # GENERATE
  kubectl apply -f f.yaml                        # declarative create/update
  kubectl apply -f k8s/                          # apply a whole directory
  kubectl apply -k overlays/prod/                # apply a Kustomize overlay
  kubectl apply -f f.yaml --dry-run=client       # local shape validation
  kubectl apply -f f.yaml --dry-run=server       # full apiserver validation
  kubectl diff -f f.yaml                          # preview change vs live
  kubectl apply -f f.yaml --server-side          # server-side apply (ownership)
  kubectl apply -f f.yaml --server-side --force-conflicts  # take ownership
  kubectl create -f f.yaml / kubectl replace -f f.yaml      # imperative config

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 7  (work the answer, THEN read the explanation)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 Q1. A manifest uses a tab for indentation (and one bad indent level). Fix
         it so it applies.
     ANSWER: Replace every tab with spaces and align to 2-space levels. Confirm
       with `kubectl apply -f m.yaml --dry-run=server`. Quick detection:
       `cat -A m.yaml | grep '\^I'` shows tabs as `^I`.
     WHY: YAML forbids tabs entirely; the parser cannot infer intended depth, so
       it errors before Kubernetes ever sees the object.

  🧪 Q2. A Deployment manifest is missing a required field. Add it.
     ANSWER: Ensure all four are present — apiVersion (apps/v1), kind
       (Deployment), metadata (with a name), spec. The most commonly missing one
       is `apiVersion` or a `metadata.name`. Validate with `--dry-run=server`.
     WHY: The apiserver rejects any object lacking one of the four required
       top-level fields; the error names the missing field.

  🧪 Q3. Find the apiVersion you need for an Ingress (by command).
     ANSWER: `kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress` → networking.k8s.io/v1,
       or `kubectl explain ingress | head -2` → VERSION: networking.k8s.io/v1.
     WHY: api-resources / explain read the live cluster's schema, so you get the
       version THIS cluster actually serves — not a guess that may be deprecated.

  🧪 Q4. Convert `kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:v1` into a YAML
         manifest (don't create the object yet).
     ANSWER: kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:v1 \
               --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
     WHY: `--dry-run=client` builds the object locally without sending it, and
       `-o yaml` prints it — the canonical exam way to get a correct skeleton
       fast, then edit it.

  🧪 Q5. Put a Deployment AND a Service in one file and apply both.
     ANSWER: Write both objects in one file separated by a `---` line (see the
       k8s/easypj.yaml example in 7.4), then `kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml`.
     WHY: `---` makes a YAML document stream; kubectl submits each document
       independently, in file order, in a single command.

  🧪 Q6. Validate a manifest against the apiserver WITHOUT creating the object.
     ANSWER: `kubectl apply -f m.yaml --dry-run=server`.
     WHY: Server dry-run runs schema validation, defaulting, and admission on
       the real apiserver but skips the final persist — the strongest check
       short of actually creating it.

  🧪 Q7. Preview EXACTLY what `apply` would change on a live object.
     ANSWER: `kubectl diff -f m.yaml` — prints a unified diff of live vs
       proposed state (exit code 1 means there ARE differences).
     WHY: It lets you see additions/removals/changes before committing them,
       like a `git diff` for cluster state.

  🧪 Q8. A Service has no endpoints even though Pods are Running. The Service
         selector is `app: easypj` but the Pods are labelled `app: easjpj`
         (typo). Why, and how do you fix it?
     ANSWER: The selector matches NO Pods, so no endpoints are created. Fix the
       typo on whichever side is wrong (make Pod labels and Service selector
       identical), e.g. relabel the Pods or correct the Service. Verify with
       `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`.
     WHY: Services route to Pods PURELY by label match. A one-character
       mismatch means an empty Endpoints object and traffic that goes nowhere —
       no error is raised, which is what makes it sneaky.

  🧪 Q9. Applying a manifest fails with "expected map, got list" (or "got
         string, want map"). Fix it.
     ANSWER: A field's SHAPE is wrong. Example — `containers:` must be a LIST of
       maps:
         containers:
         - name: web
           image: easypj:v1
       not a bare map (`containers:` then `name:` with no `- `). Add/remove the
       `- ` and correct the indent so the value type matches the schema.
     WHY: Each field has an expected type; a missing `- ` turns a list into a
       map (or vice versa), and the structural schema rejects the mismatch.

  🧪 Q10. Force the string "true" and a numeric-looking port to be treated as
          strings. Why might you care?
     ANSWER: Quote them: `note: "true"`, `port: "8080"` (e.g. when a field or a
       ConfigMap value must be a string). ConfigMap `data:` values, for
       instance, must all be strings.
     WHY: Unquoted `true` parses as a BOOLEAN and unquoted `8080` as an INTEGER.
       If the field expects a string (ConfigMap data, certain env values), the
       wrong type causes a validation error or surprising behaviour downstream.

  🧪 DRILL: Take a working manifest, break ONE indent level, run
     `kubectl apply -f m.yaml --dry-run=server`, read the exact error, fix it,
     re-validate. Repeat until reading-the-error-then-fixing is reflexive — that
     loop IS the exam skill.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 7
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        THE MANIFEST SKELETON, COLOUR-CODED BY THE 4 REQUIRED FIELDS
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ [1] apiVersion: apps/v1   ← GROUP/VERSION (api-resources) │
        │ [2] kind: Deployment      ← OBJECT TYPE                   │
        │ [3] metadata:             ← IDENTITY                      │
        │       name: easypj-web                                    │
        │       labels: {app: easypj}                               │
        │ [4] spec:                 ← DESIRED STATE (the meat)      │
        │       replicas: 3                                         │
        │       selector.matchLabels: {app: easypj} ──┐ MUST       │
        │       template.metadata.labels:{app: easypj}◄┘ match     │
        │       template.spec.containers:                          │
        │         - {name: jobpost, image: easypj:v1, port: 8000}  │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          spaces not tabs · space after every colon · selector==labels
          generate → edit → diff → apply --dry-run=server → apply

  VISUAL SUMMARY (prose): A Kubernetes manifest is always four blocks stacked in
  the same order — apiVersion (which API group/version, found via
  `kubectl api-resources`), kind (the object type), metadata (identity: name,
  namespace, labels), and spec (the desired state, where most of your editing
  happens). For any object that carries a Pod template, the selector's
  matchLabels must exactly equal the template's labels, or the object is
  rejected. Write YAML with spaces (never tabs) and a space after every colon.
  In practice you don't author manifests by hand: you GENERATE them with
  `--dry-run=client -o yaml`, EDIT, preview with `kubectl diff`, VALIDATE with
  `--dry-run=server`, and finally APPLY. Manage each object with one consistent
  style — imperative for throwaways, declarative `apply` for Git-tracked
  manifests, and server-side apply (with managedFields ownership) when several
  actors share one object.

================================================================================
  Chapter 8: Deploying easypj — Your First Kubernetes Application      🟡 🧪
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · The payoff: a real app on a real cluster.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  This is where Parts 1-2 fuse into a running system you can SEE. Everything you
  have learned — Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, kubectl, YAML
  — comes together to put easypj (a real Django job-posting platform) onto a real
  cluster. By the end of this chapter you will have taken raw application code,
  wrapped it in declarative manifests, and watched the Kubernetes control plane
  bring it to life. This is the single most motivating moment of the whole guide:
  the abstract becomes concrete.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  - Deploy easypj step-by-step from an empty namespace to a reachable web page.
  - Inject non-secret config via a ConfigMap and sensitive config via a Secret.
  - Expose the Deployment with a ClusterIP Service.
  - Access the running app via kubectl port-forward.
  - Verify the deployment, then EXPLAIN exactly what Kubernetes did with your YAML.
  - Understand the full ConfigMap & Secret picture (consumption, live updates,
    limits, types) — a heavily examined topic.

  CKA RELEVANCE  🎯
  ----------------
  kubectl mastery is essential for EVERY single exam question. The deploy
  pipeline in this chapter (namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment →
  Service → access → verify) is the exact muscle memory the exam tests under
  time pressure. ConfigMaps & Secrets (Section 8.10) map directly to the
  "Workloads & Scheduling" domain. Speed = passing.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
    8.1   The easypj Application Overview
    8.2   Step 1 — Create the Namespace
    8.3   Step 2 — Create the ConfigMap
    8.4   Step 3 — Create the Secret
    8.5   Step 4 — Create the Deployment
    8.6   Step 5 — Create the Service
    8.7   Step 6 — Access Your Application
    8.8   Step 7 — Verify Everything
    8.9   What Just Happened? — Full Walkthrough
    8.10  ConfigMaps & Secrets — The Full Picture  🎯
    🔧 Under-the-Hood / DEEPER
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A


  ── 8.1  The easypj Application Overview ─────────────────────────────────  🟡

     We are deploying the Django WEB tier of easypj now; the PostgreSQL database
     tier arrives later (Part 6). For this chapter, easypj talks to a database
     placeholder (DB_HOST: easypj-db) but the focus is getting the web app live.

         📖 The easypj stack
         - Django PROJECT: easypj (the job-posting platform)
         - Django APP:     jobpost
         - Models:         Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, auth.User
         - Stack:          Python 3.13, Django 5.2.5, Docker, SQLite (dev)
                           → PostgreSQL (Kubernetes)
         - What we deploy: Django web app (this chapter) + PostgreSQL (Part 6)

     The deployment order — and it is the SAME order on the exam — is:
         Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service → reachable on /jobs/.

         [EASYPJ IN KUBERNETES — target architecture]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  NAMESPACE: easypj-dev                                │
         │                                                       │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
         │  │ Deployment: easypj-web (1 replica)            │     │
         │  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐         │     │
         │  │ │ 📦 Pod: easypj-django             │         │     │
         │  │ │ Image: easypj:v1                  │         │     │
         │  │ │ Port: 8000                        │         │     │
         │  │ │ Env: from ConfigMap + Secret      │         │     │
         │  │ └──────────────────────────────────┘         │     │
         │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
         │                    │                                   │
         │  ┌────────────────▼────────────────┐                 │
         │  │ Service: easypj-web (ClusterIP)  │                 │
         │  │ Port: 80 → targetPort: 8000      │                 │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────┘                 │
         │                                                       │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐                 │
         │  │ ConfigMap: easypj-config          │                 │
         │  │ DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE            │                 │
         │  │ ALLOWED_HOSTS · DEBUG · DB_HOST   │                 │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────┘                 │
         │                                                       │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐                 │
         │  │ Secret: easypj-secret             │                 │
         │  │ SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD            │                 │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────┘                 │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     .vs-prose — Reading the diagram: the easypj-dev namespace is a logical box
     that holds the entire app. Inside it, a Deployment manages one replica Pod
     running the easypj:v1 image on port 8000. The Pod's environment is filled
     from two objects — a ConfigMap (non-secret settings) and a Secret (sensitive
     settings). A ClusterIP Service named easypj-web sits in front of the Pod,
     accepting traffic on port 80 and forwarding it to the Pod's targetPort 8000.
     Nothing is exposed outside the cluster yet; we reach it with port-forward.


  ── 8.2  Step 1 — Create the Namespace ───────────────────────────────────  🟡

     A namespace is the logical container that scopes every other object we make.

         $ kubectl create namespace easypj-dev

     Or the equivalent declarative manifest (namespace.yaml):

         apiVersion: v1
         kind: Namespace
         metadata:
           name: easypj-dev

         $ kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml

     From here on, EVERY object sets `namespace: easypj-dev` (or you pass
     `-n easypj-dev`). Forgetting the namespace is the #1 reason objects "vanish."


  ── 8.3  Step 2 — Create the ConfigMap ───────────────────────────────────  🟡

     The ConfigMap holds NON-secret configuration — settings that are safe to read
     in plaintext and commit to git.

         apiVersion: v1
         kind: ConfigMap
         metadata:
           name: easypj-config
           namespace: easypj-dev
         data:
           DEBUG: "False"
           ALLOWED_HOSTS: "*"
           DB_HOST: "easypj-db"
           DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"

         $ kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
         $ kubectl get cm easypj-config -n easypj-dev -o yaml

     💡 INSIGHT: Keep ALL knobs an operator might tune (host names, feature flags,
        log levels) in the ConfigMap. Anything you would be embarrassed to print
        in a log belongs in the Secret instead (next step).


  ── 8.4  Step 3 — Create the Secret ──────────────────────────────────────  🟡

     The Secret holds SENSITIVE configuration. We use `stringData` so we can type
     plaintext and let Kubernetes base64-encode it for us at rest.

         apiVersion: v1
         kind: Secret
         metadata:
           name: easypj-secret
           namespace: easypj-dev
         type: Opaque
         stringData:                  # plaintext in → base64 at rest
           SECRET_KEY: "change-me-in-prod"
           DB_PASSWORD: "supersecret"

         $ kubectl apply -f secret.yaml

     If you instead use the `data:` field you must supply already-base64 values:

         $ echo -n 'supersecret' | base64        # → c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQ=

         data:
           DB_PASSWORD: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQ=

     ⚠️ WARNING — Never commit real Secrets to git! base64 is ENCODING, not
        encryption. Anyone can `base64 -d` it. Protect Secrets with encryption-at-
        rest (etcd) plus RBAC; keep manifests out of version control or use a
        sealed-secrets / external-secrets workflow.


  ── 8.5  Step 4 — Create the Deployment ──────────────────────────────────  🟡

     The Deployment is the heart of the chapter: it declares the desired state of
     the easypj web tier — image, replica count, env injection, resources, probes.

         apiVersion: apps/v1
         kind: Deployment
         metadata:
           name: easypj-web
           namespace: easypj-dev
         spec:
           replicas: 1                         # dev environment — single replica
           selector:
             matchLabels:
               app: easypj
               tier: web
           template:
             metadata:
               labels:
                 app: easypj
                 tier: web
             spec:
               containers:
               - name: web
                 image: easypj:v1
                 ports:
                 - containerPort: 8000
                 envFrom:                       # inject ALL keys as env vars
                 - configMapRef:
                     name: easypj-config
                 - secretRef:
                     name: easypj-secret
                 resources:
                   requests:
                     cpu: 100m
                     memory: 128Mi
                   limits:
                     cpu: 500m
                     memory: 256Mi
                 readinessProbe:                # gate traffic until /jobs/ is up
                   httpGet:
                     path: /jobs/
                     port: 8000
                 livenessProbe:                 # restart if the app wedges
                   httpGet:
                     path: /jobs/
                     port: 8000
                   initialDelaySeconds: 10

         $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

     Annotated highlights:
       - Image: easypj:v1 — must be built AND available to the cluster (loaded
         into Minikube/Kind, or pushed to a registry the nodes can reach).
       - Replicas: 1 — fine for dev; scale up in production.
       - envFrom pulls EVERY key from the ConfigMap and the Secret into the
         container's environment in one shot.
       - Resource requests/limits let the scheduler place the Pod and protect the
         node from a runaway container.
       - The readiness probe means the Service only sends traffic once /jobs/
         answers; the liveness probe restarts a hung container.

     🧭 DECISION GUIDE — env vs envFrom: use `envFrom` to bulk-import a whole
        ConfigMap/Secret; use an individual `env:` entry with `configMapKeyRef`/
        `secretKeyRef` when you only need ONE key or need to RENAME it.


  ── 8.6  Step 5 — Create the Service ─────────────────────────────────────  🟡

     The Service gives the Pod a stable virtual IP and load-balances across
     replicas. ClusterIP is the default and is internal-only.

         apiVersion: v1
         kind: Service
         metadata:
           name: easypj-web
           namespace: easypj-dev
         spec:
           selector:                          # MUST match the pod template labels
             app: easypj
             tier: web
           ports:
           - port: 80                         # the Service's port
             targetPort: 8000                 # the container's port
           # type: ClusterIP is the default and may be omitted

         $ kubectl apply -f service.yaml
         $ kubectl get svc -n easypj-dev
         $ kubectl get svc,ep -n easypj-dev     # endpoints should list pod IPs

     🔑 The Service `selector` MUST match the Pod template `labels`. If they
        differ, the Service has ZERO endpoints and silently drops traffic. Always
        verify with `kubectl get endpoints`.


  ── 8.7  Step 6 — Access Your Application ────────────────────────────────  🟡

     ClusterIP is internal, so we tunnel from the laptop with port-forward:

         $ kubectl -n easypj-dev port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80
         → Open browser: http://localhost:8000/jobs/   ✅

         [SCREENSHOT: easypj running in Kubernetes!]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  🌐  http://localhost:8000/jobs/              │
         │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
         │ │   easypj — Job Board                      │ │
         │ │   ─────────────────────────────────────   │ │
         │ │   [ Senior K8s Engineer  · Remote ]       │ │
         │ │   [ Django Developer     · Berlin ]       │ │

         │  Served by Pod easypj-web in namespace        │
         │  easypj-dev — running in Kubernetes! 🎉       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     💡 port-forward is a DEBUG/dev tool — it tunnels from your machine straight
        to the Service. For real external access you would use a NodePort,
        LoadBalancer, or Ingress (covered later).
