  ── 8.9  What Just Happened? — Full Walkthrough ──────────────────────────  🟡

     You wrote a few lines of YAML; the control plane did the rest. Here is the
     end-to-end flow of what Kubernetes did with your manifests:

         [END-TO-END DEPLOYMENT FLOW — what K8s did with your YAML]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                          │
         │  YOU:  $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml                │
         │        $ kubectl apply -f service.yaml                   │
         │             │                                            │
         │   ┌─────────▼──────────┐                                │
         │   │  1. API SERVER      │  Receives YAML, validates,     │
         │   │     stores in etcd  │  authenticates, authorizes     │
         │   └─────────┬──────────┘                                │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │   ┌────────────────────┐                                │
         │   │  2. CONTROLLER MGR  │  Sees new Deployment →         │
         │   │     creates objects │  creates ReplicaSet →          │
         │   │                     │  creates Pod objects            │
         │   └─────────┬──────────┘                                │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │   ┌────────────────────┐                                │
         │   │  3. SCHEDULER       │  Sees unassigned Pod →         │
         │   │     assigns node   │  evaluates nodes →             │
         │   │                     │  assigns best worker            │
         │   └─────────┬──────────┘                                │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │   ┌────────────────────┐                                │
         │   │  4. KUBELET         │  Sees Pod assigned to its     │
         │   │     (on worker)    │  node → pulls image →          │
         │   │                     │  starts container via         │
         │   │                     │  containerd                    │
         │   └─────────┬──────────┘                                │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │   ┌────────────────────┐                                │
         │   │  5. KUBE-PROXY      │  Updates iptables rules →     │
         │   │     (all nodes)    │  Service ClusterIP now         │
         │   │                     │  routes to new Pod             │
         │   └─────────┬──────────┘                                │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │   ┌────────────────────┐                                │
         │   │  6. PORT-FORWARD    │  You: port-forward 8000:80    │
         │   │     (your laptop)  │  Browser: http://localhost:8000│
         │   └────────────────────┘  easypj is LIVE! 🎉            │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - You applied YAML → API server stored in etcd
         - Controller created ReplicaSet → created Pod
         - Scheduler placed Pod on a node
         - kubelet pulled image and started container
         - Service created endpoints pointing to the Pod
         - port-forward tunneled traffic to the Service

     Condensed one-liner (memorize this chain):
       apply ─►📡 apiserver ─►🗄️ etcd ─►🔄 ctrl-mgr (RS→Pod) ─►📋 scheduler ─►
       🤖 kubelet (pull + run) ─►🌐 kube-proxy (route) ─► 🎉 easypj LIVE

     .vs-prose — The whole system is a feedback loop of controllers watching etcd.
     You never tell Kubernetes HOW to run the app, only WHAT you want. The
     apiserver records your intent in etcd; the controller manager notices a
     Deployment with no ReplicaSet and creates one, which notices it has no Pod and
     creates one; the scheduler notices an unbound Pod and binds it to a node; the
     kubelet on that node notices a Pod assigned to it and pulls the image and runs
     the container; kube-proxy notices a new endpoint and programs iptables so the
     Service IP routes to it. Each step is independent and self-healing.


  ── 8.10  ConfigMaps & Secrets — The Full Picture ───────────────────────  🟡 🎯

     You used both objects above; here is the complete examinable picture.

     CONSUMPTION — four ways to feed a ConfigMap/Secret into a container:
       1. env (single key)  — `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` / `secretKeyRef`;
          pick ONE key, optionally rename it.
       2. envFrom (all keys) — every key becomes an env var (what we used).
       3. VOLUME mount       — each key becomes a FILE in a mounted directory.
       4. command/args       — reference the injected env vars on the cmdline.

         [CONSUMPTION MODES — ConfigMap / Secret → container]
         ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
         │ Mode         │ How                   │ Live update?           │
         ├──────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
         │ env (1 key)  │ configMapKeyRef /     │ NO — fixed at start    │
         │              │ secretKeyRef          │ (restart pod)          │
         │ envFrom (all)│ configMapRef /        │ NO — fixed at start    │
         │              │ secretRef             │ (restart pod)          │
         │ volume mount │ volumes + volumeMounts│ YES — auto-syncs       │
         │              │                       │ (≈ kubelet period)     │
         │ subPath mount│ volumeMounts.subPath  │ NO — no live update    │
         └──────────────┴───────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

     LIVE UPDATES: env vars are FIXED at container start — changing the source
       requires a pod restart. A VOLUME-mounted ConfigMap/Secret updates
       automatically (within ≈ the kubelet sync period). BUT a `subPath` mount
       does NOT receive updates — it is a one-time copy.

     LIMITS: each ConfigMap/Secret is ≤ 1 MiB. Both support `immutable: true`
       (v1.19+), which blocks edits and cuts apiserver/etcd watch load.

     SECRETS specifics:
       - base64 is ENCODING, not encryption — Secrets sit UNENCRYPTED in etcd by
         default → protect with encryption-at-rest + RBAC.
       - `data` (base64 values you supply) vs `stringData` (plaintext in, encoded
         for you).
       - Built-in TYPES:
           Opaque · kubernetes.io/service-account-token ·
           kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson · kubernetes.io/basic-auth ·
           kubernetes.io/ssh-auth · kubernetes.io/tls ·
           bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token

     📖 KEY TERM — immutable ConfigMap/Secret: marked `immutable: true` so it can
        only be deleted+recreated, never edited — safer and lighter on the
        control plane (the kubelet stops watching it for changes).

     🧠 ANALOGY: env-injected config is printed in the startup banner (fixed for
        the life of the process); a mounted volume is a live noticeboard (it
        updates while the app keeps running).


  ── 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER ──────────────────────────────────────────  🔧

     🔧 UTH — How injection actually works:
       - `envFrom` is resolved by the kubelet at container START. The kubelet
         reads the named ConfigMap/Secret from the apiserver, turns each key into
         an environment variable, and hands them to the container runtime. That is
         why an env-injected value is frozen until the next restart.
       - Readiness gating: when the readiness probe passes, the kubelet marks the
         Pod Ready; the endpoints controller then ADDS the Pod IP to the Service's
         EndpointSlice. kube-proxy programs that endpoint into iptables/IPVS. A
         not-Ready Pod is REMOVED from endpoints, so the Service never routes to it.

     🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
       - initContainers for DB migrations: run `python manage.py migrate` in an
         initContainer so the schema is ready BEFORE the web container starts.
       - Readiness-gated rolling updates: combine readinessProbe + `maxSurge`/
         `maxUnavailable` so new Pods only take traffic after they are healthy.
       - env-over-envFrom precedence: an explicit `env:` entry OVERRIDES the same
         key coming from `envFrom`.
       - The Downward API: inject Pod metadata (name, namespace, node, labels,
         resource limits) as env vars or files without a ConfigMap.
       - `minReadySeconds`: make a Pod wait N seconds after Ready before counting
         as available — smooths out flapping rollouts.
       - Recreate vs RollingUpdate for schema migrations: use the `Recreate`
         strategy when old and new code cannot share a database schema at once.

  ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 8
  ----------------------
    ⚠️ Image not built/pushed (or not loaded into Minikube/Kind) → ImagePullBackOff.
    ⚠️ targetPort ≠ containerPort → traffic goes nowhere; they must line up.
    ⚠️ Secret `data` values not base64-encoded → apply error; use `stringData`.
    ⚠️ Service selector ≠ Pod labels → empty endpoints, silent traffic drop.
    ⚠️ Forgetting `-n easypj-dev` → objects "disappear" (they're in `default`).
    ⚠️ env-injected config is frozen at start — editing the ConfigMap does NOT
       update a running Pod's env vars; you must restart the Pod.
    ⚠️ A `subPath` volume mount does NOT receive ConfigMap/Secret live updates.
    ⚠️ Each ConfigMap/Secret is capped at 1 MiB.


  ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 8
  ------------------------
    ⚡ Scaffold the Deployment imperatively, then tweak the YAML:
         kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev $do > dep.yaml
       (where `$do` = `--dry-run=client -o yaml`).
    ⚡ Make the Service in one line: `kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 \
         --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev`.
    ⚡ Create config/secrets imperatively:
         kubectl create cm easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False -n easypj-dev
         kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=x -n easypj-dev
    ⚡ Always verify endpoints first when a Service "doesn't work": `kubectl get ep`.
    ⚡ Restart a Deployment to pick up new env config: `kubectl rollout restart \
         deploy/easypj-web -n easypj-dev`.
    ⚡ Set your namespace once: `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev`.

  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 8  (union of both editions; full answers)
  --------------------------------------------------------------

    Q1. Create a namespace + Deployment + Service for easypj (imperative).
        A:
          kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
          kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev
          kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev
        WHY: `create deploy` builds the ReplicaSet + Pod; `expose` builds a
        ClusterIP Service whose selector auto-matches the Deployment's labels.

    Q2. Inject DB_HOST into the Pod from a ConfigMap (single key).
        A: add to the container spec:
          env:
          - name: DB_HOST
            valueFrom:
              configMapKeyRef:
                name: easypj-config
                key: DB_HOST
        WHY: configMapKeyRef pulls ONE key; use this when you don't want all keys.

    Q3. Expose SECRET_KEY from a Secret as an env var.
        A:
          env:
          - name: SECRET_KEY
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: easypj-secret
                key: SECRET_KEY
        WHY: secretKeyRef is the Secret analogue of configMapKeyRef; the value is
        decoded from base64 before it reaches the container.

    Q4. The Pod is ImagePullBackOff — diagnose and fix.
        A: `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj-dev` → read the Events; you'll see
        "Failed to pull image easypj:v1". Fixes: build the image and load it into
        the cluster (`minikube image load easypj:v1` or `kind load docker-image
        easypj:v1`), or push it to a reachable registry and fix the image
        reference / imagePullSecrets.
        WHY: the kubelet can't find/pull the image; the Events list names the cause.

    Q5. Port-forward the Service and hit /jobs/.
        A:
          kubectl -n easypj-dev port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80
          # then: curl http://localhost:8000/jobs/   (or open in a browser)
        WHY: ClusterIP is internal; port-forward tunnels localhost → Service.

    Q6. Scale easypj-web to 3 replicas (command).
        A: kubectl scale deploy easypj-web --replicas=3 -n easypj-dev
        WHY: the Deployment controller creates 2 more Pods; the Service load-
        balances across all Ready endpoints automatically.

    Q7. Add a readiness probe so traffic flows only when /jobs/ is up.
        A: in the container spec:
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /jobs/
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
        WHY: the Pod is added to Service endpoints only after the probe passes, so
        no request hits the app before it's ready.

    Q8. Confirm the Service has endpoints; what if it doesn't?
        A: kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj-dev
        If empty: the Service `selector` doesn't match the Pod `labels`, or no Pod
        is Ready. Compare `kubectl get svc easypj-web -o yaml` (spec.selector) with
        `kubectl get pods --show-labels`; fix the mismatch or the readiness probe.
        WHY: endpoints are the Pods a Service routes to; empty = broken routing.

    Q9. Roll the image to easypj:v2 and watch the rollout.
        A:
          kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web web=easypj:v2 -n easypj-dev
          kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n easypj-dev
          # roll back if needed:
          kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web -n easypj-dev
        WHY: a RollingUpdate spins up new Pods and waits for readiness before
        retiring old ones; `rollout status` blocks until it completes.

    Q10. A Pod is Pending — which command shows why, and where do you look?
        A: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj-dev → read the Events at the
        bottom. Pending usually means the SCHEDULER couldn't place it: insufficient
        CPU/memory, an unsatisfiable nodeSelector/affinity, or a taint with no
        toleration. `kubectl get events -n easypj-dev --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`
        gives the same story chronologically.
        WHY: Pending = unscheduled; the Events explain the scheduler's reasoning.

    🧪 DRILL: deploy easypj end-to-end (ns → cm → secret → deployment → service →
       port-forward → /jobs/ returns 200) from scratch in UNDER 10 MINUTES.

  [VISUAL SUMMARY] easypj-dev is running: a single easypj-web Pod (image
  easypj:v1) fed by easypj-config + easypj-secret, fronted by a ClusterIP Service
  on 80→8000, reachable from your laptop via port-forward at /jobs/. Traffic path:
  laptop → port-forward → Service (ClusterIP 80) → endpoint (Pod IP:8000) → Django.
  .vs-prose — In one sentence: you turned a few declarative YAML files into a
  live, self-healing web application, and you can trace every request from your
  browser, through the Service's iptables rule, into the running container.

  ║     kubectl config use-context <ctx>                                     ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  [PART 2 VISUAL SUMMARY]: the full deploy pipeline, easypj edition — from
  Dockerfile and image, through Namespace/ConfigMap/Secret/Deployment/Service
  manifests, to a port-forwarded /jobs/ page served by a self-healing Pod.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [PART 3 INTRO]
  This is the heart of the administrator's job and a quarter of the exam.
  Minikube hid the hard parts; now you build a cluster from bare machines with
  kubeadm, configure the control plane by editing its static-pod manifests,
  and master the single most important admin skill — etcd backup & restore.
  ⚠️ This part is mostly done over SSH on the nodes, not just via kubectl.

  Up to now you have treated the cluster as a black box that "just runs."
  In this part you pry the lid off and assemble it yourself: you will prepare
  bare Linux nodes (swap off, kernel modules, sysctls, a container runtime),
  call kubeadm init to bootstrap a control plane, lay a CNI over it so Pods can
  talk, and kubeadm join your worker nodes. Then you will configure the parts
  you bootstrapped — the kube-apiserver, the kubelet, and admission control —
  by editing files on disk rather than by asking the API to change itself.
  Finally you will treat etcd, the cluster's single source of truth, with the
  respect it deserves: snapshot it, prove the snapshot is real by restoring
  from it, and only then trust your cluster in production. By the end, easypj
  will be running on a cluster that YOU built and that YOU can rebuild.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 3 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch9 INSTALL (kubeadm) ─▶ Ch10 CONFIGURE (apiserver/kubelet/admission)   │
  │        │                          │                                     │
  │        ▼                          ▼                                     │
  │ Ch11 etcd (backup/restore) ◀─▶ Ch12 MANAGE control plane (static pods)  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read the map as a build-then-operate loop. Ch9 stands the cluster up; Ch10
  tunes the components Ch9 created; Ch11 protects the state those components
  depend on; Ch12 closes the loop by teaching you to operate, upgrade, and
  repair the control plane that Ch9–11 produced. The double arrow between
  Ch11 and Ch12 is deliberate: managing the control plane (Ch12) and owning
  etcd (Ch11) are two halves of the same job — you cannot safely upgrade or
  recover a control plane without a known-good etcd snapshot.

  ┌──────────┬──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
  │ Chapter  │ You learn to…                │ Why the exam cares             │
  ├──────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch 9     │ kubeadm init / join, CNI,    │ "Provision a cluster" tasks;   │
  │ INSTALL  │ node prep over SSH           │ join a node that fell out      │
  ├──────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch 10    │ edit apiserver / kubelet     │ change a flag, enable an       │
  │ CONFIG   │ flags, admission plugins     │ admission plugin, fix kubelet  │
  ├──────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch 11    │ etcdctl snapshot save /      │ THE classic CKA task — back up │
  │ etcd     │ snapshot restore            │ and restore etcd               │
  ├──────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch 12    │ static-pod manifests,        │ control-plane upgrade,         │
  │ MANAGE   │ kubeadm upgrade, recovery    │ "apiserver won't start" fixes  │
  └──────────┴──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

  [PART 3 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: prep nodes (swap off, kernel modules, containerd) ->
  kubeadm init -> CNI -> join workers -> configure apiserver/kubelet/admission
  -> back up etcd (and prove you can restore) -> redeploy easypj on YOUR
  cluster. The visual to anchor on is the kubeadm cluster-creation flow:

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            THE kubeadm CLUSTER-CREATION FLOW (anchor diagram)           │
  │                                                                         │
  │  [Bare node]                                                            │
  │     │  swapoff -a · load br_netfilter/overlay · sysctl ip_forward       │
  │     ▼                                                                    │
  │  [containerd ready]                                                      │
  │     │  install kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl                                  │
  │     ▼                                                                    │
  │  control-plane:  kubeadm init ──▶ static pods written to                │
  │     │            /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (apiserver, etcd,           │
  │     │            controller-manager, scheduler) + admin.conf            │
  │     ▼                                                                    │
  │  apply a CNI (Calico/Flannel) ──▶ CoreDNS goes Ready, nodes Ready       │
  │     │                                                                    │
  │     ▼            kubeadm token + CA hash                                 │
  │  worker nodes:   kubeadm join <cp>:6443 ──▶ kubelet registers Node      │
  │     │                                                                    │
  │     ▼                                                                    │
  │  [Cluster Ready] ──▶ deploy easypj (jobpost app + PostgreSQL) on it     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 EXTENSION INTERFACES (official competency) introduced here and revisited:
     CRI (Ch 2/3) · CNI (Ch 9/17) · CSI (Ch 21) — "the three plug points."

  ┌──────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Plug │ Interface             │ What plugs in / where it appears          │
  ├──────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CRI  │ Container Runtime     │ containerd / CRI-O — how the kubelet runs │
  │      │ Interface             │ containers (Ch 2/3, node prep here)       │
  ├──────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CNI  │ Container Network     │ Calico / Flannel — how Pods get IPs and   │
  │      │ Interface             │ talk (applied in Ch 9, deep in Ch 17)     │
  ├──────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CSI  │ Container Storage     │ EBS / Ceph / local — how PVs are          │
  │      │ Interface             │ provisioned (Ch 21)                       │
  └──────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 PART-LEVEL MUST-REMEMBER
     • kubeadm writes the control plane as STATIC POD MANIFESTS under
       /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — edit the file, the kubelet restarts the pod.
     • The single highest-value admin skill (and a near-guaranteed exam task)
       is etcdctl snapshot save followed by a proven snapshot restore.
     • Most of this part is done over SSH on the nodes, not from your laptop's
       kubectl — know where the configs and certs live on disk.

  ⚡ PART-LEVEL SPEED TIPS
     • Forget swapoff -a (and the fstab edit) and kubeadm init/kubelet fails —
       check this FIRST when a node won't come up.
     • A NotReady node almost always means the CNI is missing or broken — apply
       or fix the CNI before chasing anything exotic.
     • Always export ETCDCTL_API=3 and pass --cacert/--cert/--key from
       /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ when driving etcdctl.

    [A] META: 🟡 · ⏱️ ~3h · HEAVILY TESTED. Domain: Cluster Architecture,
        Installation & Configuration (~25% of the exam).

    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS:
        The exam may hand you a half-built or broken cluster, and you must
        know every install step to finish it or fix it. This is one of the
        highest-yield chapters: "prepare infrastructure" and "create a cluster
        with kubeadm" are explicit syllabus items. If a worker is NotReady, a
        token is expired, or a port is blocked, you need the muscle memory to
        diagnose it in minutes.
        💡 INSIGHT: kubeadm does not provision machines — it bootstraps
        Kubernetes ONTO machines you already have. Knowing exactly where its
        responsibility starts and stops is half the battle.

    [C] OBJECTIVES:
        • Prepare node infrastructure (swap, kernel modules, sysctl, runtime).
        • Initialize a control-plane node with kubeadm init.
        • Install a CNI plugin so pods can network and nodes go Ready.
        • Join worker nodes to the cluster.
        • Verify the cluster end-to-end and deploy easypj as a smoke test.
        • Recover a lost or expired join token; cleanly remove a worker.

    [D] CKA RELEVANCE: 🎯 Directly maps to "prepare underlying infrastructure
        for installing a Kubernetes cluster" and "create and manage Kubernetes
        clusters using kubeadm." Expect hands-on join/verify/troubleshoot tasks.

    SECTION MAP:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.1  What is kubeadm?                                              🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         - Official Kubernetes installer tool.
         - Creates production-grade clusters.
         - Handles: certificate generation, control plane bootstrap,
           joining worker nodes.
         - NOT for: provisioning machines (you provide the VMs).

         📖 KEY TERM — kubeadm: a CLI that bootstraps a minimum viable,
         conformant Kubernetes cluster (certs + control-plane static pods +
         etcd + join mechanics). It is opinionated but does NOT install a CNI,
         provision VMs, or set up load balancers — those are your job.

         [KUBEADM: WHAT IT DOES AND WHAT IT DOESN'T]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  YOU provide:           kubeadm handles:             │
         │                                                      │
         │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌───────────────────────┐    │
         │  │ 🖥️ VMs/Servers│     │ ✅ Bootstrap control   │    │
         │  │ OS installed  │     │    plane components    │    │
         │  │ Network ready │     │ ✅ Generate TLS certs  │    │
         │  │ Swap disabled │     │ ✅ Create etcd cluster │    │
         │  │ Container     │     │ ✅ Join worker nodes   │    │
         │  │ runtime ready │     │ ✅ Configure kubelet   │    │
         │  └──────────────┘     │ ✅ Set up networking   │    │
         │                        │    prerequisites       │    │
         │  NOT kubeadm:          └───────────────────────┘    │
         │  ❌ VM provisioning                                  │
         │  ❌ OS installation                                  │
         │  ❌ CNI plugin install (you pick and install)        │
         │  ❌ Load balancer setup                              │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🧠 ANALOGY: kubeadm is like a flat-pack furniture assembly robot.
         You supply the room (VMs) and the toolbox (container runtime); kubeadm
         assembles the cabinet (control plane) and bolts on each drawer
         (workers). It will NOT build the room or paint the walls (CNI/LB).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.2  Pre-requisites for All Nodes                                  🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
         Run these on EVERY node (control plane AND workers) before any init
         or join. Skipping one is the #1 cause of a failed bootstrap.

         a) System requirements
            - 2 CPUs minimum (control plane)
            - 2 GB RAM minimum
            - Unique hostname, MAC, and product_uuid per node
            - Full network connectivity between nodes

         b) Disable swap — kubeadm REFUSES to run with swap on
            $ sudo swapoff -a
            $ sudo sed -i '/swap/d' /etc/fstab
            # Edition-2 variant (comment instead of delete, survives reboot):
            $ sudo swapoff -a && sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab

         c) Kernel modules
            $ sudo modprobe overlay
            $ sudo modprobe br_netfilter

            # /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf — load them on every boot:
            $ cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
            overlay
            br_netfilter
            EOF

         d) Sysctl parameters — let bridged pod traffic reach iptables and
            enable IP forwarding (required for the CNI and Services):

            # /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
            $ cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
            net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  = 1
            net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
            net.ipv4.ip_forward                 = 1
            EOF
            $ sudo sysctl --system

         e) Install container runtime (containerd)
            # Step-by-step containerd installation:
            $ sudo apt-get update
            $ sudo apt-get install -y containerd
            $ sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd
            $ containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml

            # Configure containerd for the SYSTEMD cgroup driver — this MUST
            # match the kubelet's cgroup driver or the kubelet crash-loops:
            #   /etc/containerd/config.toml →
            #     [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options]
            #       SystemdCgroup = true
            $ sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' \
                /etc/containerd/config.toml
            $ sudo systemctl restart containerd
            $ sudo systemctl enable containerd

         f) Install kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl
            # Add the Kubernetes apt repo and install packages:
            $ sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg
            $ curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.31/deb/Release.key \
                | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
            $ echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] \
                https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.31/deb/ /' \
                | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
            $ sudo apt-get update
            $ sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm kubelet kubectl

            # HOLD the package versions so an apt upgrade can't silently break
            # the node (version skew with the rest of the cluster):
            $ sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl

         ⚠️ GOTCHA: the cgroup driver mismatch in (e) is silent at install time
         and only shows up as a crash-looping kubelet AFTER init. Always set
         SystemdCgroup = true with containerd + systemd.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.3  Initialize the Control Plane Node                             🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
         Run ONLY on the control-plane node, once prerequisites are done:

         $ sudo kubeadm init \
             --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 \
             --apiserver-advertise-address=<CONTROL_PLANE_IP>

         # Full kubeadm init with the flags that matter on the exam:
         $ sudo kubeadm init \
             --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 \      # MUST match your CNI
             --apiserver-advertise-address=10.0.0.10 \
             --control-plane-endpoint=10.0.0.10 \    # set for HA-capable cluster
             --cri-socket=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock \
             --upload-certs                          # for HA control-plane joins

         EXPECTED OUTPUT (abridged): preflight checks pass, certificates are
         generated in /etc/kubernetes/pki, static-pod manifests are written to
         /etc/kubernetes/manifests, components start, and finally a printed
         "kubeadm join ..." command for your workers.

         Post-init steps (as a regular, non-root user):
         $ mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
         $ sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
         $ sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

         ⚠️ WARNING: SAVE THE kubeadm join COMMAND! You need it for the workers.
         If you lose it, you can regenerate it (see 9.5) — but save it anyway.

         🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: kubeadm init does not "run" the control plane as a
         service — it writes static-pod manifests that the kubelet watches and
         starts as pods (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler,
         etcd all run as static pods on the control-plane node).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.4  Install a CNI Plugin (Pod Networking)                        🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
         - Without a CNI: pods cannot communicate across nodes, and nodes stay
           NotReady. Installing the CNI is what flips nodes to Ready.
         - Popular choices: Calico, Flannel, Cilium, Weave.

         📖 KEY TERM — CNI (Container Network Interface): the plug point
         Kubernetes uses for pod networking. kubeadm leaves this slot empty on
         purpose so you can choose the implementation that fits your needs.

         $ kubectl apply -f https://docs.projectcalico.org/manifests/calico.yaml
         # (Flannel example — note the matching pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16:)
         $ kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flannel-io/flannel/master/Documentation/kube-flannel.yml

         [CNI COMPARISON]
         ┌───────────┬────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┬────────────┐
         │ CNI       │ Features                       │ Performance │ Complexity │
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
         │ Calico    │ Network policies, BGP          │ High        │ Medium     │
         │ Flannel   │ Simple overlay (VXLAN)         │ Medium      │ Low        │
         │ Cilium    │ eBPF-based, advanced security  │ Very High   │ High       │
         │ Weave     │ Simple, encrypted              │ Medium      │ Low        │
         └───────────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┘

         ⚠️ GOTCHA: the --pod-network-cidr you passed to kubeadm init MUST match
         what the CNI expects (Flannel defaults to 10.244.0.0/16; Calico can be
         told otherwise). A mismatch yields pods that schedule but never get a
         working IP, and nodes that never go Ready.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.5  Join Worker Nodes                                            🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
         On each worker node (after its prerequisites are done):

         $ sudo kubeadm join <CONTROL_PLANE_IP>:6443 \
             --token <TOKEN> \
             --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<HASH>

         If you lost the join command (tokens expire after 24h by default):
         $ kubeadm token create --print-join-command

         # To join an ADDITIONAL control-plane node (HA):
         $ sudo kubeadm join <CP_ENDPOINT>:6443 \
             --token <TOKEN> \
             --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<HASH> \
             --control-plane --certificate-key <KEY>

         [VERIFY: kubectl get nodes → all nodes Ready]

         [CLUSTER SETUP FLOW — complete journey]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  KUBEADM CLUSTER CREATION — step by step               │
         │                                                         │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ Step 1: Prerequisites │  All nodes: swap off,        │
         │  │ (all nodes)           │  containerd, kubeadm         │
         │  └──────────┬───────────┘                               │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ Step 2: kubeadm init │  Control plane node only      │
         │  │ (control plane)      │  → generates certs + configs  │
         │  └──────────┬───────────┘                               │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ Step 3: Setup kubeconfig│  Copy admin.conf to ~/.kube │
         │  │ (control plane)      │                               │
         │  └──────────┬───────────┘                               │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ Step 4: Install CNI  │  kubectl apply -f calico.yaml │
         │  │ (control plane)      │  → enables pod networking     │
         │  └──────────┬───────────┘                               │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ Step 5: kubeadm join │  Worker nodes join cluster    │
         │  │ (worker nodes)       │  → nodes show as Ready        │
         │  └──────────┬───────────┘                               │
         │             ▼                                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
         │  │ ✅ Cluster Ready!    │  kubectl get nodes → all Ready │
         │  └──────────────────────┘                               │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: kubeadm join uses a bootstrap token + the CA cert
         hash to mutually authenticate. The token proves the joiner is allowed
         in; the --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash proves the API server the
         worker is talking to is the real one (prevents man-in-the-middle).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.6  Verifying the Cluster
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         $ kubectl get nodes
         $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system
         $ kubectl cluster-info
         $ kubectl get cs            # component status (deprecated but still asked)

         EXPECTED OUTPUT: control plane + all workers show STATUS Ready; all
         kube-system pods (apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, etcd,
         coredns, kube-proxy, and the CNI pods) are Running.

         [POST-INSTALL VERIFICATION CHECKLIST]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ☐ kubectl get nodes        → every node Ready          │
         │  ☐ kubectl get pods -A      → no CrashLoopBackOff       │
         │  ☐ coredns pods Running     → DNS works                 │
         │  ☐ CNI pods Running on all  → pod networking up         │
         │  ☐ kubectl cluster-info     → API + CoreDNS endpoints   │
         │  ☐ smoke test: deploy easypj → it schedules & serves    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🧪 SMOKE TEST — deploy easypj as the real end-to-end check:
         $ kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj/jobpost:latest
         $ kubectl expose deployment easypj --port=8000 --type=NodePort
         $ kubectl get pods -l app=easypj -o wide   # confirm it lands on a worker
         If the easypj jobpost app comes up and answers, your cluster is
         genuinely usable — not just "Ready" on paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.7  🧪 PRACTICE EXERCISES — Chapter 9
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Exercise 9.1: Build a cluster from scratch            │
         │  • Create 3 VMs (1 control, 2 workers) with Vagrant   │
         │  • Install container runtime (containerd) on all       │
         │  • Run kubeadm init on control plane                   │
         │  • Install Calico CNI plugin                           │
         │  • Join both workers with kubeadm join                 │
         │  • Verify: kubectl get nodes (all 3 Ready)            │
         │                                                        │
         │  Exercise 9.2: kubeadm token recovery                  │
         │  • Pretend the join token expired                       │
         │  • Generate a new join token:                           │
         │    kubeadm token create --print-join-command            │
         │  • Join a new worker node                               │
         │                                                        │
         │  Exercise 9.3: Add a control plane node               │
         │  • Use --control-plane flag with kubeadm join          │
         │  • Verify etcd member list shows new member            │
         │                                                        │
         │  Exercise 9.4: Fix a NotReady worker                   │
         │  • Identify why a worker is NotReady (CNI? kubelet?)   │
         │  • Check journalctl -u kubelet and kube-system CNI pod │
         │  • Restore it to Ready                                  │
         │                                                        │
         │  ⏱️ Target time: Complete 9.1 in under 30 minutes     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    9.8  Required Ports (open these between nodes)                    🟡 🎯
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         A blocked firewall port is a classic "broken cluster" exam scenario.
         Know which ports each node type must accept inbound.

         [REQUIRED PORTS]
         ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Node         │ Port(s)      │ Purpose                               │
         ├──────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ CONTROL PLANE│ 6443         │ kube-apiserver (every client & node)  │
         │ (inbound)    │ 2379-2380    │ etcd client (2379) + peer/Raft (2380) │
         │              │ 10259        │ kube-scheduler                        │
         │              │ 10257        │ kube-controller-manager               │
         │              │ 10250        │ kubelet API (control plane → kubelet) │
         ├──────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ WORKER       │ 10250        │ kubelet API                           │
         │ (inbound)    │ 10256        │ kube-proxy health                     │
         │              │ 30000-32767  │ NodePort Service range                │
         └──────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘

         💡 INSIGHT — what breaks when a port is blocked:
            • blocked 6443       → joins & kubectl fail
            • blocked 10250      → `kubectl logs/exec` + metrics fail
            • blocked 2379-2380  → etcd can't form quorum (control plane down)
            • blocked 30000-32767→ NodePort Services unreachable from outside

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    📊 KEY DIAGRAM — Build a cluster with kubeadm (the order that matters)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ALL NODES (prep):  swapoff -a · load overlay+br_netfilter · sysctl
                      bridge-nf-call+ip_forward · install containerd
                      (SystemdCgroup=true) · install kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl + hold
        │
        ▼  CONTROL PLANE only
   kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16  ─► generates certs+manifests
        │  then: mkdir ~/.kube; cp admin.conf; chown   (+ SAVE the join cmd!)
        ▼
   kubectl apply -f <CNI>   (Calico/Cilium) ─► nodes go Ready (NOT before!)
        │
        ▼  EACH WORKER
   kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
        │   (lost it? kubeadm token create --print-join-command)
        ▼
   ✅ kubectl get nodes  ─ all Ready  ─► deploy easypj as the smoke test
   ⚠️ NotReady everywhere = no CNI · token expired = regenerate · swap on = fail

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 The kubeadm init sequence runs as ordered PHASES (you can run any phase
       alone with `kubeadm init phase <name>`):
         preflight → certs (CA + apiserver/etcd/front-proxy certs)
         → kubeconfig (admin/controller-manager/scheduler/kubelet configs)
         → control-plane static-pod manifests → etcd static-pod manifest
         → wait-control-plane (kubelet starts the static pods)
         → upload-config (kubeadm-config + kubelet-config ConfigMaps)
         → upload-certs (HA only) → mark-control-plane (taint + label)
         → bootstrap-token → kubelet-finalize → addons (CoreDNS + kube-proxy).

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
       • The kubeadm-config ConfigMap in kube-system records how the cluster
         was built; `kubeadm upgrade` reads it. Inspect with
         `kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml`.
       • Declarative install: `kubeadm init --config kubeadm-config.yaml`
         pins versions, CIDRs, the CRI socket, and feature gates reproducibly.
       • TLS bootstrapping: a worker joins with a bootstrap token, gets a
         short-lived cert, then the kubelet auto-rotates to a node-specific cert
         signed by the cluster CA.
       • --upload-certs stores the control-plane certs (encrypted) in a Secret
         so additional control-plane nodes can fetch them during HA joins.
       • Air-gapped installs: `kubeadm config images pull` to a local registry
         first; pass `--image-repository <your-registry>`.
       • --ignore-preflight-errors=<check> to bypass a known-safe failing check
         (e.g. in lab VMs); `--cri-socket` to select a non-default runtime.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • You provide the machines + runtime; kubeadm bootstraps the cluster
      (certs, control-plane static pods, etcd, join mechanics).
    • Prep EVERY node first: swap off, load overlay + br_netfilter, set the
      bridge-nf-call + ip_forward sysctls, install containerd with
      SystemdCgroup=true, install + apt-mark hold kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl.
    • Order: prereqs (all) → kubeadm init (CP) → set up kubeconfig (CP) →
      install a CNI (CP) → kubeadm join (workers) → verify.
    • Nodes stay NotReady until a CNI is installed — that is normal, not a bug.
    • Always SAVE the join command; if lost, regenerate it.
    • The control-plane components run as STATIC PODS managed by the kubelet
      from /etc/kubernetes/manifests.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Swap left on → kubeadm refuses to run (preflight failure).
    • No CNI installed → all nodes NotReady; people think the cluster failed.
    • Join token expired (24h default) → new workers can't join; regenerate it.
    • cgroup-driver mismatch (containerd vs kubelet) → kubelet crash-loops.
    • --pod-network-cidr overlaps the host/LAN network, or doesn't match the
      CNI → pods get no working IP.
    • Blocked ports (6443, 10250, 2379-2380, 30000-32767) → joins, logs/exec,
      etcd quorum, or NodePort access fail.
    • Forgetting apt-mark hold → an unrelated apt upgrade bumps the kubelet and
      introduces version skew, breaking the node.
    • Running kubeadm init on a worker, or join on the control plane — direction
      matters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • `kubeadm token create --print-join-command` regenerates a lost/expired
      join command in one line.
    • `kubeadm reset` cleanly undoes an init/join so you can retry from clean.
    • `--upload-certs` (init) + `--control-plane --certificate-key` (join) for
      HA control-plane joins without manually copying certs.
    • `kubeadm config images pull` pre-pulls images so init doesn't stall on a
      slow network during the timed exam.
    • `journalctl -u kubelet -f` is your first stop for any "node won't come up."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    kubeadm init [--pod-network-cidr --apiserver-advertise-address --config]
    kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
    kubeadm token create --print-join-command
    kubeadm token list
    kubeadm reset
    kubeadm config images pull
    kubeadm init phase <phase>
    systemctl status kubelet   ·   systemctl restart containerd
    journalctl -u kubelet
    kubectl get nodes   ·   kubectl get pods -n kube-system
    kubectl cluster-info
    sudo swapoff -a   ·   sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 9
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Q1. Disable swap permanently on a node. Give the commands.
        A: Turn it off now and stop it mounting at boot:
             sudo swapoff -a
             sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab   # (or '/swap/d')
        WHY: kubeadm's preflight check fails if swap is active; commenting the
        fstab line makes it survive a reboot.

    Q2. Name the 3 commands you run right after `kubeadm init` (to use kubectl
        as a regular user).
        A: mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
           sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
           sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
        WHY: admin.conf is the cluster-admin kubeconfig; copying it under
        $HOME/.kube/config (owned by you) lets kubectl authenticate.

    Q3. All nodes are NotReady right after init. Most likely cause and fix.
        A: No CNI installed yet. Fix: kubectl apply -f <CNI manifest>
        (e.g. Calico/Flannel). Nodes flip to Ready once CNI pods are Running.
        WHY: the kubelet reports NotReady until the network plugin is up; this
        is expected immediately after init, not a failure.

    Q4. The join token expired. Add a new worker anyway.
        A: On the control plane:  kubeadm token create --print-join-command
        Copy the printed line and run it (with sudo) on the worker.
        WHY: tokens expire after 24h by default; this mints a fresh token and
        prints a ready-to-run join command including the CA cert hash.

    Q5. Why must --pod-network-cidr match the CNI's expectation?
        A: kube-controller-manager hands each node a slice of that CIDR for pod
        IPs, and the CNI also expects to allocate from it. If they disagree,
        pods get no usable IP and cross-node pod traffic fails. Flannel, for
        instance, defaults to 10.244.0.0/16, so you init with that CIDR.

    Q6. The kubelet is crash-looping on a fresh node. Where do you look?
        A: journalctl -u kubelet -f and systemctl status kubelet. The usual
        culprit is a cgroup-driver mismatch (set containerd SystemdCgroup=true),
        a missing/misconfigured CRI socket, or swap still enabled.

    Q7. Which kernel modules and sysctls are required, and why?
        A: Modules: overlay (containerd's overlayfs snapshotter) and
        br_netfilter (so bridged traffic is seen by iptables). Sysctls:
        net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 and net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 so the
        CNI and kube-proxy can route pod/Service traffic.

    Q8. Cleanly remove a worker node.
        A: From the control plane:
             kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
             kubectl delete node <node>
           On the worker itself:
             sudo kubeadm reset
        WHY: drain evicts workloads safely, delete removes it from the API,
        and reset undoes kubeadm's changes so the box is clean.

    Q9. Which ports must be open between the control plane and workers?
        A: Control plane inbound: 6443 (apiserver), 2379-2380 (etcd),
        10259 (scheduler), 10257 (controller-manager), 10250 (kubelet).
        Workers inbound: 10250 (kubelet), 10256 (kube-proxy health),
        30000-32767 (NodePort). Blocking 6443 breaks joins/kubectl; blocking
        2379-2380 breaks etcd quorum; blocking 10250 breaks logs/exec/metrics.

    Q10. Pin the toolchain so an apt upgrade can't break the node.
        A: sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl
        WHY: holding the packages prevents an unrelated `apt upgrade` from
        bumping the kubelet and introducing version skew with the cluster.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧭 VISUAL SUMMARY — the full kubeadm build, one flow
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    PREP (all)──►INIT (CP)──►KUBECONFIG (CP)──►CNI (CP)──►JOIN (workers)──►VERIFY
      swap off    certs +     ~/.kube/config    nodes go    bootstrap     all Ready
      modules     static       from              Ready       token + CA    + easypj
      sysctl      pods +       admin.conf        (not        hash auth     smoke
      containerd  etcd +                         before!)                  test
      hold pkgs   join cmd
    .vs-prose: A kubeadm cluster is built strictly in order. Every node is
    prepped identically (swap off, kernel modules, sysctls, containerd with the
    systemd cgroup driver, held packages). The control plane is initialized
    once with kubeadm init, which generates the TLS certs and the control-plane
    static pods (plus etcd) and prints a join command — save it. You then wire
    up kubeconfig from admin.conf and install a CNI; only now do the nodes go
    Ready. Each worker joins with kubeadm join using a bootstrap token and the
    CA cert hash for mutual trust. Finally you verify with kubectl get nodes
    and prove the cluster is genuinely usable by deploying the easypj jobpost
    app as a smoke test. The three failure modes to memorize: NotReady
    everywhere means no CNI; "token expired" means regenerate it with
    `kubeadm token create --print-join-command`; and a refusal to init usually
    means swap is still on.

  Chapter 10: Cluster Configuration & kubeconfig                       🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation
        & Configuration (25%) · Difficulty climbs in 10.3–10.5.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Configuring the apiserver, kubelet and admission chain is HOW you bend a
  cluster to your requirements — and HOW you accidentally break it. In the
  exam you will jump between several clusters from a single kubeconfig, so a
  fluent `use-context` reflex is worth real points. Day-2, every guardrail
  you care about (default resource limits on easypj Pods, blocking privileged
  containers, namespace quotas) is wired in here. 💡 Insight: there is no
  central "settings panel" in Kubernetes — the control plane is configured by
  editing the static-pod manifests the kubelet is watching, and the kubelet
  itself by a file plus a systemd unit. Master those two surfaces and you can
  reshape almost anything.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OBJECTIVES
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Deep-read a kubeconfig: clusters / users / contexts, and how they bind.
    □ Manage many clusters from one file; understand KUBECONFIG merge order.
    □ Configure the API server via its static-pod manifest and key flags.
    □ Configure the kubelet via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml + systemd.
    □ Enable and reason about admission controllers (mutating vs validating).
    □ Navigate API groups and versioning (core vs named groups).

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🎯 Context switching is a near-certain skill across multiple tasks.
    🎯 "Enable admission plugin X" / "find apiserver flag Y" are classic asks.
    🎯 kubelet config + journalctl troubleshooting overlaps with node debug.
    🏢 Beyond exam: encryption-at-rest (KMS), audit webhooks, OIDC, API
       Priority & Fairness — the levers you tune on real production clusters.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SECTION MAP
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    10.4  kubelet Configuration
    10.5  Admission Controllers
    10.6  API Groups and Versioning


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.1  kubeconfig File Deep Dive                                          🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    📖 KEY TERM — kubeconfig: a YAML file that tells kubectl (and any client)
       three things: WHICH clusters exist (where the apiserver is + its CA),
       WHO you are (your credentials), and WHICH cluster+user+namespace combo
       is "current". It does NOT live inside the cluster — it is a client-side
       file on your machine.

      - Location: ~/.kube/config (or wherever $KUBECONFIG points).
      - 3 sections: clusters, users, contexts.
      - A context is the GLUE: context = cluster + user (+ optional namespace).
      - You can merge multiple kubeconfig files (see 10.2).

      [ANATOMY OF A kubeconfig — the three lists + the binding]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  apiVersion: v1                                                  │
      │  kind: Config                                                    │
      │  current-context: easypj-dev   ◄── the active context           │
      │                                                                  │
      │  clusters:        ── WHERE  (apiserver URL + CA to trust)        │
      │  ─ name: dev                                                     │
      │    cluster:                                                      │
      │      server: https://10.0.0.10:6443                             │
      │      certificate-authority-data: <base64 CA>                    │
      │                                                                  │
      │  users:           ── WHO    (your credentials)                  │
      │  ─ name: dev-admin                                              │
      │    user:                                                        │
      │      client-certificate-data: <base64 cert>                    │
      │      client-key-data:         <base64 key>                     │
      │                                                                  │
      │  contexts:        ── BINDING (cluster + user + namespace)        │
      │  ─ name: easypj-dev                                             │
      │    context:                                                    │
      │      cluster:   dev                                            │
      │      user:      dev-admin                                      │
      │      namespace: easypj                                         │
      │                                                                  │
      │  💡 current-context just NAMES one entry in contexts:           │
      │     contexts ─► (cluster, user, namespace)                      │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [CODE: Complete kubeconfig with multiple clusters/users/contexts]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Config
      current-context: easypj-dev

      clusters:
      - name: dev
        cluster:
          server: https://10.0.0.10:6443
          certificate-authority-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJU...   # base64 CA
      - name: prod
        cluster:
          server: https://prod.k8s.easypj.io:6443
          certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/prod-ca.crt  # file path also ok

      users:
      - name: dev-admin
        user:
          client-certificate-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJU...
          client-key-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBSU0Eg...
      - name: prod-admin
        user:
          token: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6...   # bearer token instead of certs

      contexts:
      - name: easypj-dev
        context:
          cluster: dev
          user: dev-admin
          namespace: easypj
      - name: easypj-prod
        context:
          cluster: prod
          user: prod-admin
          namespace: easypj

      🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: when you run `kubectl get pods`, kubectl reads the
      current-context, follows it to a cluster (gets the server URL + CA) and a
      user (gets your cert/token), then makes an authenticated HTTPS call. The
      namespace on the context is what makes `kubectl get pods` (no -n) target
      easypj instead of default. Three credential styles appear in `users`:
      client cert/key (most common in CKA), bearer token (ServiceAccounts,
      OIDC), and `exec` plugins (cloud auth like aws/gcloud).

      ⚠️ GOTCHA: `*-data` fields hold BASE64 of the cert/key/CA contents;
      the non-`-data` variants (certificate-authority, client-certificate)
      hold a FILE PATH instead. Don't mix them up.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.2  Managing Multiple Clusters                                         🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — you'll switch contexts during the exam]

      $ kubectl config view                       # show merged config (redacted)
      $ kubectl config view --raw                 # include secret data
      $ kubectl config get-contexts               # list all contexts (* = current)
      $ kubectl config current-context            # name of the active context
      $ kubectl config use-context <context-name> # SWITCH active context
      $ kubectl config set-context <name> --cluster=X --user=Y --namespace=Z
      $ kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj   # set ns only

      [MULTI-CLUSTER MANAGEMENT]
      ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  YOUR LAPTOP — ONE kubeconfig, MANY clusters         │
      │                                                      │
      │  ~/.kube/config                                      │
      │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
      │  │ contexts:                                    │     │
      │  │ ├── dev    → cluster: dev   + user: dev    │     │
      │  │ ├── staging→ cluster: stg   + user: admin  │     │
      │  │ └── prod   → cluster: prod  + user: admin  │     │
      │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
      │       │              │              │                 │
      │       ▼              ▼              ▼                 │
      │  ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐              │
      │  │dev clstr│   │stg clstr│   │prd clstr│              │
      │  │ 2 nodes │   │ 3 nodes │   │ 5 nodes │              │
      │  └────────┘   └────────┘   └────────┘              │
      │                                                      │
      │  $ kubectl config use-context prod  ← switch!       │
      └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      📖 KEY TERM — the KUBECONFIG env var: instead of editing one file you can
      LAYER several. kubectl reads every path in $KUBECONFIG (colon-separated on
      Linux, semicolon on Windows) and merges them in order.

      [KUBECONFIG MERGE — precedence is FIRST-WINS]
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/prod.conf           │
      │                                                              │
      │     file A (config)         file B (prod.conf)              │
      │     ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐                │
      │     │ cluster: dev │        │ cluster: prod│                │
      │     │ user: dev    │        │ user: prod   │                │
      │     │ ctx: dev *   │        │ ctx: prod    │                │
      │     └──────┬───────┘        └──────┬───────┘                │
      │            └──────────┬────────────┘                        │
      │                       ▼                                     │
      │              MERGED VIEW (in memory)                        │
      │              clusters: dev, prod                            │
      │              users:    dev, prod                            │
      │              contexts: dev, prod                            │
      │                                                              │
      │  ⚠️ If both files define the SAME name, the FIRST file in    │
      │     the list wins. current-context = first non-empty one.   │
      │  💡 `kubectl config view --flatten > merged.yaml` writes the │
      │     merged result (with embedded data) to a single file.    │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      🧪 [LAB] During the exam each task says "set context to clusterX". Just
      run `kubectl config use-context clusterX` FIRST, before touching anything
      — operating on the wrong cluster is a silent way to lose points.

      🧠 ANALOGY: a context is a saved "connection profile", like an SSH config
      Host block — one short name (`easypj-prod`) bundles the address, the
      identity, and the default working directory (namespace).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.3  API Server Configuration                                           🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

      - API server flags live in the static-pod manifest:
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
      - Key flags:
          --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
          --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...
          --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
          --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/12
      - Modifying: edit the static pod manifest → the kubelet notices the file
        change and AUTO-RESTARTS the apiserver pod (no systemctl needed).

      [CODE: kube-apiserver.yaml key sections]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: kube-apiserver
        namespace: kube-system
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: kube-apiserver
          image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0
          command:
          - kube-apiserver
          - --advertise-address=10.0.0.10
          - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
          - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
          - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
          - --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
          - --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/12
          - --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
          - --tls-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
          - --tls-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.key

      [STATIC-POD RECONCILE LOOP — how an apiserver flag change propagates]
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │   you: vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml      │
      │        (add a flag, :wq)                                     │
      │                       │                                      │
      │                       ▼                                      │
      │   kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ ──► sees diff  │
      │                       │                                      │
      │                       ▼                                      │
      │   kubelet KILLS old apiserver pod, starts a NEW one with     │
      │   the updated command line                                  │
      │                       │                                      │
      │                       ▼                                      │
      │   for ~10–40s the apiserver is DOWN → kubectl errors         │
      │                       │                                      │
      │                       ▼                                      │
      │   new pod healthy ──► kubectl works again, flag is live      │
      │                                                              │
      │   watch it: crictl ps | grep apiserver                       │
      │             kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w               │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [WARNING: Misconfiguring the API server can break the ENTIRE cluster]
      ⚠️ A typo (bad flag, broken YAML, wrong cert path) means the apiserver
      pod will not start. Because kubectl TALKS to the apiserver, kubectl
      itself stops working — you cannot `kubectl edit` your way out.

      🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING / RECOVERY:
        1. Logs from the failing static pod (kubectl is dead, use crictl):
             crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
             crictl logs <container-id>
           or check the kubelet's view:
             journalctl -u kubelet -f
        2. Fix the manifest by hand:
             vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        3. The kubelet re-reconciles on save; wait for the pod to come back.
      ⚡ SPEED TIP: ALWAYS back up before editing —
             cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/kas.bak
         If the edit breaks it, `cp /tmp/kas.bak <back>` and you're restored.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.4  kubelet Configuration                                              🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

      - Config file: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml  (KubeletConfiguration object)
      - Drop-in flags / unit: /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
      - Service: systemctl status kubelet
      - Key settings: clusterDNS, clusterDomain, cgroupDriver, staticPodPath.
      - Troubleshooting: journalctl -u kubelet -f

      [CODE: kubelet config.yaml key fields]
      apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
      kind: KubeletConfiguration
      clusterDomain: cluster.local
      clusterDNS:
        - 10.96.0.10                 # CoreDNS ClusterIP — Pods get this as resolver
      cgroupDriver: systemd          # MUST match the container runtime's driver
      staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests
      authentication:
        x509:
          clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
      authorization:
        mode: Webhook
      serverTLSBootstrap: true

      [KUBELET CONFIG SURFACES — two places, two restart rules]
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  (1) /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   (the KubeletConfiguration) │
      │       edit ──► systemctl restart kubelet     (no reload)      │
      │                                                              │
      │  (2) systemd unit / drop-in (.service.d/*.conf)   FLAGS      │
      │       edit ──► systemctl daemon-reload                       │
      │           ──► systemctl restart kubelet                      │
      │                                                              │
      │  ⚠️ Change the UNIT and you MUST daemon-reload FIRST, or      │
      │     systemd keeps running the old command line.             │
      │                                                              │
      │  check health: systemctl status kubelet                     │
      │  follow logs:  journalctl -u kubelet -f                      │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: the kubelet is NOT a static pod — it is a host-level
      systemd service (the one daemon that bootstraps everything else). It reads
      config.yaml at start, registers the node with the apiserver, then runs its
      sync loop: watch assigned Pods + watch staticPodPath, reconcile both
      against the container runtime via CRI. clusterDNS is injected into every
      Pod's /etc/resolv.conf so easypj containers can resolve `db.easypj.svc`.

      ⚠️ GOTCHA — cgroupDriver mismatch: if the kubelet says `systemd` but the
      runtime (containerd) is configured for `cgroupfs` (or vice-versa), the
      kubelet flaps and nodes go NotReady. They MUST agree.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.5  Admission Controllers                                              🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

      📖 KEY TERM — admission controller: a plugin that intercepts an API
      request AFTER authentication and authorization but BEFORE the object is
      persisted to etcd. Two flavors:
        • MUTATING   — may CHANGE the request (add defaults, inject sidecars).
        • VALIDATING — may only ACCEPT or REJECT it (enforce policy).
      Order is fixed: mutating runs FIRST, then schema validation, then
      validating. (Some built-ins do both.)

      [ADMISSION CONTROLLER PIPELINE — request lifecycle]
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  kubectl apply -f pod.yaml                                │
      │       │                                                    │
      │       ▼                                                    │
      │  ┌──────────────┐   Who are you?                          │
      │  │ AUTHENTICATE │   Client certs / Bearer token / OIDC   │
      │  └──────┬───────┘                                         │
      │         ▼                                                  │
      │  ┌──────────────┐   Are you ALLOWED to do this?           │
      │  │  AUTHORIZE   │   RBAC checks: verb + resource          │
      │  │  (RBAC)      │   → allowed or denied                   │
      │  └──────┬───────┘                                         │
      │         ▼                                                  │
      │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
      │  │           ADMISSION CONTROLLERS                   │    │
      │  │                                                    │    │
      │  │  ┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐              │    │
      │  │  │  MUTATING    │───▶│  VALIDATING   │              │    │
      │  │  │  Webhooks    │    │  Webhooks     │              │    │
      │  │  │              │    │               │              │    │
      │  │  │ "Add default │    │ "Is this valid?│              │    │
      │  │  │  limits if   │    │  Reject if no │              │    │
      │  │  │  missing"    │    │  limits set"  │              │    │
      │  │  └─────────────┘    └──────┬───────┘              │    │
      │  │                             │                      │    │
      │  │  Examples:                  │                      │    │
      │  │  • LimitRanger (mutating)   │                      │    │
      │  │  • PodSecurity (validating) │                      │    │
      │  │  • NamespaceLifecycle       │                      │    │
      │  │  • ResourceQuota            │                      │    │
      │  └─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘    │
      │                                ▼                           │
      │                         ┌────────────┐                    │
      │                         │   PERSIST   │                    │
      │                         │  in etcd 💾 │                    │
      │                         └────────────┘                    │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [THE API REQUEST PIPELINE — compact view, every kubectl apply travels it]
       kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
            ▼
       🔐 AUTHENTICATION   who are you?   (client cert / token / OIDC)
            ▼
       🛂 AUTHORIZATION    allowed?       (RBAC: verb + resource)
            ▼
       🧪 ADMISSION  ── MUTATING webhooks (add defaults, e.g. LimitRanger)
            │         ── schema validation
            │         ── VALIDATING webhooks / PodSecurity (reject if invalid)
            ▼
       🗄️ PERSIST in etcd  ─► controllers + scheduler take over
       💡 Mutating runs BEFORE validating. Enable plugins via
          --enable-admission-plugins on the kube-apiserver static-pod manifest.

      - Key admission controllers:
        • NamespaceLifecycle: prevent ops in terminating namespaces.
        • LimitRanger: enforce default resource limits (MUTATES Pods to add them).
        • ResourceQuota: enforce namespace quotas (rejects over-budget creates).
        • PodSecurity: enforce Pod Security Standards (replaced PodSecurityPolicy).
        • NodeRestriction: limit what each kubelet can modify (only its own Node
          + Pods bound to it) — a key defense-in-depth control.
        • DefaultStorageClass: stamp the default StorageClass onto PVCs that omit one.
      - Enable: --enable-admission-plugins flag on the API server manifest.
        Disable a default one with --disable-admission-plugins.

      [TABLE: Important admission controllers and what they do]
      ┌──────────────────────┬────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Controller           │ Type       │ What it does                        │
      ├──────────────────────┼────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
      │ NamespaceLifecycle   │ validating │ Blocks creates in a terminating ns; │
      │                      │            │ stops deleting system namespaces.   │
      │ LimitRanger          │ mutating   │ Injects default requests/limits from│
      │                      │            │ a LimitRange; rejects out-of-range. │
      │ ResourceQuota        │ validating │ Rejects objects that would exceed a │
      │                      │            │ namespace ResourceQuota.            │
      │ PodSecurity          │ validating │ Enforces privileged/baseline/       │
      │                      │            │ restricted Pod Security Standards.  │
      │ NodeRestriction      │ validating │ A kubelet may only modify its own   │
      │                      │            │ Node + Pods scheduled to it.        │
      │ DefaultStorageClass  │ mutating   │ Sets the default StorageClass on a  │
      │                      │            │ PVC that doesn't name one.          │
      │ ServiceAccount       │ mutating   │ Auto-mounts the SA token; assigns   │
      │                      │            │ the default SA if none is given.    │
      │ MutatingAdmission-   │ mutating   │ Calls external mutating webhooks    │
      │   Webhook            │            │ (e.g. a sidecar injector).          │
      │ ValidatingAdmission- │ validating │ Calls external validating webhooks  │
      │   Webhook            │            │ (e.g. OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno).     │
