      └──────────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

      🧪 [LAB] easypj wants every Pod in the easypj namespace to get default CPU
      and memory limits even when the manifest forgets them. Create a LimitRange
      in the namespace — LimitRanger (a mutating controller, enabled by default)
      then stamps those defaults onto each new easypj Pod at admission time.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10.6  API Groups and Versioning
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      - Core API group: /api/v1 (pods, services, configmaps) — NO group name
        in apiVersion (just `v1`).
      - Named groups: /apis/<group>/<version> (apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1).
      - Discovering: kubectl api-resources, kubectl api-versions.
      - Version maturity: vNalpha (off by default, may vanish) → vNbeta (on by
        default historically, may change) → vN (stable, GA, long-term).

      [KUBERNETES API GROUP MAP]
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │                  KUBERNETES API TREE                      │
      │                                                          │
      │  /api/v1  (CORE GROUP — no group name in apiVersion)     │
      │  ├── Pod                    apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── Service                apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── ConfigMap              apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── Secret                 apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── PersistentVolume       apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── Namespace              apiVersion: v1               │
      │  ├── Node                   apiVersion: v1               │
      │  └── ServiceAccount         apiVersion: v1               │
      │                                                          │
      │  /apis/<GROUP>/<VERSION>  (NAMED GROUPS)                 │
      │  ├── apps/v1                                             │
      │  │   ├── Deployment                                      │
      │  │   ├── ReplicaSet                                      │
      │  │   ├── StatefulSet                                     │
      │  │   └── DaemonSet                                       │
      │  ├── networking.k8s.io/v1                                │
      │  │   ├── Ingress                                         │
      │  │   └── NetworkPolicy                                   │
      │  ├── rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1                       │
      │  │   ├── Role / ClusterRole                              │
      │  │   └── RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding                │
      │  ├── batch/v1                                            │
      │  │   ├── Job                                             │
      │  │   └── CronJob                                         │
      │  └── storage.k8s.io/v1                                  │
      │      └── StorageClass                                    │
      │                                                          │
      │  💡 kubectl api-resources — shows ALL resources + groups │
      │  💡 kubectl api-versions  — shows ALL available versions │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [TABLE: Key API groups and their resources]
      ┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
      │ API group / version          │ apiVersion   │ Resources (selected)     │
      ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
      │ core (no group)              │ v1           │ Pod, Service, ConfigMap, │
      │                              │              │ Secret, PV, PVC, Node,   │
      │                              │              │ Namespace, ServiceAccount│
      │ apps                         │ apps/v1      │ Deployment, ReplicaSet,  │
      │                              │              │ StatefulSet, DaemonSet   │
      │ batch                        │ batch/v1     │ Job, CronJob             │
      │ networking.k8s.io            │ networking.  │ Ingress, NetworkPolicy,  │
      │                              │ k8s.io/v1    │ IngressClass             │
      │ rbac.authorization.k8s.io    │ rbac.        │ Role, ClusterRole,       │
      │                              │ ...k8s.io/v1 │ RoleBinding, CRBinding   │
      │ storage.k8s.io               │ storage.     │ StorageClass,            │
      │                              │ k8s.io/v1    │ VolumeAttachment, CSI*   │
      │ policy                       │ policy/v1    │ PodDisruptionBudget      │
      │ autoscaling                  │ autoscaling/ │ HorizontalPodAutoscaler  │
      │                              │ v2           │                          │
      │ apiextensions.k8s.io         │ ...k8s.io/v1 │ CustomResourceDefinition │
      └──────────────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

      ⚡ SPEED TIP: to find which version serves a kind, ask kubectl directly:
             kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
             kubectl explain ingress      # top line shows the GROUP/VERSION


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 How control-plane config actually propagates: the kubelet runs a file
     watcher on staticPodPath (/etc/kubernetes/manifests). On any write it
     diffs the desired PodSpec against the running container; a changed command
     line means tear-down + recreate. That is why "edit the YAML and save" is
     the entire deploy mechanism for the apiserver, controller-manager,
     scheduler and etcd — there is no `systemctl restart kube-apiserver`,
     because it is a pod, not a unit. The kubelet itself, by contrast, is the
     one true systemd service that boots before any pod exists.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    • API Priority & Fairness (APF): replaces the old max-inflight flags;
      classifies requests into FlowSchemas/PriorityLevelConfigurations so a
      noisy client can't starve the apiserver.
    • Audit logging: --audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path, or an audit
      WEBHOOK backend that streams events to an external sink.
    • Encryption at rest: EncryptionConfiguration via --encryption-provider-config;
      KMS v2 plugins encrypt Secrets in etcd with an external KMS DEK/KEK.
    • --feature-gates=Name=true/false toggles alpha/beta features per component.
    • Aggregation layer / front-proxy: --requestheader-* and --proxy-client-*
      certs let extension apiservers (metrics-server, custom APIs) plug in.
    • OIDC: --oidc-issuer-url / --oidc-client-id / --oidc-username-claim wire
      an external identity provider into authentication.
    • Admission-plugin ORDERING is fixed by the apiserver, not by the order you
      list them in --enable-admission-plugins; mutating always precedes
      validating regardless of flag order.


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 A kubeconfig has three lists — clusters (WHERE), users (WHO), contexts
       (the BINDING of cluster+user+namespace); current-context names one.
    🔑 `*-data` fields are base64 inline content; the plain fields are file paths.
    🔑 Switch clusters with `kubectl config use-context` — do it FIRST in every
       exam task. Set the default namespace with `set-context --current --namespace`.
    🔑 $KUBECONFIG merges multiple files; on name clashes the FIRST file wins.
       `config view --flatten` writes a single merged file.
    🔑 Configure the control plane by editing its STATIC-POD MANIFESTS in
       /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet auto-restarts the pod on save.
    🔑 Configure the kubelet via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (then restart) or
       its systemd unit (then daemon-reload AND restart).
    🔑 Admission runs AFTER authN+authZ, BEFORE etcd; MUTATING then VALIDATING.
       Enable plugins with --enable-admission-plugins.
    🔑 Core resources use apiVersion `v1`; named groups use `group/version`
       (apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1). Discover with api-resources/api-versions.


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ A manifest typo crashes the apiserver — and since kubectl TALKS to the
       apiserver, kubectl dies too. Recover by fixing the file with vi + crictl,
       not kubectl.
    ⚠️ Run `systemctl daemon-reload` BEFORE restarting the kubelet after editing
       its systemd unit, or systemd keeps the stale command line.
    ⚠️ cgroupDriver in kubelet config MUST match the container runtime's driver,
       or nodes flap NotReady.
    ⚠️ Don't confuse --client-ca-file (verifies clients) with the etcd
       --etcd-cafile, or the apiserver's --tls-cert-file with etcd's
       --peer-cert-file — wrong cert path = apiserver won't start.
    ⚠️ Don't mix base64 `*-data` fields with file-path fields in kubeconfig.
    ⚠️ KUBECONFIG merge is first-wins on duplicate names — order matters.
    ⚠️ Listing a plugin in --enable-admission-plugins does NOT change its run
       order; mutating-before-validating is fixed by the apiserver.


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ ALWAYS back up a manifest before editing: cp x.yaml /tmp/x.bak
    ⚡ Watch a control-plane pod come back: crictl ps | grep apiserver  OR
       kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w
    ⚡ Set the working namespace once: kubectl config set-context --current
       --namespace=easypj — saves typing -n on every command.
    ⚡ Find a kind's group/version fast: kubectl explain <kind> (top line) or
       kubectl api-resources | grep -i <kind>.
    ⚡ Tail kubelet trouble live: journalctl -u kubelet -f
    ⚡ `kubectl config view --minify` shows only the current context — quick
       sanity check that you're on the right cluster.


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    kubectl config view [--raw|--minify|--flatten]   # show config
    kubectl config get-contexts                       # list contexts (* = current)
    kubectl config current-context                    # active context name
    kubectl config use-context <name>                 # switch cluster
    kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
    kubectl config set-context <n> --cluster=C --user=U --namespace=N
    export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/prod.conf # merge files
    vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml  # configure apiserver
    cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/kas.bak   # back up first
    crictl ps -a | grep apiserver ; crictl logs <id>  # debug when kubectl is down
    vi /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml ; systemctl restart kubelet
    systemctl daemon-reload ; systemctl restart kubelet   # after unit edit
    systemctl status kubelet ; journalctl -u kubelet -f
    kubectl api-resources                             # all resources + groups
    kubectl api-versions                              # all available versions
    kubectl explain <kind>                            # shows the GROUP/VERSION


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 10
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Q1. Name the 3 kubeconfig sections and what each holds.
  A.  clusters (WHERE — apiserver server URL + the CA to trust), users (WHO —
      your credentials: client cert/key, bearer token, or exec plugin), and
      contexts (the BINDING — a named tuple of cluster + user + optional
      namespace). current-context simply names which context is active.
      EXPLANATION: a context is the glue; kubectl follows current-context to a
      cluster and a user to make one authenticated call.

  Q2. Merge two kubeconfig files into one session.
  A.  export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/prod.conf
      kubectl config get-contexts          # both files' contexts now visible
      # to bake it into one physical file:
      KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/prod.conf kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged
      EXPLANATION: $KUBECONFIG is a path list (':' on Linux). On duplicate names
      the FIRST file wins; --flatten embeds the cert data into a single output.

  Q3. Enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin (which file, which flag).
  A.  Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and add NodeRestriction
      to the --enable-admission-plugins flag, e.g.:
        - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
      Save; the kubelet restarts the apiserver pod automatically.
      EXPLANATION: comma-separate multiple plugins. Verify with:
        ps -ef | grep apiserver | grep enable-admission   (or check the manifest)

  Q4. Find the current --service-cluster-ip-range of the apiserver.
  A.  grep service-cluster-ip-range /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
      (or `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-<node> -o yaml | grep
      service-cluster-ip-range`). EXPLANATION: every effective flag is in the
      static-pod manifest's command list — read it straight from the file.

  Q5. The apiserver won't start after an edit — how do you recover?
  A.  kubectl is dead, so use the node directly:
        crictl ps -a | grep apiserver ; crictl logs <container-id>   # see the error
        cp /tmp/kas.bak /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml # restore backup
      or hand-fix the YAML/flag in the manifest. The kubelet re-reconciles on
      save; wait ~30s for the pod to come healthy. EXPLANATION: this is exactly
      why you `cp` the manifest to /tmp before editing.

  Q6. Core API group vs a named group — an example apiVersion of each.
  A.  Core group: apiVersion: v1 (e.g. Pod, Service, ConfigMap) — served at
      /api/v1, no group name. Named group: apiVersion: apps/v1 (e.g. Deployment)
      — served at /apis/apps/v1. EXPLANATION: any apiVersion containing a slash
      is a named group; a bare version like `v1` is the core group.

  Q7. Change the kubelet's clusterDNS and apply it.
  A.  Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml:
        clusterDNS:
          - 10.96.0.10
      then: systemctl restart kubelet
      Verify: a new Pod's /etc/resolv.conf shows the new nameserver.
      EXPLANATION: clusterDNS is the CoreDNS ClusterIP injected into Pods; a
      config.yaml change needs only a restart (no daemon-reload).

  Q8. Set a context's default namespace to easypj.
  A.  kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
      (or for a named context: kubectl config set-context easypj-dev --namespace=easypj)
      Verify: kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
      EXPLANATION: this writes namespace into the context so `kubectl get pods`
      (no -n) targets easypj.

  Q9. Where do mutating vs validating webhooks run in the request flow?
  A.  After authentication and authorization, before persistence to etcd.
      MUTATING admission runs FIRST (may change the object — add defaults/inject
      sidecars), then schema validation, then VALIDATING admission (accept or
      reject only). EXPLANATION: order is enforced by the apiserver, not by your
      --enable-admission-plugins ordering.

  Q10. Discover which API version serves Ingress.
  A.  kubectl explain ingress        # top line: networking.k8s.io/v1
      or: kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
      EXPLANATION: Ingress lives in the networking.k8s.io group at v1, so its
      manifests use `apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1`.


  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 10
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   [REQUEST LIFECYCLE — left to right, the road into etcd]

     kubectl ─► 🔐 authN ─► 🛂 authZ ─► 🧪 admission ─► 🗄️ etcd
                (who?)      (RBAC:      (mutate then     (persisted;
                            allowed?)    validate)        controllers +
                                                          scheduler act)

   .vs-prose: A kubectl request first PROVES IDENTITY (authentication — client
   cert, token or OIDC), then is CHECKED FOR PERMISSION (authorization — RBAC
   evaluates verb + resource). If both pass it enters ADMISSION, where mutating
   controllers may rewrite it (LimitRanger stamps default limits onto easypj
   Pods) and validating controllers may reject it (PodSecurity, ResourceQuota).
   Only then is the object WRITTEN TO etcd, after which controllers and the
   scheduler take over to make it real. You shape every stage of this road by
   editing two surfaces: the apiserver's STATIC-POD MANIFEST in
   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (kubelet auto-restarts it on save) and the
   KUBELET's own config.yaml + systemd unit. And from your laptop, ONE
   kubeconfig — clusters, users, contexts — lets you point that whole road at
   dev, staging or the easypj prod cluster with a single `use-context`.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 11: etcd — The Cluster Database (Backup & Restore)           🔴 🎯
================================================================================

  META: 🔴 HARD · ⏱️ ~2.5h · ALMOST-GUARANTEED EXAM TASK · Domain: Cluster
        Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Backup & restore is
        one of the highest-yield single tasks on the entire CKA.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  etcd is the cluster's ENTIRE memory. Every Pod, Deployment, Service, Secret,
  ConfigMap, Node and namespace you have ever created lives as a key in etcd.
  Lose etcd without a backup and the cluster is simply gone — there is no other
  copy of that state anywhere. This makes "take a verified snapshot" and
  "restore from a snapshot" THE highest-value admin skills you own. On the exam
  you will almost certainly be asked to back up etcd, and very likely to restore
  it. 🧠 ANALOGY: etcd is the cluster's brain/memory — wipe the brain and the
  body (the worker nodes, the kubelets, the running containers) keeps twitching
  for a moment, but the control plane no longer knows what is supposed to exist.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  - Explain what etcd is and how Raft consensus keeps it consistent.
  - Take a VERIFIED snapshot using etcdctl with the correct TLS flags.
  - Restore a snapshot to a NEW data directory and repoint the static pod.
  - Secure etcd with TLS and turn on encryption at rest for Secrets.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
  🎯 Backup & restore is heavily tested and almost guaranteed to appear.
  🎯 You must be able to find the cert paths, run the command from memory, and
     repoint the static-pod manifest correctly. Partial credit is rare here —
     a restore either comes back or it does not.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
    11.1  What is etcd?
    11.2  etcd Architecture & Raft
    11.3  etcd Backup — THE Most Important Admin Task
    11.4  etcd Restore
    11.5  etcd Security & Encryption at Rest
    🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  11.1  What is etcd?                                                        🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    - Distributed key-value store.
    - Stores ALL Kubernetes cluster state.
    - Uses Raft consensus for distributed consistency.
    - If etcd dies: the cluster loses its memory.
    📖 KEY TERM: every object the API server serves is persisted under a
       /registry/<resource>/<namespace>/<name> key in etcd.
    🧠 ANALOGY: etcd = the cluster's brain/memory.
    ⚠️ GOTCHA: Secrets are stored UNENCRYPTED (base64 only) in etcd by default.
       Anyone who can read the etcd data files or a raw snapshot can read every
       Secret — which is exactly why section 11.5 exists.

          [ETCD — THE CLUSTER'S MEMORY]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  EVERYTHING IN KUBERNETES IS STORED IN ETCD          │
          │                                                      │
          │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
          │  │  etcd key-value store                          │   │
          │  │                                                │   │
          │  │  /registry/pods/easypj-dev/easypj-abc123      │   │
          │  │  /registry/deployments/easypj-dev/easypj      │   │
          │  │  /registry/services/easypj-dev/easypj-svc     │   │
          │  │  /registry/secrets/easypj-dev/easypj-secret   │   │
          │  │  /registry/configmaps/easypj-dev/easypj-config│   │
          │  │  /registry/nodes/worker-1                      │   │
          │  │  /registry/nodes/worker-2                      │   │
          │  │  ... every K8s object lives here ...           │   │
          │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
          │                                                      │
          │  ⚠️ LOSE ETCD = LOSE EVERYTHING                      │
          │  ✅ BACKUP ETCD = CAN RESTORE EVERYTHING             │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: The /registry prefix above is not cosmetic — when the API
    server stores your easypj Deployment, it serializes the object (protobuf by
    default) and PUTs it at /registry/deployments/easypj-dev/easypj. A
    `kubectl get` is, underneath, a range read against that key prefix. This is
    why "etcd has all state" is literally true: there is no second database.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  11.2  etcd Architecture & Raft                                            🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    - Runs as a static pod (kubeadm clusters) or as a systemd service.
    - Default ports: 2379 (client API), 2380 (peer/replication).
    - Certificate-based authentication on both ports.
    - Data directory: default /var/lib/etcd.
    - One LEADER, the rest FOLLOWERS; the leader serializes all writes.

          [ETCD RAFT CONSENSUS — 3-node cluster]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  ETCD CLUSTER (odd number for quorum)                │
          │                                                      │
          │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐      │
          │  │ etcd-0   │◄──▶│ etcd-1   │◄──▶│ etcd-2   │      │
          │  │ (LEADER) │    │ (follower)│    │ (follower)│      │
          │  │ port 2379│    │ port 2379│    │ port 2379│      │
          │  │ port 2380│    │ port 2380│    │ port 2380│      │
          │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘      │
          │       │                                              │
          │       │ Raft consensus: majority needed              │
          │       │ 3 nodes → can survive 1 failure              │
          │       │ 5 nodes → can survive 2 failures             │
          │       │ Always odd numbers! (3, 5, 7)                │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [etcd RAFT — quorum keeps the cluster's memory consistent]
           ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
           │ etcd-0   │◄─►│ etcd-1   │◄─►│ etcd-2   │   3 members
           │ LEADER   │   │ follower │   │ follower │   quorum = N/2+1 = 2
           │ :2379/80 │   │          │   │          │   tolerate 1 failure
           └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘
           WRITE: client ─► LEADER ─► replicate ─► commit once a MAJORITY ack ─► ✅
           ⚠️ Always ODD members (3,5,7). 5 ⇒ tolerate 2. Lose quorum ⇒ read-only/down.

    📖 QUORUM MATH: quorum = floor(N/2) + 1. With N=3, quorum=2, so the cluster
    keeps working with 1 member down. With N=5, quorum=3, so it tolerates 2 down.
    Even counts buy you NOTHING extra (4 still only tolerates 1) while costing an
    extra machine — that is why production etcd is always 3, 5 or 7 members.
    ⚠️ If you lose quorum, etcd goes read-only / unavailable: the API server can
    still serve cached reads briefly but no writes succeed, so `kubectl apply`
    hangs or fails. Recovery from quorum loss means restoring from a snapshot.

    🔧 STACKED vs EXTERNAL: In a default kubeadm cluster, etcd runs as a static
    pod ON the control-plane node alongside the API server — "stacked" topology.
    In larger clusters etcd runs on its own dedicated machines — "external"
    topology — and the API server reaches it over the network with
    --etcd-servers. The backup/restore commands are identical; only WHERE you
    run them and which manifest/unit you repoint differs (see Q8).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  11.3  etcd Backup — THE Most Important Admin Task                         🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — almost guaranteed to appear]
    - Tool: etcdctl (the command-line client for etcd).
    - Always export ETCDCTL_API=3 (the v3 data API is what Kubernetes uses).

    Backup command:
    $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
        --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
        --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
        --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
        --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

    Verify backup (ALWAYS do this — a snapshot you have not verified is a
    snapshot you do not have):
    $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db --write-table

    The status output gives you HASH, REVISION, TOTAL KEYS and TOTAL SIZE — a
    sane non-zero key count is your confirmation the file is a real snapshot and
    not an empty/truncated file.

          [ETCD BACKUP CHECKLIST]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  ETCD BACKUP — know these by heart for CKA           │
          │                                                      │
          │  You need 4 things:                                  │
          │  1. 📁 --endpoints   (where etcd listens)           │
          │  2. 🔐 --cacert      (CA certificate)               │
          │  3. 📜 --cert        (server certificate)           │
          │  4. 🔑 --key         (server private key)           │
          │                                                      │
          │  Find them:                                          │
          │  $ kubectl describe pod etcd-master -n kube-system  │
          │  (look in --command section for cert paths)          │
          │                                                      │
          │  Or from the static pod manifest:                    │
          │  $ cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml           │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — where do the 4 values come from?
      --endpoints : the --listen-client-urls / --advertise-client-urls in
                    etcd.yaml; on a stacked cluster this is https://127.0.0.1:2379.
      --cacert    : --trusted-ca-file in etcd.yaml (usually .../etcd/ca.crt).
      --cert      : --cert-file in etcd.yaml (.../etcd/server.crt).
      --key       : --key-file in etcd.yaml (.../etcd/server.key).
    ⚡ SPEED TIP: rather than type four long --flags every time, alias them:
       $ export ETCDCTL_API=3
       $ alias e='etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
           --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
           --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
           --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key'
       then simply: e snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db ; e snapshot status ... ;
       e member list ; e endpoint health.

    🏢 DAY-2: In production you do not run this by hand — you schedule it. A
    Kubernetes CronJob (see Q10) or a host cron entry runs the snapshot nightly
    and ships the file off-box (object storage / another host). A backup that
    lives only on the dying control-plane node is not a backup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  11.4  etcd Restore                                                        🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    Restore command (restore into a NEW directory, never the live one):
    $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
        --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

    Note: `snapshot restore` does NOT need the TLS flags — it operates on a file
    on disk, not on a running server. It writes a fresh, self-consistent member
    data directory under --data-dir.

    Post-restore steps:
    a) Update the etcd manifest to point at the new data directory.
       Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
         → change the --data-dir flag to /var/lib/etcd-restored
         → update the hostPath VOLUME that backs the data dir to
           /var/lib/etcd-restored  (this is the step people forget!)
    b) Wait for the etcd pod to restart. The kubelet watches the manifests
       directory and auto-restarts static pods when the file changes.
    c) Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system  (and your restored objects
       reappear: kubectl get deploy -n easypj-dev should show easypj again).

          [FLOWCHART: Backup → Disaster → Restore → Verify]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  ETCD BACKUP & RESTORE FLOW                         │
          │                                                     │
          │  Normal ops:    etcdctl snapshot save               │
          │       │         (scheduled backup, e.g., CronJob)   │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  💾 Backup file saved: /backup/etcd-snapshot.db     │
          │       │                                              │
          │  ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ DISASTER HAPPENS ─ ─ ─ ─ ─           │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  etcdctl snapshot restore → new data directory      │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  Update etcd.yaml → --data-dir = new path           │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  kubelet restarts etcd pod automatically            │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  ✅ Cluster restored to backup point!               │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [BACKUP ▶ DISASTER ▶ RESTORE — the #1 admin skill]
           snapshot save ──► 💾 /opt/etcd-backup.db  (needs --cacert --cert --key)
                │
           ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ ─ 💥 DISASTER ─ ─ ─ ─
                ▼
           snapshot restore ──data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-RESTORED  (a NEW dir!)
                ▼
           edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
                change --data-dir  AND  the hostPath volume  ──► both!
                ▼
           🤖 kubelet auto-restarts etcd ──► ✅ cluster back at the snapshot point

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING the restart: if etcd does not come back after you edit the
    manifest, move etcd.yaml OUT of /etc/kubernetes/manifests momentarily so the
    kubelet kills the old pod, confirm the old container is gone with
    `crictl ps | grep etcd`, then move the file back so the kubelet starts the
    new one with the new --data-dir. Watch `crictl logs` for the etcd container
    if it crash-loops — a mismatched data-dir vs hostPath is the usual cause.

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: If you restore on top of the LIVE /var/lib/etcd you will hit
    "data-dir not empty" (or corrupt the live store). Always pick a fresh path.
    ⚡ SPEED TIP: Before ANY restore, take one more fresh snapshot of the current
    (broken) state — restores are destructive and you want a fallback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  11.5  etcd Security & Encryption at Rest                                 🎯 🏢
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - All etcd communication uses TLS certificates (client AND peer).
    - Certificate locations: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/
    - Encrypt Secrets at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server.

          [/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ — the etcd cert directory]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  $ ls -1 /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/                    │
          │                                                       │
          │  ca.crt            ← etcd CA certificate (--cacert)   │
          │  ca.key            ← etcd CA private key              │
          │  server.crt        ← etcd server cert  (--cert)       │
          │  server.key        ← etcd server key   (--key)        │
          │  peer.crt          ← peer (member↔member) cert        │
          │  peer.key          ← peer private key                 │
          │  healthcheck-client.crt ← client cert for health/probe│
          │  healthcheck-client.key                               │
          │                                                       │
          │  apiserver-etcd-client.crt  (lives in ../pki/)        │
          │  apiserver-etcd-client.key  ← API server → etcd auth  │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    📖 ENCRYPTION AT REST: TLS protects etcd traffic on the wire, but the data
    FILES (and your snapshots) still contain Secrets in plaintext base64 unless
    you enable encryption at rest. You do that with an EncryptionConfiguration
    handed to the API server via --encryption-provider-config.

          [EncryptionConfiguration — encrypt Secrets at rest]
          # /etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml  (root-readable only, mode 0600)
          apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
          kind: EncryptionConfiguration
          resources:
            - resources:
                - secrets
              providers:
                - aescbc:
                    keys:
                      - name: key1
                        secret: <BASE64_32_BYTE_KEY>   # head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64
                - identity: {}    # fallback so existing plaintext stays readable

    Wire it into the API server static pod manifest
    (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml):
      - add flag:   --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
      - add a hostPath volume + volumeMount mapping /etc/kubernetes/enc into the
        pod so the API server container can read the file.
    The kubelet restarts the API server when you save the manifest.

    ⚠️ ORDER MATTERS: list aescbc FIRST under providers (so NEW writes are
    encrypted) and keep identity LAST (so already-written plaintext Secrets are
    still readable until you rewrite them). Putting identity first means nothing
    ever gets encrypted.

    Re-encrypt EXISTING Secrets — enabling the config only affects future writes,
    so force every Secret to be re-written through the new encrypter:
      $ kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
    Confirm at the etcd layer that the value is now ciphertext (prefixed with
    k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:), e.g.:
      $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/easypj-dev/easypj-secret \
          --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
          --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
          --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
          --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key | hexdump -C | head

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 STORAGE ENGINE: etcd v3 stores data in a memory-mapped B+tree file via
    BoltDB, fronted by a Write-Ahead Log (WAL). A write is first appended to the
    WAL (durable), then applied to the B+tree. On restart, etcd replays the WAL.
    This is why a snapshot is a single consistent point-in-time .db file.

    🔧 MVCC & REVISIONS: etcd is multi-version. Every write bumps a global
    revision; old key versions accumulate. This powers watches (the API server
    watches etcd for changes), but the history must be reclaimed.

    🔧 COMPACTION vs DEFRAG: Two distinct cleanups, often confused.
      • Compaction discards historical revisions older than a point — frees
        logical space (--auto-compaction-mode=periodic, --auto-compaction-retention).
      • Defragmentation (`etcdctl defrag`) returns the freed space to the OS by
        rewriting the .db file — compaction alone leaves the file the same size.

    🔧 WRITE PATH (Raft): client ▶ LEADER appends to its log ▶ replicates to
    followers ▶ once a MAJORITY (quorum) has persisted the entry it is COMMITTED
    and applied ▶ leader acks the client. This is why an even member count gives
    no extra safety: commitment needs N/2+1 regardless.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
      • --auto-compaction-mode (periodic|revision) and --auto-compaction-retention
        tuning to keep the DB from growing unbounded.
      • Scheduled `etcdctl defrag` (one member at a time, off-peak) to shrink the
        file after compaction.
      • Membership ops: `etcdctl member add/remove`, and LEARNER members (non-voting
        members that catch up before being promoted — safer cluster growth).
      • Quorum-loss / split-brain recovery: when you cannot regain a majority, the
        recovery path is restore-from-snapshot with --force-new-cluster on a single
        surviving member, then re-add members.
      • NOSPACE alarm: when the DB hits --quota-backend-bytes, etcd raises a NOSPACE
        alarm and goes read-only; you compact + defrag, then
        `etcdctl alarm disarm` to clear it.
      • Lease & transaction (txn) semantics: TTL leases back things like Events and
        leader-election; txn gives compare-and-swap.
      • Perf tuning: --heartbeat-interval and --election-timeout for high-latency
        or large clusters; etcd is extremely sensitive to disk fsync latency (use
        fast SSDs, never network disks with high latency).
      • External-etcd topology: dedicated etcd nodes, API server points at them via
        --etcd-servers and apiserver-etcd-client certs.

    🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: etcd does NOT back up PersistentVolume DATA. A snapshot
    captures the PV/PVC OBJECTS (the API definitions) but not the bytes on the
    underlying disk/NFS/cloud volume. Those need their own backup (Velero, volume
    snapshots, etc.).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 etcd holds ALL cluster state — lose it without a backup and the cluster is
       gone; back it up and you can restore everything.
    🔑 `snapshot save` needs the endpoint plus the 3 TLS flags: --cacert, --cert,
       --key (and ETCDCTL_API=3).
    🔑 ALWAYS verify with `snapshot status --write-table` before trusting a file.
    🔑 Restore goes to a NEW --data-dir, then you repoint etcd.yaml in TWO places:
       the --data-dir flag AND the hostPath volume.
    🔑 `snapshot restore` needs NO TLS flags (it works on the file, not the server).
    🔑 Odd member count (3,5,7); quorum = N/2+1; 3 tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2.
    🔑 etcd backs up the PV/PVC OBJECTS, not the PV DATA.
    🔑 Secrets are plaintext-base64 at rest by default — enable
       EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc) to encrypt them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ Forgetting one of --cacert / --cert / --key → "context deadline exceeded"
       or a TLS handshake error (it looks like etcd is down; it is auth).
    ⚠️ Restoring into the LIVE /var/lib/etcd → "data-dir not empty" or corruption.
    ⚠️ Editing --data-dir in etcd.yaml but forgetting the matching hostPath volume
       → etcd starts against the OLD data and your restore "didn't work."
    ⚠️ For EXTERNAL etcd, not stopping the API server / handling all members during
       a restore → inconsistent cluster.
    ⚠️ Assuming etcd backs up PersistentVolume data — it does not.
    ⚠️ Putting `identity` before `aescbc` in EncryptionConfiguration → nothing is
       ever actually encrypted.
    ⚠️ Even member counts (e.g. 4) give NO extra fault tolerance over 3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ Alias the four etcdctl TLS flags (and `export ETCDCTL_API=3`) so you type
       `e snapshot save ...` instead of four long lines.
    ⚡ ALWAYS take a fresh snapshot of the current state right before any restore.
    ⚡ Cert paths and the endpoint all live in
       /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml — `cat` it instead of guessing.
    ⚡ If a static pod won't pick up your manifest edit, move the file out of the
       manifests dir and back in to force the kubelet to recreate it.
    ⚡ `etcdctl endpoint health` and `etcdctl member list` are your fast sanity
       checks that etcd is actually up and has quorum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    export ETCDCTL_API=3
    etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
      --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=... --cert=... --key=...
    etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table
    etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
    etcdctl member list --write-out=table   (with TLS flags)
    etcdctl endpoint health                  (with TLS flags)
    etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
    etcdctl defrag                           (reclaim disk after compaction)
    etcdctl alarm list / etcdctl alarm disarm
    kubectl describe pod etcd-master -n kube-system   (find cert paths)
    cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml           (find flags/paths)
    kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -   (re-encrypt Secrets)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 11
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 DRILL: back up etcd, delete the easypj Deployment, restore the snapshot,
       and confirm the Deployment is back.

    Q1. 🟢 Write the full `etcdctl snapshot save` command with TLS flags.
        A:
          ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
            --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
            --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
            --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
            --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
        WHY: etcdctl needs a target (--endpoints) and three TLS materials to
        authenticate as a client to the etcd server: the CA to trust the server,
        and a client cert+key etcd trusts. Without all four you get a TLS/timeout
        error. Use ETCDCTL_API=3 because Kubernetes uses the v3 store.

    Q2. 🔴 Restore a snapshot and repoint the static pod — every step.
        A:
          1) ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
               --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
          2) Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
               - change the container arg  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
                 to        --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
               - change the hostPath volume for the data dir from
                 /var/lib/etcd to /var/lib/etcd-restored
          3) Save. The kubelet detects the manifest change and recreates the etcd
             static pod. (If it stalls, move etcd.yaml out and back in.)
          4) Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system  → etcd-master Running, and
             your objects (e.g. kubectl get deploy -n easypj-dev) are back.
        WHY: restore builds a fresh member directory; etcd must be told to USE it
        in BOTH the flag and the hostPath, or it boots against the old data.

    Q3. 🟢 Where do you find the 3 cert paths etcdctl needs?
        A: In the etcd static pod manifest, /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml —
        read the --trusted-ca-file (→ --cacert), --cert-file (→ --cert) and
        --key-file (→ --key) args. Equivalently:
        `kubectl describe pod etcd-master -n kube-system` and read the Command
        section. They normally live under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/.

    Q4. 🟢 Verify a snapshot file before trusting it.
        A: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table
        Check that TOTAL KEYS is a sane non-zero number and note the HASH/REVISION.
        An empty or truncated file shows 0 keys or errors — do not trust it.

    Q5. 🟢 Quorum math: how many failures does a 5-member cluster tolerate?
        A: 2. quorum = floor(5/2)+1 = 3, so up to 5−3 = 2 members can be down and
        the cluster still commits writes. (3 members tolerate 1; 7 tolerate 3.)

    Q6. 🟡 A restore failed with "data-dir not empty" — why, and the fix?
        A: You pointed --data-dir at an existing/populated directory (often the
        LIVE /var/lib/etcd). Fix: restore into a brand-new path
        (--data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored), then repoint etcd.yaml to it. Never
        restore on top of the running data directory.

    Q7. 🔴 Enable encryption at rest for Secrets (EncryptionConfiguration).
        A:
          1) Generate a 32-byte key: head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64
          2) Write /etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml with kind: EncryptionConfiguration,
             resources: [secrets], providers: [aescbc{keys:[key1]}, identity{}]
             — aescbc FIRST, identity LAST.
          3) Add --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml to
             kube-apiserver.yaml, plus a hostPath volume+mount for /etc/kubernetes/enc.
          4) Save; kubelet restarts the API server.
          5) Re-encrypt existing Secrets:
             kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
          6) Confirm in etcd the value is prefixed k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: (ciphertext).
        WHY: TLS protects the wire, not the disk; without this, Secrets sit in
        snapshots as plaintext base64.

    Q8. 🟡 External vs stacked etcd — one operational difference.
        A: STACKED etcd runs as a static pod on the control-plane node, so you
        repoint /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml and the kubelet restarts it.
        EXTERNAL etcd runs on dedicated machines (systemd, not a static pod), so a
        restore is performed on the etcd hosts, you restart the etcd SERVICE
        (systemctl), and you typically stop the API server(s) while restoring to
        keep the cluster consistent. The API server reaches external etcd via
        --etcd-servers and apiserver-etcd-client certs.

    Q9. 🟢 Check etcd cluster health from the command line.
        A: With the TLS flags set (or the alias from 11.3):
           etcdctl endpoint health                 # is this endpoint healthy?
           etcdctl member list --write-out=table    # who are the members?
           etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table # leader, DB size, revision
        These confirm etcd is up and has quorum before/after maintenance.

    Q10. 🔴 Automate a nightly etcd backup with a CronJob.
        A: Run a CronJob in kube-system that mounts the etcd certs and writes a
        timestamped snapshot to a hostPath / off-box volume:
          apiVersion: batch/v1
          kind: CronJob
          metadata: { name: etcd-backup, namespace: kube-system }
          spec:
            schedule: "0 2 * * *"          # 02:00 daily
            jobTemplate:
              spec:
                template:
                  spec:
                    hostNetwork: true
                    nodeSelector: { node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: "" }
                    tolerations:
                      - operator: Exists
                    containers:
                      - name: backup
                        image: registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.5.12-0
                        command:
                          - /bin/sh
                          - -c
                          - >
                            ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save
                            /backup/etcd-$(date +%F-%H%M).db
                            --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379
                            --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
                            --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt
                            --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
                        volumeMounts:
                          - { name: certs,  mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd, readOnly: true }
                          - { name: backup, mountPath: /backup }
                    restartPolicy: OnFailure
                    volumes:
                      - name: certs
                        hostPath: { path: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd }
                      - name: backup
                        hostPath: { path: /var/backups/etcd, type: DirectoryOrCreate }
        WHY: it must land on the control-plane node (nodeSelector + toleration),
        use hostNetwork to reach 127.0.0.1:2379, and mount the etcd certs. 🏢 In
        production also copy /var/backups/etcd off the node so a node loss doesn't
        take the backups with it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  📊 VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 11 (one timeline)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ✅ HEALTHY ──► 💾 snapshot save (verify!) ──► 💥 DISASTER ──►
   🔧 snapshot restore (NEW data-dir) ──► ✏️ repoint etcd.yaml (--data-dir + hostPath)
   ──► 🤖 kubelet restarts etcd ──► ✅ cluster back at the snapshot point

   .vs-prose: etcd is the cluster's single source of truth. The whole admin
   lifecycle is one line: keep a VERIFIED snapshot at all times; when disaster
   strikes, restore that snapshot into a NEW data directory, repoint the static
   pod manifest in BOTH the --data-dir flag and the hostPath volume, and let the
   kubelet restart etcd. Remember the three TLS flags for save (none for
   restore), the odd-member quorum rule (N/2+1), that PV data is NOT included,
   and that Secrets are plaintext at rest until you enable EncryptionConfiguration.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 12: Managing the Control Plane                              🔴  🎯
================================================================================

    [A] META: 🔴 Hard · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Cluster Architecture 25% +
        Troubleshooting 30%. The single most exam-dense chapter in the guide.

    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS:
        When the control plane misbehaves you fix it by reading logs and
        editing static-pod manifests — and the cruel twist is that you are
        often doing this with the API server itself DOWN, which means kubectl
        is dead too. If you only know how to debug "through kubectl" you are
        helpless the moment the apiserver crash-loops. This chapter teaches the
        two-layer skill: drive the control plane through kubectl when it is
        healthy, and drop down to crictl + journalctl when it is not. For the
        easypj cluster, this is the difference between a 30-second recovery and
        a rebuilt cluster.

        💡 INSIGHT: The control plane is "just pods." There is no magic daemon
        managing the apiserver — it is a Pod whose manifest happens to live in
        a directory the kubelet watches. Once you internalize "edit a file,
        kubelet restarts the pod," the whole control plane stops being a black
        box.

    [C] OBJECTIVES:
        - Manage the control plane AS static pods (find them, edit them).
        - Inspect control-plane health BOTH with kubectl and without it.
        - Safely modify components (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager).
        - Recover from a bad manifest / bad config.
        - Understand the CRI / CNI / CSI extension interfaces as ONE set —
          the three plug points that make Kubernetes pluggable.

    [D] CKA RELEVANCE:
        This material sits at the intersection of Cluster Architecture (25%)
        and Troubleshooting (30%) — together more than half the exam. Expect:
        a kubeadm/etcd task, a "the apiserver/scheduler won't start, fix it"
        task, and a "add a flag to a component" task. These are near-certain.

    [E] SECTION MAP:
        12.1  Control Plane as Static Pods                              🎯
        12.2  Inspecting Control Plane Health                           🎯
        12.3  Modifying API Server Configuration                        🎯
        12.4  Scheduler Configuration                                   🏢
        12.5  Controller Manager Tuning                                 🏢
        12.6  Extension Interfaces Together (CRI / CNI / CSI)           🎯


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.1  Control Plane as Static Pods                                   🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        - All control plane components run as STATIC PODS.
        - Manifests location: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
        - The kubelet watches this directory and manages the pods directly —
          NOT the scheduler, NOT the apiserver. That is why control-plane
          pods can exist even when the apiserver is down: the kubelet starts
          them from local files.

        [CONTROL PLANE = STATIC PODS — edit a file, kubelet restarts the pod]

           /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
             ├── etcd.yaml                     ┐
             ├── kube-apiserver.yaml           ├─ 🤖 kubelet WATCHES this dir
             ├── kube-controller-manager.yaml  │   edit  -> auto-restart (~30-60s)
             └── kube-scheduler.yaml           ┘   remove file -> pod deleted

        💡 INSIGHT: There is no `kubectl` involved in starting these. The
        kubelet polls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (the `staticPodPath` in its
        config) and reconciles the running containers against the files. A
        static pod then surfaces in the API as a read-only "mirror pod" so you
        CAN see it with `kubectl get pods -n kube-system`, but you cannot
        delete it via the API — to remove it you remove the FILE.

        ⚡ TIP: To modify a control plane component, edit its YAML in
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet auto-detects the change (mtime)
        and restarts the pod. No `systemctl restart`, no `kubectl apply`.

        📖 KEY TERM — Static Pod: a pod defined by a manifest file on a node's
        disk and managed directly by that node's kubelet, not by the API
        server. The control plane bootstraps itself this way.

        📖 KEY TERM — Mirror Pod: the read-only API object the kubelet creates
        so a static pod is visible cluster-wide. Its name is the static pod
        name plus the node name (e.g. kube-apiserver-master).

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: The kubelet's static pod path is set in
        /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml via `staticPodPath:`. Change that value
        (then restart the kubelet) and the kubelet watches a different
        directory. This is how you move the control plane manifests, and it is
        a favourite "gotcha" exam variant (see Lab Q5).


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.2  Inspecting Control Plane Health                                🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        WITH kubectl (apiserver is UP):

          $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system
          $ kubectl logs kube-apiserver-master           -n kube-system
          $ kubectl logs kube-scheduler-master           -n kube-system
          $ kubectl logs kube-controller-manager-master  -n kube-system
          $ kubectl logs etcd-master                      -n kube-system

        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  COMPONENT LOG — WHAT TO LOOK FOR                                      │
        ├────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  Component             │  What its logs / failure tells you             │
        ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  kube-apiserver        │  TLS/cert errors, etcd connection refused,     │
        │                        │  bad flag -> "unknown flag"; if down, kubectl  │
        │                        │  itself stops working.                         │
        │  kube-scheduler        │  Leader-election churn; new pods stay Pending  │
        │                        │  (no node assigned) when it is down.           │
        │  kube-controller-mgr   │  Reconcile loops failing; Deployments don't    │
        │                        │  scale, endpoints/SA tokens not created.       │
        │  etcd                  │  "connection refused", "no leader", disk slow  │
        │                        │  / fsync warnings, cert mismatch.              │
        │  kubelet (systemd)     │  Node NotReady, image pull errors, CNI not     │
        │                        │  ready, static-pod manifest parse errors.      │
        └────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        Component health endpoints (curl through the kubelet/loopback or via
        `kubectl get --raw`):
          /healthz            overall health (legacy)
          /livez?verbose      liveness, per-check breakdown
          /readyz?verbose     readiness (is it OK to serve traffic?)

          $ kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
          $ kubectl get --raw='/livez?verbose'

        WITHOUT kubectl (apiserver is DOWN) — the exam scenario:

           kubectl dead?  ─►  crictl ps -a            (list containers, incl. exited)
                          ─►  crictl logs <id>         (read that container's logs)
                          ─►  journalctl -u kubelet -f (why didn't the pod start?)

          $ sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
          $ sudo crictl logs <container-id>
          $ sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f
          $ sudo systemctl status kubelet

        🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING ORDER when "everything is down":
          1. systemctl status kubelet      — is the kubelet even running?
          2. journalctl -u kubelet         — is it failing to parse a manifest?
          3. crictl ps -a                  — which static-pod containers exist /
                                             exited?
          4. crictl logs <id>              — WHY did apiserver/etcd exit?
          5. fix the manifest / cert / etcd, wait ~30-60s, recheck.

        ⚠️ GOTCHA: crictl needs a runtime endpoint. If `crictl ps` errors,
        set it: `export CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock`
        or pass `crictl --runtime-endpoint ...`. Some exam images ship a
        /etc/crictl.yaml already; check before fighting it.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.3  Modifying API Server Configuration                             🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        - Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        - Add / modify command flags under the container's `command:` list.
        - Example: enable admission controllers
            --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity
        - After the edit: the kubelet auto-restarts the API server pod
          (~30-60s). You do NOT restart anything yourself.

        SAFE WORKFLOW (back up → edit → wait → verify → recover):

           1. cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /root/kas.bak
           2. edit the manifest (add/change exactly one flag)
           3. wait ~30-60s (watch `crictl ps` — old container exits, new starts)
           4. verify: kubectl get --raw='/readyz' ; kubectl get nodes
           5. if it never comes back: read crictl logs, fix the YAML
              (or restore the backup), wait again.

        ⚠️ WARNING: Test changes carefully — wrong config = API server won't
        start, and the moment it doesn't start, kubectl stops working. A
        single mistyped flag or a YAML indentation error takes down the whole
        management plane.

        🩺 RECOVERY: Because the manifest is just a FILE the kubelet keeps
        re-reading, recovery is local and does not need the apiserver:
          - find why it died:  crictl ps -a ; crictl logs <apiserver-id>
          - fix the YAML in place (or `cp /root/kas.bak <manifest>`)
          - the kubelet detects the new mtime and restarts the pod (~30-60s).

        ⚠️ GOTCHA — the silent-crash case: if the apiserver container starts
        then immediately exits and crictl shows nothing for it, the kubelet may
        be rejecting the manifest BEFORE creating a container. In that case the
        evidence is in `journalctl -u kubelet`, NOT in crictl logs. Always
        check the kubelet journal when no container appears at all.

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: secure ports & --bind-address determine where the
        apiserver listens; --secure-port (default 6443) serves TLS. Several
        endpoints aid debugging: /healthz, /livez, /readyz (with ?verbose),
        plus profiling (--profiling) and the metrics endpoint. Knowing
        /readyz?verbose lets you see exactly which sub-check (etcd, informer
        sync, admission) is failing.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.4  Scheduler Configuration                                        🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        - Custom scheduler profiles (KubeSchedulerConfiguration).
        - Priority classes for pod preemption.
        - Multiple schedulers in a single cluster (a pod picks one via
          `spec.schedulerName`).

        WHAT THE SCHEDULER DOES (one job): it watches for pods with no
        `nodeName` set and decides WHICH node each should run on (filter +
        score), then writes the binding. If the scheduler is down, new pods
        stay Pending forever — existing pods are unaffected.

        PriorityClass — easypj web pods outrank batch jobs:

          apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
          kind: PriorityClass
          metadata:
            name: easypj-high-priority
          value: 1000000
          globalDefault: false
          preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
          description: "easypj web tier — may preempt batch jobs under pressure."
          ---
          apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
          kind: PriorityClass
          metadata:
            name: batch-low-priority
          value: 1000
          globalDefault: false
          description: "Background jobpost batch jobs — preemptible."

        Use it in a pod:

          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Pod
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web
          spec:
            priorityClassName: easypj-high-priority
            containers:
            - name: web
              image: easypj:latest

        💡 INSIGHT: A higher `value` means higher priority. When a high-
        priority easypj pod cannot be scheduled, the scheduler may PREEMPT
        (evict) lower-priority batch pods to make room — that is what
        `preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority` enables.

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — leader election: there is only ONE active scheduler
        even if you run several replicas for HA. They contend for a Lease
        object (kube-system/kube-scheduler); the holder is the active leader,
        the rest stand by. Lease churn in the logs ("attempting to acquire
        leader lease...") usually means a connectivity or clock problem.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.5  Controller Manager Tuning                                      🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        WHAT THE CONTROLLER-MANAGER DOES (one job): it runs the reconcile
        loops — Node, Deployment/ReplicaSet, Endpoints, ServiceAccount token,
        Job, etc. It is the "make reality match desired state" engine. If it is
        down, Deployments stop scaling, new ServiceAccount tokens/secrets and
        endpoints stop being created, and dead nodes are never marked NotReady.

        Key tuning flags (edit kube-controller-manager.yaml):

        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  FLAG                          │ DEFAULT │ IMPACT                       │
        ├────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
        │  --node-monitor-grace-period   │   40s   │ How long an unresponsive     │
        │                                │         │ node may go before it is     │
        │                                │         │ marked NotReady. Lower =     │
        │                                │         │ faster failover detection,   │
        │                                │         │ more false positives.        │
        │  --node-monitor-period         │   5s    │ How often node health is     │
        │                                │         │ checked.                     │
        │  --pod-eviction-timeout        │   5m    │ How long after a node is     │
        │  (legacy; taint-based eviction │         │ NotReady before its pods are │
        │   via tolerationSeconds in     │         │ evicted/rescheduled. Lower = │
        │   newer versions)              │         │ faster recovery, riskier on  │
        │                                │         │ flaky networks.              │
        │  --terminated-pod-gc-threshold │  12500  │ How many terminated pods to  │
        │                                │         │ keep before GC kicks in.     │
        └────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

        These matter for: SLA requirements (how fast must we react to a dead
        node?) and failover speed. Tightening them makes the cluster react
        faster but raises the chance of evicting pods during a transient blip.

        🧭 DECISION GUIDE — tighten eviction timing only when:
          - the network between control plane and nodes is reliable, AND
          - workloads can tolerate being rescheduled quickly.
        On flaky infrastructure, KEEP the defaults — premature eviction storms
        are worse than a slightly slow failover.

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: like the scheduler, the controller-manager uses
        leader election (Lease kube-system/kube-controller-manager); only one
        replica reconciles at a time. The "modern" eviction path is taint-based
        (node gets node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute; pods carry a default
        tolerationSeconds), which is why --pod-eviction-timeout is increasingly
        a legacy knob.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    12.6  Extension Interfaces Together — CRI / CNI / CSI                🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        Kubernetes is pluggable through THREE socket-style interfaces. Learn
        them as a set; each is "the kubelet/cluster talking to a swappable
        implementation."

        📖 CRI — Container Runtime Interface: how the kubelet starts/stops
             containers. Implementations: containerd, CRI-O. (crictl talks to
             this socket.)
        📖 CNI — Container Network Interface: how pods get an IP and connect.
             Implementations: Calico, Flannel, Cilium, Weave. No CNI -> nodes
             stay NotReady and pods can't network.
        📖 CSI — Container Storage Interface: how volumes are provisioned and
             attached. Implementations: cloud CSI drivers, Ceph, Longhorn, etc.

        [THE THREE PLUG POINTS — what plugs into what]

           ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
           │                                                              │
           │   kubelet ──── CRI ────▶  [ runtime ]   containerd / CRI-O   │
           │                                                              │
           │   pod net ──── CNI ────▶  [ network ]   Calico / Flannel ... │
           │                                                              │
           │   volumes ──── CSI ────▶  [ storage ]   cloud / Ceph / ...   │
           │                                                              │
           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

           📖 plug points:  kubelet─CRI─runtime · pods─CNI─net · volumes─CSI─storage

        💡 ANALOGY: Think of three wall sockets. Kubernetes provides the
        sockets (the interfaces); vendors provide the appliances (the plugins).
        You can swap the runtime, the network plugin, or the storage driver
        without changing Kubernetes itself — that is the whole point of the
        interfaces.


  ┌──────────────────────── 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER ──────────────────────┐
  │                                                                              │
  │  • Static -> mirror pod: the kubelet creates a read-only API object for     │
  │    each static pod so it is cluster-visible; you manage the FILE, not the   │
  │    API object.                                                              │
  │  • Leader election: scheduler & controller-manager each hold a Lease        │
  │    object; only the leader acts. Lease timing (lease-duration, renew-       │
  │    deadline, retry-period) governs failover speed of the control plane      │
  │    itself.                                                                   │
  │  • Secure ports / --bind-address: where each component listens; apiserver   │
  │    --secure-port 6443 serves TLS.                                           │
  │  • Health endpoints: /livez, /readyz, /healthz — add ?verbose to see the    │
  │    per-check breakdown (etcd, informer sync, admission, etc.).              │
  │  • Profiling & metrics endpoints exist on each component for deep debugging.│
  │  • Controller-manager timing flags (node-monitor-grace-period,             │
  │    pod-eviction-timeout) tune how fast the cluster reacts to dead nodes.    │
  │                                                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 12                                       ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ The control plane runs AS static pods you edit IN PLACE.        ║
  ║     Manifests live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and the kubelet   ║
  ║     watches that directory and auto-starts/restarts them.          ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ Control plane components run as static pods: kube-apiserver,    ║
  ║     kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler (and etcd).            ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ Edit a manifest -> kubelet auto-restarts the pod (~30-60s).     ║
  ║     No systemctl, no kubectl apply.                                ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ When kubectl is DEAD (apiserver down), debug WITHOUT it:        ║
  ║     crictl ps -a · crictl logs <id> · journalctl -u kubelet.       ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ kubelet is the ONLY control-plane-side component that runs as a ║
  ║     systemd service — everything else is a (static) pod.           ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ Three extension interfaces: CRI (run) · CNI (network) ·         ║
  ║     CSI (storage) — the three plug points that make K8s pluggable. ║
  ║                                                                    ║

  ║     a CNI is mandatory or nodes stay NotReady.                     ║
  ║                                                                    ║

  ║  ⚠️ Editing the WRONG manifest — double-check the filename before   ║

  ║  ⚠️ Not waiting ~30-60s for the kubelet to notice the change and    ║

  ║  ⚠️ A typo or bad indentation in kube-apiserver.yaml takes the      ║
