  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 12  (full answer + explanation each)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    🧪 Q1 — List the control-plane static pods and the directory they live in.
      A: The directory is /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. It contains etcd.yaml,
         kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml and
         kube-scheduler.yaml.
           $ ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
           $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system   # mirror pods, *-<nodename>
      WHY: These four manifests are static pods owned by the kubelet. They show
      up in the API as mirror pods named e.g. kube-apiserver-master, but the
      source of truth is the FILE, not the API object.

    🧪 Q2 — The scheduler is down. What symptom on new pods, and how to fix?
      A: SYMPTOM: newly created pods stay Pending with no node assigned (no
         scheduling events; `nodeName` never set). Existing pods keep running.
         FIX: inspect why — `kubectl logs kube-scheduler-master -n kube-system`
         (or crictl if the apiserver is also affected), check
         /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml for a bad flag/typo,
         fix it, wait ~30-60s for the kubelet to restart the pod.
      WHY: The scheduler is the only thing that binds Pending pods to nodes. No
      scheduler = nothing gets a node, so pods pile up Pending.

    🧪 Q3 — Add a `--feature-gates=...` flag to a component safely.
      A:  1. Back up: cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /root/kas.bak
          2. Edit the manifest; add the flag under the container's command:
               - --feature-gates=SomeGate=true
          3. Save; wait ~30-60s (watch `crictl ps`).
          4. Verify: kubectl get --raw='/readyz' and kubectl get nodes.
          5. If it won't start: crictl logs the container / read journalctl,
             fix the YAML or restore the backup.
      WHY: The manifest is read by the kubelet on every change. A clean
      back-up-edit-wait-verify loop means a mistake is always recoverable
      locally — no apiserver needed to fix the apiserver.

    🧪 Q4 — ALL control-plane components are down. What is your debugging order?
      A:  1. systemctl status kubelet  — is the kubelet running at all?
          2. journalctl -u kubelet     — manifest parse errors? cert problems?
          3. crictl ps -a              — which static-pod containers exist/exited?
          4. crictl logs <id>          — WHY did etcd/apiserver exit?
          5. Fix root cause (often etcd or apiserver), wait ~30-60s, recheck.
      WHY: With kubectl dead you must work bottom-up: kubelet -> containers ->
      logs. etcd or the apiserver is usually the root; everything else fails
      downstream of them.

    🧪 Q5 — Change the kubelet's staticPodPath.
      A: Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml and set `staticPodPath:` to the new
         directory, move the manifests there, then restart the kubelet:
           $ sudo systemctl restart kubelet
         The kubelet now watches the new path and starts the static pods from
         it.
      WHY: staticPodPath is what tells the kubelet WHICH directory to watch.
      Changing it (and the kubelet config requires a kubelet restart to reload)
      relocates the entire control plane's manifest source.

    🧪 Q6 — Scheduler vs controller-manager: one job each.
      A: SCHEDULER: decides which NODE each unscheduled pod runs on (binding).
         CONTROLLER-MANAGER: runs the reconcile loops (Node, Deployment/RS,
         Endpoints, ServiceAccount, Job, ...) to make actual state match
         desired state.
      WHY: Scheduler = placement decision (one-time, per pod). Controller-
      manager = continuous reconciliation. Different symptoms when each fails:
      Pending pods (scheduler) vs no scaling / no endpoints (controller-mgr).

    🧪 Q7 — Check a component's health endpoint.
      A: $ kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
         $ kubectl get --raw='/livez?verbose'
         $ kubectl get --raw='/healthz'
         (Or curl the component's secure port directly on the node.)
      WHY: The ?verbose form lists each sub-check (etcd, informer-sync,
      admission), so you see precisely which one is red instead of a bare
      "unhealthy."

    🧪 Q8 — The controller-manager is crash-looping. Where do you look?
      A: kubectl logs kube-controller-manager-master -n kube-system (if the
         apiserver is up); otherwise crictl ps -a | grep controller, then
         crictl logs <id>; and journalctl -u kubelet if no container appears.
         Common causes: bad flag/typo in kube-controller-manager.yaml, missing
         /unreadable cert, or unreachable apiserver.
      WHY: A crash loop means the container starts then dies — the reason is in
      the container logs (or, if it never starts, in the kubelet journal).

    🧪 Q9 — Create a static pod on a WORKER node, then remove it.
      A: On the worker, drop a pod manifest into its staticPodPath
         (default /etc/kubernetes/manifests/), e.g.:
           apiVersion: v1
           kind: Pod
           metadata: { name: easypj-static }
           spec:
             containers:
             - name: web
               image: easypj:latest
         The kubelet starts it; it appears as mirror pod easypj-static-<node>.
         To REMOVE it, delete the FILE — `kubectl delete pod` will not stick
         because the kubelet re-creates it from the manifest.
      WHY: Static pods are file-driven. The file is the desired state; the API
      object is just a read-only mirror, so removal must happen at the file.

    🧪 Q10 — Match CRI / CNI / CSI to runtime / network / storage.
      A: CRI -> Container Runtime Interface -> RUNTIME (containerd, CRI-O).
         CNI -> Container Network Interface -> NETWORK (Calico, Flannel, ...).
         CSI -> Container Storage Interface -> STORAGE (cloud/Ceph/Longhorn).
      WHY: These are the three plug points: kubelet─CRI─runtime,
      pods─CNI─network, volumes─CSI─storage. Memorize the triplet as a set.

    🧪 DRILL: Add a harmless flag (e.g. --v=4) to kube-controller-manager.yaml,
      confirm via crictl/logs that it restarted with the flag, then REVERT and
      confirm it returns to normal. Practising the back-up/edit/wait/revert
      loop until it is muscle memory is the single best prep for the exam's
      control-plane tasks.


  [N] 🖼️ VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 12

        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  THE CONTROL PLANE AS STATIC PODS + THE 3 PLUG POINTS              │
        │                                                                    │
        │   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/   ── 🤖 kubelet watches ──▶ restarts │
        │     etcd · apiserver · controller-manager · scheduler              │
        │                                                                    │
        │   kubectl dead?  ─► crictl ps -a · crictl logs · journalctl -u    │
        │                                              kubelet               │
        │                                                                    │
        │   kubelet ─CRI─▶ runtime   pods ─CNI─▶ network   vol ─CSI─▶ storage│
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      .vs-prose SUMMARY: The Kubernetes control plane is not a set of mystical
      daemons — it is four static pods (etcd, kube-apiserver,
      kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler) whose manifests sit in
      /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet, the one piece that runs as a
      plain systemd service, watches that directory and (re)starts those pods
      whenever a file changes — typically within 30 to 60 seconds. You
      configure the control plane by editing those YAML files in place; a typo
      takes the apiserver (and kubectl) down, but because the fix is a local
      file the kubelet keeps re-reading, recovery never needs the apiserver.
      When kubectl is dead, you debug bottom-up with crictl ps -a, crictl logs,
      and journalctl -u kubelet. The scheduler places pods on nodes; the
      controller-manager runs the reconcile loops — distinct failure symptoms
      (Pending pods vs stalled scaling) tell you which one broke. Finally,
      Kubernetes stays pluggable through three interfaces learned as one set:
      CRI for the runtime, CNI for the network, CSI for storage.

  [PART 3 VISUAL SUMMARY]: bare nodes -> kubeadm -> configured, backed-up
  cluster running easypj.

  .vs-prose SUMMARY: Part 3 takes you from bare Linux nodes to a configured,
  backed-up Kubernetes cluster running easypj. kubeadm init stands up the
  control plane and kubeadm join attaches workers; a CNI plugin is non-optional
  or the nodes never go Ready. From there you operate the cluster by editing
  static-pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and you protect it with
  etcd snapshots — save with the etcd certs, restore into a fresh data-dir and
  repoint etcd.yaml. The whole stack stays extensible through CRI, CNI and CSI.
  These are the highest-yield skills on the exam: roughly a quarter of it lives
  in this part, and etcd plus kubeadm tasks are all but guaranteed.

PART 4: WORKLOADS & SCHEDULING                                       🟡 🎯

  What you'll build: easypj scaled to 3 self-healing replicas with zero-
  downtime rollouts, autoscaling, smart placement, and the right workload
  type for every job (web, db, batch, per-node agent).
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [PART 4 INTRO]
  A Pod alone is fragile. Kill its node and it's gone; bump the image and you
  must hand-edit and re-create it; flood it with traffic and it has no way to
  grow. This part is about the controllers and policies that make workloads
  ROBUST and SELF-HEALING: Deployments for stateless apps, rolling updates &
  rollbacks, autoscaling under load, scheduling so the right pod lands on the
  right node, resource governance so no pod starves another, and the
  specialized workload types (Job / CronJob / DaemonSet / StatefulSet).

  Where Part 3 taught you to RUN a single Pod and wire it with a Service,
  Part 4 teaches you to RUN MANY, KEEP THEM RUNNING, PLACE THEM WISELY, and
  BUDGET their resources. This is the bridge from "I can launch a container"
  to "I operate a fleet."

  🧠 ANALOGY: A bare Pod is a single employee with no manager. A Deployment is
  the manager who notices when someone quits, hires a replacement to keep
  headcount at the target, and rolls out new policy one team-member at a time
  so the office never goes dark. The scheduler is HR deciding which desk each
  hire sits at; requests/limits are the office budget that stops one team from
  hogging every meeting room.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 4 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch13 RUN & SCALE ──▶ Ch14 PLACE (scheduling) ──▶ Ch15 GOVERN (resources)│
  │  Deploy/RS/HPA          affinity/taints/topology     requests/limits/QoS │
  │            └────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘            │
  │                                 ▼                                        │
  │            Ch16 SPECIALIZE: Job · CronJob · DaemonSet · StatefulSet      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read it left-to-right as a pipeline: first you make easypj durable and
  scalable (Ch13), then you control WHERE its pods land (Ch14), then you set
  the resource budget so the cluster stays fair and stable (Ch15), and finally
  you reach for the right specialized controller when a plain Deployment is the
  wrong tool — a batch job, a scheduled backup, a per-node agent, or a sticky
  stateful database (Ch16).

  🧭 WORKLOAD-TYPE DECISION GUIDE — pick the controller before you write YAML
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Is the work a one-shot task that should run to completion and stop?       │
  │     YES, once .................................................. Job      │
  │     YES, but on a schedule (e.g. nightly db-backup) ........... CronJob   │
  │ NO — it's a long-running service. Does each replica need a stable         │
  │ identity / its own persistent volume / ordered start (a database)?        │
  │     YES ................................................... StatefulSet   │
  │ NO — must exactly one copy run on EVERY node (logs, metrics, CNI)?        │
  │     YES ..................................................... DaemonSet   │
  │ NO — plain stateless, interchangeable replicas (the easypj web tier)?     │
  │     YES ............................. Deployment (manages a ReplicaSet)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [PART 4 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread (one continuous story across the four chapters):
    1. Turn the easypj web tier into a Deployment (3 replicas, self-healing).
    2. Roll out v2 of easypj with ZERO downtime, then practice a rollback.
    3. Autoscale the Deployment under load with an HPA.
    4. Pin the postgres db pods to fast-disk nodes via affinity / taints.
    5. Set requests/limits so QoS classes are sane and no pod starves another.
    6. Add a CronJob (db-backup) that dumps the jobpost data on a schedule.
    7. Run the postgres tier as a StatefulSet with stable identity + storage.

  By the end, easypj is no longer a fragile hand-launched Pod — it is a fleet
  that survives node loss, upgrades cleanly, grows under traffic, lands its
  pods on the right hardware, and lives inside a fair resource budget.

  📖 NOTE: ConfigMaps & Secrets (an official Workloads competency in the CKA
  curriculum) are taught in depth in Ch 23 (Part 6) and merely USED here — when
  this part references a ConfigMap for easypj settings or a Secret for the
  postgres password, treat it as a forward reference and lean on Ch 23 for the
  full mechanics.

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE: This 15% domain is where the exam spends the most "build
  something and make it survive" tasks — scale a Deployment, perform a rolling
  update and a rollback, schedule a pod onto (or away from) a node with
  taints/tolerations/affinity, fix a pod stuck Pending because of resource
  requests, and create a Job/CronJob/DaemonSet. Every chapter here closes with
  a 🧪 LAB Q&A drilling exactly those imperative + declarative moves.

================================================================================
  Chapter 13: Deployments, ReplicaSets & Scaling                       🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Workloads & Scheduling (15%).
      🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC] — this is one of the most heavily tested chapters.

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS:
      Deployments are HOW you ship and update easypj safely. A bare Pod is a
      pet — kill it and it stays dead. A Deployment is a herd manager: it keeps
      N replicas of easypj-web alive, rolls out a new image one pod at a time
      with zero downtime, and lets you instantly roll back when the v3 image
      turns out to be broken. In the exam and in production, you will create,
      scale, update, roll back, pause/resume, and autoscale Deployments far more
      than any other object. VISUAL: the rolling-update timeline below is the
      mental model to burn in.

      🧠 ANALOGY: A ReplicaSet is a thermostat — it has ONE job: keep the room
      at exactly N pods. A Deployment is the smart home that owns several
      thermostats over time (one per version) and switches between them
      gracefully so the house never goes cold during the changeover.

  [C] OBJECTIVES:
      - Create and scale Deployments (imperative + declarative YAML).
      - Perform and WATCH rolling updates; tune maxSurge / maxUnavailable.
      - Roll back to any previous revision; pause/resume to batch edits.
      - Understand ReplicaSets under the hood (selectors, revision history).
      - Autoscale with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).
      - Configure liveness / readiness / startup probes for robust
        self-healing.

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE:
      Expect tasks like "scale deploy X to N", "update the image and confirm
      the rollout", "a rollout is stuck — roll it back", "create an HPA min 3
      max 10 at 70% CPU", and "add a readiness probe so traffic only hits ready
      pods". These are fast, high-value points if your imperative speed is good.

  [E] SECTION MAP:
      13.1  Deployments — Complete Lifecycle
      13.2  ReplicaSets — Under the Hood
      13.3  Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
      13.4  Deployment Strategies
      13.5  Health Probes & Self-Healing Primitives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  13.1  Deployments — Complete Lifecycle                       🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The object hierarchy you must never forget:

       Deployment  ──owns──►  ReplicaSet  ──owns──►  Pods
       (desired state,        (keeps N copies        (your easypj
        rollout history)       of one pod template)   containers)

  a) Creating a Deployment

     Imperative (fast — exam-friendly):
       $ kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3

     Declarative Deployment YAML (all key fields):

       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: Deployment
       metadata:
         name: easypj
         labels:
           app: easypj
       spec:
         replicas: 3
         revisionHistoryLimit: 10        # how many old ReplicaSets to keep
         selector:
           matchLabels:
             app: easypj                 # MUST match template labels (immutable)
         strategy:
           type: RollingUpdate
           rollingUpdate:
             maxSurge: 1                  # +1 extra pod allowed during update
             maxUnavailable: 0           # never drop below desired during update
         minReadySeconds: 5              # pod must stay ready 5s before "available"
         progressDeadlineSeconds: 600    # mark rollout failed if no progress in 10m
         template:
           metadata:
             labels:
               app: easypj               # selected by the ReplicaSet
           spec:
             containers:
               - name: django
                 image: easypj:v1
                 ports:
                   - containerPort: 8000
                 resources:
                   requests:             # REQUIRED for HPA to work!
                     cpu: 100m
                     memory: 128Mi
                   limits:
                     cpu: 500m
                     memory: 256Mi

       💡 INSIGHT: selector.matchLabels MUST be a subset of template labels, and
       the selector is IMMUTABLE once created — you cannot re-point a live
       Deployment at a different label set; you must delete and recreate.

  b) Scaling

     $ kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5

     Three ways to scale (memorize for Q4):
       1. Imperative:   kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
       2. Declarative:  edit replicas: in YAML, then kubectl apply -f
       3. Automatic:    HPA (see 13.3) adjusts replicas for you

     $ kubectl autoscale deployment easypj --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70

     HPA YAML (autoscaling/v2):

       apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
       kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
       metadata:
         name: easypj
       spec:
         scaleTargetRef:
           apiVersion: apps/v1
           kind: Deployment
           name: easypj
         minReplicas: 3
         maxReplicas: 10
         metrics:
           - type: Resource
             resource:
               name: cpu
               target:
                 type: Utilization
                 averageUtilization: 70

  c) Rolling Updates

     $ kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=easypj:v2
     $ kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj

     [ROLLING UPDATE IN ACTION]
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  ROLLING UPDATE: easypj v1 → v2                   │
     │                                                    │
     │  Time 0:  [v1] [v1] [v1]          ← all v1       │
     │  Time 1:  [v1] [v1] [v1] [v2]     ← v2 starting  │
     │  Time 2:  [v1] [v1] [v2] [v2]     ← v1 stopping  │
     │  Time 3:  [v1] [v2] [v2] [v2]     ← almost done  │
     │  Time 4:  [v2] [v2] [v2]          ← all v2 ✅    │
     │                                                    │
     │  maxSurge: 1       (1 extra pod during update)    │
     │  maxUnavailable: 0 (never fewer than 3 running)   │
     │  Zero downtime throughout! 🎉                      │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     The same timeline, annotated with the READY gate (C2 augment):

       maxSurge:1  maxUnavailable:0   (always >= 3 ready)
       t0  [v1][v1][v1]                 all v1
       t1  [v1][v1][v1][v2]+            spin up 1 new (surge)
       t2  [v1][v1][v2][v2]             old one removed once new is READY
       t3  [v1][v2][v2][v2]             repeat...
       t4  [v2][v2][v2]              ✅ all v2, never < 3 serving
       ↩️ broke it? kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj  (old RS kept at 0)

       🔑 The key invariant: a NEW pod is added (surge) and only AFTER it
       becomes Ready is an OLD pod removed. That is why maxUnavailable:0 +
       maxSurge:1 gives true zero downtime.

  d) Rollbacks                                            🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

     $ kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj
     $ kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj --revision=2
     $ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj
     $ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=2

     [ROLLBACK — v3 broken → back to v2]
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  REVISION HISTORY (each = one old ReplicaSet)             │
     │                                                            │
     │   rev 1  easypj:v1   RS-aaa  replicas=0  (kept, idle)     │
     │   rev 2  easypj:v2   RS-bbb  replicas=3  ◄── healthy      │
     │   rev 3  easypj:v3   RS-ccc  replicas=0  ✗ CrashLoop      │
     │                                                            │
     │  $ kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj --to-revision=2     │
     │       │                                                    │
     │       ▼  scales RS-bbb back up, RS-ccc back to 0          │
     │   rev 4  easypj:v2   RS-bbb  replicas=3  ◄── restored ✅  │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

       🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: a rollback is NOT a delete — Kubernetes keeps the old
       ReplicaSets (scaled to 0) up to revisionHistoryLimit. "undo" simply scales
       the chosen old RS back up and scales the bad one to 0, creating a NEW
       revision number in the process.

  e) Pause / Resume — batch multiple edits into ONE rollout

     $ kubectl rollout pause deployment/easypj
     $ kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=easypj:v2
     $ kubectl set resources deployment/easypj -c=django --limits=cpu=600m
     $ kubectl rollout resume deployment/easypj     # ← single combined rollout

       💡 Without pause, EACH edit triggers its own rollout. Pause first, make
       all the changes, then resume to roll them out together — far fewer pod
       churns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  13.2  ReplicaSets — Under the Hood                           🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  - Deployments create and manage ReplicaSets — you almost never create a
    ReplicaSet directly.
  - A ReplicaSet's ONLY job: keep exactly spec.replicas pods matching its
    selector alive. Pod dies / node fails → RS makes a replacement.
  - ReplicaSets use label selectors to track their pods.
  - matchLabels vs matchExpressions: matchLabels is simple equality;
    matchExpressions adds set-based operators (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist).
  - revisionHistoryLimit (on the Deployment) controls how many old RS are kept
    for rollback.

  ReplicaSet YAML (for understanding — rarely created directly):

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: ReplicaSet
    metadata:
      name: easypj-rs
    spec:
      replicas: 3
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: easypj
        matchExpressions:                 # set-based selector example
          - key: tier
            operator: In
            values: [web, api]
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: easypj
            tier: web
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: django
              image: easypj:v1
              ports:
                - containerPort: 8000

  ⚠️ NEVER edit a ReplicaSet directly when it is owned by a Deployment — the
  Deployment controller will fight you and revert the change. Edit the
  Deployment instead.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  13.3  Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)                        🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  - Automatically scales the number of pods based on CPU / memory / custom
    metrics.
  - REQUIRES the Metrics Server installed (or another metrics provider).
  - REQUIRES resource requests on the containers — utilization is computed as a
    percentage of the request; no request = HPA has no denominator and does
    nothing.

  $ kubectl autoscale deployment easypj --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
  $ kubectl get hpa
  $ kubectl describe hpa easypj            # shows current vs target & decisions

  [HPA SCALING FLOW]
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HPA: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler                        │
  │                                                         │
  │  📊 Metrics Server reports: CPU = 85%                  │
  │       │                                                  │
  │       ▼                                                  │
  │  🤖 HPA evaluates: target is 70%                       │
  │       │                                                  │
  │       ▼                                                  │
  │  📈 HPA decides: need more replicas                    │
  │       │                                                  │
  │       ▼                                                  │
  │  ⚙️ HPA updates: deployment.spec.replicas = 5          │
  │       │                                                  │
  │       ▼                                                  │
  │  📦📦📦📦📦  5 pods running, CPU drops to 65%          │
  │       │                                                  │
  │  ... traffic decreases ...                              │
  │       │                                                  │
  │  📊 CPU = 30%  →  HPA scales down to 3 replicas       │
  │  📦📦📦                                                 │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  The control loop, formalized:
       desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × (currentMetric / targetMetric) )
       e.g. 3 × (85 / 70) = ceil(3.64) = 4 replicas

  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: HPA edits the Deployment's /scale subresource (not the YAML
  you wrote). It re-evaluates roughly every 15s. By design it scales UP fast and
  DOWN slow — a stabilization window (default 5m for scale-down) prevents
  flapping when traffic is bursty.

  🔬 DEEPER — HPA v2 (autoscaling/v2):
    - Multiple metrics: HPA picks the recommendation that yields the MOST
      replicas (safest).
    - Custom & external metrics: requests-per-second, queue depth, etc.
    - behavior block tunes scaleUp / scaleDown with policies and
      stabilizationWindowSeconds.

  🏢 DAY-2 / BEYOND — the three autoscalers (know WHEN to use each):
    ┌─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ HPA (this section)  │ adds/removes POD replicas based on load        │
    │ VPA                 │ right-sizes a pod's CPU/mem REQUESTS (not count)│
    │ Cluster Autoscaler  │ adds/removes NODES when pods can't be scheduled │
    └─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    ⚠️ Don't run HPA and VPA on the SAME metric (CPU) for the same workload —
    they conflict.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  13.4  Deployment Strategies                                  🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  a) RollingUpdate (default)
     - Replace pods gradually.
     - maxSurge + maxUnavailable control the pace (see 13.1c).
     - maxSurge: how many EXTRA pods above desired during the update.
     - maxUnavailable: how many BELOW desired you tolerate during the update.
     - Both accept counts (e.g. 1) or percentages (e.g. 25%).

  b) Recreate
     - Kill ALL old pods first, then create the new ones.
     - Causes downtime! Use only when versions are mutually incompatible
       (e.g. a breaking DB schema migration where v1 and v2 cannot run at once).

  [COMPARISON TABLE]
  ┌───────────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy      │ Downtime │ When to use                         │
  ├───────────────┼──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ RollingUpdate │ None     │ Most cases (default)                │
  │ Recreate      │ Yes      │ Breaking changes, DB migrations     │
  └───────────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

  🏢 DAY-2 / BEYOND — strategies Kubernetes does NOT build in natively:
    ┌───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Blue-Green│ run v2 (green) fully alongside v1 (blue), then flip the   │
    │           │ Service selector all at once. Instant rollback = flip back│
    │ Canary    │ send a small % of traffic to v2 (e.g. 1 of 10 replicas or │
    │           │ a 2nd Deployment behind the same Service), watch metrics, │
    │           │ then ramp up. Done with two Deployments or a service mesh. │
    └───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    💡 A poor-man's canary: a 2nd Deployment (easypj-canary, replicas=1) sharing
    the Service's selector labels — ~10% of traffic hits the new version.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  13.5  Health Probes & Self-Healing Primitives               🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  📖 KEY TERMS — the three probe types:
    - livenessProbe  — "is it ALIVE?" Fails → kubelet RESTARTS the container.
                       Use to recover from deadlocks / hung processes.
    - readinessProbe — "is it READY for traffic?" Fails → pod is removed from
                       Service Endpoints (no traffic) but is NOT restarted.
    - startupProbe   — "has it FINISHED booting?" Protects slow-starting apps;
                       while it runs, liveness & readiness are suspended. Once it
                       passes once, it never runs again.

  Probe HANDLERS (the same four for all three probe types):
    HTTP (httpGet) · TCP (tcpSocket) · Exec (command) · gRPC (grpc).

  Tuning knobs:
    initialDelaySeconds · periodSeconds · timeoutSeconds ·
    failureThreshold · successThreshold.

  easypj-web container with all three probes:

    startupProbe:                 # protect a slow boot; gates the others
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 5            # up to 150s to start before liveness applies
    readinessProbe:               # gate traffic (endpoints) — no restart
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8000 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
    livenessProbe:                # restart if truly dead
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 20
      failureThreshold: 3

  THE "robust self-healing" trio (an official competency) =
    ReplicaSet (replace lost pods) + Probes (detect sick pods) +
    PodDisruptionBudget (survive voluntary disruption).

  [PROBE-DECISION CARD — which probe, when]
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Symptom      │ Use which probe          │ Effect on failure            │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
  │ App hangs /  │ livenessProbe            │ container RESTARTED           │
  │ deadlocks    │                          │                              │
  │ Warming up / │ readinessProbe           │ removed from endpoints; NO    │
  │ DB not ready │                          │ traffic; NO restart           │
  │ Slow boot    │ startupProbe             │ suspends liveness/readiness   │
  │ (migrations) │                          │ until boot done               │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  [THE SELF-HEALING LOOP]
        probe runs (HTTP/TCP/Exec/gRPC)
                │
        ┌───────┴────────┐
        │                │
   liveness fail    readiness fail
        │                │
        ▼                ▼
   kubelet RESTARTS  drop pod from
   the container     Service Endpoints
                     (503s, no restart)

  [SELF-HEALING TRIO — the official "robust deployment" primitives]
   ┌────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🔁 ReplicaSet   │ pod/node lost  ─► recreate to keep replica count│
   │ ❤️ Probes       │ liveness fails ─► restart;  readiness fails ─►  │
   │                │ drop from endpoints (no traffic, no restart)    │
   │ 🛡️ PDB          │ drain/upgrade  ─► keep minAvailable up          │
   └────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   ⚠️ aggressive liveness ⇒ restart storms · readiness ≠ liveness.

  ⚠️ A too-aggressive liveness probe causes restart storms (it kills a pod that
  was merely slow); readiness != liveness; a failing readiness empties endpoints
  (clients get 503s) WITHOUT restarting the pod. When in doubt, prefer readiness.

================================================================================
  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 13 (quick-reference)
================================================================================

  [ROLLING UPDATE — easypj v1 -> v2 with ZERO downtime]
   maxSurge:1  maxUnavailable:0   (always >= 3 ready)
   t0  [v1][v1][v1]                 all v1
   t1  [v1][v1][v1][v2]+            spin up 1 new (surge)
   t2  [v1][v1][v2][v2]             old one removed once new is READY
   t3  [v1][v2][v2][v2]             repeat...
   t4  [v2][v2][v2]              ✅ all v2, never < 3 serving
   ↩️ broke it? kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj  (old ReplicaSet kept at 0)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UTH: the rolling-update math — each step the Deployment scales the NEW
     ReplicaSet up and the OLD one down, respecting maxSurge/maxUnavailable, so
     the running total stays inside [desired - maxUnavailable, desired +
     maxSurge]. `kubectl rollout status` reads .status.conditions (Progressing /
     Available) plus updatedReplicas/availableReplicas to decide "done". Each
     revision maps to a distinct old ReplicaSet kept (scaled to 0) for rollback.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
     - progressDeadlineSeconds: if no progress within this window, the rollout's
       Progressing condition flips to False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded
       (a "stuck" rollout) — your cue to `rollout undo`.
     - minReadySeconds: a new pod must stay Ready this long before it counts as
       Available (catches pods that crash seconds after starting).
     - Available vs Progressing conditions: Available = enough ready pods now;
       Progressing = the rollout is still advancing.
     - HPA v2 behavior: stabilizationWindowSeconds + scaleUp/scaleDown policies.
     - The /scale subresource is what `kubectl scale` and HPA both write to.
     - Canary via two Deployments sharing a Service selector.

================================================================================
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
================================================================================
  - Hierarchy: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Manage the Deployment; let it
    manage the rest.
  - Rolling update + `rollout undo` = safe ship + instant rollback.
  - maxSurge / maxUnavailable control pace; maxSurge:1 + maxUnavailable:0 with
    a "remove old only after new is Ready" rule = true zero downtime.
  - HPA needs BOTH resource requests AND the metrics-server; it edits /scale.
  - The robust self-healing trio = ReplicaSet + Probes + PodDisruptionBudget.
  - liveness = restart; readiness = traffic gate; startup = boot protection.
  - Old ReplicaSets are kept (scaled to 0) up to revisionHistoryLimit — that is
    what makes `--to-revision` possible.

================================================================================
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
================================================================================
  - The selector is IMMUTABLE — you cannot change matchLabels on a live
    Deployment; delete and recreate.
  - HPA does NOTHING without resource requests (no denominator for %).
  - HPA does nothing without metrics-server (or another metrics API).
  - A stuck rollout (bad image, ImagePullBackOff/CrashLoop) → `rollout undo`.
  - An aggressive liveness probe causes RESTART STORMS — it kills slow-but-fine
    pods. Give it a startup probe or a higher failureThreshold/initialDelay.
  - readiness ≠ liveness: a failing readiness drops traffic, does NOT restart.
  - Recreate strategy = downtime; never use it unless versions are incompatible.
  - Never hand-edit a Deployment-owned ReplicaSet — the controller reverts it.

================================================================================
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
================================================================================
  - Update image fast:    kubectl set image deploy/easypj django=easypj:v2
  - Always confirm:        kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj
  - Scale fast:            kubectl scale deploy/easypj --replicas=N
  - Roll back fast:        kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj
  - Roll back to a rev:    kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj --to-revision=N
  - Generate YAML, don't type it:
        kubectl create deploy easypj --image=easypj:v1 \
          --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
  - Watch pods churn live:  kubectl get pods -w

================================================================================
  🔑 COMMANDS
================================================================================
  kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3
  kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
  kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=easypj:v2
  kubectl rollout status   deployment/easypj
  kubectl rollout history  deployment/easypj
  kubectl rollout history  deployment/easypj --revision=2
  kubectl rollout undo     deployment/easypj
  kubectl rollout undo     deployment/easypj --to-revision=2
  kubectl rollout pause    deployment/easypj
  kubectl rollout resume   deployment/easypj
  kubectl autoscale deployment easypj --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
  kubectl get rs        # see the ReplicaSets a Deployment owns
  kubectl get hpa ; kubectl describe hpa easypj

================================================================================
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 13  (union of both editions)
================================================================================

  🧪 DRILL: roll easypj v1 → v2 → a bad image → undo, watching each step with
            `kubectl rollout status` and `kubectl get pods -w`.

  Q1. Update easypj to v2 with zero downtime — give the command AND the fields
      that control it.
      A: kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=easypj:v2
         then kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj.
         Zero downtime is controlled by strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge (allow an
         extra pod) and maxUnavailable (set to 0 so the count never drops below
         desired). A new pod is added and only after it is Ready is an old one
         removed.

  Q2. A rollout is stuck on a bad image — diagnose and roll back.
      A: Diagnose: kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj (hangs / shows
         "waiting"), kubectl get pods (ImagePullBackOff or CrashLoopBackOff),
         kubectl describe pod <p> for the event, and the Progressing condition
         may read ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Fix: kubectl rollout undo
         deployment/easypj (or --to-revision=N for a specific good revision).

  Q3. RollingUpdate vs Recreate — when is each correct?
      A: RollingUpdate (default) for almost everything — no downtime, gradual
         replacement. Recreate only when old and new versions cannot coexist
         (e.g. a breaking DB schema migration); it kills all old pods first, so
         it incurs downtime.

  Q4. Give 3 ways to scale a Deployment.
      A: (1) Imperative: kubectl scale deploy easypj --replicas=5.
         (2) Declarative: edit replicas: in YAML, kubectl apply -f.
         (3) Automatic: an HPA adjusting replicas based on metrics.

  Q5. Name the chain for pod easypj-web-7d4-x9k2.
      A: Deployment easypj-web → ReplicaSet easypj-web-7d4 → Pod
         easypj-web-7d4-x9k2. The middle hash segment identifies the ReplicaSet
         (pod-template hash); the last segment is the pod's random suffix.

  Q6. Create an HPA 3→10 at 70% CPU — what prerequisite is required?
      A: kubectl autoscale deployment easypj --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70.
         Prerequisites: the metrics-server must be installed AND the containers
         must declare CPU resource requests (utilization is a % of the request).

  Q7. maxSurge:1 / maxUnavailable:0 with 3 replicas — how many pods peak?
      A: 4 pods at peak (3 desired + 1 surge). The count never drops below 3
         because maxUnavailable is 0.

  Q8. Pause a Deployment, make 2 edits, resume as ONE rollout.
      A: kubectl rollout pause deploy/easypj ; kubectl set image
         deploy/easypj django=easypj:v2 ; kubectl set resources deploy/easypj
         -c=django --limits=cpu=600m ; kubectl rollout resume deploy/easypj.
         Resume triggers a single combined rollout instead of one per edit.

  Q9. Add a startup probe so a slow-booting easypj isn't killed early.
      A: Add a startupProbe (e.g. httpGet /healthz:8000, periodSeconds 5,
         failureThreshold 30 → up to ~150s grace). While it runs, liveness and
         readiness are suspended, so a slow migration boot won't trip liveness
         and cause restart storms.

  Q10. A failing readiness probe — what happens to traffic vs the pod?
      A: The pod is removed from the Service's Endpoints, so it receives NO new
         traffic (clients see it as not-ready). The pod is NOT restarted — only
         a failing LIVENESS probe restarts the container.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: one Deployment owns many ReplicaSets over time (one per
      revision); a rolling update shifts pods from the old RS to the new RS one
      at a time while the count stays at or above desired, and `rollout undo`
      simply scales a kept old RS back up — giving you safe ship plus instant
      rollback.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 14: Scheduling & Node Management                             🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~3h · Domain: Workloads & Scheduling 15%
      (Pod admission & scheduling). Exam weight is high — placement questions
      (affinity, taints, cordon/drain) appear almost every attempt.

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS: the scheduler decides WHERE your pods run. You need to
      control placement (put easypj near its cache, spread replicas for HA, keep
      pods off GPU nodes) AND keep nodes maintainable (patch the OS without
      dropping traffic). Get this wrong and pods sit Pending forever, or all your
      replicas land on one node and a single reboot takes the app down.

  [C] OBJECTIVES:
      • Explain the scheduler's filter → score → bind pipeline.
      • Place pods with nodeSelector and node affinity (required vs preferred).
      • Co-locate and spread pods with pod (anti-)affinity.
      • Repel pods with taints and permit them with tolerations.
      • Maintain nodes safely: cordon → drain → uncordon (+ PodDisruptionBudget).
      • Spread evenly with topology spread constraints.
      • Rank pods with PriorityClass and understand preemption.

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE: 🎯 Scheduling is a named exam objective. Expect tasks like
      "make this pod run only on nodes labelled disk=ssd", "taint a node and add a
      toleration", "drain node01 for maintenance", and "why is this pod Pending?".
      Node management (cordon/drain/uncordon) is a near-guaranteed question.

  [E] SECTION MAP:
      14.1  How the Scheduler Works
      14.2  Node Selectors — Simple Placement
      14.3  Node Affinity — Advanced Placement
      14.4  Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity
      14.5  Taints and Tolerations
      14.6  Node Management for Admins
      14.7  Topology Spread Constraints
      14.8  Priority and Preemption
      14.9  🏋️ Practice Exercises
      🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
      🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.1  How the Scheduler Works                                          🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    The kube-scheduler watches for pods with no node assigned (spec.nodeName is
    empty) and runs each through a three-step pipeline:

      - Filtering phase: which nodes CAN run this pod? (a yes/no predicate test)
      - Scoring phase: which passing node is the BEST fit? (a 0–100 ranking)
      - Binding phase: write the winning node into the pod, then kubelet runs it.

    📖 Filtering is also called "predicates"; scoring is also called "priorities"
    in older docs. Criteria that feed these phases: free resources (CPU/memory),
    node affinity, taints/tolerations, topology, volume constraints.

          [SCHEDULER DECISION FLOWCHART]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  NEW POD NEEDS SCHEDULING (easypj: 256Mi, 250m CPU)    │
          │       │                                                  │
          │       ▼                                                  │
          │  ═══════════════ PHASE 1: FILTERING ═══════════════    │
          │  "Which nodes CAN run this pod?"                        │
          │                                                          │
          │  Node 1 (512Mi free, 500m free)  → ✅ PASSES            │
          │  Node 2 (128Mi free, 100m free)  → ❌ Insufficient mem  │
          │  Node 3 (1Gi free, 1000m free)   → ✅ PASSES            │
          │  Node 4 (taint: gpu=true)        → ❌ No toleration     │
          │       │                                                  │
          │       ▼ (only passing nodes continue)                   │
          │  ═══════════════ PHASE 2: SCORING ════════════════     │
          │  "Which passing node is the BEST fit?"                  │
          │                                                          │
          │  Node 1: score 65  (good fit, balanced resources)       │
          │  Node 3: score 82  (better fit, more headroom,          │
          │                     affinity match, spread bonus)       │
          │       │                                                  │
          │       ▼                                                  │
          │  ═══════════════ PHASE 3: BINDING ════════════════     │
          │  Winner: Node 3 (highest score: 82)                     │
          │  Pod "easypj-xyz" → assigned to Node 3                  │
          │  kubelet on Node 3 → pulls image → starts container    │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [FLOWCHART: Pod → Filter → Score → Bind]

    A second, lighter rendering of the same pipeline (handy on the exam):

          [THE SCHEDULER — filter ▶ score ▶ bind  (easypj pod: 256Mi, 250m)]
           New Pod (unbound)
                │
                ▼  ── FILTER: which nodes CAN run it? ──
           Node1 (512Mi free) ✅   Node2 (128Mi free) ❌ too small
           Node3 (1Gi free)   ✅   Node4 taint gpu=true ❌ no toleration
                │  (only survivors continue)
                ▼  ── SCORE: which fits BEST? ──
           Node1 = 65        Node3 = 82  ◄ more headroom + affinity + spread
                │
                ▼  ── BIND ──   Pod ─► Node3 ─► 🤖 kubelet starts it

    📖 Levers, weakest → strongest pull on placement:
       nodeSelector < nodeAffinity < taints/tolerations < topologySpread.
       nodeSelector/affinity ATTRACT pods toward nodes; taints REPEL pods away.

    🧠 ANALOGY: the scheduler is a recruiter. Filtering is the résumé screen
    (do you even meet the hard requirements?). Scoring is the interview ranking
    (of the qualified candidates, who's the best?). Binding is the signed offer.

    ⚠️ If NO node passes filtering, the pod stays Pending and the scheduler emits
    a FailedScheduling event — `kubectl describe pod` shows the reason.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.2  Node Selectors — Simple Placement                                🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The simplest placement tool: label a node, then demand that label in the pod
    spec. It is a HARD, exact-match requirement (key=value). If no node has the
    label, the pod stays Pending.

          $ kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd
          $ kubectl get nodes --show-labels

          # Pod with nodeSelector
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Pod
          metadata:
            name: easypj
          spec:
            nodeSelector:
              disk: ssd
            containers:
              - name: easypj
                image: easypj:latest
                resources:
                  requests:
                    cpu: 250m
                    memory: 256Mi

    💡 nodeSelector cannot express "OR", ranges, or "preferred". The moment you
    need anything richer, reach for node affinity (14.3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.3  Node Affinity — Advanced Placement                               🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    Node affinity is nodeSelector's expressive successor. Two flavours:
      - requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution  (HARD — must match, else
        Pending)
      - preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution (SOFT — try to match,
        weighted; falls back to any node if none match)

    📖 "IgnoredDuringExecution" means: once the pod is running, later label
    changes on the node do NOT evict it. The rule is only enforced at scheduling
    time.

    Operators: In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt — far richer than the
    exact-match-only nodeSelector.

          # Deployment with node affinity (required + preferred)
          apiVersion: apps/v1
          kind: Deployment
          metadata:
            name: easypj
          spec:
            replicas: 3
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj
            template:
              metadata:
                labels:
                  app: easypj
              spec:
                affinity:
                  nodeAffinity:
                    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                      nodeSelectorTerms:
                        - matchExpressions:
                            - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                              operator: In
                              values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
                    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                      - weight: 50
                        preference:
                          matchExpressions:
                            - key: disk
                              operator: In
                              values: ["ssd"]
                containers:
                  - name: easypj
                    image: easypj:latest

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE:
      • Exact single label, must-match  → nodeSelector (shortest to type).
      • OR / set / numeric / soft rule  → nodeAffinity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.4  Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity                                   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Where node affinity attracts pods to NODES by their labels, pod affinity
    attracts/repels pods relative to OTHER PODS, scoped by a topologyKey.

      - Pod Affinity:      place easypj NEAR its Redis cache (same node/zone) to
                           cut latency.
      - Pod Anti-Affinity: SPREAD easypj replicas across nodes so one node loss
                           doesn't take the whole app down (HA).

    📖 topologyKey defines the "domain" of co-location/spread:
       kubernetes.io/hostname = per node; topology.kubernetes.io/zone = per zone.

          # easypj Deployment with pod anti-affinity for HA
          apiVersion: apps/v1
          kind: Deployment
          metadata:
            name: easypj
          spec:
            replicas: 3
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj
            template:
              metadata:
                labels:
                  app: easypj
              spec:
                affinity:
                  podAntiAffinity:
                    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                      - labelSelector:
                          matchLabels:
                            app: easypj
                        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
                  podAffinity:
                    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                      - weight: 80
                        podAffinityTerm:
                          labelSelector:
                            matchLabels:
                              app: redis-cache
                          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
                containers:
                  - name: easypj
                    image: easypj:latest

    ⚠️ REQUIRED anti-affinity with topologyKey=hostname means you cannot have more
    replicas than nodes — the surplus stays Pending. Use preferred (soft) for
    elastic HA, or prefer topology spread constraints (14.7) for "spread evenly".

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.5  Taints and Tolerations                                           🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — very common question]

    Taints and tolerations are the INVERSE of affinity. Affinity is the pod
    asking to be near a node; a taint is the NODE pushing pods away unless they
    explicitly opt in.

      - Taint      = "keep pods away from this node" (set on the NODE)
      - Toleration = "I can handle that taint"       (set on the POD)
      - Effects:
          NoSchedule        → never schedule new pods that don't tolerate it
          PreferNoSchedule  → soft; avoid if possible, but allowed if needed
          NoExecute         → also EVICTS already-running pods that don't tolerate

          $ kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule
          $ kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-   # remove taint

    📖 Taint syntax is strictly key=value:Effect. The trailing dash removes it.

          [TAINTS & TOLERATIONS — CKA must-know concept]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  NODE TAINT: "Do not schedule here"                  │
          │  POD TOLERATION: "I can tolerate that taint"         │
          │                                                      │
          │  ┌─────────────── Node: gpu-node ──────────────┐   │
          │  │ Taint: gpu=true:NoSchedule   🚫              │   │
          │  │                                               │   │
          │  │  easypj pod (no toleration)                │   │
          │  │  → ❌ REJECTED — no toleration                │   │
          │  │                                               │   │
          │  │  ml-job pod (toleration: gpu=true)             │   │
          │  │  → ✅ SCHEDULED — has matching toleration     │   │
          │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
          │                                                      │
          │  Control plane nodes are tainted by default:         │
          │  node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule   │
          │  That's why your pods don't run on master nodes!    │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    A compact second view of the same idea:

          [TAINTS & TOLERATIONS — nodes repel, pods opt-in]
           🚫 Node taint: gpu=true:NoSchedule
                ├─ 📦 easypj pod (no toleration)      ─► ❌ rejected
                └─ 📦 ml-job pod (tolerates gpu=true) ─► ✅ scheduled
           💡 Control-plane nodes carry node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:
              NoSchedule by default — that's why your pods don't land there.

          # Toleration in a pod spec (matches the gpu taint above)
          spec:
            tolerations:
              - key: "gpu"
                operator: "Equal"
                value: "true"
                effect: "NoSchedule"
            containers:
              - name: ml-job
                image: ml-job:latest

    🔧 A toleration only PERMITS scheduling onto a tainted node — it does not
    ATTRACT. To both keep a node exclusive AND force certain pods onto it, combine
    a taint (repel others) with node affinity (pull the right pods in).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.6  Node Management for Admins                                       🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    The patch-a-node-without-downtime workflow:

      a) Cordon — mark node as unschedulable (no NEW pods; existing keep running)
         $ kubectl cordon worker-1
      b) Drain — cordon + safely EVICT existing pods so they reschedule elsewhere
         $ kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
      c) Uncordon — mark node schedulable again
         $ kubectl uncordon worker-1

    📖 Common drain flags:
       --ignore-daemonsets    DaemonSet pods can't move; skip them (almost always
                              needed, or drain refuses).
       --delete-emptydir-data acknowledge that emptyDir data on this node is lost.
       --force                also evict "bare" pods not managed by a controller
                              (otherwise drain refuses them).

          [FLOWCHART: Maintenance → Cordon → Drain → Work → Uncordon]

          [NODE MAINTENANCE FLOW]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  NODE MAINTENANCE — the admin workflow              │
          │                                                     │
          │  Step 1: 🚫 cordon worker-1                        │
          │          (stop new pods being scheduled here)       │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  Step 2: 🏗️ drain worker-1                          │
          │          (safely move all pods to other nodes)      │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  Step 3: 🔧 Perform maintenance                    │
          │          (OS upgrade, kernel patch, reboot)         │
          │       │                                              │
          │       ▼                                              │
          │  Step 4: ✅ uncordon worker-1                       │
          │          (allow pods to be scheduled again)         │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — PodDisruptionBudget makes drain SAFE:
    A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) sets spec.minAvailable OR spec.maxUnavailable
    plus a label selector. `kubectl drain` HONORS it: evictions proceed gradually
    and BLOCK rather than ever dropping the app below its budget. This is the
    official way to "safely drain" — without a PDB, drain can evict all replicas
    at once and cause an outage.

          # Keep at least 2 easypj pods serving during any voluntary disruption
          apiVersion: policy/v1
          kind: PodDisruptionBudget
          metadata:
            name: easypj-pdb
          spec:
            minAvailable: 2
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj

    ⚠️ cordon vs drain: cordon only stops NEW scheduling; existing pods stay put.
    drain cordons AND evicts. For a reboot you want drain. Don't forget to
    uncordon afterward, or the node sits idle forever.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.7  Topology Spread Constraints                                      🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The modern, declarative way to spread pods EVENLY across failure domains
    (zones, nodes, regions) — cleaner than required anti-affinity.

      - maxSkew:           max allowed difference in pod count between domains
      - topologyKey:       the domain label (e.g. topology.kubernetes.io/zone)
      - whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule (hard) | ScheduleAnyway (soft)
      - labelSelector:     which pods are counted toward the spread

          # TopologySpreadConstraint for easypj across zones
          apiVersion: apps/v1
          kind: Deployment
          metadata:
            name: easypj
          spec:
            replicas: 6
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj
            template:
              metadata:
                labels:
                  app: easypj
              spec:
                topologySpreadConstraints:
                  - maxSkew: 1
                    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
                    labelSelector:
                      matchLabels:
                        app: easypj
                containers:
                  - name: easypj
                    image: easypj:latest

    💡 maxSkew: 1 across 3 zones with 6 replicas → 2 pods per zone. If a zone is
    full and whenUnsatisfiable is DoNotSchedule, surplus pods stay Pending; use
    ScheduleAnyway to let them in anyway as a best-effort.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    14.8  Priority and Preemption                                          🏢
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🏢 [DAY-2 / BEYOND]

    A PriorityClass assigns an importance value to pods. When the cluster is full
    and a high-priority pod can't schedule, the scheduler can PREEMPT (evict)
    lower-priority pods to make room.

          # PriorityClass for easypj (high) vs batch jobs (low)
          apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
          kind: PriorityClass
          metadata:
            name: easypj-high
          value: 1000000
          globalDefault: false
          description: "Critical web tier — easypj job board."
          ---
          apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
          kind: PriorityClass
          metadata:
            name: batch-low
          value: 100
          globalDefault: false
          description: "Best-effort batch jobs, preemptable."
          ---
          # reference it in the pod spec:
          spec:
            priorityClassName: easypj-high

    ⚠️ Preemption only evicts pods of STRICTLY LOWER priority, and respects PDBs
    on a best-effort basis. Higher value = more important. globalDefault:true on a
    class makes it apply to pods that name no priorityClassName.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER — Chapter 14
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UTH:
      • Predicates vs priorities: filtering uses predicate plugins (hard yes/no);
        scoring uses priority plugins (weighted 0–100 ranking).
      • The scheduler maintains an in-memory CACHE of node state so it doesn't
        re-query the API server for every decision — kept in sync via watches.
      • NoExecute eviction: a NoExecute taint evicts running, non-tolerating pods.
        A toleration may set tolerationSeconds — how long the pod is allowed to
        stay before eviction (e.g. ride out a brief node-not-ready blip).

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
      • The SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK: filter/score/bind are extension points with
        pluggable plugins (PreFilter, Filter, PreScore, Score, Reserve, Permit,
        PreBind, Bind, PostBind) — this is how custom scheduling is built.
      • MULTIPLE SCHEDULERS: run a second scheduler and target it per pod with
        spec.schedulerName. Pods naming an absent scheduler stay Pending forever.
      • The DESCHEDULER: a separate component that evicts already-running pods
        that violate current policy (e.g. after nodes are added) so they can be
        rescheduled more optimally. The scheduler itself never re-balances.
      • POD OVERHEAD via RuntimeClass: accounts for the runtime's own resource
        cost (e.g. a sandboxed runtime) in scheduling math.
      • nodeName BYPASS: setting spec.nodeName directly skips the scheduler
        entirely — kubelet just runs it (used by static pods).
      • PreferNoSchedule vs NoSchedule: Prefer is a soft "avoid", NoSchedule is a
        hard "never (unless tolerated)".
      • WELL-KNOWN taints auto-applied by the node controller:
        node.kubernetes.io/not-ready, /unreachable, /memory-pressure,
        /disk-pressure, /pid-pressure, /network-unavailable.
      • BIN-PACKING vs SPREADING: score weights decide whether the scheduler
        packs pods tightly (cost-efficient) or spreads them (resilient).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 14
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 Scheduler = FILTER (can it run here?) → SCORE (best fit?) → BIND (assign).
    🔑 Placement levers escalate in strength:
       nodeSelector < nodeAffinity < taints/tolerations < topology spread.
    🔑 nodeSelector/affinity ATTRACT pods to nodes; taints REPEL; tolerations
       merely PERMIT (they don't attract).
    🔑 required* affinity = hard (Pending if unmet); preferred* = soft (weighted,
       falls back). "IgnoredDuringExecution" = enforced only at scheduling time.
    🔑 Pod anti-affinity / topology spread = HA by spreading replicas; pod
       affinity = co-locate for latency.
    🔑 Node maintenance: cordon → drain → maintain → uncordon. A PodDisruption
       Budget makes drain honor availability and block instead of causing outage.
    🔑 Control-plane nodes carry node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
       by default — that's why ordinary pods don't land there.
    🔑 PriorityClass ranks pods; high priority can preempt (evict) strictly lower.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 14
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ Taint syntax is exactly key=value:Effect — a typo silently fails to match
       tolerations.
    ⚠️ drain is BLOCKED by a PodDisruptionBudget (good — it's protecting you) and
       refuses bare (unmanaged) pods without --force.
    ⚠️ drain without --ignore-daemonsets usually refuses to proceed (DaemonSet
       pods can't be moved).
    ⚠️ Mixing up required vs preferred affinity — required leaves pods Pending if
       unmet; people expect "preferred" behavior and get an outage.
    ⚠️ The control-plane taint silently explains "why won't my pod schedule on the
       master?" — check node taints before blaming resources.
    ⚠️ REQUIRED pod anti-affinity with topologyKey=hostname caps replicas at the
       node count; extras stay Pending.
    ⚠️ Forgetting to uncordon after maintenance leaves a healthy node idle.
    ⚠️ topology spread with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule can pin surplus pods
       Pending when a domain fills up.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 14
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ Remove a taint with a trailing dash:
       kubectl taint nodes node01 key=val:NoSchedule-
    ⚡ See actual placement instantly: kubectl get pods -o wide (NODE column).
    ⚡ Confirm a node's labels/taints fast: kubectl describe node <n> | less,
       or kubectl get nodes --show-labels.
    ⚡ Why is a pod Pending? kubectl describe pod <p> → read the Events /
       FailedScheduling message (it names the exact filter that rejected it).
    ⚡ Label a node in one line: kubectl label node node01 disk=ssd.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 14
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd
    kubectl label node worker-1 disk-                      # remove a label
    kubectl get nodes --show-labels
    kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule
    kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-       # remove a taint
    kubectl describe node worker-1                          # taints, labels, caps
    kubectl cordon worker-1
    kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data [--force]
    kubectl uncordon worker-1
    kubectl get pods -o wide                                # see node placement
    kubectl describe pod <pod>                              # FailedScheduling why
    kubectl get priorityclass
    kubectl get pdb

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 14 (union of both editions)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    🧪 Q1. Pin easypj to nodes labelled disk=ssd (nodeSelector).
       ANSWER:
         kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd
         # pod spec:
         spec:
           nodeSelector:
             disk: ssd
       WHY: nodeSelector is a hard exact-match. If no node carries disk=ssd the
       pod stays Pending — verify with kubectl get pods -o wide.

    🧪 Q2. Require pods in specific zones using node affinity (required).
       ANSWER:
         spec:
           affinity:
             nodeAffinity:
               requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                 nodeSelectorTerms:
                   - matchExpressions:
                       - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                         operator: In
                         values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
       WHY: required = hard rule; operator In allows OR across multiple zones,
       which nodeSelector cannot express.

    🧪 Q3. Spread 3 easypj replicas across nodes with anti-affinity.
       ANSWER:
         spec:
           affinity:
             podAntiAffinity:
               requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                 - labelSelector:
                     matchLabels:
                       app: easypj
                   topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
       WHY: topologyKey=hostname forbids two easypj pods on the same node →
       1 replica per node. Verify all three land on different nodes with
       kubectl get pods -o wide. (Needs ≥3 schedulable nodes.)

    🧪 Q4. Taint a node and give one pod a matching toleration.
       ANSWER:
         kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule
         # pod that may run there:
         spec:
           tolerations:
             - key: "gpu"
               operator: "Equal"
               value: "true"
               effect: "NoSchedule"
       WHY: the taint repels all pods; only pods whose toleration matches
       key+value+effect are permitted. A toleration permits but does not attract.

    🧪 Q5. Cordon vs drain — what does each do?
       ANSWER: cordon marks the node unschedulable so NO NEW pods land there, but
       existing pods keep running. drain does the cordon AND evicts the existing
       pods so they reschedule elsewhere. Use cordon to "stop adding work"; use
       drain to "empty the node" before maintenance.

    🧪 Q6. Drain a node for maintenance, then bring it back.
       ANSWER:
         kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
         # ... perform OS upgrade / reboot ...
         kubectl uncordon worker-1
       WHY: --ignore-daemonsets is needed because DaemonSet pods can't move;
       --delete-emptydir-data acknowledges emptyDir loss. uncordon re-enables
       scheduling. Add --force if any bare (unmanaged) pods exist.

    🧪 Q7. Even-spread easypj across 3 zones (topologySpreadConstraints).
       ANSWER:
         spec:
           topologySpreadConstraints:
             - maxSkew: 1
               topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
               whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
               labelSelector:
                 matchLabels:
                   app: easypj
       WHY: maxSkew:1 keeps zone pod-counts within 1 of each other (6 replicas →
       2 per zone). DoNotSchedule enforces it hard; ScheduleAnyway makes it soft.

    🧪 Q8. Make easypj higher priority than batch jobs (PriorityClass).
       ANSWER:
         apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
         kind: PriorityClass
         metadata: { name: easypj-high }
         value: 1000000
         ---
         # in the pod spec:
         spec:
           priorityClassName: easypj-high
       WHY: when the cluster is full, the scheduler can preempt (evict)
       strictly-lower-priority pods (e.g. value 100 batch jobs) to fit easypj.

    🧪 Q9. A pod is Pending — list the scheduling reasons to check.
       ANSWER: run kubectl describe pod <p> and read the FailedScheduling event.
       Common causes:
         • Insufficient cpu/memory on every node (no node passes filtering).
         • An untolerated taint (e.g. the control-plane taint).
         • nodeSelector / required nodeAffinity matches no node.
         • required podAntiAffinity with more replicas than nodes.
         • topology spread DoNotSchedule with all domains full.
         • PVC unbound / volume-node affinity mismatch.
         • spec.schedulerName names a scheduler that isn't running.

    🧪 Q10. Remove a taint from a node (command).
       ANSWER:
         kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-
       WHY: the trailing dash on the exact key=value:Effect string deletes that
       taint. (Same trailing-dash trick removes a label: disk-.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧭 VISUAL SUMMARY — a pod's path from "unscheduled" to a chosen node
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  easypj pod created (spec.nodeName = "" → unscheduled)    │
          │        │                                                  │
          │        ▼                                                  │
          │  FILTER  ─ drop nodes too small / wrong labels /          │
          │            untolerated taints / unsatisfied affinity      │
          │        │                                                  │
          │        ▼                                                  │
          │  SCORE   ─ rank survivors: headroom + affinity + spread   │
          │        │                                                  │
          │        ▼                                                  │
          │  BIND    ─ write winning node into pod                    │
          │        │                                                  │
          │        ▼                                                  │
          │  🤖 kubelet on that node pulls image, starts container    │
          │                                                          │
          │  Admin override knobs along the way:                      │
          │    nodeSelector · nodeAffinity · pod (anti)affinity ·     │
          │    taints/tolerations · topology spread · priority ·      │
          │    cordon/drain (take a node out) → uncordon (back in)    │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    .vs-prose — A new easypj pod starts life unscheduled (no nodeName). The
    scheduler first FILTERS out every node that physically can't host it (too
    little CPU/memory, missing required labels, untolerated taints, unmet
    affinity), then SCORES the survivors so the one with the most headroom and the
    best affinity/spread match wins, then BINDS that choice into the pod so the
    node's kubelet can pull the image and run it. As an admin you bias every step:
    nodeSelector and node affinity attract pods to the right nodes, pod
    (anti-)affinity and topology spread co-locate or spread replicas,
    taints/tolerations fence pods off nodes, and PriorityClass decides who wins
    when the cluster is full. To service hardware you cordon a node (stop new
    pods), drain it (evict existing pods, protected by a PodDisruptionBudget), do
    the work, then uncordon it to let scheduling resume.
