================================================================================
  Chapter 15: Resource Management                                      🟡 🎯
================================================================================
  [A] META: 🟡 INTERMEDIATE · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Workloads & Scheduling 15%
      (requests/limits, QoS, admission via LimitRange/ResourceQuota).

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      Requests and limits decide three things at once: WHERE a pod lands
      (scheduling), HOW HARD it can run (throttling), and WHO DIES FIRST when a
      node runs out of memory (eviction). Get them wrong and easypj either never
      schedules, gets CPU-starved under load, or gets OOMKilled at 2 a.m. In the
      exam, every "the pod won't schedule" or "the pod keeps restarting" ticket
      eventually comes back to these four fields.
      💡 INSIGHT: a "request" is a promise the SCHEDULER trusts; a "limit" is a
      fence the KUBELET enforces. Two different components, two different jobs.

  [C] OBJECTIVES
      - Set CPU/memory requests and limits on a container (easypj).
      - Explain the three QoS classes and the eviction order they imply.
      - Enforce per-container defaults/min/max with a LimitRange.
      - Cap a whole namespace's totals with a ResourceQuota.
      - Debug OOMKills, throttling, and "unschedulable due to requests".

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE
      Part of the Workloads & Scheduling domain (15%). Expect at least one task
      that asks you to add requests/limits, create a LimitRange or ResourceQuota,
      or diagnose a pod that is OOMKilling or stuck Pending. `kubectl describe`
      (QoS Class, Last State, Events) is your primary evidence-gathering tool.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      15.1  Resource Requests and Limits
      15.2  QoS Classes — Quality of Service
      15.3  LimitRange — Namespace Default Limits
      15.4  ResourceQuota — Namespace Capacity Control

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  15.1  Resource Requests and Limits                                  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    - Requests: guaranteed minimum resources (used for SCHEDULING). The
      scheduler sums the requests of all containers in a pod and only places it
      on a node whose allocatable capacity can cover them.
    - Limits: maximum resources (ENFORCED by the kubelet via cgroups).
    - CPU: measured in millicores (1000m = 1 CPU core). CPU is COMPRESSIBLE —
      exceeding the limit means the container is throttled (slowed), not killed.
    - Memory: measured in bytes (Mi, Gi). Memory is INCOMPRESSIBLE — exceeding
      the limit means the container is OOMKilled (exit code 137).

    📖 KEY TERM — millicore: 1000m == 1 vCPU. "250m" = a quarter of a core.
    📖 KEY TERM — Mi vs M: Mi = mebibyte (1024^2), M = megabyte (1000^2).
       Kubernetes accepts both; prefer Mi/Gi for predictability.

    [CODE: easypj Pod with resources.requests and resources.limits]
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: easypj
      namespace: easypj-dev
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: easypj:5.2.5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "512Mi"

    [REQUESTS vs LIMITS — CKA must-know]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  RESOURCE REQUESTS & LIMITS                       │
          │                                                   │
          │  resources:                                       │
          │    requests:        ← "I need at least this much" │
          │      cpu: "250m"   ← 0.25 CPU cores              │
          │      memory: "256Mi" ← 256 MB RAM                │
          │    limits:          ← "Don't use more than this"  │
          │      cpu: "500m"   ← 0.5 CPU cores               │
          │      memory: "512Mi" ← 512 MB RAM                │
          │                                                   │
          │  CPU exceeded limit?    → Throttled (slowed) ⏳   │
          │  Memory exceeded limit? → OOMKilled (killed) 💀   │
          │                                                   │
          │  No requests set?  → Scheduler doesn't know needs │
          │  No limits set?    → Pod can consume ALL node RAM  │
          │  ⚠️ ALWAYS set both in production!                │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    [REQUESTS vs LIMITS — and what happens when you cross a limit]
     resources:
       requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }  ◄ scheduling FLOOR (guaranteed)
       limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }  ◄ hard CEILING (enforced)
     Over CPU limit  ─► ⏳ THROTTLED (slowed, not killed)
     Over MEM limit  ─► 💀 OOMKilled (137)
     No requests ─► scheduler is blind   ·   No limits ─► pod can eat the node

    🧠 ANALOGY: a REQUEST is your hotel reservation (the room is held for you
    even if you arrive late); a LIMIT is the room's fire-code occupancy (cross
    it for memory and security throws you out; cross it for CPU and they just
    slow the elevator).

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: a request that exceeds any node's allocatable capacity leaves the
    pod Pending forever with "0/N nodes are available: Insufficient cpu/memory".
    This is a SCHEDULING failure, not a runtime failure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  15.2  QoS Classes — Quality of Service                              🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    Kubernetes derives a pod's Quality-of-Service class automatically from how
    its requests and limits are set. You never set QoS directly — it is COMPUTED.

    - Guaranteed: every container has requests == limits for BOTH cpu and memory
      (and both are set). Safest; evicted last.
    - Burstable: at least one container sets a request or limit, but it does not
      qualify as Guaranteed. Most real workloads.
    - BestEffort: no requests or limits set on any container. Evicted first.

    Order of eviction under node memory pressure:
       BestEffort (first) → Burstable → Guaranteed (last)

    [QOS CLASSES — eviction order]
    | QoS Class    | When                      | Eviction priority | easypj? |
    | Guaranteed   | requests == limits        | Last (safest)     | ✅ Prod |
    | Burstable    | requests < limits         | Middle            | ⚠️ Dev  |
    | BestEffort   | No requests or limits     | First (risky!)    | ❌ Never|

    [QoS & GOVERNANCE NESTING]
     ResourceQuota (namespace TOTAL: 8 cpu / 16Gi / 30 pods)
       └─ LimitRange (per-container default/min/max)
            └─ Pod spec (this easypj: 250m req / 500m lim)
     QoS:  req==lim ⇒ Guaranteed (evicted last) · partial ⇒ Burstable ·
           none ⇒ BestEffort (evicted first)

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: the QoS class is computed at admission and stored in
    `status.qosClass`. See it with:
       kubectl get pod easypj -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
       kubectl describe pod easypj   # QoS Class: line near the top

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: to be Guaranteed, requests must equal limits for BOTH cpu AND
    memory. Setting them equal for memory only still yields Burstable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  15.3  LimitRange — Namespace Default Limits                         🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    - A LimitRange is a namespace-scoped admission policy. It can:
      · inject DEFAULT requests/limits into containers that omit them,
      · enforce MIN and MAX per container,
      · enforce a default request/limit RATIO.
    - It prevents pods from running without limits and stops a single container
      from requesting absurd amounts.

    [CODE: LimitRange YAML for easypj-dev namespace]
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: LimitRange
    metadata:
      name: easypj-defaults
      namespace: easypj-dev
    spec:
      limits:
        - type: Container
          default:            # applied as LIMIT if container sets none
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          defaultRequest:     # applied as REQUEST if container sets none
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          min:                # reject containers below this
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          max:                # reject containers above this
            cpu: "1"
            memory: "1Gi"

    💡 INSIGHT: `default` populates the LIMIT; `defaultRequest` populates the
    REQUEST. If a pod sets a limit but no request, the request defaults to the
    limit value (not to `defaultRequest`).

    🧪 DRILL: apply the LimitRange above, then create a pod with NO resources
    block and run `kubectl describe pod` — you will see the injected defaults
    under the container's Limits/Requests.

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: a container that requests below `min` or above `max` is REJECTED
    at admission ("forbidden: minimum/maximum ... per Container"). The pod is
    never created — it does not just get clamped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  15.4  ResourceQuota — Namespace Capacity Control                    🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    - A ResourceQuota limits the TOTAL resource consumption of a namespace:
      aggregate cpu/memory requests and limits, plus object counts (pods, PVCs,
      services, configmaps, secrets, etc.).
    - It prevents one team from using all cluster resources.

    [CODE: ResourceQuota YAML — max 10 pods, 4 CPU, 8Gi memory]
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: easypj-quota
      namespace: easypj-dev
    spec:
      hard:
        pods: "10"
        requests.cpu: "4"
        requests.memory: "8Gi"
        limits.cpu: "8"
        limits.memory: "16Gi"
        persistentvolumeclaims: "5"

    [RESOURCE CONTROL HIERARCHY]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  RESOURCE CONTROL — 3 levels                     │
          │                                                   │
          │  Level 1: ResourceQuota (namespace total)        │
          │  "easypj-dev can use max 4 CPUs total"           │
          │       │                                           │
          │       ▼                                           │
          │  Level 2: LimitRange (per-container defaults)    │
          │  "Each container gets max 500m CPU by default"   │
          │       │                                           │
          │       ▼                                           │
          │  Level 3: Pod spec (per-container specific)      │
          │  "This easypj container: 250m request, 500m limit"│
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ⚠️ GOTCHA (exam favourite): once a ResourceQuota sets `requests.cpu` /
    `limits.cpu` (or the memory equivalents) for a namespace, EVERY new pod in
    that namespace MUST specify the corresponding request/limit, or creation is
    rejected: "must specify limits.cpu,requests.cpu". The standard fix is to add
    a LimitRange so defaults are injected automatically.

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING: inspect usage vs. hard with
       kubectl describe quota easypj-quota -n easypj-dev
    The "Used" vs "Hard" columns show exactly what is exhausted.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 How QoS is computed: at admission the apiserver inspects every container.
       requests==limits (cpu AND memory, all containers) ⇒ Guaranteed; any
       request/limit present but not fully matched ⇒ Burstable; nothing set ⇒
       BestEffort. Result lands in status.qosClass.

    🔧 How limits are enforced: the kubelet translates limits into cgroup
       settings. CPU limit → CFS quota (cpu.cfs_quota_us / cpu.max), producing
       THROTTLING when the quota is spent in a 100ms period. Memory limit →
       memory.limit_in_bytes / memory.max; crossing it triggers the kernel OOM
       killer, which kills the process and the kubelet reports OOMKilled (137).
       Requests map to cpu.shares (relative CPU weight) — they affect contention,
       not a hard cap.

    🔧 Eviction thresholds & node pressure: the kubelet watches node memory and
       ephemeral-storage against eviction thresholds (e.g.
       memory.available<100Mi). Under pressure it evicts pods in QoS order, and
       within a class prefers pods exceeding their requests by the most.

    🔬 DEEPER:
       - cgroup v1 vs v2: v2 uses a unified hierarchy (cpu.max, memory.max,
         memory.high for soft pressure). Modern distros default to v2.
       - CPU CFS quota & throttling metrics: watch
         container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total — high throttling means the
         CPU limit is too tight even though CPU% looks "fine".
       - Memory QoS & PSI: Pressure Stall Information (some/full) gauges real
         memory/cpu/io contention beyond raw utilization.
       - ephemeral-storage requests/limits: scratch disk (logs, emptyDir,
         writable layer) is a schedulable, limitable resource too; over-limit →
         eviction.
       - Extended resources & device plugins (GPU): nvidia.com/gpu and friends
         are requested/limited like cpu/memory; for them request MUST equal limit.
       - node-allocatable & overcommit: allocatable = capacity −
         kube-reserved − system-reserved − eviction-threshold. Summed REQUESTS
         must fit allocatable; summed LIMITS may exceed it (overcommit), which is
         exactly why nodes can OOM.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 15
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 Requests = scheduling FLOOR (guaranteed, trusted by the scheduler);
       limits = hard CEILING (enforced by the kubelet via cgroups).
    🔑 CPU over limit → THROTTLED (slowed); memory over limit → OOMKilled (137).
    🔑 QoS (Guaranteed / Burstable / BestEffort) is COMPUTED from requests vs
       limits and sets the eviction order: BestEffort dies first, Guaranteed last.
    🔑 Guaranteed requires requests == limits for BOTH cpu AND memory.
    🔑 LimitRange = per-container defaults/min/max within a namespace.
    🔑 ResourceQuota = namespace-wide totals (cpu/mem requests & limits, pods,
       PVCs, object counts).
    🔑 With a cpu/mem ResourceQuota, every pod MUST set the matching request/limit
       (or a LimitRange supplies it).
    🔑 No requests → the scheduler is blind; no limits → a pod can eat the node.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 15
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ With a ResourceQuota in place, every pod MUST set limits (or a LimitRange
       supplies defaults) — otherwise "must specify limits.cpu/requests.cpu".
    ⚠️ A too-low memory limit causes a CrashLoopBackOff via repeated OOMKilled —
       the fix is raising the limit, not restarting the pod.
    ⚠️ No requests → the scheduler cannot reason about fit and may overcommit a
       node into OOM.
    ⚠️ A request larger than any node's allocatable leaves the pod Pending with
       "Insufficient cpu/memory" — a scheduling failure, not a crash.
    ⚠️ Guaranteed needs cpu AND memory matched; matching only one keeps it
       Burstable.
    ⚠️ LimitRange min/max REJECT out-of-range containers at admission; they are
       not silently clamped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 15
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ Set BOTH requests and limits — it is the safest default and yields a known
       QoS class.
    ⚡ Use a LimitRange to inject defaults once instead of editing every pod.
    ⚡ `kubectl describe pod` shows the QoS Class line and Last State
       (Terminated: OOMKilled) — your fastest diagnosis.
    ⚡ `kubectl describe quota` shows Used vs Hard at a glance.
    ⚡ `kubectl top pod` reveals live consumption to size requests/limits sanely.
    ⚡ For OOMKill tickets, jump straight to describe → Last State / Reason.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 15
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Set resources imperatively on a deployment
    kubectl set resources deploy/easypj \
      --requests=cpu=250m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi

    # Create a quota imperatively
    kubectl create quota easypj-quota -n easypj-dev \
      --hard=pods=10,requests.cpu=4,requests.memory=8Gi,limits.cpu=8,limits.memory=16Gi

    # Inspect governance objects
    kubectl get limitrange,resourcequota -n easypj-dev
    kubectl describe limitrange easypj-defaults -n easypj-dev
    kubectl describe quota easypj-quota       -n easypj-dev

    # Live usage and QoS / failure evidence
    kubectl top pod -n easypj-dev
    kubectl get pod easypj -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
    kubectl describe pod easypj -n easypj-dev   # QoS Class, Last State, Events

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 15 (union of both sources)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Q1. Set CPU/memory requests and limits on the easypj container.
        A: Add a resources block (or `kubectl set resources deploy/easypj
        --requests=cpu=250m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi`).
        EXPLANATION: requests inform scheduling; limits cap runtime. Equal
        values make it Guaranteed; unequal make it Burstable.

    Q2. Determine a given pod's QoS class and justify it.
        A: `kubectl get pod X -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'` or describe.
        EXPLANATION: Guaranteed if requests==limits for cpu AND memory on every
        container; Burstable if some request/limit is set but not fully matched;
        BestEffort if nothing is set.

    Q3. Create a LimitRange with default + max for a namespace.
        A: Apply a LimitRange (type Container) with `default`, `defaultRequest`,
        and `max`. EXPLANATION: `default` fills the limit, `defaultRequest` the
        request, for containers that omit them; `max` rejects oversize containers.

    Q4. Create a ResourceQuota capping cpu/mem/pods/PVCs.
        A: Apply a ResourceQuota with hard: requests.cpu, requests.memory,
        limits.cpu, limits.memory, pods, persistentvolumeclaims. EXPLANATION:
        caps namespace TOTALS; subsequent pods are validated against remaining
        headroom at admission.

    Q5. A pod keeps OOMKilling — root cause and two fixes.
        A: Memory usage exceeds the memory LIMIT (Last State: Terminated,
        Reason: OOMKilled, exit 137). FIXES: (1) raise the memory limit to a
        realistic value; (2) reduce the app's memory footprint (e.g. lower
        worker/cache size). EXPLANATION: memory is incompressible, so the kernel
        OOM killer terminates the process.

    Q6. A pod won't schedule due to requests — what do you check?
        A: `kubectl describe pod` Events ("0/N nodes available: Insufficient
        cpu/memory") and compare the pod's requests against
        `kubectl describe node` Allocatable. EXPLANATION: the sum of requests
        must fit a single node's allocatable capacity.

    Q7. Why is BestEffort risky in production?
        A: BestEffort pods are evicted FIRST under node memory pressure and have
        no guaranteed share. EXPLANATION: with no requests, the scheduler can't
        reserve resources, so these pods are the first sacrifice.

    Q8. A pod create is rejected by the quota — why, and the fix.
        A: The namespace ResourceQuota sets cpu/mem totals, so the pod must
        specify the matching requests/limits ("must specify limits.cpu,
        requests.cpu"). FIX: add the resources to the spec, or install a
        LimitRange that injects defaults. EXPLANATION: a quota on a compute
        resource forces every pod to declare that resource.

    Q9. Prove a LimitRange injected defaults into a no-limits pod.
        A: Apply the LimitRange, create a pod with no resources block, then
        `kubectl describe pod` and read the populated Limits/Requests.
        EXPLANATION: the LimitRange admission controller mutates the container to
        add default/defaultRequest values.

    Q10. CPU throttling vs OOMKill — which resource causes which?
        A: Exceeding the CPU limit → THROTTLED (compressible, slowed, never
        killed); exceeding the MEMORY limit → OOMKilled (incompressible, exit
        137). EXPLANATION: CPU is reclaimable instant-to-instant; memory once
        allocated cannot be reclaimed without killing the process.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — ResourceQuota → LimitRange → Pod spec, nested:
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  ResourceQuota  (namespace TOTAL: 4 cpu req / 8 cpu lim / 10  │
      │                  pods / 5 PVCs)                               │
      │     └── LimitRange  (per-container default 250m/256Mi req,    │
      │                      500m/512Mi lim; min 100m/128Mi;          │
      │                      max 1 cpu/1Gi)                           │
      │            └── Pod spec  (easypj: 250m req / 500m lim →        │
      │                           Burstable QoS)                      │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      .vs-prose: Resource governance nests in three layers. The ResourceQuota
      caps the namespace as a whole (aggregate cpu/memory and object counts).
      Inside it, the LimitRange supplies per-container defaults plus min/max
      guardrails so pods that omit resources still get sane values. At the
      bottom, each Pod spec declares its own requests/limits, which determine
      its QoS class and therefore its eviction priority. Reading top-down it is
      "how much the namespace may use"; reading bottom-up it is "what this one
      easypj container is promised and capped at".

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapter 16: Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets & StatefulSets               🟡 🎯
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Workloads & Scheduling 15%
        (the self-healing, run-to-completion, and stateful primitives).

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ────────────────
  Not everything is a stateless web server. The easypj Django project needs
  more than a Deployment: it needs database migrations that run ONCE and stop
  (Job), nightly backups that run on a SCHEDULE (CronJob), a log/monitoring
  agent on EVERY node (DaemonSet), and a PostgreSQL database with STABLE
  identity and durable per-pod storage (StatefulSet). This chapter teaches you
  to look at a need and instantly pick the correct workload type.

  🧠 ANALOGY: A Deployment is a pool of interchangeable temp workers — any one
  will do, and you can swap them freely. A StatefulSet is a numbered team with
  assigned desks (db-0, db-1) and personal lockers (PVCs) that survive even if
  the person goes home. A Job is a contractor hired for one task who leaves
  when it's done. A CronJob is the cleaning crew that shows up on a schedule.
  A DaemonSet is the smoke detector you install in every room of the building.

  OBJECTIVES
  ──────────
  • Choose and build the RIGHT workload type for each need (decision tree 🧭).
  • Write a Job with completions, parallelism, and a backoffLimit.
  • Schedule a CronJob with cron syntax and a concurrencyPolicy.
  • Deploy a DaemonSet that lands exactly one pod per eligible node.
  • Deploy a StatefulSet with stable names, stable DNS, and volumeClaimTemplates.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────
  🎯 Part of the 15% Workloads & Scheduling domain. Expect to be asked to
  create a Job or CronJob (often `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/...`),
  reason about why a StatefulSet needs a headless Service, and identify the
  correct workload type for a described scenario. Fast, high-yield points.

  ───────────

  16.1  Jobs — Run to Completion                                       🎯
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    📖 KEY TERM — Job: a controller that runs one or more pods until a
       specified number SUCCESSFULLY complete, then stops. Unlike a Deployment
       (which keeps pods running forever), a Job is "done" and exits.

    • Run a pod until it completes successfully (then stops).
    • Use case: database migration, batch processing, one-off scripts.
    • completions: how many pods must succeed for the Job to be complete.
    • parallelism: how many pods run simultaneously.
    • backoffLimit: retry count before the Job is marked as Failed.
    • restartPolicy MUST be OnFailure or Never (NOT Always — Always is the
      Deployment default and is illegal in a Job's pod template).

    Job YAML — Django manage.py migrate for easypj:

       apiVersion: batch/v1
       kind: Job
       metadata:
         name: easypj-migrate
         namespace: easypj
       spec:
         backoffLimit: 4              # retries before the Job is marked Failed
         template:
           spec:
             restartPolicy: Never
             containers:
             - name: migrate
               image: easypj:v1
               command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
               envFrom:
               - configMapRef: { name: easypj-config }
               - secretRef:    { name: easypj-secret }

    [JOB LIFECYCLE — RUN TO COMPLETION (not forever)]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Job: "easypj-migrate"   completions: 1   backoffLimit: 4   │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │                                                            │
    │   create Job ──► spawn Pod ──► run command                 │
    │                       │                                    │
    │             ┌─────────┴──────────┐                         │
    │             ▼                    ▼                         │
    │        exit 0 (success)     exit ≠0 (failure)              │
    │             │                    │                         │
    │             ▼                    ▼                         │
    │     ✅ Job COMPLETE       retry (up to backoffLimit=4)     │
    │     (pod stays as           │                              │
    │      Completed, NOT         ▼                              │
    │      restarted)        retries exhausted ──► ❌ Job Failed │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 Parallel Job — 5 completions, 2 at a time:

       apiVersion: batch/v1
       kind: Job
       metadata: { name: batch-process, namespace: easypj }
       spec:
         completions: 5             # 5 pods must succeed total
         parallelism: 2             # but only 2 run at once
         backoffLimit: 6
         template:
           spec:
             restartPolicy: OnFailure
             containers:
             - name: worker
               image: easypj:v1
               command: ["python", "manage.py", "process_batch"]

    💡 INSIGHT: completions vs parallelism. completions is the FINISH LINE
    (how many successes you need); parallelism is the LANE COUNT (how many
    run concurrently). Set completions=5, parallelism=2 and the Job keeps two
    pods running, replacing each as it succeeds, until five have finished.


  16.2  CronJobs — Scheduled Tasks                                     🎯
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    📖 KEY TERM — CronJob: a controller that creates a Job on a recurring
       SCHEDULE. Like Unix cron, but Kubernetes-native. The CronJob is the
       schedule; each firing produces a fresh Job object.

    • Like Unix cron, but in Kubernetes.
    • Creates Jobs on a schedule.
    • cron expression: "minute hour day month weekday".
    • concurrencyPolicy controls what happens if a run is still going when the
      next is due: Allow (default), Forbid (skip), or Replace (kill & restart).
    • successfulJobsHistoryLimit / failedJobsHistoryLimit cap retained Jobs.

    CronJob YAML — daily database backup for easypj:

       apiVersion: batch/v1
       kind: CronJob
       metadata:
         name: easypj-db-backup
         namespace: easypj
       spec:
         schedule: "0 2 * * *"        # 02:00 daily (min hr dom mon dow)
         concurrencyPolicy: Forbid    # don't overlap runs
         successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
         jobTemplate:
           spec:
             template:
               spec:
                 restartPolicy: OnFailure
                 containers:
                 - name: backup
                   image: postgres:16
                   command:
                   - "sh"
                   - "-c"
                   - "pg_dump -h easypj-db -U easypj easypj > /backup/easypj-$(date +%F).sql"

    [TABLE: Cron expression examples]
    ┌────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Schedule       │ Meaning                                    │
    ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ */5 * * * *    │ Every 5 minutes                            │
    │ 0 2 * * *      │ Daily at 2:00 AM                           │
    │ 0 0 * * 0      │ Every Sunday at midnight                   │
    │ 0 */6 * * *    │ Every 6 hours                              │
    │ 30 8 * * 1-5   │ 08:30 on weekdays (Mon–Fri)                │
    │ 0 0 1 * *      │ Midnight on the 1st of every month         │
    └────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

    [THE FIVE CRON FIELDS]
       ┌───────────── minute        (0 - 59)
       │ ┌───────────  hour          (0 - 23)
       │ │ ┌─────────  day of month  (1 - 31)
       │ │ │ ┌───────  month         (1 - 12)
       │ │ │ │ ┌─────  day of week    (0 - 6, Sun = 0)
       │ │ │ │ │
       *  *  *  *  *
       Special: *=every  */n=every n  a-b=range  a,b=list

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: A CronJob fires in the kube-controller-manager's clock/timezone
    (UTC unless spec.timeZone is set). "02:00" is not your laptop's 02:00 — it
    is the cluster's. If the controller is down past the window,
    startingDeadlineSeconds decides whether a missed run is still launched.


  16.3  DaemonSets — One Pod Per Node                                  🎯
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    📖 KEY TERM — DaemonSet: a controller that ensures exactly ONE copy of a
       pod runs on every (or every selected) node. There is no replicas field —
       the count tracks the node count automatically.

    • Ensures exactly ONE pod on every (or selected) node.
    • New node added → DaemonSet pod auto-created.
    • Node removed → DaemonSet pod auto-deleted.
    • Use cases: log collectors, monitoring agents, CNI, kube-proxy.
    • Targets a subset of nodes with nodeSelector / nodeAffinity; tolerates
      control-plane taints with tolerations to also land on masters.

    DaemonSet YAML — Fluentd log collector:

       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: DaemonSet
       metadata:
         name: fluentd-logging
         namespace: kube-system
       spec:
         selector:
           matchLabels: { app: fluentd }
         template:
           metadata:
             labels: { app: fluentd }
           spec:
             tolerations:
             - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
               operator: Exists
               effect: NoSchedule          # also run on control-plane nodes
             containers:
             - name: fluentd
               image: fluent/fluentd:v1.16
               volumeMounts:
               - { name: varlog, mountPath: /var/log }
             volumes:
             - name: varlog
               hostPath: { path: /var/log }

    [DAEMONSET — ONE POD PER NODE (GUARANTEED)]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  DaemonSet: "fluentd-logging"   replicas: N/A (auto)     │
    │  (scheduler places exactly ONE pod per eligible node)     │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │                                                            │
    │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐      │
    │  │  worker-1    │ │  worker-2    │ │  worker-3    │      │
    │  │              │ │              │ │              │      │
    │  │ ┌──────────┐ │ │ ┌──────────┐ │ │ ┌──────────┐ │      │
    │  │ │ fluentd  │ │ │ │ fluentd  │ │ │ │ fluentd  │ │      │
    │  │ │  📋 logs │ │ │ │  📋 logs │ │ │ │  📋 logs │ │      │
    │  │ └──────────┘ │ │ └──────────┘ │ │ └──────────┘ │      │
    │  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘      │
    │                                                            │
    │  ┌──────────────┐                                         │
    │  │  worker-4    │  ← new node joins cluster               │
    │  │              │                                         │
    │  │ ┌──────────┐ │  DaemonSet controller                  │
    │  │ │ fluentd  │ │  AUTOMATICALLY schedules                │
    │  │ │  📋 logs │ │  a pod here too!                       │
    │  │ └──────────┘ │                                         │
    │  └──────────────┘                                         │
    │                                                            │
    │  Common DaemonSet use cases:                               │
    │  • 📋 Log collectors    (fluentd, filebeat)               │
    │  • 📊 Monitoring agents (node-exporter, datadog)          │
    │  • 🌐 Network plugins   (calico-node, cilium)            │
    │  • 💾 Storage daemons   (ceph, glusterd)                  │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: A DaemonSet does not go through the default scheduler
    the way a Deployment does in spirit — the DaemonSet controller creates a
    pod already bound (via nodeAffinity to a specific nodeName) for each
    eligible node. Its update strategy is RollingUpdate by default; setting
    updateStrategy.type: OnDelete means new pods are only created when you
    manually delete the old ones — handy when restarting an agent is risky.


  16.4  StatefulSets — Stateful Applications                           🎯
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    📖 KEY TERM — StatefulSet: a controller for applications that need a STABLE
       identity (predictable pod names + stable DNS) and STABLE per-pod storage
       (each replica gets its own PersistentVolumeClaim). Pods are created,
       scaled, and deleted in a defined ORDER.

    • For applications that need stable identity and storage.
    • Features: stable pod names, stable network identity, stable storage
      (per-pod PVC), ordered operations.
    • Use case: PostgreSQL for easypj, Kafka, Redis Cluster.
    • Requires a HEADLESS Service (clusterIP: None) named in serviceName to
      give each pod its own DNS A-record.
    • Per-pod storage comes from volumeClaimTemplates — one PVC PER replica.

    StatefulSet YAML — PostgreSQL for easypj:

       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: StatefulSet
       metadata:
         name: easypj-db
         namespace: easypj
       spec:
         serviceName: easypj-db        # the Headless Service (clusterIP: None)
         replicas: 1
         selector:
           matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
         template:
           metadata:
             labels: { app: easypj-db }
           spec:
             containers:
             - name: postgres
               image: postgres:16
               ports:
               - { containerPort: 5432 }
               envFrom:
               - secretRef: { name: easypj-secret }   # POSTGRES_PASSWORD ...
               volumeMounts:
               - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }
         volumeClaimTemplates:         # each replica gets its OWN durable PVC
         - metadata:
             name: data
           spec:
             accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
             storageClassName: easypj-fast
             resources:
               requests:
                 storage: 10Gi

    And the companion headless Service the StatefulSet requires:

       apiVersion: v1
       kind: Service
       metadata:
         name: easypj-db
         namespace: easypj
       spec:
         clusterIP: None               # ← HEADLESS: no virtual IP, DNS per-pod
         selector: { app: easypj-db }
         ports:
         - { port: 5432, targetPort: 5432 }

    [STATEFULSET — ORDERED PODS WITH STABLE IDENTITY + PER-POD STORAGE]
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  StatefulSet: "mysql"    replicas: 3                        │
    │  serviceName: "mysql-headless"                               │
    ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │                                                              │
    │  Deployment pods:        StatefulSet pods:                   │
    │  (random names)          (ordered, predictable names)       │
    │  ┌────────────┐          ┌────────────┐                     │
    │  │ app-x7k2z  │          │ mysql-0    │ ← created FIRST    │
    │  ├────────────┤          │  (primary) │   (must be ready   │
    │  │ app-m9p4q  │          ├────────────┤    before mysql-1)  │
    │  ├────────────┤          │ mysql-1    │ ← created SECOND   │
    │  │ app-j3r8w  │          │  (replica) │                     │
    │  └────────────┘          ├────────────┤                     │
    │                          │ mysql-2    │ ← created THIRD    │
    │                          │  (replica) │                     │
    │                          └────────────┘                     │
    │                                                              │
    │  Per-Pod Persistent Volumes (stable across restarts):       │
    │  ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐        │
    │  │ mysql-0    │    │ mysql-1    │    │ mysql-2    │        │
    │  │ ┌────────┐ │    │ ┌────────┐ │    │ ┌────────┐ │        │
    │  │ │data-0  │ │    │ │data-1  │ │    │ │data-2  │ │        │
    │  │ │ 10Gi   │ │    │ │ 10Gi   │ │    │ │ 10Gi   │ │        │
    │  │ │PVC     │ │    │ │PVC     │ │    │ │PVC     │ │        │
    │  │ └───┬────┘ │    │ └───┬────┘ │    │ └───┬────┘ │        │
    │  └─────┼──────┘    └─────┼──────┘    └─────┼──────┘        │
    │        ▼                 ▼                 ▼                │
    │  ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐          │
    │  │  PV-0   │       │  PV-1   │       │  PV-2   │          │
    │  │ (disk)  │       │ (disk)  │       │ (disk)  │          │
    │  └─────────┘       └─────────┘       └─────────┘          │
    │                                                              │
    │  Key guarantees:                                             │
    │  ✅ Stable network identity  (mysql-0.mysql-headless)       │
    │  ✅ Ordered deployment       (0 → 1 → 2)                   │
    │  ✅ Ordered deletion         (2 → 1 → 0)                   │
    │  ✅ Stable storage           (PVC survives pod restart)     │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    [STATEFULSET vs DEPLOYMENT — names & storage]
       Deployment pods: easypj-web-7d4-x9k2
                        (random, interchangeable, shared/no PVC)
       StatefulSet pods: db-0 ▶ db-1 ▶ db-2
                        (ordered, stable DNS, OWN PVC each)
       ⚠️ A StatefulSet needs a headless Service; scaling DOWN does NOT
          delete the PVCs (your data is intentionally preserved).

    💡 INSIGHT — stable DNS: with serviceName "easypj-db", pod easypj-db-0
    is reachable at easypj-db-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local. That stable
    address is why clustered databases (Postgres replicas, Kafka brokers) can
    find each other reliably — a random Deployment pod name could never do that.

    [WORKLOAD TYPES COMPARISON — when to use what]
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  WHICH WORKLOAD TYPE DO I NEED?                          │
    │                                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────┐  Need stable storage/identity?        │
    │  │ easypj Django │  NO → Deployment ✅                   │
    │  └──────────────┘                                        │
    │                                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────┐  Need stable storage/identity?        │
    │  │ PostgreSQL   │  YES → StatefulSet ✅                  │
    │  └──────────────┘                                        │
    │                                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────┐  Need one per node?                   │
    │  │ Log collector│  YES → DaemonSet ✅                    │
    │  └──────────────┘                                        │
    │                                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────┐  Run once and done?                   │
    │  │ DB migration │  YES → Job ✅                          │
    │  └──────────────┘                                        │
    │                                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────┐  Run on a schedule?                   │
    │  │ Nightly backup│  YES → CronJob ✅                     │
    │  └──────────────┘                                        │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE
    [WHICH WORKLOAD TYPE? — a decision tree for easypj]
     Need stable identity + per-pod storage?
       ├─ YES ─► 🗄️ StatefulSet      (🐘 postgres: db-0, db-1 + PVCs)
       └─ NO
           Need exactly one pod per node?
             ├─ YES ─► 🔁 DaemonSet   (log/monitoring agent)
             └─ NO
                 Runs once to completion?
                   ├─ YES ─► ⚡ Job       (easypj manage.py migrate)
                   │         on a schedule? ─► ⏰ CronJob (nightly db-backup)
                   └─ NO ─► 🔄 Deployment  (easypj-web: stateless, scalable)


  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER BLOCK
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UTH — how the controllers actually work:
    • Job: the Job controller watches its pods and counts SUCCEEDED ones
      against .spec.completions. backoffLimit caps total failures; on the Nth
      failure the Job is marked Failed and stops creating pods.
    • CronJob: the CronJob controller wakes roughly every 10s, compares "now"
      against the schedule, and CREATES a Job object per due tick. Missed
      schedules (controller was down) are launched only if within
      startingDeadlineSeconds, else counted as a miss.
    • StatefulSet: ordinal index drives everything. PVC names follow the pattern
      <volumeClaimTemplate>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>, e.g. data-easypj-db-0.
      Pods come up 0→1→2 (each Ready before the next) and go down 2→1→0.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    • Job completionMode: Indexed gives each pod a fixed index (for sharded
      work); podFailurePolicy lets you treat specific exit codes as fatal vs
      retryable; spec.suspend: true pauses a Job/CronJob without deleting it.
    • CronJob concurrencyPolicy (Allow/Forbid/Replace) and
      startingDeadlineSeconds govern overlap and missed-run handling.
    • StatefulSet podManagementPolicy: Parallel brings pods up/down all at once
      (skip ordering); partitioned rollouts (updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.
      partition: N) update only pods with ordinal ≥ N — a canary for stateful
      apps.
    • DaemonSet updateStrategy OnDelete vs RollingUpdate for controlled agent
      restarts.

  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ Pick the type: Deployment (stateless, scalable),             ║
  ║     StatefulSet (stable id + per-pod storage),                    ║
  ║     DaemonSet (one pod per node), Job (run-to-completion),        ║
  ║     CronJob (scheduled). Know WHEN to use each.                   ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ A Job runs to completion and STOPS; completions = how many    ║
  ║     successes, parallelism = how many at once, backoffLimit =     ║
  ║     retries before Failed. restartPolicy must be OnFailure/Never. ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ A CronJob creates a Job per scheduled tick; concurrencyPolicy ║
  ║     (Allow/Forbid/Replace) controls overlap; schedule runs in the ║
  ║     cluster's timezone (UTC unless spec.timeZone set).            ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ A DaemonSet runs exactly one pod per eligible node and        ║
  ║     auto-adds/removes pods as nodes join/leave — no replicas.     ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ A StatefulSet needs a HEADLESS Service; it gives ordered      ║
  ║     stable names (db-0, db-1), stable DNS, and a PVC per pod via  ║
  ║     volumeClaimTemplates. Scaling DOWN does NOT delete the PVCs.  ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  ✅ Deployments manage ReplicaSets manage Pods; rolling update +  ║
  ║     `rollout undo` give safe ships and instant rollbacks.         ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  🎯 CKA Relevance: part of the 15% Workloads domain. Expect       ║
  ║     create job/cronjob, --from=cronjob, and "pick the type" Qs.   ║
  ║                                                                    ║
  ║  🔑 Must-Remember Commands:                                       ║
  ║     kubectl create job easypj-migrate --image=easypj:v1          ║
  ║     kubectl create cronjob backup --schedule="0 2 * * *" ...     ║
  ║     kubectl create job run-now --from=cronjob/easypj-db-backup   ║
  ║     kubectl get jobs / cronjobs / ds / sts                       ║
  ║     kubectl scale sts easypj-db --replicas=3                     ║

  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ A Job's pod template restartPolicy MUST be OnFailure or Never — the
       default Always is illegal in a Job and the API will reject it.
    ⚠️ CronJob schedule runs in the controller-manager's TIMEZONE (UTC by
       default). "0 2 * * *" is cluster 02:00, not your local 02:00.
    ⚠️ concurrencyPolicy defaults to Allow — long-running CronJobs can OVERLAP
       and pile up. Use Forbid for backups so two pg_dumps never run at once.
    ⚠️ A StatefulSet REQUIRES a headless Service (clusterIP: None) named in
       serviceName, or the pods get no stable DNS.
    ⚠️ Scaling a StatefulSet DOWN does NOT delete the orphaned PVCs — by design,
       to protect your data. You must delete PVCs manually if you want them gone.
    ⚠️ DaemonSet pods will NOT land on tainted control-plane nodes unless you add
       the matching toleration.
    ⚠️ Completed Job pods linger as "Completed" (not auto-deleted) until you
       delete the Job or set ttlSecondsAfterFinished.


  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ Trigger a one-off run from an existing CronJob immediately:
         kubectl create job run-now --from=cronjob/easypj-db-backup
    ⚡ Generate a CronJob fast with imperative create:
         kubectl create cronjob backup --image=postgres:16 \
           --schedule="0 2 * * *" -- /bin/sh -c "pg_dump ..."
    ⚡ Generate a Job imperatively:
         kubectl create job easypj-migrate --image=easypj:v1 \
           -- python manage.py migrate
    ⚡ Watch a Job finish: kubectl get jobs -w  (or `kubectl wait --for=
       condition=complete job/easypj-migrate`).
    ⚡ Inspect StatefulSet ordering/storage at a glance:
         kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-db  /  kubectl get pvc


  🔑 COMMANDS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    kubectl create job NAME --image=IMG -- CMD          # imperative Job
    kubectl create cronjob NAME --image=IMG --schedule="..." -- CMD
    kubectl create job NAME --from=cronjob/CRONJOB       # one-off from CronJob
    kubectl get jobs                                     # list Jobs
    kubectl get cronjobs   (kubectl get cj)              # list CronJobs
    kubectl get ds                                       # list DaemonSets
    kubectl get sts                                      # list StatefulSets
    kubectl scale sts NAME --replicas=N                  # scale a StatefulSet
    kubectl describe job NAME                            # completions/failures
    kubectl logs job/NAME                                # logs from Job pods
    kubectl delete job NAME                              # remove Job + its pods


  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 16  (merged union, 12)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Q1. Create a Job that runs `manage.py migrate` once for easypj.
        A: A Job with completions defaulting to 1.
           kubectl create job easypj-migrate --image=easypj:v1 \
             -n easypj -- python manage.py migrate --noinput
        WHY: Migrations must run exactly once and STOP — a Deployment would
        loop forever. The Job's restartPolicy (Never/OnFailure) and backoffLimit
        handle transient failures.

    Q2. Create a CronJob that backs up the database nightly at 02:00.
        A: schedule "0 2 * * *", concurrencyPolicy Forbid.
           kubectl create cronjob easypj-db-backup --image=postgres:16 \
             --schedule="0 2 * * *" -n easypj -- /bin/sh -c \
             "pg_dump -h easypj-db -U easypj easypj > /backup/db.sql"
        WHY: A CronJob creates a Job each tick. Forbid stops two backups
        overlapping. Remember: 02:00 is the cluster's timezone (UTC default).

    Q3. Run a logging agent on EVERY node. Which workload type?
        A: A DaemonSet. It guarantees one pod per eligible node and auto-creates
        a pod when a new node joins / removes it when a node leaves.
        WHY: Deployments place replicas wherever the scheduler likes — they
        cannot guarantee coverage of every node. Add control-plane tolerations
        if the agent must run on masters too.

    Q4. Give the postgres tier stable identity + per-pod storage.
        A: A StatefulSet with serviceName pointing at a headless Service and a
        volumeClaimTemplates entry, so each replica gets its own PVC and the
        pods are named easypj-db-0, easypj-db-1, ...
        WHY: Stable names + stable DNS + dedicated PVCs are exactly what a
        clustered database needs; a Deployment provides none of these.

    Q5. Pick the type for: web · db · migration · nightly backup · node agent.
        A: web → Deployment; db → StatefulSet; migration → Job;
           nightly backup → CronJob; node agent → DaemonSet.
        WHY: Each maps to a core need — stateless/scalable, stable+stored,
        run-once, scheduled, one-per-node respectively.

    Q6. Run a Job with 5 completions, 2 in parallel.
        A: spec.completions: 5 and spec.parallelism: 2 in the Job YAML.
        WHY: completions is the finish line (total successes required),
        parallelism is the lane count (how many pods run at once). The Job keeps
        two pods running, replacing each as it succeeds, until five complete.

    Q7. Trigger a Job immediately from an existing CronJob.
        A: kubectl create job run-now --from=cronjob/easypj-db-backup -n easypj
        WHY: --from copies the CronJob's jobTemplate into a standalone Job so you
        can run the backup on demand without waiting for the next schedule.

    Q8. Why does a StatefulSet need a headless Service?
        A: The headless Service (clusterIP: None) creates a per-pod DNS A-record
        (e.g. easypj-db-0.easypj-db...), giving each replica a stable network
        identity so peers can address pods individually.
        WHY: A normal ClusterIP load-balances across all pods and hides identity
        — useless for a database whose members must find each other by name.

    Q9. What are the PVC names for a StatefulSet "db" with 2 replicas, whose
        volumeClaimTemplate is named "data"?
        A: data-db-0 and data-db-1.
        WHY: PVC names follow <volumeClaimTemplate>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>.
        These PVCs persist even if you scale the StatefulSet down.

    Q10. Why do StatefulSet pods start and stop in order?
        A: Ordered operations guarantee correctness for stateful apps — db-0
        (often the primary) must be Ready before db-1 joins as a replica;
        deletion reverses (2→1→0) so the primary is the last to go.
        WHY: Many clustered systems require a deterministic bring-up sequence;
        random ordering could corrupt replication or quorum.

    Q11. A Job pod keeps CrashLooping but the Job won't fail. What's wrong?
        A: Likely restartPolicy: Always (invalid for a Job) was forced, or
        backoffLimit is very high. Set restartPolicy: OnFailure/Never and a
        sensible backoffLimit (e.g. 4) so failures eventually mark the Job Failed.
        WHY: Always would make the kubelet restart the container in place forever;
        the Job needs distinct pod failures to count toward backoffLimit.

    Q12. You deleted a StatefulSet but your data is "still there" / "still using
         storage." Why, and how do you clean up?
        A: StatefulSet PVCs are NOT garbage-collected on delete or scale-down.
        Delete them explicitly: kubectl delete pvc -l app=easypj-db
        WHY: This is intentional data protection — Kubernetes assumes the volumes
        may hold irreplaceable state and refuses to remove them automatically.

  CKA Exam Weight: 20% (the single largest scored domain on the exam)

  What you'll build: easypj reachable from the internet via Ingress AND the
  modern Gateway API, talking to its database internally, with traffic locked
  down by NetworkPolicies and names resolved by CoreDNS.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  📖 PART 5 INTRO
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A running pod nobody can reach is useless. This part is the plumbing: how
  pods get IPs and talk (flat network + CNI), how Services give them stable
  names and load-balance, how DNS resolves those names, how external traffic
  enters (Ingress AND the new Gateway API), and how NetworkPolicies firewall
  it all. 🆕 2025: Gateway API is now an official exam competency.

  Networking is where the most CKA points are concentrated, and also where the
  most candidates lose time. The reason is layering: a single failing request
  ("easypj.example.com returns 503") can break at the CNI (pod has no IP), at
  the Service (selector matches nothing -> no endpoints), at DNS (CoreDNS down
  or wrong search domain), at the Ingress (no controller, wrong path), or at a
  NetworkPolicy (default-deny with no allow rule). Mastering this part means
  being able to walk that stack top-to-bottom in the exam and fix the one
  broken layer fast.

  🧠 ANALOGY — the building's wiring & mail system:
    • CNI / pod network = the electrical wiring + flat floor plan: every room
      (pod) gets a power outlet (IP) and any room can reach any other room.
    • Service = the front desk extension number: people (pods) move offices,
      but the extension (ClusterIP) never changes and routes you to whoever
      is on shift (a healthy endpoint).
    • DNS / CoreDNS = the company phone book: you dial a name ("easypj-db"),
      it looks up the extension (ClusterIP) for you.
    • Ingress / Gateway API = the lobby reception that takes outside visitors
      (internet traffic) and directs them to the right department by the name
      on the door (host/path L7 routing).
    • NetworkPolicy = the keycard doors between departments: by default
      everyone can roam (allow-all), until you install locks (default-deny)
      and then issue keycards (allow rules) for exactly who may pass.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 5 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch17 POD NET (CNI) ─▶ Ch18 SERVICES ─▶ Ch19 DNS (CoreDNS)               │
  │   IPs & flat net        stable VIPs       name -> ClusterIP             │
  │                              │                                          │
  │                              ▼                                          │
  │ Ch20 INGRESS + NETWORKPOLICY ──▶ Ch20b GATEWAY API (modern ingress)     │
  │   L7 routing + firewall            Gateway/HTTPRoute, role-oriented     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 READING ORDER & DEPENDENCIES
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Layer in the stack        │ Chapter │ Answers the question             │
  ├───────────────────────────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤

  │ L4 stable virtual IPs     │  Ch18   │ "How do I get a name/IP that      │
  │   (Services, kube-proxy)  │         │  survives pod churn + LB?"        │
  │ Name resolution           │  Ch19   │ "How does easypj-db become an     │
  │   (CoreDNS)               │         │  IP I can dial?"                  │
  │ L7 north-south ingress    │  Ch20   │ "How does the internet reach my   │
  │   + east-west firewall    │         │  app, and how do I lock it down?" │

  └───────────────────────────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘
  Read in order: each layer assumes the one above it already works. You cannot
  debug a Service (Ch18) without understanding pod IPs (Ch17); you cannot debug
  an Ingress (Ch20) without a working Service + DNS (Ch18/Ch19).

  [PART 5 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: easypj-web Pods get CNI IPs -> a ClusterIP Service
  fronts them -> CoreDNS resolves easypj-db -> an Ingress (then a Gateway/
  HTTPRoute) exposes easypj.example.com -> a default-deny NetworkPolicy only
  allows web->db on 5432. VISUAL: the full north-south + east-west traffic map.

  VISUAL — the full easypj traffic map (north-south + east-west):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   INTERNET (user hits https://easypj.example.com)                         │
  │        │                                                                  │
  │        ▼  north-south (L7)                                                │
  │   ┌─────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │   │ Ingress / Gateway API   │ ───▶ │ Ingress Controller / Gateway Pod │  │
  │   │  host+path routing      │      │  (nginx, Envoy, ...)             │  │
  │   └─────────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                              │                            │
  │                                              ▼                            │
  │   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │   │ Service: easypj-web  (ClusterIP, stable VIP)                       │  │
  │   │   selector app=easypj-web  ─▶  Endpoints/EndpointSlice            │  │
  │   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │            │ kube-proxy DNATs VIP ─▶ a healthy backend                    │
  │            ▼                                                              │
  │   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐                          │
  │   │ web Pod 1 │   │ web Pod 2 │   │ web Pod 3 │   (CNI IPs, flat net)     │
  │   └───────────┘   └───────────┘   └───────────┘                          │
  │            │ east-west: dials "easypj-db" ─▶ CoreDNS ─▶ ClusterIP        │
  │            ▼                                                              │
  │   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │   │ Service: easypj-db (ClusterIP) ─▶ PostgreSQL Pod  :5432            │  │
  │   │   🔒 NetworkPolicy: default-deny; allow ONLY web ─▶ db on 5432     │  │
  │   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  north-south = traffic in/out of the cluster (internet <-> Ingress/Gateway).
  east-west   = traffic between pods inside the cluster (web <-> db),
                governed by CoreDNS for naming and NetworkPolicy for access.

  🎯 WHY THIS PART CARRIES 20% OF THE EXAM
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Networking is the connective tissue of every other domain: Workloads (Part 4)
  are pointless if they can't be reached, Storage talks over the network, and
  Cluster Architecture depends on a healthy CNI and CoreDNS. Expect tasks that
  ask you to: create/expose a Service of a given type, fix a Service whose
  selector doesn't match its pods, configure an Ingress with host/path rules,
  troubleshoot CoreDNS, and author a NetworkPolicy that implements default-deny
  plus a single allow rule. The 2025 syllabus adds Gateway API resources
  (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) as fair game.

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER ACROSS THIS PART
    • Pod network is FLAT: every pod can reach every other pod by IP with no
      NAT — until a NetworkPolicy says otherwise.
    • A Service with no matching Endpoints silently drops traffic; always check
      "kubectl get endpoints <svc>" first.
    • In-cluster names resolve via CoreDNS as
      <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local; the search domain lets a pod reach
      "easypj-db" short-name within its own namespace.
    • NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE allow-lists and only take effect if your CNI
      supports them (Calico, Cilium — NOT plain flannel).
    • Ingress needs a running Ingress Controller; the Ingress object alone does
      nothing. Same idea for Gateway API: a Gateway needs an implementation.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Services & Networking (20%).
    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS: every networking bug you will ever chase — a pod that
        won't reach the database, a Service that returns "connection refused", a
        node stuck NotReady, a DNS lookup that times out — traces back to the
        four rules in this chapter. Get the model straight and troubleshooting
        becomes a checklist instead of a guessing game.
        VISUAL: the 4 fundamental networking rules card (below).
    [C] OBJECTIVES:
        - State the Kubernetes network model (the 4 rules) from memory.
        - Explain what CNI is and whose job it is to install/troubleshoot it.
        - Trace a pod-to-pod packet, same-node AND cross-node.
        - Explain kube-proxy's role and its three modes.
        - Perform basic network debugging from inside the cluster.
    [D] CKA RELEVANCE: Services & Networking is 20% of the exam. The grader does
        not ask you to recite theory, but you cannot fix a broken Service, a
        failing NetworkPolicy, or a NotReady node without this mental model. This
        chapter is the foundation the Services, DNS, NetworkPolicy and Ingress
        chapters all build on.

    [E] SECTION MAP
        17.1  The Kubernetes Networking Model        🎯  the 4 rules, flat net
        17.2  CNI Plugins — How Networking Is Built  🎯  the plug point, you install it
        17.3  Pod-to-Pod Communication               🎯  same node vs cross node
        17.4  kube-proxy — Service Networking        🎯  DaemonSet, iptables/IPVS/nftables
        17.5  Network Troubleshooting for Admins     🩺  checks + common issues table

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17.1  The Kubernetes Networking Model
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          The whole model rests on four rules. Memorize them; everything else
          is implementation detail.
          - Every Pod gets its own unique IP address.
          - All Pods can reach all other Pods WITHOUT NAT.
          - All Nodes can reach all Pods WITHOUT NAT.
          - The IP a Pod sees itself as = the IP others see it as.

          💡 INSIGHT: this is deliberately a FLAT layer-3 network. There are no
          port-mapping games like classic Docker (-p 8080:80). A pod is a
          first-class network citizen with a real, routable IP. That is why you
          can curl one pod from another by IP and it "just works" — any pod can
          talk to any pod.

          🧠 ANALOGY: think of the cluster as one big office building where every
          desk (pod) has its own direct phone extension. You dial the extension
          and you are connected — no switchboard operator translating numbers
          (no NAT). The extension a person gives out is the same one that rings
          their phone (a pod sees its own real IP).

          📖 KEY TERM — NAT (Network Address Translation): rewriting source/dest
          IPs as packets cross a boundary. The K8s model FORBIDS NAT between
          pods/nodes precisely so addresses stay meaningful end-to-end.

          [KUBERNETES NETWORKING RULES]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  THE 4 FUNDAMENTAL NETWORKING RULES                     │
          │                                                          │
          │  Rule 1: Every Pod gets a unique IP                     │
          │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                          │
          │  │Pod A │  │Pod B │  │Pod C │                          │
          │  │10.1.1│  │10.1.2│  │10.2.1│                          │
          │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                          │
          │                                                          │
          │  Rule 2: Pod-to-Pod — direct communication              │
          │  Pod A (10.1.1) → Pod C (10.2.1) ✅ No NAT needed     │
          │                                                          │
          │  Rule 3: Node-to-Pod — direct communication             │
          │  Node 1 → Pod C (10.2.1) on Node 2 ✅ No NAT          │
          │                                                          │
          │  Rule 4: Pod sees its own real IP                       │
          │  Inside Pod A: "my IP is 10.1.1"                        │
          │  From Pod B:   "Pod A is 10.1.1"  ✅ Same IP           │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: kube-proxy is NOT in the pod-to-pod path. Pod A
          curling Pod B by pod IP never touches kube-proxy. kube-proxy only
          matters when you target a Service VIP (Section 17.4).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17.2  CNI Plugins — How Networking Is Implemented
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - CNI = Container Network Interface.
          - The plugin actually CREATES the pod network — it gives each pod its
            IP, wires up the veth pair, and arranges cross-node routing.
          - Admin responsibility: choose, install, and troubleshoot the CNI.
            Kubernetes ships NO networking out of the box.

          📖 KEY TERM — CNI: a thin spec/contract. When kubelet starts a pod it
          calls the CNI plugin binary, which sets up the pod's network namespace
          (assigns IP, creates the veth, adds routes) and hands the result back.
          The CNI is the network "plug point" of the cluster.

          ⚠️ GOTCHA: no CNI installed → every node reports NotReady and pods sit
          Pending/ContainerCreating forever, because kubelet cannot complete pod
          network setup. The fix is "install a CNI", not "restart kubelet".

          [CNI PLUGINS — COMPARISON]
          ┌────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
          │ Plugin     │ Dataplane    │ NetworkPol? │ Notes / when to pick      │
          ├────────────┼──────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
          │ Flannel    │ VXLAN overlay│ ❌ NO       │ Simplest; great for labs. │
          │            │              │             │ Policies silently ignored.│
          │ Calico     │ BGP routing  │ ✅ YES      │ Production default; rich  │
          │            │ (or VXLAN)   │             │ NetworkPolicy; scalable.  │
          │ Cilium     │ eBPF         │ ✅ YES      │ Modern; eBPF dataplane,   │
          │            │              │             │ L7 policy, observability. │
          │ Weave Net  │ VXLAN/mesh   │ ✅ YES      │ Easy mesh; less common    │
          │            │              │             │ now, lower performance.   │
          └────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

          🧭 DECISION GUIDE:
            - Just need a cluster to come up for practice  → Flannel.
            - Need NetworkPolicy / production               → Calico.
            - Want eBPF, L7 policy, deep observability      → Cilium.
            - Inherited a mesh you must keep                → Weave.

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: the CNI creates a veth (virtual ethernet) PAIR per
          pod — one end becomes eth0 inside the pod's netns, the other end lands
          on the host and attaches to the node bridge (cbr0). The plugin also
          installs the routes that send cross-node pod traffic out the node NIC.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17.3  Pod-to-Pod Communication
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - Same node: via the local Linux bridge (cbr0). Pod's veth → cbr0 →
            destination pod's veth. Pure local switching, no encapsulation.
          - Different nodes: the CNI either ENCAPSULATES the packet (VXLAN
            overlay) or ROUTES it natively (BGP, e.g. Calico) out the node NIC,
            across the physical network, into the peer node's bridge.

          [POD-TO-POD NETWORKING — cross-node]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  Node 1                          Node 2               │
          │  ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐ │
          │  │ Pod A (10.244.1.2)│          │ Pod C (10.244.2.3)│ │
          │  │ easypj-django    │          │ postgres          │ │
          │  └────────┬─────────┘          └────────▲─────────┘ │
          │           │                              │            │
          │  ┌────────▼──────────┐        ┌──────────┴────────┐ │
          │  │   cbr0 (bridge)   │        │   cbr0 (bridge)   │ │
          │  └────────┬──────────┘        └──────────▲────────┘ │
          │           │                              │            │
          │  ┌────────▼──────────┐        ┌──────────┴────────┐ │
          │  │   eth0 (node NIC) │───────▶│   eth0 (node NIC) │ │
          │  │   192.168.1.10    │  CNI   │   192.168.1.11    │ │
          │  └───────────────────┘ overlay └───────────────────┘ │
          │                        (VXLAN)                        │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          📊 KEY DIAGRAM — the same path, annotated (C2 view):
          [POD-TO-POD ACROSS NODES — the flat network, no NAT]
           Node 1                                Node 2
           📦 web (10.244.1.5)                   📦 db (10.244.2.8)
               │                                     ▲
           ┌───▼─────────┐  CNI overlay (VXLAN)  ┌───┴─────────┐
           │ cbr0 bridge │                        │ cbr0 bridge │
           └───┬─────────┘                        └───▲─────────┘
           ┌───▼─────────┐   eth0 ──────────► eth0 ┌──┴──────────┐
           │ 192.168.1.10│ ====== physical net ====│ 192.168.1.11│
           └─────────────┘                         └─────────────┘
           📖 Rules: every pod a unique IP · pod<->pod direct (no NAT) · a pod
              sees its OWN real IP. kube-proxy only matters for Service VIPs, not
              pod-to-pod.

          🧪 PACKET TRACE (cross-node, easypj-web → easypj-db):
            web's eth0 → web's veth → node1 cbr0 → CNI encapsulates (VXLAN) or
            routes (BGP) → out node1 eth0 → physical net → node2 eth0 →
            decapsulate/route → node2 cbr0 → db's veth → db's eth0. No NAT
            anywhere; db sees web's REAL pod IP (10.244.1.5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17.4  kube-proxy — Service Networking
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - Runs on EVERY node as a DaemonSet.
          - Implements Service → Pod routing rules (turns a Service VIP into a
            real pod endpoint IP).
          - Modes: iptables (default), IPVS (higher performance at scale),
            nftables (newer).
          - When a Service is created/changed, kube-proxy updates the dataplane
            routing rules on ALL nodes so the VIP resolves to current endpoints.

          [kube-proxy — ClusterIP DNAT]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  curl easypj-web (ClusterIP 10.96.0.20:80)                │
          │                  │                                         │
          │                  ▼                                         │
          │   ┌───────────────────────────────────┐                  │
          │   │ kube-proxy dataplane (iptables/IPVS)│                 │
          │   │  match VIP 10.96.0.20:80           │                  │
          │   │  DNAT → one READY endpoint:        │                  │
          │   └───────────────┬───────────────────┘                  │
          │        ┌──────────┼──────────┐                            │
          │        ▼          ▼          ▼                            │
          │  10.244.1.5  10.244.2.8  10.244.3.4   (pod endpoints,     │
          │   :8080       :8080       :8080        load-balanced)     │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: a request to a ClusterIP is matched by a kube-proxy
          rule and DNAT'd (destination NAT) to one of the Service's READY
          endpoint pod IPs:targetPort, load-balanced (random/round-robin). The
          connection is tracked in the kernel conntrack table so replies return
          correctly.

          🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
            - iptables vs IPVS: iptables rules grow linearly with Services and are
              evaluated sequentially → O(n) lookups that hurt at thousands of
              Services. IPVS uses kernel hash tables → near-constant lookups and
              real load-balancing algorithms (rr, lc, etc.). Pick IPVS at scale.
            - eBPF dataplane (Cilium) can REPLACE kube-proxy entirely, doing
              Service load-balancing and NetworkPolicy in-kernel without iptables.
            - BGP (Calico) advertises pod CIDRs as real routes — no overlay
              encapsulation, lower overhead — vs VXLAN overlay (works anywhere but
              adds a header and shrinks usable MTU).
            - Dual-stack IPv4/IPv6: pods/Services can carry both families.
            - Per-node pod-CIDR allocation: each node owns a slice of the cluster
              pod CIDR (e.g. node1 = 10.244.1.0/24) so IPs never collide.
            - conntrack limits: busy nodes can exhaust nf_conntrack_max →
              dropped connections; tune net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max.
            - MTU/overlay overhead: VXLAN adds ~50 bytes; mismatched MTU causes
              large packets to hang/drop while small ones work.
            - NetworkPolicy can be enforced at the eBPF layer (Cilium) for speed.
            - Service mesh at a glance: sidecar (Istio classic, a proxy per pod)
              vs ambient/sidecarless (shared node proxy) — adds L7 routing, mTLS,
              and observability on top of this base network.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17.5  Network Troubleshooting for Admins
          🩺 [TROUBLESHOOTING]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - Check CNI pods:    kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -Ei 'calico|cilium|flannel'
          - Check kube-proxy:  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep proxy
          - Confirm pod IPs:   kubectl get pods -A -o wide
          - Test connectivity: kubectl exec -it pod -- curl <service-ip>
          - DNS resolution:    kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default

          ⚡ SPEED TIP: don't debug from your app pod (it may lack curl/nslookup).
          Spin up a throwaway diagnostics pod that has every tool:
            kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
          (or busybox for a minimal shell).

          [COMMON NETWORK ISSUES AND FIXES]
          ┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
          │ Symptom                     │ Likely cause         │ Fix / check              │
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ All nodes NotReady, pods    │ No CNI installed /   │ Install/repair CNI;      │
          │ Pending/ContainerCreating   │ CNI DaemonSet crash  │ kubectl apply -f cni.yaml│
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
