          │                             │ crashing             │ -o wide; check its logs  │
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ Service VIP unreachable but │ kube-proxy down or   │ Check kube-proxy DS;     │
          │ pod IP works                │ no endpoints         │ kubectl get endpoints svc│
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ nslookup fails / DNS times  │ CoreDNS down or net  │ get pods -n kube-system; │
          │ out                         │ broken to it         │ nslookup kubernetes.default│
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ ping works, large HTTP hangs│ MTU mismatch (overlay│ Align CNI/iface MTU;     │
          │ across nodes                │ overhead ~50B)       │ ip -d link show flannel.1│
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ NetworkPolicy not enforcing │ CNI is Flannel (no   │ Switch to Calico/Cilium  │
          │                             │ policy support)      │                          │
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │ Random dropped connections  │ conntrack table full │ Raise                    │
          │ on busy node                │                      │ nf_conntrack_max         │
          └─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

    [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER — Chapter 17
================================================================================
        - How a packet to a ClusterIP is DNAT'd to a real pod IP by iptables,
          and tracked through conntrack so replies return to the caller.
        - IPVS vs iptables at scale: hash-table O(1) lookups + LB algorithms vs
          sequential O(n) rule chains.
        - How the CNI sets up veth pairs (pod eth0 <-> host bridge) and the
          routes that carry cross-node pod traffic.
        - eBPF dataplane (Cilium) replacing kube-proxy; BGP (Calico) vs VXLAN
          overlay; dual-stack IPv4/IPv6; per-node pod-CIDR allocation; conntrack
          limits & tuning; MTU/overlay overhead; NetworkPolicy enforced in eBPF;
          service mesh (sidecar vs ambient) at a glance.

================================================================================
    [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 17
================================================================================
        • The K8s network model has 4 rules: every pod gets a unique IP; pods
          talk to pods WITHOUT NAT; nodes talk to pods without NAT; a pod sees
          its own real IP (the same IP others use to reach it). One flat network.
        • CNI (a plugin you install — Calico/Cilium/Flannel/Weave) implements
          that model. No CNI = nodes stay NotReady and pods never get an IP.
        • Choosing and troubleshooting the CNI is the ADMIN's job; Kubernetes
          ships no networking by itself.
        • kube-proxy is NOT in the pod-to-pod path. It only programs the
          dataplane (iptables/IPVS/nftables) that turns a Service VIP into a real
          pod IP.
        • Same-node traffic crosses a local bridge (veth → cbr0); cross-node
          traffic is encapsulated (VXLAN) or routed (BGP) by the CNI, then hits
          the peer node's bridge.
        • Flannel cannot enforce NetworkPolicy — pick Calico or Cilium when you
          need a pod firewall.

================================================================================
    [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 17
================================================================================
        • No CNI installed → every node shows NotReady, CoreDNS is Pending. The
          fix is "install a CNI", not "restart kubelet".
        • Flannel does NOT enforce NetworkPolicy — policies silently do nothing.
          Use Calico or Cilium when you need a pod firewall.
        • MTU mismatch (overlay adds ~50 bytes) → large packets hang/drop while
          ping/small requests work. Classic "curl hangs at TLS handshake" symptom.
        • conntrack table full on busy nodes → dropped connections; tune
          net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max.
        • Debugging from the app pod fails because it lacks curl/nslookup — use a
          netshoot/busybox pod instead.

================================================================================
    [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 17
================================================================================
        • Debug with a throwaway pod: kubectl run tmp --rm -it
          --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash (or busybox for a minimal shell).
        • kubectl get pods -A -o wide shows pod IPs and which node — the fastest
          way to confirm the CNI assigned addresses.
        • A NotReady node almost always means the CNI DaemonSet pod on that node
          is crashing — check kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide.
        • To prove the flat network in one shot: curl a Service ClusterIP, then
          curl a pod IP directly — both should work.

================================================================================
    [K] 🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 17
================================================================================
        kubectl get pods -A -o wide                 # pod IPs + nodes
        kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep -Ei 'calico|cilium|flannel|kube-proxy'
        kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
        kubectl exec net -- curl -s http://easypj-web.default.svc.cluster.local
        kubectl exec net -- nslookup easypj-db
        kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default
        kubectl get endpoints easypj-web            # do Services have READY pods?
        ip route ; ip -d link show flannel.1        # on a node: overlay device/MTU

    [L] 🧪 DRILL: from a temp netshoot pod, curl the easypj-web ClusterIP, then
        curl a pod IP directly; confirm both work (proves the flat network).
        Scale down the CNI DaemonSet on one node and watch that node go NotReady.

    [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 17 (10 questions, full answer + explanation)
================================================================================
      Q1. State the 4 rules of the Kubernetes network model.
          A. (1) Every pod has a unique IP. (2) Pods communicate pod-to-pod with
          no NAT. (3) Nodes communicate with pods with no NAT. (4) A pod sees its
          own IP as the same IP others use. Together: one flat L3 network.

      Q2. All nodes are NotReady and pods are stuck Pending/ContainerCreating.
          What is the most likely cause and fix?
          A. No CNI plugin installed (or its DaemonSet is crashing). kubelet
          can't set up pod networking, so it reports NotReady. Fix: install/repair
          a CNI (e.g. kubectl apply -f calico.yaml) and confirm its pods Running.

      Q3. Is kube-proxy involved when pod A curls pod B by pod IP? Explain.
          A. No. Pod-to-pod by IP uses the CNI's flat network directly.
          kube-proxy only matters when you target a Service VIP, which it DNATs
          to a pod IP.

      Q4. Trace a packet from web on node1 to db on node2 (different nodes).
          A. web's veth → node1 bridge (cbr0) → CNI encapsulates (VXLAN) or
          routes (BGP) out node1 eth0 → physical net → node2 eth0 → decapsulate →
          node2 bridge → db's veth → db. No NAT; db sees web's real pod IP.

      Q5. How do you debug "web can't reach db" at the network layer?
          A. Run a netshoot pod; nslookup easypj-db (DNS?), curl <db-podIP>:5432
          (pod reachable?), curl easypj-db:5432 (Service path?). Narrow whether
          it's DNS, Service/endpoints, NetworkPolicy, or the CNI.

      Q6. What kube-proxy modes exist and how do you check which is in use?
          A. iptables (default), IPVS (better at scale), nftables (newer). Check
          the kube-proxy ConfigMap mode: field, or kubectl -n kube-system logs
          ds/kube-proxy | grep -i proxier.

      Q7. How does a request to a ClusterIP reach a real pod?
          A. kube-proxy installs iptables/IPVS rules that DNAT the Service
          VIP:port to one of the READY endpoint pod IPs:targetPort, load-balanced.

      Q8. You need NetworkPolicy but it isn't enforcing. Which CNI did you pick?
          A. Probably Flannel, which ignores NetworkPolicy. Switch to a policy-
          aware CNI like Calico or Cilium.

      Q9. ping works but large HTTP responses hang across nodes. Likely cause?
          A. MTU mismatch — the overlay's encapsulation overhead shrinks the
          usable MTU; oversized packets get dropped. Align the CNI/interface MTU.

      Q10. What is a veth pair and where is it used here?
          A. A virtual ethernet cable with two ends: one inside the pod's network
          namespace (eth0), one on the host attached to the bridge. It connects
          the pod to the node's network so the CNI can route its traffic.

================================================================================
    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — a packet's journey pod → Service → pod
================================================================================
        easypj-web pod ──curl easypj-db (ClusterIP)──┐
                                                      ▼
                                  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                                  │ kube-proxy DNAT: VIP → pod IP    │
                                  │ (iptables/IPVS, conntrack-tracked)│
                                  └────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                                   ▼
                          CNI flat network (cbr0 bridge; VXLAN/BGP cross-node)
                                                   ▼
                                          easypj-db pod (real pod IP)

        .vs-prose SUMMARY: A request that names a Service first hits kube-proxy's
        dataplane, where the Service VIP is DNAT'd to one READY pod endpoint and
        recorded in conntrack. From that point the packet is just pod-to-pod
        traffic on the CNI's flat network: it crosses the local bridge if the
        target pod is on the same node, or is encapsulated (VXLAN) / routed (BGP)
        across the physical network to the peer node's bridge if not. No NAT is
        applied between pods, so the destination pod sees the caller's real pod
        IP. If you remember just one picture: kube-proxy resolves WHICH pod, the
        CNI delivers the packet TO that pod, and pod-to-pod by IP skips
        kube-proxy entirely.

================================================================================


================================================================================
  Chapter 18: Services Deep Dive                                       🟡 🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]   ·   Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate

  [META] 🟡 · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Services & Networking (20% of the exam).

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  Services are how everything finds everything in Kubernetes. Pods are
  ephemeral — they are created, killed, rescheduled, and re-IP'd constantly.
  Hard-coding a pod IP is a guaranteed outage. A Service is the stable façade:
  one virtual IP and one DNS name that never changes, sitting in front of a
  moving set of pods. Your easypj-web pods come and go; the easypj-web Service
  endures, and easypj-db, the browser, and other pods all reach the app
  through it. If you cannot wire a selector to its endpoints in your head, you
  cannot debug a broken Service on exam day — and "no endpoints" is one of the
  most common live-cluster failures.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  • Explain how a Service maps a stable VIP + DNS name to a moving set of pods
    via label selectors and an auto-maintained Endpoints/EndpointSlice list.
  • Choose and configure all five Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort,
    LoadBalancer, ExternalName, Headless.
  • Resolve services by DNS (<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local) and understand the
    short-form names.
  • Diagnose empty endpoints, port/targetPort mismatches, and pending LBs.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
  Services & Networking is 20% of the exam. Expect to expose a Deployment
  imperatively under time pressure, fix a Service whose endpoints are empty,
  pick the right type for a stated access requirement, and reason about DNS
  names. This is bread-and-butter exam work — fast, deterministic points.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
  18.1  How Services Work — Under the Hood    🎯
  18.2  ClusterIP Services                     🎯
  18.3  NodePort Services                      🎯
  18.4  LoadBalancer Services                  🎯
  18.5  ExternalName Services                  🎯
  18.6  Headless Services                      🎯
  18.7  Service Discovery — How Pods Find Services  🎯

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.1  How Services Work — Under the Hood   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - Service = stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) + DNS name
    - Endpoints: list of pod IPs that match the Service selector
    - When a pod dies/starts, Endpoints are updated automatically
    - Only READY pods are listed — readiness gates endpoint membership

          [SERVICE ROUTING — HOW TRAFFIC REACHES YOUR PODS]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                                                            │
          │  kubectl apply:                                           │
          │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐                     │
          │  │ kind: Service                    │                     │
          │  │ metadata:                        │                     │
          │  │   name: easypj-web               │                     │
          │  │ spec:                            │                     │
          │  │   selector:                      │                     │
          │  │     app: easypj  ──────────────────┐                  │
          │  │   ports:                         │  │ label match     │
          │  │     - port: 80                   │  │                  │
          │  │       targetPort: 8000           │  │                  │
          │  └──────────────────────────────────┘  │                  │
          │                                        │                  │
          │  Service (ClusterIP: 10.96.45.2)      │                  │
          │       │                                │                  │
          │       ▼ auto-created                   │                  │
          │  ┌──────────────────┐                  │                  │
          │  │   Endpoints      │  ← K8s watches   │                  │
          │  │   object         │    for pods with  │                  │
          │  │                  │    matching labels │                  │
          │  │  10.244.1.5:8000 │◄─────────────────┘                  │
          │  │  10.244.2.8:8000 │ ← pod IPs auto-discovered          │
          │  │  10.244.3.2:8000 │                                     │
          │  └────────┬─────────┘                                     │
          │           │ kube-proxy distributes traffic                │
          │     ┌─────┼──────┬──────────┐                             │
          │     ▼     ▼      ▼          │                             │
          │  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ │                             │
          │  │Pod 1 │ │Pod 2 │ │Pod 3 │ │                             │
          │  │easypj│ │easypj│ │easypj│ │                             │
          │  │:8000 │ │:8000 │ │:8000 │ │                             │
          │  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ │                             │
          │                             │                             │
          │  If Pod 3 dies:             │                             │
          │  Endpoints auto-removes     │                             │
          │  10.244.3.2 — traffic only  │                             │
          │  goes to Pod 1 & Pod 2      │                             │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    The same wiring, seen as a pipeline (note: modern clusters use
    EndpointSlice, the scalable successor to the single Endpoints object):

          [HOW A SERVICE FINDS ITS PODS — selector -> endpoints -> load-balance]
           apply Service{ selector: app=easypj, port 80 -> targetPort 8000 }
                │
                ▼  K8s watches for Pods with matching labels
           🔌 Service  ClusterIP 10.96.45.2:80
                │
                ▼  auto-built
           📇 EndpointSlice  ── only READY pods are listed ──┐
                │  10.244.1.5:8000  10.244.2.8:8000  10.244.3.2:8000
                ▼  🌐 kube-proxy load-balances (iptables/IPVS)
           📦 web-0        📦 web-1        📦 web-2

    💡 [INSIGHT] Pod 2 fails its readiness probe? It is DROPPED from the slice
       — traffic only flows to healthy pods, and clients never see a 500. No
       endpoints at all = selector/label mismatch.

    📖 [KEY TERM] port vs targetPort. `port` is the Service's own port (what
       clients dial); `targetPort` is the container's listening port (what the
       app actually binds). They are independent: port 80 → targetPort 8000 is
       normal for easypj-web because Django/Gunicorn listens on 8000.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.2  ClusterIP Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - Default type — accessible ONLY within the cluster
    - easypj Django app → reached by other pods (e.g. a worker, or the
      ingress controller) via the ClusterIP / DNS name
    - This is the right default for east-west, in-cluster traffic

          [CODE: ClusterIP Service YAML for easypj-web]
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Service
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            type: ClusterIP            # default — may be omitted
            selector:
              app: easypj
            ports:
              - name: http
                port: 80               # Service port (clients dial this)
                targetPort: 8000       # container port (Gunicorn listens here)

    Imperative equivalent (fastest on the exam):
          kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.3  NodePort Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    - Exposes the Service on EACH node's IP at a static port (30000-32767)
    - Access from outside: <NodeIP>:<NodePort>
    - A NodePort Service still has a ClusterIP underneath it (superset of
      ClusterIP); good for dev/test or bare-metal external access

          [CODE: NodePort Service YAML]
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Service
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            type: NodePort
            selector:
              app: easypj
            ports:
              - port: 80               # internal ClusterIP port
                targetPort: 8000       # container port
                nodePort: 30080        # external port on every node (optional;
                                       # auto-assigned in 30000-32767 if omitted)

    Imperative:
          kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --type=NodePort \
            --port=80 --target-port=8000

    ⚠️ nodePort must fall within 30000-32767 (the default range). Outside that
       range the API server rejects it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.4  LoadBalancer Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - Creates an EXTERNAL load balancer (cloud providers only)
    - Distributes traffic across nodes; provisions a real external IP
    - Superset of NodePort (which is a superset of ClusterIP)

          [CODE: LoadBalancer Service YAML]
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Service
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            type: LoadBalancer
            selector:
              app: easypj
            ports:
              - port: 80
                targetPort: 8000
          # EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until the cloud controller assigns one.
          # On bare-metal you need MetalLB (or similar) or it stays <pending>.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.5  ExternalName Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - DNS alias for an external service — a CNAME, no proxying, no selector,
      no endpoints, no ClusterIP
    - Maps a Service name to an external DNS name (e.g. a managed database)
    - Lets app config stay cluster-internal (talk to "easypj-db") while the
      real host lives outside the cluster

          [CODE: ExternalName Service pointing to a managed PostgreSQL host]
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Service
          metadata:
            name: easypj-db
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            type: ExternalName
            externalName: prod-pg.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
          # In-cluster, "easypj-db" now resolves (via CNAME) to the RDS host.
          # The app's settings.py keeps HOST: 'easypj-db' regardless of backend.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.6  Headless Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    - clusterIP: None — NO virtual IP is assigned
    - DNS returns the individual pod IPs instead of one VIP
    - Required for StatefulSets: gives stable, per-pod DNS names
      (e.g. postgres-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local)

          [CODE: Headless Service YAML for a PostgreSQL StatefulSet]
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Service
          metadata:
            name: easypj-db
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            clusterIP: None            # ← headless: no VIP, DNS returns pod IPs
            selector:
              app: easypj-db
            ports:
              - port: 5432
                targetPort: 5432
          # With a StatefulSet named "postgres", each replica gets a stable name:
          #   postgres-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
          #   postgres-1.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
          # Clients can address a SPECIFIC replica (e.g. the primary, postgres-0).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    18.7  Service Discovery — How Pods Find Services   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - DNS:  <svc-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
    - Short forms work too (same-namespace lookups are shortest)
    - Environment variables are also injected into every pod at start
      (e.g. EASYPJ_WEB_SERVICE_HOST), but DNS is preferred — env vars only
      exist for services created BEFORE the pod started

          [CODE: DNS resolution from an easypj pod to the postgres service]
          # from inside an easypj-web pod:
          $ nslookup easypj-db
          $ wget -qO- http://easypj-web:80/jobs/

          [SERVICE DISCOVERY — DNS]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  HOW easypj FINDS postgres                            │
          │                                                       │
          │  Full DNS:  easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local        │
          │  Short DNS: easypj-db.easypj                          │
          │  Same NS:   easypj-db                                 │
          │                                                       │
          │  In Django settings.py:                                │
          │  DATABASES = {                                        │
          │      'default': {                                     │
          │          'HOST': 'easypj-db',  ← K8s DNS resolves!    │
          │          'PORT': '5432',                               │
          │      }                                                │
          │  }                                                    │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER  (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 [UNDER-THE-HOOD]
    • Endpoints vs EndpointSlice: the legacy single `Endpoints` object listed
      every backend IP in one resource — it didn't scale (every change rewrote
      the whole object). `EndpointSlice` shards backends across multiple
      objects (~100 endpoints each), which scales to large Services and adds
      topology metadata. kube-proxy programs the same iptables/IPVS rules from
      either; `kubectl get endpoints` still works as a friendly view.
    • Readiness gates membership: an endpoint only appears once its pod passes
      its readiness probe; failing readiness silently removes it from rotation
      (graceful drain, no client-visible errors).
    • sessionAffinity: ClientIP — pins a given client IP to one backend pod for
      a timeout window instead of load-balancing every request (sticky
      sessions).
    • externalTrafficPolicy — Cluster (default) load-balances across all nodes
      but SNATs (hides client IP, adds a hop); Local preserves the client
      source IP and skips the extra hop, but only routes to pods on the
      receiving node.

    🔬 [DEEPER]
    • EndpointSlice scaling & topology-aware routing hints let kube-proxy
      prefer same-zone endpoints to cut cross-zone traffic and latency/cost.
    • internalTrafficPolicy: Local restricts in-cluster traffic to node-local
      endpoints (the internal mirror of externalTrafficPolicy).
    • Dual-stack Services can carry both IPv4 and IPv6 ClusterIPs
      (ipFamilyPolicy / ipFamilies).
    • Service IP allocation comes from the configured service CIDR; ClusterIPs
      are allocated by the API server (and can be reserved with a fixed
      `clusterIP:`).
    • allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false lets a LoadBalancer skip allocating
      node ports when the cloud LB targets pods directly.
    • Headless DNS for StatefulSets returns one A record per ready pod plus the
      stable per-pod SRV/A records that give ordinal identity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • A Service is a stable VIP + DNS name in front of a moving set of pods. It
      selects pods by label; K8s auto-maintains an EndpointSlice of their IPs.
    • Only READY pods appear in the endpoints. A failing readiness probe
      silently removes the pod from rotation (graceful, no 500s to clients).
    • Endpoints are updated automatically as pods die and start — you never
      hand-edit the IP list.
    • Five types: ClusterIP (internal default), NodePort (node IP:30000-32767),
      LoadBalancer (cloud LB), ExternalName (DNS CNAME to an external host),
      Headless (clusterIP:None → returns pod IPs, used by StatefulSets).
    • port is the Service's port; targetPort is the container's port. They are
      independent — port 80 → targetPort 8000 is normal for easypj-web.
    • Type layering: NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP, and LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort — the
      richer types still carry a ClusterIP underneath.
    • Service discovery is DNS-first: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local, with short
      forms for same-namespace lookups. Django just sets HOST: 'easypj-db'.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Empty endpoints (`<none>`) = the selector matches no pods OR no pod is
      Ready. Check pod labels vs the Service selector and the readiness probe.
    • targetPort must match the containerPort the app actually listens on, not
      the Service port. Mismatch = connection refused.
    • NodePort must be in 30000-32767 (default range). Outside = rejected.
    • LoadBalancer stays `<pending>` with no cloud controller (bare-metal needs
      MetalLB or similar).
    • ExternalName has no selector and no endpoints — don't go hunting for
      endpoints when an ExternalName "isn't working"; it's pure DNS/CNAME.
    • A headless Service (clusterIP: None) has no VIP — `kubectl get svc` shows
      CLUSTER-IP as None, which is correct, not broken.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Fastest expose: `kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80
      --target-port=8000`. Add `--type=NodePort` for external dev access.
    • `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=easypj-web`
      shows exactly which pod IPs back a Service.
    • To debug, curl the ClusterIP from a temp pod — if the pod IP works but the
      VIP doesn't, it's a kube-proxy/endpoints problem, not the app.
    • `kubectl describe svc easypj-web` shows selector AND endpoints in one
      view — the fastest single command to diagnose a broken Service.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000
    kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=8000
    kubectl get svc easypj-web -o wide
    kubectl get endpoints easypj-web
    kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=easypj-web
    kubectl describe svc easypj-web        # selector + endpoints in one view
    kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- easypj-web:80/jobs/
    kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup easypj-db.easypj

    🧪 [LAB DRILL] Expose easypj-web, verify the endpoint pod IPs match the
       running pods, then edit the Deployment's pod labels so the selector no
       longer matches — watch endpoints go empty — and fix it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 LAB Q&A  (10)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Q1. Expose easypj-web (port 80) to its container port 8000 imperatively.
        A. `kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000`. This
        creates a ClusterIP Service selecting the deployment's pod labels.

    Q2. `kubectl get endpoints easypj-web` shows <none>. List the two causes.
        A. (1) Selector/label mismatch — no pod carries the labels the Service
        selects. (2) Pods exist but none is Ready (readiness probe failing).

    Q3. When would you choose NodePort over ClusterIP vs LoadBalancer?
        A. ClusterIP for internal-only (default). NodePort to reach a Service
        from outside on <nodeIP>:3xxxx in dev/test/bare-metal. LoadBalancer for
        a real cloud external IP in production.

    Q4. Why do StatefulSets need a Headless Service?
        A. clusterIP:None makes DNS return each pod's IP and gives stable
        per-pod names (postgres-0.easypj-db...), so clients address specific
        replicas — required for ordered, identity-bound workloads.

    Q5. What does ExternalName do and when is it useful?
        A. Maps a Service name to an external DNS name via CNAME (no proxying).
        Use it to alias a managed PostgreSQL host as `easypj-db` so app config
        stays cluster-internal.

    Q6. Give the full DNS name for easypj-db in namespace easypj.
        A. `easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local`. Short forms: `easypj-db`
        (same ns) and `easypj-db.easypj`.

    Q7. The app connects but gets "connection refused". port=80 works elsewhere.
        A. targetPort likely doesn't match the container's listening port. The
        app listens on 8000, so targetPort must be 8000, not 80.

    Q8. How do you serve two ports (e.g. 80 web + 9000 metrics) from one Service?
        A. Define multiple named entries under `ports:` (each with name/port/
        targetPort). Named ports are required when there is more than one.

    Q9. What does sessionAffinity: ClientIP do?
        A. Pins a given client IP to the same backend pod for a timeout window,
        instead of load-balancing every request — useful for sticky sessions.

    Q10. externalTrafficPolicy Local vs Cluster — what's the trade-off?
        A. Cluster (default) load-balances across all nodes but SNATs, hiding
        the client IP and adding a hop. Local preserves the client source IP
        and avoids the extra hop, but only sends to pods on the receiving node.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    📊 VISUAL SUMMARY — THE 5 SERVICE TYPES (who can reach them)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
   │ ClusterIP    │ inside cluster only (def.) │ easypj-web internal  │
   │ NodePort     │ <anyNodeIP>:30000-32767    │ dev/test external    │
   │ LoadBalancer │ cloud external LB -> nodes  │ prod on cloud        │
   │ ExternalName │ DNS CNAME to external host  │ managed psql alias   │
   │ Headless     │ clusterIP:None -> pod DNS   │ StatefulSet (db-0..) │
   └──────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

   .vs-prose — In plain words: a ClusterIP Service is the internal default,
   reachable only by other pods (this is how easypj-web is consumed in-
   cluster). A NodePort opens a static port (30000-32767) on every node's IP
   so you can hit the app from outside in dev/test or on bare-metal. A
   LoadBalancer asks the cloud for a real external IP and front-ends the nodes
   for production. An ExternalName is not a real proxy at all — it is a DNS
   CNAME that aliases an outside host (like a managed PostgreSQL endpoint) so
   the app keeps using a friendly in-cluster name. A Headless Service sets
   clusterIP:None so DNS returns the individual pod IPs and gives each
   StatefulSet replica a stable per-pod name (postgres-0.easypj-db...). Each
   richer type builds on the simpler one: NodePort includes a ClusterIP, and
   LoadBalancer includes a NodePort.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 19: DNS & CoreDNS                                              🟡 🎯
================================================================================

    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]   🩺 [TROUBLESHOOTING-HEAVY]   🟡 Intermediate

    META: 🟡 · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Domain: Services & Networking 20% (CoreDNS focus).
          Stack: easypj (Django project) / jobpost (app); Postgres backend.

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    ----------------
    When something "can't connect" inside a Kubernetes cluster, the cause is
    almost always DNS — a wrong namespace, a CoreDNS pod that's down, or an
    ndots surprise. Service discovery in Kubernetes is name-based: your easypj
    web pod doesn't hard-code the database IP, it asks for "easypj-db" and lets
    cluster DNS turn that name into a ClusterIP. Understand the resolution flow
    and you can fix the single most common class of cluster bugs in seconds.

    OBJECTIVES
    ----------
    • Explain how cluster DNS works end to end (pod resolv.conf → CoreDNS →
      ClusterIP → Endpoints → pod).
    • Read and safely edit the CoreDNS configuration (the Corefile ConfigMap).
    • Know every DNS record form: Service A/AAAA, pod records, headless,
      SRV, and the search-domain / ndots mechanics behind short names.
    • Troubleshoot resolution failures methodically with nslookup and logs.

    CKA RELEVANCE
    -------------
    DNS sits squarely in the Services & Networking domain (≈20% of the exam).
    Expect tasks that hand you a "service unreachable" symptom whose real fix
    is a namespace-qualified name, a restored Corefile, or restarting CoreDNS.
    Being fast at `nslookup kubernetes.default` is worth real points.

    SECTION MAP
    -----------
    19.1  How Kubernetes DNS Works            🎯
    19.2  CoreDNS Configuration (the Corefile) 🎯 🏢
    19.3  DNS Records in Kubernetes            🎯
    19.4  Troubleshooting DNS Issues          🎯 🩺
    🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    19.1  How Kubernetes DNS Works                                          🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    📖 KEY TERM — Cluster DNS: an in-cluster name service that maps Kubernetes
    object names (Services, pods) to IP addresses, so workloads find each other
    by stable name instead of by ephemeral pod IP.

    • CoreDNS is the default DNS server in Kubernetes.
    • It runs as a Deployment in the kube-system namespace, fronted by a
      Service named kube-dns (the ClusterIP is commonly 10.96.0.10).
    • Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points its nameserver at that ClusterIP.
    • DNS records are created automatically for every Service — you do not
      author them; CoreDNS synthesizes them by watching the API server.

    🧠 ANALOGY — CoreDNS is the cluster's phone book operator. Your easypj-web
    pod doesn't memorize the database's number (its IP changes on every
    restart); it asks the operator for "easypj-db" and gets connected to
    whatever number is current right now.

    [DNS RESOLUTION FLOW — HOW PODS FIND SERVICES BY NAME]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                                            │
    │  Pod "easypj-frontend" wants to reach "easypj-db"        │
    │                                                            │
    │  Step 1: App code calls → http://easypj-db:5432           │
    │       │                                                    │
    │       ▼                                                    │
    │  Step 2: Pod checks /etc/resolv.conf                      │
    │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                         │
    │  │ nameserver 10.96.0.10        │ ← CoreDNS ClusterIP    │
    │  │ search default.svc.cluster.local                       │
    │  │        svc.cluster.local                                │
    │  │        cluster.local                                    │
    │  └──────────────────────────────┘                         │
    │       │                                                    │
    │       ▼ DNS query: "easypj-db"                            │
    │  Step 3: CoreDNS resolves the name                        │
    │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                         │
    │  │ 🔍 CoreDNS (10.96.0.10)     │                         │
    │  │                              │                         │
    │  │ Try: easypj-db.default.      │                         │
    │  │      svc.cluster.local       │                         │
    │  │                              │                         │
    │  │ Found! → 10.96.45.2          │                         │
    │  │ (Service ClusterIP)          │                         │
    │  └──────────────────────────────┘                         │
    │       │                                                    │
    │       ▼                                                    │
    │  Step 4: Traffic reaches Service → Endpoints → Pod        │
    │  10.96.45.2 → kube-proxy → 10.244.2.8:5432               │
    │                                                            │
    │  DNS Name Formats:                                         │
    │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
    │  │ Same namespace:  easypj-db                       │     │
    │  │ Cross namespace: easypj-db.prod                  │     │
    │  │ Full FQDN:      easypj-db.prod.svc.cluster.local│     │
    │  │ Headless:       mysql-0.mysql.default.svc...     │     │
    │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    The same flow again, namespace-qualified, for the Postgres backend that
    backs easypj's jobpost app:

    [DNS RESOLUTION FLOW]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Pod requests: "postgres-svc"                           │
    │       │                                                  │
    │       ▼                                                  │
    │  /etc/resolv.conf                                       │
    │  nameserver 10.96.0.10  ← CoreDNS ClusterIP            │
    │  search easypj-dev.svc.cluster.local                   │
    │         svc.cluster.local                               │
    │         cluster.local                                    │
    │       │                                                  │
    │       ▼                                                  │
    │  CoreDNS resolves:                                      │
    │  postgres-svc.easypj-dev.svc.cluster.local              │
    │  → 10.96.45.123 (ClusterIP)                             │
    │       │                                                  │
    │       ▼                                                  │
    │  Pod connects to 10.96.45.123:5432                      │
    │  kube-proxy routes to actual Pod IP                     │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    A compact icon view of the same chain (easypj-web finding easypj-db):

      📦 easypj-web  needs  http://easypj-db:5432
           │ 1. read /etc/resolv.conf
           ▼  nameserver 10.96.0.10 (CoreDNS)   search easypj.svc.cluster.local ...
      🔍 CoreDNS (Deployment in kube-system)
           │ 2. match "kubernetes" plugin -> watch API for Services
           ▼ 3. easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local  ⇒  10.96.45.9 (ClusterIP)
      🔌 Service easypj-db ─► 📦 db pod(s)
      📖 Name forms:  easypj-db  (same ns)  ·  easypj-db.easypj  ·  full FQDN
      ⚠️ Most "can't connect" bugs are DNS: wrong namespace, ndots, CoreDNS down.

    💡 INSIGHT — DNS gives you a ClusterIP, not a pod IP. The ClusterIP is a
    stable virtual address; kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) does the final hop to a
    live pod. So a successful nslookup proving DNS works does NOT prove the
    Service has healthy endpoints — those are two separate failures.


    💡 RELATED ENTRY POINT — INGRESS (external traffic into the cluster)
    -------------------------------------------------------------------
    DNS resolves names INSIDE the cluster. The mirror-image concern is how
    traffic gets IN from outside — that's Ingress, which often relies on
    external DNS (app.example.com) pointing at a load balancer. The diagram
    below is the external counterpart to the internal resolution flow above;
    keep both mental models side by side.

    [INGRESS — EXTERNAL TRAFFIC ROUTING INTO THE CLUSTER]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                                            │
    │  🌐 Internet User                                         │
    │       │                                                    │
    │       │ https://app.example.com/api                       │
    │       ▼                                                    │
    │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐                     │
    │  │  ☁️  Load Balancer (cloud/bare)   │                     │
    │  │  External IP: 52.168.1.100       │                     │
    │  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘                     │
    │                 │ port 443                                │
    │                 ▼                                          │
    │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐                     │
    │  │  🔀 Ingress Controller Pod       │                     │
    │  │  (nginx / traefik / haproxy)     │                     │
    │  │                                  │                     │
    │  │  Reads Ingress rules:            │                     │
    │  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐  │                     │
    │  │  │ /       → frontend-svc:80 │  │                     │
    │  │  │ /api    → backend-svc:80  │  │                     │
    │  │  │ /admin  → admin-svc:80    │  │                     │
    │  │  └────────────────────────────┘  │                     │
    │  └────────┬───────┬───────┬─────────┘                     │
    │           │       │       │                                │
    │     ┌─────┘       │       └─────┐                         │
    │     ▼             ▼             ▼                          │
    │  ┌───────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐                     │
    │  │frontend│   │backend │   │ admin  │ ← Services         │
    │  │svc :80 │   │svc :80 │   │svc :80 │                     │
    │  └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘                     │
    │      ▼            ▼            ▼                          │
    │  ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐                       │
    │  │ Pods │    │ Pods │     │ Pods │                       │
    │  └──────┘    └──────┘     └──────┘                       │
    │                                                            │
    │  Without Ingress: need separate LoadBalancer per service  │
    │  With Ingress:    ONE entry point, path-based routing     │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    19.2  CoreDNS Configuration (the Corefile)                         🎯 🏢
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    📖 KEY TERM — Corefile: CoreDNS's configuration file, delivered as a
    ConfigMap named `coredns` in the kube-system namespace and mounted into the
    CoreDNS pods. It is a chain of plugins, evaluated per query.

    • ConfigMap: coredns (in the kube-system namespace).
    • Corefile: the CoreDNS configuration itself.
    • Plugins you will see: kubernetes, forward, cache, loop, reload, errors,
      health, ready, prometheus.

    [CODE: inspect the CoreDNS ConfigMap / Corefile]
    $ kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml

    A typical Corefile looks like this (read the plugin chain top to bottom):

    [CODE: Corefile — annotated]
    .:53 {
        errors                         # log errors to stdout
        health   { lameduck 5s }       # /health endpoint on :8080
        ready                          # /ready endpoint on :8181
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
            pods insecure              # synth pod records on request
            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
            ttl 30
        }
        prometheus :9153               # metrics
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf {   # everything else → node upstream DNS
            max_concurrent 1000
        }
        cache 30                       # cache positive+negative answers 30s
        loop                           # detect forwarding loops, crash if found
        reload                         # auto-reload Corefile changes (~30s)
        loadbalance                    # round-robin A/AAAA responses
    }

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — the `kubernetes` plugin opens a watch on the API server
    for Services, Endpoints/EndpointSlices and (optionally) pods. It builds an
    in-memory map and answers `*.cluster.local` queries from it — no per-query
    API call. The `forward` plugin sends every non-cluster name (like
    api.example.com) to the upstream resolvers in the node's /etc/resolv.conf.

    EDITING & RELOADING
    -------------------
    $ kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns      # change a plugin/block
    The `reload` plugin re-reads the Corefile within ~30s; to force it now:
    $ kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy coredns

    ⚠️ Always keep a backup before editing — a syntax error here breaks name
    resolution for the entire cluster (see GOTCHAS). Save the original first:
    $ kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml > coredns-backup.yaml

    🏢 DAY-2 — stub domains & upstream forwarding: to route a private zone to a
    specific resolver, add a dedicated server block, e.g.:
        example.internal:53 { forward . 10.0.0.53 }
    This is the standard pattern for letting cluster workloads resolve
    on-prem/internal corporate names.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    19.3  DNS Records in Kubernetes                                        🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    • Service:            <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local       → ClusterIP
    • Pod (optional):     <pod-ip-dashed>.<ns>.pod.cluster.local
    • Headless Service:   returns the individual pod IPs (no ClusterIP)
    • SRV records:        _<port-name>._<protocol>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local

    [TABLE: DNS record types and their formats]
    ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
    │ Record / Object  │ DNS name format                          │ Resolves to             │
    ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
    │ Service (normal) │ easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local       │ ClusterIP (one A record)│
    │ Headless Service │ easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local       │ all ready pod IPs       │
    │ StatefulSet pod  │ postgres-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster… │ that pod's IP           │
    │ Pod (by IP)      │ 10-244-1-5.easypj.pod.cluster.local      │ that pod's IP           │
    │ SRV (named port) │ _pg._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster…   │ port + target host      │
    │ kube-apiserver   │ kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local     │ API server ClusterIP    │
    └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘

    📖 KEY TERM — search domain & ndots: resolv.conf lists `search` suffixes and
    an `options ndots:5`. Any query with FEWER than 5 dots gets each search
    suffix appended and tried first; only if all fail is the name tried as-is.
    That is exactly why a bare short name like "easypj-db" works.

    SHORT NAME EXPANSION (why "easypj-db" resolves)
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Query "easypj-db" (0 dots, < ndots:5) → append search list:   │
    │   1. easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local      ✅ FOUND, stop   │
    │   2. easypj-db.svc.cluster.local             (not tried)      │
    │   3. easypj-db.cluster.local                 (not tried)      │
    │                                                              │
    │ Query "api.example.com" (2 dots, still < 5) → tries search    │
    │ suffixes FIRST (all NXDOMAIN), THEN the bare name → slow.     │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — headless Services (clusterIP: None) skip the virtual-IP
    layer entirely: the kubernetes plugin returns one A record per ready pod, so
    the client load-balances itself. StatefulSets pair with headless Services to
    give each pod a stable, individually-resolvable name (postgres-0, -1, …).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    19.4  Troubleshooting DNS Issues                                   🎯 🩺
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    🩺 The methodical order: prove DNS itself is up, then prove the NAME is
    right, then prove the Service has endpoints, then inspect CoreDNS.

    [CODE: core troubleshooting commands]
    $ kubectl run dnstest --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it -- nslookup kubernetes.default
    $ kubectl run dnstest --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it -- nslookup easypj-svc.easypj-dev
    $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
    $ kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

    ⚡ Use busybox:1.28 specifically — newer busybox images ship a flaky musl
    resolver that gives false negatives.

    [TABLE: DNS issue → symptom → fix]
    ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Problem                          │ Fix                              │
    ├──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
    │ nslookup fails from pod          │ Check CoreDNS pods running       │
    │ "server can't find NXDOMAIN"     │ Check service exists and NS      │
    │ DNS slow / timeouts              │ Check CoreDNS logs, ndots config │
    │ DNS works but connection fails   │ Service selector doesn't match   │
    └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — "easypj-web can't reach easypj-db"
      1. nslookup kubernetes.default  → fails? DNS plane is down → 19.4 CoreDNS.
      2. nslookup easypj-db           → NXDOMAIN? wrong namespace → use
         easypj-db.easypj or full FQDN; confirm the Service exists.
      3. Name resolves but connect fails? → `kubectl get endpoints easypj-db`;
         empty endpoints = selector/label mismatch, NOT a DNS problem.
      4. Still stuck? → CoreDNS pod logs + check the Corefile didn't get broken.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER  (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    • Record synthesis: the kubernetes plugin watches the API and builds records
      in memory; there is no per-query API hit, which is what makes it fast.
    • ndots:5: short names get search domains appended first — great for
      in-cluster names, a latency trap for external FQDNs. A trailing dot
      ("api.example.com.") or a custom dnsConfig with ndots:1 bypasses it.
    • cache & negative caching: the `cache` plugin caches both hits and misses
      (NXDOMAIN) for its TTL; a stale negative cache can mask a now-existing
      Service until the TTL expires.
    • Corefile plugin chain & rewrite: plugins run in a fixed order; the
      `rewrite` plugin can transform queries (e.g. legacy → new name); `autopath`
      can short-circuit the search-domain walk to cut lookups.
    • Pod dnsPolicy / dnsConfig: Default uses the node resolver; ClusterFirst
      (the default for most pods) uses CoreDNS; ClusterFirstWithHostNet is
      needed when a pod runs with hostNetwork: true, or it would bypass CoreDNS.
      dnsConfig lets a pod add nameservers, searches, or override ndots.
    • NodeLocal DNSCache: a per-node DNS cache DaemonSet that answers most
      lookups locally over the node, cutting CoreDNS load and tail latency on
      large clusters and avoiding conntrack races on UDP.
    • Stub domains & upstream forwarding: extra server blocks forward specific
      zones to specific resolvers (corporate/internal DNS integration).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Cluster DNS is CoreDNS — a Deployment in kube-system fronted by the
      kube-dns Service (commonly 10.96.0.10). Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf
      points its nameserver at that ClusterIP.
    • DNS records are created AUTOMATICALLY for Services; you never write them.
    • The Corefile (a ConfigMap) configures CoreDNS via plugins: kubernetes
      (synthesizes Service/pod records by watching the API), forward (sends
      everything else upstream), cache, errors, health, ready, reload.
    • Service A records resolve to the ClusterIP; headless Services and pods
      resolve to pod IPs. SRV records exist for named ports.
    • Name forms: bare name = same namespace; <svc>.<ns> = cross namespace;
      <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local = full FQDN.
    • Short names work because of search domains + ndots:5 in resolv.conf — the
      resolver tries `<name>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` etc. automatically.
    • A successful nslookup proves DNS, not connectivity — check endpoints too.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • A malformed Corefile → CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff → the WHOLE cluster loses
      name resolution. Edit it carefully; keep a backup.
    • Using the wrong namespace in an FQDN resolves to nothing — `easypj-db`
      from another namespace must be `easypj-db.easypj`.
    • ndots:5 means names with fewer than 5 dots get search domains appended
      first; an external name like `api.example.com` may do extra failed lookups.
    • Scaling CoreDNS to 0 (or eviction during node pressure) silently breaks
      everything that resolves names.
    • DNS works but the connection still fails → the Service selector doesn't
      match any pod (empty endpoints). That is NOT a DNS bug.
    • A stale negative cache (NXDOMAIN cached) can hide a Service you just
      created until the cache TTL expires.
    • hostNetwork: true pods need dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet, or they
      bypass CoreDNS and use the node's resolver.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Sanity check from any pod: `nslookup kubernetes.default` — if that fails,
      DNS itself is broken, not your Service.
    • Use a busybox:1.28 pod for nslookup (newer busybox has a flaky resolver).
    • `kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns` then delete CoreDNS pods
      to reload — or rely on the `reload` plugin / `rollout restart`.
    • Append a trailing dot to external FQDNs (`api.example.com.`) to skip the
      ndots search-domain walk and speed up the lookup.
    • Back up the Corefile to a file before any edit so recovery is instant.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
    kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml          # the Corefile
    kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml > coredns-backup.yaml
    kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns
    kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns                 # edit Corefile
    kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy coredns         # reload
    kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.28 -- nslookup easypj-db.easypj
    kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.28 -- nslookup kubernetes.default
    kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n easypj                     # DNS ok but no conn?
    kubectl exec POD -- cat /etc/resolv.conf                      # inspect search/ndots


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 LAB Q&A
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 DRILL: from a temp pod, resolve easypj-db three ways (short, ns-qualified,
    full FQDN). Then introduce a typo into the Corefile, watch CoreDNS
    CrashLoop and DNS break cluster-wide, and restore it from your backup.

    Q1. Give the FQDN of Service easypj-db in namespace easypj.
        A. `easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local` — pattern
        <svc>.<ns>.svc.<clusterDomain>.

    Q2. easypj-web can't resolve easypj-db. How do you debug it step by step?
        A. nslookup kubernetes.default (is DNS up?) → nslookup easypj-db (right
        ns?) → check the Service exists and has endpoints → check CoreDNS pods/
        logs. Most failures are wrong namespace or CoreDNS down.

    Q3. Add an upstream forward for example.internal to CoreDNS. How?
        A. Edit the coredns ConfigMap, add a server block:
        `example.internal:53 { forward . 10.0.0.53 }`, save; CoreDNS reloads.

    Q4. CoreDNS is CrashLoopBackOff after an edit. Cause and recovery?
        A. The Corefile is invalid. `kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=
        kube-dns` shows the parse error; fix or restore the previous Corefile
        (from your backup), then restart the pods.

    Q5. What DNS name does a headless Service hand back?
        A. The pod IPs of its ready members (A records), plus per-pod names like
        `postgres-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local` for StatefulSets.

    Q6. Does a normal pod get a DNS record? In what form?
        A. Optionally, as `<pod-ip-dashed>.<ns>.pod.cluster.local`
        (e.g. 10-244-1-5.easypj.pod.cluster.local). Services are the usual path.

    Q7. What is ndots:5 and why can it cause slow external lookups?
        A. Names with <5 dots get search domains appended and tried first, so an
        external FQDN may incur several failed cluster lookups before the real
        one. Use a trailing dot or dnsConfig to limit it.

    Q8. From namespace web, how do you address Service db in namespace data?
        A. `db.data` (or the full `db.data.svc.cluster.local`). A bare `db`
        would only resolve within namespace web.

    Q9. CoreDNS is overloaded on a large cluster. What do you do?
        A. Scale the CoreDNS Deployment up (more replicas) and/or deploy
        NodeLocal DNSCache to offload per-node lookups and cut latency.

    Q10. How do you confirm CoreDNS is healthy without exec-ing into it?
        A. Check its pods are Running/Ready, its health/ready plugins
        (:8080 /health, :8181 /ready), and run `nslookup kubernetes.default`
        from a test pod.

    Q11. nslookup succeeds but easypj-web still can't connect to easypj-db. Why?
        A. DNS resolved the ClusterIP correctly, but the Service has no
        endpoints — its selector doesn't match the db pod's labels, or the pods
        aren't Ready. Check `kubectl get endpoints easypj-db`.

    Q12. A pod runs with hostNetwork: true and can't resolve cluster names. Fix?
        A. Set `dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet` on the pod spec — otherwise
        a hostNetwork pod uses the node's resolver and bypasses CoreDNS.

    VISUAL SUMMARY: name → CoreDNS → ClusterIP → kube-proxy → pods.
    .vs-prose — A workload asks for a name; CoreDNS (the kube-system Deployment
    at the kube-dns ClusterIP) answers from records it synthesized by watching
    the API, returning a Service ClusterIP (or pod IPs for headless). kube-proxy
    then routes that ClusterIP to a live pod. Break any link — CoreDNS down, a
    bad Corefile, the wrong namespace, an ndots surprise, or empty endpoints —
    and the symptom looks identical ("can't connect"), which is why the fixed
    nslookup-first troubleshooting order is the fastest path to the real cause.

    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]   🟡 INTERMEDIATE   🆕 includes 2025 Gateway API

    META:  🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~5h · Domain: Services & Networking (20%).
           Folds the classic Ingress/NetworkPolicy material together with the
           NEW (2025 syllabus) Gateway API competency.

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Ingress is how the world reaches easypj over HTTP(S) — north-south
    traffic. NetworkPolicy is the firewall that protects the database and
    controls east-west traffic between pods. Gateway API is the modern,
    role-oriented successor to Ingress and is now an exam competency. Get
    these three right and you can expose easypj safely AND lock its data
    plane down to exactly the flows you intend.

    OBJECTIVES
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Deploy an Ingress controller and write Ingress rules (host/path, TLS).
    • Write NetworkPolicies: default-deny, allow web→db, allow-DNS egress.
    • Test policies live (allowed pod succeeds, blocked pod hangs).
    • Explain the Gateway API resource model and route easypj with it.
    • Decide between Ingress and Gateway API and migrate between them.

    CKA RELEVANCE
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🎯 Services & Networking is 20% of the exam. NetworkPolicy and Ingress
    are heavily tested; Gateway API is the newest staple. PRACTICE writing
    policies and Ingress/HTTPRoute skeletons from scratch and from the docs.

    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
