    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.1  Ingress — HTTP/HTTPS Routing
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          - Routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to internal Services (Layer 7)
          - Requires an Ingress Controller (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy)
          - Features: path-based routing, host-based routing, TLS termination
          - 📖 KEY TERM: ingressClassName ties an Ingress to a specific
            controller. pathType is Exact / Prefix / ImplementationSpecific.
            TLS is a secret reference (type kubernetes.io/tls) in spec.tls.

          [INTERNET → INGRESS CONTROLLER → SERVICE → PODS]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  INTERNET                                             │
          │       │                                                │
          │  ┌────▼──────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
          │  │  INGRESS CONTROLLER (NGINX)                    │   │
          │  │                                                 │   │
          │  │  easypj.example.com/       → easypj-svc:80    │   │
          │  │  easypj.example.com/api/   → easypj-api:80    │   │
          │  │  admin.example.com/        → admin-svc:80      │   │
          │  └─────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┘   │
          │        │                   │                          │
          │  ┌─────▼─────┐    ┌──────▼──────┐                   │
          │  │ easypj-svc │    │ admin-svc   │                   │
          │  │ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  │    │ ┌──┐        │                   │
          │  │ │📦│ │📦│  │    │ │📦│        │                   │
          │  │ └──┘ └──┘  │    │ └──┘        │                   │
          │  └────────────┘    └─────────────┘                   │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [CODE: Ingress YAML — host and path-based routing for easypj, with TLS]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Ingress
          metadata:
            name: easypj
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            ingressClassName: nginx
            tls:
            - hosts: [easypj.example.com]
              secretName: easypj-tls       # kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls ...
            rules:
            - host: easypj.example.com
              http:
                paths:
                - path: /jobs
                  pathType: Prefix
                  backend:
                    service:
                      name: easypj-web
                      port:
                        number: 80
                - path: /api
                  pathType: Prefix
                  backend:
                    service:
                      name: easypj-api
                      port:
                        number: 80

          [CODE: Create the TLS secret the Ingress references]
          kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls \
            --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n easypj

          🧠 ANALOGY: an Ingress object is a routing TABLE pinned to the wall.
          It describes where traffic SHOULD go — but it's just paper. The
          Ingress CONTROLLER is the receptionist who actually reads the table
          and walks each visitor to the right office.


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.2  Ingress Controller Setup
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          - The Ingress resource does NOTHING without a controller. The object
            is inert; a controller watches Ingress objects and programs the
            actual proxy (nginx) to serve traffic.
          - NGINX Ingress Controller (most common):
            $ kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/...
          - Minikube: minikube addons enable ingress
          - Install ingress-nginx (Helm or manifest), confirm its pods are
            Running in the ingress-nginx namespace, and that an IngressClass
            named `nginx` exists; ONLY then does an Ingress object route traffic.

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: the controller is a Deployment of nginx pods plus a
          control loop. It watches the API for Ingress + IngressClass + Secret
          objects, renders an nginx.conf from them, and reloads nginx. The
          `kubectl get ingress` ADDRESS column is populated by the controller
          once it has programmed the rule — empty ADDRESS = controller missing
          or not yet reconciled.

          ⚡ TIP: the CKA exam usually has an Ingress Controller pre-installed.
          If `kubectl get ingressclass` shows nothing, that's your first clue
          you need to install one (or it's a deliberate part of the task).


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.3  Network Policies — Firewall for Pods
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — very commonly tested]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          - By default: ALL pods can talk to ALL pods (open, flat network).
          - NetworkPolicy: restrict which pods can communicate, by label.
          - 📖 KEY TERM: a pod is allow-all UNTIL a policy SELECTS it. Once
            selected, only what the policy permits is allowed (implicit deny).
            Multiple policies on one pod combine as a UNION (no ordering, no
            deny-override).
          - Requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicies (Calico, Cilium, Weave).
          - ⚠️ Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicies — policies appear
            applied but do nothing.

          - Structure: podSelector (which pods this policy guards) + policyTypes
            (Ingress and/or Egress) + ingress/egress rules with from/to + ports.

          [CODE: default-deny ALL ingress to every pod in the namespace]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: NetworkPolicy
          metadata:
            name: default-deny-ingress
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            podSelector: {}                  # selects EVERY pod in the ns
            policyTypes: [Ingress]           # no ingress rules = deny all inbound

          [CODE: allow ONLY easypj-web -> easypj-db on 5432]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: NetworkPolicy
          metadata:
            name: allow-web-to-db
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            podSelector:
              matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
            policyTypes: [Ingress]
            ingress:
            - from:
              - podSelector:
                  matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
              ports:
              - protocol: TCP
                port: 5432


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.4  Network Policy Types
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — know these patterns]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          a) Ingress rules — control INCOMING traffic to pods
          b) Egress rules  — control OUTGOING traffic from pods
          c) Default deny all — best-practice starting point, then allow

          [NETWORK POLICY — easypj security example]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  NAMESPACE: easypj-prod (default deny all)           │
          │                                                      │
          │  ┌────────────┐                                      │
          │  │  Internet   │                                      │
          │  └─────┬──────┘                                      │
          │        │ ✅ port 443 (allowed by Ingress policy)     │
          │  ┌─────▼──────┐                                      │
          │  │  Ingress    │                                      │
          │  └─────┬──────┘                                      │
          │        │ ✅ port 8000 (NetworkPolicy allows)         │
          │  ┌─────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐     │
          │  │  📦 easypj pods (app: easypj)               │     │
          │  └───────┬────────────────┬──────────────────┘     │
          │          │                 │                          │
          │    ✅ port 5432      ✅ port 53                     │
          │          ▼                 ▼                          │
          │  ┌────────────┐   ┌────────────┐                    │
          │  │ 🗄️ Postgres │   │ 🌐 CoreDNS │                    │
          │  └────────────┘   └────────────┘                    │
          │                                                      │
          │  ❌ Everything else: DENIED                          │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [NETWORKPOLICY — default-deny then allow (the safe pattern)]
           1) default-deny: podSelector:{} , policyTypes:[Ingress]  ─► db rejects ALL
           2) allow web->db:
                to:   podSelector app=easypj-db
                from: podSelector app=easypj-web   ports: 5432
           3) ⚠️ don't forget egress allow-DNS (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system)
              or names break.

          [CODE: allow ingress -> easypj on port 8000]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: NetworkPolicy
          metadata:
            name: allow-ingress-to-web
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            podSelector:
              matchLabels: { app: easypj }
            policyTypes: [Ingress]
            ingress:
            - from:
              - namespaceSelector:
                  matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx }
              ports:
              - protocol: TCP
                port: 8000


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.5  Network Policy YAML Patterns
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — know these patterns cold]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          [CODE: default deny all EGRESS]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: NetworkPolicy
          metadata: { name: default-deny-egress, namespace: easypj }
          spec:
            podSelector: {}
            policyTypes: [Egress]

          [CODE: allow specific pod-to-pod by label]
          ingress:
          - from:
            - podSelector:
                matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }

          [CODE: allow by NAMESPACE selector (a whole namespace, not pods)]
          ingress:
          - from:
            - namespaceSelector:
                matchLabels: { team: platform }

          [CODE: allow by IP block (CIDR), with an exception]
          ingress:
          - from:
            - ipBlock:
                cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
                except: [10.0.5.0/24]

          [CODE: allow DNS egress so name lookups keep working]
          egress:
          - to:
            - namespaceSelector:
                matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
            ports:
            - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
            - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

          [CODE: combined ingress + egress policy on the db]
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: NetworkPolicy
          metadata: { name: db-lockdown, namespace: easypj }
          spec:
            podSelector:
              matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
            policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
            ingress:
            - from:
              - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: easypj-web } }
              ports:
              - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
            egress:
            - to:
              - namespaceSelector:
                  matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
              ports:
              - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
              - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20.6  Testing Network Policies
          🩺 [TROUBLESHOOTING]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          $ kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- wget -qO- http://easypj-svc:80
          $ kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- nc -zv postgres-svc 5432
          $ kubectl exec web   -- curl -m3 easypj-db:5432   # should SUCCEED
          $ kubectl exec other -- curl -m3 easypj-db:5432   # should HANG/REFUSE

          ⚡ TIP: always test policies after applying — a mistake can lock out
          everything, including DNS. Exec into an ALLOWED pod and a DISALLOWED
          pod and curl the same target: one connects, one times out. That's the
          fastest proof a policy works, with no external tooling.


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20b.1  Why Gateway API
           🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]  🆕 NEW 2025 COMPETENCY
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          - Gateway API is the role-oriented SUCCESSOR to Ingress, now on the
            exam. Ingress packed everything into one object plus a sprawl of
            controller-specific annotations and a single role. Gateway API
            splits the concern across three resources owned by different teams.
          - It is a real, portable Kubernetes API (CRDs) rather than nginx
            annotations, and natively supports header matching, weighted traffic
            splitting, and GRPC/TLS routes.

           [Ingress vs Gateway API]
           ┌───────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
           │ Ingress       │ one object + annotations│ single role, limited     │
           │ Gateway API   │ GatewayClass/Gateway/   │ role-separated, portable,│
           │               │ HTTPRoute               │ header/weight/traffic-split│
           └───────────────┴───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20b.2  The Gateway API Resource Model
           🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          GatewayClass (infra type) -> Gateway (listener/IP/TLS, platform team)
          -> HTTPRoute (rules, app team) -> Service.

          [GATEWAY API — roles split across resources (vs one Ingress blob)]
           🛠️ Cluster ops   ──►  GatewayClass   (which controller/infra type)
                                      │ implemented by
           🏗️ Platform team ──►  Gateway        (listeners: :80/:443, IP, TLS)
                                      │ routes attach to a listener
           👩‍💻 App team      ──►  HTTPRoute      (host/path/header/weight rules)
                                      │ backendRefs
                                      ▼
                                 🔌 easypj-web Service ─► 📦 pods

          - Routes ATTACH to a Gateway listener via parentRefs; backends are
            referenced by backendRefs (Services). Status conditions (Accepted,
            Programmed) tell you whether attachment and provisioning succeeded.


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20b.3  Routing easypj with Gateway API
           🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          - Supports header / path / weight matching and traffic splitting.

          [CODE: Gateway + HTTPRoute for easypj]
          apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Gateway
          metadata:
            name: easypj-gw
          spec:
            gatewayClassName: nginx          # which controller implements it
            listeners:
            - name: http
              protocol: HTTP
              port: 80
          ---
          apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: HTTPRoute
          metadata:
            name: easypj-route
          spec:
            parentRefs:
            - name: easypj-gw                # attach to the Gateway listener
            hostnames: ["easypj.example.com"]
            rules:
            - matches:
              - path:
                  type: PathPrefix
                  value: /jobs
              backendRefs:
              - name: easypj-web
                port: 80

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: a controller (nginx-gateway, Envoy Gateway, etc.)
          reconciles GatewayClass/Gateway/HTTPRoute, provisions the data plane
          (an Envoy/nginx fleet + an IP), and reports back via status
          conditions. Header matching and weighted backendRefs map to data-plane
          routing rules — a 90/10 split is two backendRefs with weights 90 and 10.


    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    20b.4  Ingress vs Gateway API (decision guide)
           🧭 [DECISION GUIDE]
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          Pick Ingress when: a needed controller only speaks Ingress, the
          cluster lacks the Gateway API CRDs, or routing is trivial/single-role.
          Pick Gateway API when: you want role separation (ops/platform/app),
          portability across controllers, header-based routing, weighted traffic
          splitting, or GRPC/TLS routes. New designs lean Gateway API.

          Migration notes: install the CRDs + a Gateway controller, recreate the
          Ingress's host/path rules as an HTTPRoute attached to a Gateway
          listener, validate via status conditions, then cut DNS/LB over.


    ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER                                    ║
    ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔧 UTH (NetworkPolicy): a policy compiles down to CNI rules —     ║
    ║     iptables chains (Calico) or eBPF programs (Cilium). "Deny" is  ║
    ║     IMPLICIT: the moment ANY policy selects a pod, traffic not     ║
    ║     explicitly allowed is dropped. Multiple policies = UNION of    ║
    ║     their allows.                                                  ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔧 UTH (Ingress): controllers WATCH Ingress objects, render an    ║
    ║     nginx.conf, and reload. ADDRESS appears once programmed.       ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔧 UTH (Gateway API): a controller reconciles GatewayClass/       ║
    ║     Gateway/HTTPRoute, provisions an Envoy/nginx data plane, and   ║
    ║     reports status Accepted/Programmed conditions + attachment.    ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔬 DEEPER (Ingress/NetPol): IngressClass & default class;         ║
    ║     pathType Exact/Prefix/ImplementationSpecific; NetworkPolicy    ║
    ║     endPort & ipBlock except; multiple policies on one pod = UNION;║
    ║     default-deny EGRESS patterns (re-allow DNS!).                  ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔬 DEEPER (Gateway API): listener TLS modes Terminate/Passthrough;║
    ║     ReferenceGrant for cross-namespace routes; route precedence;   ║
    ║     GRPCRoute/TLSRoute; policy attachment; status Accepted/        ║
    ║     Programmed conditions.                                         ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝


    ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS                                                 ║
    ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 Ingress = Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS routing: host + path rules map   ║
    ║     to backend Services. The Ingress OBJECT is inert — an Ingress ║
    ║     CONTROLLER (nginx, Traefik) must be installed or Ingress does ║
    ║     NOTHING.                                                       ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 ingressClassName ties an Ingress to a controller. TLS is a    ║
    ║     secret reference (type kubernetes.io/tls) named in spec.tls.  ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 NetworkPolicy = firewall rules for pods. Pods are allow-all   ║
    ║     UNTIL a policy selects them; once selected, only what the     ║
    ║     policy permits is allowed (implicit deny). Multiple policies  ║
    ║     on a pod are a UNION.                                         ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 NetworkPolicy needs a policy-aware CNI (Calico ✅, Cilium ✅, ║
    ║     Flannel ❌). It has SEPARATE ingress and egress rules; the    ║
    ║     safe pattern is default-deny + explicit allows — and you MUST ║
    ║     re-allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system) or names break.║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 DNS pattern still applies: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local;      ║
    ║     CoreDNS resolves it — most "can't connect" bugs are DNS.      ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🔑 Gateway API is the role-oriented SUCCESSOR to Ingress: it     ║
    ║     splits one blob into GatewayClass (cluster ops — controller), ║
    ║     Gateway (platform team — listeners/IP/TLS), HTTPRoute (app    ║
    ║     team — host/path/header/weight rules). Routes ATTACH via      ║
    ║     parentRefs; backends via backendRefs; status conditions       ║
    ║     (Accepted, Programmed) confirm it. It ships as CRDs you must  ║
    ║     install and is now an exam competency.                        ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ║  🎯 CKA Relevance: 20% of exam. NetworkPolicy, Ingress, CoreDNS   ║
    ║     and Gateway API are staples. PRACTICE writing policies and    ║
    ║     routes from scratch.                                          ║
    ║                                                                    ║
    ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝


    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • No Ingress controller installed → the Ingress object exists but nothing
      routes. ADDRESS stays empty; requests time out.
    • Flannel ignores NetworkPolicy entirely — policies appear applied but do
      nothing. Verify your CNI before relying on them.
    • A default-deny ingress+egress policy breaks DNS — you MUST add an egress
      allow to kube-system on UDP/TCP 53, or every name lookup fails.
    • extensions/v1beta1 Ingress is REMOVED — use networking.k8s.io/v1 (backend
      shape changed to service.name / service.port).
    • pathType matters: Prefix vs Exact vs ImplementationSpecific route
      differently; omitting it is INVALID in v1.
    • The Gateway API CRDs are NOT built in — install them first or every
      Gateway/HTTPRoute apply fails with "no matches for kind".
    • gatewayClassName must match a RUNNING controller (nginx-gateway, Envoy
      Gateway); otherwise the Gateway never becomes Programmed.
    • An HTTPRoute with no valid parentRef (wrong Gateway name/namespace) stays
      unattached and silently routes nothing — check its status conditions.
    • Cross-namespace routing requires a ReferenceGrant; without it the
      attachment is refused.


    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Don't hand-write policies — copy a known-good one from the docs and swap
      the podSelector/ports. Same for Ingress and HTTPRoute skeletons.
    • Test policies live: exec into an allowed pod and a disallowed pod and
      curl the target; one should succeed, one should hang/refuse.
    • `kubectl get ingress` ADDRESS column tells you if the controller has
      programmed it yet (empty = controller missing or not reconciled).
    • `kubectl get gateway easypj-gw -o yaml` → check status.conditions for
      Accepted/Programmed BEFORE debugging anything else.
    • `kubectl describe httproute easypj-route` shows ParentRef attachment
      status — the fastest way to spot an unattached route.
    • Keep the Gateway (platform) and HTTPRoute (app) in separate files so you
      can hand each to the right owner.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (union — Ingress/NetworkPolicy + Gateway API)
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    DRILL A: install ingress-nginx, expose easypj-web via a host/path Ingress
    with TLS, then apply a default-deny on the db namespace plus an allow
    web→db:5432 and an allow-DNS egress; verify web reaches db and a third pod
    cannot.

    Q1. Write an Ingress that routes easypj.example.com/jobs to easypj-web:80.
        A. networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, ingressClassName: nginx, rule host
        easypj.example.com, http.paths: path /jobs, pathType: Prefix, backend
        service.name easypj-web service.port.number 80.

    Q2. How do you add TLS to that Ingress?
        A. Create a tls secret (`kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls
        --cert=... --key=...`) and add spec.tls: [{hosts: [easypj.example.com],
        secretName: easypj-tls}].

    Q3. You applied an Ingress but nothing is reachable. First thing to check?
        A. Whether an Ingress CONTROLLER is installed and running (e.g.
        ingress-nginx). Without it the Ingress object does nothing; ADDRESS
        stays empty.

    Q4. Write a default-deny ingress policy for namespace easypj.
        A. NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} (all pods) and
        policyTypes: [Ingress], no ingress rules → all inbound denied.

    Q5. Allow ONLY easypj-web to reach easypj-db on 5432.
        A. Policy on podSelector app=easypj-db, ingress.from podSelector
        app=easypj-web, ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}].

    Q6. After a default-deny egress, DNS breaks. Fix?
        A. Add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the kube-system
        namespace (CoreDNS), or names won't resolve.

    Q7. Two policies select the same pod. How do they combine?
        A. As a UNION — traffic is allowed if ANY selecting policy permits it.
        There's no ordering or deny-override.

    Q8. Allow traffic from an entire namespace (not specific pods). How?
        A. Use a namespaceSelector (matching the namespace's labels) in the
        from/to block instead of (or combined with) a podSelector.

    Q9. Your NetworkPolicy seems ignored — pods still talk freely. Why?
        A. The CNI isn't policy-aware (e.g. Flannel). Switch to Calico/Cilium;
        NetworkPolicy is only enforced by a CNI that implements it.

    Q10. How do you prove a policy works without external tools?
        A. Exec into an allowed pod and curl the target (succeeds), then exec
        into a non-selected pod and curl the same target (times out/refused).

    DRILL B: install the Gateway API CRDs and a controller, create a Gateway
    with an HTTP :80 listener and an HTTPRoute sending /jobs to easypj-web,
    then confirm the Gateway is Programmed and the route Accepted.

    Q11. Map the three core Gateway API resources to their owning roles.
        A. GatewayClass = cluster ops (selects the controller/infra). Gateway =
        platform team (listeners, IP, TLS). HTTPRoute = app team (host/path/
        header/weight routing rules).

    Q12. Create a Gateway with an HTTP listener on port 80.
        A. kind Gateway, gatewayClassName: <controller>, listeners: [{name:
        http, protocol: HTTP, port: 80}].

    Q13. Route easypj.example.com/jobs to easypj-web:80 with an HTTPRoute.
        A. HTTPRoute parentRefs: [easypj-gw], hostnames: [easypj.example.com],
        rules.matches path PathPrefix /jobs, backendRefs: [{name: easypj-web,
        port: 80}].

    Q14. How do you match on an HTTP header instead of a path?
        A. In rules.matches add headers: [{name: X-Env, value: canary}] — only
        requests with that header take the rule's backend.

    Q15. Split traffic 90/10 between easypj-web v1 and v2.
        A. One rule with two backendRefs, each given a weight (90 and 10); the
        controller load-balances proportionally.

    Q16. When would you still pick Ingress over Gateway API?
        A. When a needed controller only speaks Ingress, the cluster lacks the
        CRDs, or the routing is trivial single-role. New designs lean Gateway API.

    Q17. `kubectl apply` of a Gateway returns "no matches for kind Gateway". Fix?
        A. The Gateway API CRDs aren't installed. Apply the CRD bundle first,
        then re-apply the Gateway.

    Q18. Your HTTPRoute routes nothing. How do you diagnose it?
        A. `kubectl describe httproute` and check status: parentRef Accepted? If
        unattached, the parentRefs name/namespace or listener is wrong, or a
        ReferenceGrant is missing for cross-namespace.

    Q19. Terminate TLS on a Gateway listener — what's required?
        A. A listener with protocol: HTTPS, port 443, tls.mode: Terminate, and
        certificateRefs pointing at a TLS secret.

    Q20. An HTTPRoute in namespace app targets a Service in namespace data.
         What extra object is needed?
        A. A ReferenceGrant in the data namespace permitting HTTPRoutes from
        namespace app to reference its Services.

    VISUAL SUMMARY (.vs-prose)
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    [NORTH-SOUTH + EAST-WEST — traffic into easypj and locked down]
              🌍 internet
                  │  HTTPS easypj.example.com/jobs
                  ▼
        🌍 Ingress Controller (nginx)  ── reads Ingress rules
                  │  host/path -> backend
                  ▼
        🔌 easypj-web Service ─► 📦 web pods
                  │  app traffic
                  ▼  🧯 NetworkPolicy: ONLY easypj-web may reach db:5432
        🔌 easypj-db Service ─► 🐘 postgres
     ⚠️ Ingress needs a CONTROLLER or it does nothing; NetworkPolicy needs a
        policy-aware CNI (Calico/Cilium — NOT Flannel).

    [GATEWAY API SUMMARY] GatewayClass -> Gateway -> HTTPRoute -> easypj Service.

    In prose: easypj's traffic story runs in two directions. NORTH-SOUTH,
    requests arrive from the internet over HTTPS, hit the Ingress controller
    (or, in the modern model, a Gateway listener), get matched by host/path
    rules, and land on the easypj-web Service and its pods. EAST-WEST, the web
    pods reach the database — but ONLY because a NetworkPolicy explicitly allows
    easypj-web → easypj-db on 5432, while a default-deny blocks everything else,
    and an allow-DNS egress keeps name resolution alive. Ingress objects are
    inert without a controller; NetworkPolicies are inert without a policy-aware
    CNI; Gateway/HTTPRoute objects are inert without their CRDs and a Gateway
    controller. Install the machinery, write the rules, then PROVE them by
    curling from an allowed and a denied pod.

PART 6: STORAGE                                                         🟡 🎯
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapters 21-23  ·  CKA DOMAIN WEIGHT: 10%  ·  "Don't lose the data"
  CKA Exam Weight: 10%

  What you'll build: persistent, dynamically-provisioned storage for easypj's
  PostgreSQL, plus clean config/secret injection — data that survives pod
  death, rescheduling, and rollouts.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [PART 6 INTRO]
  Containers are ephemeral — kill a pod and its writable layer is gone. That's
  fine for stateless easypj-web, fatal for the database. This part is the third
  plug point (CSI): how Kubernetes attaches durable storage via the PV/PVC
  model and StorageClasses (dynamic provisioning), plus how ConfigMaps and
  Secrets feed configuration into easypj cleanly.

  Where Parts 4 and 5 made easypj-web reachable and resilient, Part 6 makes its
  state durable. The Django app itself is stateless — any easypj-web replica can
  serve any request — but the data it serves (Skills, Author, Location, JobPost,
  auth.User rows) lives in PostgreSQL, and PostgreSQL must not lose a single
  byte when its pod is rescheduled onto another node. That is the whole job of
  the storage subsystem: decouple the lifetime of data from the lifetime of the
  pod that happens to be using it.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 6 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch21 VOLUMES (why & types) ─▶ Ch22 PV/PVC/StorageClass (durable, dynamic)│
  │                                          │                              │
  │                                          ▼                              │
  │                 Ch23 CONFIGMAPS & SECRETS (configuration, not bytes)     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 READING ORDER — why this sequence:
    • Ch21 establishes the volume abstraction and shows why the container
      writable layer and emptyDir are not enough for a database.
    • Ch22 introduces the PersistentVolume / PersistentVolumeClaim contract and
      StorageClasses, so storage is durable AND requested on demand.
    • Ch23 covers ConfigMaps and Secrets — configuration and credentials that
      are mounted/injected like storage but are not bulk data.

  [PART 6 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: see easypj lose data on restart -> attach an emptyDir
  (still ephemeral) -> understand the PV/PVC contract -> a StorageClass
  dynamically provisions a PVC for postgres -> the StatefulSet mounts it ->
  config via ConfigMap, credentials via Secret (encrypted at rest). VISUAL:
  the PV->PVC->Pod binding chain (reuse+augment cka_1).

  THE BINDING CHAIN (what you will assemble across Ch21-23):

    StorageClass ──(dynamic provision)──▶ PersistentVolume (real disk)
         ▲                                          │
         │ claims by class                          │ bound 1:1
         │                                          ▼
    PersistentVolumeClaim ◀───── requested by ──── Pod / StatefulSet
         │                                          │
         │ mounted at                               │ env / files
         ▼                                          ▼
    /var/lib/postgresql/data                  ConfigMap + Secret
    (PostgreSQL durable data)                 (settings, DB password)

  📖 EXTENSION INTERFACE recap: CSI = the storage plug point. CSI drivers are
  the out-of-tree plugins that provision and attach real disks (cloud block
  storage, NFS, Ceph, local SSD), exactly as CNI plugs networking and CRI plugs
  the container runtime. Kubernetes core stays storage-vendor-agnostic; the
  StorageClass names which CSI provisioner to call.

  🔑 PART 6 MUST-REMEMBER:
    • A Pod's writable layer and emptyDir die WITH the pod — never store a
      database there.
    • PV = cluster-level durable storage; PVC = a namespaced request for it;
      they bind 1:1.
    • A StorageClass enables DYNAMIC provisioning: create a PVC and a PV is
      created for you on demand.
    • ConfigMaps hold non-secret configuration; Secrets hold credentials
      (base64-encoded, and encrypt-at-rest if configured) — both injectable as
      env vars or mounted files.
    • Stateful workloads (PostgreSQL for easypj) use a StatefulSet +
      volumeClaimTemplates so each replica gets its own stable PVC.

================================================================================
  Chapter 21: Volumes & Persistent Storage                              🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Storage 10% (volume types,
      access modes, reclaim policies). Builds the foundation for Chapter 22's
      PV/PVC and StorageClass machinery.

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      🏢 easypj lets users upload resumes and profile photos, and 🐘 PostgreSQL
      writes its database files to disk. The instant a pod restarts, anything
      written to the container's own filesystem is GONE. Volumes are how
      Kubernetes attaches storage whose lifecycle outlives the container — the
      difference between "the resume upload survived a redeploy" and "all user
      data vanished." VISUAL: the ephemeral-storage problem panel below.

  [C] OBJECTIVES
      • Explain why container storage is ephemeral and what breaks because of it.
      • Map the full volume-type spectrum and each type's lifecycle/scope.
      • Use emptyDir (incl. medium: Memory) and hostPath correctly.
      • Understand CSI as the storage plug point that replaced in-tree plugins.
      • Distinguish a `volume` (the source) from a `volumeMount` (the path).

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE
      Storage is a graded 10% domain. Expect tasks like "share a directory
      between two containers," "mount a node path into a pod," "create an
      in-memory scratch volume," and "explain why an upload disappeared." This
      chapter covers the pod-local volume types; Chapter 22 covers cluster-
      durable PV/PVC/StorageClass.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      21.1  The Problem: Container Storage is Ephemeral        🎯
      21.2  Volume Types Overview                              🎯
      21.3  emptyDir — Temporary Shared Storage                🎯
      21.4  hostPath — Node-Level Storage                      🎯
      21.5  CSI & the Storage Plug Point                       🎯 🏢

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  21.1  The Problem: Container Storage is Ephemeral                          🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      - The container filesystem (the writable layer) is temporary — it dies
        with the container.
      - Pod restart = all data written inside the container is GONE.
      - easypj users upload resumes and profile photos → that data MUST persist!
      - 🐘 PostgreSQL's data directory must survive pod reschedules or you lose
        the database.

      [WHY VOLUMES? — THE DATA LOSS PROBLEM]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  WITHOUT VOLUMES:              WITH VOLUMES:            │
      │                                                         │
      │  ┌────────────┐               ┌────────────┐           │
      │  │ 📦 Pod v1   │               │ 📦 Pod v1   │           │
      │  │ 📄 data.db  │               │ 📄 data.db ─┼──┐       │
      │  └──────┬─────┘               └──────┬─────┘  │       │
      │         │ pod dies                    │ pod dies│       │
      │         ▼                             ▼        │       │
      │  ┌────────────┐               ┌────────────┐  │       │
      │  │ 📦 Pod v2   │               │ 📦 Pod v2   │  │       │
      │  │ 📄 (empty!) │ 💀            │ 📄 data.db ─┼──┤       │
      │  │ DATA LOST!  │               │ DATA SAFE!  │  │       │
      │  └────────────┘               └────────────┘  │       │
      │                                        ┌──────▼──┐    │
      │                                        │ 💾 Volume│    │
      │                                        │ persists!│    │
      │                                        └─────────┘    │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      🧠 ANALOGY: the container's writable layer is a hotel-room whiteboard —
      wiped clean the moment the next guest (pod) checks in. A volume is a USB
      stick you carry out of the room: plug it into the next room and your notes
      are still there.

      📖 KEY TERM — writable layer: the thin read-write layer the container
      runtime stacks on top of the image's read-only layers. All in-container
      writes land here, and it is discarded when the container is removed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  21.2  Volume Types Overview                                                🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Kubernetes offers many volume sources. The right choice is driven by ONE
      question: how long must the data live?

      [COMMON VOLUME TYPES]
      ┌──────────────────┬───────────┬─────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
      │ Type             │ Persists? │ Scope       │ Use case                   │
      ├──────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
      │ emptyDir         │ No (pod)  │ Pod         │ Temp files, cache, shared  │
      │ hostPath         │ No (node) │ Node        │ Dev/testing, single node   │
      │ PersistentVolume │ Yes       │ Cluster     │ Databases, uploads         │
      │ configMap        │ N/A       │ Cluster     │ Config files               │
      │ secret           │ N/A       │ Cluster     │ Sensitive config           │
      │ nfs              │ Yes       │ Network     │ Shared storage             │
      │ csi              │ Yes       │ Provider    │ Cloud storage (EBS, etc.)  │
      └──────────────────┴───────────┴─────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

      [VOLUME LIFECYCLE SPECTRUM — how long does the data live?]
       container-only      pod-scoped         node-scoped      cluster-durable
       (writable layer) ◄─ emptyDir ─►    ◄─ hostPath ─►   ◄─ PVC ─► PV ─►
       dies with         dies with the      tied to ONE      survives pod delete,
       CONTAINER         POD (survives a     node             reschedule & scaling
                         container restart)

       📖 configMap/secret volumes = read-only config files · CSI = real disks.
       easypj: web = stateless (no PVC)   ·   🐘 postgres = PVC (MUST persist!).

      💡 INSIGHT: every volume in the spec is two halves. You declare the SOURCE
      once under pod.spec.volumes, then each container that wants it adds a
      volumeMount referencing that volume's name. Many containers can mount the
      same source — that is exactly how sidecars share files.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  21.3  emptyDir — Temporary Shared Storage                                  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      - Created when the pod starts, deleted when the pod dies.
      - Survives a CONTAINER restart (it is pod-scoped), but NOT pod deletion or
        reschedule.
      - Shared between all containers in the same pod that mount it.
      - Use case: a sidecar container sharing data with the main container
        (e.g. Nginx serving static files written by Django).

      [CODE: Pod with emptyDir — Django + Nginx sharing static files]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web
      spec:
        volumes:
          - name: static-files          # the SOURCE, declared once
            emptyDir: {}
        containers:
          - name: django
            image: easypj/jobpost:latest
            command: ["sh", "-c", "python manage.py collectstatic --noinput \
              && gunicorn easypj.wsgi"]
            volumeMounts:
              - name: static-files       # references the volume above
                mountPath: /app/static
          - name: nginx
            image: nginx:1.27
            volumeMounts:
              - name: static-files
                mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html/static
                readOnly: true           # nginx only reads what Django wrote

      [IN-MEMORY emptyDir — medium: Memory]
      volumes:
        - name: cache
          emptyDir:
            medium: Memory               # tmpfs — fast RAM-backed scratch
            sizeLimit: 256Mi

      ⚠️ GOTCHA: medium: Memory is a tmpfs. It is fast, but it COUNTS AGAINST the
      pod's memory limit and is lost on a node reboot. Use it for hot caches, not
      for anything you need to keep.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  21.4  hostPath — Node-Level Storage                                        🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      - Maps a directory (or file) from the node's filesystem into the pod.
      - ⚠️ NOT PORTABLE — the pod can only reach that data on that specific node.
        If the pod reschedules elsewhere, the path is empty or absent.
      - Use case: accessing node-level logs or sockets (node agents), testing.

      [CODE: Pod with hostPath volume]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: node-log-reader
      spec:
        volumes:
          - name: host-logs
            hostPath:
              path: /var/log            # directory on the node
              type: Directory           # must already exist
        containers:
          - name: reader
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -f /host/var/log/syslog"]
            volumeMounts:
              - name: host-logs
                mountPath: /host/var/log
                readOnly: true

      [hostPath `type` VALUES — the guardrail]
      ┌────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ type               │ Behavior                                         │
      ├────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
      │ "" (default)       │ No checks — mount whatever is there              │
      │ Directory          │ Path must exist and be a directory               │
      │ DirectoryOrCreate  │ Create an empty dir (0755) if missing            │
      │ File               │ Path must exist and be a file                    │
      │ FileOrCreate       │ Create an empty file (0644) if missing           │
      │ Socket             │ Path must be a UNIX socket                        │
      │ CharDevice         │ Path must be a character device                  │
      │ BlockDevice        │ Path must be a block device                      │
      └────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      ⚠️ WARNING: Avoid hostPath in production — use PV/PVC instead. It pins the
      pod to one node and exposes the host filesystem (a real security and
      portability hazard). It is acceptable only for node-level agents (log
      shippers, monitoring) and local dev.

      ⚠️ GOTCHA: the wrong `type` keeps a pod stuck in ContainerCreating. If the
      path may not exist yet, use DirectoryOrCreate / FileOrCreate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  21.5  CSI & the Storage Plug Point                                      🎯 🏢
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      📖 KEY TERM — CSI (Container Storage Interface): a standard plug point that
      lets storage vendors ship drivers OUT-OF-TREE that provision and attach
      real storage (AWS EBS, GCE PD, Ceph, Portworx, etc.).

      Before CSI, every storage backend had to be compiled into Kubernetes
      itself ("in-tree" volume plugins). That bloated the codebase and tied
      storage release cadence to Kubernetes releases. CSI moved all of that to
      external drivers that speak a common gRPC contract, and the old in-tree
      plugins have since been migrated/removed.

      [CSI — WHO DOES WHAT]
      ┌──────────────┐     provision/attach      ┌─────────────────────────┐
      │  Kubernetes  │ ───────────────────────►  │  CSI Driver (vendor)    │
      │  (PVC/PV)    │  ◄─── disk ready ─────────  │  EBS · PD · Ceph · ...  │
      └──────────────┘                            └──────────┬──────────────┘
                                                             │ real disk
                                                             ▼
                                                       ┌───────────┐
                                                       │ 💾 Volume  │
                                                       └───────────┘

      🏢 DAY-2: in the cloud, easypj's PostgreSQL PVC is satisfied by a CSI
      driver that carves out a real cloud disk and attaches it to whichever node
      the pod lands on — that is what makes the data survive reschedules.

      🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which volume do I reach for?
        • Just sharing scratch between containers in one pod  → emptyDir
        • Hot cache that must be fast and can be lost         → emptyDir Memory
        • Read node logs / mount a host socket (agent only)   → hostPath
        • Inject config files                                 → configMap volume
        • Inject credentials                                  → secret volume
        • Anything that MUST survive pod delete/reschedule    → PVC (→ Ch.22)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD
      When a pod is scheduled, the kubelet's volume manager realizes each
      volume: for CSI/disk-backed volumes it runs Attach (controller plugin
      attaches the disk to the node), then on the node it runs Mount/NodeStage
      and NodePublish to mount the volume into the container's mount namespace at
      the requested mountPath. emptyDir and hostPath skip the attach stage — the
      kubelet just creates/binds a directory locally and bind-mounts it in.

      🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
      • Projected volumes — combine configMap + secret + serviceAccountToken +
        downwardAPI into a single mounted directory.
      • Ephemeral CSI volumes — a pod-inline CSI volume created/destroyed with
        the pod (no PVC), for secrets-store / scratch CSI use.
      • subPath / subPathExpr — mount just one file or subdirectory of a volume
        at a path; subPathExpr expands env vars (e.g. per-pod subdir).
      • mountPropagation — Bidirectional / HostToContainer for sharing mounts
        between the host and container (CSI node drivers need this).
      • fsGroupChangePolicy — Always vs OnRootMismatch controls whether the
        kubelet recursively chowns the volume to the pod's fsGroup (huge perf
        win on big volumes).
      • readOnly mounts — set readOnly: true to expose a volume read-only to a
        container even when the source is writable.

  [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      • A container's writable layer is ephemeral — it dies with the CONTAINER.
        Volumes attach storage with longer lifecycles outside that layer.
      • The lifecycle spectrum: emptyDir (lives with the POD, survives container
        restarts) → hostPath (lives on ONE node) → PVC/PV (cluster-durable,
        survives pod delete/reschedule/scale).
      • A `volume` is declared at pod level (the source); a `volumeMount` places
        it at a path inside a container. Many containers can mount the same
        volume — that is how sidecars share files.
      • CSI is the storage extension interface: out-of-tree drivers provision and
        attach real disks (EBS/PD/Ceph), replacing the old in-tree plugins.
      • configMap and secret volumes mount as read-only config files; they are
        not durable storage.
      • easypj-web is stateless (no PVC needed); 🐘 PostgreSQL needs a PVC because
        its data MUST persist.

  [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      • emptyDir survives a container crash/restart but is DELETED when the pod is
        removed or rescheduled — it is not durable storage.
      • hostPath pins a pod to whichever node holds that path and exposes the host
        filesystem — fine for node agents/dev, dangerous for app data.
      • The wrong hostPath `type` (e.g. Directory when the path doesn't exist)
        keeps the pod stuck in ContainerCreating; use DirectoryOrCreate when
        unsure.
      • medium: Memory emptyDir counts against the pod's memory limit and is lost
        on reboot.
      • Forgetting that the volume name in volumeMounts must EXACTLY match a name
        under pod.spec.volumes — a typo yields a validation error.

  [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      • For a quick scratch share between containers, an emptyDir is one block of
        YAML — no PVC, no provisioner.
      • `kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes` lists every volume source if you forget
        the field name in the exam.
      • Mount the same volume readOnly in consumers and read-write only where
        writes happen, to avoid accidental corruption.
      • `kubectl describe pod | sed -n '/Volumes/,/Events/p'` shows exactly which
        sources mounted where when debugging a mount failure.

  [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
      kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes
      kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.volumeMounts
      kubectl exec -it web -c sidecar -- ls /shared
      kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes}'
      kubectl describe pod web | sed -n '/Volumes/,/Events/p'

  [L] 🧪 DRILL
      Build a pod with two containers sharing one emptyDir — a writer that
      appends to /shared/out.log and a reader that tails it — and prove the file
      is visible to both (kubectl exec into each container).

  [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10)
      Q1. Share a single file between two containers in one pod. How?
          A. Declare an emptyDir volume at pod level and mount it (same name)
          into both containers' volumeMounts at chosen paths; both see the same
          files.
      Q2. Does an emptyDir survive a container crash? A pod deletion?
          A. It survives a container restart (it is pod-scoped) but is destroyed
          when the pod is deleted or rescheduled to another node.
      Q3. Mount the node's /var/log into a pod. Which volume type?
          A. hostPath with path /var/log. Use it only for node-level agents; it
          ties the pod to that node and exposes host files.
      Q4. What does the hostPath `type` field guard against?
          A. It validates/creates the target: Directory (must exist), File,
          DirectoryOrCreate (create if missing), Socket, etc. Wrong type =
          ContainerCreating failure.
      Q5. Create an in-memory scratch volume. How and what's the cost?
          A. emptyDir with `medium: Memory` (tmpfs). It is fast but counts
          against the pod's memory and is lost on node reboot.
      Q6. easypj-web restarts and the uploaded file is gone. Why and fix?
          A. It was on the container writable layer (or an emptyDir on a
          rescheduled pod). Use a PVC for anything that must persist.
      Q7. What problem does CSI solve?
          A. It lets storage vendors ship drivers out-of-tree that provision and
          attach real volumes, instead of baking every backend into Kubernetes.
      Q8. Difference between a volume and a volumeMount?
          A. The volume (pod.spec.volumes) defines the storage source; the
          volumeMount (container) maps it to a path inside that container.
      Q9. Can one volume be mounted into several containers at once?
          A. Yes — reference the same volume name in each container's
          volumeMounts; that is the basis of sidecar log/file sharing.
      Q10. How do you mount a volume read-only into a container?
          A. Set readOnly: true on that container's volumeMount, so the container
          can read but not modify the shared data.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
      [VOLUME LIFECYCLE SPECTRUM — how long does the data live?]
       container-only      pod-scoped         node-scoped      cluster-durable
       (writable layer) ◄─ emptyDir ─►    ◄─ hostPath ─►   ◄─ PVC ─► PV ─►
       dies with         dies with the      tied to ONE      survives pod delete,
       CONTAINER         POD (survives a     node             reschedule & scaling
                         container restart)

      .vs-prose — Storage in Kubernetes is a lifecycle ladder. At the bottom, the
      container's writable layer dies with the container. One rung up, emptyDir
      lives as long as the POD and is shared between its containers (the sidecar
      pattern), with an optional RAM-backed Memory medium. hostPath reaches the
      node's own filesystem but pins the pod to that node and is reserved for
      agents and dev. At the top, PVC/PV (backed by CSI drivers) give cluster-
      durable storage that survives pod deletion, reschedule and scaling — which
      is why easypj's web tier stays stateless while PostgreSQL and user uploads
      ride on PVCs. Always remember: a volume is the source declared once at pod
      level; a volumeMount places it inside a container, and many containers can
      mount the same source.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Chapter 22: PersistentVolumes, PVCs & StorageClasses                  🟡 🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — heavily tested]      🟡 INTERMEDIATE

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Storage (10% of exam) —
        PV/PVC model, access modes, reclaim policies, dynamic provisioning.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  This is how easypj's database gets durable, on-demand disk. Containers are
  ephemeral: kill a pod and its writable layer evaporates. PostgreSQL backing
  the JobPost / Skills / Author / Location data CANNOT lose its files on a
  restart or reschedule. PersistentVolumes (PV), PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC)
  and StorageClasses are the Kubernetes machinery that hands a pod a piece of
  real disk that OUTLIVES the pod. The mental model that wins exam questions is
  separation of concerns: the ADMIN supplies storage, the DEVELOPER requests it,
  and Kubernetes binds the two.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  • Explain the PV/PVC separation-of-concerns model and the binding lifecycle.
  • Create PersistentVolumes (capacity, access modes, reclaim policy, backend).
  • Create PersistentVolumeClaims and understand why one binds (or stays Pending).
  • Mount a PVC inside a Pod / Deployment via volumes + volumeMounts.
  • Use StorageClasses for dynamic provisioning (provisioner, binding mode,
    expansion, default class).
  • Give PostgreSQL durable per-replica storage with volumeClaimTemplates.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
  Storage is 10% of the exam and almost always appears as a task: "create a PV
  and a PVC that binds to it and mount it in a pod," or "this PVC is Pending —
  fix it." You must be able to author PV/PVC/StorageClass YAML from memory, read
  `kubectl get pv,pvc,sc`, and debug a Pending claim from its Events. Fast,
  accurate, no Googling.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------

    22.2  Creating PersistentVolumes
    22.3  Creating PersistentVolumeClaims
    22.4  Using PVCs in Pods
    22.5  StorageClasses — Dynamic Provisioning
