    🔧 Under-the-Hood / DEEPER
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.1  The PV/PVC Model — Separation of Concerns          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • PersistentVolume (PV): a cluster-level storage resource (created by an admin,
    or carved out automatically by a StorageClass). It is the ACTUAL storage.
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): a user's REQUEST for storage, created by a
    developer in their own namespace. It is a request, not the disk itself.
  • The flow: Admin provisions PV → Developer creates PVC → Kubernetes binds the
    PVC to a matching PV → Pod references the PVC by name and mounts it.

  📖 KEY TERM — Binding: Kubernetes' control loop matches a PVC to a PV whose
     storageClassName, accessModes and capacity satisfy the request, then locks
     them together one-to-one. A bound PV serves exactly one PVC.

  🧠 ANALOGY: A PV is like a furnished apartment the landlord (admin) lists. A
     PVC is your rental application stating "2 bedrooms, pet-friendly, near
     downtown." The agency (Kubernetes) matches your application to an apartment
     and hands you the keys (binds). You (the pod) move in. When you move out
     (delete the PVC), the landlord decides whether to re-rent or demolish
     (reclaimPolicy).

  Status lifecycle of a PV:  Available → Bound → Released → (Failed / reused)
  Status lifecycle of a PVC: Pending → Bound  (→ Lost if its PV vanishes)

          [DIAGRAM: Admin creates PV → PVC matches and binds → Pod uses PVC]

          [PV/PVC — THE STORAGE MODEL]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  THE PV / PVC MODEL                                   │
          │                                                       │
          │  🔧 ADMIN creates:              👨‍💻 DEVELOPER creates: │
          │  ┌────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐ │
          │  │ PersistentVolume   │        │ PersistentVolume │ │
          │  │ (PV)               │        │ Claim (PVC)      │ │
          │  │                    │        │                  │ │
          │  │ capacity: 10Gi    │◄──────▶│ request: 10Gi    │ │
          │  │ accessMode: RWO   │ bind!  │ accessMode: RWO  │ │
          │  │ storageClass: ssd │        │ storageClass: ssd│ │
          │  │ hostPath/NFS/EBS  │        │                  │ │
          │  └────────────────────┘        └───────┬──────────┘ │
          │                                        │              │
          │                                        ▼              │
          │                                ┌──────────────┐      │
          │                                │ Pod spec     │      │
          │                                │ volumes:     │      │
          │                                │ - pvc:       │      │
          │                                │   claimName: │      │
          │                                │   data-pvc   │      │
          │                                └──────────────┘      │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT: The developer never names a PV. They name a PVC. This decoupling
     is the whole point — the developer says "I need 10Gi RWO of class fast"
     without knowing whether the disk is EBS, a Ceph volume, or an NFS export.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.2  Creating PersistentVolumes                        🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  A PV declares: capacity, access modes, a reclaim policy, an optional
  storageClassName, and a backend (hostPath / NFS / CSI / cloud disk).

  [CODE: PV YAML — 10Gi with hostPath (for local testing)]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolume
      metadata:
        name: easypj-pv-hostpath
      spec:
        capacity:
          storage: 10Gi
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
        storageClassName: manual
        hostPath:                      # NODE-LOCAL path — single-node / dev only
          path: /mnt/data/easypj

  [CODE: PV YAML — NFS volume]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolume
      metadata:
        name: easypj-pv-nfs
      spec:
        capacity:
          storage: 10Gi
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteMany              # NFS can serve many nodes read-write
        persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
        storageClassName: nfs
        nfs:
          server: 10.0.0.5
          path: /exports/easypj

  Access Modes (⚠️ describe NODES, not pods):
    • ReadWriteOnce  (RWO)  — single node read-write (block storage default)
    • ReadOnlyMany   (ROX)  — multiple nodes, read-only
    • ReadWriteMany  (RWX)  — multiple nodes read-write (needs NFS/CephFS, etc.)
    • ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) — exactly one POD read-write (newer; pod-scoped)

          [ACCESS MODES — WHO CAN MOUNT IT]
          ┌──────────┬───────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
          │  Mode    │  How many?    │  Access     │  Typical backend         │
          ├──────────┼───────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
          │  RWO     │  one node     │  read-write │  EBS, GCE PD, most block │
          │  ROX     │  many nodes   │  read-only  │  NFS, prepopulated CSI   │
          │  RWX     │  many nodes   │  read-write │  NFS, CephFS, GlusterFS  │
          │  RWOP    │  one POD      │  read-write │  CSI (single-pod lock)   │
          └──────────┴───────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
          ⚠️ "Once"/"Many" count NODES, not pods (except RWOP). Two pods on the
             SAME node can both use an RWO volume.

  Reclaim Policies (what happens to the disk after the PVC is deleted):
    • Retain  — keep the data; PV goes Released; admin cleans up manually.
    • Delete  — delete the underlying storage automatically (cloud default).
    • Recycle — DEPRECATED (used to `rm -rf` the volume); do not use.

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: hostPath is single-node only. It binds to a path on whatever
     node the pod lands on — useless for a real multi-node cluster, fine for
     kind/minikube labs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.3  Creating PersistentVolumeClaims                   🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  A PVC binds to a PV that matches on THREE things: storageClassName,
  access modes, and size (requested ≤ PV capacity). If nothing matches, the PVC
  stays Pending.

  [CODE: PVC YAML — requesting 10Gi storage]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db-data
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        storageClassName: manual       # must match a PV's class (or "" / default)
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi

  • PVC binds to a PV that matches: size (request ≤ capacity), access mode, and
    storage class.
  • If no matching PV exists: the PVC stays in Pending state until one appears
    (static) or the StorageClass provisions one (dynamic).
  • You can force a specific PV with spec.volumeName, or narrow matches with a
    label selector.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING: A Pending PVC almost always means class mismatch, no PV big
     enough, incompatible access mode, or no provisioner. `kubectl describe pvc`
     names the reason in its Events.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.4  Using PVCs in Pods                                🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  The pod references the PVC by name. Two stanzas matter:
    • volumes:       a volume whose source is persistentVolumeClaim.claimName
    • volumeMounts:  where inside the container that volume appears

  [CODE: Pod/Deployment YAML with PVC as volume]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: postgres
            image: postgres:16
            volumeMounts:
              - name: data
                mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data   # where storage appears
        volumes:
          - name: data
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: easypj-db-data                # reference to the PVC

  • volumeMounts.mountPath: the path INSIDE the container that shows the storage.
  • volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName: the PVC this pod is consuming.

          [PV → PVC → POD — THE CONSUMPTION CHAIN]
          ┌────────────┐  binds  ┌────────────┐  claimName  ┌────────────┐
          │ PV 10Gi    │◄───────►│ PVC        │◄────────────│ Pod        │
          │ RWO, ssd   │  match  │ req 10Gi   │   reference │ volumeMount│
          │ (real disk)│         │ RWO, ssd   │             │ /var/lib/..│
          └────────────┘         └────────────┘             └────────────┘
              admin                developer                  developer
          ⚠️ The pod never names the PV — only the PVC. Decoupling by design.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.5  StorageClasses — Dynamic Provisioning             🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • Eliminates the need for an admin to pre-create PVs.
  • A developer creates a PVC with a storageClassName → a matching PV is created
    AUTOMATICALLY by the class's provisioner.
  • Provisioner: cloud/CSI-specific (ebs.csi.aws.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io,
    disk.csi.azure.com, rbd.csi.ceph.com, …).

  Key StorageClass fields:
    • provisioner          — the CSI driver that creates the disk.
    • parameters           — backend-specific (e.g. type: gp3).
    • reclaimPolicy        — Retain or Delete for dynamically created PVs.
    • allowVolumeExpansion — true lets PVCs be grown later (never shrunk).
    • volumeBindingMode    — Immediate vs WaitForFirstConsumer (see below).

  [CODE: StorageClass YAML]
      apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
      kind: StorageClass
      metadata:
        name: easypj-fast
        annotations:
          storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
      provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com        # the CSI driver that creates disks
      parameters:
        type: gp3
      reclaimPolicy: Retain                # keep the disk when the PVC is deleted
      allowVolumeExpansion: true           # PVCs may be grown later
      volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer   # bind once a pod is scheduled
      # A PVC with storageClassName: easypj-fast now auto-creates a matching PV.

  [CODE: PVC using StorageClass for dynamic provisioning]
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db-data
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        storageClassName: easypj-fast      # triggers dynamic provisioning
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
      # No admin action needed — the class provisions a PV on demand.

          [STATIC vs DYNAMIC PROVISIONING]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  STATIC (manual)              DYNAMIC (automatic)    │
          │                                                      │
          │  Admin creates PV             Developer creates PVC  │
          │       │                             │                │
          │       ▼                             ▼                │
          │  Dev creates PVC           StorageClass provisions   │
          │       │                    PV automatically          │
          │       ▼                             │                │
          │  PVC binds to PV                    ▼                │
          │       │                     PVC binds to new PV      │
          │       ▼                             │                │
          │  Pod uses PVC                Pod uses PVC             │
          │                                                      │
          │  More work for admin 😰     Admin sets up once! 🎉  │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERM — volumeBindingMode:
     • Immediate — the PV is created/bound as soon as the PVC exists. Risky in
       multi-zone clusters: the disk may land in a zone where the pod can't run.
     • WaitForFirstConsumer — binding is DELAYED until a pod that uses the PVC is
       scheduled, so the volume is provisioned in the SAME zone/topology as the
       pod. The correct default for zonal cloud storage.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — static vs dynamic:
     • Dynamic (StorageClass): the norm in cloud/managed clusters; self-service.
     • Static (hand-made PV): pre-existing disks, NFS exports, on-prem volumes,
       or exam tasks that explicitly say "create a PV."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  22.6  PostgreSQL Storage for easypj   🧪 [COMPLETE EXAMPLE]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Goal: give easypj's PostgreSQL durable storage that survives pod restarts,
  rescheduling and scaling. StatefulSets do this with volumeClaimTemplates —
  EACH replica gets its own PVC (data-easypj-db-0, data-easypj-db-1, …) bound to
  its own PV.

  a) StorageClass for database storage
      apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
      kind: StorageClass
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db-storage
      provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
      parameters:
        type: gp3
      reclaimPolicy: Retain                 # never auto-destroy database disks
      allowVolumeExpansion: true
      volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

  b) PVC for PostgreSQL data (10Gi) — standalone form (for a single pod / Deployment)
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db-data
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        storageClassName: easypj-db-storage
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi

  c) StatefulSet using volumeClaimTemplates (the production pattern)
      apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: StatefulSet
      metadata:
        name: easypj-db
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        serviceName: easypj-db
        replicas: 1
        selector:
          matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
        template:
          metadata:
            labels: { app: easypj-db }
          spec:
            containers:
              - name: postgres
                image: postgres:16
                env:
                  - name: POSTGRES_DB
                    value: easypj
                  - name: POSTGRES_USER
                    value: easypj
                  - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
                    valueFrom:
                      secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-db-secret, key: password }
                  - name: PGDATA
                    value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
                ports:
                  - containerPort: 5432
                volumeMounts:
                  - name: data
                    mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        volumeClaimTemplates:                 # one PVC PER replica, auto-created
          - metadata:
              name: data
            spec:
              accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
              storageClassName: easypj-db-storage
              resources:
                requests:
                  storage: 10Gi

  d) Verify storage binding
      kubectl get pv,pvc,sc -n easypj
      kubectl get pvc -n easypj            # data-easypj-db-0  Bound  10Gi  RWO
      kubectl describe pvc data-easypj-db-0 -n easypj

          [POSTGRES STORAGE ARCHITECTURE — easypj]
   👩‍💻 Developer                       🤖 Kubernetes              🛠️ Admin
   ┌──────────────┐  binds to   ┌──────────────┐  provisioned  ┌──────────┐
   │ PVC          │◄───────────►│ PV (10Gi,    │◄──────────────│ 🧱 Storage│
   │ request 10Gi │  if class & │ RWO, Retain) │  on-demand by │ Class    │
   │ RWO, class=  │  size match │              │  the class    │ (provisn)│
   │ easypj-fast  │             └──────┬───────┘               └──────────┘
   └──────┬───────┘                    │ real disk (CSI: EBS/PD/Ceph)
          │ mounted into                ▼
   📦 postgres-0 ─ volumeMounts ─► /var/lib/postgresql/data  🐘
   Status flow:  PVC Pending ─► Bound ─► (PV) Released (after PVC delete)
   ⚠️ PVC stuck Pending = no matching PV / wrong storageClassName / no provisioner.
   Access modes: RWO (one node) · ROX (many read) · RWX (many r/w) · RWOP (one pod)

  💡 INSIGHT: With reclaimPolicy Retain, deleting the StatefulSet does NOT delete
     its PVCs (K8s keeps volumeClaimTemplate PVCs by default), and deleting the
     PVC does NOT destroy the disk. The data survives restart, reschedule and
     scale — exactly what a database needs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 The PersistentVolume binder controller (part of kube-controller-manager)
     continuously matches Pending PVCs against Available PVs. For dynamic
     classes, the external-provisioner sidecar of the CSI driver watches PVCs,
     calls the storage backend's CreateVolume, and creates the resulting PV.

  🔧 WaitForFirstConsumer & topology-aware provisioning: with this binding mode,
     the scheduler picks a node FIRST (considering CPU/memory/affinity), then the
     provisioner creates the disk in that node's zone and stamps the PV with
     topology (nodeAffinity) so it can only attach where the pod runs. This is
     why zonal disks must use WaitForFirstConsumer.

  🔧 Online volume expansion: patch the PVC's requests.storage upward; the
     CSI driver calls ControllerExpandVolume (and NodeExpandVolume to grow the
     filesystem) — often without restarting the pod. Requires
     allowVolumeExpansion: true on the class. Shrinking is never allowed.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
     • volumeMode: Filesystem (default, mounted dir) vs Block (raw device given
       to the container at a devicePath — for databases that manage their own FS).
     • CSI VolumeSnapshots & clones: snapshot a PVC (VolumeSnapshot →
       VolumeSnapshotContent), then restore it into a new PVC via
       spec.dataSource; or clone an existing PVC directly. Great for backups.
     • Zonal binding with WaitForFirstConsumer (above) avoids cross-zone attach
       failures.
     • RWX storage: block devices (EBS/PD) are RWO; for many-node read-write you
       need a network filesystem — NFS, CephFS, or an EFS/Filestore CSI driver.
     • fsGroup / fsGroupChangePolicy in securityContext set group ownership of the
       mounted volume so a non-root container can write; "OnRootMismatch" avoids
       expensive recursive chown on every mount.
     • Reclaiming Released PVs: a Retain PV stays Released and won't rebind until
       you clear its spec.claimRef (kubectl edit / patch) — otherwise it leaks.
     • Generic ephemeral CSI volumes: pod-lifetime volumes declared inline in the
       pod spec (volumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate) — created and deleted
       with the pod.
     • mountOptions and subPath pitfalls: subPath does NOT receive updates when a
       referenced ConfigMap/Secret changes, and a subPath into a hostPath can
       expose unexpected host data — prefer subPathExpr / full mounts where you can.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • PV/PVC is separation of concerns: an admin (or a StorageClass) supplies the
    PV (the actual storage); a developer files a PVC (a request). Kubernetes
    binds them: PVC Pending → Bound; after the PVC is deleted the PV goes
    Released (and is cleaned up or kept per reclaimPolicy).
  • A pod NEVER names a PV — it names a PVC. That decoupling is the whole design.
  • A StorageClass enables DYNAMIC provisioning — its provisioner creates a PV on
    demand the moment a matching PVC appears, so you never pre-create PVs.
  • Access modes describe NODES, not pods: RWO = one node read-write, ROX = many
    nodes read-only, RWX = many nodes read-write, RWOP = one pod read-write.
    Most block storage is RWO; RWX needs a network filesystem.
  • reclaimPolicy controls the disk's fate after the PVC is gone: Delete
    (destroy it) or Retain (keep it, manual cleanup). Recycle is deprecated.
  • StatefulSets use volumeClaimTemplates so each replica gets its own durable
    PVC/PV that survives restart, reschedule and scale.
  • A PVC binds on three criteria: storageClassName match, compatible access
    modes, and request ≤ capacity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • PVC stuck Pending = no matching PV, wrong storageClassName, no provisioner
    for that class, or (with WaitForFirstConsumer) no pod scheduled yet.
  • Access-mode mismatch: a PVC asking RWX bound to an RWO backend won't attach
    on multiple nodes. Most block storage is RWO only.
  • Retain leaves PVs in Released state that won't rebind until you manually
    clear claimRef — a silent capacity leak.
  • Editing a PVC's size only works if allowVolumeExpansion: true on the class,
    and you can only GROW, never shrink.
  • hostPath PVs are node-local: a pod that reschedules to another node sees an
    empty/different directory. Lab-only.
  • storageClassName: "" (empty string) explicitly disables dynamic provisioning
    and forces static binding — different from omitting the field (which uses the
    default class).
  • Deleting a StatefulSet does NOT delete its volumeClaimTemplate PVCs; you must
    delete them by hand if you really want the storage gone.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • `kubectl get pv,pvc,sc` in one shot shows binding state across all three.
  • describe a Pending PVC FIRST — its Events line usually names the exact reason
    (no provisioner / waiting for first consumer / no matching PV).
  • `kubectl get sc` — the one marked (default) is what PVCs without a
    storageClassName use.
  • To force static binding (no class), set storageClassName: "" on both the PV
    and the PVC.
  • Patch to grow: one-liner `kubectl patch pvc NAME -p '{"spec":{"resources":
    {"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  kubectl get pv,pvc,sc -o wide
  kubectl describe pvc easypj-db-data          # Events explain Pending
  kubectl get sc                               # which is (default)?
  kubectl patch pvc easypj-db-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'
  kubectl get pv -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.phase}{"\n"}{end}'
  kubectl apply -f pv.yaml -f pvc.yaml
  kubectl get pvc -n easypj -w                 # watch a claim move Pending→Bound
  kubectl delete pvc easypj-db-data -n easypj  # release the PV (per reclaimPolicy)

  🧪 DRILL: create a StorageClass-backed PVC, mount it in a pod, write a file,
     delete the pod, recreate it bound to the same PVC, and confirm the file
     survived. Then make the PVC Pending (wrong class) and debug it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Q1. Create a static PV, a matching PVC, and a pod that mounts it.
      A. PV with capacity/accessModes/storageClassName; PVC requesting the same
      class, ≤ capacity, compatible accessModes; pod volumes with
      persistentVolumeClaim.claimName → volumeMount at a mountPath.

  Q2. What is dynamic provisioning and what triggers it?
      A. A StorageClass with a provisioner auto-creates a PV when a PVC
      referencing that class is created — no admin pre-provisioning needed.

  Q3. Explain RWO vs ROX vs RWX vs RWOP.
      A. RWO = read-write by one node; ROX = read-only by many nodes; RWX =
      read-write by many nodes; RWOP = read-write by a single pod. Modes are
      node-scoped (except RWOP, which is pod-scoped).

  Q4. reclaimPolicy Delete vs Retain — what happens to the disk?
      A. Delete destroys the underlying volume when the PVC is removed; Retain
      keeps it (PV → Released) for manual recovery/cleanup. Recycle is deprecated.

  Q5. A PVC is stuck Pending. List the likely causes.
      A. No PV matches (size/accessModes/class), wrong storageClassName, no
      provisioner for the class, or WaitForFirstConsumer waiting on a pod.
      `kubectl describe pvc` shows the reason in Events.

  Q6. How does a PVC bind to a specific PV?
      A. The binder matches storageClassName, requested ≤ capacity, and
      compatible accessModes; you can force it with spec.volumeName or a label
      selector.

  Q7. Grow an existing PVC from 10Gi to 20Gi. Requirements?
      A. The StorageClass must have allowVolumeExpansion: true; patch the PVC's
      requests.storage upward (shrinking is not allowed). The CSI driver expands
      the disk and filesystem, often online.

  Q8. How do you set/identify the default StorageClass?
      A. The class with annotation
      storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" (shown as (default) in
      `kubectl get sc`) is used by PVCs that omit storageClassName.

  Q9. Why use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
      A. It delays PV creation/binding until a pod is scheduled, so the volume is
      provisioned in the same zone/topology as the pod (avoids cross-zone attach
      failures with zonal disks).

  Q10. Give postgres durable per-replica storage in a StatefulSet.
       A. Use volumeClaimTemplates in the StatefulSet — each replica gets its own
       PVC (e.g. data-easypj-db-0) bound to its own PV that persists across
       restarts and rescheduling.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  📊 VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 22
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       StorageClass ──provisions──► dynamic PV ──binds──► PVC ──mounted──► postgres pod
       (Available → Bound → Released)        request ≤ capacity, class & accessModes match

  .vs-prose: A StorageClass (provisioner + parameters + binding mode + reclaim
  policy) dynamically provisions a PV the moment a matching PVC is created. The
  PVC binds to that PV when storageClassName, access modes and size all agree,
  moving Pending → Bound. A pod consumes the PVC by claimName and mounts it at a
  path; for easypj's PostgreSQL a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates give each
  replica its own durable PVC. With reclaimPolicy Retain the disk and its data
  survive pod deletion, restart, reschedule and scale — and after the PVC is
  deleted the PV goes Released until an admin cleans it up.

================================================================================
  Chapter 23: ConfigMaps & Secrets                                     🟡 🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]   🟢 intro · 🟡 core · 🔴 encryption-at-rest

    META: 🟡 · ⏱️ ~2h · Official "Workloads & Scheduling" competency
          (configure applications). Difficulty 🟡; the encryption-at-rest
          tie-in is 🔴.

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    ----------------
    easypj's settings (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, DB_HOST, DB_NAME) and its
    credentials (SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD) must live OUTSIDE the container
    image. Bake them in and you get one image per environment, secrets in
    Git history, and a rebuild for every config tweak. ConfigMaps and
    Secrets let ONE easypj image run unchanged in dev, staging and the
    Kubernetes cluster — only the injected config differs. 💡 The image is
    the recipe; the ConfigMap/Secret is the seasoning added at serve time.

    OBJECTIVES
    ----------
    • Create & consume ConfigMaps (literal / file / env-file) and Secrets.
    • Inject config three ways: env (one key), envFrom (all keys), volume.
    • Know secret types (generic/Opaque, tls, docker-registry).
    • 📖 Understand base64 ≠ encryption; enable encryption-at-rest.
    • Use immutability for safety and performance; version your config.

    CKA RELEVANCE
    -------------
    🎯 Part of the ~10% storage/config band. Creating ConfigMaps/Secrets
    imperatively, wiring them into a Deployment, and debugging "my app
    still sees the old value" are classic, fast-to-score exam tasks.

    SECTION MAP
    -----------
    23.1  ConfigMaps — Non-Sensitive Configuration
    23.2  Secrets — Sensitive Configuration
    23.3  ConfigMap and Secret Best Practices
    23.4  Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
    📊 KEY DIAGRAMS · 🔧 UTH / 🔬 DEEPER · 🔑 TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A


    23.1  ConfigMaps — Non-Sensitive Configuration
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - Store configuration data as key-value pairs.
          - Decouple configuration from container images.
          - Injected into pods as: environment variables OR mounted files.
          - 📖 KEY TERM — ConfigMap: an API object holding non-sensitive
            config as key/value pairs (max ~1 MiB per object).

          ConfigMap YAML for easypj Django settings:

          apiVersion: v1
          kind: ConfigMap
          metadata:
            name: easypj-config
            namespace: easypj
          data:
            DEBUG: "False"
            ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com,localhost"
            DB_HOST: "easypj-db"
            DB_NAME: "easypj"
            DB_PORT: "5432"
          # binaryData: <key>: <base64>   # for non-UTF-8 blobs

          Creating ConfigMaps (three sources, same result):
          $ kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False
          $ kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False \
              --from-literal=DB_HOST=easypj-db
          $ kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-file=settings.ini
          $ kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-env-file=.env
          # --from-literal=K=V  → inline key/value
          # --from-file=app.conf → filename becomes the key, contents the value
          # --from-env-file=.env → each NAME=VALUE line becomes a key

          Using in Pods — Deployment consuming easypj-config both ways:

          apiVersion: apps/v1
          kind: Deployment
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            replicas: 2
            selector:
              matchLabels: { app: easypj }
            template:
              metadata:
                labels: { app: easypj }
              spec:
                containers:
                - name: web
                  image: easypj:latest
                  # a) ALL keys as env vars (bulk):
                  envFrom:
                  - configMapRef:
                      name: easypj-config
                  # b) ONE key, renamed (precise):
                  env:
                  - name: DJANGO_DB_HOST
                    valueFrom:
                      configMapKeyRef:
                        name: easypj-config
                        key: DB_HOST
                  # c) As mounted files (one file per key):
                  volumeMounts:
                  - name: cfg
                    mountPath: /etc/easypj
                    readOnly: true
                volumes:
                - name: cfg
                  configMap:
                    name: easypj-config
                    # optional: items: [{key: DB_HOST, path: db_host}]
                    # optional: defaultMode: 0444

          🔧 Volume-mounted keys auto-update (~60s sync). Env vars are
          FIXED at pod start — editing the ConfigMap does NOT change them
          until the pod restarts.


    23.2  Secrets — Sensitive Configuration
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - Like ConfigMaps but for sensitive data.
          - 📖 base64 ENCODED, NOT encrypted by default! Anyone who can read
            the Secret (or etcd) can decode it.
          - Types: Opaque (generic), kubernetes.io/tls,
            kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, kubernetes.io/service-account-token,
            bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token.
          - stringData (plaintext in, K8s encodes it) vs data (you supply
            base64). defaultMode controls file permissions on volume mounts.

          Secret YAML — Django SECRET_KEY and DB password:

          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Secret
          metadata:
            name: easypj-secret
            namespace: easypj
          type: Opaque
          stringData:                  # plaintext in; K8s base64-encodes it
            SECRET_KEY: "django-insecure-CHANGE-ME"
            DB_PASSWORD: "s3cr3t-pg-pass"
          # Equivalent with pre-encoded values:
          # data:
          #   SECRET_KEY: ZGphbmdvLWluc2VjdXJlLUNIQU5HRS1NRQ==
          #   DB_PASSWORD: czNjcjN0LXBnLXBhc3M=

          Creating Secrets imperatively:
          $ kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret \
              --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=my-secret-key \
              --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=postgres123
          $ kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls \
              --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
          $ kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
              --docker-server=registry.example.com \
              --docker-username=ci --docker-password=...

          # base64 is ENCODING, not encryption — enable encryption-at-rest
          # (Ch 11) and lock down RBAC on secrets (Ch 39).

          Using in Pods — Deployment using easypj-secret as env vars AND
          volume mounts:

          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                imagePullSecrets:
                - name: regcred                 # pull private image
                containers:
                - name: web
                  image: easypj:latest
                  env:
                  - name: SECRET_KEY
                    valueFrom:
                      secretKeyRef:
                        name: easypj-secret
                        key: SECRET_KEY
                  - name: DB_PASSWORD
                    valueFrom:
                      secretKeyRef:
                        name: easypj-secret
                        key: DB_PASSWORD
                  volumeMounts:
                  - name: secret-vol
                    mountPath: /etc/easypj/secrets
                    readOnly: true
                volumes:
                - name: secret-vol
                  secret:
                    secretName: easypj-secret
                    defaultMode: 0400           # owner read-only

          Decode a secret value to verify:
          $ kubectl get secret easypj-secret \
              -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d


    23.3  ConfigMap and Secret Best Practices
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    [CHECKLIST]
          ✅ Use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config.
          ✅ Use Secrets for sensitive data.
          ✅ Use envFrom for bulk injection.
          ✅ Use volume mounts when config is a file (and for hot-reload).
          ✅ Enable encryption at rest for Secrets (Ch 11 / Ch 39).
          ✅ Use RBAC to restrict Secret access (least privilege).
          ✅ Prefer volume mounts over env for secrets (env can leak via
             `/proc`, crash dumps, child processes).
          ❌ Never commit Secrets to Git.
          ❌ Never hardcode secrets in Dockerfiles.
          ❌ Never log secret values.

          🏢 DAY-2 / BEYOND
          - Encryption at rest: configure an EncryptionConfiguration on the
            API server so Secrets aren't stored in clear text in etcd; an
            etcd backup otherwise leaks every secret.
          - External secret stores: HashiCorp Vault, the External Secrets
            Operator, or sealed-secrets keep the source of truth (and
            rotation) outside the cluster while still surfacing a native
            Secret object to pods.
          - Rotation: changing a Secret does not restart pods; pair updates
            with a `kubectl rollout restart` or use file mounts the app
            re-reads.


    23.4  Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - immutable: true → cannot be modified after creation (only
            deleted and recreated).
          - Prevents accidental changes (safety).
          - Performance: kubelet doesn't watch immutable objects, cutting
            API-server load on large clusters.
          - Versioning strategy: name configs easypj-config-v1,
            easypj-config-v2 and roll Deployments forward to the new name.

          Immutable ConfigMap YAML:

          apiVersion: v1
          kind: ConfigMap
          metadata:
            name: easypj-config-v2
            namespace: easypj
          immutable: true
          data:
            DEBUG: "False"
            ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com"
            DB_HOST: "easypj-db"

          # Same flag works on Secrets:
          # kind: Secret
          # immutable: true


    📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 23

    [3 WAYS TO INJECT CONFIG INTO easypj]
     ⚙️ ConfigMap easypj-config   /   🔒 Secret easypj-secret
          │
          ├─ envFrom ─────────► ALL keys become env vars  (DB_HOST, DEBUG, ...)
          ├─ env+valueFrom.*KeyRef ► ONE key, can rename it
          └─ volume mount ────► files at /etc/easypj/...   (hot-reloads ~60s)
     🔁 reload: volume FILES auto-update · ENV VARS do NOT (must restart the pod).
     ⚠️ Secret = base64 ENCODING, not encryption -> turn on encryption at rest.

    [CONFIGMAP vs SECRET — AT A GLANCE]
     ┌──────────────────┬────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
     │ ASPECT           │ ConfigMap              │ Secret                 │
     ├──────────────────┼────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
     │ Purpose          │ non-sensitive config   │ sensitive data         │
     │ Stored in etcd   │ plaintext              │ base64 (NOT encrypted  │
     │                  │                        │ unless encrypt-at-rest)│
     │ Plaintext field  │ data:                  │ stringData:            │
     │ Encoded field    │ binaryData:            │ data: (base64)         │
     │ Common types     │ (one kind)             │ Opaque / tls /         │
     │                  │                        │ dockerconfigjson       │
     │ env injection    │ configMapKeyRef        │ secretKeyRef           │
     │ bulk injection   │ envFrom.configMapRef   │ envFrom.secretRef      │
     │ Size limit       │ ~1 MiB                 │ ~1 MiB                  │
     └──────────────────┴────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

    [DATA FLOW — easypj POD CONSUMING CONFIG]
     ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────┐
     │  easypj-config (CM)│        │ easypj-secret (Sec)│
     │  DEBUG, DB_HOST... │        │ SECRET_KEY, DB_PW  │
     └─────────┬──────────┘        └─────────┬──────────┘
               │ envFrom / valueFrom          │ secretKeyRef
               ▼                              ▼
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                easypj-web Pod                         │
     │  ENV: DEBUG=False  DJANGO_DB_HOST=easypj-db           │
     │       SECRET_KEY=••••  DB_PASSWORD=••••               │
     │  FILES (volume): /etc/easypj/DB_HOST                  │
     │                  /etc/easypj/secrets/DB_PASSWORD      │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


    [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UTH — how injection actually works:
    • envFrom / env+valueFrom: the kubelet reads the cm/secret at pod
      creation and bakes the values into the container's environment
      block. That block is immutable for the process lifetime, which is
      WHY env vars never change without a pod restart.
    • Volume projection: cm/secret volumes are backed by a tmpfs the
      kubelet manages. The kubelet periodically syncs (~60s, plus its
      cache TTL) and atomically swaps a symlinked "..data" directory, so
      mounted FILES hot-reload while the app is running.
    • subPath caveat: a subPath mount copies the file ONCE at start and
      does NOT receive live updates — use a full-directory mount when you
      need hot-reload.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    • Immutable cm/secret: `immutable: true` stops the kubelet from
      watching them, reducing API-server load on big clusters; the object
      can only be deleted/recreated.
    • Size limit ~1 MiB per object (etcd value limit); use binaryData for
      non-UTF-8 content.
    • Secret types: kubernetes.io/tls (tls.crt+tls.key for Ingress),
      kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (imagePullSecrets), service-account-
      token, bootstrap tokens.
    • envFrom supports a `prefix:` to namespace imported keys
      (e.g. prefix: DJANGO_ → DJANGO_DB_HOST).
    • Kubelet caches secrets in memory (configurable strategy: Watch/
      Cache/Get) and only delivers a secret to nodes that run a pod
      needing it.
    • Rotation: sealed-secrets / external-secrets operators reconcile from
      an external store; pair with rollout restart for env consumers.


    [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    • ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for sensitive data.
      Inject via env vars or volume mounts. Both keep configuration OUT
      of the image so ONE easypj image runs in every environment.
    • Three injection styles: env (one key, rename via valueFrom), envFrom
      (all keys become env vars), volume mount (each key becomes a file).
    • Volume-mounted keys hot-reload (~60s); env vars are fixed at pod
      start and only change on a pod restart.
    • Secrets are base64 ENCODING, NOT encryption. Anyone with read access
      (or etcd access) can decode them — enable encryption-at-rest and
      lock down RBAC on secrets. NEVER commit to Git.
    • immutable: true buys safety (no accidental edits) and performance
      (no kubelet watch); version configs (config-v2) and roll forward.


    [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Putting plaintext under `data:` FAILS — `data` must be base64; use
      `stringData` to supply plaintext and let K8s encode it.
    • Changing a ConfigMap/Secret does NOT restart pods; env-var consumers
      keep the OLD value until the pod restarts (`kubectl rollout restart`).
    • subPath volume mounts do NOT receive live updates — copied once at
      start.
    • By default secrets sit unencrypted (only base64) in etcd; a backup or
      etcd read leaks them. Turn on EncryptionConfiguration.
    • A referenced cm/secret that doesn't exist (and isn't marked optional)
      keeps the pod stuck in ContainerCreating / CreateContainerConfigError.
    • Env-var names from envFrom must be valid shell identifiers; keys with
      `.` or `-` are skipped (an event is logged).


    [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Imperative create is fastest:
      kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False
      kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=...
    • Generate then edit: add `--dry-run=client -o yaml` to any create
      command to get a YAML skeleton you can pipe to a file.
    • Mark config immutable (`immutable: true`) for hot paths — fewer API
      watches and protection against accidental edits.
    • Decode in one line:
      kubectl get secret S -o jsonpath='{.data.K}' | base64 -d
    • Force consumers to pick up new env values fast:
      kubectl rollout restart deploy easypj-web


    [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
      kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False --from-literal=DB_HOST=easypj-db
      kubectl create configmap myconfig --from-literal=key=val
      kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-file=settings.ini
      kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-env-file=.env
      kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t
      kubectl create secret generic mysecret --from-literal=pw=123
      kubectl get secret easypj-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
      kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
      kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
      kubectl get cm,secret -n easypj
      kubectl describe configmap easypj-config
      kubectl rollout restart deploy easypj-web        # pick up new env values


    [L] 🧪 DRILL
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    Inject easypj config three ways into a single pod — one env var via
    valueFrom, all keys via envFrom, and the Secret as files under
    /etc/easypj — then `kubectl exec` in and verify each is present
    (`env | grep DB_HOST`, `env`, `ls /etc/easypj`).


    [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
      Q1. Create a ConfigMap three different ways.
          A. --from-literal=K=V (inline), --from-file=app.conf (filename
          becomes key, contents the value), and --from-env-file=app.env
          (each NAME=VALUE line a key). All produce the same kind: ConfigMap.

      Q2. Difference between envFrom and env+valueFrom?
          A. envFrom imports ALL keys of a cm/secret as env vars;
          env+valueFrom.configMapKeyRef/secretKeyRef pulls ONE key and lets
          you rename it (e.g. DB_HOST → DJANGO_DB_HOST).

      Q3. Mount easypj-config as files. Where do the keys appear?
          A. As a volume → each key becomes a file under the mountPath
          (e.g. /etc/easypj/DB_HOST containing the value).

      Q4. Create a generic Secret with DB_PASSWORD.
          A. `kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret
          --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=...` (type Opaque, value base64-encoded).

      Q5. Create a TLS secret for Ingress.
          A. `kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=tls.crt
          --key=tls.key` (type kubernetes.io/tls).

      Q6. Is a Secret encrypted? Justify.
          A. No by default — values are base64-ENCODED and stored in etcd in
          the clear. Real protection needs encryption-at-rest
          (EncryptionConfiguration) + RBAC restrictions on the secret.

      Q7. What does immutable: true buy you on a ConfigMap?
          A. The cm/secret can't be updated (only replaced), which reduces
          kubelet watch load and prevents accidental live edits.

      Q8. You edited a ConfigMap but the app still sees the old value. Why?
          A. The app reads it as an env var, which is fixed at pod start.
          Restart the pods (`kubectl rollout restart`) — or mount it as a
          file for ~60s hot-reload.

      Q9. Pull a private image — what Secret type and wiring?
          A. A kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson secret (create via
          `kubectl create secret docker-registry`) referenced via
          imagePullSecrets on the pod or its ServiceAccount.

      Q10. Rotate DB_PASSWORD with minimal disruption.
           A. Update the Secret, then trigger a rolling restart of the
           consumers (`kubectl rollout restart`) so new pods pick up the new
           value; or use a file-mounted secret that hot-reloads if the app
           re-reads it.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  easypj-config (CM) ──envFrom/valueFrom──┐                        │
     │  easypj-secret (Secret) ──secretKeyRef──┐│                        │
     │                                         ▼▼                        │
     │                              ┌──────────────────┐                 │
     │                              │  easypj-web pod  │                 │
     │                              │  ENV: DEBUG,     │                 │
     │                              │  DB_HOST, SECRET │                 │
     │                              │  FILES: /etc/    │                 │
     │                              │  easypj/...      │                 │
     │                              └──────────────────┘                 │
     │  🔁 files hot-reload ~60s · env fixed at start · base64≠encrypt   │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     .vs-prose: ConfigMaps and Secrets externalize easypj's config and
     credentials. The same image consumes them as environment variables
     (one key via valueFrom, all keys via envFrom) or as mounted files.
     File mounts hot-reload in about a minute; env vars are frozen at pod
     start and need a rollout restart. Secret data is only base64-encoded,
     so encryption-at-rest plus tight RBAC are mandatory for real safety.

  [PART 7 INTRO]
  Security in Kubernetes answers two questions: WHO are you (authentication via
  certificates / ServiceAccount tokens) and WHAT may you do (authorization via
  RBAC). On top sits workload security — what a pod itself is allowed to do.
  This part makes easypj's humans and pods least-privileged by default.

  Every request that reaches the API server runs a three-stage gauntlet:
  authentication (prove identity), authorization (check permission), then
  admission control (validate/mutate the object). Get any stage wrong and a
  request is rejected with 401 (who?), 403 (forbidden), or an admission error.
  For easypj this means: developers carry signed kubeconfigs, the easypj-web
  pod carries a scoped ServiceAccount token, RBAC Roles spell out exactly what
  each may touch, and Pod Security Admission stops a compromised pod from
  running as root or breaking out of its container.

  🧠 ANALOGY — The office building. AuthN is the badge that proves you are an
  employee (TLS cert / SA token). AuthZ is the access-control list that says
  which doors your badge opens (RBAC). Admission control is the security guard
  at the door who can still refuse you (or make you wear a visitor sticker)
  even with a valid badge — that's Pod Security enforcing house rules.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 7 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WHO ARE YOU?                         WHAT CAN YOU DO?                   │
  │  Ch26 TLS/PKI (humans) ─┐    ┌─▶ Ch24 RBAC (Roles/Bindings)             │
  │  Ch25 ServiceAccounts ──┴────┘                                          │
  │                                  └─▶ Ch27 POD SECURITY (what pods may do)│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Chapter guide:
    • Ch24 RBAC ............ Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, verbs/resources
    • Ch25 ServiceAccounts . pod identity, projected tokens, imagePullSecrets
    • Ch26 TLS / PKI ....... the cluster cert web, CSR API, signing kubeconfigs
    • Ch27 Pod Security .... Pod Security Standards, PSA labels, securityContext

  [PART 7 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: an easypj-web ServiceAccount with a tight Role (read
  its own ConfigMap only) -> a developer kubeconfig signed via a CSR -> Pod
  Security Admission set to "restricted" on the easypj namespace -> easypj pods
  run non-root, read-only-rootfs, no extra capabilities.

  VISUAL — the request pipeline every kubectl/pod API call must survive:

  ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
  │  Client  │──▶│ AUTHENTICATION│──▶│ AUTHORIZATION │──▶│   ADMISSION    │──▶ etcd
  │ kubectl  │   │   "WHO?"      │   │   "WHAT?"     │   │  "ALLOWED AS    │   write
  │  / pod   │   │ cert / token  │   │     RBAC      │   │   SHAPED?"      │
  └──────────┘   └───────┬───────┘   └───────┬───────┘   └───────┬────────┘
                         │ fail              │ fail             │ deny/mutate
                         ▼                   ▼                   ▼
                    401 Unauth          403 Forbidden     admission error
                  (Ch25/Ch26)             (Ch24)              (Ch27)

  Read the pipeline left to right: a TLS client cert or ServiceAccount token
  (Ch26/Ch25) establishes WHO; RBAC Roles and Bindings (Ch24) decide WHAT; and
  the admission stage — where Pod Security Admission lives (Ch27) — gets the
  final word on whether the object is allowed in the shape it was submitted.
  Master this single diagram and the whole security domain snaps into place:
  every 401 is an identity bug, every 403 is an RBAC bug, and every rejected
  pod create is an admission/securityContext bug.

  🔑 PART MUST-REMEMBER: 401 = AuthN (identity), 403 = AuthZ (RBAC),
  admission denial = Pod Security / policy. Diagnose in that order.

================================================================================
  Chapter 24: RBAC — Role-Based Access Control                          🟡 🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — heavily tested · EXAM STAPLE]

    META: 🟡 · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture 25% (RBAC).
          Every "Forbidden" error and every access grant you make in the exam
          is RBAC. Expect at least one task that creates a Role/ClusterRole and
          binds it to a user or ServiceAccount, plus verification with
          `kubectl auth can-i`.

    WHY THIS MATTERS
       RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is the gatekeeper of the Kubernetes API.
       It answers the single question: "Is THIS subject allowed to perform
       THIS verb on THIS resource (in THIS namespace)?" Without it, anyone who
       can reach the API server can do everything — read every Secret, delete
       every node, drain your whole cluster. With it, you express least
       privilege: each human, group and ServiceAccount gets exactly the verbs
       and resources it needs, and nothing more. The mental model is one short
       chain you will draw a hundred times:

            WHO (subject) ──► BINDING ──► WHAT (role / rules)

    OBJECTIVES
       • Name and place the FOUR RBAC objects (Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding,
         ClusterRoleBinding) on a scope matrix.
       • Distinguish Role vs ClusterRole and RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding.
       • Author rules from apiGroups + resources + verbs; know "" = core group.
       • Bind permissions to Users, Groups and ServiceAccounts.
       • Test and audit effective permissions with `kubectl auth can-i`.
       • Apply least privilege to a real workload (easypj).

    CKA RELEVANCE
       Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%) lists RBAC
       explicitly. Tasks are fast to do imperatively and easy to verify, so
       graders love them. Master the imperative generators and the can-i check
       and these become guaranteed points.

    SECTION MAP
       24.1  What is RBAC and Why It Matters         🎯
       24.2  The Four RBAC Objects                   🎯
       24.3  Creating Roles and ClusterRoles         🎯
       24.4  Creating RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings   🎯
       24.5  Testing RBAC                            🎯
       24.6  RBAC for easypj — Practical Example     🧪
       24.7  🏋️ Practice Exercises
       🔧 Under-the-Hood / DEEPER · 🔑 Takeaways · ⚠️ Gotchas · ⚡ Speed Tips
       🔑 Commands · 🧪 Lab Q&A

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.1  What is RBAC and Why It Matters                                   🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - Controls WHO can do WHAT on WHICH resources.
          - Authorization happens AFTER authentication — first the API server
            decides WHO you are (authN), then RBAC decides WHAT you may do
            (authZ). RBAC denies by default.
          - Enabled via --authorization-mode=RBAC on the API server (almost
            always present; usually as Node,RBAC).
          - Without RBAC: anyone with API access can do everything 💀

          📖 KEY TERM — deny by default: if no binding grants you a verb on a
             resource, the answer is "no". There are NO deny rules in RBAC; your
             effective access is simply the UNION of every binding that applies.

          [DIAGRAM: RBAC Gate — request → authentication → authorization →
           admission → action]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                THE REQUEST PIPELINE (where RBAC sits)           │
          │                                                                │
          │   kubectl / pod ─► [ AuthN ] ─► [ AuthZ ] ─► [ Admission ] ─►   │
          │                      WHO?         WHAT?        mutate/validate   │
          │                       │            │                │           │
          │                  cert / token   RBAC rules     webhooks /        │
          │                   / SA JWT      (this chap)     quotas      ──► etcd
          │                                                                │
          │   Fail AuthN  ─► 401 Unauthorized                              │
          │   Fail AuthZ  ─► 403 Forbidden  ◄── RBAC says "no"             │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          💡 INSIGHT: a 401 means "I don't know who you are"; a 403 means
             "I know who you are, but you may not do that." RBAC produces 403s.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.2  The Four RBAC Objects                                            🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          Two objects hold PERMISSIONS (rules); two objects GRANT them to
          subjects. Multiply by scope (namespace vs cluster) and you get four.

          [TABLE: RBAC objects explained]
          ┌────────────────────┬───────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ Object             │ Scope     │ Purpose                               │
          ├────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
          │ Role               │ Namespace │ Define permissions within a namespace │
          │ ClusterRole        │ Cluster   │ Define permissions cluster-wide       │
          │ RoleBinding        │ Namespace │ Bind Role/ClusterRole to subject (ns) │
          │ ClusterRoleBinding │ Cluster   │ Bind ClusterRole to subject (cluster) │
          └────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘

          [RBAC RELATIONSHIP MAP]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │          WHO          BINDING           WHAT           │
          │                                                        │
          │   ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────┐  │
          │   │  User     │    │ RoleBinding   │   │  Role      │  │
          │   │  Group    │───▶│ (namespace)   │──▶│ (namespace)│  │
          │   │  ServiceAc│    └──────────────┘   └────────────┘  │
          │   └──────────┘                                        │
          │                                                        │
          │   ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────┐  │
          │   │  User     │    │ ClusterRole   │   │ ClusterRole│  │
          │   │  Group    │───▶│ Binding       │──▶│ (cluster)  │  │
          │   │  ServiceAc│    └──────────────┘   └────────────┘  │
          │   └──────────┘                                        │
          │                                                        │
          │   You can also bind a ClusterRole to a namespace      │
          │   using a RoleBinding (limits scope!)                  │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [RBAC — WHO ─► (BINDING) ─► WHAT]   (the canonical chain)
           👤 WHO (subject)            🔗 BINDING                 📜 WHAT (rules)
           ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
           │ User / Group     │   │ RoleBinding (ns)     │   │ Role (ns)        │
           │ ServiceAccount   │──►│  -or-                │──►│  -or-            │
           │ system:sa:ns:name│   │ ClusterRoleBinding   │   │ ClusterRole      │
           └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘   │ apiGroups+        │
                                                              │ resources+verbs   │
                                                              └──────────────────┘

          [SCOPE MATRIX — the 2x2 you must memorize]
          ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ Role + RoleBinding    │ permissions in ONE namespace               │
          │ ClusterRole +         │ permissions across the WHOLE cluster       │
          │   ClusterRoleBinding  │ (and cluster-scoped resources)             │
          │ ClusterRole +         │ reuse a cluster-defined permission SET,    │
          │   RoleBinding         │ but APPLY it inside ONE namespace only     │
          │ Role +                │ ❌ INVALID — a RoleBinding's roleRef can   │
          │   ClusterRoleBinding  │ never point at a Role                      │
          └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

          🔑 Test it:  kubectl auth can-i create deploy \
                         --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:web
          💡 Deny by default; permissions are the UNION of all bindings
             (there are no deny rules).

          🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which pair do I use?
             • Need it in one namespace, permission unique to that namespace?
               → Role + RoleBinding.
             • Need cluster-scoped resource (nodes, PVs, namespaces) or the
               same perms everywhere? → ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.
             • Want a built-in permission set (view/edit/admin) but only inside
               one namespace? → ClusterRole + RoleBinding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.3  Creating Roles and ClusterRoles                                  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          A rule has three parts: apiGroups + resources + verbs.
          - Verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete (and
            deletecollection). The trio get/list/watch is "read".
          - apiGroups: "" (empty string) is the CORE group (pods, services,
            configmaps, secrets, nodes, namespaces). Named groups like apps
            (deployments), batch (jobs), rbac.authorization.k8s.io are spelled
            out explicitly.
          - resourceNames: optionally scope a rule to one named object (only
            for verbs that target a single object — get/update/patch/delete;
            you cannot resourceName-restrict list/watch/create).

          [CODE: Role — allow read pods in easypj namespace]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Role
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: pod-reader
          rules:
          - apiGroups: [""]                 # "" = the core API group
            resources: ["pods"]
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create role pod-reader -n easypj \
          #     --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods

          [CODE: Role — scope to ONE ConfigMap named easypj-config]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Role
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-role
          rules:
          - apiGroups: [""]                    # "" = the core API group
            resources: ["configmaps"]
            resourceNames: ["easypj-config"]   # scope to ONE object (optional)
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create role easypj-role -n easypj \
          #     --verb=get,list,watch --resource=configmaps \
          #     --resource-name=easypj-config

          [CODE: ClusterRole — allow read nodes cluster-wide]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: ClusterRole          # NOTE: no namespace — cluster-scoped
          metadata:
            name: node-viewer
          rules:
          - apiGroups: [""]
            resources: ["nodes"]     # nodes are cluster-scoped → must be a ClusterRole
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create clusterrole node-viewer \
          #     --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes

          ⚠️ A Role is ALWAYS namespaced; it cannot grant access to
             cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces). For those you
             MUST use a ClusterRole.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.4  Creating RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings                    🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          A binding has subjects (WHO) and a roleRef (WHICH role). roleRef is
          immutable once created — to change the role you delete and recreate.
          Subjects can be kind: User, kind: Group, or kind: ServiceAccount.

          [CODE: RoleBinding — bind role to user "dev-lead"]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: RoleBinding
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: dev-lead-pod-reader
          subjects:
          - kind: User
            name: dev-lead                       # name as authenticated
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          roleRef:
            kind: Role
            name: pod-reader
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create rolebinding dev-lead-pod-reader -n easypj \
          #     --role=pod-reader --user=dev-lead

          [CODE: RoleBinding — bind role to a ServiceAccount]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: RoleBinding
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-web-can-read-config
          subjects:
          - kind: ServiceAccount
            name: easypj-web-sa
            namespace: easypj
          roleRef:
            kind: Role
            name: easypj-role
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create rolebinding easypj-web-can-read-config -n easypj \
          #     --role=easypj-role --serviceaccount=easypj:easypj-web-sa

          [CODE: ClusterRoleBinding — bind cluster-admin to user]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: ClusterRoleBinding
          metadata:
            name: ops-admin-cluster-admin
          subjects:
          - kind: User
            name: ops-admin
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          roleRef:
            kind: ClusterRole
            name: cluster-admin            # built-in superuser role
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          # imperative:
          #   kubectl create clusterrolebinding ops-admin-cluster-admin \
          #     --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=ops-admin

          [CODE: ClusterRole + RoleBinding — reuse built-in `view` in one ns]
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: RoleBinding                 # namespaced binding...
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: web-view-easypj
          subjects:
          - kind: ServiceAccount
            name: easypj-web-sa
            namespace: easypj
          roleRef:
            kind: ClusterRole               # ...pointing at a ClusterRole
            name: view                      # cluster perms, scoped to easypj only
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

          ⚠️ Binding to the wrong subject kind/name (User vs ServiceAccount, or
             omitting the system:serviceaccount: prefix when impersonating)
             silently grants nothing — no error, just a quiet "no".

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.5  Testing RBAC                                                     🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          Use `kubectl auth can-i` with --as to impersonate any subject. This is
          how you both prove a grant works and debug a "Forbidden".

          $ kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=dev-lead -n easypj
          $ kubectl auth can-i delete nodes --as=dev-lead
          $ kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=system:admin
          $ kubectl auth can-i list pods \
              --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
          $ kubectl auth can-i --list \
              --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj

          [TIP: Use --as flag to impersonate users for testing; --as-group to
           impersonate group membership.]
          ⚡ SPEED TIP: `auth can-i --list --as=<subject> -n <ns>` dumps EVERY
             verb/resource a subject can do — the fastest way to see the gap
             when debugging an access problem.

          📖 SUBJECT NAMING — a ServiceAccount is referenced in --as as
             system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. A real human is just
             their authenticated username (e.g. dev-lead). Groups go through
             --as-group=<group>.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    24.6  RBAC for easypj — Practical Example                              🧪
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          [SCENARIO] Three teams need three different levels of access to the
          easypj job-board application:
          a) Developers : full access to the easypj namespace
                          (pods, services, deployments).
          b) QA Team    : read-only access to the easypj namespace.
          c) Monitoring : read access across ALL namespaces
                          (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding).

          [CODE: Complete RBAC setup for all three roles]
          # ---- (a) Developers: full access inside easypj -------------------
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Role
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-developer
          rules:
          - apiGroups: [""]                      # core: pods, services, etc.
            resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps", "secrets"]
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
          - apiGroups: ["apps"]                  # deployments live in apps
            resources: ["deployments", "replicasets"]
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
          ---
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: RoleBinding
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-developers-bind
          subjects:
          - kind: Group
            name: easypj-devs                    # everyone in this group
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          roleRef:
            kind: Role
            name: easypj-developer
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          ---
          # ---- (b) QA Team: read-only inside easypj ------------------------
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Role
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-qa-readonly
          rules:
          - apiGroups: ["", "apps"]
            resources: ["pods", "services", "deployments", "replicasets"]
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]      # read only
          ---
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: RoleBinding
          metadata:
            namespace: easypj
            name: easypj-qa-bind
          subjects:
          - kind: Group
            name: easypj-qa
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          roleRef:
            kind: Role
            name: easypj-qa-readonly
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          ---
          # ---- (c) Monitoring: read across ALL namespaces ------------------
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: ClusterRole
          metadata:
            name: easypj-monitor
          rules:
          - apiGroups: ["", "apps"]
            resources: ["pods", "services", "deployments", "nodes", "endpoints"]
            verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
          ---
          apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
          kind: ClusterRoleBinding
          metadata:
            name: easypj-monitor-bind
          subjects:
          - kind: ServiceAccount
            name: monitoring-sa
            namespace: monitoring
          roleRef:
            kind: ClusterRole
            name: easypj-monitor
            apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

          # ---- Verify each grant -------------------------------------------
          $ kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as-group=easypj-devs -n easypj   # yes
          $ kubectl auth can-i delete pods       --as-group=easypj-qa   -n easypj    # no
          $ kubectl auth can-i list pods \
              --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:monitoring-sa -n kube-system     # yes

          💡 INSIGHT: binding to a Group (easypj-devs, easypj-qa) means you add
             or remove people just by changing their identity-provider group
             membership — no new RBAC objects per person. Least-privilege at
             scale.
