--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       🔧 HOW THE AUTHORIZER EVALUATES RULES
          When a request arrives, the RBAC authorizer gathers EVERY Role and
          ClusterRole bound to your subject (directly, or via any Group you
          belong to, or via system:authenticated/system:unauthenticated), then
          asks: does ANY rule match this verb + apiGroup + resource (+ name)?
          If yes → ALLOW. If no rule matches → DENY. Crucially there are NO deny
          rules; access is the pure UNION of all bindings. You cannot subtract a
          permission once another binding grants it.

       🔧 THE AUTHORIZATION CHAIN & ORDER
          --authorization-mode is usually Node,RBAC. Modules are tried in order;
          the FIRST module to return an explicit allow or deny decides. The Node
          authorizer specially restricts what kubelets (system:nodes) may read,
          then RBAC handles everyone else. A Webhook authorizer can be appended
          to delegate to an external service.

       🔧 THE system:* DEFAULT ROLES & system:masters
          Kubernetes ships built-in ClusterRoles: cluster-admin (everything),
          admin / edit / view (the three "user-facing" tiers, namespace-friendly
          via RoleBinding), plus many system:* roles used by control-plane
          components. The GROUP system:masters is hard-wired in the authorizer to
          bypass RBAC entirely (the cert your kubeconfig uses as admin is in it).

       🔬 AGGREGATED CLUSTERROLES
          A ClusterRole may carry an aggregationRule with label selectors:
            aggregationRule:
              clusterRoleSelectors:
              - matchLabels:
                  rbac.example.com/aggregate-to-monitoring: "true"
          Kubernetes automatically MERGES the rules of any ClusterRole bearing a
          matching label into it. This is exactly how the built-in edit and view
          roles get extended by CRD operators — they add a small labeled
          ClusterRole and their resource permissions appear in view/edit without
          editing those roles.

       🔬 SUBRESOURCES, NON-RESOURCE URLs, AND VERBS YOU MUST WATCH
          • Subresources are named as resource/subresource: pods/exec, pods/log,
            pods/portforward, deployments/scale, */status. To allow `kubectl
            exec` you need verb create on pods/exec — NOT just pods.
          • nonResourceURLs (e.g. ["/healthz", "/metrics"]) can only live in a
            ClusterRole and use verbs like ["get"].
          • DANGEROUS verbs that enable privilege escalation: escalate (create a
            Role with MORE perms than you hold), bind (create a binding to a role
            you don't fully hold), and impersonate (act as another subject). The
            API server normally blocks granting perms you don't already have
            unless you hold escalate/bind.

       🔬 AUDITING & IMPERSONATION FOR TESTING
          `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user> [--as-group=<grp>] -n <ns>`
          prints the effective permission set for that subject without you ever
          logging in as them — the safest way to validate a binding before
          handing it out.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       • RBAC is authorization (WHAT you may do) — it runs AFTER authentication
         (WHO you are) and denies by default. There are NO deny rules; access is
         the UNION of every binding that applies to you.
       • Four objects: Role and ClusterRole hold permissions (apiGroups +
         resources + verbs); RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding grant them to
         subjects (User / Group / ServiceAccount).
       • Scope matrix: Role+RoleBinding = one namespace; ClusterRole+
         ClusterRoleBinding = whole cluster; ClusterRole+RoleBinding = reuse a
         cluster-defined permission set within a single namespace.
       • Cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces) and non-resource URLs
         can ONLY be granted via a ClusterRole.
       • The core API group is "" (empty string); named groups (apps, batch,
         rbac.authorization.k8s.io) are spelled out explicitly.
       • roleRef is immutable — to repoint a binding at another role, delete and
         recreate the binding.
       • Always verify a grant with `kubectl auth can-i ... --as=...`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       • A Role is always namespaced — it cannot grant access to cluster-scoped
         resources (nodes, PVs). Use a ClusterRole for those.
       • The core API group is "" (empty string), not "core" or "v1".
       • Wildcards (`*` verbs/resources) quietly grant far more than intended —
         prefer explicit least privilege.
       • Binding to the wrong subject kind/name (User vs ServiceAccount, or
         missing the system:serviceaccount: prefix) silently grants nothing.
       • resourceNames only works for object-targeting verbs (get/update/patch/
         delete) — you cannot name-restrict list, watch or create.
       • A RoleBinding's roleRef may point at a Role OR a ClusterRole; a
         ClusterRoleBinding's roleRef may ONLY point at a ClusterRole.
       • Allowing `kubectl exec`/`logs` needs the subresource (pods/exec,
         pods/log) — granting just "pods" is not enough.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       • Generate fast: `kubectl create role ... --dry-run=client -o yaml` then
         edit; same for rolebinding with --serviceaccount=ns:name.
       • Always verify with `kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE --as=<subject>
         -n ns` — and `--list` to dump everything a subject can do.
       • For a quick SA grant use the imperative `create rolebinding
         --role=... --serviceaccount=ns:sa`.
       • `kubectl create clusterrole ... --resource=... --verb=...` builds the
         YAML for you; add --aggregation-rule or --non-resource-url as needed.
       • To find existing grants in the exam: `kubectl get
         rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o wide | grep <subject>`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       kubectl create role easypj-role -n easypj --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
       kubectl create role easypj-role -n easypj --verb=get,list,watch \
         --resource=configmaps --resource-name=easypj-config
       kubectl create clusterrole node-viewer --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes
       kubectl create rolebinding rb -n easypj --role=easypj-role \
         --serviceaccount=easypj:easypj-web-sa
       kubectl create rolebinding rb -n easypj --role=pod-reader --user=jane
       kubectl create clusterrolebinding crb --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=ops-admin
       kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
       kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=jane -n exam-practice
       kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
       kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o wide | grep easypj
       kubectl describe clusterrole view

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 DRILL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       Create a ServiceAccount that can ONLY get/list/watch pods in the easypj
       namespace (Role + RoleBinding), then prove it with `auth can-i` for pods
       (allowed) and secrets (denied).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 24 (full answer + explanation each)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       Q1. Create a Role allowing read of pods in easypj and bind it to a SA.
           A. Role rules apiGroups:[""] resources:[pods] verbs:[get,list,watch];
              RoleBinding with roleRef→that Role and subject ServiceAccount
              easypj:sa. Imperatively:
                kubectl create role pod-reader -n easypj \
                  --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
                kubectl create rolebinding rb -n easypj \
                  --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=easypj:sa

       Q2. You need to grant read of NODES. Role or ClusterRole? Why?
           A. ClusterRole — nodes are cluster-scoped, so a namespaced Role can't
              express them. Grant cluster-wide with a ClusterRoleBinding.

       Q3. Bind the built-in `view` ClusterRole to SA easypj:web in one namespace.
           A. A RoleBinding (namespaced) whose roleRef is the ClusterRole `view`
              and subject is the ServiceAccount — cluster perms scoped to that ns.
                kubectl create rolebinding web-view -n easypj \
                  --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=easypj:web

       Q4. How do you test what a ServiceAccount can do?
           A. `kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:name
              -n ns`, and `auth can-i --list --as=...` for the full set.

       Q5. Restrict a Role to a single ConfigMap named easypj-config.
           A. Add resourceNames: ["easypj-config"] to the rule (note: list/watch
              can't be name-restricted, only get/update/delete/patch).

       Q6. What's the empty-string apiGroup for?
           A. "" is the CORE group (pods, services, configmaps, secrets, nodes).
              Named groups like apps, rbac.authorization.k8s.io are listed
              explicitly.

       Q7. A pod gets "Forbidden" calling the API. How do you fix it methodically?
           A. Identify its SA, run `auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa`
              to see the gap, then add a Role/ClusterRole + Binding granting
              exactly the missing verb/resource. Re-test with can-i.

       Q8. What is an aggregated ClusterRole?
           A. A ClusterRole with aggregationRule label selectors; K8s auto-merges
              rules from other ClusterRoles carrying matching labels (e.g. how
              `edit` and `view` get extended by operators).

       Q9. Grant a permission to everyone in group "easypj-devs".
           A. A binding with subject kind: Group, name: easypj-devs — RBAC matches
              the group claim from the user's authentication; add/remove people by
              changing IdP group membership, no new RBAC objects per person.

       Q10. How do you safely test a binding before handing it out?
            A. Impersonate: `kubectl auth can-i ... --as=<user> --as-group=<group>`
               to confirm the effective permissions without logging in as them.

       Q11. Distinguish a 401 from a 403 in API responses, and which one RBAC
            produces.
            A. 401 Unauthorized = authentication failed (I don't know who you
               are). 403 Forbidden = authenticated but not allowed — this is what
               RBAC emits when no binding grants the requested verb/resource.

       Q12. You want a subject to run `kubectl exec` into pods in easypj. What
            rule do you need?
            A. verb create on the subresource pods/exec (and typically get on
               pods). Granting only "pods" without the pods/exec subresource is
               insufficient.

       Q13. Can you DENY a permission that another binding already grants?
            A. No. RBAC has no deny rules; effective access is the union of all
               applicable bindings. To remove access you must remove/avoid the
               binding that grants it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 24
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
       subject ──► binding ──► role ──► allowed verbs on resources

       .vs-prose: The whole of RBAC reduces to one left-to-right chain. A SUBJECT
       (a User, a Group, or a ServiceAccount named system:serviceaccount:ns:name)
       is connected by a BINDING (a namespaced RoleBinding or a cluster-wide
       ClusterRoleBinding) to a ROLE (a namespaced Role or a cluster-wide
       ClusterRole) that lists rules of apiGroups + resources + verbs. Whether
       the grant is namespaced or cluster-wide depends on the pair you choose:
       Role+RoleBinding stays in one namespace, ClusterRole+ClusterRoleBinding
       spans the cluster, and ClusterRole+RoleBinding reuses cluster-defined
       permissions inside a single namespace. Cluster-scoped resources like nodes
       and PVs require a ClusterRole. Everything denies by default, there are no
       deny rules, and effective access is the union of every applicable binding.
       You confirm any of it with `kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE --as=<subject>
       -n <ns>` and audit the full set with `--list`.

================================================================================
  Chapter 25: Service Accounts & API Access                            🟡 🎯
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture / Workloads &
        Scheduling · Stack: easypj (project) / jobpost (app), Django 5.2.5.

  💡 WHY THIS MATTERS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Humans talk to the cluster with kubectl; pods talk to the cluster with a
  ServiceAccount (SA). The moment a workload needs to read the API — a
  controller, an operator, a sidecar, or an easypj batch job that lists its own
  pods — it must present an identity the API server can authenticate and then
  authorize via RBAC. That identity is a ServiceAccount. Get SAs wrong and you
  either break the workload (403 Forbidden) or hand every pod in a namespace a
  credential it never needed. This chapter is the bridge between "who is calling
  the API" (authentication) and "are they allowed" (RBAC, Chapter 24).

  🎯 OBJECTIVES
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Distinguish User accounts from ServiceAccounts (and when each is used).
    • Understand the per-namespace `default` ServiceAccount and its risks.
    • Create ServiceAccounts and attach them to pods/Deployments.
    • Understand token projection and the TokenRequest API (bound tokens).
    • Bind RBAC Roles/ClusterRoles to a ServiceAccount subject.
    • Disable token auto-mount for pods that never call the API.

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ServiceAccounts sit squarely in the "Cluster Architecture, Installation &
  Configuration" domain and pair with the RBAC tasks. Expect to create a SA,
  attach it to a workload, bind a Role to it, disable auto-mount, and verify
  access with `kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:...`. Fast, scriptable
  imperative commands win here.

  🧭 SECTION MAP
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    25.1  User Accounts vs Service Accounts
    25.2  Default Service Account
    25.3  Creating and Using Service Accounts
    25.4  Token Projection and Token Request API
    25.5  Binding RBAC to Service Accounts


  25.1  User Accounts vs Service Accounts                                    🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Kubernetes recognizes two kinds of identity. A USER ACCOUNT represents a
  human (or an external automation acting like a human) and is NOT a Kubernetes
  object — there is no `kubectl create user`. Users are authenticated by an
  external mechanism: client certificates, OIDC tokens, or an authenticating
  proxy. A SERVICE ACCOUNT represents an in-cluster workload (a pod) and IS a
  first-class, namespaced Kubernetes object that the API server manages.

      [TABLE: User Accounts vs Service Accounts]
      | Aspect            | User Account          | Service Account       |
      | Used by           | Humans (kubectl)      | Pods/Applications     |
      | Created by        | External system       | Kubernetes API        |
      | Scope             | Cluster-wide          | Namespaced            |
      | Credentials       | Certificates/tokens   | Mounted tokens        |
      | Managed           | Outside K8s           | Inside K8s            |
      | Is a K8s object?  | No                    | Yes (kind: SA)        |
      | Auth mechanism    | x509 cert / OIDC      | Projected JWT token   |
      | Group membership  | system:masters, etc.  | system:serviceaccounts|

  🧠 ANALOGY: a User is a contractor with their own ID badge issued by the
  building's external security firm — the building (cluster) trusts the badge
  but never printed it. A ServiceAccount is an internal employee badge the
  building's own HR (the API server) prints, files, and can revoke.

  📖 KEY TERM — subject: in RBAC, the "who" a binding grants rights to. A User
  subject is just a string; a ServiceAccount subject is the canonical name
  system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.


  25.2  Default Service Account                                              🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - Every namespace gets a "default" service account automatically.
    - Every pod that does not name a SA automatically uses its namespace's
      default SA.
    - The default SA has limited (essentially no) permissions out of the box.
    - Its token is auto-mounted into every pod at
      /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/.
    - ⚠️ Best practice: create a specific, least-privileged SA for each
      application instead of relying on (and over-granting) the default SA.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: because the default SA is mounted into EVERY pod in the namespace,
  any RBAC you grant to it spreads to all those pods at once. Treat the default
  SA as unprivileged and never bind broad rights to it.

  🧪 The mounted directory inside any pod contains three files:

      /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
        ├── token        # the projected JWT bearer token
        ├── ca.crt        # CA bundle to verify the API server's TLS cert
        └── namespace     # the pod's namespace, e.g. "easypj"


  25.3  Creating and Using Service Accounts                                  🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Create a SA imperatively, then attach it to a workload by name:

      $ kubectl create serviceaccount easypj-web-sa -n easypj

  ServiceAccount YAML, with auto-mount disabled (the SA-level default that every
  pod using it inherits):

      apiVersion: v1
      kind: ServiceAccount
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web-sa
        namespace: easypj
      automountServiceAccountToken: false   # only true if the pod calls the API

  Pod / Deployment using the specific ServiceAccount — the pod now runs with the
  identity system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa:

      ---
      apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: Deployment
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        replicas: 2
        selector:
          matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
        template:
          metadata:
            labels: { app: easypj-web }
          spec:
            serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa   # pod runs as this identity
            containers:
            - name: web
              image: easypj:v1
              ports:
              - containerPort: 8000

  Override auto-mount at the POD level (wins over the SA-level setting):

      spec:
        serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa
        automountServiceAccountToken: false   # disable token mount for this pod

  💡 INSIGHT: automountServiceAccountToken can be set on EITHER the SA or the pod
  spec. The pod-spec value takes precedence. Setting it false on the SA makes
  "no token" the default for every pod that uses that SA.

  ⚡ TIP: Disable auto-mount when a pod doesn't need API access (most app pods —
  including a plain Django web pod — never call the Kubernetes API). It removes a
  standing credential from the container and shrinks the blast radius if the pod
  is compromised.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — does this pod need a token?
      Does the workload call the Kubernetes API (controller, operator, a job
      that lists/patches resources, a sidecar that reads Secrets via the API)?
         ├─ YES → create a dedicated SA, mount the token, bind least-privilege
         │        RBAC (25.5).
         └─ NO  → automountServiceAccountToken: false. The easypj web/worker
                  pods talk to Postgres and Redis, not the API — no token.


  25.4  Token Projection and Token Request API                            🎯🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - Bound tokens: time-limited, audience-bound, pod-bound (K8s 1.22+ default
      via the BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume feature).
    - TokenRequest API: programmatic, on-demand token generation with a
      requested audience and expiry, instead of a static, never-expiring Secret.
    - The kubelet injects the token through a PROJECTED volume and rotates it
      automatically before expiry.

  Projected volume with a service-account token (this is what the auto-mount
  actually generates under the hood):

      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: easypj-api-reader
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa
        containers:
        - name: app
          image: easypj:v1
          volumeMounts:
          - name: api-token
            mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
            readOnly: true
        volumes:
        - name: api-token
          projected:
            sources:
            - serviceAccountToken:
                path: token
                audience: api                 # token only valid for this audience
                expirationSeconds: 3600        # 1h; kubelet rotates before expiry

  Generate a short-lived token by hand (uses the TokenRequest API):

      $ kubectl create token easypj-web-sa -n easypj
      $ kubectl create token easypj-web-sa -n easypj --duration=600s --audience=api

  Legacy vs bound tokens at a glance:

      ┌─────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
      │                     │ LEGACY secret token   │ BOUND projected token │
      ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
      │ Lifetime            │ never expires         │ expiry (e.g. 1h)      │
      │ Audience            │ none (any)            │ scoped (e.g. "api")   │
      │ Bound to pod        │ no                    │ yes (pod lifetime)    │
      │ Storage             │ a Secret object       │ in-memory, projected  │
      │ Rotation            │ manual                │ automatic (kubelet)   │
      │ Default since 1.22+ │ no                    │ yes                   │
      └─────────────────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: the kubelet requests a token from the API server's
  TokenRequest endpoint on the pod's behalf, writes it into the projected
  volume's tmpfs, and refreshes it once it passes ~80% of its TTL (or 24h,
  whichever is sooner). The API server signs the JWT with its service-account
  signing key; it validates incoming tokens with the matching public key, then
  checks the token's audience and expiry before handing the request to RBAC.


  25.5  Binding RBAC to Service Accounts                                     🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A ServiceAccount has NO permissions until you bind a Role (namespaced) or
  ClusterRole (cluster-wide) to it. The binding's subject must use the canonical
  ServiceAccount form.

    - Subject format: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>
    - In a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding, set subject kind: ServiceAccount,
      name: <sa-name>, namespace: <ns> (and the controller produces that subject
      string for you).

  EXAMPLE: the easypj Django pod needs to read ConfigMaps. Role + RoleBinding for
  the easypj-web-sa service account:

      apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
      kind: Role
      metadata:
        name: configmap-reader
        namespace: easypj
      rules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        resources: ["configmaps"]
        verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
      ---
      apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
      kind: RoleBinding
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web-sa-configmaps
        namespace: easypj
      subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: easypj-web-sa
        namespace: easypj
      roleRef:
        kind: Role
        name: configmap-reader
        apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  Imperative equivalent (fast in the exam):

      $ kubectl create role configmap-reader --verb=get,list,watch \
          --resource=configmaps -n easypj
      $ kubectl create rolebinding easypj-web-sa-configmaps \
          --role=configmap-reader \
          --serviceaccount=easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj

  Verify exactly as the pod would be evaluated:

      $ kubectl auth can-i list configmaps \
          --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj   # yes
      $ kubectl auth can-i list secrets \
          --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj    # no

  📖 KEY TERM — system:serviceaccounts group: every SA is a member of the
  cluster-wide group system:serviceaccounts and the per-namespace group
  system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>. You can bind a Role to a whole namespace's
  SAs by targeting that group — powerful, and easy to over-grant.


  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 25
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  [SERVICEACCOUNT — a pod's identity to the API]

   👤 User = a HUMAN (external; cert/OIDC) — NOT a K8s object
   🤖 ServiceAccount [N] = a POD's identity (in-cluster)

   📦 easypj-web pod  (serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa)
        │ auto-mounted PROJECTED token at
        │ /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
        ▼
   📡 apiserver ── validates token ──► RBAC checks
        subject = system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa

   ⚠️ set automountServiceAccountToken:false unless the pod calls the API.


  [END-TO-END REQUEST FLOW — pod to API decision]

   ┌──────────────┐   token   ┌──────────────┐  authN  ┌──────────────┐
   │ easypj-web   │──────────▶│  API server  │────────▶│ token valid? │
   │ pod (SA)     │  (Bearer) │ (apiserver)  │         │ aud + expiry │
   └──────────────┘           └──────┬───────┘         └──────┬───────┘
                                     │  identity =            │ ok
                                     ▼  system:service        ▼
                              account:easypj:easypj-web-sa  ┌──────────────┐
                                     │                      │ RBAC: verb + │
                                     └─────────────────────▶│ resource?    │
                                                            └──────┬───────┘
                                                  ┌────────────────┴────────┐
                                                  ▼                         ▼
                                            ✅ 200 Allowed            ⛔ 403 Forbidden


  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • How the projected token is mounted & rotated: the kubelet calls TokenRequest,
    writes the JWT into the pod's projected tmpfs volume, and refreshes it at
    ~80% of TTL (or every 24h). The container just re-reads the file path.
  • How the API server validates it: it verifies the JWT signature with its
    service-account public key, then enforces the token's audience and
    expiration before authorization runs.
  • BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume: the feature (GA since 1.22) that makes the
    auto-mounted token a bound, audience-scoped, expiring projected token rather
    than a long-lived Secret.
  • Audience-scoped tokens & TokenRequest expiry: a token minted for audience
    "api" is rejected by any other audience — this stops a token leaked to one
    service from being replayed against another.
  • imagePullSecrets on a SA: attach registry credentials to the SA and every
    pod using that SA inherits them automatically — no per-pod imagePullSecrets.
        $ kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred ... -n easypj
        $ kubectl patch serviceaccount easypj-web-sa -n easypj \
            -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
  • The system:serviceaccounts groups: bind to system:serviceaccounts:<ns> to
    grant a Role to every SA in a namespace at once (use sparingly).
  • OIDC discovery for cloud trust (IRSA-style): the cluster publishes its
    service-account signing keys via an OIDC issuer URL so external clouds (e.g.
    AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts) can trust pod tokens and exchange them
    for cloud credentials — no static cloud keys in the pod.


  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Users are HUMANS (external; cert/OIDC, NOT K8s objects). ServiceAccounts
      are POD identities (real namespaced objects). Pods authenticate to the API
      as their SA.
    • Every namespace has a `default` SA, auto-mounted into every pod at
      /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/. Disable the mount unless
      the pod actually calls the API.
    • A ServiceAccount has NO rights until you bind a Role/ClusterRole to it.
    • Modern tokens are short-lived PROJECTED tokens (via TokenRequest), bound to
      the pod with an expiry and audience — not the old long-lived secret token.
    • Bind RBAC to a SA using the subject name
      system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.
    • Best practice: one least-privileged SA per application; keep the default SA
      unprivileged.


  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • The default SA is mounted everywhere; if you over-grant it, every pod in
      the namespace inherits those rights. Keep it minimal.
    • Leaving automountServiceAccountToken on for pods that never call the API
      needlessly exposes a credential.
    • Binding a SA with the wrong prefix (forgetting system:serviceaccount: or
      the namespace) grants nothing — the subject string won't match.
    • Deleting/recreating a SA referenced by running pods can break their API
      access on the next token refresh.
    • A pod-spec automountServiceAccountToken overrides the SA-level value —
      check both when a token unexpectedly appears or is missing.
    • A token minted for one audience is rejected by another; mismatched
      audience looks like an auth failure, not a 403.


  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Create + attach in two commands: `kubectl create sa easypj-web-sa -n
      easypj` then `kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/easypj-web easypj-web-sa`.
    • Test exactly as the pod would: `kubectl auth can-i ... --as=system:
      serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa`.
    • Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the SA to default-deny the mount
      for all pods using it.
    • Bind a Role to a SA imperatively with
      `--serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>` on `kubectl create rolebinding`.
    • Mint an ad-hoc token to curl the API yourself with
      `kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>`.


  🔑 COMMANDS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    kubectl create serviceaccount easypj-web-sa -n easypj
    kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/easypj-web easypj-web-sa -n easypj
    kubectl get sa easypj-web-sa -n easypj -o yaml
    kubectl create token easypj-web-sa -n easypj            # short-lived token
    kubectl create token easypj-web-sa -n easypj --duration=600s --audience=api
    kubectl create role configmap-reader --verb=get,list,watch \
        --resource=configmaps -n easypj
    kubectl create rolebinding easypj-web-sa-configmaps \
        --role=configmap-reader --serviceaccount=easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
    kubectl auth can-i list pods \
        --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
    kubectl auth can-i delete deployments \
        --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj
    kubectl patch serviceaccount easypj-web-sa -n easypj \
        -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'


  🧪 DRILL
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Create a SA, bind it a Role that can list pods, run a pod as that SA, exec in
  and curl the API with the mounted token (succeeds for pods, Forbidden for
  secrets), and confirm with `kubectl auth can-i --as`. Example in-pod check:

      $ TOKEN=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)
      $ CA=/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt
      $ curl --cacert $CA -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
          https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods   # 200
      $ curl --cacert $CA -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
          https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/easypj/secrets # 403


  🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Q1. Create a ServiceAccount and run a Deployment as it.
       A. `kubectl create sa easypj-web-sa -n easypj`; then set
          spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa on the Deployment
          (or `kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/easypj-web easypj-web-sa`). The
          pods now authenticate to the API as that SA's identity.

   Q2. A pod doesn't need API access. How do you reduce its risk?
       A. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false (on the SA or the pod spec) so
          no token is mounted. No standing credential = smaller blast radius if
          the container is compromised.

   Q3. Grant a SA permission to read configmaps. What's the subject string?
       A. Bind a Role with get/list/watch on configmaps; in the RoleBinding the
          subject is kind: ServiceAccount, name: easypj-web-sa, namespace:
          easypj — which RBAC evaluates as
          system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa.

   Q4. Why is the default SA a risk?
       A. It's mounted into every pod in the namespace, so any privilege you give
          it spreads to all those pods. Keep it unprivileged and use dedicated
          SAs per app.

   Q5. What's a projected/bound token and why is it better?
       A. A short-lived token issued via TokenRequest, scoped to an audience and
          expiry and tied to the pod's lifetime, auto-rotated by the kubelet —
          far safer than a static, never-expiring Secret token.

   Q6. Difference between a User and a ServiceAccount?
       A. Users are external humans NOT stored in K8s (authenticated by cert/
          OIDC); ServiceAccounts are in-cluster, namespaced API objects used by
          pods.

   Q7. What does a token's audience do?
       A. It restricts where the token is valid (e.g. the API server, or a named
          external service), preventing a leaked token from being replayed across
          audiences.

   Q8. Test whether a SA can delete deployments.
       A. `kubectl auth can-i delete deployments
          --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj`. It prints
          yes/no without changing anything.

   Q9. A pod gets 403 from the API. SA-side fix?
       A. Its SA lacks RBAC — create a Role/ClusterRole with the needed verb/
          resource and bind it to system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. Confirm with
          `auth can-i --as`.

   Q10. Pull from a private registry as a SA. How?
        A. Create a docker-registry Secret, then attach it via imagePullSecrets
           on the ServiceAccount (`kubectl patch sa ...`). Pods using that SA
           inherit the registry credentials automatically — no per-pod config.


  🟢 VISUAL SUMMARY (.vs-prose)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  The path of a pod's API call is: pod (running as its ServiceAccount) presents
  its auto-mounted, audience-scoped, expiring projected token as a Bearer
  credential → the API server authenticates it (signature, audience, expiry) and
  resolves the identity to system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> → RBAC checks whether
  any Role/ClusterRole bound to that subject permits the requested verb on the
  requested resource → the request is Allowed (200) or Forbidden (403). Users are
  external humans the cluster trusts but never created; ServiceAccounts are
  in-cluster objects the cluster mints and can revoke. Default deny is the rule:
  a SA starts with zero rights, the default SA should stay unprivileged, and any
  pod that doesn't call the API should have its token mount turned off.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Chapter 26: TLS Certificates & PKI                                   🔴 🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — frequently tested]    🔴 [HARD]

    [A] META: 🔴 difficulty · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation
        & Configuration (25%). Cross-cuts Security/Authentication.

    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
        The entire Kubernetes control plane talks to itself over MUTUAL TLS —
        every component proves who it is with a certificate signed by the cluster
        CA. When those certs expire, the cluster simply STOPS: you can't kubectl
        your way out of an expired apiserver cert. The exam regularly tests the
        CSR approval flow (generate key → submit CertificateSigningRequest →
        `kubectl certificate approve` → embed in kubeconfig) and cert renewal.
        VISUAL: think of it as the cluster's PKI web — one CA at the center,
        spokes of client/server certs reaching every component and every admin.

    [C] OBJECTIVES
        • Map the Kubernetes PKI: which CA signs what, and where the keys live.
        • Know every certificate location under /etc/kubernetes/pki/ and its
          purpose.
        • Create, submit, and approve CertificateSigningRequests for new users.
        • Check certificate expiry with kubeadm and openssl.
        • Renew certificates AND make the cluster actually use them.

    [D] CKA RELEVANCE
        Certificates appear in two forms on the exam: (1) "a new developer needs
        access — create a client cert + kubeconfig" (the CSR workflow), and
        (2) "the cluster is broken / certs are about to expire — check and renew."
        Both are pure muscle-memory tasks; speed and exact flags win points.

    [E] SECTION MAP
        26.1  Kubernetes PKI Overview
        26.2  Certificate Locations and Purpose
        26.3  Certificate Signing Requests (CSR)
        26.4  Checking Certificate Expiry
        26.5  Renewing Certificates

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    26.1  Kubernetes PKI Overview
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - All cluster communication uses TLS.
          - A Certificate Authority (CA) signs all certificates.
          - Each component has its own certificate (and most have both a SERVER
            cert to identify themselves and a CLIENT cert to call others).

          📖 KEY TERM — PKI (Public Key Infrastructure): the system of a CA plus
          the certs it signs that lets parties authenticate each other and
          encrypt traffic without sharing secrets in advance.

          [K8S CERTIFICATE ARCHITECTURE]
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                   ROOT CA                               │
          │                   /ca.crt                               │
          │                   /ca.key                               │
          │                      │                                  │
          │          ┌───────────┼───────────┐                     │
          │          ▼           ▼           ▼                     │
          │   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐             │
          │   │API Server│ │  etcd    │ │  kubelet │             │
          │   │ .crt     │ │  .crt   │ │  .crt    │             │
          │   │ .key     │ │  .key   │ │  .key    │             │
          │   └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘             │
          │        ▲                          ▲                   │
          │        │                          │                   │
          │   ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────┐              │
          │   │scheduler │             │kube-proxy│              │
          │   │.crt .key │             │.crt .key │              │
          │   └──────────┘             └──────────┘              │
          │                                                       │
          │   Default location: /etc/kubernetes/pki/              │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          🧠 ANALOGY: the cluster CA is the passport office. Every component
          carries a passport (its leaf cert) stamped by that one office. When
          two components meet, each checks the other's passport against the
          office's seal (the CA cert) — no central login server needed. An admin
          is just another passport holder whose CN field is their username.

          [THE CLUSTER PKI — everything speaks mutual TLS]
              🏛️ cluster CA  (/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt, ~10y)
        ┌──────────┬─────────┴────────┬──────────────────┐
   📡 apiserver  🤖 kubelet      🗄️ etcd (own CA)    👩‍💻 admin
   (server+client)(client)       (peer+server)      CN=user, O=group
                                                     (client cert -> RBAC ids)
   🔑 new user: openssl CSR ─► kubectl certificate approve ─► embed in kubeconfig
   ⏰ check: kubeadm certs check-expiration   ·   renew: kubeadm certs renew all
   ⚠️ leaf certs ~1y -> RESTART the control plane / kubelet AFTER renewing.

          💡 INSIGHT: there is NO separate "user object" in Kubernetes for
          certificate auth. Identity lives entirely IN the certificate — the CN
          is the username, the O entries are the groups. RBAC then authorizes
          that user/group. This is why issuing a cert == creating a user.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    26.2  Certificate Locations and Purpose
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          Every request into the cluster passes the full security pipeline below
          before anything is written to etcd. TLS (authentication via x509 client
          cert) is the very first gate.

          [FULL API REQUEST PIPELINE — SECURITY AT EVERY LAYER]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                                                          │
          │  kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=pw │
          │       │                                                  │
          │       ▼                                                  │
          │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐   │
          │  │  🔐      │   │  ✅      │   │  🔍              │   │
          │  │  AUTH-N   │──▶│  AUTH-Z  │──▶│  ADMISSION       │   │
          │  │          │   │          │   │                   │   │
          │  │ x509     │   │ RBAC     │   │ Mutating:        │   │
          │  │ token    │   │ ABAC     │   │  - add defaults  │   │
          │  │ OIDC     │   │ webhook  │   │  - inject sidecar│   │
          │  │          │   │          │   │                   │   │
          │  │ WHO?     │   │ CAN?     │   │ Validating:      │   │
          │  │          │   │          │   │  - enforce policy │   │
          │  │          │   │          │   │  - check limits   │   │
          │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └───────┬───────────┘   │
          │                                        │               │
          │                          ┌─────────────▼─────────┐     │
          │                          │  💾 PERSIST TO ETCD   │     │
          │                          │  (encrypted at rest)  │     │
          │                          │                       │     │
          │                          │  /registry/secrets/   │     │
          │                          │    default/db-pass    │     │
          │                          └───────────────────────┘     │
          │                                                          │
          │  ❌ Rejection at ANY stage → request denied              │
          │  ✅ All stages pass → object persisted in etcd           │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [CERTIFICATE INVENTORY — /etc/kubernetes/pki/]
          | Certificate           | Used by       | Purpose                    |
          |-----------------------|---------------|----------------------------|
          | ca.crt / ca.key       | Cluster CA    | Sign all other certs       |
          | apiserver.crt / .key  | API Server    | Serve HTTPS API            |
          | apiserver-kubelet.crt | API Server    | Talk to kubelets           |
          | etcd/server.crt       | etcd          | etcd peer communication    |
          | kubelet.crt           | Kubelet       | Authenticate to API server |
          | front-proxy-ca.crt    | Aggregation   | API aggregation layer      |

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — the actual directory layout kubeadm creates:
          /etc/kubernetes/pki/
          ├── ca.crt              ca.key            (cluster CA, ~10y)
          ├── apiserver.crt       apiserver.key     (apiserver SERVING cert)
          ├── apiserver-kubelet-client.crt/.key     (apiserver → kubelet CLIENT)
          ├── apiserver-etcd-client.crt/.key        (apiserver → etcd CLIENT)
          ├── front-proxy-ca.crt  front-proxy-ca.key
          ├── front-proxy-client.crt/.key           (aggregation layer)
          ├── sa.key  sa.pub                        (ServiceAccount token signer)
          └── etcd/
              ├── ca.crt          ca.key            (etcd's OWN CA — separate!)
              ├── server.crt      server.key        (etcd serving)
              ├── peer.crt        peer.key          (etcd peer-to-peer)
              └── healthcheck-client.crt/.key

          ⚠️ etcd uses a DIFFERENT CA from the rest of the cluster. An etcd cert
          expiring breaks the datastore independently of the apiserver CA — and
          if etcd is down, nothing else works either.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    26.3  Certificate Signing Requests (CSR)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          The process for generating new user certificates:
          a) Generate private key:    openssl genrsa -out user.key 2048
          b) Create CSR:              openssl req -new -key user.key \
                                        -subj "/CN=dev-user/O=dev-team"
          c) Create K8s CSR object:   kubectl apply -f csr.yaml
          d) Approve CSR:             kubectl certificate approve dev-user
          e) Extract certificate:     kubectl get csr dev-user \
                                        -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}'

          🧪 FULL WORKED EXAMPLE — onboard developer "dev" into group
          "easypj-devs" (so a RoleBinding can grant them access to the easypj /
          jobpost namespaces):

          # 1) generate a key + CSR (CN becomes the username, O the group)
          openssl genrsa -out dev.key 2048
          openssl req -new -key dev.key -out dev.csr -subj "/CN=dev/O=easypj-devs"

          # 2) submit it to the K8s certificates API
          cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
          apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
          kind: CertificateSigningRequest
          metadata:
            name: dev
          spec:
            request: $(base64 -w0 dev.csr)
            signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
            usages: ["client auth"]
          EOF

          # 3) approve and fetch the signed cert
          kubectl certificate approve dev
          kubectl get csr dev -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' \
            | base64 -d > dev.crt

          # 4) wire dev.crt/dev.key into a kubeconfig
          kubectl config set-credentials dev \
            --client-certificate=dev.crt --client-key=dev.key
          kubectl config set-context dev --cluster=kubernetes --user=dev
          kubectl --context=dev get pods -n jobpost   # allowed/denied per RBAC

          📖 KEY TERM — signerName: tells the apiserver which built-in signer
          should issue the cert and what it may be used for:
            • kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client  → client certs for users that
              authenticate TO the apiserver (usages: ["client auth"]).
            • kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving         → kubelet SERVING certs.
            • kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet → kubelet client certs.
          Picking the wrong signerName (or wrong usages) makes the cert unusable
          even after you approve it.

          🧭 DECISION GUIDE — request.field must be base64 of the CSR FILE
          (PEM), not the key. `base64 -w0` avoids line wraps that corrupt YAML.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    26.4  Checking Certificate Expiry
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          $ kubeadm certs check-expiration
          $ openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout
          $ openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates -subject

          ⚡ SPEED TIP: `kubeadm certs check-expiration` is the ONE command that
          lists every kubeadm-managed cert AND the CA with their expiry dates in
          a single table — start here every time.

          [TIP: Certificates default to 1 year — monitor and renew!]

          🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING: if kubectl returns
              x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid
          the apiserver's serving cert (or your admin kubeconfig's embedded
          client cert) has expired. You must fix this ON the node with
          kubeadm/openssl — the API is unreachable, so kubectl can't help.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    26.5  Renewing Certificates
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          $ kubeadm certs renew all
          $ kubeadm certs renew apiserver
          [IMPORTANT: Restart control plane components after renewal]

          🔑 The complete renewal recipe:
          1. kubeadm certs renew all
          2. Restart the control-plane static pods so they RELOAD the new certs.
             Easiest: bounce the kubelet, or move the manifests out of
             /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and back:
               systemctl restart kubelet
             (or `kill` the apiserver/controller-manager/scheduler/etcd pods)
          3. Refresh the admin kubeconfig if it embedded the OLD client cert:
               kubeadm init phase kubeconfig admin
             then copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf back to ~/.kube/config.

          ⚠️ This is the #1 gotcha: renewing the files on disk does NOTHING until
          the process re-reads them. A renewed-but-not-restarted cluster is still
          a broken cluster.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        🔧 UTH — the mutual TLS handshake: when kubelet calls the apiserver, the
        apiserver presents apiserver.crt (signed by ca.crt); the kubelet verifies
        it against the CA. The kubelet ALSO presents its own client cert; the
        apiserver verifies it against the same CA and then reads the cert's
        Subject — CN → username, each O → a group. That mapping is the entire
        "authentication" step; RBAC takes over from there. CA certs are long-lived
        (~10y) because rotating a CA is disruptive; leaf certs are short (~1y) so
        a leaked component cert has limited blast radius.

        🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
        • Certificates API signers: kube-apiserver-client (user clients),
          kubelet-serving and kube-apiserver-client-kubelet (kubelet TLS
          bootstrap), and the legacy/aggregation front-proxy CA. Each enforces
          allowed key usages.
        • Key usages: "client auth" vs "server auth" (TLS WWW auth) vs
          "digital signature"/"key encipherment". A serving cert needs server
          auth + SANs; a user cert needs client auth.
        • External-CA mode: kubeadm can run with the CA private key absent
          (ca.key missing) — you sign certs out-of-band; `certs renew` then can't
          renew leaves automatically.
        • front-proxy CA: a SEPARATE trust chain for the API aggregation layer
          (extension apiservers like metrics-server) — don't confuse it with the
          cluster CA.
        • Rotating the cluster CA is hard: you must distribute the new CA to every
          node and component before retiring the old one; plan a bundle/overlap.
        • cert-manager: for APPLICATION TLS (Ingress, webhooks), not control-plane
          certs — it automates issuance/renewal from Let's Encrypt or an internal
          CA via Certificate/Issuer CRDs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        • Kubernetes runs on MUTUAL TLS. A cluster CA
          (/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt, ~10y) signs client/server certs for the
          apiserver, kubelet, controller-manager, scheduler, and admins; etcd
          usually has its OWN CA.
        • Each component has its own certificate; the default home for all of them
          is /etc/kubernetes/pki/ (etcd certs live in the etcd/ subdir).
        • A client certificate's CN is the username and O is the group — that is
          how a cert maps to an RBAC identity. No separate "user object" exists.
        • New human access = generate a key+CSR (CN=user, O=group), submit a
          CertificateSigningRequest, `kubectl certificate approve` it, then embed
          the signed cert in a kubeconfig.
        • Leaf certs expire (~1y). `kubeadm certs check-expiration` reports them
          and `kubeadm certs renew all` renews them — and you MUST restart the
          control plane / kubelet afterward so the new certs are loaded.
        • The cluster CA (~10y) outlives leaf certs (~1y); an expired leaf breaks
          its component even while the CA is perfectly valid.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        • Forgetting to restart components after `certs renew` leaves them using
          the old (renewed-but-not-loaded) certs — the cluster still breaks.
        • CN/O drive identity: a typo in CN gives a different (unauthorized) user;
          the group in O must EXACTLY match your RoleBindings.
        • Mixing up cert flags (client vs serving usages, wrong signerName) makes
          the CSR unusable even after approval.
        • An expired apiserver/etcd cert takes the whole control plane down — you
          can't kubectl your way out; fix on the node with kubeadm/openssl.
        • etcd has a separate CA — renewing the cluster CA does not fix etcd certs.
        • The CSR's `request` field must be base64 of the PEM CSR (use `base64 -w0`
          so no newlines corrupt the YAML).
        • After renewing, the admin kubeconfig may still embed the OLD client cert;
          regenerate it (`kubeadm init phase kubeconfig admin`).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        • `kubeadm certs check-expiration` is the one-command health check for
          every cert and the CA at once.
        • Decode any cert with `openssl x509 -in cert.crt -noout -text` to read its
          CN/O, SANs, and validity; add `-dates -subject` for the quick version.
        • After approving a CSR, pull the cert straight from the object:
          `kubectl get csr <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d`.
        • `base64 -w0` (no wrap) when stuffing the CSR into YAML — saves a debugging
          detour.
        • Restart the control plane fast by bouncing the kubelet
          (`systemctl restart kubelet`) instead of editing each manifest.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        kubeadm certs check-expiration
        kubeadm certs renew all          # then restart control-plane static pods + kubelet
        kubeadm certs renew apiserver
        kubectl get csr
        kubectl certificate approve dev   # or `deny`
        kubectl get csr dev -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > dev.crt
        openssl genrsa -out dev.key 2048
        openssl req -new -key dev.key -out dev.csr -subj "/CN=dev/O=easypj-devs"
        openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates -subject
        openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout
        kubectl config set-credentials dev --client-certificate=dev.crt --client-key=dev.key
        kubectl config set-context dev --cluster=kubernetes --user=dev
        kubeadm init phase kubeconfig admin   # refresh admin.conf after renewal

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [L] 🧪 DRILL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Create a key+CSR for user "dev" in group "easypj-devs", approve it, fetch
        the signed cert, build a kubeconfig context, and confirm that
        `kubectl --context=dev get pods` is allowed/denied per a matching
        RoleBinding (e.g. a Role granting get/list on pods in the jobpost
        namespace bound to group easypj-devs).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Q1. Approve a pending CertificateSigningRequest named "dev".
            A. `kubectl get csr` to see it Pending, then
            `kubectl certificate approve dev`; fetch the signed cert from
            `.status.certificate` (base64-decode it). Approval is what triggers
            the signer to actually issue the certificate.

        Q2. Create a client cert + kubeconfig for a new user.
            A. openssl key+CSR (CN=user / O=group) → submit a
            CertificateSigningRequest → `kubectl certificate approve` → decode the
            cert → `kubectl config set-credentials` + `set-context` with the
            cert+key. CN sets the username, O sets the group for RBAC.

        Q3. How do you check when the cluster certs expire?
            A. `kubeadm certs check-expiration` lists all kubeadm-managed certs
            plus the CA with their dates; for a single cert use
            `openssl x509 -noout -dates -in <cert>`.

        Q4. Renew all certs and make the cluster use them. Steps?
            A. `kubeadm certs renew all`, then restart the control-plane static
            pods (move/replace the manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests or
            `systemctl restart kubelet`) so they reload the new certs. Finally
            refresh any admin kubeconfig that embedded the old cert.

        Q5. Where do the cluster certs live and name two.
            A. /etc/kubernetes/pki/ — e.g. ca.crt (cluster CA) and apiserver.crt
            (apiserver serving cert), plus an etcd/ subdir holding etcd's own
            CA and server/peer certs.

        Q6. How does a client cert become a Kubernetes identity?
            A. The apiserver maps the cert's CN to the username and each O to a
            group; RBAC then authorizes that user/group. There is no separate
            user object — the cert IS the identity.

        Q7. CA vs leaf cert validity — typical and implication?
            A. CA ~10y, leaf certs ~1y. Leaves must be renewed yearly; an expired
            leaf breaks that component even though the CA is still valid.

        Q8. You renewed certs but the apiserver still rejects connections. Why?
            A. The component wasn't restarted, so it is still serving the OLD cert
            held in memory. Restart the apiserver static pod / kubelet so it
            reloads the new cert from disk.

        Q9. etcd uses a different cert chain — why does that matter?
            A. etcd typically has its OWN CA and peer/server certs. etcd cert
            expiry breaks the datastore independently of the apiserver CA, and a
            down etcd takes the whole cluster with it.

        Q10. The whole control plane is down with x509 "certificate has expired".
             Recovery outline?
             A. On the control-plane NODE (kubectl is useless now):
             `kubeadm certs renew all` (or regenerate the specific expired cert),
             restart kubelet / the static pods so the new certs load, then update
             any admin kubeconfig that embedded the old cert
             (`kubeadm init phase kubeconfig admin`).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: the certificate web of a kubeadm cluster
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        One cluster CA at the center (~10y) signs leaf certs (~1y) for the
        apiserver (server+client), kubelet (client + serving), controller-manager,
        scheduler, and every admin (CN=user, O=group → RBAC identity). etcd hangs
        off its OWN CA with peer+server certs; the front-proxy CA serves the
        aggregation layer. To onboard a user you openssl a CSR, submit it as a
        CertificateSigningRequest, `kubectl certificate approve` it, and embed the
        signed cert in a kubeconfig. To keep the cluster alive you
        `kubeadm certs check-expiration`, `kubeadm certs renew all`, and then —
        critically — RESTART the control plane / kubelet so the fresh certs are
        actually loaded.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
