  Chapter 27: Pod Security & Admission Control                         🟡 🎯
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Workloads & Scheduling /
      Cluster Architecture · Icons: 🎯 exam · 🏢 day-2 · 🧪 lab · ⚠️ gotcha ·
      ⚡ speed · 🔑 must-remember · 🔧 under-the-hood

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      A compromised container should never own the node it runs on. The
      Django easypj app may pull an image off the internet, run third-party
      Python wheels, or expose an endpoint that gets exploited — and the very
      first question an attacker asks is "can I break out of this pod onto the
      host?" Pod Security closes that door: it forces pods to run as non-root,
      drop Linux capabilities, refuse privilege escalation, and ride a seccomp
      filter so a single popped container can't pivot to kubelet, the host
      filesystem, or other tenants. The VISUAL to burn in: the three Pod
      Security Standards levels — privileged, baseline, restricted — and the
      namespace labels that enforce them.

  [C] OBJECTIVES
      • Explain the three Pod Security Standards (PSS) and what each blocks.
      • Enforce PSS at the namespace level with Pod Security Admission (PSA),
        in enforce / warn / audit modes, and pin the enforce-version.
      • Write a SecurityContext that passes the restricted profile:
        runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false,
        drop ALL capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault.
      • Place PSA in the wider admission-controller pipeline and know where
        custom webhooks / ValidatingAdmissionPolicy fit (Ch 40).

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE 🎯
      Pod Security lives in the Workloads/Cluster-Architecture domains. Expect
      a task that says "lock down namespace easypj to the restricted standard"
      (a one-line label) and/or "fix this pod so it can be admitted" (add the
      SecurityContext fields). Reading the admission rejection message and
      naming the exact violated control is a fast point.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      27.1  Pod Security Standards (PSS) — the three levels
      27.2  Pod Security Admission (PSA) — namespace labels & modes
      27.3  Security Contexts — pod-level and container-level hardening
      27.4  Admission Controllers — the gatekeeper pipeline
      🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
      🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A


  27.1  Pod Security Standards (PSS)                         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
        Three levels of security restrictions, from "anything goes" to
        "maximum lockdown." You don't write PSS directly — you select a level
        and let Pod Security Admission enforce it (27.2).

          [POD SECURITY STANDARDS]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  🔓 PRIVILEGED      🟡 BASELINE       🔒 RESTRICTED   │
          │                                                        │
          │  No restrictions    Sensible defaults   Maximum lock   │
          │  Full access        Block known          down           │
          │  For system pods    escalations          For sensitive  │
          │                     Good starting         workloads     │
          │  Examples:          point                               │
          │  - kube-system      Examples:            Examples:      │
          │  - monitoring       - easypj app         - payment svc  │
          │  - CNI plugins      - web frontends      - auth service │
          │                     - API services       - data stores  │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          A second view — what each level actually blocks, and where it fits:

          [POD SECURITY STANDARDS — 3 levels, enforced by namespace labels]
           ┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
           │ privileged  │ no restrictions                    │ kube-system  │
           │ baseline    │ blocks privileged/hostNet/hostPID  │ general apps │
           │ restricted  │ + non-root, drop ALL caps, seccomp,│ prod / multi-│
           │             │   read-only-ish rootfs             │ tenant 🔒    │
           └─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

        • privileged — open. No restrictions at all; used by the system pods
          that legitimately need host access (kube-system, CNI plugins, node
          monitoring agents).
        • baseline — blocks the obvious container escapes: privileged
          containers, hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, hostPath volumes, host
          ports, dangerous capabilities. A good starting point for the easypj
          web frontend and most general apps.
        • restricted — everything baseline blocks, plus the hardening that
          actually matters for multi-tenant / sensitive workloads: must run as
          non-root, drop ALL capabilities, set allowPrivilegeEscalation:false,
          and apply a seccomp profile. This is the target for payment, auth,
          and data-store pods.

        💡 INSIGHT: PSS is a spec; PSA is the enforcer. Think of PSS as the
        rulebook and PSA as the referee standing at the namespace door.


  27.2  Pod Security Admission (PSA)                         🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
        PSA is a built-in admission controller that enforces a chosen PSS
        level at the NAMESPACE level, driven entirely by labels. Three modes,
        which can point at different levels simultaneously:
          - enforce : reject pods that violate the level (blocks admission)
          - audit   : log violations to the audit log, but allow the pod
          - warn    : print a warning to the client (stderr), but allow the pod

        [CODE: Namespace with PSA labels — declarative]
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Namespace
        metadata:
          name: easypj
          labels:
            pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
            pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.31   # PIN the version
            pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted     # warn before enforcing
            pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
        # or imperatively:
        # kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

        [CODE: Namespace with PSA labels — imperative, mixed levels]
        $ kubectl label ns easypj \
          pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
          pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

        Modes recap: enforce (block) · warn (stderr) · audit (log).
        ⚡ Best practice: roll out with warn+audit=restricted FIRST, watch the
        warnings, fix the pods, THEN flip enforce=restricted.

        ⚠️ PSA is per-namespace and does NOT evict already-running pods — it
        only evaluates pods at admission time (create / update / recreate).


  27.3  Security Contexts                                    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
        SecurityContext is where you actually harden a pod so it passes the
        restricted profile. Two scopes:
          - Pod-level settings: fsGroup, runAsUser, runAsNonRoot,
            seccompProfile (apply to all containers, and to volume ownership)
          - Container-level settings: capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem,
            allowPrivilegeEscalation (override / refine per container)

        [CODE: Hardened pod — run as non-root, drop all caps, RO rootfs, seccomp]
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Pod
        metadata:
          name: easypj-web
          namespace: easypj
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            seccompProfile:
              type: RuntimeDefault
          containers:
          - name: web
            image: easypj:v1
            securityContext:
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
              capabilities:
                drop: ["ALL"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp        # writable scratch for the RO rootfs
          volumes:
          - name: tmp
            emptyDir: {}

        [CODE: Drop all capabilities, add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE]
        # Need to bind a low port (e.g. 80) without running as root?
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
            add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]   # the ONE cap that allows binding < 1024
        # Alternative: listen on a high port (8080) and let the Service map
        # port 80 -> targetPort 8080, so you can keep drop:[ALL] with nothing added.

        Hardened easypj pod, in one breath: runAsNonRoot,
        allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, readOnlyRootFilesystem:true (+ an
        emptyDir for anything it must write), capabilities.drop:[ALL],
        seccompProfile RuntimeDefault.

        🧠 ANALOGY: a SecurityContext is a building pass with the lowest
        clearance that still lets you do your job — no master key, can't prop
        the fire door, can't promote yourself to admin while inside.


  27.4  Admission Controllers
        - Gatekeepers that intercept API requests AFTER authentication and
          authorization, but BEFORE the object is persisted to etcd.
        - Built-in plugins: NamespaceLifecycle, LimitRanger, ServiceAccount,
          PodSecurity (this is the PSA controller from 27.2), ResourceQuota,
          DefaultStorageClass, and more.
        - Custom: dynamic admission webhooks —
          MutatingAdmissionWebhook (can change the object on the way in) and
          ValidatingAdmissionWebhook (accept/reject only). The in-cluster,
          CEL-based ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is the newer, webhook-free option
          (covered in Ch 40).

        [DIAGRAM: the API request admission pipeline guarding easypj]
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  kubectl apply -f easypj-pod.yaml                                   │
        │        │                                                            │
        │        ▼                                                            │
        │  ┌──────────────┐   WHO are you?  (certs / SA token)                │
        │  │ AUTHENTICATION│                                                  │
        │  └──────┬───────┘                                                   │
        │         ▼                                                           │
        │  ┌──────────────┐   WHAT may you do?  (RBAC)                        │
        │  │ AUTHORIZATION │                                                  │
        │  └──────┬───────┘                                                   │
        │         ▼                                                           │
        │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                               │
        │  │ ADMISSION CONTROL               │                               │
        │  │  1. MUTATING  webhooks/plugins  │  (may rewrite the pod)         │
        │  │  2. schema / object validation  │                               │
        │  │  3. VALIDATING (incl. PodSecurity)│ (reject if PSS violated) ◀── │
        │  └──────┬──────────────────────────┘                               │
        │         ▼                                                           │
        │      💾 etcd  (object persisted → scheduler/kubelet act on it)      │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Request → Authentication → Authorization → Admission → etcd

        [CODE: Check which admission controllers are enabled on the API server]
        # On a kubeadm control-plane node, inspect the static-pod manifest:
        $ grep enable-admission-plugins \
            /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        # or query a running apiserver for its defaults:
        $ kube-apiserver -h | grep -A2 enable-admission-plugins
        # PodSecurity is enabled by default in modern clusters (v1.25+).


  [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD
      • How PSA evaluates a pod: at admission, the PodSecurity controller reads
        the namespace labels, picks the level + version, and checks the pod
        spec field-by-field against that profile's controls. A single failed
        control under enforce = rejected admission; the rejection message names
        the exact control (e.g. "allowPrivilegeEscalation != false").
      • How SecurityContext maps to kernel features: capabilities.drop:[ALL]
        clears the process capability bounding set; allowPrivilegeEscalation:
        false sets the kernel's no_new_privs bit (so setuid binaries / file
        capabilities can't regain privilege); readOnlyRootFilesystem mounts the
        container's "/" read-only; seccompProfile installs a syscall filter.
        runAsNonRoot makes the kubelet refuse to start a container whose image
        resolves to UID 0.

      🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
      • restricted, field-by-field: disallow privileged; hostNetwork/PID/IPC
        false; no hostPath; allowPrivilegeEscalation must be false; runAsNonRoot
        true (or a non-zero runAsUser); capabilities must drop ALL (add back
        only NET_BIND_SERVICE); seccompProfile must be RuntimeDefault or
        Localhost; volume types restricted to the safe set.
      • PSA exemptions: a cluster admin can exempt by usernames, runtimeClasses,
        or namespaces so privileged system components aren't held to restricted.
      • Cluster-wide defaults: instead of labeling every namespace, set defaults
        and exemptions in an AdmissionConfiguration file referenced by the
        apiserver's --admission-control-config-file. Per-namespace labels still
        override the cluster default.
      • NET_BIND_SERVICE nuance: it's the single capability that lets a non-root
        process bind ports below 1024; pairing drop:[ALL] with add:
        [NET_BIND_SERVICE] is the canonical "non-root web server on :80."
      • seccomp Localhost profiles: type: Localhost + a localhostProfile path
        lets you ship a custom JSON seccomp filter (under the kubelet's seccomp
        dir) when RuntimeDefault is too permissive or too strict.


  [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      • Pod Security Standards define three levels: privileged (anything),
        baseline (blocks the obvious escapes — hostNet/hostPID/privileged), and
        restricted (also non-root, drop ALL caps, seccomp, no privilege
        escalation).
      • Pod Security Admission enforces them per NAMESPACE via labels, in three
        modes: enforce (reject), warn (stderr message), audit (log). Start with
        warn/audit before flipping to enforce.
      • SecurityContext is where you actually harden a pod: runAsNonRoot,
        readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false,
        capabilities.drop:[ALL], seccompProfile RuntimeDefault.
      • PSA is admission-time only — it does NOT evict already-running pods, and
        it complements (doesn't replace) RBAC and NetworkPolicy.
      • Admission control runs AFTER authn/authz and BEFORE etcd: mutating
        webhooks first, then validating (PodSecurity is a validating plugin).
      • SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL
        capabilities — defense in depth for pods.


  [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      • Labeling a namespace restricted does nothing to pods already running —
        only new/updated/recreated pods are evaluated.
      • A read-only root filesystem breaks apps that write to disk; add writable
        emptyDir mounts for /tmp, caches, Django's static collection dir, etc.
      • restricted requires runAsNonRoot AND a seccomp profile — images that
        default to root (UID 0) are rejected at admission.
      • Pin enforce-version so a cluster upgrade doesn't silently tighten the
        policy and break admissions.
      • Don't confuse the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy (PSP, removed in v1.25)
        with Pod Security Admission — the exam is on PSA / PSS labels.
      • A pod can pass `warn` and still be `enforce`-rejected if you set warn to
        a looser level than enforce — keep them aligned during rollout.


  [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      • Roll out safely: set warn+audit=restricted first, watch the warnings,
        fix the pods, THEN set enforce=restricted.
      • `kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`
        is the one-liner; add `--overwrite` to change an existing label.
      • Test a manifest against a level with a dry-run apply into a labeled ns —
        the rejection message names the exact violated control.
      • `kubectl get ns easypj --show-labels` instantly tells you the current
        PSA level/mode — faster than describing the namespace.


  [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
      kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
      kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted --overwrite
      kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
      kubectl get ns easypj --show-labels
      kubectl apply -f hardened-pod.yaml -n easypj     # see the admission verdict
      kubectl run root --image=nginx -n easypj         # rejected under restricted
      grep enable-admission-plugins \
        /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml  # which controllers are on


  [L] 🧪 DRILL
      Label the easypj namespace enforce=restricted, try to run a stock nginx
      (rejected for running as root and missing the required fields), then
      deploy the hardened easypj pod from 27.3 and watch it get admitted.


  [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each:

      Q1. Enforce the restricted standard on namespace easypj.
          A. kubectl label ns easypj
             pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
             (optionally pin pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.31).
             PSA reads the namespace labels and validates every pod at
             admission against the restricted profile.

      Q2. Harden a container to pass restricted. Which fields?
          A. Pod-level: runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
             Container-level: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false,
             readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]. Those are
             exactly the controls the restricted profile checks.

      Q3. A stock nginx pod is rejected in the namespace. Why?
          A. It runs as root (UID 0) and doesn't set the required restricted
             fields (allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, drop ALL caps, seccomp), so
             PSA's enforce=restricted blocks admission. The rejection message
             lists each violated control.

      Q4. The app needs to write but rootfs is read-only. Fix?
          A. Keep readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and mount writable emptyDir
             volumes at the paths it writes (e.g. /tmp, cache dirs). The "/" stays
             immutable while specific paths remain writable.

      Q5. Drop all Linux capabilities but keep binding to port 80. How?
          A. capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] then add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE — the
             one capability that allows a non-root process to bind ports < 1024.
             Alternatively run on a high port and front it with a Service that
             maps port 80 -> targetPort 8080, keeping drop:[ALL] with no adds.

      Q6. What does seccompProfile RuntimeDefault do?
          A. Applies the container runtime's default seccomp filter, blocking
             dangerous/unused syscalls — required by the restricted profile and
             a major hardening win for little effort.

      Q7. Difference between warn and enforce modes?
          A. warn emits a message to the client (stderr) but still admits the
             pod; enforce rejects the pod outright; audit only records the
             violation to the audit log. You can set all three at once, even at
             different levels.

      Q8. Why pin pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version?
          A. So the policy is evaluated against a fixed Kubernetes version; a
             cluster upgrade won't silently add new restricted controls that
             suddenly break pods that used to be admitted.

      Q9. kube-system runs privileged pods. How is that allowed?
          A. Its namespace is labeled (or exempted) at the privileged level —
             PSA is per-namespace, so system components and CNI/monitoring pods
             aren't held to restricted.

      Q10. Does enforcing restricted kill the pods already running as root?
           A. No — PSA only acts at admission. Existing pods keep running; they're
              only blocked on recreate/update. Evict/recreate (e.g. roll the
              Deployment) to make the new policy take effect.

      Q11. Where does PSA sit relative to RBAC in request handling?
           A. After authentication and authorization (RBAC), during admission
              control. RBAC decides WHO may create a pod; PSA decides whether
              that pod's SPEC is allowed. They are complementary, not a
              substitute for one another.

      Q12. How do you find which admission controllers are enabled?
           A. On a kubeadm node, grep enable-admission-plugins in
              /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. PodSecurity is on by
              default in v1.25+.


  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: a hardened easypj pod admitted under the restricted PSS.

          ┌──────────── easypj namespace (enforce=restricted) ────────────┐
          │  label: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted          │
          │                                                                │
          │   apply easypj-web pod ──▶ ┌─ PSA validating check ─┐          │
          │                            │ runAsNonRoot ........ ✅ │          │
          │                            │ allowPrivEsc:false .. ✅ │          │
          │                            │ readOnlyRootFS ...... ✅ │          │
          │                            │ drop: ["ALL"] ....... ✅ │          │
          │                            │ seccomp RuntimeDefault ✅│          │
          │                            └──────────┬─────────────┘          │
          │                                       ▼                        │
          │                              ✅ ADMITTED → etcd → scheduled     │
          │                                                                │
          │   stock nginx (root) ──▶  ❌ REJECTED: "runAsNonRoot != true,  │
          │                              allowPrivilegeEscalation != false" │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      .vs-prose — A namespace labeled enforce=restricted turns Pod Security
      Admission into a gate at the door. The hardened easypj-web pod sets all
      five restricted controls (non-root, no privilege escalation, read-only
      rootfs, drop ALL caps, seccomp RuntimeDefault), so PSA admits it and it
      reaches etcd and the scheduler. A stock nginx image running as root sets
      none of them, so PSA rejects it with a message naming each violated
      control. Already-running pods are untouched until they are recreated.


  ┌──────────────────────── PART 7 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ─────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ AuthN (certs / SA tokens) = WHO; RBAC = WHAT (deny by default, union  │
  │    of bindings, no deny rules). Role/RoleBinding (ns) vs ClusterRole/    │

  │ ✅ ServiceAccounts are pod identities; disable automount when unused;    │
  │    bind RBAC as system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>. Users are for humans, │
  │    every namespace has a "default" ServiceAccount.                       │
  │ ✅ The control plane runs on mutual TLS; approve CSRs, check & renew      │

  │ ✅ Pod Security Standards (privileged/baseline/restricted) via namespace │
  │    labels; SecurityContext makes pods non-root & least-capability.       │
  │ 🎯 EXAM: RBAC Role+Binding and `auth can-i`, plus CSR approval and the   │
  │    PSA labels, are high-frequency tasks (25% cluster domain).            │
  │ 🔑 create role/rolebinding · auth can-i · certificate approve · kubeadm  │
  │    certs renew · label ns pod-security...enforce=restricted              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  [PART 7 VISUAL SUMMARY]: the AuthN -> AuthZ -> Admission pipeline guarding

  controllers (PodSecurity included) validate the object before it ever
  reaches etcd.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapters 28-30  ·  Cluster lifecycle competency (25%)  ·  "Keep it alive"
  CKA Exam Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration
                   (25% — includes cluster upgrades & lifecycle)

  What you'll build: a safe upgrade of your kubeadm cluster, automated etcd
  backups with a tested restore, and a drain/patch/uncordon node-maintenance
  routine that keeps easypj available throughout.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  [PART 8 INTRO]
  Clusters aren't "set and forget." Versions age out, disks fill, nodes need
  kernel patches, and disasters happen. This part is the admin's recurring
  calendar: upgrade Kubernetes safely (control plane first, then workers),
  guarantee recoverability (backup + DR), and take nodes down for maintenance
  WITHOUT taking easypj down (drain + PodDisruptionBudgets).

  Up to now you have BUILT the cluster and the easypj/jobpost workloads that
  live on it. This part is about KEEPING it alive over months and years. Three
  recurring operational duties define a Kubernetes administrator's calendar:

    1. UPGRADE  — Kubernetes ships a minor release roughly every ~4 months and
                  supports only the latest three. Falling behind means losing
                  patches and support, so you upgrade — control plane first,
                  one minor at a time, respecting version skew.
    2. BACKUP   — etcd is the single source of truth. If it is lost and you
                  have no snapshot, the cluster's entire desired state (every
                  Deployment, Secret, RBAC rule, the JobPost data plane config)
                  is gone. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a
                  plan — so you also practice DISASTER RECOVERY.
    3. MAINTAIN — Real nodes need kernel patches, hardware swaps and reboots.
                  You drain a node so its Pods reschedule elsewhere, do the
                  work, then uncordon it — and a PodDisruptionBudget guarantees
                  easypj never drops below its minimum replica count meanwhile.

  💡 Mental model: think of this part as the cluster's "health, insurance and
     scheduled-maintenance" trio. Upgrade = staying current; Backup/DR =
     insurance against catastrophe; Node maintenance = routine servicing done
     without an outage.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 8 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch28 UPGRADE (kubeadm, version skew) ─▶ Ch30 NODE MAINTENANCE (drain/PDB)│
  │                 │                                                        │
  │                 ▼                                                        │
  │ Ch29 BACKUP & DISASTER RECOVERY (etcd snapshots, automation, Velero)     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read it as a single operational loop. An upgrade (Ch28) ALWAYS begins with a
  fresh etcd snapshot from Ch29 — that snapshot is your undo button if the
  control-plane upgrade misbehaves. The actual mechanics of taking a node out
  of service to upgrade its kubelet (Ch28) are the SAME drain/uncordon
  mechanics you use for kernel patching in Ch30, just applied for a different
  reason. So the three chapters share one toolbox:

  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CHAPTER              │ CORE QUESTION IT ANSWERS                          │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch28 Cluster Upgrade │ How do I move from vX to vX+1 with zero data loss │
  │                      │ and minimal disruption? (kubeadm, version skew)   │
  │ Ch29 Backup & DR     │ If etcd dies, how do I get the cluster's brain    │
  │                      │ back? (snapshot save / snapshot restore, Velero)  │
  │ Ch30 Node Maintenance│ How do I service a node without an app outage?    │
  │                      │ (cordon / drain / uncordon, PDB)                  │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [PART 8 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: snapshot etcd FIRST -> `kubeadm upgrade plan/apply`
  on the control plane -> drain+upgrade kubelet on each worker -> verify easypj
  unaffected (PDB kept minAvailable). VISUAL: the upgrade order + version-skew
  rules below.

  THE END-TO-END LIFECYCLE RUN (the thread that stitches Ch28-30 together):

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 0  SNAPSHOT FIRST (Ch29)                                             │
  │    ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-pre-upgrade.db          │
  │    ...with --endpoints + --cacert/--cert/--key. Verify --write-out=table.   │
  │                                   │                                         │
  │                                   ▼                                         │
  │  STEP 1  CONTROL PLANE (Ch28)                                              │
  │    apt upgrade kubeadm -> kubeadm upgrade plan -> kubeadm upgrade apply vX  │
  │    -> drain CP node -> upgrade kubelet+kubectl -> systemctl restart kubelet │
  │    -> uncordon CP node.                                                     │
  │                                   │                                         │
  │                                   ▼                                         │
  │  STEP 2  WORKERS, ONE AT A TIME (Ch28 + Ch30 share the drain)              │
  │    kubectl drain wkr --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data            │
  │    -> apt upgrade kubeadm -> kubeadm upgrade node                          │
  │    -> apt upgrade kubelet kubectl -> systemctl restart kubelet            │
  │    -> kubectl uncordon wkr.                                                 │
  │                                   │                                         │
  │                                   ▼                                         │
  │  STEP 3  VERIFY (all three chapters)                                       │
  │    kubectl get nodes  (all Ready, all at new version)                       │
  │    easypj Deployment never went below its PDB minAvailable; jobpost serving.│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE UPGRADE ORDER + VERSION-SKEW RULES (the single most-tested visual here):

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  UPGRADE DIRECTION  ───────────────────────────────▶  (always top-down)     │
  │                                                                             │
  │   1. kubeadm (the tool)        on each node, BEFORE anything else           │
  │   2. CONTROL PLANE             kube-apiserver, controller-manager,          │
  │      ┌──────────────┐          scheduler, etcd  ──  upgrade FIRST           │
  │      │  apiserver   │                                                       │
  │      └──────┬───────┘                                                       │
  │             ▼                                                               │
  │   3. WORKER NODES              kubelet + kube-proxy  ──  upgrade AFTER       │
  │      ┌──────────────┐          drain → upgrade → uncordon, one by one       │
  │      │   kubelet    │                                                       │
  │      └──────────────┘                                                       │
  │                                                                             │
  │  ONE MINOR VERSION AT A TIME:  1.31 → 1.32 → 1.33   (never skip a minor)    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  VERSION-SKEW POLICY (memorize the allowed gaps — exam favourite):
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
  │ COMPONENT         │ ALLOWED RELATIVE TO       │ MEANING                       │
  │                   │ kube-apiserver            │                               │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ kube-apiserver    │ baseline (newest)         │ Upgrade this FIRST.           │
  │ controller-mgr /  │ same or 1 minor older     │ Within the control plane.     │
  │   scheduler       │                          │                               │
  │ kubelet           │ up to 3 minors older      │ So workers may lag CP — but   │
  │                   │   (≤3)                    │ NEVER be newer than apiserver.│
  │ kube-proxy        │ matches its node's kubelet│ Per-node, with kubelet.       │
  │ kubectl           │ ±1 minor of apiserver     │ Client may be 1 ahead/behind. │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
  🔑 Golden rule: NOTHING is ever newer than kube-apiserver. Upgrade the
     apiserver first; everything else follows downhill.

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: kubeadm doesn't replace binaries by magic. `kubeadm
     upgrade apply` re-renders the static Pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/
     manifests/ with new image tags; the kubelet (watching that directory)
     notices the changed manifest and restarts each control-plane component as
     a new static Pod. etcd's data is untouched — only the etcd container image
     is bumped — which is exactly why a pre-upgrade snapshot is cheap insurance.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: the apt package upgrade and the `kubeadm upgrade apply` are TWO
     separate acts. Upgrading the kubeadm package alone changes nothing on the
     cluster; you must then run `kubeadm upgrade apply`. And upgrading the
     kubelet package does nothing until you `systemctl daemon-reload &&
     systemctl restart kubelet`.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: in the exam, `kubeadm upgrade plan` prints the exact target
     version and the precise commands for the next steps — read its output
     instead of guessing version strings.

  🩺 If a drained worker shows Pods stuck Terminating, look for a missing
     --ignore-daemonsets or local emptyDir data needing --delete-emptydir-data;
     a PDB that can never be satisfied will also block the drain indefinitely.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

          should be able to perform end-to-end under time pressure.

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    ────────────────
    Clusters do not stand still. New Kubernetes minor versions ship roughly
    every four months, each one eventually dropping out of support. Keeping a
    cluster current is both a near-certain CKA exam task and an ordinary day-2
    operations chore: you upgrade kubeadm, the control plane, then the workers,
    one minor version at a time, without taking the whole cluster down. Get the
    ORDER wrong (workers before the control plane, or skipping a minor) and you
    can wedge or corrupt the control plane. This chapter drills the exact,
    repeatable pipeline.

    🎯 OBJECTIVES
    ─────────────
      • Explain the Kubernetes release cycle and the component version-skew
        rules (kubelet, kubectl, etcd vs. the API server).
      • Upgrade the CONTROL PLANE with kubeadm (plan → apply → kubelet/kubectl).
      • Upgrade WORKER nodes safely (drain → upgrade node → kubelet → uncordon).
      • Verify cluster health and version after each step.

    CKA RELEVANCE
    ─────────────
    🎯 Expect a live task: "upgrade this cluster from 1.X to 1.X+1." You are
    graded on doing it in the correct order, on the control plane AND the
    worker, ending with all nodes Ready on the new VERSION. The apt-mark
    hold/unhold dance and `systemctl restart kubelet` are the steps people
    most often forget.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    28.1  Kubernetes Release Cycle & Version Skew                          🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - Minor versions every ~4 months (1.30 → 1.31 → 1.32); about 3
            minor releases per year.
          - Patch versions for bug/security fixes (1.31.0 → 1.31.1).
          - Support window: the latest 3 minor versions are supported.
          - Component version skew rules:
            • kubelet: can TRAIL the API server (up to n-3 minor versions in
              modern releases), but must NEVER lead it.
            • kubectl: can be ±1 minor version of the API server.
            • etcd: must satisfy the version compatibility matrix for the
              target apiserver — `kubeadm upgrade apply` bumps the bundled etcd
              static-pod image for you.
            • Always upgrade: control plane FIRST → then workers.
            • Never SKIP a minor (1.30 → 1.32 ✗ — go 1.30 → 1.31 → 1.32).

          [VERSION SKEW RULES — who may trail whom]
          ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
          │ COMPONENT    │ RELATIVE TO kube-apiserver│ DIRECTION            │
          ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
          │ kube-apiserver│ —  (the reference)       │ upgrade FIRST        │
          │ kubelet      │ up to n-3 minor BEHIND    │ may TRAIL, not lead  │
          │ kube-proxy   │ matches its node's kubelet│ trails apiserver     │
          │ controller-  │ same minor as apiserver   │ moves with CP        │
          │  manager/sched│  (one minor older OK mid-│                      │
          │              │   upgrade)                │                      │
          │ kubectl      │ ±1 minor of apiserver     │ either direction     │
          └──────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
          🔑 The whole reason control plane goes first: kubelet may LAG but
             never LEAD the apiserver.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    28.2  Upgrade Strategy                                                 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          💾 BACKUP etcd FIRST — always, before you touch anything. One minor
          at a time, control plane before workers, one worker at a time so the
          cluster keeps serving traffic.

          [CLUSTER UPGRADE ORDER]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  STEP 0: 💾 Back up etcd (snapshot) — always first      │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 1: Upgrade kubeadm on control plane node          │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 2: kubeadm upgrade plan (check what's available)  │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 3: kubeadm upgrade apply v1.XX.0                  │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 4: Drain control plane node                       │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 5: Upgrade kubelet & kubectl on control plane     │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 6: Uncordon control plane node                    │
          │       ▼                                                 │
          │  STEP 7: For EACH worker node (one at a time):          │
          │          a) Drain node                                  │
          │          b) Upgrade kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl           │
          │          c) kubeadm upgrade node                        │
          │          d) Uncordon node                               │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    28.3  Hands-On: Upgrading the Control Plane                            🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          Generic form (substitute your target minor for 1.XX.0):

          $ apt-mark unhold kubeadm
          $ apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.XX.0-00
          $ apt-mark hold kubeadm
          $ kubeadm upgrade plan
          $ kubeadm upgrade apply v1.XX.0
          $ kubectl drain <control-plane-node> --ignore-daemonsets
          $ apt-get install -y kubelet=1.XX.0-00 kubectl=1.XX.0-00
          $ apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
          $ systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
          $ kubectl uncordon <control-plane-node>

          Worked example (target v1.31.1, on the control-plane node):

          # on the control-plane node (example target v1.31.1)
          apt-mark unhold kubeadm
          apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.31.1-1.1
          apt-mark hold kubeadm
          kubeadm upgrade plan                  # shows the exact upgrade path
          kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.1         # re-renders manifests, rotates certs
          kubectl drain <cp-node> --ignore-daemonsets
          apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl
          apt-get install -y kubelet=1.31.1-1.1 kubectl=1.31.1-1.1
          apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
          systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
          kubectl uncordon <cp-node>

          📖 Note the package-name skew between Kubernetes generations: older
          repos use the "=1.XX.0-00" suffix, the community pkgs.k8s.io repos use
          "=1.31.1-1.1". Use whichever your `apt-cache madison kubeadm` lists.
          📖 The unhold → install → re-hold pattern: `apt-mark hold` pins the
          kube* packages so a routine `apt upgrade` can't bump them out from
          under the cluster; you unhold only long enough to install the chosen
          version, then re-hold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    28.4  Hands-On: Upgrading Worker Nodes                                 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          Generic form:

          (From control plane): $ kubectl drain <worker-node> --ignore-daemonsets
          (SSH into worker):    $ apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.XX.0-00
                                $ kubeadm upgrade node
                                $ apt-get install -y kubelet=1.XX.0-00
                                $ systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
          (From control plane): $ kubectl uncordon <worker-node>
          ⚡ [TIP: Upgrade one worker at a time to maintain availability]

          Worked example (target v1.31.1):

          # from a control-plane/admin context: drain the worker first
          kubectl drain <worker> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
          # then ON the worker node:
          apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.31.1-1.1 && apt-mark hold kubeadm
          kubeadm upgrade node                  # updates the local kubelet config
          apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl
          apt-get install -y kubelet=1.31.1-1.1 kubectl=1.31.1-1.1
          apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
          systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
          # back on admin:
          kubectl uncordon <worker>

          📖 The KEY difference from the control plane: workers run
          `kubeadm upgrade node` (NOT `upgrade apply`). On a worker there is no
          static-pod control plane to re-render — `upgrade node` just refreshes
          the local kubelet config (and, on extra control-plane nodes, applies
          the same manifests `apply` already computed). `--delete-emptydir-data`
          lets the drain evict pods that use emptyDir volumes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 28
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [CLUSTER UPGRADE — order & version skew (one minor at a time)]
     0  💾 BACKUP etcd first (always)
     1  CONTROL PLANE node:
          apt-mark unhold kubeadm ; install kubeadm vX
          kubeadm upgrade plan  ─►  kubeadm upgrade apply vX
          apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl ; install vX ; restart kubelet
     2  EACH WORKER (one at a time):
          kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
          kubeadm upgrade node ; upgrade kubelet ; restart kubelet
          kubectl uncordon <node>
     ⚠️ NEVER skip a minor (1.30 -> 1.32 ✗). kubelet may TRAIL the apiserver,
        never lead it.

    [CONTROL PLANE vs WORKER — the one command that differs]
    ┌───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
    │  CONTROL PLANE            │  WORKER NODE              │
    ├───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
    │  kubeadm upgrade PLAN     │  (no plan step)           │
    │  kubeadm upgrade APPLY vX │  kubeadm upgrade NODE     │
    │  re-renders CP manifests, │  refreshes local kubelet  │
    │  rotates certs, bumps      │  config only              │
    │  addons (CoreDNS,kube-proxy)│                          │
    └───────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 What `kubeadm upgrade apply vX` actually does on the control plane:
       • Re-renders the static-pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests for
         kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler (and etcd
         if it manages etcd). The kubelet notices the changed manifest files
         and restarts those pods with the new images.
       • Rotates control-plane certificates as needed (the kubeadm-managed
         certs are renewed during the upgrade).
       • Updates the cluster-wide `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap in kube-system to
         record the new version and config.
       • Upgrades the bundled addons: CoreDNS and kube-proxy DaemonSet/Deployment
         images are bumped to versions compatible with the target.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
       • Full skew policy: kubelet may be up to n-3 minor versions behind the
         apiserver; kube-proxy tracks its node's kubelet; kubectl is ±1.
         controller-manager/scheduler run the apiserver's minor (one older is
         tolerated transiently mid-upgrade).
       • etcd version compatibility: each apiserver minor expects an etcd
         version range; `kubeadm` upgrades etcd's static-pod image to stay in
         range. If you run etcd EXTERNALLY (not as a kubeadm static pod), you
         must upgrade it yourself per the matrix.
       • Migrating deprecated/removed APIs ACROSS versions: before a minor
         upgrade, audit manifests/Helm charts for removed apiVersions (e.g.
         betas that graduated or were dropped). Tools like `kubectl convert`
         and pluto/kubent help. The apiserver will refuse objects on removed
         versions after the bump.
       • Addon upgrades: if a CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel) is involved,
         it has its OWN upgrade procedure independent of kubeadm — check its
         compatibility with the target Kubernetes minor.
       • Rollback considerations: kubeadm upgrades are largely forward-only.
         The real safety net is the etcd snapshot you took in STEP 0 plus the
         pre-upgrade static-pod manifest backups kubeadm writes to
         /etc/kubernetes/tmp. For a multi-node control plane, upgrade nodes one
         at a time so quorum is never lost.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • Upgrade order is FIXED: back up etcd → control plane → workers, ONE
        minor version at a time (1.30→1.31, never 1.30→1.32).
      • Version skew: kubelet may TRAIL the apiserver (up to n-3) but must never
        lead it; kubectl is ±1. Upgrade the control plane BEFORE the kubelets.
      • Control plane: `kubeadm upgrade plan` then `kubeadm upgrade apply vX`
        (re-renders static-pod manifests, rotates certs, bumps addons); then
        upgrade kubelet/kubectl and restart kubelet.
      • Workers: drain → `kubeadm upgrade node` → upgrade+restart kubelet →
        uncordon. The apt-mark hold/unhold dance pins package versions.
      • Support window is the latest 3 minors; a new minor lands ~every 4 months
        (~3/year). Stay current to keep getting security patches.
      • Upgrade workers ONE at a time so the application (easypj) stays
        available while pods reschedule onto the not-yet-upgraded nodes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • Skipping a minor is unsupported and can corrupt the control plane.
      • Forgetting `apt-mark unhold` leaves packages pinned (install does
        nothing); forgetting to RE-hold lets an unplanned upgrade slip in later.
      • Not draining a worker before upgrading risks disrupting running pods
        abruptly.
      • Forgetting `systemctl restart kubelet` (or `daemon-reload`) after
        installing the new kubelet means the node keeps running the OLD version
        — `kubectl get nodes` still shows the old VERSION.
      • Forgetting the control plane's OWN kubelet: the CP is also a node and
        appears in skew checks — upgrade and restart its kubelet too.
      • Running `kubeadm upgrade apply` on a worker (instead of `upgrade node`)
        is wrong — workers have no control-plane manifests to apply.
      • Picking the wrong package suffix (=1.XX.0-00 vs =1.31.1-1.1) — confirm
        with `apt-cache madison kubeadm`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • `kubeadm upgrade plan` prints the exact component versions and the
        target — read it before touching anything.
      • `kubectl get nodes` after each step confirms the VERSION column moved
        and the node is Ready.
      • Upgrade the control plane's kubelet too — it's also a node and shows in
        skew checks.
      • `apt-cache madison kubeadm` lists the exact installable version strings
        so you don't guess the suffix.
      • Drain and uncordon are run from your admin/control-plane context; the
        package installs and `kubeadm`/`systemctl` steps run ON the node.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      kubeadm upgrade plan
      kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.1            # control plane
      kubeadm upgrade node                     # workers / extra CP nodes
      apt-mark unhold kubeadm kubelet kubectl ; apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl
      apt-cache madison kubeadm                # list installable versions
      apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.31.1-1.1
      kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
      kubectl uncordon <node>
      systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
      kubectl get nodes -o wide                # VERSION column

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 DRILL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      On a 2-node kubeadm cluster, upgrade one minor end to end — control plane
      (plan/apply, kubelet) then the worker (drain, upgrade node, kubelet,
      uncordon) — verifying versions and Ready at each step.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 28 (full answer + explanation each)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Q1. Give the full control-plane upgrade sequence.
          A. Back up etcd → unhold+install new kubeadm → `kubeadm upgrade plan`
          → `kubeadm upgrade apply vX` → drain CP → unhold+install
          kubelet/kubectl → restart kubelet → uncordon.

      Q2. Upgrade a worker node. Steps?
          A. drain (--ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data) → unhold+install
          kubeadm → `kubeadm upgrade node` → install+restart kubelet → uncordon.

      Q3. State the version-skew rule for kubelet vs apiserver.
          A. kubelet may be up to 3 minor versions behind the apiserver but
          never ahead — so always upgrade the control plane first.

      Q4. Why drain a node before upgrading its kubelet?
          A. To evict pods gracefully and reschedule them elsewhere, so the
          kubelet restart/reboot doesn't abruptly kill running workloads.

      Q5. What do apt-mark hold/unhold accomplish here?
          A. hold pins kube* packages so routine `apt upgrade` can't bump them;
          you unhold only to install the chosen version, then re-hold.

      Q6. What does `kubeadm upgrade plan` show?
          A. The current versions, the available target(s), the exact upgrade
          path, and component/addon versions that will change.

      Q7. You upgraded packages but `kubectl get nodes` still shows the old
          version. Why?
          A. kubelet wasn't restarted (or daemon-reload skipped). Run
          `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet`.

      Q8. Can you jump from 1.29 to 1.31 directly?
          A. No — upgrade one minor at a time (1.29→1.30→1.31). Skipping minors
          is unsupported.

      Q9. What does `kubeadm upgrade apply` actually change on the CP?
          A. Re-renders the static-pod manifests for apiserver/controller-
          manager/scheduler, rotates certs as needed, and updates kubeadm
          config + addons (CoreDNS, kube-proxy).

      Q10. After upgrading, how do you verify the cluster is healthy?
           A. `kubectl get nodes` (all Ready, new VERSION), check control-plane
           pods in kube-system Running, and that workloads (easypj) are intact.

      Q11. What is the single command difference between upgrading a control
           plane node and a worker node?
           A. The control plane runs `kubeadm upgrade apply vX`; a worker runs
           `kubeadm upgrade node`. Only the control plane re-renders manifests.

      Q12. How long is a Kubernetes minor version supported, and how often do
           new minors ship?
           A. The latest 3 minor versions are supported; a new minor lands
           roughly every 4 months (~3 per year), so each minor is supported
           about a year.

      Q13. You run etcd externally (not as a kubeadm static pod). Does
           `kubeadm upgrade apply` upgrade etcd?
           A. No — kubeadm only upgrades the etcd static pod it manages. With
           external etcd you upgrade etcd yourself per the compatibility matrix.

      Q14. Before a minor upgrade, what should you audit in your manifests?
           A. Deprecated/removed apiVersions — graduated or dropped beta APIs.
           After the bump the apiserver rejects objects on removed versions;
           use `kubectl convert` / pluto / kubent to find and migrate them.

      Q15. On a 3-node control plane, why upgrade the nodes one at a time?
           A. To keep etcd/raft quorum and apiserver availability — taking more
           than one CP node out at once can lose quorum and stall the cluster.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🖼️ VISUAL SUMMARY — the upgrade pipeline, control plane then workers
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      💾 etcd backup
           │
           ▼
      ┌──────────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────────┐
      │  CONTROL PLANE               │      │  EACH WORKER (one at a time)  │
      │  unhold+install kubeadm vX   │ ───► │  drain --ignore-daemonsets    │
      │  upgrade plan → apply vX     │      │  unhold+install kubeadm vX    │
      │  (re-render manifests, certs,│      │  kubeadm upgrade node         │
      │   addons)                    │      │  install kubelet/kubectl vX   │
      │  drain → install kubelet/    │      │  daemon-reload; restart kubelet│
      │   kubectl vX → restart       │      │  uncordon                     │
      │  uncordon                    │      │                               │
      └──────────────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────────┘
           │                                        │
           ▼                                        ▼
      kubectl get nodes -o wide  →  all Ready, VERSION column advanced

      .vs-prose: The upgrade is a strict pipeline. First snapshot etcd as your
      safety net. Then take the control plane up one minor: install the new
      kubeadm, run `kubeadm upgrade plan` to read the exact path, `kubeadm
      upgrade apply vX` to re-render the static-pod manifests / rotate certs /
      bump CoreDNS and kube-proxy, then drain the node, install and restart the
      new kubelet/kubectl, and uncordon. Only after the control plane is on the
      new version do you touch workers — and only one at a time so the app
      stays up. Each worker is drained, gets the new kubeadm, runs `kubeadm
      upgrade node` (NOT apply), gets the new kubelet, restarts it, and is
      uncordoned. Verify with `kubectl get nodes -o wide` after every step: the
      node must come back Ready with its VERSION advanced. Never skip a minor,
      never let a kubelet lead the apiserver, and never forget to restart the
      kubelet or re-hold the packages.

    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
        Chapter 11 taught you the raw commands; THIS chapter turns backup into a
        RELIABLE, automated, TESTED process — the difference between knowing and
        surviving. etcd stores ALL cluster state; lose etcd and you lose the
        entire cluster configuration. A backup you have never restored is not a
        backup. The exam will almost certainly ask you to take a snapshot and/or
        perform a restore under time pressure, and in real life the etcd
        backup/restore runbook is what stands between a bad afternoon and a
        resume-generating event.
        VISUAL: backup cadence + DR runbook.

    [C] OBJECTIVES
        - Explain why etcd backup is critical and what a snapshot does and does
          NOT capture (RPO/RTO).
        - Take and VERIFY an etcd snapshot using the four critical cert flags.
        - Perform a full restore (restore → repoint → verify) end to end.
        - Schedule, rotate and ship backups off-node (CronJob / systemd timer).
        - Recover broader app + PersistentVolume state with Velero.

    [D] CKA RELEVANCE
        Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). "Implement
        etcd backup and restore" is an explicit competency. Expect a live task:
        save a snapshot with the right certs, OR restore a snapshot and repoint
        the static pod. Speed and getting the cert flags right are everything.

    [E] SECTION MAP
        29.1  Why etcd Backup is Critical 🎯
        29.2  etcd Backup (recap + verify) 🎯
