--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.1  Why etcd Backup is Critical
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          - etcd stores ALL cluster state.
          - Lose etcd = lose entire cluster configuration.
          - Must have a regular backup strategy.

          📖 KEY TERMS
          RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = the maximum amount of data you can
              afford to LOSE. It drives how OFTEN you back up. A 6-hour RPO means
              snapshots at least every 6 hours.
          RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = the maximum DOWNTIME you can tolerate.
              It drives how FAST your restore must run — and therefore how well
              rehearsed your runbook is.

          💡 INSIGHT: etcd is the single source of truth. Every Deployment,
          Service, Secret, ConfigMap and RBAC rule you ever applied lives there.
          Snapshot etcd and you've snapshotted the cluster's "brain." But the
          brain does NOT include the data on disk inside your PersistentVolumes.

          [DIAGRAM: etcd contains → all pods, services, secrets, configs, RBAC]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  WHAT etcd HOLDS — the cluster "brain"                            │
          │                                                                  │
          │            ┌────────────────────────────────┐                  │
          │            │            etcd                  │                  │
          │            │   (key-value store, MVCC)        │                  │
          │            └────────────────────────────────┘                  │
          │                          │                                       │
          │     ┌───────────┬────────┼────────┬───────────┬───────────┐    │
          │     ▼           ▼        ▼        ▼           ▼           ▼    │
          │  ┌──────┐   ┌────────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌──────┐ │
          │  │ Pods │   │Deploys │ │ Svcs │ │Secrets │ │Config-│ │ RBAC │ │
          │  │      │   │        │ │      │ │        │ │ Maps  │ │      │ │
          │  └──────┘   └────────┘ └──────┘ └────────┘ └───────┘ └──────┘ │
          │                                                                  │
          │  ✅ ALL of the above = API object STATE = in the snapshot       │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [WHAT etcd DOES (and DOESN'T) BACK UP]
           ✅ in the snapshot: pods, deploys, services, secrets, configmaps,
                               RBAC, namespaces, CRDs ... (all API objects)
           ❌ NOT in it: PersistentVolume DATA (the 🐘 postgres files on disk!)
                └─► back PV data up SEPARATELY: Velero + volume snapshots.

          ⚠️ The classic trap: a team snapshots etcd nightly, the easypj
          PostgreSQL volume corrupts, they "restore from backup" — and discover
          the snapshot never contained a single row of postgres data. etcd backs
          up the CLAIM to the volume, not the bytes inside it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.2  etcd Backup (recap + verify)
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
            --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
            --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
            --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
            --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

          Verify backup (ALWAYS — an unverified snapshot is a guess):
          $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
            --write-table

          Example status output:
          +----------+----------+------------+------------+
          |   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE |
          +----------+----------+------------+------------+
          | fe01cf57 |   210309 |       1281 |     4.9 MB |
          +----------+----------+------------+------------+

          [ETCD BACKUP — THE CRITICAL 4 FLAGS]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  🎯 MEMORIZE THESE FLAGS:                              │
          │                                                        │
          │  --endpoints    Where etcd is running                  │
          │  --cacert       CA certificate for etcd                │
          │  --cert         Server certificate for etcd            │
          │  --key          Server private key for etcd            │
          │                                                        │
          │  Default cert paths:                                   │
          │  /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt                       │
          │  /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt                   │
          │  /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key                   │
          │                                                        │
          │  [TIP: Check etcd pod YAML for actual paths]           │
          │  $ kubectl describe pod etcd-master -n kube-system     │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          ⚡ SPEED TIP — set the flags once, then forget them:
          $ export ETCDCTL_API=3
          $ alias e='etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
              --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
              --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
              --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key'
          $ e snapshot save /backup/snap.db
          $ e snapshot status /backup/snap.db --write-table

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: where do the real cert paths come from? The etcd
          static pod manifest. If the default paths fail, read the source:
          $ grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file|listen-client-urls' \
              /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
          The --cert/--key the SERVER uses are listed there; in many clusters the
          client cert is /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt as above, but kubeadm
          variants differ — never assume, verify from the manifest.

          🏢 DAY-2: store every snapshot OFF the node immediately. A snapshot
          sitting on the same disk as etcd dies with the node it was meant to
          protect.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.3  etcd Restore (full DR drill)
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]   🧪 [DO IT END TO END]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
            --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

          (Newer toolchains: use `etcdutl snapshot restore ...` — etcdutl is the
          offline/data tool and is the recommended binary for restore; etcdctl
          restore still works on most exam images. Same --data-dir flag.)

          After restore:
          a) Update etcd pod manifest to use new --data-dir.
          b) Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml.
          c) Change the hostPath volume to /var/lib/etcd-restored.
          d) Wait for the etcd pod to restart with the restored data.

          [WALKTHROUGH: Complete backup → disaster → restore scenario]
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  FULL DR DRILL — backup → disaster → restore → validate          │
          │                                                                  │
          │  ① BACKUP        e snapshot save /backup/snap.db                 │
          │                  e snapshot status /backup/snap.db --write-table │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ② MARKER        kubectl create cm dr-marker -n default          │
          │                  (a proof object you will delete & expect back)  │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ③ DISASTER      kubectl delete cm dr-marker -n default          │
          │                  (simulate the data loss)                        │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ④ STOP CP       move kube-apiserver.yaml & etcd.yaml OUT of      │
          │                  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (kubelet stops them)  │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ⑤ RESTORE       etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/snap.db \      │
          │                    --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restored             │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ⑥ REPOINT       edit etcd.yaml hostPath → /var/lib/etcd-restored│
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ⑦ START CP      move etcd.yaml + kube-apiserver.yaml back        │
          │       ▼                                                          │
          │  ⑧ VALIDATE      kubectl get cm dr-marker -n default  ✅ it's    │
          │                  back!  Record the RTO you actually achieved.    │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          ⚠️ GOTCHA: NEVER restore into the LIVE etcd data-dir while etcd is
          running — that corrupts the store. Always restore to a NEW directory,
          stop etcd (move the static pod manifest aside), repoint the hostPath,
          then start etcd again.

          🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: an etcd snapshot is a point-in-time, internally
          consistent view because etcd uses MVCC (multi-version concurrency
          control) — the snapshot captures a single revision, so you never get a
          half-written object. On restore, in-flight objects from after that
          revision simply don't exist; anything created after the snapshot's
          REVISION is gone (that gap is your RPO made concrete).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.4  Backup Automation
          🏢 [DAY-2 / BEYOND]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          [CODE: CronJob YAML for automated etcd backups]
          apiVersion: batch/v1
          kind: CronJob
          metadata: { name: etcd-backup, namespace: kube-system }
          spec:
            schedule: "0 */6 * * *"             # every 6 hours
            jobTemplate:
              spec:
                template:
                  spec:
                    hostNetwork: true
                    nodeSelector: { node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: "" }
                    tolerations:
                    - { key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule }
                    containers:
                    - name: backup
                      image: registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.5.15-0
                      command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
                      args:
                      - >
                        etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379
                        --cacert=/pki/ca.crt --cert=/pki/server.crt --key=/pki/server.key
                        snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F-%H%M).db
                      volumeMounts:
                      - { name: pki, mountPath: /pki, readOnly: true }
                      - { name: backup, mountPath: /backup }
                    restartPolicy: OnFailure
                    volumes:
                    - { name: pki, hostPath: { path: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd } }
                    - { name: backup, hostPath: { path: /var/backups/etcd } }
          # then ship /var/backups/etcd OFF the node (object store) + prune old files.

          🧭 DECISION GUIDE — CronJob vs systemd timer:
          - CronJob (above): runs IN the cluster, scheduled by the control plane.
            Self-documenting and portable, but it depends on a healthy cluster —
            if the control plane is sick it may not fire.
          - systemd timer ON the host: runs even when Kubernetes is unhealthy,
            which is exactly when you most want a backup. Preferred for the
            control-plane node's own etcd. Example unit logic:
              ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/etcd-backup.sh   # save + status + scp off-node
              OnCalendar=*-*-* 00/6:00:00               # every 6 hours

          [BACKUP DISCIPLINE — a backup never restored is not a backup]
           ⏰ scheduled (CronJob / systemd timer)
                ▼
           🔍 verify (etcdctl snapshot status --write-table)
                ▼
           📤 copy OFF the node (object store)
                ▼
           🧪 TEST-restore periodically  ─► document RPO / RTO

          [CHECKLIST]
          ✅ Backup before every cluster upgrade.
          ✅ Store backups externally (not on same node).
          ✅ Verify every snapshot (snapshot status --write-table).
          ✅ Rotate / prune old snapshots (retention policy).
          ✅ Test restore procedure regularly.
          ✅ Document backup/restore steps for the team.

          📖 KEY TERM — retention policy: keep enough snapshot history to meet
          RPO and to recover from a problem discovered LATE (e.g. corruption that
          surfaces days later), while pruning old files so storage stays bounded.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.5  Beyond etcd — Velero
          🏢 [DAY-2 / BEYOND]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          etcd snapshots cannot restore disk data. To protect easypj's full
          state — its namespace API objects AND the PostgreSQL PersistentVolume
          — you need a tool that backs up BOTH. That tool is Velero.

          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  TWO LAYERS OF BACKUP                                             │
          │                                                                  │
          │   etcd snapshot ──────────► API object STATE (cluster brain)     │
          │   Velero        ──────────► namespace objects + PV DATA          │
          │                              (object store + volume snapshots)    │
          │                                                                  │
          │   DR for easypj on a NEW cluster:                                │
          │     velero restore create --from-backup easypj-daily             │
          │     └─► recreates the easypj namespace (Deployment, Service,     │
          │         Secret, ConfigMap, PVC) AND the postgres PV contents.     │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          - velero install ... (with a CSI or restic/node-agent plugin).
          - velero backup create easypj-daily --include-namespaces easypj \
              --snapshot-volumes
          - velero restore create --from-backup easypj-daily   (same or NEW cluster)

          💡 INSIGHT: Velero is also your cross-cluster MIGRATION tool — back up
          easypj in cluster A, restore it into cluster B. And a GitOps repo
          (re-apply all manifests) is itself a form of DR for the API objects,
          complementing volume snapshots for the data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    29.6  🧪 PRACTICE EXERCISES (timed restore drills)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          1. Take a verified snapshot, then run `snapshot status --write-table`
             and read off HASH / REVISION / TOTAL KEYS / TOTAL SIZE.
          2. Time yourself: from `snapshot save` to a validated restore, what RTO
             can you hit? Aim under 10 minutes.
          3. Write a CronJob (or systemd timer) and confirm a snapshot file lands
             in /var/backups/etcd, then add an off-node copy step.
          4. Install Velero, back up the easypj namespace WITH volume snapshots,
             delete it, and restore it.

================================================================================
    [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
================================================================================
    🔧 UTH: an etcd snapshot is a consistent point-in-time image because etcd is
    an MVCC store — a single REVISION is captured, never a partial write. PV data
    needs a SEPARATE backup because the snapshot only records the PVC/PV API
    objects, not the bytes the kubelet mounted. On restore, any object created
    after the snapshot's revision is gone — restore implications for in-flight
    objects ARE your RPO.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    - Consistent multi-resource backups: etcd gives you a cluster-wide consistent
      cut for free; Velero coordinates object + volume snapshots to approximate
      the same for app data.
    - Defragmentation: etcd accumulates free pages; `etcdctl defrag` reclaims
      space. Defrag (and `etcdctl endpoint status`) before/after large operations
      to keep the DB compact and the snapshot small.
    - Velero restic/node-agent (file-level) vs CSI volume snapshots
      (block/storage-level): restic is portable across storage backends; CSI
      snapshots are faster and crash-consistent but tied to the driver.
    - Restoring a SINGLE namespace (Velero --include-namespaces) vs a full etcd
      restore (all-or-nothing) — pick the smallest blast radius that fixes the
      problem.
    - Cross-cluster migration and GitOps re-apply as DR: re-applying manifests
      rebuilds API objects; pair with volume snapshots for the data.

================================================================================
    [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
================================================================================
    • etcd holds ALL cluster STATE (pods, deployments, services, secrets,
      configmaps, RBAC). An etcd snapshot backs that up — but NOT the data inside
      PersistentVolumes (your postgres files on disk).
    • A backup you have never test-restored is NOT a backup. Define RPO (how much
      data you can lose) and RTO (how fast you must recover) and prove them with
      drills.
    • The four critical flags are --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, --key, with
      ETCDCTL_API=3. Get them right and snapshot save/status/restore all work.
    • Automate snapshots (CronJob / systemd timer), VERIFY them (`snapshot status
      --write-table`), and copy them OFF the node to object storage with
      retention / rotation.
    • Restore to a NEW data-dir and repoint the static pod — never restore into
      the live, running data-dir.
    • For app + PV recovery (and cross-cluster migration), use Velero with volume
      snapshots — etcd alone can't restore disk data.

================================================================================
    [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
================================================================================
    • Assuming etcd backs up PV data — it doesn't. Back volumes up separately.
    • Restoring into the LIVE etcd data-dir while etcd is running corrupts it —
      restore to a NEW dir and repoint, with etcd stopped.
    • Missing/incorrect --cacert/--cert/--key (or forgetting ETCDCTL_API=3) makes
      every etcdctl command fail with a cryptic TLS error; script the flags.
    • Keeping backups only on the same node — a node loss loses both the cluster
      and its backups.
    • Forgetting to repoint the etcd static pod's hostPath after restore — the
      cluster comes back on the OLD data and your restore appears to have "done
      nothing."
    • Not stopping the API server/etcd before restore — the kubelet may rewrite
      objects mid-restore.

================================================================================
    [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
================================================================================
    • Save the cert flags once: export ETCDCTL_API=3 and an alias with
      --endpoints/--cacert/--cert/--key so snapshot save/status/restore are short.
    • `etcdctl snapshot status snap.db --write-table` instantly tells you the
      snapshot is readable (hash, revision, size) — verify before you trust.
    • In the exam, the etcd certs are under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ — read the
      static pod manifest for the EXACT paths instead of guessing.
    • To "stop" etcd/apiserver fast in the exam, move their manifests out of
      /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ ; move them back to start.

================================================================================
    [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
================================================================================
    ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
      --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
      --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /backup/snap.db
    etcdctl snapshot status /backup/snap.db --write-table
    etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore
    # then edit the etcd static pod to point hostPath at /var/lib/etcd-restore
    kubectl describe pod etcd-master -n kube-system         # find real cert paths
    grep -E 'cert-file|key-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
    velero backup create easypj-daily --include-namespaces easypj --snapshot-volumes
    velero restore create --from-backup easypj-daily

================================================================================
    [L] 🧪 DRILL
================================================================================
    Take a verified snapshot, create a marker object (e.g. a ConfigMap), delete
    it, then restore the snapshot into a NEW data-dir, repoint the etcd static
    pod, and confirm the marker object is back — timing the whole RTO.

================================================================================
    [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
================================================================================
    Q1. Schedule automated etcd backups. Approach?
        A. A CronJob (or systemd timer) on the control-plane node running
        `etcdctl snapshot save` with the etcd certs, plus an off-node copy and
        retention pruning. A host systemd timer is more robust because it fires
        even when the cluster control plane is unhealthy.

    Q2. Verify a snapshot is valid without restoring it.
        A. `etcdctl snapshot status snap.db --write-table` — shows hash,
        revision, total keys, and size; failure means a corrupt/partial file.

    Q3. Perform a full etcd restore.
        A. Stop the API/etcd (move their static pod manifests aside), run
        `etcdutl snapshot restore snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore`,
        repoint the etcd static pod's hostPath to it, start etcd, verify objects.

    Q4. What does an etcd snapshot NOT contain?
        A. The data inside PersistentVolumes (e.g. postgres files). Only API
        object state is captured.

    Q5. Why have a retention policy?
        A. To bound storage and keep enough history to meet RPO; prune old
        snapshots but keep enough points to recover from a late-discovered issue.

    Q6. Where should backups be stored and why?
        A. OFF the node, in object storage — so losing the node (or cluster)
        doesn't lose the backups too.

    Q7. How do you back up easypj's namespace AND its PV data?
        A. Velero with a volume-snapshot or restic/node-agent plugin — it
        captures the API objects and the PersistentVolume contents together.

    Q8. Restore easypj into a brand-new cluster. Tool and flow?
        A. Velero restore from the backup in object storage into the new cluster,
        which recreates the namespace objects and PV data.

    Q9. Define RPO and RTO.
        A. RPO = maximum acceptable data loss (drives backup frequency); RTO =
        maximum acceptable downtime (drives how fast restore must run).

    Q10. Give the order of a DR runbook after total control-plane loss.
         A. Provision a node → restore the latest verified etcd snapshot →
         repoint etcd → bring up the control plane → restore PV data (Velero) →
         validate workloads → document actual RPO/RTO achieved.

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING — after restore, kubectl works but my object is missing:
       the object was created AFTER the snapshot's revision (it's outside your
       RPO), OR you restored but forgot to repoint the hostPath and etcd came up
       on the old data-dir. Check the etcd static pod's volume path.

================================================================================
    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — the backup → verify → restore → validate loop
================================================================================
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                                                      │
    │    ⏰ BACKUP  ──►  🔍 VERIFY  ──►  📤 SHIP OFF-NODE  ──►  🧪 TEST    │
    │   (save snap)    (status        (object store +        RESTORE       │
    │        ▲          --write-table)  retention)            (new dir →   │
    │        │                                                 repoint →   │
    │        │                                                 ✅ validate)│
    │        └───────────────────  document RPO / RTO  ◄───────────┘       │
    │                                                                      │
    │   etcd snapshot = the cluster BRAIN (API state).                     │
    │   Velero        = the cluster BODY  (namespaces + PV DATA).          │
    │   You need BOTH for true disaster recovery.                          │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    .vs-prose SUMMARY: Disaster recovery for Kubernetes is a loop, not a one-off
    command. You SAVE an etcd snapshot (capturing all API state with the four
    cert flags), VERIFY it with `snapshot status --write-table`, SHIP it off the
    node to object storage with retention, and periodically TEST-restore it into
    a fresh data-dir, repointing the etcd static pod and validating that a marker
    object returns. etcd protects the cluster's brain (API objects) but NOT the
    body (PersistentVolume data), so pair it with Velero to back up the easypj
    namespace and its postgres volume together — and to migrate or rebuild on a
    new cluster. Define RPO and RTO, prove them with drills, and document the
    runbook: a backup you have never restored is not a backup.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 30: Node Maintenance & OS Upgrades                          🟡 🎯 🏢
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture / Workloads
        (self-healing & availability) · Weight: part of the 25% Cluster domain.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
  Real clusters need patching: kernel CVEs, OS package updates, hardware
  swaps, kubelet upgrades. The whole point of Kubernetes is that you can take
  a node OFFLINE for maintenance and your application — here easypj, the
  Django job-board project (jobpost app, served from Postgres on the cluster)
  — keeps serving traffic the entire time. This chapter is the disciplined,
  one-node-at-a-time routine that lets you patch the fleet without ever
  dropping easypj below a safe number of running pods. 💡 Maintenance is not
  an emergency; it is a planned, repeatable loop.

  🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC] — You WILL be asked to safely drain a node, create a
  PodDisruptionBudget, and reason about why a drain is hanging.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
  • cordon / drain / uncordon — what each does and the order to run them.
  • PodDisruptionBudgets (minAvailable / maxUnavailable) — gating voluntary
    disruption so easypj stays available.
  • The OS / kernel patching routine — drain → patch → reboot → uncordon,
    one node at a time.
  • Under-the-hood: the Eviction API, graceful termination, PDB internals.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
  🎯 Node drain and PodDisruptionBudgets are bread-and-butter cluster tasks.
  Expect a task like "safely take node02 out of service for a kernel patch,
  then bring it back" and "create a PDB so at least 2 web pods stay up." The
  full cluster-upgrade flow (kubeadm) and etcd backup/restore live alongside
  this in the 25% Cluster domain — see the PART 8 takeaways at the end.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
    30.1  Draining Nodes — Safe Pod Eviction        🎯
    30.2  PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB)                 🎯
    30.3  OS Upgrades & Kernel Patches              🏢
    🔧    Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER
    🔑    Key Takeaways · ⚠️ Gotchas · ⚡ Speed Tips · 🔑 Commands
    🧪    Lab Q&A (union)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


    30.1  Draining Nodes — Safe Pod Eviction
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - Gracefully move all pods off a node before maintenance
          - Node marked as unschedulable (SchedulingDisabled)
          - The flow is always: cordon → drain → (maintain) → uncordon

          📖 KEY TERMS:
          - cordon: mark a node unschedulable; running pods stay put, but no
            NEW pods land on it.
          - drain: cordon PLUS evict the pods already running on the node so
            they reschedule elsewhere.
          - uncordon: mark the node schedulable again so new pods may land.

          Drain vs Cordon vs Uncordon:
          ┌────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ Command    │ Effect                                           │
          ├────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
          │ cordon     │ Mark node unschedulable (existing pods stay)     │
          │ drain      │ Mark unschedulable + evict all pods              │
          │ uncordon   │ Mark node schedulable again                      │
          └────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          $ kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
          $ kubectl cordon <node>
          $ kubectl uncordon <node>

          [NODE MAINTENANCE FLOW]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                                                        │
          │   NORMAL         CORDON          DRAIN         BACK    │
          │  ┌──────┐      ┌──────┐       ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐  │
          │  │ Node │      │ Node │       │ Node │     │ Node │  │
          │  │ Ready│ ───▶ │ Ready│  ───▶ │ Ready│ ──▶│ Ready│  │
          │  │ Sched│      │ NoSch│       │ NoSch│     │ Sched│  │
          │  │ 🟢🟢🟢│      │ 🟢🟢🟢│       │ ⬜⬜⬜│     │ 🟢🟢🟢│  │
          │  └──────┘      └──────┘       └──────┘     └──────┘  │
          │  Pods run      Pods stay      Pods evicted  New pods  │
          │  Scheduled     No new pods    to other nodes accepted │
          │                scheduled                               │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          .vs-prose — Reading the maintenance flow: a node moves left to
          right through four states. NORMAL: the node is Ready and
          Schedulable, running its pods (🟢🟢🟢). CORDON: still Ready, but now
          SchedulingDisabled — the three pods stay running, yet no new pods
          will be placed here. DRAIN: the existing pods are evicted (⬜⬜⬜)
          and rescheduled onto other nodes; the node is empty and still
          unschedulable, ready for maintenance. BACK (after uncordon): the
          node is Ready and Schedulable again and accepts new pods. Through
          the whole cycle easypj keeps serving because its pods live on the
          OTHER nodes while this one is down.

    30.2  PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB)
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
          - Control how many pods can be unavailable during VOLUNTARY
            disruption (drain, node upgrade, scale-down by an admin).
          - Prevents a drain from killing too many pods at once.
          - 🛡️ A PDB GATES the eviction: a drain will BLOCK rather than drop
            easypj below the budget you declared.

          📖 minAvailable vs maxUnavailable — use EXACTLY ONE, never both:
          - minAvailable: the floor of healthy pods that must stay up.
          - maxUnavailable: the ceiling of pods that may be down at once.

          PDB YAML for easypj — minAvailable: 2
          ────────────────────────────────────────
          apiVersion: policy/v1
          kind: PodDisruptionBudget
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web-pdb
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            minAvailable: 2                  # keep >=2 web pods up during drains
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj-web
          # use EITHER minAvailable OR maxUnavailable, never both.
          # with 3 replicas + minAvailable:2, a drain may evict at most 1 at a time.

          PDB YAML for easypj — maxUnavailable: 1
          ────────────────────────────────────────
          apiVersion: policy/v1
          kind: PodDisruptionBudget
          metadata:
            name: easypj-web-pdb
            namespace: easypj
          spec:
            maxUnavailable: 1                # at most 1 web pod down at any moment
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj-web

          $ kubectl get pdb
          $ kubectl get pdb -n easypj        # ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column

          💡 INSIGHT: With 3 easypj-web replicas and minAvailable:2, the
          ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column reads 1 — the drain evicts one pod, waits
          for its replacement to become Ready on another node (restoring the
          count to 3), THEN evicts the next. The PDB turns a brute-force
          eviction into a safe rolling drain.

    30.3  OS Upgrades & Kernel Patches
          🏢 [DAY-2 / BEYOND]
          [PROCEDURE] — the safe loop, ONE node at a time:
          a) kubectl drain node → pods move to other nodes
          b) Perform OS upgrade / kernel patch
          c) Restart node (reboot)
          d) Verify kubelet running and healthy (node returns to Ready)
          e) kubectl uncordon node → pods can be scheduled again

          ⚡ [TIP] pod-eviction-timeout default is 5 minutes — if a node goes
          down WITHOUT a drain and stays down longer than that, its pods are
          eventually marked for deletion and rescheduled. A planned drain is
          always cleaner than relying on this timeout.

          [NODE MAINTENANCE — keep easypj up while a node goes down]
           🚫 cordon node2          (no NEW pods land here)
                ▼
           🏗️ drain node2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
                │  evicts pods -> rescheduled elsewhere
                │  🛡️ PodDisruptionBudget(minAvailable:2) GATES the eviction
                ▼  (drain BLOCKS if it would drop below minAvailable)
           🔧 patch / reboot / kernel update
                ▼
           ✅ uncordon node2        (schedulable again)
           ⚠️ drain also blocks on bare (unmanaged) pods -> --force only if intended.

          .vs-prose — Reading the keep-easypj-up flow: you first cordon node2
          so nothing new schedules there. Then you drain it with
          --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data; the existing pods are
          evicted and rescheduled onto other nodes. The eviction is gated by
          the PodDisruptionBudget — if removing a pod would drop easypj-web
          below minAvailable:2, the drain BLOCKS and waits instead of cutting
          into capacity. Once the node is clear you patch, reboot, or update
          the kernel. Finally you uncordon node2 so it is schedulable again
          and pods can return. The big warning: drain also refuses to evict
          bare (unmanaged) pods — use --force only when you genuinely mean to
          delete them permanently.

          🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which flag does the drain need?
          - Node runs DaemonSet pods (kube-proxy, CNI, log agents)? → add
            --ignore-daemonsets (those pods are pinned and can't move).
          - Pods use emptyDir scratch volumes? → add --delete-emptydir-data
            (acknowledges you accept losing that scratch data).
          - Bare pods with no controller? → drain refuses; --force deletes
            them with no replacement. Only if you truly intend it.

    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UTH:
    • How eviction respects PDBs. `kubectl drain` does NOT raw-delete pods.
      For each pod it calls the Eviction API (a POST to the pod's
      .../eviction subresource). The API server checks every PDB that
      selects the pod; if evicting it would violate a budget, the request is
      REJECTED (HTTP 429, "Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's
      disruption budget") and drain retries until the budget allows it.
    • Why DaemonSet pods need --ignore-daemonsets. DaemonSet pods are placed
      one-per-node by the DaemonSet controller, not by the scheduler. They
      can't be "moved" — a new one would just be recreated on the same node.
      Drain therefore refuses to touch them unless you explicitly skip them.
    • Graceful termination & terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Eviction sends
      SIGTERM, runs any preStop hook, and waits up to
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s) before SIGKILL — so a pod
      can finish in-flight requests, flush buffers, and deregister cleanly.

    🔬 DEEPER:
    • Eviction API vs raw deletion. `kubectl delete pod` bypasses PDBs
      entirely — it's an involuntary, immediate removal. The Eviction API
      (used by drain and the descheduler) is the ONLY path that honors
      disruption budgets. This is why "delete the pod" is NOT a substitute
      for "drain the node."
    • PDB unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy. Newer Kubernetes lets a PDB set
      unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow so that pods which are NOT
      Ready can always be evicted, even when the budget is otherwise
      exhausted. The default (IfHealthyBudget) can otherwise wedge a drain
      when broken pods count against the budget.
    • Drain timeouts & --grace-period. `--timeout` caps how long drain waits
      overall; `--grace-period` overrides the pod's termination grace. A PDB
      that can never be satisfied makes drain spin until the timeout.
    • Surge during drain. If a Deployment has spare capacity / maxSurge,
      evicted pods come up elsewhere BEFORE the budget is rechecked, so the
      drain proceeds smoothly. Tight clusters with no spare capacity stall.
    • NoExecute taint-based eviction vs drain. A drain is a VOLUNTARY,
      PDB-respecting eviction you trigger. A NoExecute taint (e.g.
      node.kubernetes.io/unreachable added when a node dies) is an
      INVOLUNTARY eviction by the node controller that does NOT consult PDBs
      and is governed by tolerationSeconds / pod-eviction-timeout instead.

    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS (merged)
    ─────────────────────────
    • Node maintenance flow: cordon (no new pods) → drain (evict existing
      pods) → patch/reboot → uncordon (schedulable again). Do ONE node at a
      time.
    • ✅ drain = evict pods + cordon. cordon = just stop scheduling.
      uncordon = make the node schedulable again.
    • `kubectl drain` needs --ignore-daemonsets (DaemonSet pods can't move)
      and usually --delete-emptydir-data (acknowledges losing emptyDir
      scratch data).
    • PodDisruptionBudgets (minAvailable / maxUnavailable) gate VOLUNTARY
      disruptions: a drain BLOCKS rather than drop easypj below the budget.
    • drain uses the Eviction API, which respects PDBs and graceful
      termination — unlike a raw pod delete.
    • ✅ Always verify after maintenance: `kubectl get nodes` should show all
      nodes Ready with the expected version, and pods rescheduled and
      healthy.
    • ✅ Cluster UPGRADE order: control plane FIRST, then workers. Never skip
      minor versions (1.30 → 1.31, NOT 1.30 → 1.32).
    • ✅ Upgrade steps: drain node → upgrade kubeadm → kubeadm upgrade apply →
      upgrade kubelet/kubectl → uncordon.
    • ✅ etcd backup is NON-NEGOTIABLE before any upgrade. Practice the
      snapshot save + restore flow until it's automatic.
    • ✅ PodDisruptionBudgets protect applications during voluntary
      disruptions (drain, upgrades, scaling).
    • 🎯 CKA Relevance: upgrades + etcd backup/restore + node drain are part
      of the 25% cluster domain. You WILL be asked to perform these.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (merged)
    ───────────────────
    • A too-strict PDB (e.g. minAvailable == replicas) makes drain hang
      FOREVER — nothing can be evicted. Scale up or relax the PDB.
    • drain refuses to evict bare/unmanaged pods (no controller) unless
      --force, which deletes them permanently with no replacement.
    • Forgetting --delete-emptydir-data stops the drain on pods with emptyDir
      volumes; forgetting --ignore-daemonsets stops it on DaemonSet pods.
    • Forgetting to UNCORDON leaves the node unschedulable after maintenance
      — capacity is silently missing and `kubectl get nodes` shows
      SchedulingDisabled.
    • `kubectl delete pod` is NOT a drain — it bypasses PDBs and gives no
      graceful, budget-aware eviction.
    • Relying on the 5-minute pod-eviction-timeout instead of a planned drain
      risks an outage window where pods are gone but not yet rescheduled.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ────────────
    • `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data` is
      the standard incantation — memorize it cold.
    • Watch a blocked drain's reason: it prints "cannot evict ... violates
      PDB"; scale up replicas or relax the PDB to proceed.
    • `kubectl get nodes` SchedulingDisabled column shows cordoned nodes at a
      glance.
    • `kubectl get pdb -n easypj` ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column tells you
      instantly how many evictions the budget currently permits.

    🔑 COMMANDS (must-remember)
    ───────────────────────────
      kubectl cordon <node>
      kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
      kubectl uncordon <node>
      kubectl create pdb easypj-web-pdb --selector=app=easypj-web --min-available=2
      kubectl get pdb -n easypj          # ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column
      kubectl get pdb -A
      kubectl get nodes                  # SchedulingDisabled = cordoned
      # --- cluster upgrade (kubeadm) context ---
      kubeadm upgrade plan
      kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.0
      apt-get install kubelet=1.31.0-00 kubectl=1.31.0-00
      systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet

    🧪 DRILL
    ────────
    Deploy easypj-web with 3 replicas + a minAvailable:2 PDB, drain its node,
    and watch the eviction proceed one pod at a time (never dropping below 2),
    then uncordon.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (union of both sources) — full answer + explanation each
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Q1. Safely take node2 down for a kernel patch. Full sequence?
        A. cordon node2 → drain node2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
        → patch/reboot → uncordon node2. Cordon stops new pods, drain evicts
        the running ones via the Eviction API, you patch while it's empty,
        then uncordon to return it to service.

    Q2. Difference between cordon and drain?
        A. cordon ONLY marks the node unschedulable (stops NEW pods, existing
        pods stay). drain also EVICTS the pods already running on it so they
        reschedule elsewhere. drain implicitly cordons first.

    Q3. Create a PDB keeping at least 2 easypj-web pods available.
        A. A PodDisruptionBudget with selector app=easypj-web and
        minAvailable: 2, or imperatively:
        `kubectl create pdb easypj-web-pdb --selector=app=easypj-web
        --min-available=2`.

    Q4. A drain hangs and won't finish. Likely cause?
        A. A PDB would be violated (or bare/DaemonSet pods block it). Check
        the ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column (`kubectl get pdb -n easypj`); relax
        the PDB or scale up replicas so an eviction is permitted.

    Q5. Why is --ignore-daemonsets needed?
        A. DaemonSet pods are pinned one-per-node and can't be rescheduled
        elsewhere, so drain refuses to proceed unless you tell it to skip
        them.

    Q6. What does --delete-emptydir-data acknowledge?
        A. That evicting pods with emptyDir volumes PERMANENTLY loses that
        scratch data; drain won't proceed on such pods without the flag.

    Q7. After maintenance the node takes no pods. What was missed?
        A. uncordon — the node is still SchedulingDisabled. Run
        `kubectl uncordon <node>`.

    Q8. Maintenance across a 5-node cluster — what order/pace?
        A. ONE node at a time (cordon/drain/patch/uncordon), verifying
        workloads stay healthy and PDBs are satisfied before moving to the
        next. Never drain multiple nodes in parallel.

    Q9. How does eviction give pods a clean shutdown?
        A. It sends SIGTERM and honors terminationGracePeriodSeconds (and
        preStop hooks) before SIGKILL, so apps can finish in-flight work and
        deregister gracefully.

    Q10. Outline the safe kernel-patch loop for the whole fleet.
         A. For each node: cordon → drain → apply patch → reboot → wait Ready
         → uncordon → confirm pods rescheduled and healthy, then move to the
         next node.

    Q11. What's the difference between a drain (voluntary) and a NoExecute
         taint eviction (involuntary)?
         A. A drain is a voluntary, PDB-respecting eviction you trigger via
         the Eviction API. A NoExecute taint (e.g. added when a node goes
         unreachable) is an involuntary eviction by the node controller that
         does NOT consult PDBs and is governed by tolerationSeconds /
         pod-eviction-timeout.

    Q12. Why isn't `kubectl delete pod` a substitute for draining a node?
         A. delete bypasses the Eviction API, so it ignores PodDisruption
         Budgets and offers no budget-aware, rolling eviction — it can drop
         easypj below its safe replica count instantly.

    🧪 VISUAL SUMMARY: a node going down and back up with easypj NEVER dropping
    below its PDB floor — cordon shuts the door to new pods, drain rolls the
    existing ones off one at a time (each replacement coming Ready elsewhere
    before the next is evicted), the node is patched and rebooted, and
    uncordon reopens it. The job board stays online the whole time.


  ┌──────────────────────── PART 8 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ─────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Upgrade order: backup etcd -> control plane -> workers; one minor at a │
  │    time; never skip a minor; mind version skew; restart kubelet.         │
  │ ✅ A backup is only real once you've test-RESTORED it; etcd does NOT back │
  │    up PV data (use Velero/volume snapshots for that).                    │
  │ ✅ cordon -> drain -> maintain -> uncordon; PodDisruptionBudgets keep     │
  │    easypj available during voluntary disruptions.                        │
  │ 🎯 EXAM: kubeadm upgrade and node drain are common, etcd restore is gold.│
  │ 🔑 kubeadm upgrade plan/apply/node · drain/cordon/uncordon · etcdctl     │
  │    snapshot save/restore                                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [PART 8 VISUAL SUMMARY]: the maintenance calendar — back up etcd, upgrade
  the control plane, then roll through the workers one drain at a time,
  patching and rebooting each, with PodDisruptionBudgets standing guard so
  easypj never goes dark.

  .vs-prose — Part 8 in one breath: the cluster lifecycle is a planned,
  ordered routine. ALWAYS snapshot etcd first and prove the restore works,
  because etcd is your only copy of cluster state (and it does not cover PV
  data — use Velero or volume snapshots for that). Upgrade the control plane
  before the workers, one minor version at a time, watching version skew, and
  restart the kubelet after each. For day-to-day patching, the cordon → drain
  → maintain → uncordon loop with PodDisruptionBudgets is what keeps easypj
  serving while individual nodes go down.

PART 9: TROUBLESHOOTING                                                 🔴 🎯
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapters 31-34  ·  CKA DOMAIN WEIGHT: 30% (THE BIGGEST)  ·  "Fix it fast"

  CKA Exam Weight: 30% — THIS IS THE HEAVIEST DOMAIN ON THE ENTIRE EXAM!

  ⚠️ CRITICAL: One in every three points lives here. If you master one Part,
     master this one. Speed and method beat raw recall.

  What you'll build: a repeatable diagnostic method and the reflexes to fix
  any broken easypj pod, node, control-plane component, or network path under
  exam time pressure.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  PART 9 INTRO
  ─────────────
  Troubleshooting is the largest slice of the exam AND the daily reality of the
  job. The secret is METHOD, not memorization: a fixed flow (gather -> read ->
  isolate -> fix -> verify) applied layer by layer (pod -> node -> control
  plane -> network). Every section here is a symptom you'll learn to read on
  easypj and a fix you'll drill until it's reflex.

  💡 INSIGHT: Candidates who fail Part 9 rarely fail from missing knowledge —
     they fail from flailing. They re-run the same command, guess at YAML, and
     burn minutes. The candidates who PASS run the SAME seven-step method on
     every single broken-thing task, regardless of what's broken. Method turns
     a panic moment into a checklist. That is the entire game of this Part.

  🧠 ANALOGY: Think like an emergency-room doctor (🩺), not a detective novelist.
     You don't theorize about the culprit; you take vitals in a fixed order
     (get -> describe -> logs -> exec -> isolate -> fix -> verify) and let the
     readings tell you where the bleed is. The body is the cluster; the layers
     (pod, node, control plane, network) are the organ systems.


  HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 9 map
  ──────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch31 PODS/CONTAINERS ─▶ Ch32 NODES/CONTROL PLANE ─▶ Ch34 SERVICES/NET   │
  │       (highest layer)        (the machines/brains)     (connectivity)   │
  │                 └──────────── Ch33 OBSERVE ───────────┘                 │
  │                    logs (output streams) + metrics (top)                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read the map top-down as a LAYER STACK. A symptom seen at the top (a Pod
  won't run) may have its ROOT CAUSE one layer down (the Node is NotReady, or
  the control plane can't schedule, or the network can't pull the image). Ch33
  (Observe) sits underneath every chapter because logs + metrics are the
  instruments you read at EVERY layer.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │                                                                            │
  │   LAYER            "IS IT HEALTHY?" CHECK            CHAPTER                │
  │   ─────────────    ─────────────────────────────    ───────                │
  │   Network/Svc      kubectl get svc,ep / curl ClusterIP   Ch34   ▲ deepest  │
  │   Control Plane    kubectl get pods -n kube-system        Ch32   │         │
  │   Node             kubectl get nodes / describe node      Ch32   │         │
  │   Pod/Container    kubectl get/describe pod / logs        Ch31   ▼ highest │
  │                                                                            │
  │   RULE: a Pod is only as healthy as the Node under it, which is only as    │
  │   healthy as the control plane scheduling it, which is only reachable      │
  │   through a working network. Start at the symptom's layer, then descend.   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


  PART 9 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION
  ────────────────────────────────
  Implementation thread: deliberately BREAK easypj in 10 classic ways and fix
  each with the SAME method. You will inflict — and then cure — image-pull
  failures, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKills, Pending pods (no resources / taints /
  PVC unbound), readiness-probe failures, a NotReady node (kubelet down),
  expired control-plane certs, a Service with no Endpoints, DNS resolution
  failure, and a NetworkPolicy that blocks traffic. Each break maps to a
  layer; each fix reinforces the flow until it is muscle memory.

  🩺 THE METHOD (memorize this — it is the spine of all four chapters):
     get  ->  describe (READ THE EVENTS!)  ->  logs (--previous)  ->  exec
       ->  isolate the layer  ->  fix  ->  verify

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: In the exam, 90% of "broken thing" tasks are SOLVED at STEP 2.
     The Events block of `kubectl describe` literally prints the reason
     (ImagePullBackOff, FailedScheduling, Unhealthy probe, FailedMount). Train
     yourself to jump straight to describe and read the bottom first.

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: `--previous` is how you read the logs of the container that
     ALREADY died in a CrashLoopBackOff. The current container may be too young
     to have logged anything useful; the crashed one holds the stack trace.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — pick your chapter by symptom:
     • Pod is Pending / CrashLooping / ImagePull / OOM / probe-failing  → Ch31
     • Node is NotReady, or a control-plane component / etcd / certs    → Ch32
     • "I can't see what's happening" — need logs, events, top, metrics → Ch33
     • Service returns nothing, DNS fails, NetworkPolicy blocks traffic → Ch34
