================================================================================
  Chapter 31: Debugging Pods & Containers                              🔴 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Troubleshooting (30% — the single
      heaviest-weighted CKA domain). 🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — 30% weight section]

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      Most failures in a Kubernetes cluster surface as a sick pod: it won't
      schedule, it won't pull its image, it boots and dies, or it runs but
      serves nothing. Debugging is not a single command — it is a DISCIPLINE: a
      fixed order of questions that routes you to the cause fast. On the exam,
      Troubleshooting is 30% of your score, and almost every task here hinges on
      one habit: read the pod STATE, then read describe Events, before you guess.
      VISUAL: a pod-status decision tree that turns "the pod is broken" into a
      precise next command.

  [C] OBJECTIVES
      • Read pod phases and container states fluently (Pending/Running/etc.).
      • Decode exit codes (0 / 1 / 137 OOM / 143 SIGTERM) and the CrashLoopBackOff
        backoff curve.
      • Apply the debug toolkit in the correct ORDER: status → describe(Events)
        → logs --previous → exec → events.
      • Use ephemeral debug containers (`kubectl debug`) for distroless images.
      • Diagnose and fix the common easypj failure modes end to end.

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE
      Troubleshooting is 30% of the exam. Expect tasks like "this pod is not
      Running, make it Running", "collect the logs of the crashed container into
      a file", or "the Service has no endpoints, fix it". Every one of these is
      solved by the method below, not by memorizing YAML.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      31.1 Pod Lifecycle & Status Codes
      31.2 The Debugging Toolkit (the ORDER)
      31.3 Essential Debug Commands
      31.4 Debugging easypj — Common Scenarios
      + 🔧 Under-the-Hood / 🔬 DEEPER, Key Takeaways, Gotchas, Speed Tips,
        Commands, Lab Q&A.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  31.1  Pod Lifecycle and Status Codes
        🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        A pod's PHASE is the high-level summary; the per-container STATE is where
        the real diagnosis lives. Read both.

        [TABLE: Pod phases and their meaning]
        | Phase        | Meaning                                          |
        | Pending      | Accepted but not yet running (scheduling/pull)   |
        | Running      | At least one container is running                |
        | Succeeded    | All containers terminated successfully           |
        | Failed       | All containers terminated, at least one failed   |
        | Unknown      | Cannot determine pod state (node comm issue)     |

        [TABLE: Common container states]
        | State                  | Common Cause                            |
        | Waiting: ErrImagePull  | Wrong image name or tag                 |
        | Waiting: CrashLoopBack | Container starts then crashes repeatedly|
        | Waiting: CreateContErr | Security context / volume mount issue   |
        | Waiting: ContainerCrea | Image pull or resource issue            |

        🧠 ANALOGY: the PHASE is the patient's triage colour (red/yellow/green);
        the STATE and Events are the chart that tells you what is actually wrong.

        EXIT CODES — the container's last words. When a container terminates,
        the kubelet records why. Memorize these four:

        ┌──────┬───────────────────┐
        │ 0    │ success           │  ← clean exit; for a Job this is "done"
        │ 1    │ app error         │  ← the application itself failed/raised
        │ 137  │ OOMKilled (mem)   │  ← 128+9: kernel SIGKILL, hit memory limit
        │ 143  │ graceful SIGTERM  │  ← 128+15: shut down on a terminate signal
        └──────┴───────────────────┘

        📖 KEY TERM — 128+signal: a non-zero exit ≥128 means the process was
        killed by a signal N where N = code − 128. 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL, OOM),
        143 = 128+15 (SIGTERM, graceful stop). This decoding is exam gold.

        [POD LIFECYCLE PILLS — phase progression]
        ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌──────────┐
        │ Pending │──►│ Running │──►│ Succeeded │   │  Failed  │
        └─────────┘   └────┬────┘   └───────────┘   └──────────┘
             ▲             │                              ▲
             │             └──── container exits ≠0 ──────┘
             │                    + restartPolicy=Never/OnFailure exhausted
             └──── stuck here = scheduling / image / config problem

        CRASHLOOPBACKOFF — THE BACKOFF CURVE. When a container keeps dying, the
        kubelet does NOT restart it instantly; it backs off exponentially so a
        broken pod can't hammer the node. The restart delay roughly doubles:

        crash → wait 10s → crash → 20s → 40s → 80s → 160s → cap 300s (5 min)
        █          █          █          █          █          █
        10s        20s        40s        80s       160s       300s (max)

        💡 INSIGHT: "CrashLoopBackOff" is a SYMPTOM, never a root cause. The pod
        is in the BackOff wait between restarts. The cause is in the previous
        container's logs (`--previous`) or in describe Events — not in the word
        "CrashLoopBackOff" itself.

        restartPolicy controls whether the kubelet retries at all:
        • Always (default for Deployments) — always restart, hence the loop.
        • OnFailure — restart only on non-zero exit (typical for Jobs).
        • Never — never restart; the pod goes Failed/Succeeded and stays.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  31.2  The Debugging Toolkit
        🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        There is ONE order. Burn it in: STATUS → DESCRIBE(Events) → LOGS
        --previous → EXEC → EVENTS. The most expensive mistake on the exam is
        skipping describe Events and guessing.

        🧭 DECISION GUIDE — the toolkit in order:
          1. STATUS    `kubectl get pod -o wide`  → what STATE is it in?
          2. DESCRIBE  `kubectl describe pod X`    → READ the Events section.
          3. LOGS      `kubectl logs X --previous` → the dead container's output.
          4. EXEC      `kubectl exec -it X -- sh`  → inspect a running container.
          5. EVENTS    `kubectl get events`        → cluster-wide timeline.

        [DEBUGGING DECISION TREE]
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  POD NOT WORKING? Follow this tree:                    │
        │                                                        │
        │  $ kubectl get pods -o wide                            │
        │       │                                                │
        │       ├── STATUS: Pending?                             │
        │       │    └── $ kubectl describe pod <name>           │
        │       │         ├── "Insufficient cpu/memory"          │
        │       │         │    → Scale cluster or adjust requests│
        │       │         ├── "No nodes match selector"          │
        │       │         │    → Check nodeSelector/affinity     │
        │       │         └── "Unbound PVC"                      │
        │       │              → Check PV/StorageClass           │
        │       │                                                │
        │       ├── STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff?                    │
        │       │    └── $ kubectl logs <pod> [--previous]       │
        │       │         ├── Application error                  │
        │       │         │    → Fix app code/config             │
        │       │         ├── Missing config/secret              │
        │       │         │    → Check ConfigMap/Secret exists   │
        │       │         └── Permission denied                  │
        │       │              → Check SecurityContext            │
        │       │                                                │
        │       ├── STATUS: ImagePullBackOff?                    │
        │       │    └── $ kubectl describe pod <name>           │
        │       │         ├── Wrong image name/tag               │
        │       │         │    → Fix image reference             │
        │       │         └── Private registry                   │
        │       │              → Add imagePullSecrets            │
        │       │                                                │
        │       └── STATUS: Running but not working?             │
        │            └── $ kubectl logs <pod>                    │
        │            └── $ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh     │
        │            └── $ kubectl port-forward <pod> 8080:8080  │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        [POD DEBUGGING DECISION TREE — read this top-down]
         kubectl get pod  ─ what STATE?
         ├─ Pending ─────► describe (Events): no resources? taint? unbound PVC?
         ├─ ImagePullBackOff ► describe: wrong image:tag / missing pull secret
         ├─ CreateContainerConfigError ► missing ConfigMap/Secret/key
         ├─ CrashLoopBackOff ► logs --previous: app error? OOM(137)? bad config?
         ├─ Running but bad ► logs + exec -it + check readiness/endpoints
         └─ Completed/Error ► it was a Job? check exit code
         🔁 ALWAYS: describe FIRST (read Events) → logs --previous → exec → fix → verify

        ⚠️ The #1 miss: skipping the Events section. describe Events almost always
        names the exact cause (FailedScheduling, Failed to pull image, OOMKilled,
        FailedMount). Read it before you theorize.

        WHERE LOGS LIVE — the cluster's logging architecture. When you run
        `kubectl logs`, the kubelet is reading container stdout/stderr from the
        node's filesystem. For fleet-wide debugging, a DaemonSet log agent ships
        those files to a central store. Know both paths:

        [KUBERNETES LOGGING ARCHITECTURE — FROM CONTAINER TO CENTRAL STORE]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                                              │
        │  ┌──────────── Worker Node 1 ─────────────┐                 │
        │  │                                         │                 │
        │  │  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐              │                 │
        │  │  │ Pod A   │  │ Pod B   │              │                 │
        │  │  │ stdout→ │  │ stdout→ │              │                 │
        │  │  └────┬────┘  └────┬────┘              │                 │
        │  │       │            │                    │                 │
        │  │       ▼            ▼                    │                 │
        │  │  /var/log/containers/*.log              │                 │
        │  │  /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>/       │                 │
        │  │       │                                 │                 │
        │  │       ▼                                 │                 │
        │  │  ┌──────────────────┐                   │                 │
        │  │  │ 📋 DaemonSet    │  fluentd /        │                 │
        │  │  │    Log Agent    │  filebeat /        │                 │
        │  │  │    (1 per node) │  fluent-bit        │                 │
        │  │  └────────┬────────┘                    │                 │
        │  │           │                             │                 │
        │  └───────────┼─────────────────────────────┘                 │
        │              │                                               │
        │  ┌───────────┼───── Worker Node 2 ──────────┐               │
        │  │           │                               │               │
        │  │  ┌────────┤  (same pattern)              │               │
        │  │  │ Pods → │ → /var/log/ → DaemonSet ──┤  │               │
        │  │  └────────┘                            │  │               │
        │  └────────────────────────────────────────┼──┘               │
        │                                           │                  │
        │              ┌────────────────────────────▼───────┐         │
        │              │  🗄️  CENTRAL LOG STORE              │         │
        │              │                                     │         │
        │              │  Elasticsearch / Loki / CloudWatch  │         │
        │              │         ▼                            │         │
        │              │  Kibana / Grafana   (visualization) │         │
        │              └─────────────────────────────────────┘         │
        │                                                              │
        │  Quick debug (no central logging needed):                   │
        │  kubectl logs <pod>           ← current logs               │
        │  kubectl logs <pod> --previous ← crashed container logs    │
        │  kubectl logs <pod> -f         ← stream live               │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: `kubectl logs` does NOT read your central store; it
        asks the kubelet, which serves the on-node container log file. That is
        why logs disappear when a node is gone — and why a DaemonSet agent that
        ships them off-node matters for day-2 forensics.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  31.3  Essential Debug Commands
        🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        $ kubectl get pods -o wide               # STATE + node + IP, one glance
        $ kubectl describe pod <name>            # Events + conditions (READ THIS)
        $ kubectl logs <pod>                     # Container stdout
        $ kubectl logs <pod> --previous          # Previous crashed container
        $ kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>      # Specific container
        $ kubectl logs <pod> -f                  # Stream live
        $ kubectl logs <pod> --since=5m          # Last 5 minutes only
        $ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh      # Shell into container
        $ kubectl exec -it <pod> -c <ctr> -- sh  # Shell into a named container
        $ kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>
                                                 # Ephemeral debug container
        $ kubectl port-forward <pod> 8080:8080   # Reach the app locally
        $ kubectl cp <pod>:/path ./local         # Pull a file out for inspection
        $ kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
        $ kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n <ns>
        $ kubectl top pod <name>                 # CPU/memory usage (metrics-server)

        🧪 EPHEMERAL DEBUG CONTAINERS — the distroless fix. You cannot
        `exec` into a container that has no shell (distroless) or won't stay up
        (CrashLoop). `kubectl debug` injects a throwaway container that SHARES
        the target's namespaces, so its tools see the target's filesystem,
        network and (optionally) processes:

        $ kubectl debug -it easypj-web --image=busybox --target=web -- sh
          # inside, you have busybox tools but see the 'web' container's network
          # and, with --target, its process namespace.

        ⚡ SPEED TIP: jump straight to the cause with
          $ kubectl describe pod X | sed -n '/Events/,$p'

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  31.4  Debugging easypj — Common Scenarios
        🧪 [LAB]
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        These are the failure modes you will actually hit running the easypj
        Django project (project = easypj, app = jobpost; Skills/Author/Location/
        JobPost/auth.User models; Gunicorn serving on :8000; PostgreSQL backend).

        [EXIT CODES & easypj real fixes]
        ┌──────┬───────────────────┐   easypj real fixes:
        │ 0    │ success           │   • CrashLoop: db refused -> initContainer wait
        │ 1    │ app error         │   • Pending: req 2Gi>free -> lower to 256Mi
        │ 137  │ OOMKilled (mem)   │   • 502: Django bound 127.0.0.1 -> 0.0.0.0:8000
        │ 143  │ graceful SIGTERM  │   • ConfigError: create easypj-config/-secret
        └──────┴───────────────────┘

        [SCENARIO 1: easypj pod in CrashLoopBackOff]
        → Symptom: easypj-web restarts in a loop; STATE CrashLoopBackOff.
        → Diagnose: `kubectl logs easypj-web --previous` shows
          "could not connect to server: Connection refused" (PostgreSQL).
        → Root cause: the web pod started before easypj-db was accepting
          connections — Django's migrate/connect fails and the process exits.
        → Fix: add an initContainer that blocks until the DB is reachable, so
          the main container only starts once easypj-db answers:

          spec:
            initContainers:
            - name: wait-for-db
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ['sh','-c',
                'until nc -z easypj-db 5432; do echo waiting for db; sleep 2; done']
            containers:
            - name: web
              image: easypj:1.0
              command: ['sh','-c','python manage.py migrate && \
                         gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application -b 0.0.0.0:8000']

        [SCENARIO 2: easypj pod Pending]
        → Symptom: easypj-web stuck Pending, never schedules.
        → Diagnose: `kubectl describe pod easypj-web` → Events:
          "0/3 nodes are available: Insufficient memory."
        → Root cause: the pod requested resources.requests.memory: 2Gi but no
          node has that much free.
        → Fix: lower the request to what the app actually needs (~256Mi), or add
          capacity:
            resources:
              requests: { memory: "256Mi", cpu: "100m" }
              limits:   { memory: "512Mi", cpu: "500m" }

        [SCENARIO 3: easypj pod Running but 502 errors]
        → Symptom: pod is Running, but the Service/Ingress returns 502.
        → Diagnose: `kubectl exec -it easypj-web -- sh`; Gunicorn is listening on
          127.0.0.1:8000 only, so traffic from the Service (a different network
          namespace) is refused.
        → Root cause: Django/Gunicorn bound to loopback, and/or ALLOWED_HOSTS
          rejects the request host.
        → Fix: bind to all interfaces and allow the host:
            gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
            # settings.py:  ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']  (or the Service/Ingress host)

        [SCENARIO 4: easypj pod ImagePullBackOff]
        → Diagnose: describe Events → "Failed to pull image easypj:latset:
          not found" or "no basic auth credentials".
        → Fix: correct the image:tag (easypj:1.0, not a typo), or for a private
          registry add an imagePullSecret:
            kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
              --docker-server=<reg> --docker-username=<u> --docker-password=<p>
            # then reference it: spec.imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]

        [SCENARIO 5: easypj pod CreateContainerConfigError]
        → Diagnose: the pod references easypj-config / easypj-secret (DB host,
          SECRET_KEY) or a key that doesn't exist.
        → Fix: create the missing object or correct the key name:
            kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DB_HOST=easypj-db
            kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret \
              --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=... --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=...

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      🔧 UTH:
      • Backoff math: the kubelet tracks per-container restart attempts and
        multiplies the delay (10s base, ×2 each time) up to a 300s cap; the
        timer resets only after the container stays up long enough.
      • Probes drive restarts AND traffic: a failing livenessProbe makes the
        kubelet KILL and restart the container (can cause CrashLoop); a failing
        readinessProbe leaves the container running but pulls it OUT of the
        Service endpoints (silent 502/no-traffic).
      • Ephemeral containers are a real pod sub-resource (`pods/ephemeralcontainers`)
        injected at runtime — they cannot be added by editing the spec normally;
        `kubectl debug` uses that API.

      🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
      • Exit code 128+signal decoding (137=SIGKILL/OOM, 143=SIGTERM, 134=SIGABRT).
      • shareProcessNamespace: true lets containers in a pod see each other's
        processes — pairs with `kubectl debug --target` to enter a process ns.
      • `kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox` gives you a host-mounted
        debug pod to inspect a sick NODE (kubelet, /var/log, disk pressure).
      • readinessGates: extend readiness with custom pod conditions.
      • terminationMessagePath / terminationMessagePolicy: the container can
        write its last words to /dev/termination-log; describe surfaces them.
      • OOM forensics: read the cgroup memory.max / memory.events on the node to
        confirm a limit hit vs. node-level memory pressure eviction.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • Read the pod STATE first, then let it route you: Pending (scheduling),
        ImagePullBackOff (image/secret), CreateContainerConfigError (missing
        cm/secret), CrashLoopBackOff (app/config), Running-but-bad (probes/net).
      • THE METHOD: describe (read Events!) → logs --previous → exec → fix →
        verify. Skipping Events is the #1 wasted-time mistake.
      • Exit codes tell the story: 0 success, 1 app error, 137 OOMKilled (memory),
        143 graceful SIGTERM. 137 is a limits problem, not a code bug.
      • CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom of the backoff timer, never the root cause —
        the cause is in `--previous` logs or Events.
      • For crashed/distroless containers use `logs --previous` and `kubectl
        debug` ephemeral containers — you can't exec a container that won't stay up.
      • A failing readinessProbe causes silent "no traffic"; a failing
        livenessProbe causes restart loops. Know which symptom maps to which.
      • `kubectl logs` reads the on-node file via the kubelet; central logging
        (DaemonSet → Elasticsearch/Loki) is what survives a dead node.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • Forgetting `--previous` shows the NEW container's (empty) logs, not the
        crash you need to see.
      • Ignoring the Events section of describe — it usually states the exact
        cause (FailedScheduling, Failed pull, OOMKilled).
      • In multi-container pods, `logs`/`exec` default to one container — use
        `-c <name>` or you read the wrong one.
      • Misreading OOMKilled (137) as an application bug — it's the memory limit;
        raise limits or fix the leak.
      • Treating "CrashLoopBackOff" as a cause — it is only the wait state; dig
        into logs/Events for the real reason.
      • `kubectl top` returning nothing means metrics-server isn't installed, not
        that the pod uses no resources.
      • Trying to `exec` into a distroless or already-dead container — use
        `kubectl debug` instead.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      • describe FIRST, always — `kubectl describe pod X | sed -n '/Events/,$p'`
        jumps straight to the cause.
      • `kubectl debug -it pod/X --image=busybox --target=app` attaches a tool
        container sharing the target's namespace — no need to rebuild the image.
      • `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` across the namespace shows
        the timeline when one pod's describe isn't enough.
      • `kubectl get pod X -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}'`
        prints the last-termination reason and exit code without scrolling.
      • `kubectl logs X --previous -c web | tail` is the fastest CrashLoop probe.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🔑 COMMANDS
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      kubectl get pod easypj-web -o wide
      kubectl describe pod easypj-web                 # READ Events
      kubectl logs easypj-web --previous -c web
      kubectl logs easypj-web -f --since=10m
      kubectl exec -it easypj-web -c web -- sh
      kubectl debug -it easypj-web --image=busybox --target=web
      kubectl port-forward easypj-web 8080:8000
      kubectl cp easypj-web:/app/logs/app.log ./app.log
      kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n easypj
      kubectl top pod easypj-web -n easypj

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 DRILL
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Deploy an easypj-web that CrashLoops because the DB connection is refused.
      Read the previous logs, add an initContainer that waits for easypj-db, and
      watch it go Running. Then break it again with a 2Gi memory request, confirm
      it goes Pending via describe Events, and fix the Pending by lowering the
      request. Finally, reproduce the 502 by binding Gunicorn to 127.0.0.1 and
      fix it by binding 0.0.0.0:8000 with ALLOWED_HOSTS set.

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪 LAB Q&A
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Q1. A pod is CrashLoopBackOff. How do you find the root cause?
          A. `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to read the dead container's output,
          plus describe Events; common causes: DB refused, bad config, missing
          env. CrashLoopBackOff itself is only the backoff wait state.

      Q2. A pod is stuck Pending. First command and likely causes?
          A. `kubectl describe pod` → Events. Causes: insufficient cpu/mem, no
          node tolerates a taint, unbound PVC, or nodeSelector/affinity unmet.

      Q3. ImagePullBackOff — how do you fix it?
          A. describe shows the pull error: fix the image:tag, the registry name,
          or add/repair an imagePullSecret for a private registry.

      Q4. How do you see logs from a container that already crashed?
          A. `kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous` — the current
          instance may have no useful logs.

      Q5. Exec into a running pod to inspect its filesystem/env.
          A. `kubectl exec -it <pod> -c <container> -- sh` (or bash), then
          inspect /env, mounted config, and connectivity.

      Q6. A pod shows exit code 137. What happened and the fix?
          A. OOMKilled — it exceeded its memory limit (137 = 128+9, SIGKILL).
          Raise the limit or reduce memory use; it is not an application crash.

      Q7. The image is distroless (no shell). How do you debug it?
          A. `kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container>` to
          attach an ephemeral debug container sharing its namespaces.

      Q8. CreateContainerConfigError — what's wrong?
          A. The pod references a ConfigMap/Secret or key that doesn't exist.
          Create the missing object (easypj-config/easypj-secret) or fix the key.

      Q9. The pod runs but the Service sends no traffic to it. Why?
          A. Its readiness probe is failing, so it's excluded from endpoints. Fix
          the probe path/port or the app so readiness passes.

      Q10. easypj returns 502 through the Service. Likely app fix?
           A. Django/Gunicorn bound to 127.0.0.1 — bind 0.0.0.0:8000 (and set
           ALLOWED_HOSTS) so the container accepts traffic from the Service.

      Q11. What is exit code 143, and is it a problem?
           A. 143 = 128+15 (SIGTERM) — a graceful shutdown, e.g. a rolling
           update or scale-down. Normal, not an error by itself.

      Q12. A pod CrashLoops only after running fine for ~30s each cycle. What
           single feature is the likely culprit?
           A. A failing livenessProbe killing the container — check the probe's
           path/port/initialDelaySeconds; loosen it or fix the endpoint.

      Q13. The whole node looks unhealthy. How do you get a shell to debug it?
           A. `kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox` — it schedules a
           privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted so you can inspect
           kubelet logs, /var/log, and disk pressure.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: the pod-debugging decision tree above is the chapter in one
      picture — read the pod STATE, branch to the matching cause (Pending →
      scheduling, ImagePullBackOff → image/secret, CreateContainerConfigError →
      missing cm/secret, CrashLoopBackOff → app/config via --previous logs,
      Running-but-bad → probes/network), and ALWAYS run describe and READ Events
      before logs → exec → fix → verify. The .vs-prose takeaway: debugging is a
      fixed order, not a guess; the pod's STATE and the describe Events tell you
      exactly where to look, and exit codes (137 OOM, 143 SIGTERM) finish the
      diagnosis.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Every other chapter assumes kubectl works. This chapter is about the moment
  it DOESN'T. When the apiserver is down, when a node falls off the cluster,
  when a single typo in a static-pod manifest silently kills the control
  plane — kubectl is useless and you must debug from the NODE itself, with
  systemd, journalctl and crictl. The CKA loves to break a cluster and time
  you on bringing it back. Mastering the "kubectl is down — now what?" flow is
  worth more raw points than any application-layer skill.

      💡 INSIGHT: Application troubleshooting (Chapter 31) is debugging things
      RUNNING ON Kubernetes. Node/control-plane troubleshooting is debugging
      KUBERNETES ITSELF. The first uses kubectl; the second assumes kubectl is
      broken and drops you to the host.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OBJECTIVES
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Diagnose a NotReady node systematically, from the node, not the API.
    • Read and interpret node Conditions (Memory/Disk/PID pressure, NetUnavail).
    • Troubleshoot the kubelet as a systemd service (config, certs, swap, runtime).
    • Troubleshoot control-plane STATIC PODS with crictl when the apiserver is down.
    • Diagnose cluster-level failures: etcd health, expired certs, full disk,
      port conflicts — and recover systematically.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CKA RELEVANCE
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🎯 Troubleshooting is 30% of the exam; cluster architecture / install /
       maintenance is another 25%. Expect a broken kubelet, a malformed
       static-pod manifest, a NotReady node, expired certs, or a wedged etcd —
       and a clock. Speed at journalctl + crictl is what passes this exam.

================================================================================
  32.1  Node Not Ready — Diagnosis                                          🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    A NotReady node means the kubelet on that node has stopped sending healthy
    status to the apiserver (or is reporting a problem condition). The golden
    rule: kubectl can TELL you a node is NotReady, but it cannot FIX it —
    everything past the diagnosis happens by SSH-ing onto the node.

    [NODE TROUBLESHOOTING FLOWCHART]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  $ kubectl get nodes                                   │
          │       │                                                │
          │       └── Node STATUS: NotReady?                       │
          │            │                                           │
          │       $ kubectl describe node <name>                   │
          │            │                                           │
          │            ├── Condition: MemoryPressure               │
          │            │    → Node running out of RAM              │
          │            │    → Evict pods or add resources          │
          │            │                                           │
          │            ├── Condition: DiskPressure                  │
          │            │    → Node running out of disk             │
          │            │    → Clean up or add storage              │
          │            │                                           │
          │            ├── Condition: PIDPressure                   │
          │            │    → Too many processes                   │
          │            │    → Find runaway process                 │
          │            │                                           │
          │            └── Condition: NetworkUnavailable            │
          │                 → CNI plugin issue                     │
          │                 → Check CNI pod status                 │
          │                                                        │
          │  SSH into the node:                                    │
          │  $ systemctl status kubelet                            │
          │  $ journalctl -u kubelet -f                            │
          │  $ systemctl restart kubelet                           │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    [NODE NotReady — diagnose from the NODE (kubectl may be useless)]
     kubectl get nodes ─ node2 NotReady
          ▼ ssh node2
     systemctl status kubelet ─ running? ──no──► systemctl start kubelet
          ▼ yes                                   (daemon-reload if config changed)
     journalctl -u kubelet -f ─ read the error:
          ├─ "cni plugin not initialized"  ─► install / fix the CNI
          ├─ "failed to run Kubelet: swap" ─► swapoff -a (+ fstab)
          ├─ x509 / certificate expired    ─► renew the kubelet cert
          └─ runtime down                  ─► systemctl restart containerd
     🔧 apiserver itself down? use crictl ps -a · crictl logs <id> (NOT kubectl).

    Common NotReady causes (memorize this list — the exam picks from it):
      • kubelet down / crashed / not enabled
      • CNI plugin missing or unhealthy (NetworkUnavailable)
      • swap left enabled on the node
      • container runtime (containerd) down
      • disk pressure / memory pressure / PID pressure
      • expired kubelet certificate (x509)

    📖 KEY TERM — Node Condition: a status flag the kubelet reports for the
       node — Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure,
       NetworkUnavailable. Read them with:
       $ kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'
       $ kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — node is NotReady:
       Is the kubelet running?   no → start it; read journalctl for WHY it died.
       Is the kubelet running but node still NotReady?
            → read its journal: CNI not initialized? swap? cert? runtime?
       Is it a pressure condition (Disk/Memory/PID)?
            → free the resource (prune images, kill runaway proc), pressure clears.

================================================================================
  32.2  Troubleshooting kubelet                                            🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    The kubelet is the ONE control component that is NOT a pod. It runs as a
    plain systemd service on every node (control-plane and worker alike). That
    is why you debug it with systemctl/journalctl, never kubectl.

      - kubelet runs as a systemd service (NOT a static pod)
      $ systemctl status kubelet
      $ journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50
      $ journalctl -u kubelet -f          # stream live — the #1 node-debug tool

    Common kubelet issues:
      a) Stopped/crashed → systemctl start kubelet
      b) Wrong config → check /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
      c) Certificate expired → check kubelet cert validity
      d) Cannot reach API server → check network/firewall
      e) Swap enabled → swapoff -a (+ remove from /etc/fstab)
      f) Container runtime down → systemctl restart containerd

    ⚠️ daemon-reload first: the kubelet's config lives in two places —
       /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (the config file) and its systemd unit /
       drop-ins (e.g. /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf).
       If you edit the unit or a drop-in you MUST run:
       $ systemctl daemon-reload
       $ systemctl restart kubelet
       Editing only config.yaml needs just a restart; editing the unit needs
       daemon-reload BEFORE restart or your change is silently ignored.

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — how a node is reported Ready:
       The kubelet has two heartbeats. (1) It posts NodeStatus (the Conditions)
       and (2) it renews a Lease object in the kube-node-lease namespace every
       few seconds. The node-controller watches the Lease; if it isn't renewed
       within the grace period the node is marked NotReady, and after a longer
       timeout its pods are evicted. So a NotReady node almost always means the
       kubelet itself is unhealthy — chase the kubelet, not the workloads.

       $ kubectl get leases -n kube-node-lease
       $ kubectl -n kube-node-lease get lease <node> -o yaml   # renewTime field

    Quick checklist when the kubelet won't start:
       1. systemctl status kubelet        # active? exited? what's the error line?
       2. journalctl -u kubelet -e         # jump to the end, read the real cause
       3. cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml # cgroupDriver, clusterDNS, etc.
       4. systemctl status containerd      # runtime must be up first
       5. free -h ; swapon --show          # swap must be OFF
       6. cert expiry (see 32.5)

================================================================================
  32.3  Troubleshooting Control Plane Components                           🎯
================================================================================
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    Control plane components run as static pods:
      - Located in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
      - kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml,
        kube-controller-manager.yaml, etcd.yaml

      $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system
      $ kubectl logs kube-apiserver-master -n kube-system
      $ kubectl logs kube-scheduler-master -n kube-system
      [TIP: If API server is down, use crictl or docker directly]
      $ crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver
      $ crictl logs <container-id>

    📖 KEY TERM — Static Pod: a pod the kubelet runs DIRECTLY from a manifest
       file on disk (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/), not from the apiserver. The
       kubelet WATCHES that directory: drop a file in and it creates the pod
       within seconds; remove or break the file and it deletes/recreates it.
       That's how the control plane bootstraps before any apiserver exists —
       and why kubectl can't manage these pods directly.

    [COMPONENT-DOWN MATRIX — which symptom maps to which static pod]
     ┌────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ SYMPTOM                 │ LIKELY COMPONENT / FIX                        │
     ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ kubectl times out /     │ kube-apiserver down. crictl ps -a | grep      │
     │ "connection refused"    │ apiserver; crictl logs <id>; check etcd too.  │
     ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Pods stay Pending,      │ kube-scheduler down. crictl logs scheduler;   │
     │ never get a node        │ check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-         │
     │                         │ scheduler.yaml.                               │
     ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Deploy doesn't create   │ kube-controller-manager down. crictl logs     │
     │ pods / nodes never      │ controller-manager; check its manifest.       │
     │ cleaned up              │                                               │
     ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ apiserver up but every  │ etcd down/unhealthy. crictl logs etcd;        │
     │ write fails / flaky     │ etcdctl endpoint health (with certs).         │
     ├────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Manifest edited, pod    │ Bad manifest (YAML/flag typo). FAILS SILENTLY │
     │ never reappears         │ via kubectl — read crictl logs / journalctl   │
     │                         │ -u kubelet; fix the file, kubelet recreates.  │
     └────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ⚠️ The silent-failure trap: a typo in a static-pod manifest does NOT
       surface as a kubectl error — kubectl simply never shows the pod, or
       shows it stuck. The kubelet logs the parse/run failure. So when a static
       pod misbehaves:
       $ journalctl -u kubelet -e | grep -i <component>
       $ crictl ps -a | grep <component>     # look for Exited containers
       $ crictl logs <container-id>

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — the recovery loop for a broken apiserver:
       1. ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/         # confirm the manifest exists
       2. Move it OUT briefly if you must stop the pod:
          mv kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/   (kubelet deletes the pod)
          ...fix it... then mv it back   (kubelet recreates the pod)
       3. crictl ps -a | grep apiserver         # is the container looping?
       4. crictl logs <id>                       # read the real error
       5. Validate flags/paths (cert paths, --etcd-servers, ports).
       Because the kubelet, not the apiserver, manages static pods, this loop
       works even with kubectl completely dead.

================================================================================
  32.4  Troubleshooting Networking                                         🩺
================================================================================
      - Pod cannot reach other pods → check CNI plugin
      - Service not responding → check endpoints
      $ kubectl get endpoints <service-name>
      - DNS not resolving → check CoreDNS pods
      $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
      $ kubectl exec -it <test-pod> -- nslookup <service-name>

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING LADDER — "my pods can't talk":
       1. CNI healthy?    kubectl get pods -n kube-system   (calico/flannel/
          cilium DaemonSet must be Running on every node). A missing CNI is the
          classic cause of both NotReady nodes (NetworkUnavailable) and
          pod-to-pod failures.
       2. Service has endpoints? kubectl get endpoints <svc> — EMPTY endpoints
          means the selector matches no Ready pods (label typo or pods not ready).
       3. DNS works? CoreDNS pods Running; nslookup <svc> from a debug pod;
          check the pod's /etc/resolv.conf points at the cluster DNS IP.
       4. kube-proxy healthy? Service IPs are realized by kube-proxy
          (iptables/IPVS) on each node — if kube-proxy is down, ClusterIPs stop
          working even though endpoints look fine.

    💡 INSIGHT — for the easypj demo app: if the jobpost pods can reach the
       'easypj-db' Service by name (PostgreSQL on Kubernetes) but a fresh
       deployment suddenly can't, check, in order: the Service's endpoints
       (did the DB pod's labels change?), then CoreDNS, then the NetworkPolicy
       (a default-deny policy silently blocking jobpost→db is a favorite trap).

================================================================================
  32.5  Cluster-Level Failures & Systematic Recovery                       🩺
================================================================================
    Beyond a single node, whole-cluster failures cluster around a few causes.
    Work them top-down and you'll recover almost any broken kubeadm cluster.

    [A] etcd unhealthy — the apiserver is only as healthy as etcd:
        $ crictl ps -a | grep etcd
        $ crictl logs <etcd-container-id>
        $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health \
            --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
            --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
            --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
            --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
        Watch for: disk too slow ("apply entries took too long"), lost quorum,
        or a database space-exceeded (NOSPACE) alarm → defrag / compact.

    [B] Expired certificates — x509 errors everywhere:
        $ kubeadm certs check-expiration
        $ kubeadm certs renew all
        ...then restart the affected static pods (move manifests out/in) and the
        kubelet. The kubelet client cert usually auto-rotates; the rest don't.

    [C] Full disk on a control-plane node:
        Symptoms: DiskPressure, etcd "no space", apiserver crashlooping.
        $ df -h ; du -sh /var/lib/*
        $ crictl rmi --prune            # remove unused images
        $ journalctl --vacuum-size=200M # trim systemd journal
        Free space, then etcd/apiserver recover on their own.

    [D] Port conflicts / firewall:
        Required ports (6443 apiserver, 2379/2380 etcd, 10250 kubelet,
        10257/10259 controller/scheduler). A blocked 6443 or 10250 looks like a
        NotReady node or a dead apiserver. Check with ss -tlnp and firewall rules.

    SYSTEMATIC RECOVERY ORDER (broken cluster, top-down):
        1. etcd healthy?        (nothing works without it)
        2. apiserver up?        (crictl, not kubectl)
        3. kubelet up on each node?
        4. controller-manager + scheduler up?
        5. CNI / kube-proxy healthy?
        6. certs valid? disk free? ports open?

================================================================================
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
================================================================================
    🔧 UTH: How the kubelet reports node conditions and the node-lease
       heartbeat; how a bad static-pod manifest fails silently (only crictl /
       journalctl reveal it); how the kubelet recreates a static pod within
       seconds of the manifest file changing.

    🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
      • kubelet FLAGS vs config.yaml PRECEDENCE: command-line flags in the
        systemd unit override config.yaml; kubeadm puts most settings in
        config.yaml and a few in the drop-in. Check BOTH when behavior is wrong.
      • node-problem-detector: a DaemonSet that surfaces kernel/hardware faults
        as node Conditions/Events — day-2 observability beyond the kubelet's own.
      • /var/log/pods and /var/log/containers: the on-disk logs the kubelet
        writes; readable even when kubectl logs can't reach the apiserver.
      • crictl inspect / crictl exec: inspect a container's full runtime state
        or shell into it directly via the CRI socket — no apiserver involved.
      • cgroup-driver MISMATCH: if the kubelet's cgroupDriver (systemd vs
        cgroupfs) disagrees with containerd's, pods fail to start with cryptic
        runtime errors and the node may flap NotReady. Both must say "systemd".
      • node-lease update frequency: the Lease in kube-node-lease is renewed
        far more often than full NodeStatus — it's the cheap, fast heartbeat the
        node-controller actually watches for liveness.
      🏢 DAY-2 / BEYOND: in production you'd add node-problem-detector, alert on
         Lease renewal gaps, monitor etcd db size and fsync latency, and
         automate cert renewal — the exam tests the manual versions of all four.

================================================================================
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
================================================================================
    • When a node is NotReady, diagnose FROM the node: `systemctl status
      kubelet` → `journalctl -u kubelet -f` → read the error → fix → restart.
    • The kubelet is a systemd service, NOT a pod. Its config is
      /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml; after editing the UNIT, daemon-reload
      before restart.
    • Control-plane components are STATIC PODS in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
      A typo there fails silently — when the apiserver is down, use `crictl ps
      -a` and `crictl logs`, not kubectl.
    • Common NotReady causes: kubelet down, CNI missing, swap on, container
      runtime down, disk/memory/PID pressure, expired certs.
    • Node Conditions (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure,
      NetworkUnavailable) tell you WHICH resource or subsystem failed — read
      them with `kubectl describe node` or jsonpath on .status.conditions.
    • The kubelet's node-lease heartbeat (kube-node-lease) is what the
      node-controller watches; a stale lease = NotReady.
    • Recover a broken cluster top-down: etcd → apiserver → kubelet →
      controller-manager/scheduler → CNI/kube-proxy → certs/disk/ports.

================================================================================
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
================================================================================
    • Reaching for kubectl when the apiserver itself is down — it can't help;
      switch to crictl/journalctl on the node.
    • Editing kubelet config or a unit and forgetting `systemctl daemon-reload`
      before restart — the change doesn't take.
    • A bad static-pod manifest doesn't show an error via kubectl; only
      crictl/journalctl/kubelet logs reveal it.
    • Swap left enabled stops the kubelet from starting (unless explicitly
      allowed) — `swapoff -a` + fix /etc/fstab so it stays off after reboot.
    • cgroup-driver mismatch (kubelet vs containerd) causes pods to fail and the
      node to flap — both must be "systemd".
    • Empty Service endpoints look like a network bug but are usually a label /
      readiness problem, not CNI.
    • etcd on a slow or full disk silently degrades the WHOLE control plane —
      check etcd before blaming the apiserver.

================================================================================
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
================================================================================
    • `journalctl -u kubelet -f` streaming the kubelet error is the single most
      useful node-debug command.
    • Editing (or moving out/in) a file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ makes the
      kubelet recreate that static pod within seconds — no restart needed.
    • `crictl ps -a | grep apiserver` then `crictl logs <id>` reads the
      apiserver's own logs when kubectl is dead.
    • `kubectl describe node <n> | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'` jumps
      straight to the Conditions block.
    • `kubeadm certs check-expiration` answers "is it the certs?" in one line.
    • `journalctl -u kubelet -e` jumps to the END of the log — the real error is
      almost always there, not at the top.

================================================================================
  🔑 COMMANDS
================================================================================
    systemctl status kubelet ; systemctl start kubelet ; systemctl restart kubelet
    systemctl daemon-reload                # after editing the kubelet unit/drop-in
    journalctl -u kubelet -f --no-pager    # stream the kubelet error
    journalctl -u kubelet -e               # jump to end of kubelet log
    systemctl status containerd ; systemctl restart containerd
    crictl ps -a                           # all CRI containers (incl. Exited)
    crictl logs <container-id>             # read a container's logs sans apiserver
    crictl inspect <container-id>          # full runtime state
    crictl rmi --prune                     # free disk: remove unused images
    kubectl get nodes
    kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'
    kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
    kubectl get leases -n kube-node-lease  # node heartbeat leases
    kubectl get pods -n kube-system        # control-plane + CNI + kube-proxy
    kubectl get endpoints <service-name>   # empty = selector/readiness problem
    kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns   # CoreDNS
    ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/          # the static-pod manifests
    swapoff -a ; swapon --show             # disable / verify swap
    kubeadm certs check-expiration ; kubeadm certs renew all
    ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
      --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
      --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
    df -h ; ss -tlnp                       # disk + listening ports

================================================================================
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 32
================================================================================
    🧪 DRILL: Stop the kubelet (or introduce a typo into the apiserver static-
    pod manifest), observe the node / control-plane break, diagnose it with
    journalctl / crictl, and restore service.

    🟢 Q1. A node is NotReady. Outline the diagnosis.
        A. ssh to it → `systemctl status kubelet` → `journalctl -u kubelet -f`
        → read the error (CNI / swap / cert / runtime) → fix → restart the
        kubelet. kubectl can only TELL you it's NotReady; the fix is on the node.

    🟢 Q2. The kubelet won't start. Where do you look?
        A. journalctl -u kubelet, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, and the
        container runtime status (systemctl status containerd); common causes
        are swap on, cert expiry, bad config, runtime down. Read journalctl -e
        for the actual failing line.

    🟡 Q3. kubectl times out — the apiserver seems down. How do you debug?
        A. On the control-plane node use `crictl ps -a` to find the apiserver
        container and `crictl logs <id>` to read why it's crashing. Do NOT use
        kubectl — it depends on the very apiserver that's down.

    🟡 Q4. You edited the apiserver static-pod manifest and now it won't come up.
        A. A manifest typo. Fix /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        (validate YAML and flags / cert paths); the kubelet recreates the static
        pod automatically within seconds. The failure won't appear via kubectl —
        read crictl logs / journalctl -u kubelet.

    🔴 Q5. Components fail with x509 errors. Cause and fix?
        A. Expired certificates. `kubeadm certs check-expiration`, then
        `kubeadm certs renew all`, and restart the affected static pods (move
        manifests out/in) and the kubelet.

    🟢 Q6. The kubelet logs "running with swap on ... failed". Fix?
        A. `swapoff -a` and remove the swap entry from /etc/fstab so it stays off
        across reboots; then restart the kubelet.

    🟡 Q7. A node shows DiskPressure. What does that do and how to clear it?
        A. The kubelet taints the node and evicts pods; free disk (prune images
        and logs: `crictl rmi --prune`, `journalctl --vacuum-size=200M`, rotate
        logs) until the pressure condition clears.

    🟡 Q8. Node NotReady with "cni plugin not initialized". Fix?
        A. The CNI isn't installed / healthy on that node — (re)apply the CNI or
        fix its DaemonSet pod (kubectl get pods -n kube-system), then the kubelet
        reports Ready.

    🟢 Q9. How do you read a node's conditions?
        A. `kubectl describe node <n>` (Conditions section) or `kubectl get node
        <n> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'` — Ready, MemoryPressure,
        DiskPressure, PIDPressure, NetworkUnavailable.

    🔴 Q10. etcd is unhealthy and the control plane is flaky. First checks?
        A. `crictl ps -a | grep etcd` + `crictl logs <id>`, and
        `etcdctl endpoint health` with the etcd certs
        (/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/...); look for disk / quorum / cert issues and
        slow-fsync warnings.

    🟡 Q11. You edited the kubelet's systemd drop-in but the change had no
        effect after restart. Why?
        A. You skipped `systemctl daemon-reload`. systemd caches unit files;
        edits to the unit / drop-in require daemon-reload BEFORE
        `systemctl restart kubelet` or the old config is used.

    🔴 Q12. A Service for the easypj 'jobpost' app returns no response, but the
        pods are Running. How do you trace it?
        A. `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` — if EMPTY, the selector matches no
        Ready pods (label or readiness issue). If endpoints exist, check CoreDNS
        (nslookup from a debug pod), then kube-proxy health, then any
        NetworkPolicy default-deny silently blocking the traffic.

  VISUAL SUMMARY — the node / control-plane diagnostic ladder:
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ kubectl works?                                                       │
     │   ├─ NO  → apiserver down → crictl ps -a | grep apiserver → logs     │
     │   │        (check etcd first — apiserver is only as healthy as etcd) │
     │   └─ YES → kubectl get nodes                                         │
     │             └─ NotReady? → ssh node → systemctl status kubelet       │
     │                  └─ journalctl -u kubelet -f → read the error:       │
     │                       swap / cert / CNI / runtime / pressure → fix   │
     │                       → restart kubelet (daemon-reload if unit edit) │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  .vs-prose — Diagnosis flows top-down. First ask whether kubectl itself works:
  if not, the apiserver (or the etcd behind it) is down and you debug with
  crictl and journalctl on the control-plane node, never kubectl. If kubectl
  works, list the nodes; a NotReady node sends you onto that node where the
  kubelet — a systemd service, not a pod — is interrogated with systemctl and
  journalctl. The streamed kubelet error names the real cause (swap, expired
  cert, missing CNI, dead runtime, or a pressure condition); you fix that, then
  restart the kubelet (running daemon-reload first if you changed its unit).
  Control-plane components are static pods in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ that
  the kubelet recreates on file change and that fail SILENTLY through kubectl —
  so crictl and journalctl, not kubectl, are the tools of last resort.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 33: Logging, Monitoring & Resource Usage                       🟡 🎯
================================================================================

    META: 🟡 INTERMEDIATE · ⏱️ ~2h · Domain: Troubleshooting (30%) — "manage and
          evaluate container output streams" + "monitor cluster & application
          resource usage."

    🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    When a Pod misbehaves, two questions dominate the exam (and real life): WHAT
    did it say, and HOW MUCH is it using? The first is answered by container
    output streams (stdout/stderr -> node log files -> `kubectl logs`). The
    second is answered by the metrics pipeline (kubelet/cAdvisor -> metrics-
    server -> `kubectl top`). Both official competencies — "manage and evaluate
    container output streams" and "monitor cluster and application resource
    usage" — live in the 30% Troubleshooting domain, so this chapter pays off
    disproportionately. Master the `kubectl logs` flag scalpel and the
    metrics-server install, and you can triage almost any failing workload fast.

    🎯 OBJECTIVES
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    • Master every `kubectl logs` flag: --previous, -f, --tail, --since,
      --since-time, -c, --all-containers, -l.
    • Know where logs physically live on the node and why they vanish on delete.
    • Understand cluster-level logging patterns: node-agent DaemonSet vs sidecar;
      EFK / Loki; log rotation via containerLogMaxSize / containerLogMaxFiles.
    • Install and use metrics-server; run `kubectl top nodes/pods --sort-by`.
    • Compare requests vs limits vs actual usage to spot resource problems.
    • Recognize the Day-2 Prometheus / Grafana monitoring story.

    🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 `kubectl logs` (every flag) is bread-and-butter Troubleshooting.
    🎯 metrics-server install + `kubectl top` appears repeatedly; in labs it
       usually needs --kubelet-insecure-tls or it stays "unavailable".
    🏢 Cluster log shipping (EFK/Loki) and Prometheus/Grafana are day-2/beyond —
       know the shapes, not the deep config.
