    33.1  Application Logging (output streams)
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The container runtime captures whatever the main process writes to stdout
    and stderr and persists it as a node-local file. `kubectl logs` is just a
    convenient reader over that file via the kubelet — no agent required.

          $ kubectl logs <pod>
          $ kubectl logs <pod> -f                  # Follow/stream
          $ kubectl logs <pod> --tail=100          # Last 100 lines
          $ kubectl logs <pod> --since=1h          # Last hour
          $ kubectl logs <pod> --since-time=2026-06-29T08:00:00Z  # Exact window
          $ kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>      # Multi-container pod
          $ kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers    # All containers in the pod
          $ kubectl logs <pod> --previous          # Prior (crashed) instance
          $ kubectl logs -l app=easypj             # By label selector
          $ kubectl logs -l app=easypj --all-containers --tail=50  # Many pods

    ⚡ TIP: For crashed pods, use the --previous flag. A container that already
    restarted has a fresh (often empty) current log; the crash reason lives in
    the PREVIOUS instance's stream. Grab it before the kubelet rotates it away.

    📖 KEY TERM — output streams: the application's stdout (normal output) and
    stderr (errors). The 12-factor convention is to log to these streams and let
    the platform handle capture/rotation/shipping — never to a file inside the
    container, which is invisible to the cluster log pipeline.

    💡 INSIGHT: `kubectl logs` does NOT search across pods by itself except via
    -l (label). `kubectl logs -l app=easypj` fans out to every matching pod; add
    --all-containers and --tail to bound the volume. This is the fastest way to
    read an entire easypj Deployment's recent output in one command.

    📦 WHERE LOGS LIVE ON THE NODE
       /var/log/containers/<pod>_<ns>_<container>-<id>.log   (symlinks)
            └─► /var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/<n>.log
    These are the kubelet's on-disk capture of stdout/stderr. `kubectl logs`
    reads exactly this. ⚠️ When the Pod is deleted, the files are removed — the
    logs are GONE. For retention you must ship them off-node (see 33.2).


    33.2  Cluster-Level Logging
          🏢 [DAY-2 / BEYOND]
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - Node-level: container runtime writes to /var/log/containers/ and
      /var/log/pods/. This is automatic but ephemeral and node-local.
    - Cluster-level: deploy a logging agent (typically as a DaemonSet — one pod
      per node) that tails those files and forwards them to a central store.

    Two architectural patterns:
      • NODE-AGENT DaemonSet — one agent per node tails /var/log/containers and
        ships to the store. Most common; zero app changes. (Fluentd/Fluent Bit
        with Elasticsearch = "EFK"; or Promtail with Loki.)
      • SIDECAR — a second container in the Pod tails the app's log file from a
        shared volume and re-emits it to stdout (or forwards directly). Used
        when the app insists on logging to a file instead of stdout, so the
        cluster pipeline can still capture it.

    🔧 Node-level log rotation is controlled by the kubelet:
       containerLogMaxSize   (e.g. 10Mi — rotate when a container log hits size)
       containerLogMaxFiles  (e.g. 5 — keep N rotated files per container)
    Without a shipper, only this rotating window survives on the node.

    [DIAGRAM: Logging architecture — nodes → DaemonSet agent → central store]
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  CLUSTER LOGGING ARCHITECTURE                                            │
    │                                                                          │
    │   NODE 1                     NODE 2                     NODE 3           │
    │   ┌──────────────┐           ┌──────────────┐           ┌────────────┐   │
    │   │ 📦 easypj-web │           │ 📦 easypj-web │           │ 📦 worker  │   │
    │   │ 📦 postgres   │           │ 📦 redis      │           │ 📦 ...     │   │
    │   └──────┬───────┘           └──────┬───────┘           └─────┬──────┘   │
    │          │ stdout/stderr            │                         │          │
    │          ▼                          ▼                         ▼          │
    │   /var/log/containers/      /var/log/containers/      /var/log/...       │
    │          │                          │                         │          │
    │   ┌──────▼───────┐           ┌──────▼───────┐           ┌──────▼─────┐   │
    │   │ 🛰 agent pod │           │ 🛰 agent pod │           │ 🛰 agent   │   │  DaemonSet
    │   │ (Fluent Bit) │           │ (Fluent Bit) │           │            │   │  = 1/node
    │   └──────┬───────┘           └──────┬───────┘           └──────┬─────┘   │
    │          └────────────────┬─────────┴────────────┬─────────────┘         │
    │                           ▼                       ▼                       │
    │                 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
    │                 │  📚 CENTRAL STORE  (Elasticsearch/Loki)  │             │
    │                 │     + 🔍 Kibana / Grafana for search     │             │
    │                 └─────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧠 ANALOGY: node-level logs are like a security camera that overwrites its
    tape every few hours. The DaemonSet agent is the off-site recorder that
    copies every frame to a vault before it is overwritten.


    33.3  Monitoring with Metrics Server
          🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - Metrics Server: a lightweight, in-cluster, in-memory aggregator of resource
      metrics. It scrapes each kubelet's summary API (which exposes cAdvisor
      data) and serves the Resource Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io).
    - Required for: `kubectl top` AND the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). No
      metrics-server -> no `top`, no CPU/memory-based autoscaling.

          $ kubectl top nodes                      # Node CPU/memory
          $ kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu        # Busiest node first
          $ kubectl top pods                       # Pod CPU/memory
          $ kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory      # Sort by usage
          $ kubectl top pods --containers          # Per-container breakdown
          $ kubectl top pods -A                    # All namespaces

    [CODE: Metrics Server deployment]
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Standard install (one manifest):
    $ kubectl apply -f \
      https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

    # LAB FIX: kubelets in kubeadm/dev clusters use self-signed certs, so the
    # scrape fails TLS verification and metrics-server stays "unavailable".
    # Patch the Deployment to skip kubelet cert verification:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: metrics-server
      namespace: kube-system
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: metrics-server
              args:
                - --cert-dir=/tmp
                - --secure-port=10250
                - --kubelet-preferred-address-types=InternalIP,Hostname,ExternalIP
                - --kubelet-use-node-status-port
                - --metric-resolution=15s
                - --kubelet-insecure-tls          # <-- the lab-critical flag
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Quick imperative patch instead of editing the file:
    $ kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json \
      -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-",
            "value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: right after install, `kubectl top` may report "Metrics API not
    available" for ~15-30s while metrics-server warms up its first scrape. Wait
    for `kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy metrics-server`, then retry.

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING `kubectl top` errors:
       1. Is metrics-server installed?  kubectl get deploy -n kube-system metrics-server
       2. Is its pod Ready?             kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics
       3. APIService healthy?           kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
       4. Logs show TLS errors?         add --kubelet-insecure-tls (labs).
       5. Just installed?               wait one scrape interval, then retry.


    33.4  Monitoring easypj Resource Usage
          🧪 🏢
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [EXAMPLE: Finding resource-hungry pods in the easypj namespace]
          $ kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=cpu
          $ kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=memory
          $ kubectl top pods -n easypj --containers   # split web vs sidecar

    Typical output for the easypj job-board stack:
          NAME                       CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
          easypj-web-7d9f-abcde      142m         310Mi
          easypj-web-7d9f-fghij      138m         298Mi
          postgres-0                 65m          540Mi
          redis-6c8-klmno            8m           42Mi

    [TABLE: Interpreting resource metrics]
    ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Signal           │ What it means / what to do                            │
    ├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ usage ≈ request  │ Healthy. The scheduler's estimate matches reality.    │
    │ usage << request │ Over-provisioned. Requests too high -> wasted node    │
    │                  │ capacity / poor bin-packing. Lower the request.       │
    │ usage >> request │ Under-provisioned. Scheduler overcommits the node;    │
    │                  │ neighbors may starve. Raise the request.              │
    │ usage near limit │ At risk: CPU -> throttling; memory -> OOMKill when it  │
    │ (memory)         │ crosses the limit. Raise the limit or fix the leak.   │
    │ usage > limit    │ Impossible for memory (kernel OOMKills first); for CPU │
    │ (cpu)            │ it is simply throttled to the limit (no kill).        │
    │ top row, sorted  │ The "hog" — start your investigation here.            │
    └──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: requests drive SCHEDULING (where a pod lands and the node's
    committed capacity); limits drive ENFORCEMENT (throttle for CPU, OOMKill for
    memory). `kubectl top` shows ACTUAL usage — compare all three to right-size.

    🏢 DAY-2: Prometheus + Grafana
    -----------------------------
    metrics-server is intentionally minimal: in-memory, no history, only CPU/mem,
    only for `top`/HPA. For dashboards, alerting and historical/custom metrics,
    teams run Prometheus (scrapes /metrics endpoints, stores a time series) with
    Grafana for visualization and Alertmanager for paging. For easypj you would
    expose app metrics (request latency, queue depth) on a /metrics endpoint and
    let Prometheus scrape them. The HPA can even consume these via the custom/
    external metrics APIs. Know the shape for the exam; deep config is beyond it.


    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
    ============================================================================
    🔧 HOW stdout/stderr BECOMES A NODE LOG FILE: the container runtime
       (containerd/CRI-O) attaches to the container's stdout/stderr file
       descriptors and writes each line, tagged with a timestamp and stream
       (stdout/stderr), into /var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/N.log.
       The kubelet creates /var/log/containers/*.log symlinks pointing at those.
       `kubectl logs` -> kubelet -> reads that file -> streams it back. No
       separate agent is involved in the basic path.

    🔧 HOW metrics-server GETS NUMBERS: every kubelet embeds cAdvisor, which
       reads cgroup accounting for CPU and memory per container. The kubelet
       exposes this on its summary API (/stats/summary, secured on port 10250).
       metrics-server scrapes each kubelet on a --metric-resolution interval
       (default 15s), aggregates, and serves the Resource Metrics API
       (metrics.k8s.io) through the aggregation layer. `kubectl top` and the HPA
       are clients of THAT API — which is why both break with no metrics-server.

    🔬 DEEPER:
      • klog levels & structured logging: Kubernetes components use klog; -v=N
        sets verbosity (higher = noisier). Newer components emit structured
        (key=value / JSON) logs for machine parsing.
      • Container log rotation: containerLogMaxSize (per-file rotate threshold)
        and containerLogMaxFiles (how many rotated files to keep) are kubelet
        settings — the only retention you get without a shipper.
      • The three metrics APIs for autoscaling:
          - Resource Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io)  -> served by metrics-server
            (CPU/mem; powers `top` and basic HPA).
          - Custom Metrics API (custom.metrics.k8s.io) -> app/object metrics
            (e.g. via Prometheus Adapter).
          - External Metrics API (external.metrics.k8s.io) -> metrics from
            outside the cluster (e.g. cloud queue length).
      • The kubelet summary API is the single source for node/pod/container
        resource stats; metrics-server is a thin aggregator on top of it.


    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ============================================================================
    • Container output streams (stdout/stderr) become node log files
      (/var/log/containers, /var/log/pods); `kubectl logs` reads them. Logs
      vanish when the pod is deleted — ship them off-node for retention.
    • `kubectl logs` flags are your scalpel: --previous (crashed instance), -f
      (follow), --tail / --since / --since-time (windowing), -c /
      --all-containers (multi-container), -l (by label across pods).
    • For a CRASHED container the current log may be empty — the crash reason is
      in --previous. Grab it before the kubelet cleans it up.
    • Cluster logging = a node-agent DaemonSet (or sidecars) forwarding to a
      store (EFK / Loki); node-level rotation is containerLogMaxSize/Files.
    • `kubectl top` (nodes/pods) needs metrics-server installed; it scrapes the
      kubelet/cAdvisor summary API and serves metrics.k8s.io. Use it to compare
      requests vs limits vs ACTUAL usage and right-size workloads.
    • metrics-server also powers the HPA. No metrics-server -> no `top`, no
      CPU/memory autoscaling.
    • Requests drive scheduling; limits drive enforcement (CPU throttle / memory
      OOMKill); `top` shows reality. All three together tell you what to fix.


    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ============================================================================
    • `kubectl top` erroring ("Metrics API not available") = metrics-server isn't
      installed/ready — it is NOT a usage problem.
    • In labs/kubeadm, metrics-server needs --kubelet-insecure-tls (self-signed
      kubelet certs) or it stays unavailable indefinitely.
    • Logs are gone after a Pod is deleted; for a crashed container you must use
      --previous BEFORE it is cleaned up.
    • Default `kubectl logs` targets ONE container; in multi-container pods add
      -c or --all-containers or you miss the relevant stream.
    • Just after install, `top` may need ~15-30s for the first scrape — wait for
      rollout, don't assume it's broken.
    • Apps that log to a file inside the container (not stdout) are INVISIBLE to
      `kubectl logs` and the cluster pipeline — that's what the sidecar pattern
      fixes.
    • CPU over-limit is throttled (no kill); MEMORY over-limit is OOMKilled —
      different failure modes for the same "near limit" reading.


    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ============================================================================
    • `kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=memory` instantly finds the hog.
    • `kubectl logs -l app=easypj --all-containers --tail=50` reads every easypj
      pod's containers at once by label.
    • `--since=1h` / `--since-time=<RFC3339>` scopes noisy logs to the incident
      window.
    • `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` is the first move on any CrashLoopBackOff.
    • `kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system ... add
      --kubelet-insecure-tls` is the one-liner that fixes "top" in labs.
    • `kubectl top pods --containers` splits a multi-container pod so you see
      which sidecar is the culprit.


    🔑 COMMANDS
    ============================================================================
    kubectl logs easypj-web --previous -c web
    kubectl logs -l app=easypj --all-containers -f --tail=100
    kubectl logs easypj-web --since=1h
    kubectl logs easypj-web --since-time=2026-06-29T08:00:00Z
    kubectl logs easypj-web --all-containers
    kubectl top nodes
    kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu
    kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=memory
    kubectl top pods -n easypj --containers
    kubectl top pods -A
    kubectl apply -f metrics-server.yaml          # (lab: add --kubelet-insecure-tls)
    kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy metrics-server
    kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
    kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json \
      -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'


    🧪 DRILL
    ============================================================================
    Install metrics-server, run `kubectl top pods -n easypj`, compare each pod's
    usage to its requests/limits, and identify which pod would OOMKill under load.


    🧪 LAB Q&A (10)
    ============================================================================
    Q1. Read the logs of a container that already crashed.
        A. `kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous` — prints the PRIOR
        instance's stdout/stderr, which holds the crash reason. The current
        instance's log is often empty after a restart.

    Q2. Follow logs of every easypj pod by label.
        A. `kubectl logs -l app=easypj --all-containers -f` streams all matching
        pods' containers together in real time.

    Q3. Show only the last hour of a noisy pod's logs.
        A. `kubectl logs <pod> --since=1h` (or `--since-time=<RFC3339>`) to
        window the output to the incident period.

    Q4. Find the node using the most CPU.
        A. `kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu` (requires metrics-server). Top row
        is the busiest node.

    Q5. `kubectl top` returns "Metrics API not available". Fix?
        A. Install metrics-server (and in labs add --kubelet-insecure-tls); wait
        for its Deployment to be Ready (`rollout status`), then retry. The error
        means the metrics pipeline is missing, not that usage is zero.

    Q6. View logs from a specific container in a multi-container pod.
        A. `kubectl logs <pod> -c <containerName>` (or `--all-containers` to see
        every container's stream).

    Q7. Which easypj pod is consuming the most memory?
        A. `kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=memory` — the top row is the hog.

    Q8. Where do container logs live on the node?
        A. /var/log/containers/ (symlinks) -> /var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/...
        — the kubelet's on-disk capture of stdout/stderr that `kubectl logs`
        reads.

    Q9. A pod's actual usage far exceeds its requests. Why does that matter?
        A. Requests drive scheduling; if usage >> requests the scheduler
        overcommits the node and pods may get CPU-throttled or OOMKilled. Raise
        the requests (and limits) to match reality.

    Q10. Describe the sidecar logging pattern.
         A. A second container in the Pod tails the app's log FILE from a shared
         volume and re-emits it to stdout (or forwards it directly), so the
         cluster log pipeline can capture apps that don't log to stdout.

    Q11. Stream the last 200 lines of all easypj web pods and keep following.
         A. `kubectl logs -l app=easypj-web --all-containers --tail=200 -f`.

    Q12. How does metrics-server obtain its numbers, and why does `top` depend
         on it?
         A. metrics-server scrapes each kubelet's summary API (cAdvisor/cgroup
         data) on an interval and serves the Resource Metrics API
         (metrics.k8s.io). `kubectl top` and the HPA are clients of THAT API, so
         both stop working without metrics-server installed.

    Q13. metrics-server pod is Running but `top` still fails; logs show kubelet
         TLS errors. Fix?
         A. Add `--kubelet-insecure-tls` to the metrics-server container args
         (self-signed kubelet certs in kubeadm/lab clusters fail verification),
         then let it restart and re-scrape.

    Q14. Name the three metrics APIs used for autoscaling and who serves the
         basic one.
         A. Resource Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io, served by metrics-server),
         Custom Metrics API (custom.metrics.k8s.io), External Metrics API
         (external.metrics.k8s.io).

    Q15. How is node-level log retention bounded without a log shipper?
         A. By the kubelet's containerLogMaxSize (rotate threshold per file) and
         containerLogMaxFiles (number of rotated files kept). Beyond that window,
         logs are lost unless a DaemonSet agent ships them off-node.

    VISUAL SUMMARY: stdout/stderr -> node log file -> (kubectl logs) and ->
    DaemonSet agent -> central store. Separately: kubelet/cAdvisor -> metrics-
    server -> kubectl top / HPA. Two independent pipelines; both are 30%-domain
    Troubleshooting staples, and both have a single classic failure (logs vanish
    on delete; `top` fails with no metrics-server).

    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


================================================================================
  Chapter 34: Troubleshooting Services & Networking + Scenario Playbook  🔴 🎯
================================================================================

    [A] META: 🔴 Hard · ⏱️ ~3h · Domain: Troubleshooting 30% (the heaviest
        domain on the exam) — with a focus on services & networking failures
        plus the full broken-cluster scenario playbook.

    [B] WHY THIS MATTERS:
        "It can't connect" is the single most common — and the most layered —
        failure you will ever debug. A request crosses the pod, the Service,
        DNS and the NetworkPolicy/kube-proxy dataplane before it ever reaches
        another container; any one of those four layers can silently swallow
        it. On top of that, the CKA hands you broken clusters and times you:
        you need a consolidated playbook of the ~12 must-know scenarios where
        you can name the symptom, fire the FIRST diagnostic command, and apply
        the fix faster than you can think it through. VISUAL: the 4-layer
        network diagnostic ladder and the symptom→first-command playbook.

    [C] OBJECTIVES:
        • Debug Service / endpoints / DNS / NetworkPolicy / kube-proxy
          failures top-down using the 4-layer diagnostic.
        • Apply ONE universal method (GATHER → READ → ISOLATE → FIX → VERIFY)
          to every canonical broken-cluster scenario.
        • Memorize the 12-scenario playbook: symptom → first command → fix.

    [D] CKA RELEVANCE:
        🎯 Troubleshooting is 30% of the exam — THE HEAVIEST domain. Networking
        and Service failures are over-represented within it. Speed and method
        win here: the candidate who knows the FIRST command for each symptom
        and never skips VERIFY clears these tasks in minutes.

    [E] SECTION MAP:
        34.1 Service & Endpoint Issues 🎯
        34.2 DNS Issues 🎯
        34.3 NetworkPolicy & kube-proxy Issues 🎯
        34.4 The CKA Scenario Playbook 🧪🎯 (12 canonical scenarios)
        34.5 Troubleshooting Methodology Checklist 🩺

    📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 34

    [THE 4-LAYER NETWORK DIAGNOSTIC — isolate top-down]
     ❓ "easypj-web can't reach easypj-db"
     L1 POD     ─ are both pods Running & Ready?           get pod -o wide
     L2 SERVICE ─ does the Service have ENDPOINTS?         get endpoints easypj-db
     │             (empty = selector/label mismatch or not Ready)
     L3 DNS     ─ does the name resolve?                   exec nslookup easypj-db
     │             (fail = CoreDNS / wrong ns / ndots)
     L4 POLICY  ─ is a NetworkPolicy blocking 5432?        get netpol; exec curl
     └─ still broken? kube-proxy mode/health · MTU · conntrack
     🔁 Method everywhere: GATHER ► READ(events/logs) ► ISOLATE layer ► FIX ► VERIFY

    🧠 ANALOGY: Debugging a connection is like a postal trace. L1 = is the
    sender/recipient even at home (pod Running/Ready)? L2 = is there a valid
    street address routed to them (Service endpoints)? L3 = does the name in
    the address book resolve to that street (DNS)? L4 = is there a checkpoint
    refusing the parcel (NetworkPolicy/kube-proxy)? You never re-write the
    letter (the app) until you've ruled out the address book and the
    checkpoint.

    [THE 12-SCENARIO PLAYBOOK — symptom ▶ first command]
     1 NotReady node ▶ ssh;systemctl kubelet   7 certs expired ▶ kubeadm certs
     2 Pod Pending ▶ describe(Events)           8 NetPol block ▶ get netpol;curl
     3 no endpoints ▶ get ep                     9 PVC Pending ▶ describe pvc
     4 CrashLoop ▶ logs --previous              10 kubeconfig ▶ config view/use
     5 DNS fail ▶ nslookup from temp pod        11 scheduler down ▶ -n kube-system
     6 etcd unhealthy ▶ crictl;etcdctl health   12 ImagePull ▶ describe(Events)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    34.1  Service & Endpoint Issues  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    A Service is just a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) plus a set of ENDPOINTS —
    the pod IPs that back it. If a Service "exists" but no traffic flows, the
    problem is almost always one of three things: the selector matches no Ready
    pod (empty endpoints), the targetPort doesn't match the container's
    listening port, or a downstream layer (DNS/policy) is blocking the call.

    📖 KEY TERM — Endpoints: the live list of pod IP:port pairs a Service
    routes to. `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` is the single fastest L2 check.
    If it shows <none>, the Service is a dead end no matter how correct its
    YAML looks.

    The fastest, most reliable test is ALWAYS from inside the cluster, from a
    throwaway debug pod — never trust an external curl until the in-cluster
    path works:

        $ kubectl run t --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
        # inside:
        $ curl -m3 easypj-db:5432
        $ nslookup easypj-db.easypj

    ⚠️ Empty endpoints silently break a Service even though `kubectl get svc`
    shows it happily with a ClusterIP. Confirm endpoints BEFORE you suspect the
    network. The two causes: (a) the Service selector doesn't match the pod
    labels, or (b) the pods are running but failing their readiness probe (a
    not-Ready pod is removed from endpoints by design).

        [WHY ENDPOINTS GO EMPTY — the two causes]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Service selector:  app: easypj-db                            │
        │  Pod labels:        app: easypj-database   ◀── MISMATCH       │
        │  Result: endpoints = <none>  → Service routes nowhere         │
        │  Fix: align selector & labels  (get pods --show-labels)       │
        │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────    │
        │  Selector matches, but pod readiness probe FAILS              │
        │  Result: pod Running but 0/1 Ready → pulled from endpoints    │
        │  Fix: make the readiness probe / health endpoint pass         │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ⚡ SPEED TIP: `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` first. Empty → stop and fix the
    selector/readiness; do NOT go chasing DNS or policy yet.

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — targetPort vs port vs containerPort:
        • port        = the port the Service VIP listens on (what clients hit).
        • targetPort  = the port on the POD the Service forwards to.
        • containerPort = the port the container actually listens on.
        If targetPort ≠ the real containerPort, you get "connection refused"
        even though endpoints are populated. Match targetPort to the real
        listening port (for easypj-db: 5432).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    34.2  DNS Issues  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    Most "connection" bugs are actually DNS bugs: a wrong namespace in the
    name, CoreDNS down or misconfigured, or an ndots/search-domain trap. A
    bare `easypj-db` only resolves within the caller's own namespace; to reach
    a Service in another namespace you must use `easypj-db.<ns>` (or the FQDN
    `easypj-db.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`).

        [DNS RESOLUTION ORDER — bare name in namespace "web"]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Pod's /etc/resolv.conf search list (typical):               │
        │    web.svc.cluster.local  svc.cluster.local  cluster.local   │
        │    nameserver = CoreDNS ClusterIP (kube-dns svc)             │
        │                                                              │
        │  Query "easypj-db"  → tries easypj-db.web.svc.cluster.local  │
        │                       (only finds it if db is in "web")     │
        │  Query "easypj-db.data" → resolves db in namespace "data"   │
        │                                                              │
        │  ndots:5 → names with <5 dots get search-domains appended;  │
        │  an FQDN ending in "." skips the search list entirely.      │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Diagnose top-down from a temp pod:

        $ kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default
          → fails  ⇒ DNS itself is broken (go check CoreDNS)
          → works  ⇒ DNS is up; your NAME is wrong (namespace/typo)

    Then check CoreDNS itself:

        $ kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
        $ kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns
        $ kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml   # Corefile typos?
        $ kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system          # ClusterIP matches
                                                           # pods' resolv.conf?

    Force a clean reload if the Corefile or pods are wedged:

        $ kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system

    ⚠️ GOTCHA: A default-deny EGRESS NetworkPolicy also blocks DNS — names stop
    resolving cluster-wide for the selected pods because they can no longer
    reach CoreDNS on UDP/TCP 53. Always pair a default-deny egress with an
    explicit allow-DNS-to-kube-system rule.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    34.3  NetworkPolicy & kube-proxy Issues  🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC]

    NetworkPolicy is allow-list, additive, and default-allow UNTIL the first
    policy selects a pod — then everything not explicitly allowed is denied for
    that pod. The classic exam break: web→db worked, you add policies, and now
    it's blocked because a policy selects db without an ingress rule allowing
    web (or a blanket default-deny with no allow at all).

        [NETWORKPOLICY BLOCK — diagnose & fix]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ 1. List policies:   kubectl get netpol -A                    │
        │ 2. Describe the one selecting db:                            │
        │      kubectl describe netpol <name> -n easypj                │
        │      → does Ingress allow "from" the web pods/labels?       │
        │ 3. Confirm labels: kubectl get pods --show-labels -n easypj  │
        │      → do web pods carry the label the policy expects?      │
        │ 4. Test:  kubectl exec web-pod -n easypj -- curl -m3 db:5432 │
        │ 5. Fix: add an ingress allow web→db:5432 (or fix the label) │
        │      kubectl apply -f fixed-netpol.yaml                       │
        │ 6. Verify: repeat the curl                                   │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ⚠️ GOTCHA — the CNI must enforce policy: Flannel (plain) IGNORES
    NetworkPolicy entirely, so a policy can look perfect and do nothing. Use a
    policy-aware CNI (Calico, Cilium, Weave) or your "fix" will silently fail.

    kube-proxy programs the Service VIPs into the node dataplane (iptables or
    IPVS). If kube-proxy is broken, Service VIPs stop working while pod IPs
    still work — a key diagnostic split:

        [SERVICE VIP DOWN vs POD IP UP — what it means]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  curl <podIP>:5432    → works                                │
        │  curl <serviceVIP>    → fails / refused                      │
        │  ⇒ App is FINE. Problem is the SERVICE layer:                │
        │     endpoints empty · targetPort wrong · kube-proxy broken   │
        │  Check: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-proxy│
        │         kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-proxy            │
        │         (mode? iptables vs IPVS — check the ConfigMap)       │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — read the dataplane by hand (on a node):
        • iptables mode:  iptables-save | grep <clusterIP>
        • IPVS mode:      ipvsadm -Ln
        • live conns:     conntrack -L
        eBPF-based CNIs (Cilium) replace much of this; observe with Hubble.
        For distroless pods with no shell, attach an ephemeral debug container:
        kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    34.4  The CKA Scenario Playbook — 10 Must-Practice Scenarios  🧪 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🎯 [CKA EXAM TOPIC — PRACTICE THESE]

          [SCENARIO 1: Worker Node Not Ready]
          Problem: kubectl get nodes shows worker01 NotReady
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. Identify: $ kubectl get nodes                      │
          │    → worker01  NotReady  <roles>  <age>  <version>   │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Describe:  $ kubectl describe node worker01        │
          │    → Look at Conditions section for clues             │
          │    → MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure?      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. SSH to node: $ ssh worker01                        │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Check kubelet:                                     │
          │    $ systemctl status kubelet                          │
          │    → If "inactive/dead": systemctl start kubelet     │
          │    → If errors: journalctl -u kubelet -f             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Common fixes:                                       │
          │    - Kubelet not running → systemctl enable kubelet   │
          │      && systemctl start kubelet                        │
          │    - Wrong kubelet config → check /var/lib/kubelet/   │
          │      config.yaml                                       │
          │    - Container runtime down → systemctl restart       │
          │      containerd                                        │
          │    - Swap enabled → swapoff -a                         │
          │                                                       │
          │ 6. Verify: $ kubectl get nodes                        │
          │    → worker01 should show Ready                       │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 2: Pod Stuck in Pending]
          Problem: easypj-web pod won't schedule
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                       │
          │    → easypj-web-xxxx  0/1  Pending  0  5m            │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. $ kubectl describe pod easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj   │
          │    → Check Events section at the bottom!              │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Common causes from Events:                         │
          │    a) "Insufficient cpu/memory"                       │
          │       → Reduce resource requests OR add nodes        │
          │    b) "node(s) had taint... pod didn't tolerate"     │
          │       → Add toleration to pod spec OR remove taint   │
          │    c) "no nodes match nodeSelector"                   │
          │       → Fix nodeSelector OR label the node           │
          │    d) "persistentvolumeclaim not found"               │
          │       → Create the missing PVC                        │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Fix and verify:                                     │
          │    $ kubectl get pods -n easypj -w  (watch)           │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 3: Service Not Accessible]
          Problem: Can't reach easypj via NodePort
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. $ kubectl get svc easypj-svc -n easypj             │
          │    → Check PORT and TYPE columns                      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. $ kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc -n easypj       │
          │    → If <none>: Service is not finding any pods!     │
          │    → Labels don't match between Service selector      │
          │      and Pod labels                                    │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Compare labels:                                     │
          │    $ kubectl get svc easypj-svc -o yaml | grep -A5   │
          │      selector                                          │
          │    $ kubectl get pods --show-labels -n easypj          │
          │    → Do they match? Fix the mismatch!                │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Check pod is actually running:                      │
          │    $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                        │
          │    → Pods must be Running + Ready (1/1)              │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Test from inside cluster:                           │
          │    $ kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it --     │
          │      wget -qO- http://easypj-svc.easypj:80           │
          │                                                       │
          │ 6. Verify: $ curl http://<node-ip>:<nodeport>         │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 4: CrashLoopBackOff]
          Problem: easypj-db keeps crashing
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                       │
          │    → easypj-db  0/1  CrashLoopBackOff  5  10m       │
          │    (restart count keeps increasing)                    │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. $ kubectl logs easypj-db -n easypj --previous      │
          │    → --previous shows logs from LAST crashed run      │
          │    → Look for error messages, stack traces            │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. $ kubectl describe pod easypj-db -n easypj          │
          │    → Check "Last State" for exit code                 │
          │    → Exit 1 = app error, Exit 137 = OOM killed       │
          │    → Exit 0 = app completed (shouldn't restart)      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Common fixes:                                       │
          │    a) Missing env vars → add ConfigMap/Secret ref    │
          │    b) Wrong command → fix container command/args      │
          │    c) OOM killed → increase memory limits             │
          │    d) Liveness probe failing → fix probe or health   │
          │       endpoint                                         │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Apply fix and verify:                               │
          │    $ kubectl logs easypj-db -n easypj -f               │
          │    → Should see clean startup, no more crashes        │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 5: DNS Resolution Failing]
          Problem: Pods can't resolve service names
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. Test DNS from a pod:                                │
          │    $ kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it --     │
          │      nslookup kubernetes.default                       │
          │    → If fails: DNS is broken                          │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Check CoreDNS pods:                                 │
          │    $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=      │
          │      kube-dns                                          │
          │    → Are they Running? Any restarts?                  │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Check CoreDNS logs:                                 │
          │    $ kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns  │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Check CoreDNS ConfigMap:                            │
          │    $ kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml    │
          │    → Check for typos in Corefile                      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Check CoreDNS Service:                              │
          │    $ kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system           │
          │    → ClusterIP should match /etc/resolv.conf in pods  │
          │                                                       │
          │ 6. Fix and restart CoreDNS:                            │
          │    $ kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns            │
          │      -n kube-system                                    │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 6: etcd Cluster Unhealthy]
          Problem: API server intermittently unavailable
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. Check etcd health:                                  │
          │    $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health \           │
          │      --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \             │
          │      --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \       │
          │      --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \     │
          │      --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key        │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Check etcd member list:                             │
          │    $ etcdctl member list (with same cert flags)        │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Check etcd pod logs:                                │
          │    $ kubectl logs etcd-master -n kube-system           │
          │    OR: $ crictl logs <etcd-container-id>               │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. If data corruption → restore from backup:          │
          │    a) Stop kube-apiserver (move manifest out)          │
          │    b) etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db \            │
          │       --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored                │
          │    c) Update etcd manifest with new data-dir           │
          │    d) Move manifests back, wait for restart            │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify: $ kubectl get nodes (should respond)       │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 7: Certificates Expired]
          Problem: kubectl commands returning "certificate has expired"
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. Check certificate expiry:                           │
          │    $ kubeadm certs check-expiration                   │
          │    → Shows expiry date for each certificate           │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Renew all certificates:                             │
          │    $ kubeadm certs renew all                           │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Restart control plane components:                   │
          │    $ systemctl restart kubelet                          │
          │    (Static pods will be restarted automatically)       │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Update kubeconfig:                                  │
          │    $ cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify:                                             │
          │    $ kubectl get nodes                                  │
          │    → Should work without certificate errors            │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 8: Network Policy Blocking Traffic]
          Problem: Frontend can't reach backend after policy applied
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. List policies:                                      │
          │    $ kubectl get networkpolicy -n easypj               │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Describe each policy:                               │
          │    $ kubectl describe netpol <name> -n easypj          │
          │    → Check: Allowing Ingress/Egress from the          │
          │      correct pods?                                     │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Check pod labels:                                   │
          │    $ kubectl get pods --show-labels -n easypj          │
          │    → Do frontend pods have labels matching the         │
          │      policy's ingress "from" selector?                 │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Test connectivity:                                   │
          │    $ kubectl exec frontend-pod -- curl backend:80     │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Fix: Add missing ingress rule or fix label          │
          │    selectors in the NetworkPolicy YAML                 │
          │    $ kubectl apply -f fixed-netpol.yaml                │
          │                                                       │
          │ 6. Verify: Repeat connectivity test                    │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 9: PVC Not Binding]
          Problem: PVC stuck in Pending state
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. $ kubectl get pvc -n easypj                         │
          │    → STATUS: Pending                                   │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. $ kubectl describe pvc <name> -n easypj             │
          │    → Events: "no persistent volumes available"        │
          │    OR: "waiting for first consumer"                    │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Check available PVs:                                │
          │    $ kubectl get pv                                     │
          │    → Is there a PV with matching:                     │
          │      - Access mode (RWO/ROX/RWX)?                     │
          │      - Storage capacity (>= PVC request)?             │
          │      - StorageClass name?                               │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Fix:                                                │
          │    a) No PV exists → create matching PV               │
          │    b) StorageClass mismatch → fix PVC or create PV    │
          │       with correct class                                │
          │    c) "waiting for consumer" → this is normal with    │
          │       WaitForFirstConsumer — PV binds when pod uses   │
          │       the PVC                                          │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify: $ kubectl get pvc (STATUS → Bound)         │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 10: kubeconfig Issues]
          Problem: kubectl can't connect to cluster
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:                             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 1. Check current context:                              │
          │    $ kubectl config current-context                   │
          │    → Is it pointing to the right cluster?             │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Check kubeconfig:                                   │
          │    $ kubectl config view                               │
          │    → Check server URL, certificate paths              │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Common causes:                                      │
          │    a) Wrong context → kubectl config use-context      │
          │    b) Wrong server URL → edit ~/.kube/config          │
          │    c) Certificate not found → copy from master node   │
          │       (cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config)  │
          │    d) KUBECONFIG env var set wrong → check with       │
          │       echo $KUBECONFIG                                 │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Test: $ kubectl cluster-info                        │
          │    → Should show cluster endpoints                     │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify: $ kubectl get nodes                         │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

    🏢 TWO MORE FROM THE 12-SCENARIO PLAYBOOK (C2 additions):

          [SCENARIO 11: Scheduler Down — pods stay Pending forever]
          Problem: every new pod sticks at Pending; no Events about resources
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ 1. Symptom: kubectl get pods → all new pods Pending,  │
          │    describe shows NO scheduling Events at all          │
          │    (nothing is even TRYING to place them).            │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. Check the scheduler static pod:                     │
          │    $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler  │
          │    → kube-scheduler-master CrashLoop / missing?       │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. If apiserver responds but scheduler pod is gone,    │
          │    inspect its manifest & runtime on the master:       │
          │    $ ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml │
          │    $ crictl ps -a | grep scheduler                     │
          │    $ crictl logs <scheduler-container-id>              │
          │    $ journalctl -u kubelet -f                          │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Common fixes: typo in the static-pod manifest      │
          │    (bad flag/path), wrong image, or kubeconfig path.  │
          │    Fix the manifest; kubelet auto-restarts the pod.   │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify: a new pod schedules onto a node.           │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

          [SCENARIO 12: ImagePullBackOff]
          Problem: easypj-web stuck pulling its image
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ 1. $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                       │
          │    → easypj-web  0/1  ImagePullBackOff               │
          │                                                       │
          │ 2. $ kubectl describe pod easypj-web -n easypj         │
          │    → Read Events: the exact pull error is there.      │
          │                                                       │
          │ 3. Common causes from Events:                         │
          │    a) "not found" / "manifest unknown" → wrong        │
          │       image name or tag (typo, missing tag)           │
          │    b) "unauthorized" / "pull access denied" →         │
          │       private registry; add an imagePullSecret        │
          │       and reference it on the pod/SA                   │
          │    c) "no such host" / timeout → registry             │
          │       unreachable / DNS / airgapped node              │
          │                                                       │
          │ 4. Fix: correct the image:tag, OR                     │
          │    $ kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \  │
          │      --docker-server=... --docker-username=... \      │
          │      --docker-password=... -n easypj                  │
          │    then reference it via imagePullSecrets.            │
          │                                                       │
          │ 5. Verify: $ kubectl get pods -n easypj (→ Running)   │
          └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ─────────────────────────────────────────────

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    34.5  Troubleshooting Methodology Checklist  🩺
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          [CHECKLIST: The 5-Step Troubleshooting Method]
          1️⃣ IDENTIFY: What is the symptom? (get → describe → events)
          2️⃣ GATHER: Collect info (logs, describe, exec)
          3️⃣ ANALYZE: What changed? What's different?
          4️⃣ FIX: Apply the smallest possible fix
          5️⃣ VERIFY: Confirm the fix worked (get, test, curl)

          [SYMPTOM ▶ FIRST-COMMAND QUICK TABLE]
          ┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
          │ SYMPTOM                     │ FIRST COMMAND                     │
          ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
          │ Node NotReady               │ ssh node; systemctl status kubelet│
          │ Pod Pending                 │ kubectl describe pod (Events!)    │
          │ Service has no traffic      │ kubectl get endpoints <svc>       │
          │ CrashLoopBackOff            │ kubectl logs <pod> --previous     │
          │ DNS / name won't resolve    │ nslookup from a temp pod          │
          │ etcd unhealthy / API flaky  │ crictl logs; etcdctl endpoint     │
          │                             │   health                          │
          │ "certificate has expired"   │ kubeadm certs check-expiration    │
          │ Connection blocked post-pol │ kubectl get netpol; exec curl     │
          │ PVC Pending                 │ kubectl describe pvc <name>       │
          │ kubectl can't connect       │ kubectl config view / use-context │
          │ All pods Pending, no Events │ -n kube-system get pods scheduler │
          │ ImagePullBackOff            │ kubectl describe pod (Events!)    │
          └─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 UTH — how a Service connection actually fails at each layer, and how to
       read the dataplane that implements it:
       • L1 POD: a pod can be Running but NOT Ready; readiness gates endpoint
         membership, so a failing probe quietly removes it from the Service.
       • L2 SERVICE: the ClusterIP is virtual — it has no host, no process. It
         only "works" because kube-proxy programs node-level rules that DNAT
         the VIP to a backend pod IP:targetPort. No endpoints ⇒ no DNAT target
         ⇒ packets dropped.
       • L3 DNS: CoreDNS is itself a Deployment behind the kube-dns Service;
         pods find it via the nameserver line in /etc/resolv.conf and append
         the search domains up to `ndots`.
       • L4 POLICY: NetworkPolicy is compiled by the CNI into the same
         iptables/eBPF dataplane; a deny is a DROP rule the packet hits before
         it ever reaches the backend.

    🔬 DEEPER:
       • Read iptables/IPVS rules & conntrack entries by hand:
         iptables-save | grep <clusterIP> · ipvsadm -Ln · conntrack -L.
       • eBPF observability: Cilium Hubble shows allowed/denied flows live
         without tcpdump.
       • Ephemeral debug containers on distroless images:
         kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<ctr>.
       • Node-level bisection when the apiserver is down: crictl ps -a,
         crictl logs, journalctl -u kubelet — debug the control plane as
         static pods, not via kubectl.
       • MTU & asymmetric-routing bugs: a too-large MTU after an overlay
         encapsulation silently drops large packets (small requests work, big
         responses hang).
       • DNS ndots/search-domain traps: high ndots turns every external lookup
         into several failed search-domain queries first — slow and flaky.
       • Systematic binary-search isolation across the 4 layers: prove each
         layer up or down before descending; never jump to the app.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS  (merged — union of both editions)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ✅ ONE method everywhere: kubectl get → describe (Events!) → logs
       (--previous) → exec → isolate the layer → fix → VERIFY. ALWAYS in
       this order; never skip VERIFY.
    ✅ "Can't connect" is LAYERED — isolate top-down: L1 pod (Running/Ready?)
       → L2 Service (has endpoints?) → L3 DNS (name resolves?) → L4
       NetworkPolicy/kube-proxy (traffic allowed/programmed?).
    ✅ Empty endpoints = selector/label mismatch OR no Ready pods. Always
       confirm endpoints before suspecting the network — a Service can "exist"
       with a ClusterIP yet route nowhere.
    ✅ A Service VIP failing while the pod IP works = the app is fine; the bug
       is Service-layer (endpoints / targetPort / kube-proxy).
    ✅ Most "connection" bugs are actually DNS (wrong namespace, CoreDNS down,
       ndots) or a NetworkPolicy with no allow-DNS egress — not the app.
    ✅ Pod statuses decode the fault: CrashLoopBackOff (app crashes
       repeatedly), ImagePullBackOff (wrong image/tag or auth), Pending (no
       node/resources/PVC/toleration), Error (container exited non-zero).
    ✅ Work the layers for cluster faults too: pod → node/kubelet (systemctl,
       journalctl) → control plane (crictl/journalctl when apiserver is down)
       → network. Control-plane components are static pods in
       /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
    ✅ Use --previous to see logs from a crashed container; use -f to follow
       live. Read Events with `get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` before
       guessing. `kubectl top` needs metrics-server.
    ✅ Memorize the 12-scenario playbook — it covers ~the whole 30%
       Troubleshooting domain. Drill symptom → first command.
    🎯 EXAM: Troubleshooting is 30% — the biggest payoff. Speed + method win
       it. Practice every scenario until you solve it in < 5 minutes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ Blaming the app when it's DNS or a NetworkPolicy — test the NETWORK path
       (endpoints → nslookup → curl from a temp pod) before touching code.
    ⚠️ Empty endpoints silently break a Service even though it "exists" with a
       ClusterIP.
    ⚠️ Wrong namespace in a name resolves to nothing; cross-namespace needs
       <svc>.<ns> (or the full FQDN).
    ⚠️ A default-deny EGRESS policy also blocks DNS — names stop resolving
       cluster-wide until you add an allow-DNS-to-kube-system rule.
    ⚠️ Plain Flannel ignores NetworkPolicy entirely — your perfect-looking
       policy does nothing without a policy-aware CNI (Calico/Cilium/Weave).
    ⚠️ targetPort ≠ the real containerPort gives "connection refused" even with
       healthy endpoints.
    ⚠️ Exit-code traps in CrashLoop: Exit 137 = OOM-killed (raise memory), Exit
       0 = app finished (it shouldn't be restarting — wrong workload type).
    ⚠️ Swap left enabled, or containerd down, will hold a node NotReady no
       matter what you do in kubectl.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚡ Always test from a temp pod:
       kubectl run t --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
       — curl/nslookup from INSIDE the cluster, not from your laptop.
    ⚡ `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` is the fastest L2 check; empty = stop and
       fix the selector/readiness before anything else.
    ⚡ Memorize the symptom→first-command table; in the exam, speed of the
       FIRST command beats deep analysis.
    ⚡ `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` goes straight to the crashed run; don't
       wait for the next crash.
    ⚡ `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A` surfaces the real cause
       fast across the whole cluster.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    kubectl describe pod <pod>              (events at the bottom!)
    kubectl logs <pod> --previous           (crashed container logs)
    kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A
    kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh
    kubectl get endpoints easypj-db ; kubectl describe svc easypj-db
    kubectl run t --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
    kubectl exec t -- nslookup easypj-db.easypj
    kubectl get netpol -A ; kubectl exec t -- curl -m3 easypj-db:5432
    kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
    kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
    kubectl get nodes -o wide
    systemctl status kubelet ; journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -l
    crictl ps -a ; crictl logs <id>        (container runtime / control plane)
    kubectl top nodes ; kubectl top pods    (needs metrics-server)
    kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource>    (RBAC check)
    kubeadm certs check-expiration ; kubeadm certs renew all

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [L] 🧪 DRILL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Run all 12 playbook scenarios under a timer, naming each symptom's FIRST
    diagnostic command and the fix BEFORE you type it. Repeat until every one
    is under 5 minutes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A  (merged union — full answer + explanation each)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Q1. A Service returns no traffic; endpoints are empty. Fix?
        A. The selector matches no Ready pod. Align the Service selector with
        the pods' labels AND ensure the readiness probe passes — a not-Ready
        pod is pulled from endpoints even if its labels match.

    Q2. Pods can't resolve easypj-db. Diagnose.
        A. From a temp pod: nslookup kubernetes.default (is DNS up at all?),
        then easypj-db / easypj-db.easypj (right namespace?). If DNS itself is
        down, check CoreDNS pods/logs and the kube-dns Service ClusterIP.

    Q3. web→db worked, now it's blocked after adding policies. Cause?
        A. A NetworkPolicy selects db without allowing web (or a default-deny
        with no allow rule). Add an ingress allow web→db on 5432. Confirm the
        web pods carry the label the policy's "from" selector expects.

    Q4. You suspect kube-proxy. What do you check?
        A. The kube-proxy DaemonSet pods are Running, its mode
        (iptables/IPVS), and its logs. A broken kube-proxy breaks Service VIPs
        while pod IPs still work.

    Q5. A Service VIP is unreachable but the pod IP works. Meaning?
        A. The app is fine; the problem is Service-layer
        (endpoints / kube-proxy / targetPort), not the pod or the app.

    Q6. Connections refused though the Service exists. Common config bug?
        A. targetPort doesn't match the container's listening port — fix the
        Service's targetPort to the real containerPort (easypj-db → 5432).

    Q7. From namespace web, reach Service db in namespace data. Name to use?
        A. `db.data` (or db.data.svc.cluster.local). A bare `db` only resolves
        within web's own namespace.

    Q8. An Ingress isn't routing. First checks?
        A. Is an Ingress controller installed and Running? Is the ADDRESS
        populated on the Ingress object? Are the host/path/backend and
        ingressClassName correct, and does the backend Service have endpoints?

    Q9. How do you peek at the dataplane rules for a Service?
        A. On a node: `iptables-save | grep <clusterIP>` (iptables mode) or
        `ipvsadm -Ln` (IPVS mode), and `conntrack -L` for live connections.

    Q10. Give the universal method you apply to every scenario.
         A. GATHER (get/describe) → READ (Events/logs) → ISOLATE the failing
         layer → FIX → VERIFY — the same loop regardless of symptom.

    Q11. A worker node shows NotReady. Where do you start, and name three
         common root causes?
         A. describe node (Conditions), then ssh and `systemctl status
         kubelet`. Common causes: kubelet dead/not enabled, container runtime
         (containerd) down, or swap left enabled. Fix and re-check get nodes.

    Q12. easypj-db is in CrashLoopBackOff. Which single flag gives you the
         crash reason, and what does Exit 137 mean?
         A. `kubectl logs easypj-db --previous` shows the LAST crashed run's
         logs. Exit 137 means the container was OOM-killed — raise the memory
         limit (vs Exit 1 = app error, Exit 0 = completed normally).

    Q13. Pods can't resolve names cluster-wide right after you applied an
         egress lockdown. Likely cause and fix?
         A. The default-deny egress policy also blocks UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS.
         Add an egress allow to the kube-system DNS pods/Service on port 53.

    Q14. A PVC is stuck Pending. Walk the checks.
         A. describe pvc (Events): "no volumes available" vs "waiting for first
         consumer". Compare get pv for matching accessMode, capacity (>=
         request) and storageClassName. WaitForFirstConsumer Pending is normal
         until a pod mounts the PVC.

    Q15. kubectl returns "certificate has expired". Recover the cluster.
         A. kubeadm certs check-expiration → kubeadm certs renew all →
         systemctl restart kubelet (static pods restart) → refresh kubeconfig
         (cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config) → verify get nodes.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: the universal 5-step method applied over the 4 network
        layers, feeding the master decision tree of symptom → fix.

    ┌──────────────────────── PART 9 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ─────────────────────────┐
    │ ✅ ONE method everywhere: get -> describe(Events!) -> logs(--previous) -> │
    │    exec -> isolate layer -> fix -> verify.                               │
    │ ✅ Work the layers: pod -> node/kubelet -> control plane (crictl/        │
    │    journalctl when apiserver down) -> network (endpoints/DNS/policy).    │
    │ ✅ Empty endpoints break a Service silently — check `get endpoints`      │
    │    before suspecting DNS or policy.                                      │
    │ ✅ Observe with logs (output streams) and `kubectl top` (needs metrics-  │
    │    server); read Events before guessing.                                │
    │ ✅ Memorize the 12-scenario playbook — it covers ~the whole 30% domain.  │
    │ 🎯 EXAM: 30% — the biggest payoff; speed + method win it.                │
    │ 🔑 describe · logs -p · get events --sort-by · crictl · top · auth can-i │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    [PART 9 VISUAL SUMMARY]: the master decision tree — symptom to fix.

PART 10: PRODUCTION & HIGH AVAILABILITY                                 🔴 🎯🏢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapters 35-36  ·  HA control plane competency (25%)  ·  "No single point"
  Beyond the exam — real-world CKA admin skills.
  What you'll build: an understanding of (and the steps for) a 3-node HA
  control plane, and how easypj's CKA skills translate to managed cloud
  Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS).
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  PART 10 INTRO
  A one-node control plane is one crash from a frozen cluster. The workloads
  already running keep limping along, but you can't schedule, scale, heal, or
  change anything — kubectl simply hangs. This part makes the cluster itself
  resilient (HA control plane + etcd quorum + load-balanced apiservers) and
  then shows how everything you've learned maps onto managed cloud Kubernetes,
  where the provider runs the control plane for you and your job shifts from
  "babysit etcd" to "design workloads that exploit the cloud."

  Up to now easypj's cluster has had exactly one control-plane node. That was
  fine for learning, but in production it is a single point of failure: lose
  that one node and the API server, scheduler, controller-manager and the
  single etcd member all vanish at once. Part 10 closes that gap two ways —
  first by making the self-managed control plane redundant (Ch35), then by
  handing the whole control plane to a cloud provider (Ch36) so you never run
  it yourself again.

  HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 10 map
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch35 HA (self-managed resilience) ─▶ Ch36 CLOUD (managed EKS/GKE/AKS)    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  The two chapters are two answers to the same question — "how do I stop the
  control plane being a single point of failure?":

  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │ Chapter      │ Strategy                     │ Who runs the control plane│
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch35  HA     │ Run it yourself, redundantly │ You — 3 stacked control   │
  │              │ (3 apiservers + etcd quorum  │ nodes behind a load       │
  │              │ behind a load balancer)      │ balancer; you own etcd    │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ Ch36  CLOUD  │ Let the provider run it      │ The cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS);  │
  │              │ (managed control plane,      │ you only own worker nodes │
  │              │ cloud LB/CSI/IAM integration)│ and workloads             │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

  Visual: from single point of failure to no single point of failure
  ┌─────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   BEFORE (fragile)      │        │      AFTER (HA — Ch35)              │
  │                         │        │                                     │
  │      ┌──────────┐       │        │            ┌────────┐               │
  │      │ control  │ ◀─ x  │        │            │   LB   │ (VIP :6443)    │
  │      │  plane   │       │        │            └───┬────┘               │
  │      │ apiserver│       │        │      ┌─────────┼─────────┐          │
  │      │  etcd ×1 │       │        │      ▼         ▼         ▼          │
  │      └────┬─────┘       │        │  ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐      │
  │           │             │        │  │ cp-1  │ │ cp-2  │ │ cp-3  │      │
  │      ┌────┴─────┐       │        │  │api+etcd│ │api+etcd│ │api+etcd│   │
  │      │ workers  │       │        │  └───┬───┘ └───┬───┘ └───┬───┘      │
  │      └──────────┘       │        │      └────quorum: 2 of 3─┘          │
  │  one crash = frozen     │        │  any one node can die, cluster lives │
  └─────────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  PART 10 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION
  Implementation thread: take easypj's cluster from 1 control plane to 3 behind
  a load balancer with quorum etcd; then map the same easypj deployment onto a
  managed cluster (cloud LB Services, cloud CSI storageclasses, IAM identity).

  Concretely, the easypj implementation arc through this part is:

    1. Stand up an external load balancer (or keepalived + HAProxy VIP) in
       front of :6443 and point kubeadm at that VIP as the controlPlaneEndpoint.
    2. kubeadm init the first control-plane node with --upload-certs, then
       `kubeadm join --control-plane` the second and third nodes so all three
       run a stacked apiserver + a stacked etcd member.
    3. Confirm etcd quorum is 2-of-3: the cluster survives losing any single
       control-plane node, but loses quorum (goes read-only / unavailable) if
       two die at once — which is exactly why you run an ODD number of members.
    4. Re-point easypj's clients (kubeconfig, Ingress, CI) at the VIP, not at
       any one node's IP, so a failover is invisible to the easypj app.
    5. Then lift-and-shift: deploy the same easypj manifests onto EKS/GKE/AKS,
       swapping the self-managed pieces for cloud equivalents — LoadBalancer
       Services for a cloud LB, cloud CSI StorageClasses for PostgreSQL PVCs,
       and IAM identity (IRSA / Workload Identity / AAD Pod Identity) instead
       of long-lived secrets.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which path is for you?
     • Bare metal / on-prem / "we must own the data plane and control plane"
       → Ch35: build the HA control plane yourself.
     • Cloud-first / small platform team / want to stop patching etcd
       → Ch36: let EKS/GKE/AKS run the control plane; you keep your CKA skills
         for workloads, networking, storage and RBAC, which all still apply.

  🔑 PART-LEVEL MUST-REMEMBER
     • etcd needs a MAJORITY (quorum) to accept writes — always run an ODD
       number of members (3 or 5). 3 members tolerate 1 failure; 5 tolerate 2.
     • controlPlaneEndpoint (a stable VIP/DNS behind a load balancer) must be
       set BEFORE the first kubeadm init — you cannot bolt HA on cleanly later.
     • Managed Kubernetes does NOT remove your CKA job: you still own RBAC,
       NetworkPolicy, storage classes, autoscaling and workload reliability —
       the provider only takes the control plane off your plate.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
