  Chapter 35: High Availability Clusters                               🔴 🎯
================================================================================

  [A] META: 🔴 Hard · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation &
      Configuration 25% (HA control plane). Format: 1 ASCII banner + 7 numbered
      sections + Under-the-Hood/DEEPER + scaffold + 10-question Lab Q&A.

  [B] WHY THIS MATTERS
      A single control-plane node is a single point of failure: lose it and you
      lose the API server, the scheduler, the controller-manager, and (if etcd is
      stacked) the cluster's entire datastore. Production clusters MUST survive a
      control-plane node loss without losing the ability to schedule, heal, and
      serve the easypj workload. High availability turns "one node dies, the
      cluster dies" into "one node dies, nobody notices." 🏢
      VISUAL — single vs HA control plane:

        SINGLE CONTROL PLANE (fragile)        HA CONTROL PLANE (resilient)
        ┌──────────────┐                      🌐 Load Balancer (:6443)
        │ CP node      │  ← dies = cluster    ╱        │        ╲
        │ API/etcd/    │     is GONE        CP-1      CP-2      CP-3
        │ sched/ctrl   │                    (1 dies → 2 survive, quorum holds)
        └──────────────┘

  [C] OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
      • Describe HA architecture: ≥3 control-plane nodes behind a load balancer.
      • Contrast stacked vs external etcd topologies and pick one.
      • Build an HA cluster with kubeadm (--control-plane-endpoint, --upload-certs).
      • Compute etcd quorum and fault tolerance (N/2+1; always odd).
      • Explain leader election for scheduler / controller-manager (Lease-based).
      • Configure a load balancer (HAProxy / nginx / keepalived) in front of :6443.
      • Make the easypj app itself HA on top of the cluster (anti-affinity + PDB).

  [D] CKA RELEVANCE 🎯
      HA control plane lives in the 25% "Cluster Architecture, Installation &
      Configuration" domain. The exam expects you to reason about quorum, know
      that scheduler/controller-manager are active-passive while apiservers are
      active-active, recognize the kubeadm HA flags, and understand why etcd
      member counts must be odd. You are unlikely to build a full LB in the exam,
      but you ARE expected to understand and troubleshoot the topology.

  [E] SECTION MAP
      35.1 HA Architecture .............. ≥3 control planes + LB; odd numbers
      35.2 Stacked vs External etcd ..... topology trade-offs table
      35.3 HA Setup with kubeadm ........ control-plane-endpoint + upload-certs
      35.4 etcd Quorum & Fault Tolerance  N/2+1; 3→1, 5→2; never even

  [HIGH AVAILABILITY — no single point of failure]
                      🌐 Load Balancer (:6443, control-plane-endpoint)
                     ╱            │            ╲
            📡 apiserver   📡 apiserver   📡 apiserver
            🗄️ etcd-0  ◄──►🗄️ etcd-1  ◄──►🗄️ etcd-2     quorum = 2 of 3

                     ╲            │            ╱

   Quorum math: 3 ⇒ tolerate 1 · 5 ⇒ tolerate 2 (ALWAYS odd).

   Build: kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint <LB> --upload-certs, then join

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.1  HA Architecture 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      • Multiple control plane nodes (minimum 3 for etcd quorum).
      • Load balancer in front of API servers (the stable endpoint clients use).
      • etcd: stacked (on control plane) vs external topology.
      • Use ODD numbers of control-plane / etcd members so quorum is meaningful.

      [HA CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │                                                        │
      │              ┌──────────────────┐                     │
      │              │  LOAD BALANCER   │                     │
      │              │  (HAProxy/nginx) │                     │
      │              └───────┬──────────┘                     │
      │           ┌─────────┼─────────┐                      │
      │           ▼         ▼         ▼                      │
      │    ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐           │
      │    │Control   │ │Control   │ │Control   │           │
      │    │Plane 1   │ │Plane 2   │ │Plane 3   │           │
      │    │ API ✓    │ │ API ✓    │ │ API ✓    │           │
      │    │ etcd ✓   │ │ etcd ✓   │ │ etcd ✓   │           │
      │    │ sched ✓  │ │ sched ✓  │ │ sched ✓  │           │
      │    │ ctrl-mgr │ │ ctrl-mgr │ │ ctrl-mgr │           │
      │    └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘           │
      │         (leader)    (standby)    (standby)           │
      │                                                       │
      │    ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐           │
      │    │ Worker 1 │ │ Worker 2 │ │ Worker 3 │           │
      │    │ 📦📦📦     │ │ 📦📦📦     │ │ 📦📦📦     │           │
      │    └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘           │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      💡 INSIGHT: The "(leader) / (standby)" labels apply to the scheduler and
      controller-manager only. The API servers are ALL active simultaneously —
      the LB spreads traffic across them. etcd members are all active too,
      replicating via the Raft consensus protocol.

      🧠 ANALOGY: Think of the control plane like an airline cockpit crew. The
      apiservers are gate agents — many of them, all serving passengers at once
      behind one "Departures" sign (the LB). The scheduler is the captain: only
      one flies the plane at a time, but a co-pilot (standby) is strapped in,
      ready to take the controls the instant the captain is incapacitated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.2  Stacked vs External etcd 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      Two supported topologies. Stacked is kubeadm's default and the most exam-
      tested. External etcd isolates the datastore for higher resilience.

      ┌───────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
      │ Aspect        │ Stacked (default)    │ External etcd        │
      ├───────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
      │ etcd location │ On control plane node│ Separate servers     │
      │ Simplicity    │ Easier to set up     │ More complex         │
      │ Fault risk    │ CP failure = etcd too│ etcd survives CP loss│
      │ Minimum nodes │ 3 (combined)         │ 3 CP + 3 etcd        │
      │ CKA Exam      │ Most tested topology │ Understand concept   │
      └───────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

      [STACKED vs EXTERNAL — visual]
        STACKED (kubeadm default)            EXTERNAL etcd
        ┌─────────────────┐                  ┌─────────────────┐
        │ CP node         │                  │ CP node         │
        │  apiserver      │                  │  apiserver ─────┼──► ┌────────┐
        │  sched/ctrl     │                  │  sched/ctrl     │    │ etcd   │
        │  etcd  ◄────────┼── on same box    └─────────────────┘    │ cluster│
        └─────────────────┘                  (etcd lives on its     │ (3 sep │
        3 boxes total                         own dedicated nodes)  │ nodes) │
                                              6 boxes total         └────────┘

      🧭 DECISION GUIDE:
        • Choose STACKED when: simplicity, fewer machines, standard prod, and the
          CKA exam. One CP node failure removes one etcd member too — still fine
          with 3 because quorum survives (2 of 3).
        • Choose EXTERNAL when: you want the datastore decoupled from control-plane
          churn, you rebuild apiservers frequently, or you need to scale/secure
          etcd independently. The cost is roughly double the machines and ops.

      ⚠️ Either way, the etcd member COUNT (not the topology) determines fault
      tolerance. Stacked 3-CP and external 3-etcd both tolerate exactly 1 loss.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.3  HA Setup with kubeadm 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      Steps:
        a) Set up the load balancer (HAProxy or nginx) fronting :6443.
        b) kubeadm init on the FIRST control plane with
           --control-plane-endpoint=LOAD_BALANCER:6443 and --upload-certs.
        c) Join additional control planes with the --control-plane flag and the
           --certificate-key printed by init.
        d) Join workers normally. Then verify etcd cluster health.

      [CODE: kubeadm init for HA setup]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      # On the FIRST control-plane node. --upload-certs stores the CA/certs
      # in a kubeadm-certs Secret so other CP nodes can fetch them.
      sudo kubeadm init \
        --control-plane-endpoint "lb.easypj:6443" \
        --upload-certs \
        --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16

      # init prints two join commands. The CONTROL-PLANE join looks like:
      kubeadm join lb.easypj:6443 \
        --token <token> \
        --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> \
        --control-plane \
        --certificate-key <certificate-key>

      # The WORKER join (no --control-plane, no --certificate-key):
      kubeadm join lb.easypj:6443 \
        --token <token> \
        --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      [CODE: HAProxy configuration for API servers]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      # /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg — TCP load balance the apiservers on 6443
      frontend kubernetes-api
          bind *:6443
          mode tcp
          option tcplog
          default_backend kube-apiservers

      backend kube-apiservers
          mode tcp
          balance roundrobin
          option httpchk GET /readyz
          http-check expect status 200
          default-server inter 5s fall 3 rise 2
          server cp1 10.0.0.11:6443 check check-ssl verify none
          server cp2 10.0.0.12:6443 check check-ssl verify none
          server cp3 10.0.0.13:6443 check check-ssl verify none
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      🔑 The --control-plane-endpoint MUST be set on the FIRST init and CANNOT be
      added later without re-bootstrapping. Always create the LB DNS name and pass
      it up front, even for a single-CP cluster you might later grow.

      ⚠️ The endpoint name (lb.easypj) must appear in the apiserver certificate's
      certSANs, or clients hitting the LB will reject the cert. kubeadm adds the
      --control-plane-endpoint to the SANs automatically; if you front an existing
      cluster with a new LB name, regenerate the apiserver cert with the new SAN.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.4  etcd Quorum and Fault Tolerance 🎯
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      • etcd requires a MAJORITY of members to function (quorum).
      • 3 members: tolerates 1 failure (quorum = 2).
      • 5 members: tolerates 2 failures (quorum = 3).
      • NEVER use even numbers for an etcd cluster size.

      [DIAGRAM: etcd quorum math]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  ETCD QUORUM FORMULA: (N/2) + 1                       │
      │                                                        │
      │  Members │ Quorum │ Tolerated Failures │ Recommended? │
      │  ────────┼────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────│
      │    1     │   1    │         0           │ Dev only ❌   │
      │    2     │   2    │         0           │ Never ❌      │
      │    3     │   2    │         1           │ Standard ✅   │
      │    5     │   3    │         2           │ Large prod ✅ │
      │    7     │   4    │         3           │ Rare ⚠️       │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      🔑 Fast rule: tolerated failures = floor(N/2). 3→1, 5→2, 7→3.

      ⚠️ Why even numbers are useless: a 4-member cluster needs quorum = 3, so it
      still only tolerates 1 failure — exactly like a 3-member cluster — but with
      one more machine to break and a higher chance of a split-brain partition
      where neither half has a majority. Even counts buy NO extra tolerance.

      🔧 What "lose quorum" actually means: if 2 of 3 members are down, the
      surviving member cannot form a majority. etcd refuses new writes; the API
      becomes read-only / unavailable. The cluster does NOT silently elect a new
      leader from a minority — that is the whole point of Raft, to avoid two
      "leaders" diverging. Recovery means restoring a member to regain quorum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.5  Leader Election Deep Dive 🔧
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      • API servers are ACTIVE-ACTIVE — every one serves requests; the LB spreads
        traffic. There is no leader among apiservers.
      • scheduler and controller-manager are ACTIVE-PASSIVE — they run on every
        control-plane node, but only the elected LEADER does work. The others are
        warm standbys, ready to take over instantly.
      • The leader holds a lease: implemented with the Lease API object in
        kube-system. The leader renews it on an interval; if it stops renewing
        (crash, network loss), the lease expires and a standby acquires it.

      [LEADER ELECTION FLOW]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  CP-1 scheduler  CP-2 scheduler  CP-3 scheduler        │
      │       │ holds        │ watch        │ watch            │
      │       ▼ lease        ▼              ▼                  │
      │   ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐           │
      │   │  Lease: kube-scheduler (kube-system)  │           │
      │   │  holderIdentity = cp-1                │           │
      │   │  renewTime = <every ~2s>              │           │
      │   └───────────────────────────────────────┘           │
      │   cp-1 dies → renewTime stale → cp-2 grabs lease →     │
      │   cp-2 becomes the new active scheduler (failover)     │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [CODE: Leader election flags in the kube-scheduler manifest]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      # /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml (static pod)
      spec:
        containers:
        - command:
          - kube-scheduler
          - --leader-elect=true          # on by default in HA
          - --leader-elect-lease-duration=15s
          - --leader-elect-renew-deadline=10s
          - --leader-elect-retry-period=2s
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      [CODE: Checking the current leaders]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      $ kubectl get lease -n kube-system
      $ kubectl describe lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system
      $ kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager
      # holderIdentity shows which node currently owns the lease (the leader).
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      💡 This is also exactly how custom controllers/operators run multiple
      replicas safely: they use the same Lease-based leader election so only one
      replica reconciles at a time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.6  Load Balancer Configuration for HA 🏢
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      The LB is the stable front door (the --control-plane-endpoint). It health-
      checks each apiserver and removes unhealthy ones from the pool so clients
      only ever reach a working API server.

      [DIAGRAM: Load balancer health check flow]
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │                                                        │
      │   Client Request                                       │
      │        │                                               │
      │        ▼                                               │
      │  ┌─────────────┐   Health Check: /healthz on :6443    │
      │  │  HAProxy /   │   If 200 → route traffic            │
      │  │  nginx LB    │   If fail → remove from pool        │
      │  └──────┬──────┘                                       │
      │    ┌────┼────┐                                         │
      │    ▼    ▼    ▼                                         │
      │  CP-1  CP-2  CP-3  (API Servers)                      │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      [CODE: HAProxy configuration example]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      frontend k8s-api
          bind *:6443
          mode tcp
          default_backend k8s-api-backend

      backend k8s-api-backend
          mode tcp
          balance roundrobin
          option httpchk GET /readyz          # apiserver readiness endpoint
          http-check expect status 200
          server cp1 10.0.0.11:6443 check check-ssl verify none
          server cp2 10.0.0.12:6443 check check-ssl verify none
          server cp3 10.0.0.13:6443 check check-ssl verify none
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      [CODE: nginx stream proxy configuration]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      # nginx.conf — L4 (TCP) stream proxy for the apiservers
      stream {
          upstream kube_apiserver {
              least_conn;
              server 10.0.0.11:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
              server 10.0.0.12:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
              server 10.0.0.13:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
          }
          server {
              listen 6443;
              proxy_pass kube_apiserver;
              proxy_timeout 10m;
              proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
          }
      }
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      🔧 keepalived for the LB itself: a single HAProxy/nginx box is a new single
      point of failure. Run two LBs and float a Virtual IP (VIP) between them with
      keepalived (VRRP); the control-plane-endpoint DNS points at the VIP, so an
      LB failure is invisible to the cluster.

      ⚠️ Use a TCP/L4 health check or the apiserver's /readyz — NOT a naive TCP
      connect alone. A node whose apiserver is up but not READY (e.g. etcd
      unreachable from it) should be pulled from the pool.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  35.7  Production HA Checklist for easypj 🧪
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      Cluster-level AND app-level HA — a resilient control plane does nothing if
      easypj runs as a single replica on one node.

      [CHECKLIST]
      ✅ 3+ control plane nodes across availability zones
      ✅ etcd backup CronJob running every 6 hours
      ✅ Load balancer with health checks on :6443/readyz (VIP via keepalived)
      ✅ PodDisruptionBudgets on the easypj Deployment (minAvailable: 2)
      ✅ Anti-affinity: spread easypj pods across nodes (and zones)
      ✅ Resource requests/limits set on all containers
      ✅ Multi-AZ storage for PostgreSQL (so a zone loss doesn't lose the DB)
      ✅ Monitoring alerts for node NotReady and pod failures
      ❌ Never run single-replica Deployments in production

      [CODE: easypj anti-affinity + PDB]
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------
      # jobpost Deployment — spread replicas across nodes
      apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: Deployment
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web
      spec:
        replicas: 3
        selector:
          matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
        template:
          metadata:
            labels: { app: easypj-web }
          spec:
            affinity:
              podAntiAffinity:
                requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                - labelSelector:
                    matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
                  topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
            containers:
            - name: web
              image: easypj:5.2.5
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
                limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
      ---
      apiVersion: policy/v1
      kind: PodDisruptionBudget
      metadata:
        name: easypj-web-pdb
      spec:
        minAvailable: 2
        selector:
          matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
      ----------------------------------------------------------------------

      💡 The PDB protects easypj during VOLUNTARY disruptions (node drains,
      upgrades): the eviction API won't take a pod below minAvailable. The
      anti-affinity protects against INVOLUNTARY ones (a node dying), because no
      single node hosts all replicas.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [G] 🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      🔧 UTH — the stable apiserver address: the --control-plane-endpoint is the
      one name every component, kubelet, and kubeconfig trusts. Because it points
      at the LB (or a keepalived VIP), the actual apiserver behind it can change,
      die, or be rebuilt and clients never notice. This indirection is what makes
      a control-plane node disposable.

      🔧 UTH — quorum loss behavior: etcd uses Raft. A write commits only when a
      MAJORITY of members acknowledge it. Below quorum, etcd will not commit
      writes and the apiserver's storage layer returns errors → the API is
      effectively read-only/unavailable. Reads of already-committed data may still
      work from a surviving member, but no mutations land. Recovery = restore a
      member to re-form a majority.

      🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
        • etcd learner members: a new member can join as a non-voting "learner"
          first, catching up on the log without affecting quorum, then be PROMOTED
          to a voting member. This avoids the risk of a slow new member stalling
          writes. (etcdctl member add --learner / member promote).
        • LB health checks on /readyz: prefer /readyz over /healthz or a bare TCP
          connect — /readyz reflects whether the apiserver is actually ready to
          serve (including its etcd connectivity).
        • certSANs for the LB endpoint: the apiserver cert must list the LB
          name/VIP in its SANs (kubeadm: apiServer.certSANs in the kubeadm config)
          or TLS clients reject the connection.
        • lease tuning: leader-elect-lease-duration / renew-deadline /
          retry-period trade failover speed against false failovers under network
          jitter. Shorter = faster failover but more flapping risk.
        • rebuilding a failed control-plane node: remove its etcd member first
          (etcdctl member remove), then `kubeadm reset` the node, then re-join it
          with --control-plane. Never just re-add a node with a stale etcd member
          still listed.
        • multi-AZ etcd latency: etcd is latency-sensitive (Raft round-trips on
          every write). Spread members across AZs for resilience, but keep them in
          the same region — cross-region etcd latency cripples write throughput.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [H] 🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      🔑 HA = ≥3 control-plane nodes behind a load balancer (the stable
         --control-plane-endpoint on :6443) + a quorum etcd cluster. Use ODD
         counts.
      🔑 etcd quorum is N/2+1: 3 members tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Lose
         quorum and the cluster goes read-only/unavailable until it's restored.
      🔑 apiservers are ACTIVE-ACTIVE (the LB spreads traffic); scheduler and
         controller-manager are ACTIVE-PASSIVE, electing one leader via a Lease.
      🔑 kubeadm builds it: `kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint <LB>
         --upload-certs`, then join the other control-plane nodes, then workers.
      🔑 Stacked etcd (default) is simpler and most exam-tested; external etcd
         decouples the datastore for resilience at higher ops cost. Either way
         the etcd member COUNT sets fault tolerance.
      🔑 Verify leaders with `kubectl get lease -n kube-system`; verify etcd with
         `etcdctl member list -w table` and `endpoint health`.
      🔑 App-level HA still matters: spread easypj with podAntiAffinity + a PDB +
         multi-AZ storage so no single failure drops all replicas.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [I] ⚠️ GOTCHAS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      ⚠️ Even numbers of etcd members buy NO extra fault tolerance (4 still only
         tolerates 1) and raise split-brain risk — stay odd.
      ⚠️ Losing quorum (e.g. 2 of 3 down) makes the API read-only/unavailable; the
         priority is restoring a quorum member, not adding workers.
      ⚠️ Forgetting --upload-certs means joining control-plane nodes can't fetch
         the certs and the join fails.
      ⚠️ The LB must health-check the apiserver (/readyz) and the cert must include
         the LB endpoint in certSANs, or clients reject it.
      ⚠️ --control-plane-endpoint cannot be added cleanly after a single-node init;
         set it on the FIRST init even if you start with one control plane.
      ⚠️ A single LB instance is itself a SPOF — pair it with keepalived/VIP.
      ⚠️ Re-joining a failed control-plane node without first removing its stale
         etcd member corrupts the member list — remove, then re-join.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [J] ⚡ SPEED TIPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      ⚡ `etcdctl member list -w table` (with etcd certs) shows the member set and
         who's healthy — first check on an HA etcd issue.
      ⚡ Spread easypj with podAntiAffinity + a PDB so a node loss never drops all
         replicas.
      ⚡ Reason quorum quickly: tolerated failures = floor(N/2). 3→1, 5→2, 7→3.
      ⚡ `kubectl -n kube-system get lease` instantly tells you which node is the
         active scheduler/controller-manager (holderIdentity).
      ⚡ `kubectl get nodes` then look at the control-plane roles to confirm how
         many CP nodes you actually have before reasoning about quorum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [K] 🔑 COMMANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "lb.easypj:6443" --upload-certs
      kubeadm join lb.easypj:6443 --control-plane --certificate-key <key>   # CP join
      kubeadm join lb.easypj:6443 ...                                       # worker join
      kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs                        # refresh certs
      etcdctl member list -w table --endpoints=... --cacert=... --cert=... --key=...
      etcdctl endpoint health --cluster -w table                           # member health
      kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager
      kubectl describe lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system                 # who is leader
      kubectl get nodes -o wide                                            # see CP nodes

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [L] 🧪 DRILL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      On a 3-control-plane cluster, reason through (and if possible simulate)
      losing 1 node (still works — quorum 2 of 3 holds) vs 2 nodes (quorum lost →
      API read-only), and identify the recovery step: restore/replace a member to
      regain a majority before doing anything else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [M] 🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Q1. How many control-plane nodes for HA, and why odd?
          A. ≥3, odd, so etcd can form quorum (N/2+1) and tolerate failures
          without split-brain. Even counts add a machine and split-brain risk but
          NO extra tolerance (4 tolerates the same 1 failure as 3).

      Q2. Stacked vs external etcd — the trade-off?
          A. Stacked (etcd on the CP nodes) is simpler and uses fewer machines but
          couples etcd to control-plane failures; external etcd isolates the
          datastore for resilience at roughly double the machines and ops cost.

      Q3. With 5 etcd members, how many failures are tolerated?
          A. 2 (quorum = 3). General rule: floor(N/2).

      Q4. What does --control-plane-endpoint provide?
          A. A single stable address (the LB/VIP) all components and kubeconfigs
          use, so any apiserver can serve traffic and the cluster survives a
          control-plane node loss. It must be set at first init.

      Q5. How do additional control-plane nodes get the certs to join?
          A. `kubeadm init --upload-certs` stores them in a kubeadm-certs Secret;
          control-plane joins use --certificate-key to fetch and install them.

      Q6. How are the scheduler and controller-manager made HA?
          A. They run on every control-plane node but only the elected leader acts
          (active-passive) via a Lease object in kube-system; on leader loss the
          lease expires and a standby acquires it and takes over.

      Q7. What is the load balancer's role?
          A. It fronts the apiservers on :6443, health-checks them (/readyz), and
          gives clients one endpoint — distributing API traffic and surviving a
          control-plane node loss. Pair LBs with keepalived/VIP to avoid a new SPOF.

      Q8. 2 of 3 control planes are down. What is the cluster state?
          A. etcd lost quorum → the API is read-only/unavailable. Restore a third
          member (or recover one) to regain quorum BEFORE anything else; adding
          workers does nothing.

      Q9. How do you check the etcd members on an HA cluster?
          A. `etcdctl member list -w table` (and `etcdctl endpoint health
          --cluster`) using the etcd CA/cert/key from /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd.

      Q10. How do you make easypj itself HA on top of the cluster?
           A. Run multiple replicas spread with podAntiAffinity across
           nodes/zones, add a PodDisruptionBudget (e.g. minAvailable: 2), set
           resource requests/limits, and use multi-AZ storage for PostgreSQL so no
           single failure drops the app.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      3 control planes + 1 stable LB endpoint + a quorum (odd) etcd cluster:

                      🌐 control-plane-endpoint (LB/VIP, :6443)
                     ╱            │            ╲
              CP-1 active    CP-2 active   CP-3 active   (apiservers ALL active)
              etcd-0 ◄──────► etcd-1 ◄──────► etcd-2     (quorum = 2 of 3)
                     ╲            │            ╱
                         workers: easypj pods (anti-affinity + PDB)

      .vs-prose: An HA cluster removes every single point of failure. Three (odd)
      control-plane nodes sit behind one stable load-balancer endpoint that every
      client and kubeconfig trusts; the apiservers are all active and the LB
      spreads traffic, while the scheduler and controller-manager run active-passive
      with one Lease-elected leader. etcd replicates via Raft and stays writable as
      long as a majority (N/2+1) survives — 3 members tolerate 1 loss, 5 tolerate 2,
      and even counts are forbidden because they add risk without tolerance. kubeadm
      assembles it all with --control-plane-endpoint plus --upload-certs, then
      control-plane and worker joins. Finally, the easypj app earns its own HA on
      top via anti-affinity, a PodDisruptionBudget, and multi-AZ storage.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Chapter 36: Cloud Kubernetes — EKS, GKE, AKS                         🟡 🏢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~1.5h · 🏢 Beyond-exam (how your CKA skills apply
        in managed clouds). Stack: easypj (Django project) + jobpost (app),
        Python 3.13, Django 5.2.5, Docker, PostgreSQL on Kubernetes.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ─────────────────
  Almost every real job runs Kubernetes on a managed service — Amazon EKS,
  Google GKE, or Azure AKS — not a hand-rolled kubeadm cluster. The CKA exam
  itself is run on self-managed clusters, but the moment you ship easypj to
  production you will land on one of these three. The crucial insight: the
  provider takes over the control plane, but YOUR skills — Pods, Deployments,
  Services, RBAC, PV/PVC, NetworkPolicy, probes, scheduling — transfer almost
  unchanged. Only the GLUE differs: storage classes, load balancers, and pod
  identity. Knowing exactly what changes and what stays the same is the whole
  point of this chapter.

  OBJECTIVES
  ──────────
  • Distinguish managed from self-managed Kubernetes and the responsibility split.
  • Identify which CKA concepts still apply in the cloud and which are abstracted.
  • Wire cloud-native storage (CSI) and networking (LoadBalancer/Ingress).
  • Use cloud identity (IRSA / Workload Identity) to give pods cloud credentials.
  • Deploy easypj to a managed cluster with the same manifests + cloud glue.
  • Understand the Cluster Autoscaler (nodes) vs the HPA (pods).

  CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────
  🎯 The exam runs on self-managed clusters, so cloud specifics are NOT directly
     tested. BUT the concepts that DO transfer — Services, PV/PVC dynamic
     provisioning via StorageClass, RBAC, NetworkPolicy — are heavily tested.
  🏢 This chapter is mostly day-2/beyond-exam context so you understand how the
     skills you are drilling map onto a real production environment.

  SECTION MAP
  ───────────
   36.1  Managed vs Self-Managed Kubernetes              🏢
   36.2  CKA Concepts in Cloud Kubernetes                🏢
   36.3  Cloud-Native Storage and Networking             🏢
   36.4  Cloud Identity Integration                      🏢
   36.5  Deploying easypj to Cloud Kubernetes            🧪
   36.6  Cluster Autoscaler                              🏢

  📊 KEY DIAGRAMS — Chapter 36
  ────────────────────────────
  [MANAGED vs SELF-MANAGED — who owns what]
   ┌──────────────── CLOUD PROVIDER (EKS/GKE/AKS) ───────────────┐
   │ 📡 apiserver  🗄️ etcd  📋 scheduler  🔄 ctrl-mgr  (managed!) │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   ┌──────────────────── YOU still own ──────────────────────────┐
   │ workloads · RBAC · NetworkPolicy · PV/PVC · ingress/gateway  │
   │ LoadBalancer Svc -> cloud LB · storageClass -> cloud CSI     │
   │ SA -> cloud IAM (IRSA / Workload Identity)                   │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   📖 Same easypj manifests; only storageClass/LB/identity glue changes.
   Cluster Autoscaler scales NODES; HPA scales PODS.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.1  Managed vs Self-Managed Kubernetes                              🏢
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  In self-managed Kubernetes (what you build with kubeadm for the CKA), YOU
  run everything: the apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager, the
  certificates, the upgrades, the backups. In managed Kubernetes the provider
  runs the control plane for you and hands you a kubeconfig. You keep the
  workloads, RBAC, networking, and storage.

  📊 Cloud Kubernetes services comparison
  ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┬────────────────┐
  │ Feature          │ EKS (AWS)       │ GKE (Google)    │ AKS (Azure)    │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────────┤
  │ Control plane    │ Managed         │ Managed         │ Managed (free) │
  │ Worker nodes     │ Self/Managed    │ Autopilot/Std   │ VMSS           │
  │ Networking       │ VPC CNI         │ VPC-native      │ Azure CNI      │
  │ Load Balancer    │ ALB/NLB         │ GCP LB          │ Azure LB       │
  │ Storage          │ EBS CSI         │ PD CSI          │ Azure Disk     │
  │ Identity         │ IAM Roles       │ Workload ID     │ Managed ID     │
  │ CKA Relevance    │ Concepts apply  │ Concepts apply  │ Concepts apply │
  └──────────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERM — Managed node pool / node group: a managed set of identical
     worker nodes (instance type, size, autoscaling policy) you can scale and
     upgrade independently of the control plane. EKS calls them "managed node
     groups", GKE "node pools", AKS "node pools" backed by VM Scale Sets (VMSS).

  💡 INSIGHT: AKS gives the control plane away for free and bills only worker
     nodes; EKS charges an hourly control-plane fee. Either way, a LoadBalancer
     Service or a dynamically-provisioned disk is BILLABLE — managed K8s makes
     it trivially easy to spend money by accident.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.2  CKA Concepts in Cloud Kubernetes                                🏢
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - Same kubectl commands work everywhere
  - Same YAML manifests (mostly)
  - Key differences: networking, storage provisioners, IAM
  - Cloud-managed: control plane, etcd backups, upgrades

  [SELF-MANAGED vs CLOUD-MANAGED — What Changes?]
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CKA SKILL             SELF-MANAGED  CLOUD-MANAGED    │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │  kubeadm init/join      You do it      Not needed ☁️   │
  │  etcd backup/restore    You do it      Auto/managed    │
  │  Certificate rotation   You do it      Auto-rotated    │
  │  Cluster upgrades       kubeadm        Cloud console   │
  │  Node scaling           Manual          Auto-scaler     │
  │  kubectl commands       Same ✅         Same ✅          │
  │  YAML manifests         Same ✅         Same ✅          │
  │  RBAC                   Same ✅         +Cloud IAM      │
  │  NetworkPolicies        Same ✅         Same ✅          │
  │  PV/PVC                 Same ✅         +Cloud Disks    │
  │  Troubleshooting        Same ✅         Same ✅          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 What's ABSTRACTED AWAY: you no longer run etcdctl backups, you don't
     rotate apiserver/kubelet certs by hand, you don't drive kubeadm upgrade.
     What STAYS YOURS: every workload object, RBAC Roles/Bindings, Services,
     PersistentVolumeClaims, NetworkPolicies, probes, scheduling constraints,
     and all the troubleshooting (a CrashLoopBackOff debugs identically on EKS
     and on a bare kubeadm box).

  💡 INSIGHT: This is why the CKA is still the right credential for a cloud
     job. The exam drills the layer you keep; the provider just removes the
     plumbing the exam already assumes works.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.3  Cloud-Native Storage and Networking                            🏢
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - CSI (Container Storage Interface) makes storage vendor-agnostic
  - Cloud providers install CSI drivers automatically
  - StorageClass uses the provisioner field to target cloud storage

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: when you create a PVC with a cloud StorageClass and a Pod
     mounts it, the cloud's CSI controller calls the provider API to create a
     real disk (EBS volume / GCE PD / Azure managed disk), attaches it to the
     node, and the kubelet mounts it into the container. When you delete the
     PVC (Delete reclaim policy) the disk is destroyed. This is dynamic
     provisioning — the exact mechanism you drilled in the storage chapters,
     just with a cloud provisioner instead of a local one.

  CODE: StorageClass for EBS (AWS) — easypj PostgreSQL data
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
  kind: StorageClass
  metadata:
    name: easypj-ebs-gp3
  provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
  parameters:
    type: gp3
    fsType: ext4
  reclaimPolicy: Delete
  allowVolumeExpansion: true
  volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

  CODE: StorageClass for Azure Disk (AKS) — easypj PostgreSQL data
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
  kind: StorageClass
  metadata:
    name: easypj-azuredisk
  provisioner: disk.csi.azure.com
  parameters:
    skuName: Premium_LRS
    fsType: ext4
  reclaimPolicy: Delete
  allowVolumeExpansion: true
  volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

  CODE: StorageClass for GCE Persistent Disk (GKE) — easypj PostgreSQL data
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
  kind: StorageClass
  metadata:
    name: easypj-pd-ssd
  provisioner: pd.csi.storage.gke.io
  parameters:
    type: pd-ssd
  reclaimPolicy: Delete
  allowVolumeExpansion: true
  volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

  📖 NETWORKING: a Service of type LoadBalancer triggers the cloud-controller-
     manager to provision a real cloud load balancer (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP LB,
     Azure LB) and write its address into the Service's EXTERNAL-IP. Ingress
     (or the newer Gateway API) routes HTTP for easypj behind that LB.

  CODE: easypj-web Service exposed via a cloud LoadBalancer
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: easypj-web
    annotations:
      # AWS NLB instead of classic ELB:
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb"
  spec:
    type: LoadBalancer
    selector:
      app: easypj
      tier: web
    ports:
      - port: 80
        targetPort: 8000

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: LB ANNOTATIONS are the per-cloud control knob. Internal
     vs internet-facing, NLB vs ALB, subnet selection, health-check paths —
     all expressed as annotations on the Service/Ingress. The spec stays
     portable; the annotations carry the cloud-specific intent.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.4  Cloud Identity Integration                                     🏢
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - Pods in cloud K8s can assume cloud IAM roles (no static keys baked in)
  - AWS: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
  - Azure: Workload Identity / Managed Identity
  - GCP: Workload Identity Federation
  - easypj example: a Pod accesses the cloud database / object store with IAM,
    not passwords embedded in the image or a Secret.

  DIAGRAM: Pod → ServiceAccount → Cloud IAM Role → Cloud Resource
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                      │
  │   easypj Pod                                                         │
  │      │ uses                                                          │
  │      ▼                                                               │
  │   ServiceAccount (annotated with cloud role ARN / client-id)        │
  │      │ projected token mounted into /var/run/secrets/...            │
  │      ▼                                                               │
  │   Cloud token exchange (STS / OIDC federation)                      │
  │      │ swaps projected SA token for short-lived cloud creds         │
  │      ▼                                                               │
  │   Cloud IAM Role  ──grants──▶  Cloud Resource (RDS, S3, KeyVault)   │
  │                                                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD (IRSA / Workload Identity token exchange): the cluster runs
     an OIDC identity provider. The kubelet mounts a *projected* ServiceAccount
     token (a short-lived, audience-scoped JWT) into the pod. The cloud SDK
     reads that token, presents it to the cloud's STS/OIDC endpoint, and — if
     the SA is annotated and the trust policy allows it — receives temporary
     cloud credentials. No long-lived access keys ever sit in the pod.

  CODE: easypj ServiceAccount annotated for IRSA (AWS)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: easypj
    annotations:
      eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/easypj-db-access

  ⚠️ A ServiceAccount ALONE is not enough — the cloud-side trust relationship
     (IAM role trust policy / federated credential) must also be configured, or
     the token exchange fails and the pod cannot reach the cloud resource.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.5  Deploying easypj to Cloud Kubernetes                          🧪
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  HIGH-LEVEL WALKTHROUGH
  a) Create the managed cluster
     - AWS:   eksctl create cluster --name easypj-prod
     - Azure: az aks create --name easypj-prod --resource-group easypj-rg
     - GCP:   gcloud container clusters create easypj-prod
  b) Configure the kubectl context
     - AWS:   aws eks update-kubeconfig --name easypj-prod
     - Azure: az aks get-credentials --name easypj-prod --resource-group easypj-rg
     - GCP:   gcloud container clusters get-credentials easypj-prod
  c) Apply the SAME manifests as the local cluster
     $ kubectl apply -f easypj-deployment.yaml
     $ kubectl apply -f easypj-service.yaml
  d) Cloud-specific glue: Ingress controller, LoadBalancer Service, PV
     provisioner (the cloud StorageClass from 36.3), and pod identity (36.4).
  💡 TIP: Focus on CKA core concepts — they transfer to any cloud. Only the
     storageClass, the LB/Ingress annotations, and the SA↔IAM identity change.

  🧪 LAB — map easypj objects to their managed-cloud equivalents:
   ┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj object              │ Managed-cloud equivalent                 │
   ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ Deployment easypj-web      │ IDENTICAL — runs unchanged               │
   │ Service type LoadBalancer  │ Cloud LB (ALB/NLB · GCP LB · Azure LB)   │
   │ PVC + StorageClass         │ Cloud CSI disk (EBS · PD · Azure Disk)   │
   │ ServiceAccount easypj      │ IRSA / Workload Identity → cloud IAM      │
   │ Ingress easypj             │ Cloud Ingress / Gateway controller        │
   │ RBAC Role/RoleBinding      │ IDENTICAL (+ optional cloud IAM mapping)  │
   │ NetworkPolicy              │ IDENTICAL (needs a policy-capable CNI)    │
   └────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: keep the cloud-specific bits (storageClass, LB annotations,
     identity) in a Kustomize OVERLAY so the base easypj manifests stay
     portable across EKS, GKE, AKS, and your local kubeadm cluster.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  36.6  Cluster Autoscaler                                            🏢
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - Automatically adds/removes NODES based on pending pods
  - Pod can't be scheduled (insufficient resources) → add a node
  - Node underutilized for 10+ minutes → remove the node

  DIAGRAM: Cluster Autoscaler decision flow
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod pending (no resources)                            │
  │        │                                               │
  │        ▼                                               │
  │  Cluster Autoscaler checks node groups                │
  │        │                                               │
  │        ▼                                               │
  │  New node provisioned by cloud provider                │
  │        │                                               │
  │        ▼                                               │
  │  Pod scheduled on new node ✅                          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which autoscaler?
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  easypj pods saturated (CPU/mem high)   → HPA scales POD replicas │
   │  pods Pending, no node has room         → Cluster Autoscaler adds │
   │                                            a NODE                 │
   │  nodes idle 10+ min                      → Cluster Autoscaler     │
   │                                            removes a NODE         │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   📖 HPA and Cluster Autoscaler work TOGETHER: HPA bumps replicas, the new
      replicas go Pending, and the Cluster Autoscaler then adds the node to
      land them on. On AWS, Karpenter is a newer alternative to the classic
      Cluster Autoscaler that provisions right-sized nodes directly.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Cloud controllers: the cloud-controller-manager watches Services of type
    LoadBalancer and PVCs, then calls provider APIs to provision LBs and disks —
    this is the seam between portable Kubernetes objects and cloud resources.
  • IRSA / Workload-Identity token exchange: the cluster's OIDC provider issues
    a projected SA token; the cloud STS/OIDC endpoint swaps it for short-lived
    creds when the SA annotation + cloud trust policy line up.
  • Cloud LB annotations: internal vs internet-facing, NLB vs ALB, subnet and
    health-check selection are all expressed as Service/Ingress annotations.
  • Per-cloud CSI drivers: ebs.csi.aws.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io,
    disk.csi.azure.com — each with its own parameters (gp3 / pd-ssd / Premium_LRS).
  • Managed node pools / groups: identical worker sets you scale and upgrade
    independently; the control plane upgrade is the provider's, the node-pool
    upgrade is yours.
  • Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter: classic CA scales fixed node groups;
    Karpenter (AWS) provisions just-in-time, right-sized nodes from a broader
    instance pool.
  • Private clusters & endpoint access: the apiserver endpoint can be public,
    private, or both — private clusters keep the control plane off the internet.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Managed K8s (EKS/GKE/AKS) runs the control plane (apiserver/etcd/scheduler/
    controller-manager) for you; you still own workloads, RBAC, NetworkPolicy,
    PV/PVC, and ingress/gateway.
  • Your CKA skills transfer directly — the same easypj manifests apply. Only
    the GLUE changes: storageClass → cloud CSI, LoadBalancer Service → cloud
    LB, ServiceAccount → cloud IAM (IRSA / Workload Identity).
  • Same kubectl commands and (mostly) the same YAML work on every cloud; the
    differences are networking, storage provisioners, and IAM.
  • Two different autoscalers: HPA scales PODS (on metrics); Cluster Autoscaler
    (or Karpenter) scales NODES when pods can't be scheduled or nodes are idle.
  • etcd backups, apiserver upgrades, certificate rotation, and control-plane HA
    become the provider's job — but you still upgrade node pools and drive app
    rollout.
  • CSI makes storage vendor-agnostic; the cloud installs the driver and the
    StorageClass provisioner targets the cloud disk.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Don't assume on-prem behavior — LoadBalancer Services provision (billable)
    cloud LBs; leaving them around costs money.
  • StorageClass names/parameters differ per cloud (gp3 vs pd-ssd vs Premium_LRS
    / managed-csi); don't hardcode an on-prem class name like "standard".
  • IRSA / Workload Identity must be configured on BOTH sides (SA annotation +
    cloud trust policy) or pods can't get cloud creds — a SA alone isn't enough.
  • Node-pool upgrades are yours to drive even though the control plane is
    managed; the two upgrade tracks are separate.
  • NetworkPolicy needs a policy-capable CNI; some default cloud CNIs enforce
    nothing until you enable it (e.g. GKE dataplane / Azure NPM).


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Keep cloud-specific bits (storageClass, LB annotations, identity) in a
    Kustomize overlay so the base easypj manifests stay portable.
  • Use an internal LB annotation for private Services to avoid exposing them
    publicly (and to cut cost).
  • Right-size with HPA for pods + Cluster Autoscaler for nodes rather than
    over-provisioning fixed capacity.
  • Use the provider CLI (eksctl / gcloud / az) for cluster + node-pool ops, but
    kubectl for everything inside the cluster.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Wire up kubectl context
  aws eks update-kubeconfig --name easypj-prod                 # AWS
  az aks get-credentials --name easypj-prod -g easypj-rg       # Azure
  gcloud container clusters get-credentials easypj-prod        # GCP

  # Inspect cloud glue
  kubectl get sc                          # cloud CSI storageclasses
  kubectl get svc easypj-web -o wide      # EXTERNAL-IP from the cloud LB
  kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone   # spread across AZs
  kubectl get nodes -L node.kubernetes.io/instance-type

  # Cluster / node-pool lifecycle (provider CLIs)
  eksctl create cluster --name easypj-prod
  az aks create --name easypj-prod -g easypj-rg
  gcloud container clusters create easypj-prod
  eksctl/gcloud/az ... update cluster     # node pools / upgrades

  # Identity & internal LB
  kubectl annotate svc easypj-web \
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-internal=true


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. In managed K8s, what does the provider own vs you?
      A. Provider: the control plane (apiserver/etcd/scheduler/controller-
      manager) plus its upgrades, HA, backups, and cert rotation. You:
      workloads, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PV/PVC, ingress, and node pools.

  Q2. Which CKA concepts still apply in the cloud?
      A. Nearly all — Pods/Deployments/Services, RBAC, PV/PVC, NetworkPolicy,
      probes, scheduling. Only the control-plane internals are abstracted away,
      and troubleshooting (CrashLoopBackOff, pending pods) is identical.

  Q3. How do you get an external IP for easypj in the cloud?
      A. A Service of type LoadBalancer; the cloud-controller-manager
      provisions a cloud LB (ALB/NLB · GCP LB · Azure LB) and populates the
      Service's EXTERNAL-IP.

  Q4. Why not hardcode storageClass: standard across clouds?
      A. Class names and provisioners differ per provider (ebs.csi.aws.com /
      pd.csi.storage.gke.io / disk.csi.azure.com); use the cloud's CSI class
      (or templatize it) so PVCs bind correctly.

  Q5. What problem do IRSA / Workload Identity solve?
      A. They bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a cloud IAM role, exchanging
      the pod's projected token for short-lived cloud credentials — no static
      keys baked into the pod or a Secret.

  Q6. Cluster Autoscaler vs HPA?
      A. HPA adds/removes POD replicas based on metrics; Cluster Autoscaler
      adds/removes NODES when pods are unschedulable or nodes sit idle. They
      complement each other.

  Q7. Deploy easypj to a managed cluster — what changes in the manifests?
      A. Mostly just the glue: storageClass, LoadBalancer/Ingress annotations,
      and SA↔IAM identity; the Deployments and Services stay the same.

  Q8. How are upgrades handled on managed K8s?
      A. The provider upgrades the control plane; you upgrade node pools (often
      a managed rolling replace) and validate the easypj workloads afterward.

  Q9. What is a node pool / group?
      A. A managed set of identical worker nodes (instance type, size,
      autoscaling) that you can scale and upgrade independently of other pools
      and of the control plane.

  Q10. Name two cloud cost levers for a K8s workload.
       A. Right-size requests + HPA/Cluster Autoscaler to avoid idle nodes, and
       use internal LBs and spot/preemptible nodes where appropriate. Also tear
       down stray LoadBalancer Services, which bill even when unused.

  Q11. Which control-plane chores disappear on managed K8s, and which remain?
       A. Gone: kubeadm init/join, etcd backup/restore, cert rotation,
       control-plane upgrades. Remain: node-pool upgrades, app rollout, RBAC,
       storage, networking, and all observability/troubleshooting.

  Q12. What is the role of CSI in cloud storage?
       A. The Container Storage Interface makes storage vendor-agnostic. The
       cloud installs its CSI driver, and a StorageClass's provisioner field
       targets the cloud disk so PVCs are dynamically provisioned — the same
       mechanism as on-prem, with a cloud backend.


  📌 VISUAL SUMMARY (.vs-prose): easypj runs on managed K8s with a clean
     responsibility split — the provider owns the control plane
     (apiserver/etcd/scheduler/controller-manager, its upgrades, HA, backups,
     and certs), while you own everything you drilled for the CKA: the
     Deployments, Services, RBAC, PV/PVC, and NetworkPolicy. Crossing into the
     cloud changes only three pieces of GLUE — the StorageClass points at a
     cloud CSI driver, a LoadBalancer Service provisions a cloud LB, and a
     ServiceAccount is bound to cloud IAM via IRSA/Workload Identity. Two
     autoscalers operate side by side: the HPA grows POD replicas on metrics,
     and the Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) grows the NODE count when those
     replicas can't be scheduled. The net message of the chapter: your
     Kubernetes skills are portable; the cloud just removes the plumbing and
     adds billable edges to watch.

PART 11: PACKAGING, DELIVERY & EXTENSIBILITY                            🔴 🎯🏢

  What you'll build: easypj packaged as a Helm chart AND a Kustomize overlay,
  extended with a Custom Resource + operator, and delivered continuously via
  GitOps.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  META │ Part 11 of 12 · Chapters 37-39 · Difficulty 🔴 · Tags 🎯 exam 🏢 day-2
       │ Stack: Python 3.13 · Django 5.2.5 · Docker · SQLite→PostgreSQL on K8s

  [PART 11 INTRO]
  Hand-applying YAML doesn't scale. Up to now we have run `kubectl apply -f`
  against a folder of static manifests, hand-editing image tags, replica
  counts and namespaces for every environment. That breaks the moment you
  have more than one cluster, more than one environment (dev/stage/prod),
  or more than one engineer. This part covers the official 2025 exam
  additions — Helm & Kustomize for templated and overlaid installs, and
  CRDs & operators for extending Kubernetes itself — then the Day-2 delivery
  layer (CI/CD & GitOps) that ships easypj automatically and safely. By the
  end you will treat easypj not as a pile of YAML you babysit, but as a
  versioned, parameterized, self-deploying product.

  🎯 EXAM NOTE: As of the 2025 syllabus the CKA explicitly lists "Use Helm
     and Kustomize to install cluster components" and "Understand CRDs,
     install and configure operators." These are no longer optional reading
     — expect at least one hands-on task that installs or customizes an
     application via Helm or Kustomize, and one that inspects or applies a
     CustomResourceDefinition.

  💡 INSIGHT: Helm vs Kustomize is not a war you must win. Helm TEMPLATES
     (Go templating + a values file) and is great for packaging software you
     SHIP to others. Kustomize OVERLAYS (patches a plain-YAML base, no
     templating) and is built into kubectl (`kubectl apply -k`), so it's
     great for environment variants of YAML you OWN. Real shops use both.

  🧠 ANALOGY: Raw manifests are a hand-written letter — fine once, painful
     to send to a hundred people. Helm is a mail-merge template with a
     values sheet. Kustomize is a base letter plus sticky-note edits per
     recipient. A CRD/operator is hiring a clerk who reads your desired
     outcome and keeps re-sending corrected letters until reality matches.

  │       "desired backup" against actual backup CronJobs/PVCs              │
  │ Ch39  CI: build image ─▶ scan ─▶ push tag ─▶ bump values in git        │
  │       CD: ArgoCD Application watches the easypj repo and syncs cluster  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which packaging tool for which job?
  ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Situation                │ Reach for    │ Why                          │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
  │ Installing 3rd-party     │ Helm         │ Charts + repos + versioning  │
  │ software (Prometheus...)  │              │ + rollback are first-class   │
  │ Many env variants of     │ Kustomize    │ No templating; patch a base; │
  │ YAML you own             │              │ built into kubectl (-k)      │
  │ Same app, complex logic, │ Helm         │ Conditionals, loops, hooks   │
  │ optional sub-components   │              │ via Go templates             │
  │ Teach Kubernetes to      │ CRD +        │ New API objects + a control  │
  │ manage a NEW resource    │ operator     │ loop that reconciles them    │
  │ Ship on every git push,  │ GitOps       │ Git is the source of truth;  │
  │ self-heal drift          │ (ArgoCD/Flux)│ controller pulls + reconciles│
  └──────────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 PART-LEVEL MUST-REMEMBER
   • Helm = template + values + release lifecycle (install/upgrade/rollback);
     `helm template` renders locally so you can see the YAML it produces.
   • Kustomize = base + overlays + patches, NO templating; `kubectl apply -k`
     or `kubectl kustomize` to render; declarative and Git-friendly.
   • A CRD defines a new KIND; an operator is the controller that watches
     those objects and drives the world toward their spec (reconcile loop).
   • GitOps inverts deployment: the cluster PULLS desired state from git and
     continuously reconciles, instead of CI pushing into the cluster.

  ⚠️ PART-LEVEL GOTCHAS
   • A CRD with no controller is inert — it just stores data; the operator
     is what makes it DO anything.
   • `helm install` is not idempotent the way `kubectl apply` is — use
     `helm upgrade --install` for repeatable runs.
   • Kustomize patches must match the target's name/kind/namespace exactly or
     they silently no-op.
