══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 37: Helm & Kustomize                                          🟡 🎯
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation
        & Configuration (25%) — "use Helm and Kustomize to install cluster
        components." Status: NEW for the 2025 syllabus.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Raw YAML is honest but it doesn't scale. The moment you need the SAME
  application — say easypj — running in dev (1 replica, DEBUG=True, SQLite),
  staging, and prod (3 replicas, DEBUG=False, PostgreSQL), copy-pasting
  manifests and hand-editing fields becomes a source of drift and outages. The
  2025 CKA makes this an explicit competency: you are expected to install
  cluster components and your own workloads using BOTH Helm and Kustomize.

  💡 INSIGHT: there are two industry-standard answers to "one app, many
  environments," and they take opposite philosophies:
    • Helm  = TEMPLATING. Parameterize manifests with {{ .Values.x }}, ship a
              versioned package (a chart), install it as a tracked RELEASE you
              can upgrade and roll back.
    • Kustomize = OVERLAYING. Keep template-FREE base manifests, then layer
              environment-specific patches on top. Built into kubectl, no
              extra binary, GitOps-friendly.
  Neither is "better." The exam wants you fluent in both, and to know when to
  reach for each (or compose them).

  🧠 ANALOGY: Helm is a cake MIX — one boxed recipe, you pour in different
  amounts of sugar (values) per occasion. Kustomize is a plain cake you bake
  once, then DECORATE differently for each party (overlays) — the cake itself
  is never reprinted.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OBJECTIVES
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Understand Helm chart anatomy (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/,
      _helpers.tpl, charts/) and the release lifecycle.
    • Install, upgrade, roll back, and uninstall a release; override values per
      environment and know the precedence rules.
    • Understand Kustomize bases, overlays, and kustomization.yaml; apply with
      `kubectl apply -k`.
    • Use strategic-merge and JSON6902 patches; use configMapGenerator /
      secretGenerator and images/replicas transformers.
    • Choose between Helm and Kustomize — and know how they compose.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CKA RELEVANCE 🎯
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Directly named in the Cluster Architecture domain. Expect a task that asks
  you to install a third-party component (e.g. ingress-nginx, metrics-server)
  via Helm, and/or to build a Kustomize overlay that changes replicas/image/env
  for an environment and `apply -k` it. Both `helm` and `kubectl` (with built-in
  kustomize) are available in the exam environment.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SECTION MAP
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    37.1  Helm Basics                  — chart/release/values/repo, lifecycle
    37.2  Helm Chart Anatomy           — Chart.yaml, values, templates, helpers
    37.3  Kustomize Basics             — base + overlays, kustomization.yaml
    37.4  Patches & Generators         — merge/JSON6902, config/secret generators
    37.5  Helm vs Kustomize            — decision guide; composing both

  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  37.1  HELM BASICS                                                        🎯
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  📖 KEY TERMS
    • CHART   — a versioned package of templated Kubernetes manifests.
    • RELEASE — an installed instance of a chart in a namespace, tracked by
                name and revision number.
    • VALUES  — the parameters that fill the templates (defaults in values.yaml,
                overridable with -f files and --set flags).
    • REPO    — an HTTP server hosting packaged charts (e.g. Bitnami).

  Helm renders the chart's templates with the supplied values into final YAML,
  then applies it to the cluster and remembers the result as a RELEASE. Because
  each install/upgrade is a numbered revision, you get one-command rollbacks.

  Core lifecycle commands — installing and operating easypj:

       helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
       helm repo update
       helm install easypj ./chart -n easypj -f prod.yaml   # release "easypj"
       helm upgrade easypj ./chart -f prod.yaml --set replicas=4
       helm rollback easypj 1                                # revert to revision 1
       helm uninstall easypj -n easypj
       helm template ./chart -f prod.yaml                    # preview (no apply)
       helm history easypj                                   # revisions + status

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: `helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart` is idempotent — it
  installs if the release is absent, upgrades if present. One command for both
  first-run and re-runs (perfect for CI and exam scripts).

  🏢 DAY-2: in production the release history is your audit log and your undo
  button. `helm history easypj` shows every revision, who/what changed, and
  status (deployed/superseded/failed); `helm rollback easypj <rev>` reverts a
  bad ship in seconds.

  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  37.2  HELM CHART ANATOMY                                                 🎯
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  📖 A chart is a directory tree. Package easypj as a chart like this:

       chart/
        ├ Chart.yaml          # name/version/appVersion (chart metadata)
        ├ values.yaml         # defaults: replicas: 2, image: easypj:v1
        ├ templates/
        │   ├ deployment.yaml # spec.replicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}
        │   ├ service.yaml
        │   └ _helpers.tpl    # named templates (labels, fullname)
        └ charts/             # subchart dependencies

    • Chart.yaml — the chart's identity card. `version` is the CHART version,
      `appVersion` is the app's version (e.g. easypj image tag). They are
      independent: you can ship chart 1.4.0 that deploys appVersion "v2".
    • values.yaml — the default parameters. Everything a consumer might want to
      tune (replicas, image, resources, env) lives here so it can be overridden
      without editing templates.
    • templates/ — the manifests, with Go-template directives. A field reads a
      value with {{ .Values.replicas }}; files starting with `_` (like
      _helpers.tpl) are NOT rendered as manifests — they hold reusable named
      templates such as a standard label block or a fullname helper.
    • charts/ — vendored SUBCHARTS (dependencies). Declaring a PostgreSQL
      subchart here lets easypj's chart pull in its database chart.

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: a deployment.yaml template fragment for easypj:

       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: Deployment
       metadata:
         name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
         labels: {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
       spec:
         replicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}
         template:
           spec:
             containers:
               - name: web
                 image: "{{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
                 env:
                   - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
                     value: easypj.settings.{{ .Values.env }}

  💡 The {{ include "easypj.labels" . }} call pulls a named template defined in
  _helpers.tpl, so every resource in the chart carries identical labels without
  copy-paste. `nindent 4` re-indents the block to fit YAML.

  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  37.3  KUSTOMIZE BASICS                                                   🎯
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  📖 Kustomize is template-FREE. You keep plain, valid manifests in a BASE, then
  create OVERLAYS that reference the base and PATCH it per environment. It is
  built into kubectl, so you apply with `kubectl apply -k` — no extra binary.

  Layout for easypj:

       base/kustomization.yaml:
         resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml]

       overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml:
         resources: ["../../base"]
         replicas: [{ name: easypj-web, count: 3 }]
         images:   [{ name: easypj, newTag: v2 }]
         patches:  [{ path: prod-env.yaml }]      # DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS

       # apply:    kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
       # preview:  kubectl kustomize overlays/prod

  How it flows:
    1. The base holds the canonical, deployable manifests (deployment.yaml,
       service.yaml) — they apply on their own.
    2. Each overlay's kustomization.yaml lists the base under `resources:` and
       then declares transformations: bump `replicas`, retag `images`, and
       apply `patches` that override env vars (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS).
    3. `kubectl apply -k overlays/prod` builds the final resource list and
       applies it. `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod` renders it to stdout so
       you can eyeball it first.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: an overlay MUST reference the base under `resources:`. Forget it
  and Kustomize builds an empty or partial set — your patches have nothing to
  patch. Paths are relative to the kustomization.yaml that contains them.

  🧠 ANALOGY: the base is a master document; each overlay is a "track changes"
  layer. The original is never edited — Kustomize merges the layer on the way
  out.

  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  37.4  PATCHES & GENERATORS                                              🎯
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Kustomize changes the base in three main ways:

  📖 STRATEGIC-MERGE PATCH (the default) — a PARTIAL manifest that Kustomize
  merges field-by-field into the matching base resource. You write only the
  fields you want to change; Kustomize finds the resource by kind/name and
  deep-merges. Example prod-env.yaml that flips DEBUG off on easypj's web
  container:

       apiVersion: apps/v1
       kind: Deployment
       metadata:
         name: easypj-web
       spec:
         template:
           spec:
             containers:
               - name: web
                 env:
                   - name: DJANGO_DEBUG
                     value: "False"

  📖 JSON6902 PATCH — a precise RFC-6902 operation list (op/path/value) for
  surgical edits, useful when a strategic merge can't express the change (e.g.
  replacing an item at a specific list index):

       patches:
         - target: { kind: Deployment, name: easypj-web }
           patch: |-
             - op: replace
               path: /spec/replicas
               value: 3

  📖 GENERATORS & TRANSFORMERS:
    • configMapGenerator / secretGenerator — build a ConfigMap/Secret from
      literals or files AND append a content HASH to the name. When the config
      changes, the name changes, which forces a rolling update automatically —
      no more "I edited the ConfigMap but the pods kept the old value."
    • images: [{ name, newTag }] — retag an image across all resources without
      touching the base.
    • replicas: [{ name, count }] — set replica counts per environment.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: the content-hash suffix on generated ConfigMaps/Secrets is a
  FEATURE, not a bug — it's what makes config rollouts atomic. If you need a
  stable name (e.g. another controller references it), set
  `generatorOptions: { disableNameSuffixHash: true }`, accepting that you then
  lose automatic rollouts.

  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  37.5  HELM vs KUSTOMIZE                                                  🧭
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Two ways to ship easypj per environment — pick by the job, not by dogma.

  [HELM vs KUSTOMIZE — two ways to ship easypj per environment]
   HELM (templating + releases)          KUSTOMIZE (overlays, no templates)
   chart/                                base/
    ├ Chart.yaml                          ├ deployment.yaml  service.yaml
    ├ values.yaml  (defaults)             └ kustomization.yaml
    └ templates/  {{ .Values.replicas }} overlays/
   helm install easypj ./chart \          ├ dev/   (patch: replicas=1, DEBUG)
     -f prod.yaml   (override per env)     └ prod/  (patch: replicas=3, image)
                                          kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
   ┌──────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
   │ Helm     │ templated, versioned  │ install 3rd-party components│
   │          │ releases, rollbacks   │ (charts), values per env    │
   │ Kustomize│ template-FREE base +  │ your own manifests, env     │
   │          │ overlays/patches      │ overlays, GitOps-friendly   │
   └──────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘
   💡 Preview first: `helm template ./chart` · `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod`.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE
    • Reach for HELM when: you're installing a third-party component shipped as
      a chart (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, a database); you need versioned
      releases with one-command rollback; you want a single package others can
      `helm install` with their own values.
    • Reach for KUSTOMIZE when: the manifests are YOUR OWN; you want template-
      free, readable YAML; you're doing GitOps (Argo CD / Flux both render
      Kustomize natively); environments differ only by a few patched fields.
    • COMPOSE both when convenient: `helm template ./chart -f prod.yaml |
      kubectl kustomize` (or feed a chart's rendered output into a Kustomize
      base) lets a Helm chart provide the manifests and Kustomize apply final
      org-wide overlays/patches on top.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • HOW HELM RENDERS: Helm renders templates CLIENT-SIDE (Helm 3 — no Tiller),
    producing plain YAML, then applies it via the Kubernetes API. The cluster
    never sees a template — only finished manifests.
  • RELEASE STORAGE: each release's metadata and rendered manifests are stored
    as a Secret of type `helm.sh/release.v1` in the release's namespace, one per
    revision. That's how `helm history`/`helm rollback` reconstruct prior
    states — and why deleting those Secrets breaks rollback.
  • VALUES PRECEDENCE: `--set` flags WIN over `-f values` files, which WIN over
    the chart's own values.yaml defaults. Later `-f` files override earlier
    ones. Mix these up and you ship the wrong config.
  • HELM HOOKS & WEIGHTS: annotate a resource with `helm.sh/hook` (pre-install,
    post-upgrade, etc.) and `hook-weight` to run jobs (migrations, backups) in
    order around the release lifecycle.
  • SUBCHARTS / DEPENDENCIES: declared in Chart.yaml (or charts/), pulled with
    `helm dependency update`; parent values can override subchart values under a
    keyed block.
  • CRDs: Helm installs CRDs from a chart's crds/ directory ONCE on first
    install and does NOT upgrade or delete them with the release — CRD upgrades
    must be managed separately.
  • HOW KUSTOMIZE BUILDS: Kustomize builds a RESOURCE LIST with NO templating —
    it reads the base, applies transformers/patches in a defined order, and
    emits final YAML. `kubectl` embeds it; standalone `kustomize` adds newer
    features: COMPONENTS (reusable opt-in overlay fragments), REPLACEMENTS
    (copy a value from one field to many), and custom TRANSFORMERS.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Helm packages manifests as a templated, versioned CHART; installing it
      creates a RELEASE you can upgrade/rollback. values.yaml (+ -f/--set
      overrides) parameterize per environment.
    • A chart = Chart.yaml (metadata) + values.yaml (defaults) + templates/
      (manifests with {{ .Values }}) + _helpers.tpl (named templates) + charts/
      (subcharts).
    • Kustomize is template-FREE: a base + overlays that patch it (replicas,
      images, env). Apply with `kubectl apply -k` — it's built into kubectl.
    • Use Helm to install 3rd-party components (charts) and when you need
      releases/rollbacks; use Kustomize for your own manifests and GitOps. They
      can even compose (`helm template | kustomize`).
    • Values precedence: --set > -f values file > chart defaults (values.yaml).
    • configMapGenerator/secretGenerator append a content hash so config changes
      trigger automatic rolling updates.
    • Always PREVIEW before applying: `helm template ./chart` and `kubectl
      kustomize overlays/prod` render the final YAML without touching the
      cluster.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • Helm release-name collisions in a namespace fail the install — names are
      unique per namespace.
    • An overlay's kustomization must reference the base under `resources:`;
      forgetting it produces an empty/partial build.
    • Helm CRDs in the crds/ dir install once and aren't upgraded/deleted with
      the release — manage CRD upgrades separately.
    • `--set` overrides win over `-f values`, which win over chart defaults; mix
      them up and you ship the wrong config.
    • Deleting a release's helm.sh/release.v1 Secrets silently breaks
      `helm history`/`helm rollback`.
    • The generated ConfigMap/Secret name-hash suffix means anything that
      references the resource by a fixed name will break — disable the hash only
      when you truly need a stable name.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    • `helm template` / `kubectl kustomize` to eyeball the rendered manifests is
      the fastest way to catch a templating/patch mistake.
    • `helm history easypj` then `helm rollback easypj <rev>` reverts a bad
      upgrade in one step.
    • `helm upgrade --install` is idempotent — installs if absent, upgrades if
      present.
    • `helm install ... --create-namespace` makes the target namespace in the
      same command — handy for one-shot component installs.
    • `--dry-run` on install/upgrade renders AND validates against the API
      without applying.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami ; helm repo update
      helm install easypj ./chart -n easypj -f prod.yaml
      helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart --set replicas=4
      helm history easypj ; helm rollback easypj 1
      helm uninstall easypj -n easypj
      helm template ./chart -f prod.yaml
      helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
        -n ingress-nginx --create-namespace
      kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
      kubectl kustomize overlays/prod          # preview

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Package easypj as a Helm chart and install it with a prod values file, then
  ALSO build a Kustomize base + dev/prod overlays (replicas/image/DEBUG differ)
  and `apply -k` prod — compare the two approaches side by side.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Install, upgrade, then roll back an easypj Helm release.
      A. `helm install easypj ./chart -f prod.yaml` → `helm upgrade easypj
         ./chart --set replicas=4` → `helm rollback easypj 1`. Verify history
         with `helm history easypj` (each step is a numbered revision).

  Q2. Override a chart value per environment. What is the precedence?
      A. Use a -f values file or --set on the command line. Precedence is
         --set > -f values file > chart defaults (values.yaml); later -f files
         override earlier ones.

  Q3. Describe a Helm chart's anatomy.
      A. Chart.yaml (metadata: name/version/appVersion), values.yaml (defaults),
         templates/ (manifests with {{ .Values }} directives), _helpers.tpl
         (named templates), charts/ (subchart dependencies).

  Q4. Create a Kustomize overlay that sets prod replicas and image tag.
      A. overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml with resources: ["../../base"],
         replicas: [{ name: easypj-web, count: 3 }], images: [{ name: easypj,
         newTag: v2 }]. Apply with `kubectl apply -k overlays/prod`.

  Q5. What is a strategic-merge patch?
      A. A partial manifest merged field-by-field into the matching base
         resource (e.g. set env or resources on a container) — the default
         Kustomize patch style. You write only the fields you want to change.

  Q6. What does configMapGenerator do?
      A. Generates a ConfigMap from literals/files and appends a content hash to
         its name, so changing the config produces a new name and triggers a
         rolling update automatically.

  Q7. Set replicas differently for dev vs prod without templating.
      A. Use Kustomize overlays — the base defines the Deployment, and each
         overlay patches replicas (and image/env) for its environment.

  Q8. Preview what Helm/Kustomize will apply.
      A. `helm template ./chart -f prod.yaml` or `kubectl kustomize
         overlays/prod` — renders the final YAML without applying it.

  Q9. Helm vs Kustomize — when each?
      A. Helm for templated/versioned releases and 3rd-party charts; Kustomize
         for template-free overlays of your own manifests and GitOps workflows.
         They can compose via `helm template | kustomize`.

  Q10. Install a cluster component (e.g. ingress-nginx) via Helm.
       A. `helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx`
          then `helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx
          -n ingress-nginx --create-namespace`.

  Q11. Where does Helm store release state, and why does it matter?
       A. As Secrets of type helm.sh/release.v1 in the release's namespace, one
          per revision. They back `helm history` and `helm rollback`; deleting
          them breaks rollback.

  Q12. A chart ships a CRD that needs a new field after upgrade. Will
       `helm upgrade` apply it?
       A. No. CRDs in a chart's crds/ directory install once on first install
          and are not upgraded or deleted with the release; manage the CRD
          upgrade separately (e.g. `kubectl apply` the new CRD).

  Q13. Make an install command that works whether or not the release exists.
       A. `helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart -f prod.yaml` — idempotent:
          installs if absent, upgrades if present.

  Q14. You need to change a single list element a strategic merge can't target.
       Which patch type and how?
       A. A JSON6902 patch — target the resource by kind/name and supply an
          op/path/value list, e.g. replace /spec/replicas with value 3.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  📌 VISUAL SUMMARY
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

      raw YAML
         │
         ├──▶  Helm chart  ──(values + -f/--set)──▶  rendered manifests
         │       templates/{{.Values}}                     │
         │                                                  ▼
         │                                            RELEASE (revisioned,
         │                                            rollback-able)  ──┐
         │                                                              │
         └──▶  Kustomize base ──(overlay patches)──▶ rendered manifests │
                 deployment.yaml   replicas/images/env                  │
                                                          │             │
                                                          ▼             ▼
                                                   ┌──────────────────────┐
                                                   │     KUBERNETES        │
                                                   │       CLUSTER         │
                                                   └──────────────────────┘

  .vs-prose — Both tools turn raw YAML into what the cluster actually runs, by
  opposite routes. Helm TEMPLATES the manifests: you parameterize fields with
  {{ .Values }}, supply per-environment values via -f files and --set flags
  (precedence --set > -f > defaults), and each install/upgrade becomes a
  numbered, rollback-able RELEASE stored as Secrets. Kustomize OVERLAYS the
  manifests: a template-free base is patched per environment (replicas, images,
  env) and applied with `kubectl apply -k`, with no templates and no release
  objects. Use Helm for third-party charts and versioned releases, Kustomize for
  your own manifests and GitOps — and preview either with `helm template` or
  `kubectl kustomize` before it ever touches the cluster.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 38: Extending Kubernetes — CRDs & Operators                  🔴 🎯
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Domain: Cluster Architecture, Installation &
        Configuration (25%) — "Understand CRDs; install and configure
        operators." NEW in the 2025 syllabus.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 💡 WHY THIS MATTERS                                                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │ Kubernetes is not a fixed product — it is an extensible PLATFORM. Every  │
  │ built-in object (Pod, Deployment, Service) is just an entry in the API   │
  │ server's resource registry plus a controller that acts on it. A Custom   │
  │ Resource Definition (CRD) lets YOU add a brand-new object type to that   │
  │ same registry, and an OPERATOR adds the controller that brings it to     │
  │ life. This is how cert-manager, Prometheus, ArgoCD and the postgres-     │
  │ operator turn "kubectl apply" into automated, self-healing software.     │
  │                                                                          │
  │ For easypj this is the leap from "I run my Django job-board on K8s" to   │
  │ "K8s knows what an easypj application IS and reconciles it for me." The  │
  │ official competency reads: understand CRDs, then install and configure   │
  │ an operator — both of which this chapter drills end to end.              │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🎯 OBJECTIVES
     • Register a CRD (group / versions / scope / OpenAPIv3 schema).
     • Create and manage custom resources as first-class API objects.
     • Explain the OPERATOR pattern (CRD + controller reconcile loop).
     • Install and configure an operator (Helm / manifests / OLM) and verify
       its CRDs.
     • Author RBAC for custom resources (apiGroup + plural + /status).
     • Know when to reach for the API Aggregation Layer instead of a CRD.

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
     Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration is the heaviest single
     domain (25%) and now explicitly names CRDs and operators. Expect a task
     that asks you to apply a CRD, create an instance, list it, explain its
     schema, and/or install an operator and confirm its CRDs are present — then
     grant RBAC so a subject can manage the new resource.

  ┌─ SECTION MAP ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 38.1  Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)              🎯                   │
  │ 38.2  The Operator Pattern                            🎯                   │
  │ 38.3  Installing & Configuring Operators              🎯                   │
  │ 38.4  The API Aggregation Layer                       🔧                   │
  │ 38.5  RBAC for Custom Resources                       🎯                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERMS
     CRD ............ Custom Resource Definition: a manifest that registers a
                      new API type (group/version/kind + schema).
     CR ............. Custom Resource: an INSTANCE of a CRD-defined kind.
     Operator ....... CRD + a controller that runs a reconcile loop.
     Reconcile loop . WATCH → COMPARE (desired vs actual) → ACT → update status.
     Aggregation .... An extension API server plugged into the main apiserver.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  38.1  Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)                                  🎯
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  A CRD teaches the Kubernetes API server a NEW kind. You declare a group, one
  or more versions, the scope (Namespaced or Cluster), the names, and an
  OpenAPI v3 schema that validates instances. The instant it is applied,
  `kubectl get/create <kind>` works exactly like a built-in resource and the
  objects you create are persisted in etcd.

  🔑 The single naming rule that trips everyone:
     metadata.name MUST equal  <plural>.<group>

       apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
       kind: CustomResourceDefinition
       metadata:
         name: easypjapps.apps.easypj.io        # MUST be plural.group
       spec:
         group: apps.easypj.io
         scope: Namespaced
         names:
           plural: easypjapps
           singular: easypjapp
           kind: EasypjApp
           shortNames: ["eapp"]
         versions:
         - name: v1
           served: true
           storage: true                         # exactly one version is storage
           schema:
             openAPIV3Schema:
               type: object
               properties:
                 spec:
                   type: object
                   properties:
                     replicas: { type: integer, minimum: 1 }
                     version:  { type: string }
       # now: kubectl get easypjapp  (eapp) works as a first-class API type

  ┌─ ANATOMY OF A CRD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │   metadata.name ─── easypjapps . apps.easypj.io                          │
  │                     └─plural─┘   └────group────┘                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │   spec.group ........ apps.easypj.io   →  API path /apis/apps.easypj.io  │
  │   spec.scope ........ Namespaced | Cluster                              │
  │   spec.names ........ plural / singular / kind / shortNames             │
  │   spec.versions[] ... name · served:true · storage:(exactly one true)   │
  │        └─ schema.openAPIV3Schema  ─ validates every instance            │
  │                                                                          │
  │   AFTER apply →  kubectl api-resources shows:                           │
  │     NAME         SHORTNAMES  APIVERSION             NAMESPACED  KIND     │
  │     easypjapps   eapp        apps.easypj.io/v1      true        EasypjApp│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ served vs storage: every version you want callable sets served: true, but
     EXACTLY ONE version may set storage: true (that is the form etcd persists).
     Two storage versions → the CRD is rejected as invalid.

  🔧 What happens under the hood: applying the CRD makes the apiserver mount a
     new REST path (/apis/apps.easypj.io/v1/namespaces/<ns>/easypjapps) and a
     new etcd prefix (/registry/apps.easypj.io/easypjapps/...). No restart, no
     recompile — the resource registry is dynamic.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  38.2  The Operator Pattern                                                🎯
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  A CRD by itself is inert storage — `kubectl create easypjapp` writes a row in
  etcd and nothing happens. An OPERATOR adds the missing half: a CONTROLLER
  that watches those custom resources and continuously drives the cluster to
  match their spec. CRD + controller = operator.

  📊 KEY DIAGRAM — Chapter 38
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ [CRD + CONTROLLER = OPERATOR — extend Kubernetes itself]                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1) Install CRD (kind: EasypjApp, group apps.easypj.io) ─► a NEW API type│
  │       ▼  kubectl get easypjapp  now works                               │
  │  2) Create a custom resource:  EasypjApp{ replicas: 3, version: v2 }     │
  │       ▼  stored in etcd at /registry/apps.easypj.io/easypjapps/...       │
  │  3) The OPERATOR (a controller) runs the reconcile loop:                 │
  │       WATCH ─► COMPARE (spec vs cluster) ─► ACT (make Deploy/Svc/...) ─►  │
  │       update STATUS ─► repeat                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  📖 Real operators: cert-manager, Prometheus, postgres-operator, ArgoCD. │
  │  ⚠️ CRD metadata.name MUST be plural.group · add RBAC for the new resource│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧠 ANALOGY: the CRD is a new entry in a restaurant's menu ("Easypj Special").
     Writing it on the menu changes nothing on its own — the OPERATOR is the
     chef who reads the order ticket (spec), checks what's already plated
     (actual state), cooks the difference, and keeps the dish topped up if a
     diner takes a bite. WATCH → COMPARE → ACT → repeat, forever.

  ┌─ THE RECONCILE LOOP (level-triggered, not edge-triggered) ───────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐            │
  │            │              easypj-operator                  │            │
  │            │                                                │            │
  │   etcd ──► │  WATCH EasypjApp  ──►  desired: replicas=3     │            │
  │   (CRs)    │        │                                       │            │
  │            │        ▼                                       │            │
  │            │  COMPARE  desired (spec)  vs  actual (cluster) │            │
  │            │        │                                       │            │
  │            │   diff? ▼ yes                                  │            │
  │            │  ACT: create/scale Deployment, Service, ...    │ ──► cluster│
  │            │        │                                       │            │
  │            │        ▼                                       │            │
  │            │  UPDATE status.subresource (observedGeneration)│            │
  │            └────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘            │
  │                             └──────► requeue / re-watch ──────► (repeat) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: the loop is driven by INFORMERS. An informer maintains a
     local cache of the watched objects and fires add/update/delete events onto
     a work queue; the controller pops keys, fetches the latest object from the
     cache, and reconciles. Because reconciliation is level-triggered (it acts
     on current state, not on the event), a missed event just gets healed on
     the next sync — which is why operators are resilient.

  💡 INSIGHT: every Kubernetes built-in works this way too. The Deployment
     controller, the Job controller, kube-scheduler — all reconcile loops. An
     operator is simply you writing one of those loops for YOUR domain.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  38.3  Installing & Configuring Operators                                  🎯
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Operators ship as a bundle: their CRDs plus a controller Deployment plus the
  RBAC the controller needs. You install them three common ways:

  ┌─ THREE INSTALL PATHS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  Helm        helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io          │
  │              helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \          │
  │                --set installCRDs=true -n cert-manager --create-namespace │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Manifests   kubectl apply -f https://.../cert-manager.yaml             │
  │              (one big YAML: CRDs + Deployment + RBAC)                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OLM         Operator Lifecycle Manager: a Subscription object pulls the │
  │  (Operator   operator from a catalog and manages upgrades for you.       │
  │   Lifecycle  install OLM, then apply a Subscription / OperatorGroup.     │
  │   Manager)                                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧪 The golden install-and-verify sequence (memorize the ORDER):

       # 1. install the operator (its CRDs + controller)
       kubectl apply -f cert-manager.yaml
       # 2. VERIFY the CRDs landed BEFORE you create any custom resource
       kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager.io
       # 3. confirm the controller is running
       kubectl -n cert-manager get pods
       # 4. NOW create custom resources to configure it
       kubectl apply -f my-clusterissuer.yaml

  ⚠️ If you create a custom resource before its CRD exists, the apply fails with
     `error: no matches for kind "ClusterIssuer" in version "cert-manager.io/v1"`.
     Always verify CRDs first.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  38.4  The API Aggregation Layer                                           🔧
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  CRDs cover ~95% of extension needs, but they have limits: Kubernetes stores
  and serves the data for you (in etcd) and you cannot inject arbitrary
  server-side logic. When you need a CUSTOM API SERVER — with its own storage,
  computed/on-the-fly responses, or protocol logic a static schema can't express
  — you use the API Aggregation Layer instead.

  ┌─ CRD  vs  API AGGREGATION ───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │                       CRD                    API Aggregation             │
  │  ───────────────────  ─────────────────────  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  Storage              etcd (K8s manages)     YOUR apiserver decides      │
  │  Logic                schema validation +    arbitrary server-side code  │
  │                       your controller                                    │
  │  Data shape           declarative objects    computed / virtual (no etcd │
  │                                               row needed)                │
  │  Effort               low (one YAML)          high (build+run a server)  │
  │  Example              EasypjApp, ClusterIssuer  metrics-server           │
  │                                               (metrics.k8s.io)           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE
     • Declarative custom objects you want K8s to store?  → CRD (default).
     • Need a NEW apiserver with its own storage/computed responses (like
       metrics-server serving live CPU/memory that has no etcd row)? → register
       an APIService that aggregates an extension apiserver.

  🔧 An APIService object tells the main kube-apiserver "for group
     metrics.k8s.io, proxy requests to THIS service" — the aggregator routes
     /apis/metrics.k8s.io/... to the metrics-server pod.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  38.5  RBAC for Custom Resources                                           🎯
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  A custom resource is a first-class API object, so it is governed by the SAME
  RBAC rules as Pods or Deployments — and by default no one (not even your
  operator) can touch it until you grant verbs on its apiGroup + plural.

       apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
       kind: ClusterRole
       metadata:
         name: eapp-admin
       rules:
       - apiGroups: ["apps.easypj.io"]
         resources: ["easypjapps", "easypjapps/status"]   # include /status
         verbs: ["get","list","watch","create","update","patch","delete"]

  Imperative equivalent:

       kubectl create clusterrole eapp-admin \
         --verb=get,list,watch,create,update,delete \
         --resource=easypjapps.apps.easypj.io

  🔑 Note the resource is named with apiGroup form on the CLI
     (easypjapps.apps.easypj.io) but as plain plural in the YAML rules. Include
     the /status subresource if controllers or users must write status.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING: a user or operator getting `Forbidden` on a custom
     resource almost always means missing RBAC — `kubectl auth can-i create
     easypjapps.apps.easypj.io --as <subject>` to confirm, then add the verbs.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  • How a CRD adds a REST path & /registry key: apiserver registers the new
    group/version dynamically; instances persist at
    /registry/<group>/<plural>/<ns>/<name> in etcd — no apiserver restart.

  • The reconcile loop + informers: informers cache watched objects and feed a
    work queue; the controller reconciles level-triggered state, so missed
    events self-heal on resync. This is the controller-runtime pattern that
    kubebuilder/Operator SDK generate.

  • FINALIZERS: a string in metadata.finalizers blocks deletion — the object
    gets a deletionTimestamp but is NOT removed until the operator does its
    cleanup (drain external resources, deregister) and REMOVES the finalizer.
    A stuck-Terminating custom resource usually = an operator that never
    cleared its finalizer (patch it out only as a last resort, manually).

  • CRD VERSIONS & CONVERSION WEBHOOKS: serve v1alpha1 and v1 simultaneously;
    a conversion webhook translates between them so old and new clients coexist
    while exactly one version is the storage version.

  • STRUCTURAL SCHEMAS + x-kubernetes-* + CEL: structural schemas are required
    for many features; x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields, x-kubernetes-
    int-or-string, and x-kubernetes-validations (CEL rule expressions) let you
    enforce cross-field invariants the basic OpenAPI types can't.

  • SUBRESOURCES: /status splits spec (user-owned) from status (controller-
    owned) so they don't race and can be RBAC'd separately; /scale makes the
    custom resource work with `kubectl scale` and the HPA.

  • additionalPrinterColumns: surface custom columns (REPLICAS, VERSION, AGE)
    in `kubectl get easypjapp` output.

  • OLM (Operator Lifecycle Manager): catalogs, Subscriptions, install plans
    and automatic upgrades for operators — the productionized install path.


  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • A CRD registers a NEW API type (group/version/kind + OpenAPIv3 schema).
    Once applied, `kubectl get/create <kind>` works like any built-in resource
    and instances are stored in etcd.
  • An OPERATOR = a CRD + a controller running the reconcile loop: WATCH the
    custom resources → COMPARE desired spec vs live state → ACT (create/update
    Deployments/Services/…) → update status → repeat. CRD + controller =
    operator.
  • Real operators (cert-manager, Prometheus, postgres-operator, ArgoCD)
    install via Helm/manifests/OLM; the exam expects you to install/configure
    one and verify its CRDs are present BEFORE creating custom resources.
  • The API Aggregation Layer is the OTHER extension path — register an
    extension apiserver (e.g. metrics-server) when you need custom storage/
    logic a CRD can't express.
  • The CRD naming rule is absolute: metadata.name = <plural>.<group>, and
    exactly one version may be the storage version.
  • Custom resources obey normal RBAC — grant verbs on the CRD's apiGroup +
    plural (and /status) or subjects get Forbidden.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • CRD metadata.name MUST be exactly <plural>.<group> (e.g.
    easypjapps.apps.easypj.io) or the apply is rejected.
  • Exactly one version may have storage: true; multiple → invalid CRD.
  • A missing/loose schema lets bad data in; always define an openAPIV3Schema
    (and ideally x-kubernetes-validations / CEL rules).
  • Forgetting RBAC for the new resource means users/controllers get Forbidden
    — grant verbs on the CRD's apiGroup + plural (and /status).
  • Creating a custom resource before its CRD exists fails with "no matches for
    kind" — install/verify CRDs first.
  • A custom resource stuck in Terminating usually means an operator never
    removed its finalizer; fix the operator, don't blindly strip finalizers.
  • On the CLI the resource is referenced as plural.group
    (easypjapps.apps.easypj.io); in RBAC rule YAML it is the plain plural.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • `kubectl get crd` lists installed types; `kubectl explain easypjapp.spec`
    works once the schema is registered.
  • `kubectl api-resources | grep <group>` (or --api-group=<group>) confirms
    the new kind and its short names.
  • After installing an operator, verify its CRDs exist BEFORE creating custom
    resources, or the apply fails with "no matches for kind".
  • `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <plural>.<group> --as <subject>` quickly proves
    whether RBAC is the cause of a Forbidden.
  • `kubectl get <kind> -o yaml` shows status/finalizers when an instance is
    misbehaving or stuck Terminating.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl apply -f easypj-crd.yaml
  kubectl get crd
  kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps.easypj.io
  kubectl explain easypjapp.spec
  kubectl get easypjapp -A                 # short name: eapp
  kubectl get eapp -o yaml                 # see spec/status/finalizers
  kubectl create clusterrole eapp-admin \
    --verb=get,list,watch,create,update,delete \
    --resource=easypjapps.apps.easypj.io
  kubectl auth can-i create easypjapps.apps.easypj.io --as alice
  # operator install/verify:
  kubectl apply -f cert-manager.yaml
  kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager.io
  kubectl -n cert-manager get pods

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Apply the easypjapp CRD, create an EasypjApp instance with replicas/version,
  list it (`kubectl get eapp`), and `kubectl explain` its schema — then add a
  Role/ClusterRole granting access to it and prove it with `kubectl auth can-i`.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Create a CRD for a new kind EasypjApp. Key fields?
      A. apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 CRD; metadata.name = easypjapps.apps.easypj.io
         (plural.group); spec.group/scope/names plus versions[].schema
         (openAPIV3Schema); exactly one version storage:true, served versions
         served:true.

  Q2. Create an instance of that custom resource.
      A. A manifest with apiVersion: apps.easypj.io/v1, kind: EasypjApp, and
         spec.replicas/version; apply it with kubectl like any other object.

  Q3. List all installed custom resource types.
      A. `kubectl get crd` (and `kubectl api-resources` to see kinds + short
         names; `--api-group=apps.easypj.io` to filter).

  Q4. Explain the operator pattern.
      A. A controller watches custom resources and reconciles desired spec to
         actual cluster state (creating/updating real objects), updating status
         — CRD + controller = operator; the loop is WATCH → COMPARE → ACT →
         update status → repeat, level-triggered via informers.

  Q5. Install an operator. General steps?
      A. Apply its CRDs + controller (Helm/manifests/OLM), VERIFY the CRDs with
         `kubectl get crd` and the controller pod is Running, THEN create its
         custom resources to configure it.

  Q6. Grant RBAC to manage a custom resource.
      A. A Role/ClusterRole with apiGroups: ["apps.easypj.io"], resources:
         ["easypjapps","easypjapps/status"], the needed verbs, bound to the
         subject via a (Cluster)RoleBinding.

  Q7. CRD vs API aggregation — when each?
      A. CRD for declarative custom objects stored by K8s in etcd (most cases);
         aggregation when you need a custom apiserver with its own storage/logic
         or computed responses (e.g. metrics-server, metrics.k8s.io).

  Q8. What does a /status subresource give you?
      A. It splits spec and status so controllers update status without racing
         user spec edits, enables separate RBAC on status, and (with /scale)
         makes the resource work with kubectl scale and the HPA.

  Q9. State the CRD naming rule.
      A. metadata.name must equal <plural>.<group>; the kind is CamelCase and
         plural/singular/shortNames live under spec.names.

  Q10. Inspect a custom resource's fields like a built-in.
       A. `kubectl explain <kind>.spec` (works from the registered
          openAPIV3Schema) and `kubectl get <kind> -o yaml`.

  Q11. After applying a CRD, `kubectl get eapp` returns "no matches for kind".
       Why?
       A. The CRD hasn't fully registered yet, the short name/scope differs, or
          you're querying the wrong namespace; wait for the apiserver to serve
          the new path and confirm with `kubectl get crd` + `kubectl
          api-resources --api-group=apps.easypj.io`.

  Q12. An EasypjApp is stuck in Terminating. Diagnose.
       A. A finalizer in metadata.finalizers is blocking deletion — the
          operator must finish cleanup and remove the finalizer. Inspect with
          `kubectl get eapp <n> -o yaml`; fix/restart the operator. Only as a
          last resort patch the finalizer out manually.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  📊 VISUAL SUMMARY — CRD + operator extending easypj's API
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   apply CRD          create CR              OPERATOR reconciles           │
  │  ┌──────────┐      ┌─────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ kind:    │      │ EasypjApp   │        │ WATCH EasypjApp            │ │
  │  │ Easypj-  │ ───► │ replicas: 3 │ ─────► │   ▼                        │ │
  │  │ App CRD  │      │ version: v2 │  etcd  │ COMPARE spec vs cluster     │ │
  │  └──────────┘      └─────────────┘        │   ▼                        │ │
  │   new API type      stored object         │ ACT: Deployment+Service     │ │
  │   (eapp)            in /registry           │   ▼                        │ │
  │                                            │ UPDATE status ─► repeat     │ │
  │                                            └────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  .vs-prose — In words: applying the EasypjApp CRD adds a new API type to the
  Kubernetes registry, so `kubectl get eapp` becomes a first-class command.
  Creating an EasypjApp resource (replicas: 3, version: v2) stores an object in
  etcd but does nothing on its own. The easypj operator — a controller running
  the reconcile loop — WATCHES those resources, COMPARES the desired spec to the
  live cluster, ACTS by creating the matching Deployment and Service, then
  UPDATES status and loops forever. That CRD-plus-controller pairing is exactly
  how cert-manager, Prometheus, ArgoCD and the postgres-operator extend
  Kubernetes; the API Aggregation Layer (metrics-server) is the alternate path
  when a custom apiserver is needed. Throughout, the new resource obeys normal
  RBAC, so granting verbs on apps.easypj.io/easypjapps (and /status) is the
  final step that lets users and controllers actually manage it.
