  Chapter 39: CI/CD & GitOps                                            🟡 🏢
================================================================================

  META: 🟡 INTERMEDIATE · ⏱️ ~2h · Beyond-exam (how easypj actually ships).

  ┌─────────────────────────── WHY THIS MATTERS ──────────────────────────────┐
  │  Real teams don't `kubectl apply` by hand. Git is the source of truth.     │
  │  A CI pipeline builds, tests, scans and pushes the easypj image, then      │
  │  bumps the image tag in a manifest repo. A CD/GitOps controller WATCHES    │
  │  that repo and continuously reconciles the live cluster to match it. This  │
  │  gives you an audit trail (every change is a commit), trivial rollback     │
  │  (`git revert`), and drift detection/self-heal (manual edits get reverted).│
  │  These are the skills you need the day AFTER you pass the CKA.             │
  │  VISUAL: CI (build/test/push) ──▶ CD/GitOps (sync) pipeline.               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🎯 OBJECTIVES
     • Build a K8s CI/CD pipeline (code → build → test → image → push → deploy).
     • Run GitOps with ArgoCD / Flux: git = desired state; controller syncs;
       drift detection + self-heal.
     • Deploy easypj via GitOps (an Application/Kustomization pointing at the
       easypj repo/overlay).
     • Combine GitOps with Helm and Kustomize (render from chart/overlay in the
       pipeline).

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
     Not a direct exam objective by name, but Helm, Kustomize, CRDs & operators
     ARE 2025 Cluster-Architecture topics, and the GitOps mental model (declare
     desired state, let a controller reconcile) is exactly how Kubernetes itself
     works. Master it once and the whole platform makes more sense.

  🧭 SECTION MAP
     39.1  CI/CD Pipeline for Kubernetes        🏢
     39.2  GitOps with ArgoCD (and Flux)        🏢
     39.3  ArgoCD for easypj — Practical Setup  🧪
     39.4  Helm — Kubernetes Package Manager    🏢
     39.5  Kustomize — Built-in Customization   🏢
     39.6  Helm vs Kustomize — When to Use Each 🧭
     39.7  Helm/Kustomize in GitOps             🏢


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.1  CI/CD Pipeline for Kubernetes   🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        The pipeline takes a git push of easypj source and turns it into a
        running workload: build the image, test it, scan it for CVEs, push it to
        a registry, then update the manifest so the new tag rolls out.

          [DIAGRAM: CI/CD Pipeline]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  CODE → BUILD → TEST → IMAGE → PUSH → DEPLOY → VERIFY│
          │                                                        │
          │  Git    Docker  Unit   Docker  Registry  kubectl      │
          │  Push   Build   Tests  Tag     Push      apply        │
          │                                                        │
          │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌──────────┐  │
          │  │ 📝 │→│ 🔨 │→│ ✅ │→│ 🏷️  │→│ 📦  │→│ ☸️ K8s   │  │
          │  └────┘ └────┘ └────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘ └──────────┘  │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        📖 KEY TERMS
           CI (Continuous Integration) = build / test / scan / push the image
           (and bump the manifest). CI produces ARTIFACTS.
           CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) = sync the cluster to the
           manifests. CD DEPLOYS those artifacts.

        🔍 In a GitOps world, the last steps change: instead of the CI runner
        having cluster credentials and running `kubectl apply` (push-based), CI
        only commits the new image tag to a manifest repo. A controller running
        INSIDE the cluster pulls and applies it (pull-based). This keeps cluster
        credentials out of CI and makes git the deployment record.

        💡 INSIGHT: the image tag bump is itself a git commit — that commit IS
        your deployment record and your rollback point.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.2  GitOps with ArgoCD (and Flux)   🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        - GitOps: Git is the single source of truth.
        - ArgoCD (or Flux) watches the Git repo → syncs changes to the cluster.
        - Benefits: auditable, reversible, declarative.

          [DIAGRAM: GitOps flow — Git commit → ArgoCD detects → Sync to cluster]
          [CI/CD + GITOPS — git is the source of truth]
           👩‍💻 git push (easypj code)
                ▼  CI: build → test → 🔍 scan → push image easypj:v2
                ▼  bump image tag in the manifests/overlay repo
           📦 Git repo (desired state)
                ▼  CD/GitOps controller (ArgoCD / Flux) WATCHES the repo
           ☸️ Cluster  ── controller SYNCS: live state → matches git
                └─ drift? manual kubectl edit gets REVERTED (self-heal)
           ⚠️ don't store raw Secrets in git (sealed-secrets / external-secrets).

          [GITOPS vs TRADITIONAL CI/CD]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  TRADITIONAL CI/CD:              GITOPS:               │
          │                                                        │
          │  Dev pushes code                 Dev pushes code       │
          │       │                               │                │
          │       ▼                               ▼                │
          │  CI builds image                 CI builds image       │
          │       │                               │                │
          │       ▼                               ▼                │
          │  CD runs kubectl apply           CD updates Git        │
          │  (push-based) ⚠️                  manifest repo         │
          │                                       │                │
          │  Problem:                             ▼                │
          │  - Who ran what?                  ArgoCD detects        │
          │  - No audit trail                 change, syncs         │
          │  - Hard to rollback               (pull-based) ✅       │
          │                                                        │
          │                                  Benefits:             │
          │                                  - Full Git history    │
          │                                  - git revert = rollback│
          │                                  - Drift detection     │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        🧠 ANALOGY: a thermostat. You set the desired temperature (commit to
        git). The thermostat (controller) continuously compares the room (live
        cluster) to the setpoint and acts until they match. Open a window
        (manual `kubectl edit`) and it keeps pushing back toward the setpoint.

        🔑 The core reconciliation loop: the controller continuously DIFFS git
        (desired) against the live cluster (actual) and APPLIES the difference.
        If they already match, it does nothing. If you hand-edit a live object,
        the next sync detects the drift and re-applies git — self-heal.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.3  ArgoCD for easypj — Practical Setup   🧪
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          [ARCHITECTURE]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │                                                        │
          │  ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────────┐                │
          │  │ Git Repo │  watch  │   ArgoCD     │                │
          │  │ manifests│◀────────│  Controller  │                │
          │  └──────────┘         └──────┬───────┘                │
          │                              │ sync                    │
          │                              ▼                         │
          │                      ┌──────────────┐                 │
          │                      │  K8s Cluster │                 │
          │                      │  ┌─────────┐ │                 │
          │                      │  │ easypj  │ │                 │
          │                      │  │  pods   │ │                 │
          │                      │  └─────────┘ │                 │
          │                      └──────────────┘                 │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [CODE: ArgoCD Application YAML for easypj]
          apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
          kind: Application
          metadata:
            name: easypj
            namespace: argocd
          spec:
            project: default
            source:
              repoURL: https://github.com/easypj/easypj-manifests.git
              targetRevision: main
              path: overlays/prod          # Kustomize overlay (or Helm chart)
            destination:
              server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
              namespace: easypj
            syncPolicy:
              automated:
                prune: true                 # delete objects removed from git
                selfHeal: true              # revert manual drift back to git
              syncOptions:
                - CreateNamespace=true

        🧪 easypj ships as an Application (ArgoCD) or Kustomization (Flux)
        pointing at the manifest repo/overlay. Helm or Kustomize renders the
        actual Deployment/Service/Ingress/ConfigMap/Secret in the pipeline.

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: how a GitOps controller diff/syncs vs the live
        cluster, and image-updater patterns —
           • ArgoCD's application-controller runs a reconcile loop: it renders
             the source (kustomize build / helm template), computes a diff
             against the live cluster via the API server, and shows Synced /
             OutOfSync / Healthy status. Auto-sync applies the diff; self-heal
             re-applies when live drifts; prune removes objects no longer in git.
           • Argo CD Image Updater (or CI itself) writes the new image tag back
             into the manifest repo, which then triggers the normal sync — the
             image change reaches the cluster as a commit, not a kubectl call.

        🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
           • App-of-apps: one parent Application that points at a repo full of
             child Applications — bootstrap an entire cluster from one commit.
           • Sync waves & hooks: annotate resources with
             `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` so CRDs/namespaces apply before the
             objects that depend on them; PreSync/PostSync hooks run jobs around
             a sync (e.g. DB migrations for easypj before the new pods roll).
           • Auto-prune & drift detection: removing a manifest from git deletes
             the object; manual edits are flagged OutOfSync and (with self-heal)
             reverted.
           • Progressive delivery: Argo Rollouts / Flagger do canary and
             blue-green releases on top of GitOps (shift traffic gradually,
             auto-rollback on bad metrics).
           • Image automation: Flux image-reflector/-automation controllers, or
             Argo Image Updater, commit new tags automatically.
           • GitOps secret management: sealed-secrets (encrypt → commit →
             controller decrypts in-cluster) or external-secrets (git stores a
             REFERENCE; an operator pulls the real value from Vault/AWS SM).
           • Projects & multi-tenancy: ArgoCD AppProjects scope which repos,
             clusters and namespaces a set of apps may touch — RBAC for GitOps.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.4  Helm — Kubernetes Package Manager   🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        - Package K8s manifests into reusable, versioned charts.
        - Values files for environment-specific config.
        - Chart structure: templates/ + values.yaml + Chart.yaml.
        $ helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --values prod-values.yaml

          [HELM CHART STRUCTURE — easypj example]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  easypj-chart/                                         │
          │  ├── Chart.yaml          # Chart metadata              │
          │  ├── values.yaml         # Default configuration       │
          │  ├── templates/                                         │
          │  │   ├── deployment.yaml  # {{ .Values.replicas }}     │
          │  │   ├── service.yaml     # {{ .Values.serviceType }}  │
          │  │   ├── ingress.yaml     # {{ .Values.host }}         │
          │  │   ├── configmap.yaml   # {{ .Values.dbHost }}       │
          │  │   ├── secret.yaml      # {{ .Values.dbPassword }}   │
          │  │   └── _helpers.tpl     # Template helpers           │
          │  └── values-prod.yaml    # Production overrides        │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

          [HELM ESSENTIAL COMMANDS]
          $ helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
          $ helm search repo nginx
          $ helm install my-release bitnami/nginx
          $ helm upgrade my-release bitnami/nginx --values custom.yaml
          $ helm rollback my-release 1
          $ helm list -A
          $ helm history my-release

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: Helm 3 renders Go templates against your values into
        plain manifests, then applies them and records a "release" (a versioned
        revision) in a Secret in the target namespace. `helm upgrade` bumps the
        revision; `helm rollback N` re-applies a previous stored revision; `helm
        history` lists them. No Tiller — Helm 3 talks straight to the API server
        with your kubeconfig RBAC.

        💡 For easypj, Helm shines when the SAME app must ship to many envs (dev
        / staging / prod) with only values differing, and when you want a single
        installable artifact (chart) to share via a chart repo.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.5  Kustomize — Built-in Manifest Customization   🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        - Kubernetes-native configuration management.
        - Base + overlays pattern (dev, staging, prod).
        - No templates — patch-based approach.
        $ kubectl apply -k overlays/production/

          [KUSTOMIZE DIRECTORY STRUCTURE — easypj]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  easypj-kustomize/                                     │
          │  ├── base/                                             │
          │  │   ├── kustomization.yaml                            │
          │  │   ├── deployment.yaml    # easypj base deployment   │
          │  │   ├── service.yaml       # easypj base service      │
          │  │   └── configmap.yaml     # shared config            │
          │  └── overlays/                                          │
          │      ├── dev/                                           │
          │      │   ├── kustomization.yaml  # replicas: 1         │
          │      │   └── patch-replicas.yaml                       │
          │      ├── staging/                                       │
          │      │   ├── kustomization.yaml  # replicas: 2         │
          │      │   └── patch-resources.yaml                       │
          │      └── production/                                    │
          │          ├── kustomization.yaml  # replicas: 5         │
          │          ├── patch-replicas.yaml                       │
          │          └── patch-resources.yaml                      │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: `kubectl apply -k` (or `kustomize build`) takes a
        BASE set of plain manifests and applies strategic-merge / JSON patches
        from an OVERLAY on top — no templating language. Each overlay's
        kustomization.yaml references the base and lists its patches, plus
        cluster-wide transforms (namePrefix, commonLabels, namespace, images:
        newTag). It's built into kubectl, so there's nothing extra to install.

        💡 For easypj, Kustomize is ideal for internal config drift between
        envs: keep ONE base, then patch only what differs (replicas, resources,
        hostnames) per overlay.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.6  Helm vs Kustomize — When to Use Each   🧭
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
          [COMPARISON TABLE]
          | Feature          | Helm                | Kustomize              |
          | Approach         | Templates + values   | Patches on base YAML   |
          | Learning curve   | Moderate             | Low                     |
          | Package sharing  | ✅ Charts repos      | ❌ Not designed for     |
          | Complexity mgmt  | Go templates         | Strategic merge patches |
          | Built into kubectl| No (separate binary) | Yes (kubectl apply -k) |
          | Best for         | Shared/public charts | Internal config mgmt   |

          [TIP: You can use BOTH together — Helm renders, Kustomize patches]

        🧭 DECISION GUIDE
           • Need a packaged, versioned, shareable release with per-env values
             and rollback history?            → Helm.
           • Need template-free, kubectl-native base + overlays for your own
             internal manifests?              → Kustomize.
           • Installing third-party software (databases, ingress, operators)?
                                              → usually a Helm chart.
           • Want both? Render the Helm chart, then post-render with Kustomize
             to patch the output for your cluster.


  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  39.7  Helm / Kustomize in GitOps   🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        GitOps doesn't replace Helm or Kustomize — it CONSUMES them. The
        Application/Kustomization points at a chart or overlay path, and the
        controller renders + applies it on every sync.

          [GITOPS SOURCE TYPES]
          ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  ArgoCD/Flux source: path in git                       │
          │                                                        │
          │  overlays/prod/   (Kustomize)  ─┐                      │
          │  easypj-chart/    (Helm + values)─┼─▶ controller       │
          │  raw manifests/   (plain YAML)  ─┘   renders → applies │
          │                                                        │
          │  per-env = different path / values file → easypj live  │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        ⚡ Point the GitOps app at a Kustomize overlay (or Helm chart with a
        values file) so per-env config is just a different path/values file —
        one app definition, many environments.


  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 39                                           ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • CI builds/tests/scans/pushes the image and bumps the manifest;        ║
  ║    CD/GitOps SYNCS the cluster to those manifests. Git is the single     ║
  ║    source of truth for desired state.                                    ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • A GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) continuously diffs git vs live and  ║
  ║    applies the difference; manual `kubectl edit` drift is detected and   ║
  ║    self-healed (reverted) back to git.                                   ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • easypj ships as an Application/Kustomization pointing at the repo/     ║
  ║    overlay; Helm or Kustomize renders the actual manifests in the        ║
  ║    pipeline.                                                             ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • Rollbacks are just `git revert` — the controller syncs the cluster    ║
  ║    back to the previous known-good commit.                               ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) is the production standard for deployments —     ║
  ║    pull-based, auditable, declarative.                                   ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  • Helm = templated, versioned releases (values per env); Kustomize =    ║
  ║    template-free base + overlays/patches. Know both, use what fits.      ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  🎯 CKA Relevance: Helm, Kustomize, CRDs & operators are 2025 Cluster-   ║
  ║     Architecture topics; GitOps is what you use the day AFTER you pass.  ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
     • Hand-editing live objects is futile under GitOps — the controller reverts
       them on the next sync. Change git instead.
     • Never commit raw Secrets to git — use sealed-secrets / external-secrets so
       only encrypted or reference data is stored.
     • Resource ordering (CRDs before CRs, namespaces before objects) needs sync
       waves/hooks, or the first sync fails.
     • Auto-prune deletes objects removed from git — powerful, but can wipe
       things if the repo is wrong.
     • Push-based CD puts cluster credentials in CI; pull-based GitOps keeps them
       in-cluster. Don't hand kubeconfig to your CI runner if you can avoid it.

  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
     • Point the GitOps app at a Kustomize overlay (or Helm chart) so per-env
       config is just a different path/values file.
     • Enable self-heal + prune deliberately; start in "manual sync" mode to
       observe diffs before automating.
     • Treat the image-tag bump as a git commit — that commit is your deployment
       record and your rollback point.
     • You can use Helm and Kustomize together: Helm renders, Kustomize patches.

  🔑 COMMANDS
     # GitOps — ArgoCD
     argocd app create easypj --repo <git> --path overlays/prod \
       --dest-namespace easypj
     argocd app sync easypj
     argocd app get easypj
     # GitOps — Flux
     flux create kustomization easypj --source=easypj-repo --path=./overlays/prod
     # Rollback = revert + auto-sync
     git revert <bad-commit>
     # What the controller does for you (Kustomize)
     kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
     # Helm
     helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --values prod-values.yaml
     helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --values prod-values.yaml
     helm rollback easypj 1
     helm list -A ; helm history easypj

  🧪 DRILL
     Sketch (or wire) the easypj git→cluster flow: CI pushes easypj:v2 and bumps
     the overlay; the GitOps controller syncs it; then make a manual
     `kubectl scale` change and watch it get reverted to git.

  🧪 LAB Q&A (10) — full answer + explanation each
     Q1. Difference between CI and CD here?
         A. CI = build/test/scan/push the image (+ bump the manifest); CD/GitOps
         = sync the cluster to the manifests. CI produces artifacts; CD deploys
         them.

     Q2. State the core GitOps principle.
         A. Git holds the declarative desired state; a controller continuously
         reconciles the live cluster to match it (no manual kubectl apply).

     Q3. What is an ArgoCD Application?
         A. An object that points at a git repo/path (and target cluster/ns) and
         tells ArgoCD what to sync — the unit of GitOps deployment.

     Q4. How does GitOps handle configuration drift?
         A. It detects the live/git difference and self-heals by re-applying git,
         reverting unauthorized manual changes.

     Q5. Use a Helm chart in GitOps. How?
         A. The controller renders the chart (with values) from the repo and
         applies the output — ArgoCD/Flux both support Helm sources.

     Q6. How are Secrets handled in GitOps?
         A. Store only encrypted/sealed secrets (sealed-secrets) or references
         (external-secrets) in git; the controller/operator materializes the
         real Secret in-cluster.

     Q7. What are sync waves for?
         A. Ordering — apply CRDs/namespaces before the resources that depend on
         them, using wave annotations/hooks so the sync doesn't fail.

     Q8. Roll back a bad deploy under GitOps.
         A. `git revert` the offending commit; the controller syncs the cluster
         back to the previous state automatically.

     Q9. How does an image update reach the cluster?
         A. CI (or an image-updater) commits the new tag to the manifest repo;
         the GitOps controller syncs the changed Deployment.

     Q10. You edited a live Deployment and it changed back. Why?
          A. GitOps self-heal reverted your manual edit to match git — make the
          change in the repo instead.

     Q11. When would you pick Helm over Kustomize (and vice-versa)?
          A. Helm for packaged, versioned, shareable releases with per-env values
          and rollback history (and for installing third-party software);
          Kustomize for template-free, kubectl-native base + overlays for your
          own internal manifests. They can also be combined.

     Q12. Why is pull-based GitOps safer than push-based CD?
          A. Push-based CD needs cluster credentials in the CI runner and leaves
          no audit trail of who applied what. Pull-based GitOps keeps creds
          in-cluster, makes every change a commit, and adds drift detection and
          easy `git revert` rollback.

  [N] VISUAL SUMMARY: git push → pipeline (build/test/scan/push + manifest bump)
      → GitOps controller syncs → easypj live; drift self-heals back to git.

PART 12: HARDENING & POLICY                                             🔴 🏢
  Chapters 40-42  ·  Beyond-exam depth + admission/policy mastery
  What you'll build: a hardened easypj namespace governed by layered policy —
  Pod Security Standards, resource governance, CEL admission policies, and an
  external policy engine — plus the admission-webhook machinery underneath.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  PART INTRO
  ───────────
  Security isn't one switch; it's layers. This part stacks them: harden the
  cluster surface (apiserver flags, audit, supply chain), then ENFORCE rules
  automatically with Pod Security Admission, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL,
  no webhook), and external engines (OPA Gatekeeper / Kyverno) — and shows the
  admission-webhook plumbing that powers it all.

  💡 The mental model: a single hardened pod is a one-off; a GOVERNED cluster
  makes the secure choice the DEFAULT and the insecure choice IMPOSSIBLE. Every
  chapter in this part moves you one rung up that ladder — from "I configured
  it right this once" to "the cluster will not let anyone configure it wrong."

  🧠 Analogy: think of cluster security like an airport. Chapter 40 is the
  perimeter fence, locked doors and the audit cameras (harden the surface and
  record who did what). Chapter 41 is the security checkpoint that EVERY
  passenger must clear — Pod Security Standards, ResourceQuota and CEL policies
  that screen each workload before it boards. Chapter 42 is the X-ray machine
  itself: the admission-webhook engine that the checkpoint runs on, the
  machinery you can extend with your own scanners.

  📖 KEY TERMS THIS PART INTRODUCES
    • Pod Security Admission (PSA) / Pod Security Standards (PSS) — built-in,
      namespace-labelled enforcement at three levels: privileged, baseline,
      restricted.
    • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP) — in-tree, CEL-based admission rules that
      run inside the apiserver with NO external webhook to deploy or maintain.
    • Admission webhook — an external HTTP callback (validating or mutating)
      the apiserver invokes during the admission phase of every API request.
    • OPA Gatekeeper / Kyverno — external policy engines that plug in via
      admission webhooks to enforce, mutate, and generate cluster resources.
    • Audit policy — rules that decide WHICH API events the apiserver logs and
      at WHAT level (Metadata / Request / RequestResponse).

  HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 12 map
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch40 HARDEN (surface, audit, supply chain) ─▶ Ch41 POLICY (enforce)     │
  │                                                     │                   │
  │                                                     ▼                   │
  │                 Ch42 ADMISSION WEBHOOKS & API EXTENSION (the engine)     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read it as a stack you build bottom-up, then operate top-down:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    THE LAYERED POLICY STACK (easypj)                       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 4  EXTERNAL ENGINE   Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper                       │
  │           (Ch41/Ch42)       "require team & cost-center labels"           │
  │                             ▲  admission webhook callback                  │
  │  Layer 3  CEL ADMISSION     ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (in-tree, no hook)   │
  │           (Ch41)            "min 2 replicas, approved registries only"     │
  │                             ▲  runs inside kube-apiserver                  │
  │  Layer 2  RESOURCE GOVERN.  ResourceQuota + LimitRange                     │
  │           (Ch41)            "namespace capped; every pod has limits"       │
  │                             ▲                                              │
  │  Layer 1  POD SECURITY      PSA label: enforce=restricted                  │
  │           (Ch41)            "no privileged, no host*, drop ALL caps"       │
  │                             ▲                                              │
  │  Layer 0  HARDENED SURFACE  apiserver flags · audit log · supply chain     │
  │           (Ch40)            "secure defaults, recorded, signed images"     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  💡 Each higher layer ASSUMES the one below it. A CEL policy that demands an
  approved registry is meaningless if the apiserver itself is wide open, so we
  harden the surface (Layer 0) FIRST, then stack enforcement on top.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which layer enforces what?
    • "Block privileged / hostNetwork / writable root fs"  → PSA restricted
        (Layer 1) — zero config beyond a namespace label.
    • "Cap total CPU/memory; force every pod to set limits" → ResourceQuota +
        LimitRange (Layer 2) — governance, not security per se.
    • "Custom rule, no external component" (replica floor,   → VAP / CEL
        registry allow-list, label shape)                       (Layer 3).
    • "Rich rules, mutation, generation, reporting, audit"  → Kyverno / OPA
        across many clusters                                    Gatekeeper (4).
    • "Understand or build the plumbing itself"             → Admission webhooks
                                                                (Ch42).

  CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────
  🎯 Hardening and admission control are explicit, high-weight items in the
  2025 "Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration" and security
  domains. The exam reliably tests: labelling a namespace for Pod Security
  Admission at a given level, reading an apiserver/audit misconfiguration,
  and reasoning about why a pod was ADMITTED or REJECTED. ⚡ The fastest marks
  here come from PSA labels (one kubectl label command) and from knowing the
  three PSS levels cold — privileged < baseline < restricted.

  PART SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION
  ──────────────────────────────
  Implementation thread: lock the easypj namespace with PSA=restricted +
  ResourceQuota + a CEL policy ("min 2 replicas, approved registries only") +
  a Kyverno rule ("require labels"), and understand the validating/mutating
  webhook flow that enforces them. VISUAL: the layered policy stack (above).

  By the end of this part the easypj namespace looks like this:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  namespace/easypj                                                         │
  │    labels:                                                                │
  │      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted   ◀── Layer 1 (PSA)   │
  │      pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn:    restricted                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ResourceQuota: requests.cpu=4 memory=8Gi  limits ...   ◀── Layer 2   │ │
  │  │ LimitRange:    default request/limit per container                  │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ValidatingAdmissionPolicy "easypj-guardrails"        ◀── Layer 3    │ │
  │  │   CEL: object.spec.replicas >= 2                                    │ │
  │  │   CEL: image starts with "registry.easypj.internal/"               │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Kyverno ClusterPolicy "require-labels"               ◀── Layer 4    │ │
  │  │   validate: every Pod must carry team & cost-center labels          │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD PREVIEW — the admission pipeline every layer rides on:

      kubectl apply ─▶ kube-apiserver
                          │
                          ├─ (1) authentication        who are you?
                          ├─ (2) authorization (RBAC)  may you?
                          ├─ (3) MUTATING admission    rewrite the object
                          │        • built-in plugins  • mutating webhooks
                          │        • Kyverno mutate     (Layer 4)
                          ├─ (4) object schema validation
                          ├─ (5) VALIDATING admission   accept / reject
                          │        • PSA                 (Layer 1)
                          │        • ResourceQuota       (Layer 2)
                          │        • VAP / CEL            (Layer 3)
                          │        • validating webhooks → Kyverno/OPA (Layer 4)
                          └─ (6) persist to etcd
  ⚠️ Order matters: ALL mutating admission runs BEFORE any validating admission,
  so a mutating webhook can inject a default that a later validating policy then
  approves. Within each phase, webhook order is not guaranteed — never write a
  webhook that depends on another webhook having run first.

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER FOR THIS PART
    • PSA is enforced by NAMESPACE LABELS, not by a CRD or a controller pod.
    • The three PSS levels, weakest→strongest: privileged → baseline →
      restricted.
    • VAP/CEL runs INSIDE the apiserver — no pod, no webhook, no TLS cert to
      manage; prefer it over a custom webhook when CEL can express the rule.
    • failurePolicy on a webhook decides what happens if the webhook is DOWN:
      Fail (closed, safe) vs Ignore (open, available). For security policy,
      lean Fail.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 40: Security Hardening & Best Practices                       🔴 🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2.5h · 🏢 Beyond-exam (production security; CKS
        on-ramp). The CKA touches RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ServiceAccounts and
        admission; this chapter ties them into one coherent hardening posture.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A passing cluster isn't a secure cluster. easypj can be perfectly healthy —
  pods Running, Services routing, Ingress serving traffic — and still be one
  leaked token, one `:latest` image, or one cluster-admin binding away from a
  full compromise. Security is not a feature you bolt on at the end; it is a
  property of how every other object is configured. The mental model is
  DEFENSE IN DEPTH: stack independent controls so that defeating any single one
  doesn't hand an attacker the cluster. This chapter is the on-ramp to the CKS
  (Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist) world, but every control here pays
  off the day-2 operation of easypj in production.

  💡 INSIGHT: every prior chapter contributed one layer. RBAC (Ch. authZ),
  NetworkPolicy (Ch. networking), ServiceAccounts (Ch. auth), Pod Security
  Admission (Ch. admission), Secrets/etcd encryption (Ch. config) and image
  management (Ch. workloads) are not separate topics — they are the bricks of
  a single wall. This chapter is where you mortar them together.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OBJECTIVES
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
    • Apply a 6-layer hardening checklist to easypj end-to-end.
    • Harden RBAC to least privilege and spot the dangerous verbs (escalate,
      bind, impersonate, *) that let a subject grant itself more power.
    • Manage Secrets safely: encryption at rest, volume over env, automount off,
      external stores.
    • Lock down the API server and configure an audit policy that captures the
      right events at the right level without leaking secret bodies.
    • Apply runtime security: seccomp RuntimeDefault, AppArmor, read-only root
      filesystem, dropped capabilities.
    • Secure the supply chain: pin digests, scan, sign, and allowlist registries.
    • Compose per-namespace controls into safe multi-tenancy.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CKA RELEVANCE
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🎯 Exam: RBAC (create least-privilege Role/RoleBinding), ServiceAccount token
  automount, NetworkPolicy default-deny, and Pod Security Admission labels are
  all directly testable. 🏢 Beyond-exam: KMS encryption, audit policy authoring,
  seccomp/AppArmor profile attachment, image signing/scanning and ImagePolicy
  admission are CKS / production-security territory — know the shape, even if
  the CKA only scratches the surface.

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SECTION MAP
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    40.1  Hardening Checklist — the 6 layers                         🏢
    40.2  RBAC Hardening — least privilege & dangerous verbs         🏢
    40.3  Secrets Management — encrypt, mount, scope                 🏢
    40.4  API Server & Audit — anonymous-auth, admission, audit      🏢
    40.5  Runtime Security — seccomp, AppArmor, rootfs, caps         🏢
    40.6  Supply Chain — pin, scan, sign, allowlist                  🏢
    40.7  Multi-Tenancy — stacking per-namespace controls            🏢

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.1  HARDENING CHECKLIST — THE 6 LAYERS                                  🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Defense in depth means no single control is load-bearing. Picture six
  concentric rings around the easypj workload; an attacker must defeat ALL of
  them, in order, to reach the data.

  [DEFENSE IN DEPTH — 6 LAYERS AROUND easypj]

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 1 🏗️  INFRA      hardened nodes, restricted kubelet, firewalled ports  │
   │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
   │  │ 2 🔐 AuthN/Z   least-privilege RBAC, no anonymous-auth, SA      │    │
   │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │    │
   │  │  │ 3 🧪 Admission  PodSecurity=restricted, ValidatingAd- │      │    │
   │  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │ 4 📦 Workload  non-root, ro-rootfs, drop    │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │ 5 🧯 Network  default-deny NetPol │       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  ┌────────────────────────┐       │       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  │ 6 💾 DATA              │       │       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  │   encrypt Secrets at   │       │       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  │   rest, audit log,     │  ◀── easypj   │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  │   signed+scanned imgs  │     JobPost    │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  │  └────────────────────────┘       │       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────┘       │       │      │    │
   │  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │      │    │
   │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │    │
   │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     💡 a breach must defeat EVERY layer — one is never enough.

  ┌────┬──────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ #  │ LAYER        │ WHAT IT BUYS YOU (for easypj)                           │
  ├────┼──────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 1  │ 🏗️ Infra     │ Hardened nodes, kubelet anonymous-auth off, only the    │
  │    │              │ kube ports open; an attacker on the network can't reach │
  │    │              │ the kubelet or etcd directly.                           │
  │ 2  │ 🔐 AuthN/Z   │ Least-privilege RBAC + no anonymous-auth + SA hygiene;  │
  │    │              │ a stolen easypj-web-sa token can do almost nothing.     │
  │ 3  │ 🧪 Admission │ PodSecurity=restricted + ValidatingAdmissionPolicy      │
  │    │              │ reject insecure pods at create time, before they run.   │
  │ 4  │ 📦 Workload  │ non-root, read-only rootfs, dropped caps, seccomp, no   │
  │    │              │ automount; a compromised JobPost process is boxed in.   │
  │ 5  │ 🧯 Network   │ default-deny NetworkPolicy + egress control; a breached  │
  │    │              │ pod can't pivot laterally or call out.                  │
  │ 6  │ 💾 Data      │ Secrets encrypted at rest, audit logging, signed+scanned│
  │    │              │ images; even etcd access doesn't yield plaintext creds.  │
  └────┴──────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — where does a given control belong?
    Is it about the host/node?  → Layer 1 (Infra).
    Who can call the API?       → Layer 2 (AuthN/Z).
    Can this pod even be made?  → Layer 3 (Admission).
    What can the pod do once up?→ Layer 4 (Workload).
    Who can it talk to?         → Layer 5 (Network).
    Is the data/at-rest safe?   → Layer 6 (Data).

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.2  RBAC HARDENING — LEAST PRIVILEGE & DANGEROUS VERBS                  🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  RBAC hardening = least privilege + watching the verbs that let a subject
  grant ITSELF more power. The single most common real-world misconfiguration
  is over-broad RBAC: wildcards in rules, or cluster-admin handed out "just to
  make it work."

  📖 KEY TERM — privilege escalation verbs. Certain RBAC verbs are special
  because they let a subject increase its own authority:
    • escalate — create/update a Role with permissions you don't yourself hold.
    • bind     — create a RoleBinding referencing a Role you don't hold.
    • impersonate — act AS another user/group/SA (--as).
    • *  (wildcard verb or resource) — effectively unlimited within scope.

  [LEAST PRIVILEGE FOR easypj-web-sa — READ ITS OWN CONFIGMAP]

   apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
   kind: Role
   metadata:
     namespace: easypj
     name: easypj-cm-reader
   rules:
   - apiGroups: [""]
     resources: ["configmaps"]
     resourceNames: ["easypj-config"]    # ← narrowed to ONE object for get
     verbs: ["get"]
   - apiGroups: [""]
     resources: ["configmaps"]
     verbs: ["list", "watch"]            # list/watch can't use resourceNames
   ---
   apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
   kind: RoleBinding
   metadata:
     namespace: easypj
     name: easypj-cm-reader-bind
   subjects:
   - kind: ServiceAccount
     name: easypj-web-sa
     namespace: easypj
   roleRef:
     kind: Role
     name: easypj-cm-reader
     apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  ⚠️ resourceNames restricts get/update/delete/patch but NOT list/watch/create
  (the name isn't known yet for those). So list/watch rules can't be name-scoped
  — keep them as narrow as the resource type allows.

  [AUDITING WHO CAN DO WHAT]

   # What can this SA actually do?
   kubectl auth can-i --list \
     --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj

   # Find cluster-admin / wildcard bindings
   kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep -i cluster-admin

   # Invert the question (krew plugin): who can delete pods in easypj?
   kubectl who-can delete pods -n easypj

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING — "it works only with cluster-admin." That's a smell, not a
  fix. Use `auth can-i --list` to enumerate exactly which verbs/resources the
  workload needs, then write a Role granting precisely those and nothing more.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.3  SECRETS MANAGEMENT — ENCRYPT, MOUNT, SCOPE                          🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  By default, Secrets are stored in etcd merely base64-encoded — NOT encrypted.
  Anyone who can read etcd (a node compromise, an etcd backup) reads every
  credential in the cluster. Four practices close that gap.

  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PRACTICE             │ WHY / HOW                                            │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Encrypt at rest      │ EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc) or KMS v2 provider; │
  │                      │ apiserver flag --encryption-provider-config.         │
  │ Volume over env      │ env vars leak via `kubectl describe`, crash dumps,    │
  │                      │ child processes & logs; mounted files don't.         │
  │ Disable automount    │ automountServiceAccountToken:false unless the pod     │
  │                      │ actually calls the API — fewer live tokens.          │
  │ External stores      │ Vault / cloud SM via CSI Secrets Store or External    │
  │                      │ Secrets Operator; rotate centrally, sync on demand.  │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [ENCRYPTION-AT-REST CONFIG (on the control-plane host)]

   # /etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
   apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
   kind: EncryptionConfiguration
   resources:
   - resources: ["secrets"]
     providers:
     - aescbc:                       # or: kms: { ... } for KMS v2
         keys:
         - name: key1
           secret: <base64 32-byte key>
     - identity: {}                  # fallback so existing data still reads

   # kube-apiserver static-pod manifest gains:
   #   --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
   # then re-encrypt everything already written:
   kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

  🔑 ORDER MATTERS: list `identity: {}` LAST when enabling encryption (read
  plaintext, write encrypted). To DECRYPT, put identity FIRST and re-run the
  replace. The first provider listed is the one used for writes.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: to prove a secret is encrypted in etcd:
   ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/easypj/easypj-secret \
     --cacert=... --cert=... --key=... | hexdump -C | head
   Plaintext → you'll see "k8s:enc:aescbc" prefix instead of readable values.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.4  API SERVER & AUDIT — ANONYMOUS-AUTH, ADMISSION, AUDIT POLICY        🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  The API server is the front door; everything authenticates through it. Two
  hardening axes: shut the unauthenticated paths, and record what happened.

  [API-SERVER HARDENING FLAGS]
   --anonymous-auth=false              # no unauthenticated requests
   --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,...
   --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml
   --audit-log-path=/var/log/kube-audit.log
   --audit-log-maxage=30 --audit-log-maxbackup=10

  📖 KEY TERM — audit levels (least → most verbose):
    None  → don't log this.
    Metadata → who/what/when/verb, but NOT request/response bodies.
    Request → metadata + request body.
    RequestResponse → metadata + request AND response bodies.

  [AUDIT POLICY — RIGHT LEVEL PER RESOURCE]

   apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
   kind: Policy
   rules:
   # Secrets at Metadata ONLY — never log their bodies
   - level: Metadata
     resources:
     - group: ""
       resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
   # RBAC changes at full RequestResponse — high-value, no sensitive bodies
   - level: RequestResponse
     resources:
     - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
       resources: ["roles","rolebindings","clusterroles","clusterrolebindings"]
   # Catch-all
   - level: Metadata

  [HOW AN AUDIT EVENT FLOWS]

     request ──▶ apiserver ──▶ [audit stages]
                                 │
        RequestReceived ─────────┤  (verb authorized?)
        ResponseStarted ─────────┤  (for long-running/watch)
        ResponseComplete ────────┤  ◀── policy decides LEVEL here
        Panic ───────────────────┘
                                 ▼
                          /var/log/kube-audit.log (or webhook backend)

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: a rule of `RequestResponse` on Secrets writes the secret VALUES
  into the audit log — a plaintext leak in a file you ship to a SIEM. Always
  cap Secrets at Metadata level.

  🔬 DEEPER: audit stages let you log a watch when it STARTS (ResponseStarted)
  vs. when it ends. KMS v2 adds key-hierarchy and per-object DEKs for faster
  rotation. The ImagePolicyWebhook admission plugin can defer image decisions to
  an external service. NodeRestriction limits what a kubelet can modify (only
  its own Node/Pods), blocking a compromised node from editing other nodes.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.5  RUNTIME SECURITY — SECCOMP, APPARMOR, ROOTFS, CAPABILITIES          🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Layer 4 boxes in the running process. Even if the JobPost app is exploited,
  these controls limit what the resulting shell can do on the node.

  [HARDENED easypj POD securityContext]

   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     name: easypj-web
     namespace: easypj
   spec:
     automountServiceAccountToken: false
     securityContext:
       runAsNonRoot: true
       runAsUser: 10001
       seccompProfile:
         type: RuntimeDefault              # default syscall filter
     containers:
     - name: web
       image: registry.example.com/easypj@sha256:<digest>
       securityContext:
         allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
         readOnlyRootFilesystem: true      # tamper-proof image layers
         capabilities:
           drop: ["ALL"]                   # add back only what's needed
       volumeMounts:
       - name: tmp
         mountPath: /tmp                    # writable scratch via emptyDir
     volumes:
     - name: tmp
       emptyDir: {}

  ┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CONTROL                 │ WHAT IT STOPS                                     │
  ├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ runAsNonRoot / UID      │ root-in-container → root-on-node escapes          │
  │ seccomp RuntimeDefault  │ dangerous syscalls (ptrace, mount, etc.)          │
  │ AppArmor profile        │ file/network access beyond the profile            │
  │ readOnlyRootFilesystem  │ writing malware/persistence into image layers     │
  │ drop ALL capabilities   │ raw sockets, chroot, NET_ADMIN, etc.              │
  │ allowPrivilegeEscalation│ setuid binaries gaining more than the parent      │
  │ automount token off     │ a shell silently using the SA token vs the API    │
  └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 ANALOGY: a read-only root filesystem is like welding the engine bay shut —
  the car still runs (it reads from the image), but nobody can swap parts while
  it's moving. Apps that legitimately need to write get explicit emptyDir/PVC
  mounts, the only unlocked panels.

  🔬 DEEPER: AppArmor profiles attach via the annotation/field
  `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/<name>`
  (newer: the appArmorProfile field) and must be loaded on every node. seccomp
  profiles can be custom JSON in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/profiles. For true
  sandboxing, a RuntimeClass pointing at gVisor or Kata runs the workload in a
  micro-VM / user-space kernel. Falco watches syscalls at runtime and alerts on
  anomalies (a shell spawned in a container, an unexpected outbound connection).

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.6  SUPPLY CHAIN — PIN, SCAN, SIGN, ALLOWLIST                           🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  You can harden the cluster perfectly and still lose if the image you run is
  compromised. Four practices protect the path from source to running container.

  [SUPPLY-CHAIN PIPELINE]

    source ─▶ build ─▶ SCAN (Trivy/Grype) ─▶ SIGN (cosign) ─▶ push by DIGEST
                            │ fail on CRITICAL          │              │
                            ▼                           ▼              ▼
                       block build              verify in admission   pull
                                                 (allowlist registry) immutable

  ┌───────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PRACTICE      │ HOW (easypj)                                                  │
  ├───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Pin digests   │ image: registry/easypj@sha256:<digest> — NOT :latest. Same   │
  │               │ digest = byte-identical, reproducible, scan/sign still valid. │
  │ Scan          │ `trivy image easypj:v1` in CI; fail the build on CRITICAL/HIGH│
  │ Sign          │ `cosign sign` at build; verify signature in admission         │
  │ Allowlist     │ Kyverno/Gatekeeper or ImagePolicyWebhook reject any registry  │
  │ registries    │ not on the approved list.                                     │
  └───────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: `:latest` (or any tag with no digest) makes deployments
  non-reproducible AND bypasses scan/sign guarantees — the tag can be retagged
  out from under you. Pin tags to digests in production.

  🔬 DEEPER: an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists every package in the
  image so you can answer "are we affected by CVE-X?" instantly. SLSA provenance
  attests HOW the image was built (which CI, which source commit), so a forged
  build is detectable. cosign stores signatures in the OCI registry alongside
  the image; admission verifies them against your public key before the pod runs.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  40.7  MULTI-TENANCY — STACKING PER-NAMESPACE CONTROLS                     🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Namespaces are a soft boundary, not a security boundary by themselves. Safe
  multi-tenancy = STACK independent controls on each tenant namespace so one
  tenant can't read, starve, reach, or escalate against another.

  [THE TENANCY STACK — APPLIED TO ns/easypj]

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ namespace: easypj                                            │
   │  ┌──────────────┐  least-privilege Role + RoleBinding         │
   │  │ 🔐 RBAC      │  (scoped to this ns, no cluster verbs)      │
   │  ├──────────────┤                                             │
   │  │ 📊 Quota     │  ResourceQuota — caps total cpu/mem/objects │
   │  ├──────────────┤                                             │
   │  │ 📏 LimitRange│  per-pod defaults & max (fair share)        │
   │  ├──────────────┤                                             │
   │  │ 🧯 NetPol    │  default-deny ingress+egress, allow-listed  │
   │  ├──────────────┤                                             │
   │  │ 🧪 PSA       │  pod-security.../enforce=restricted         │
   │  └──────────────┘                                             │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [APPLY THE STACK]
   kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
   kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted
   # + ResourceQuota, LimitRange, default-deny NetworkPolicy, scoped RBAC

  💡 INSIGHT: each control blocks a different attack: RBAC stops "read the
  neighbor's secrets," Quota/LimitRange stop "starve the neighbor" (noisy
  neighbor / DoS), NetworkPolicy stops "reach the neighbor's pods," PSA stops
  "run a privileged pod that escapes to the node." Remove any one and that
  attack class reopens.

  ⚠️ For HARD multi-tenancy (untrusted tenants), namespaces alone are not
  enough — you need separate node pools, RuntimeClass sandboxing (gVisor/Kata),
  or even separate clusters. The stack above is SOFT multi-tenancy for
  cooperating teams.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔧 UTH:
    • Audit events flow through stages (RequestReceived → ResponseStarted →
      ResponseComplete → Panic); the policy picks a LEVEL at decision time and
      writes to the log file or a webhook backend.
    • seccomp/AppArmor profiles attach per-container and must exist on the node;
      RuntimeDefault uses the container runtime's built-in syscall filter.
    • An image digest (sha256:...) is content-addressed and immutable — the same
      digest can never refer to different bytes, which is what makes pinning,
      scanning and signing meaningful.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    • Audit policy stages & levels; omitStages to drop noisy RequestReceived.
    • KMS v2: per-object DEKs, key hierarchy, faster rotation than aescbc.
    • ImagePolicyWebhook for external image admission decisions.
    • Falco for runtime anomaly detection (unexpected shells / connections).
    • SBOM + SLSA provenance for supply-chain attestation.
    • gVisor / Kata via RuntimeClass for kernel-level sandboxing.
    • AppArmor profile authoring and per-node loading.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • Security is DEFENSE IN DEPTH across 6 layers — infra, authN/Z, admission,
    workload, network, data. A breach must defeat EVERY layer; one is never
    enough.
  • RBAC hardening = least privilege + watching the dangerous verbs (escalate,
    bind, impersonate, and wildcard *) that let a subject grant itself more.
    Broad RBAC is the most common real-world misconfiguration — audit bindings.
  • Secrets: encrypt at rest (EncryptionConfiguration / KMS), prefer volume
    mounts over env, disable token automount, and consider external stores.
  • API server / audit / runtime / supply chain all matter:
    --anonymous-auth=false; an audit policy that uses Metadata for secrets and
    RequestResponse for RBAC; seccomp/AppArmor; and scanned + signed + pinned
    images from allowlisted registries.
  • resourceNames narrows get/update/delete but NOT list/watch/create — name
    your secrets/configmaps in the get rule, keep list/watch as tight otherwise.
  • Multi-tenancy is a STACK: RBAC + ResourceQuota + LimitRange + NetworkPolicy
    (default-deny) + PSA=restricted, per namespace.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • Audit at RequestResponse on Secrets logs their BODIES — use Metadata level
    for secrets so you don't leak them into the audit log.
  • `:latest` (or no digest) makes deployments non-reproducible and bypasses
    scan/sign guarantees — pin tags/digests.
  • Broad RBAC (wildcards, cluster-admin handed out) is the most common real
    misconfiguration — audit ClusterRoleBindings regularly.
  • Leaving automountServiceAccountToken ON across all pods needlessly exposes
    API credentials to any process (or attacker) in the pod.
  • EncryptionConfiguration only protects NEW writes — existing secrets stay
    plaintext in etcd until you re-`replace` them.
  • Namespaces are NOT a hard security boundary on their own; untrusted tenants
    need sandboxing or separate clusters.
  • A read-only root filesystem breaks apps that write to disk unless you add
    explicit emptyDir/PVC mounts for their writable paths.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=...` audits what a subject can really do;
    the krew `who-can` plugin inverts it (who can do X).
  • Stack per-namespace controls together for tenancy in one go:
    RBAC + ResourceQuota + LimitRange + NetworkPolicy + PSA=restricted.
  • Scan images in CI (Trivy/Grype) and fail the build on criticals — far
    cheaper than catching it in the running cluster.
  • Verify encryption-at-rest by reading the raw etcd value: a `k8s:enc:aescbc`
    prefix means it worked; readable text means it didn't.
  • `kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`
    is the one-liner that turns on the strongest built-in pod hardening.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔑 COMMANDS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # Audit what a ServiceAccount can do
  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj

  # Find risky cluster-admin / wildcard bindings
  kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep -i cluster-admin

  # Invert: who can perform an action (krew plugin)
  kubectl who-can delete pods -n easypj

  # Turn on restricted Pod Security on the namespace
  kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

  # Verify a secret is encrypted in etcd
  kubectl get secret easypj-secret -o yaml      # then check raw etcd value

  # Re-encrypt all existing secrets after enabling encryption-at-rest
  kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

  # Supply-chain scan in CI (fail on criticals)
  trivy image easypj:v1

  # API-server hardening flags (static-pod manifest)
  --anonymous-auth=false
  --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
  --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml --audit-log-path=...

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🧪 DRILL — END-TO-END HARDEN easypj
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Harden the easypj namespace end-to-end: apply restricted PSA on the
  namespace; write a least-privilege Role for its ServiceAccount with automount
  off; enable encryption-at-rest for secrets and re-encrypt existing ones; add a
  default-deny NetworkPolicy; and deploy with a scanned, digest-pinned image and
  a hardened securityContext (non-root, ro-rootfs, drop ALL, seccomp
  RuntimeDefault). Verify each layer with `auth can-i --list`, a raw etcd read,
  and a denied test pod.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Q1. Give easypj's ServiceAccount the minimum it needs (read its own
      ConfigMap). How?
      A. A Role scoped to get on that ConfigMap (with resourceNames for get) plus
      list/watch on configmaps, bound to the SA — no wildcards, nothing
      cluster-wide. resourceNames narrows get; list/watch can't be name-scoped.

  Q2. Enable encryption at rest for Secrets.
      A. Configure an EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc or KMS) and point the
      apiserver at it with --encryption-provider-config. List a real provider
      first and identity last. Then re-`replace` existing secrets so they're
      re-encrypted (the config only protects new writes).

  Q3. List the controls that harden a workload (pod) itself.
      A. runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false,
      drop ALL capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault, and automount token off.

  Q4. Set an audit policy that won't leak secret contents.
      A. Log Secrets (and ConfigMaps) at Metadata level and sensitive RBAC
      objects at RequestResponse; never RequestResponse on Secret bodies.

  Q5. What does seccomp RuntimeDefault provide?
      A. The container runtime's default syscall filter, blocking dangerous
      syscalls — a baseline runtime-security control required by the restricted
      Pod Security standard.

  Q6. Why a read-only root filesystem, and how do apps still write?
      A. It prevents tampering/persistence by an attacker (no writing into image
      layers). Apps that must write get explicit emptyDir or PVC mounts for just
      those paths (e.g. /tmp).

  Q7. Restrict which registries images may come from.
      A. An admission policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper or an ImagePolicyWebhook) that
      allowlists approved registries and rejects everything else.

  Q8. Reduce the attack surface of the default ServiceAccount.
      A. Set automountServiceAccountToken:false and keep it unprivileged, so no
      pod silently inherits API access via a mounted token.

  Q9. Isolate tenants sharing a cluster. Which objects per namespace?
      A. Scoped RBAC, ResourceQuota + LimitRange (fair share), a default-deny
      NetworkPolicy, and PSA=restricted — stacked together.

  Q10. Find risky cluster bindings.
      A. Audit ClusterRoleBindings for cluster-admin and wildcards, and look for
      the escalate/bind/impersonate verbs (`kubectl get clusterrolebindings`,
      `kubectl auth can-i --list`, the who-can plugin).

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧠 VISUAL SUMMARY — THE 6-LAYER DEFENSE AROUND easypj
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  easypj's security is six independent rings — Infra, AuthN/Z, Admission,
  Workload, Network, Data — wrapped around the JobPost workload and its etcd
  data. Each ring answers a different question (whose host? who can call the
  API? can this pod be created? what can it do? who can it reach? is the data
  safe at rest?) and stops a different class of attack. RBAC enforces least
  privilege and guards the escalate/bind/impersonate verbs; Secrets are
  encrypted at rest, mounted as volumes, and have automount off; the API server
  refuses anonymous auth and audits at the right level (Metadata for secrets,
  RequestResponse for RBAC); the workload runs non-root with a read-only rootfs,
  dropped capabilities and seccomp; NetworkPolicy defaults to deny; and images
  are scanned, signed and pinned by digest from allowlisted registries. The
  whole point: a breach must defeat EVERY layer — one is never enough.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 41: Policies Deep Dive                                       🔴 🎯 🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  META: 🔴 hard · ⏱️ ~2.5h · PSS and ResourceQuota are exam-relevant; external
        policy engines (Gatekeeper / Kyverno) are Day-2 / beyond-the-exam.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHY THIS MATTERS                                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │ Policy is how a cluster enforces its standards AUTOMATICALLY instead of  │
  │ trusting every human to remember the rules. Without policy, one          │
  │ developer ships a root container, another forgets resource requests and  │
  │ starves a node, a third deploys a single-replica "production" workload   │
  │ that dies on the next drain. Policy moves all of that from "please be    │
  │ careful" to "the API server will refuse the request." For the easypj    │
  │ platform this means the jobpost workload (Django + Gunicorn talking to   │
  │ PostgreSQL) is FORCED to run non-root, with capped resources, with a     │
  │ sane replica floor — guaranteed at admission time, before a single bad   │
  │ pod ever schedules.                                                      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT: There is no single "policy" object in Kubernetes. "Policy" is a
     LAYERED stack of independent controls — each one guards a different aspect
     of a request, and each one says yes/no (or quietly mutates) at a different
     point in the admission pipeline. Master the layers and their ORDER and the
     whole subject collapses into something simple.

  🧠 ANALOGY: Think of admission as airport security for pods. Pod Security
     Admission is the metal detector (no weapons / no root). The
     ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is the gate agent checking your boarding pass
     rules ("you must travel with at least one companion → replicas >= 2").
     LimitRange is the helpful clerk who fills in the blank fields on your form
     (default cpu/mem). ResourceQuota is the flight's total weight limit. And
     NetworkPolicy + PDB are the in-flight rules once you're already aboard.

  OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
    • Apply the three Pod Security Standards (privileged / baseline /
      restricted) in enforce / warn / audit modes, version-pinned.
    • Distinguish LimitRange (per-pod defaults & bounds) from ResourceQuota
      (namespace totals) and make them work together.
    • Use PID limits to protect nodes from fork bombs.
    • Use topology spread constraints as a governance / reliability control.
    • Author a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL (in-cluster, no webhook).
    • Compare OPA Gatekeeper (Rego) vs Kyverno (YAML) and choose between them.
    • Assemble the complete layered policy stack and reason about its order.

  CKA RELEVANCE: 🎯 Pod Security Standards, LimitRange and ResourceQuota are
     fair game and frequently appear. 🎯🏢 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) is
     newer, partially exam-relevant and increasingly important Day-2. 🏢 OPA
     Gatekeeper and Kyverno are beyond the exam but expected of a real admin.

  ┌──────────────────────────── SECTION MAP ────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 41.1 Pod Security Standards — 3 levels            🎯                      │
  │ 41.2 LimitRange vs ResourceQuota                  🎯                      │
  │ 41.3 PID Limits                                   🏢                      │
  │ 41.4 Topology Spread as Policy                    🎯                      │
  │ 41.5 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)              🎯 🏢                   │
  │ 41.6 External Engines — OPA Gatekeeper & Kyverno  🏢                      │
  │ 41.7 The Complete Policy Stack                    🧭                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — "which policy tool do I reach for?"

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Need ...                                  │ Reach for ...             │
   ├───────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
   │ block root / privileged / dangerous caps  │ Pod Security Admission    │
   │ inject default cpu/mem on bare pods       │ LimitRange                │
   │ cap a namespace's TOTAL cpu/mem/objects   │ ResourceQuota             │
   │ stop fork bombs / runaway processes       │ podPidsLimit (PID limit)  │
   │ force even spread across zones/nodes       │ topologySpreadConstraints │
   │ a simple cluster-native rule (CEL)        │ ValidatingAdmissionPolicy │
   │ rich validate + MUTATE + GENERATE rules   │ Kyverno (YAML)            │
   │ Rego-based org policy with constraints    │ OPA Gatekeeper (Rego)     │
   │ who-may-talk-to-whom at runtime           │ NetworkPolicy             │
   │ survive node drains / voluntary disruption│ PodDisruptionBudget       │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.1 Pod Security Standards — 3 levels 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — Pod Security Standards (PSS): a set of three predefined
     security profiles. Pod Security Admission (PSA) is the BUILT-IN admission
     controller that enforces them, configured by labels ON THE NAMESPACE.

  The three levels, from most permissive to most locked-down:

   ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Level        │ What it allows / requires                                 │
   ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ privileged   │ Wide open. No restrictions. For system / infra workloads. │
   │ baseline     │ Blocks known privilege escalations: no hostNetwork,       │
   │              │ no hostPID, no privileged containers, limited hostPath.   │
   │              │ A sane "minimum bar" for general apps.                    │
   │ restricted   │ Hardened. MUST run non-root, MUST drop ALL capabilities,  │
   │              │ seccompProfile RuntimeDefault, no privilege escalation,   │
   │              │ read-only-friendly. The target for easypj/jobpost.        │
   └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Each level is applied in one (or more) of three MODES via namespace labels:

   ┌──────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Mode      │ Effect on a violating pod                                     │
   ├──────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ enforce   │ REJECT the pod at admission. Hard block.                      │
   │ warn      │ Allow, but return a user-facing warning to kubectl.           │
   │ audit     │ Allow, but write an annotation to the audit log.              │
   └──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Each mode label can ALSO be version-pinned so a cluster upgrade doesn't
  silently tighten the rules under you:

      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.31
      pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
      pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted

  Apply restricted enforcement to the easypj namespace:

      kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: PSA is PER-NAMESPACE and it does NOT evict already-running pods.
     Only NEW or UPDATED pods are evaluated. Labelling an existing busy
     namespace enforce=restricted will not kill the violators already there —
     but it WILL block their next rollout. Always go warn/audit first.

  💡 INSIGHT — the safe rollout pattern: set warn + audit to the target level
     first, watch what would break, fix the manifests, THEN flip enforce.

      # 1) observe only — nobody is blocked
      kubectl label ns easypj \
        pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
        pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
      # 2) fix offending manifests (drop caps, runAsNonRoot, etc.)
      # 3) commit to the hard block
      kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

  🧪 LAB: label the easypj namespace enforce=baseline, try to create a pod with
     `securityContext.privileged: true`, watch it get rejected; relabel to
     privileged and watch the same pod succeed.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.2 LimitRange vs ResourceQuota 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  These two are constantly confused. They operate on different SCOPES and they
  are designed to be used TOGETHER.

   ┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ LimitRange                  │ ResourceQuota                            │
   ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ Scope: a single CONTAINER / │ Scope: the entire NAMESPACE (aggregate). │
   │   pod.                      │                                          │
   │ Injects DEFAULT requests &  │ Caps the SUM of requests/limits across   │
   │   limits when a container   │   all pods, plus object COUNTS (pods,    │
   │   omits them.               │   services, pvcs, secrets ...).          │
   │ Sets MIN / MAX bounds per   │ Rejects the request that would push the  │
   │   container.                │   namespace total over its hard cap.     │
   │ "Every pod gets sane        │ "This whole team can't exceed N cpu /    │
   │   defaults and stays in     │   M memory / K pods."                     │
   │   range."                   │                                          │
   └─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Example LimitRange (per-container defaults + bounds) for easypj:

      apiVersion: v1
      kind: LimitRange
      metadata:
        name: easypj-limits
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        limits:
        - type: Container
          default:            # used as the container's LIMIT if unset
            cpu: "500m"
