            memory: "512Mi"
          defaultRequest:     # used as the container's REQUEST if unset
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          min:
            cpu: "50m"
            memory: "64Mi"
          max:
            cpu: "2"
            memory: "2Gi"

  Example ResourceQuota (namespace totals) for easypj:

      apiVersion: v1
      kind: ResourceQuota
      metadata:
        name: easypj-quota
        namespace: easypj
      spec:
        hard:
          requests.cpu: "4"
          requests.memory: 8Gi
          limits.cpu: "8"
          limits.memory: 16Gi
          pods: "20"
          persistentvolumeclaims: "10"

  Imperative quick form:

      kubectl create quota easypj-quota -n easypj \
        --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi,pods=20

  🔧 THE INTERPLAY (why you almost always pair them):

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ If a ResourceQuota constrains requests.cpu / requests.memory, then     │
   │ EVERY pod in that namespace MUST declare those requests — otherwise    │
   │ the quota cannot account for it and the pod is REJECTED.               │
   │                                                                        │
   │ A bare pod (no resources block) would therefore fail ...               │
   │   ...UNLESS a LimitRange is present to INJECT defaultRequest/default.  │
   │                                                                        │
   │ ⇒ LimitRange fills in the blanks → ResourceQuota can then count it.    │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: A too-tight ResourceQuota with NO LimitRange defaults will reject
     every pod that omits requests/limits. The error ("must specify ...") looks
     like a quota bug but the fix is to add a LimitRange. PAIR THEM.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: `kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj -o yaml` shows `status:`
     with used vs hard side by side — you instantly see which resource is
     exhausted instead of guessing why pods are pending/rejected.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.3 PID Limits 🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — PID limit (podPidsLimit): a kubelet-level cap on the number of
     PROCESSES a single pod may create. It protects the NODE from a fork bomb
     or a runaway process loop in one pod consuming the kernel's PID table and
     taking down every other pod on that node.

  Configured on the kubelet (node-level), e.g. in the KubeletConfiguration:

      apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
      kind: KubeletConfiguration
      podPidsLimit: 1024          # max processes per pod on this node

  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: this maps to the cgroup `pids.max` controller for the
     pod's cgroup. When a process in the pod tries to fork past the cap, the
     kernel returns EAGAIN ("Resource temporarily unavailable") to the
     offending pod ONLY — neighbours are unaffected. That blast-radius
     containment is the whole point.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING: a pod whose app logs "fork: retry: Resource temporarily
     unavailable" or "cannot allocate memory" while the node has free RAM is
     very often hitting podPidsLimit, not actual memory pressure.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.4 Topology Spread as Policy 🎯
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  topologySpreadConstraints are normally taught as a SCHEDULING feature, but
  they are equally a GOVERNANCE / reliability control: you are mandating "the
  easypj/jobpost replicas must be EVENLY distributed so no single zone or node
  failure takes them all out."

      spec:
        topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule     # the "policy" teeth
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: jobpost

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ maxSkew=1 across zones, 3 replicas, 3 zones:                           │
   │                                                                        │
   │   zone-a [ pod ]      zone-b [ pod ]      zone-c [ pod ]               │
   │   ▲ even — skew 0/1, all schedule                                      │
   │                                                                        │
   │   vs. piling 3 in one zone → skew 3 > maxSkew 1                        │
   │   whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule ⇒ the lopsided pod stays Pending.   │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION: whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule = HARD policy (refuse to place
     a pod that would violate even spread). ScheduleAnyway = SOFT preference
     (best-effort balance, never block). Use DoNotSchedule when even spread is
     a real reliability requirement, not a nice-to-have.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.5 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) 🎯 🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP): a built-in, IN-CLUSTER
     admission policy that evaluates CEL (Common Expression Language)
     expressions against incoming objects — with NO external webhook to
     deploy, secure, or keep alive. It is the cluster-native answer to "I just
     want one simple validation rule."

  💡 INSIGHT: Before VAP, even a trivial rule like "Deployments must have >= 2
     replicas" meant standing up a validating admission WEBHOOK — a service, a
     TLS cert, a deployment to keep healthy, a single point of failure in the
     admission path. VAP runs the same logic IN-PROCESS in the API server.
     Less to break, nothing to host.

  A VAP has TWO objects: the POLICY (the rule) and the BINDING (where it
  applies + what action to take). Example — require >= 2 replicas, scoped to
  the easypj namespace:

      apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
      kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
      metadata:
        name: require-min-replicas
      spec:
        failurePolicy: Fail
        matchConstraints:
          resourceRules:
          - apiGroups:   ["apps"]
            apiVersions: ["v1"]
            operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
            resources:   ["deployments"]
        validations:
        - expression: "object.spec.replicas >= 2"
          message: "easypj Deployments must have at least 2 replicas"
      ---
      apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
      kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
      metadata:
        name: require-min-replicas-binding
      spec:
        policyName: require-min-replicas
        validationActions: ["Deny"]
        matchResources:
          namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: easypj

  Apply and inspect:

      kubectl apply -f vap.yaml
      kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy
      kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybinding

  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — the CEL object model and richer features:
   • `object`    = the resource being submitted (e.g. object.spec.replicas).
   • `oldObject` = the prior version (on UPDATE) — diff-based rules.
   • `request`   = admission metadata (operation, userInfo, namespace).
   • `params`    = an optional bound PARAMETER resource (a CRD/ConfigMap) so
                   one policy can be parameterised per binding (e.g. a
                   per-namespace minReplicas value).
   • `messageExpression` = a CEL expression that BUILDS the rejection message
                   dynamically (e.g. embed the actual replica count).
   • `variables` = named sub-expressions reused across validations.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: a CEL syntax error, or referencing a field that doesn't exist on
     the object, makes the VAP misbehave (depending on failurePolicy it may
     fail-open or fail-closed). TEST the expression first. failurePolicy: Fail
     means "if evaluation errors, REJECT"; Ignore means "let it through."

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.6 External Engines — OPA Gatekeeper & Kyverno 🏢
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  When the built-in CEL VAP isn't enough — you need MUTATION, GENERATION,
  image verification, or a large library of org-wide policies — you reach for
  a full external policy engine, wired in via admission WEBHOOKS.

   ┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ OPA Gatekeeper          │ Kyverno                                      │
   ├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ Policy language: Rego   │ Policy language: native Kubernetes YAML       │
   │   (Open Policy Agent).  │   (no new DSL to learn).                      │
   │ Authoring model:        │ Authoring model: a single Policy /            │
   │   ConstraintTemplate    │   ClusterPolicy resource with rules.         │
   │   (defines the Rego) +  │                                              │
   │   Constraint (applies    │                                             │
   │   it with params).      │                                              │
   │ Capabilities: VALIDATE, │ Capabilities: VALIDATE, MUTATE, GENERATE,     │
   │   plus mutation.        │   verifyImages — the broadest set.           │
   │ Best when: org already   │ Best when: team wants YAML, fast onboarding, │
   │   knows Rego / wants the │   mutate+generate out of the box.            │
   │   OPA ecosystem.        │                                              │
   └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔧 Both publish results via the PolicyReport CRD (a standardised report of
     what passed/failed), and both register as webhooks in the admission
     chain. Gatekeeper expresses rules in Rego inside ConstraintTemplates and
     can mutate; Kyverno expresses validate/mutate/generate/verifyImages
     directly in YAML rules.

  🧭 PICK BY: team familiarity. Rego shop or existing OPA usage → Gatekeeper.
     "We just want YAML and we need mutate/generate too" → Kyverno. Need
     neither, just one simple native rule → don't install either; use a VAP.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  41.7 The Complete Policy Stack 🧭
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  All of these compose. A single create-pod request must satisfy EVERY layer
  that applies to it; each layer guards a different aspect and they do not
  conflict — they stack.

  ┌──────────────── 📊 THE LAYERED POLICY STACK (easypj namespace) ──────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │   request to create a pod                                                │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │   🛡️  Pod Security Admission    (enforce=restricted: non-root, drop caps)│
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │   🧮  ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL, no webhook: e.g. "replicas >= 2")  │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │   📏  LimitRange                (inject default cpu/mem if missing)      │
  │        ▼                                                                 │
  │   📦  ResourceQuota             (namespace totals not exceeded)          │
  │        ▼  scheduled                                                      │
  │   🧯  NetworkPolicy (who may talk)      🛟  PDB (survive disruptions)    │
  │                                                                          │
  │   🧭 engines: built-in CEL · OPA Gatekeeper (Rego) · Kyverno (YAML).     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 .vs-prose SUMMARY: Read the stack top to bottom. A pod-create request for
     easypj first hits Pod Security Admission, which enforces the restricted
     standard (non-root, all capabilities dropped). If it survives that, the
     ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs its in-cluster CEL rule (e.g. Deployments
     must have at least 2 replicas) — no webhook involved. Next the LimitRange
     quietly INJECTS default cpu/memory requests and limits into any container
     that omitted them, so the request is now fully specified. Only then does
     the ResourceQuota check that adding this pod won't push the namespace over
     its aggregate cpu/memory/object caps. If all admission-time layers pass,
     the pod schedules — and at RUNTIME two more controls take over:
     NetworkPolicy governs who the pod may talk to, and a PodDisruptionBudget
     guarantees a minimum number of replicas survive voluntary disruptions
     like node drains. The engine column reminds you that the CEL rule can be
     built-in, or upgraded to OPA Gatekeeper (Rego) or Kyverno (YAML) when you
     outgrow native CEL.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD / DEEPER — how each layer actually executes
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  • PSA evaluates at ADMISSION using the namespace's pod-security labels: the
    built-in controller inspects the pod's securityContext / capabilities /
    host-namespace fields against the named standard and rejects (enforce),
    warns (warn) or annotates the audit log (audit). It is stateless and runs
    in the API server — nothing to install.

  • CEL expressions in a VAP run IN-PROCESS in the API server. There is no
    network hop, no TLS cert, no external service. The cost is a fast,
    sandboxed expression evaluation per matching request.

  • Gatekeeper / Kyverno hook in via ADMISSION WEBHOOKS — the API server makes
    an outbound call to their service during admission. That gives full power
    (mutate/generate/Rego) at the cost of an external dependency in the
    critical path (hence failurePolicy and timeout tuning matter).

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
    • CEL: variables, built-in functions, and messageExpression for dynamic
      rejection messages; bind PARAM resources so one policy is reused with
      different values per binding.
    • VAP: matchConstraints (resourceRules) define WHAT is matched;
      ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding defines WHERE (namespaceSelector /
      objectSelector) and the validationActions (Deny / Warn / Audit).
    • Gatekeeper: ConstraintTemplates define reusable Rego; Constraints
      instantiate them with parameters; supports mutation.
    • Kyverno: a single ClusterPolicy can validate, mutate, generate and
      verifyImages; results surface as PolicyReport CRDs.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS — Chapter 41
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Policy is LAYERED at admission: PSA (pod security) → ValidatingAdmission-
    Policy (CEL rules, in-cluster, NO webhook) → LimitRange (inject defaults)
    → ResourceQuota (namespace totals) → then NetworkPolicy + PDB at runtime.
  • Pod Security Standards have THREE levels (privileged / baseline /
    restricted) applied in THREE modes (enforce / warn / audit) via namespace
    labels, and can be version-pinned.
  • PSA is per-namespace, does NOT evict running pods, and only checks new/
    updated pods — always roll out warn/audit before enforce.
  • LimitRange sets per-pod/container DEFAULTS and min/max BOUNDS;
    ResourceQuota caps the namespace's TOTAL requests/limits AND object counts.
    They are designed to work together.
  • A ResourceQuota on requests/limits forces every pod to declare them; a
    LimitRange injects defaults so bare pods still schedule under that quota.
  • podPidsLimit bounds processes per pod (via cgroup pids.max) to protect the
    node from fork bombs.
  • topologySpreadConstraints (maxSkew + DoNotSchedule) enforce even
    distribution as a reliability/governance control.
  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs CEL expressions IN-PROCESS (e.g.
    "object.spec.replicas >= 2") — no external webhook to deploy or maintain.
  • External engines add power via webhooks: OPA Gatekeeper = Rego
    (ConstraintTemplates), Kyverno = YAML and also mutate/generate/verifyImages.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS — Chapter 41
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • PSA is per-namespace and doesn't evict already-running pods — only new/
    updated ones are checked.
  • Roll policies out as warn/audit BEFORE enforce, or you instantly block
    legitimate deploys (an outage from a too-strict rollout).
  • CEL syntax errors (or referencing missing fields) make a VAP misbehave;
    test the expression first, and understand failurePolicy Fail vs Ignore.
  • A too-tight ResourceQuota with NO LimitRange defaults rejects pods that
    omit requests/limits — pair them.
  • Not version-pinning the PSS label means a cluster upgrade can silently
    tighten the standard and start rejecting previously-valid pods.
  • Gatekeeper/Kyverno are webhooks in the critical admission path — a down or
    slow webhook with failurePolicy: Fail can block ALL admissions.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS — Chapter 41
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Use a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for simple cluster-native rules before
    reaching for a full Gatekeeper/Kyverno install.
  • LimitRange with default + defaultRequest means pods without resources still
    schedule sanely under a Quota.
  • `kubectl get resourcequota -o yaml` shows used vs hard — instantly see
    what's exhausted.
  • Label a namespace warn + audit at the target PSS level first to preview
    breakage with zero blocking.
  • `kubectl create quota ... --hard=...` is the fastest imperative path to a
    namespace cap in an exam.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 41
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
  kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
                          pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
  kubectl create quota easypj-quota -n easypj --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi,pods=20
  kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj -o yaml        # used vs hard
  kubectl get limitrange -n easypj -o yaml
  kubectl apply -f vap.yaml
  kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy
  kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybinding

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  On the easypj namespace, stack PSA=restricted + a LimitRange (default
  cpu/mem) + a ResourceQuota + the "replicas >= 2" VAP, then try to create a
  1-replica ROOT pod and watch each layer reject or adjust it in turn.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A — Chapter 41 (full answer + explanation each)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Apply the restricted Pod Security Standard to a namespace.
      A. `kubectl label ns easypj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`
         — apply warn/audit first to preview breakage, then enforce. The label
         lives on the NAMESPACE; PSA is built-in, nothing to install.

  Q2. What does a LimitRange do vs a ResourceQuota?
      A. LimitRange sets PER-CONTAINER defaults / min / max (and injects
         defaults into bare containers); ResourceQuota caps the namespace's
         AGGREGATE requests/limits and object counts. Different scope, paired.

  Q3. Create a ResourceQuota capping the namespace.
      A. `kubectl create quota easypj-quota --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi,pods=20 -n
         easypj`. Once it constrains requests/limits, pods must declare them
         within the cap (use a LimitRange to default the ones that don't).

  Q4. What are PID limits for?
      A. podPidsLimit bounds the number of processes per pod (cgroup pids.max)
         to protect the node from fork bombs / runaway process creation, so one
         pod can't exhaust the kernel PID table for its neighbours.

  Q5. Use topology spread as a policy. How?
      A. topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew + topologyKey (e.g. zone) +
         whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule + a labelSelector force even
         distribution across zones/nodes, governing placement as a reliability
         control.

  Q6. Write a VAP that requires >= 2 replicas on Deployments.
      A. A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL `object.spec.replicas >= 2`
         matching apps/v1 deployments on CREATE/UPDATE, plus a
         ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding with validationActions:[Deny] scoped
         to the easypj namespace via namespaceSelector.

  Q7. OPA Gatekeeper vs Kyverno — key difference?
      A. Gatekeeper uses Rego (ConstraintTemplates + Constraints); Kyverno uses
         native YAML policies and ALSO does mutate/generate/verifyImages. Pick
         by team familiarity (Rego shop → Gatekeeper; YAML + mutate → Kyverno).

  Q8. Why warn before enforce?
      A. warn/audit surface violations WITHOUT blocking deploys, so you can fix
         the manifests first, then flip to enforce — avoiding an instant outage
         from a too-strict rollout. PSA also never evicts running pods.

  Q9. Combine multiple policies on one namespace — do they conflict?
      A. No, they COMPOSE: PSA + VAP + LimitRange + Quota + NetworkPolicy + PDB
         each guard a different aspect; a request must satisfy ALL that apply.

  Q10. What is the admission enforcement order?
       A. authN → authZ → MUTATING webhooks → schema validation → VALIDATING
          (PSA / VAP / validating webhooks) → persist. Defaults (LimitRange) are
          applied during admission BEFORE the ResourceQuota is checked, which is
          why a LimitRange lets bare pods pass a quota.

  Q11. A pod is rejected with "must specify cpu" under a quota — why and fix?
       A. The ResourceQuota constrains requests.cpu, so the pod must declare a
          cpu request; it omitted one. Fix by adding a LimitRange with
          defaultRequest.cpu so the omitted value is injected automatically.

  Q12. How do you stop a cluster upgrade from silently tightening PSS?
       A. Version-pin the label, e.g.
          pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.31, so the standard is
          evaluated at a fixed version regardless of the cluster's upgrade.

  📊 VISUAL SUMMARY: the layered policy stack over easypj — PSA → VAP →
     LimitRange → ResourceQuota at admission, then NetworkPolicy + PDB at
     runtime, with built-in CEL / Gatekeeper / Kyverno as the rule engines.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  Chapter 42: Admission Webhooks & API Extension                        🔴 🏢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  META: 🔴 Hard · ⏱️ ~2h · 🏢 Beyond-exam (the machinery under policy).
        The dynamic-admission engine that mutates and validates EVERY write
        to the API server, plus the ways you extend the API surface itself.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Every object you ever applied to easypj — every Deployment, Service,
  PVC, NetworkPolicy — was inspected, possibly rewritten, and either
  accepted or rejected before it ever touched etcd. That inspection layer
  is dynamic admission control: mutating webhooks that MODIFY a request,
  then validating webhooks that ACCEPT or REJECT it. Service meshes inject
  their sidecar here. Policy engines (Gatekeeper, Kyverno) enforce "no
  :latest", "must have resource limits", "registry allowlist" here. And the
  same machinery, misconfigured, can WEDGE a whole cluster — a webhook with
  failurePolicy:Fail whose backing pod is down will reject the very
  requests you'd use to fix it. Understanding this engine is the difference
  between "the cluster mysteriously rejects everything" being a 4-hour
  outage or a 2-minute `kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration`.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  OBJECTIVES
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Distinguish mutating vs validating webhooks: order, purpose, and the
    shared AdmissionReview request/response JSON.
  • Trace the full admission flow: authN → authZ → mutating → schema →
    validating → persist.
  • Configure and reason about failurePolicy (Fail vs Ignore), TLS, and
    caBundle — and recover a wedged cluster.
  • Extend the kubectl CLI itself with plugins via krew (ctx, ns, neat,
    tree, who-can).
  • Recap API aggregation (APIService) vs CRDs as ways to extend the API
    surface.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🎯 Mostly Day-2 / beyond-exam depth — the CKA rarely asks you to author a
     webhook from scratch. BUT: recognizing a webhook-induced outage and
     knowing the emergency `kubectl delete ...webhookconfiguration` recovery
     is genuinely useful, and `kubectl get apiservices` / krew tooling speed
     you up. Treat this chapter as the "what's really happening" layer
     beneath PSA, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, LimitRange and ResourceQuota.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SECTION MAP
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  42.1 Mutating vs Validating Webhooks 🏢 — order, purpose, AdmissionReview.
  42.2 The Admission Flow 🏢 — authN → authZ → mutating → schema →
       validating → persist.
  42.3 Failure Policy & TLS 🏢 — Fail vs Ignore; caBundle; timeouts.
  42.4 kubectl Plugins & krew 🏢 — extend the CLI (ctx, ns, neat, tree,
       who-can).
  42.5 API Aggregation (recap) 🔧 — apiservices; extending the API surface.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  42.1  Mutating vs Validating Webhooks                                  🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Dynamic admission control hooks the API server out to YOUR HTTP endpoints
  at write time. There are two kinds, registered by two configuration
  objects, and they run in a fixed order:

  📖 KEY TERM — MutatingWebhookConfiguration: registers webhook endpoints
     that may CHANGE the incoming object (via a JSON Patch) before it is
     stored. Examples: inject an Envoy/Istio sidecar, set a default
     securityContext, add labels/annotations, set defaults the schema can't.

  📖 KEY TERM — ValidatingWebhookConfiguration: registers endpoints that may
     only say YES or NO. They CANNOT change the object. Examples: reject
     :latest images, reject images from non-allowlisted registries, require
     resource limits. Gatekeeper and Kyverno are validating-webhook engines.

  ┌──────────────────────── MUTATING vs VALIDATING ────────────────────────┐
  │                  MUTATING WEBHOOK        │   VALIDATING WEBHOOK         │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────── │
  │ Config object  MutatingWebhook-          │  ValidatingWebhook-          │
  │                Configuration             │  Configuration               │
  │ Can change?    ✅ YES (returns a patch)  │  ❌ NO (accept / reject only)│
  │ Runs           FIRST                     │  AFTER mutating + schema     │
  │ Typical use    sidecar inject, defaults  │  policy enforcement, deny    │
  │ Response       allowed + patch +         │  allowed + status message    │
  │                patchType: JSONPatch      │  (no patch)                  │
  │ Engines        Istio/Linkerd injector,   │  OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno     │
  │                cert-manager              │                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT — why mutating runs BEFORE validating: a mutating webhook may
  add the very field a validating webhook checks for. If a sidecar injector
  adds a container, and a validating policy requires every container to have
  limits, validation must see the FINAL (mutated) object — otherwise you'd
  validate something that won't actually be stored. So the pipeline mutates
  to a final shape, THEN validates that shape, THEN persists.

  📖 KEY TERM — AdmissionReview: the single JSON envelope both webhook types
  speak. The API server POSTs an AdmissionReview REQUEST to your webhook;
  your webhook returns an AdmissionReview RESPONSE.

  [ADMISSIONREVIEW — request the apiserver sends to a webhook]

   {
     "apiVersion": "admission.k8s.io/v1",
     "kind": "AdmissionReview",
     "request": {
       "uid": "705ab...c3",            ← echo this back in the response
       "operation": "CREATE",          ← CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE / CONNECT
       "userInfo": { "username": "easypj-deployer", "groups": [...] },
       "resource": { "group":"", "version":"v1", "resource":"pods" },
       "object":    { ...the new object... },
       "oldObject": null,              ← populated on UPDATE/DELETE
       "dryRun":    false
     }
   }

  [ADMISSIONREVIEW — response a MUTATING webhook returns]

   {
     "apiVersion": "admission.k8s.io/v1",
     "kind": "AdmissionReview",
     "response": {
       "uid": "705ab...c3",            ← MUST match the request uid
       "allowed": true,
       "patchType": "JSONPatch",
       "patch": "<base64 of a JSON-Patch array>"   ← e.g. add a sidecar
     }
   }

  [ADMISSIONREVIEW — response a VALIDATING webhook returns]

   {
     "apiVersion": "admission.k8s.io/v1",
     "kind": "AdmissionReview",
     "response": {
       "uid": "705ab...c3",
       "allowed": false,               ← reject
       "status": {
         "code": 403,
         "message": "image must not use the :latest tag"
       }
     }
   }

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — the patch a mutating webhook returns is a base64-
  encoded RFC-6902 JSON Patch array, e.g.:
   [ { "op":"add",
       "path":"/spec/containers/-",
       "value": { "name":"envoy", "image":"envoy:v1.30", ... } } ]
  The API server decodes it, applies it to the object, and the patched
  object continues down the pipeline.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  42.2  The Admission Flow                                               🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Every write request (CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE) the API server receives walks
  the SAME chain. Reads (GET/LIST/WATCH) skip admission entirely.

  [ADMISSION WEBHOOKS — mutate THEN validate]

   request ─► authN ─► authZ
        ▼
   🔧 MutatingWebhookConfiguration   (can MODIFY: inject sidecar, set defaults)
        ▼
   📋 schema validation
        ▼
   ✅ ValidatingWebhookConfiguration (accept / REJECT only)
        ▼
   🗄️ persist in etcd
   ⚠️ failurePolicy: Fail + webhook DOWN ⇒ requests blocked (can wedge the
      cluster). Webhooks need TLS + caBundle.
   🧰 kubectl plugins (krew): ctx · ns · neat · tree · who-can.

  [THE FULL ADMISSION PIPELINE — annotated]

   ┌──────────┐   who are you?        ┌──────────┐   are you allowed?
   │  authN   │ ────────────────────► │  authZ   │ ──────────────────►
   └──────────┘  (certs, tokens,      └──────────┘  (RBAC / Node / ABAC
                  OIDC, webhook)                      / webhook)
                                                          │
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐  built-in mutating plugins (e.g.
   │  MUTATING admission           │  DefaultStorageClass, ServiceAccount)
   │  • built-in plugins           │  run, THEN your registered
   │  • MutatingWebhookConfig(s)   │  MutatingWebhookConfigurations.
   └──────────────────────────────┘  Object may be REWRITTEN here.
        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐  decode → validate against the
   │  OBJECT SCHEMA VALIDATION     │  OpenAPI schema / CRD structural
   │  (+ defaulting)               │  schema. Bad fields rejected here.
   └──────────────────────────────┘
        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐  built-in validating plugins
   │  VALIDATING admission         │  (ResourceQuota, PodSecurity / PSA,
   │  • built-in plugins           │  LimitRanger checks), then
   │  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy  │  ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL),
   │  • ValidatingWebhookConfig(s) │  then your validating webhooks.
   └──────────────────────────────┘  Accept / REJECT only — no changes.
        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │  PERSIST to etcd 🗄️           │  only now is the object durable.
   └──────────────────────────────┘

  💡 ANALOGY (🧠): admission is airport security. authN = passport check
  (who you are). authZ = boarding pass check (are you allowed on this
  flight). Mutating = the agent who makes you take off your belt and put
  your laptop in a bin (they REARRANGE your stuff). Schema check = the
  scanner that only understands certain shapes. Validating = the final
  officer who can wave you through or pull you aside — but can't repack your
  bag. Only after all of it do you reach the gate (etcd).

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — ordering nuances:
  • Built-in admission controllers (compiled into the apiserver, enabled
    via --enable-admission-plugins) run AROUND the webhooks: built-in
    mutators first, then mutating webhooks; built-in validators, VAP, then
    validating webhooks.
  • reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded — if a LATER mutating webhook changes the
    object, earlier mutating webhooks may be re-invoked so they can react to
    the change. (Default Never means each mutating webhook is called once.)
  • matchPolicy: Equivalent (default) vs Exact — Equivalent matches a
    resource even when the client used a different but equivalent API
    version (e.g. apps/v1beta1 vs apps/v1); Exact matches only the literal
    group/version/resource you listed. Equivalent is almost always what you
    want so version skew doesn't silently bypass your webhook.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond) — selectors and dry-run:
  • namespaceSelector / objectSelector — scope WHICH objects the webhook
    sees. Use a namespaceSelector to EXCLUDE kube-system so a broken webhook
    can't lock out control-plane components.
  • sideEffects — declare whether the webhook mutates external state. Values:
    None, NoneOnDryRun, Some (deprecated), Unknown. If you don't declare
    None/NoneOnDryRun, `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` and `kubectl diff`
    break, because the API server won't call a webhook that might cause real
    side effects during a dry run.
  • timeoutSeconds (default 10, max 30) — how long the apiserver waits for
    the webhook before applying failurePolicy.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  42.3  Failure Policy & TLS                                            🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  A webhook is an out-of-process HTTP service. It can be slow, down, or
  unreachable. failurePolicy tells the API server what to do then.

  ┌─────────────────────── failurePolicy DECISION ────────────────────────┐
  │  webhook unreachable / times out / errors ...                          │
  │                                                                        │
  │   failurePolicy: Fail   ──►  REJECT the request  (default; safe-by-    │
  │                              default for SECURITY policies)            │
  │                                                                        │
  │   failurePolicy: Ignore ──►  ALLOW the request   (availability-by-     │
  │                              default; webhook is "best effort")        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — Fail or Ignore?
   ┌─ Is the webhook enforcing a SECURITY/COMPLIANCE invariant
   │   that MUST hold (e.g. block privileged pods)?
   │     ├─ YES ─► failurePolicy: Fail  (better to block than to leak),
   │     │        BUT scope it tightly (objectSelector / namespaceSelector)
   │     │        and EXCLUDE kube-system so you can still recover.
   │     └─ NO, it's a convenience/defaulting/injection nicety?
   │              └─► failurePolicy: Ignore  (don't let it wedge writes).
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ⚠️ THE CLASSIC WEDGE: failurePolicy:Fail + a broadly-scoped webhook +
  its backing pod is Pending/CrashLoopBackOff = EVERY matching CREATE/UPDATE
  is rejected, including attempts to scale up or fix the webhook's own
  Deployment. The cluster appears "frozen". Recovery is to DELETE the
  offending webhook configuration (see commands), then redeploy it.

  TLS & caBundle
  ──────────────
  The API server calls webhooks over HTTPS ONLY. It must trust the
  webhook's serving certificate. The clientConfig of each webhook carries a
  caBundle (base64 CA cert) the apiserver uses to verify the webhook's TLS
  cert.

  [WEBHOOK clientConfig — service-backed]

   webhooks:
   - name: inject.easypj.example.com
     clientConfig:
       service:
         name: easypj-injector
         namespace: easypj-system
         path: /mutate
         port: 443
       caBundle: <base64 CA cert>      ← apiserver trusts certs signed by this
     rules:
     - apiGroups:   [""]
       apiVersions: ["v1"]
       operations:  ["CREATE"]
       resources:   ["pods"]
     namespaceSelector:                ← scope: only easypj namespaces
       matchLabels: { easypj-injection: enabled }
     failurePolicy: Ignore             ← don't wedge pod creation if down
     sideEffects: None
     admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
     timeoutSeconds: 5

  ⚠️ GOTCHA — caBundle rotation: when the webhook's serving cert is rotated,
  the caBundle must still chain to it. cert-manager's ca-injector or a
  controller usually keeps caBundle in sync. A stale caBundle → TLS
  handshake failure → with failurePolicy:Fail, requests blocked.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING — webhook symptoms:
   • "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" in apiserver logs
     → caBundle wrong/stale, or cert rotated without updating caBundle.
   • "context deadline exceeded" / "i/o timeout"
     → webhook slow or unreachable; check the Service/Endpoints and the
       webhook pod. failurePolicy decides allow vs reject.
   • Everything suddenly rejected → list webhook configs, find the culprit.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  42.4  kubectl Plugins & krew                                          🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  You can extend kubectl ITSELF. Any executable on your PATH named
  `kubectl-foo` becomes the subcommand `kubectl foo`. krew is the plugin
  MANAGER that installs and updates these for you.

  📖 KEY TERM — krew: the package manager for kubectl plugins. Installs
  plugins into ~/.krew/bin (add it to PATH). `kubectl krew install <name>`.

  ┌──────────────────────── HIGH-VALUE krew PLUGINS ───────────────────────┐
  │ ctx       │ switch kube-context fast            kubectl ctx prod        │
  │ ns        │ switch current namespace fast       kubectl ns easypj       │
  │ neat      │ strip managedFields/status noise    kubectl neat -f po.yaml │
  │ tree      │ show ownership tree (Deploy→RS→Pod) kubectl tree deploy web │
  │ who-can   │ reverse-RBAC: who can do X          kubectl who-can get pods│
  │ access-   │ show what the CURRENT user can do   kubectl access-matrix   │
  │  matrix   │                                                            │
  │ stern     │ multi-pod log tailing               stern easypj-web        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT — `neat` is a lifesaver in exams/audits: it turns a
  server-fetched object back into something you can re-apply, dropping
  status, managedFields, creationTimestamp, resourceVersion, uid, etc.
  `tree` instantly answers "what owns this pod?". `who-can`/`access-matrix`
  reverse RBAC — instead of "what can this subject do?", they ask "who can
  do THIS?".

  🏢 Plugins are CLIENT-side only — they run on your machine, not in the
  cluster. They are never required by the CKA but they shave real seconds.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  42.5  API Aggregation (recap)                                         🔧
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Webhooks extend BEHAVIOR on existing types. To add NEW types or NEW API
  surface, you have two tools — and it's a common exam-adjacent distinction:

  ┌──────────────────── CRD vs API AGGREGATION ───────────────────────────┐
  │                 CRD                       │   API AGGREGATION          │
  │ ───────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────── │
  │ What         a new declarative TYPE        │  a SECOND apiserver        │
  │              (kind), stored by K8s in etcd │  registered behind the     │
  │              for you                       │  main apiserver            │
  │ Object       CustomResourceDefinition      │  APIService (+ a Service   │
  │                                            │  pointing at your server)  │
  │ Storage      etcd (K8s manages it)         │  YOUR backend (any store)  │
  │ Custom logic │ via a separate controller   │  built INTO the aggregated │
  │              │ watching the CR             │  apiserver (full control)  │
  │ Examples     Certificate (cert-manager),   │  metrics-server            │
  │              CronTab, your easypj CRDs     │  (metrics.k8s.io),         │
  │                                            │  custom-metrics adapters   │
  │ Effort       low — just YAML               │  high — write & run a      │
  │                                            │  whole apiserver           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

  [API AGGREGATION — request routing]

      kubectl get pods.metrics.k8s.io
            │
            ▼
   ┌───────────────────┐  group not built-in? look up APIService.
   │  kube-apiserver    │  metrics.k8s.io → registered to a Service
   │  (aggregator)      │ ─────────────────────────────────────────►
   └───────────────────┘                                            │
                                                                     ▼
                                                    ┌────────────────────────┐
                                                    │  metrics-server         │
                                                    │  (aggregated apiserver) │
                                                    │  serves metrics.k8s.io  │
                                                    └────────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — `kubectl get apiservices` lists every API group and
  whether it is Local (built-in) or backed by a Service (aggregated). A
  metrics-server that's down shows its APIService as not Available, which is
  why `kubectl top` fails — the aggregation layer can't reach the backend.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — extending the API:
   • Just need a new declarative object + a controller?  → CRD.
   • Need custom storage, on-the-fly computed values, or
     a different backend (like live metrics)?           → Aggregation.
   • Need to change/validate EXISTING objects at write?  → Webhooks (42.1).
   • Just want lighter-weight cluster-side validation?   → CRD validation
     schema + ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL), no webhook pod to run.


  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / DEEPER
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • The AdmissionReview request carries object, oldObject, operation, and
    userInfo; the response carries allowed, an optional base64 JSON-Patch
    (mutating only), and a status message. The response uid MUST equal the
    request uid or the apiserver errors.
  • Mutating runs before validating so the FINAL mutated object is what gets
    validated and persisted.
  • matchPolicy: Equivalent vs Exact controls whether version-equivalent
    resources are matched. reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded re-runs mutating
    webhooks when a later webhook changed the object.
  • objectSelector / namespaceSelector scope a webhook — essential to keep
    it off kube-system. sideEffects + dryRun support keep `--dry-run` and
    `diff` working. timeoutSeconds (≤30) bounds the wait before failurePolicy.
  • caBundle rotation must track the webhook's serving cert.
  • TRADE-OFF — webhook vs ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP): VAP runs CEL
    expressions INSIDE the apiserver — no pod to keep alive, no TLS to
    rotate, no failurePolicy-wedge risk for the common validation cases.
    Prefer VAP for validation you can express in CEL; reach for a webhook
    only when you need external data, mutation, or logic CEL can't express.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • The admission chain: authN → authZ → MUTATING webhooks → schema
    validation → VALIDATING webhooks → persist. Mutating runs BEFORE
    validating so the final (mutated) object is what gets validated.
  • Mutating webhooks MODIFY objects (inject sidecars, set defaults);
    validating webhooks only ACCEPT or REJECT. Both speak the AdmissionReview
    request/response JSON, and the response uid must echo the request uid.
  • failurePolicy decides what happens when the webhook is unreachable: Fail
    (block the request) or Ignore (allow it). Fail + a down webhook can wedge
    the whole cluster.
  • Webhooks require TLS with a caBundle the apiserver trusts. Reads skip
    admission; only writes (CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE) walk the chain.
  • Prefer ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL, in-apiserver) over a validating
    webhook when you can — no pod, no TLS, no wedge risk.
  • krew extends kubectl ITSELF (ctx, ns, neat, tree, who-can) — client-side
    convenience, never required by the exam.
  • Extend the API: CRD = new type stored by K8s (+ a controller);
    aggregation = a separate apiserver behind an APIService (e.g.
    metrics-server). Webhooks change/validate EXISTING objects.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • failurePolicy: Fail + the webhook pod down = every matching request is
    rejected — including the ones you'd use to fix it. Scope match narrowly
    and consider Ignore for non-critical webhooks.
  • A stale/incorrect caBundle (cert rotation) breaks the webhook with TLS
    "certificate signed by unknown authority" errors.
  • Webhook ORDER matters: a mutating webhook's output feeds validation;
    design for it (and reinvocationPolicy if webhooks chain).
  • Webhooks that don't declare sideEffects/dryRun support break
    `--dry-run=server` and `kubectl diff`.
  • A webhook NOT excluding kube-system can lock out control-plane writes —
    always namespaceSelector-exclude system namespaces.
  • A down metrics-server makes its APIService not Available, which is why
    `kubectl top` fails — that's the aggregation layer, not a webhook.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • If the cluster suddenly rejects everything, suspect a webhook:
    `kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations`
    and delete/fix the offender.
  • Prefer ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) over a validating webhook when you
    can — no pod to keep alive, no TLS to rotate.
  • Use namespaceSelector/objectSelector to scope a webhook so it can't
    affect kube-system and lock you out.
  • `kubectl get apiservices | grep -v Local` finds the aggregated APIs fast;
    a `False`/not-Available row points at a down backend.
  • `kubectl neat` before saving an object you fetched, so it re-applies
    cleanly; `kubectl tree` to see what owns a pod.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
  kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
  kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration <name> -o yaml      # inspect rules
  kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <bad-one>      # emergency unwedge
  kubectl delete mutatingwebhookconfiguration <bad-one>        # emergency unwedge
  kubectl get apiservices                                      # aggregation layer
  kubectl get apiservices | grep -v Local                      # only aggregated
  kubectl krew install ns ctx neat tree who-can
  kubectl ctx prod ; kubectl ns easypj                         # fast switching
  kubectl tree deployment easypj-web                           # ownership tree
  kubectl who-can create pods -n easypj                        # reverse RBAC
  kubectl neat -f pod.yaml                                     # strip noise

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Trace a pod-create request through the admission chain (authN → authZ →
  mutating → schema → validating → persist), then simulate a down webhook
  with failurePolicy:Fail and recover by deleting the configuration.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A (10)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Mutating vs validating webhook — purpose of each?
      A. Mutating MODIFIES the object (defaults, sidecar injection);
         validating only ACCEPTS or REJECTS it. Mutating runs first because
         validation must see the final (mutated) object.

  Q2. Give the full admission order.
      A. authN → authZ → mutating webhooks → schema validation → validating
         webhooks (and PSA/VAP) → persist to etcd. Reads skip admission.

  Q3. What does failurePolicy: Fail do when the webhook is down?
      A. Matching requests are REJECTED (blocked). Ignore would let them
         through. Fail can wedge the cluster if the webhook is broadly
         scoped — including the requests you'd use to fix it.

  Q4. Why do webhooks need TLS/caBundle?
      A. The apiserver calls the webhook over HTTPS and must trust its cert;
         the caBundle in the configuration validates the webhook's server
         certificate. A stale caBundle after cert rotation breaks it.

  Q5. The cluster rejects all creates after a webhook broke. Recovery?
      A. List the webhook configs, then delete/fix the offending
         Validating/MutatingWebhookConfiguration (or restore its webhook pod
         / caBundle):
         kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations
         kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <bad-one>

  Q6. What is krew and give two useful plugins.
      A. krew is the kubectl plugin manager; e.g. `ctx`/`ns` (fast context/
         namespace switching) and `who-can`/`neat`/`tree`. Plugins are any
         executable on PATH named `kubectl-<x>`, runnable as `kubectl <x>`.

  Q7. CRD vs API aggregation — recap the distinction.
      A. A CRD adds declarative types stored by K8s in etcd (paired with a
         controller); aggregation registers a SEPARATE apiserver via an
         APIService for custom logic/storage (e.g. metrics-server serving
         metrics.k8s.io).

  Q8. What's in an AdmissionReview?
      A. The REQUEST (object, oldObject, operation, userInfo, uid, dryRun)
         the apiserver sends to the webhook, and the RESPONSE (allowed, the
         echoed uid, an optional base64 JSON-Patch for mutating, and a status
         message).

  Q9. Give an example of a mutating webhook in practice.
      A. A service-mesh injector (Istio/Linkerd) adding an Envoy sidecar to
         every pod in labeled namespaces, or defaulting securityContext/
         labels on creation.

  Q10. Give an example of a validating webhook in practice.
      A. Rejecting pods using :latest images or images from non-allowlisted
         registries — exactly what OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno enforce. (Many
         such checks can now move to ValidatingAdmissionPolicy/CEL instead.)

  VISUAL SUMMARY: a request flowing through the admission chain.
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  📋 .vs-prose — A write to easypj enters at the left as a raw API request.
  authN confirms WHO is calling, authZ confirms they're ALLOWED. Then the
  request hits MUTATING admission, where built-in mutators and your
  MutatingWebhookConfigurations may rewrite it — injecting sidecars or
  setting defaults. The rewritten object is checked against its SCHEMA, then
  passed to VALIDATING admission (built-in checks, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
  CEL rules, and your ValidatingWebhookConfigurations) which can only accept
  or reject. Survive all of that and the object is PERSISTED to etcd. The
  danger spot: any webhook with failurePolicy:Fail whose pod is down rejects
  every matching request — scope webhooks narrowly, exclude kube-system, and
  know the emergency `kubectl delete ...webhookconfiguration` unwedge.


  ┌──────────────────────── PART 12 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Security is layered: infra -> authN/Z -> admission -> workload ->      │
  │    network -> data; harden each.                                        │
  │ ✅ Enforce automatically: PSS (namespace labels), ValidatingAdmission-   │
  │    Policy (CEL, no webhook), OPA Gatekeeper/Kyverno (webhook engines).   │
  │ ✅ Resource governance: LimitRange (per-pod) + ResourceQuota (ns total). │
  │ ✅ Webhooks: mutating runs before validating; failurePolicy=Fail can     │
  │    lock the cluster if the webhook is down.                             │
  │ 🎯 EXAM: PSS, LimitRange, ResourceQuota appear; the rest is Day-2 depth. │
  │ 🔑 label ns pod-security · ValidatingAdmissionPolicy · get quota/limits  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  [PART 12 VISUAL SUMMARY]: the policy & admission engine guarding easypj.
  📋 .vs-prose — Part 12 hands easypj a layered guard: PodSecurity Standards
  set a baseline by namespace label; ValidatingAdmissionPolicy enforces CEL
  rules right inside the apiserver with no pod to babysit; Gatekeeper/Kyverno
  add webhook-powered policy; LimitRange caps each pod and ResourceQuota caps
  the namespace total. Beneath them all runs the admission engine of this
  chapter — mutate, then validate, then persist — the machinery every one of
  those policies plugs into.

  [PART 13 INTRO]
  Passing the exam means you CAN operate a cluster; SRE practice means you
  operate it WELL. This part goes beyond `kubectl top`: a real observability
  stack (the three pillars), alerting and SLOs, and the multi-cluster /
  capacity / cost concerns of running easypj at scale.

  Up to this point the guide has been mostly about MAKING easypj run on
  Kubernetes — Pods scheduled, Services routed, Ingress terminated, storage
  bound, RBAC enforced. Day-2 SRE is the discipline of KEEPING it running,
  and proving — with numbers — that it is healthy. The two chapters here
  answer two different questions:

    Ch43 — "Is easypj healthy RIGHT NOW, and how do I know BEFORE my users
            do?"  (observability: metrics, logs, traces, alerts, SLOs)
    Ch44 — "How do I run easypj like this across many clusters and regions
            without going broke?"  (multi-cluster, capacity, cost)

  🧠 ANALOGY  Observability is the difference between a smoke detector and a
     security camera. `kubectl get pods` (a green "Running") is the smoke
     detector — it tells you something is on fire only once flames are
     visible. A real observability stack is the camera + motion sensor +
     thermostat: it shows you the room heating up, names the corner it
     started in, and pages you while the fire is still a spark.

  📖 KEY TERM — Observability  The property of a system that lets you ask
     ARBITRARY questions about its internal state from the OUTSIDE, using
     only the signals it emits, WITHOUT shipping new code to add a probe.
     Contrast with "monitoring," which watches a PRE-DEFINED set of checks.
     You monitor for the failures you predicted; you need observability for
     the ones you didn't.

  📖 KEY TERM — Day-2 operations  "Day 0" is design, "Day 1" is install/
     deploy, "Day 2" is everything after: upgrades, scaling, incident
     response, capacity planning, cost control. Most of a cluster's life —
     and most of its risk — lives in Day 2.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  [THE THREE PILLARS — at a glance]
  Observability rests on three complementary signal types. None is a
  superset of the others; you correlate across all three during an incident.

  ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
  │ PILLAR       │ ANSWERS THE QUESTION       │ TYPICAL TOOL (in this guide) │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
  │ 📊 Metrics   │ "Is something wrong, and   │ Prometheus + Grafana         │
  │              │  HOW wrong?" (rates,       │ (scrapes /metrics, stores    │
  │              │  latencies, error %, RPS)  │  time-series, alerts)        │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
  │ 📜 Logs      │ "WHAT exactly happened on  │ Loki / Elasticsearch +       │
  │              │  THIS request?" (discrete  │ Fluent Bit (ships container  │
  │              │  events, stack traces)     │  stdout/stderr)              │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
  │ 🔗 Traces    │ "WHERE in the request path │ Jaeger / Tempo via           │
  │              │  did the time / error go?" │ OpenTelemetry (spans across  │
  │              │  (spans across services)   │  service hops)               │
  └──────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT  Metrics tell you a problem EXISTS and is getting worse; logs
     tell you WHAT broke on a specific request; traces tell you WHERE in the
     chain (which hop, which dependency) the time or the error was spent. An
     incident is usually solved by starting at a metric alert, jumping to the
     trace of a slow request, then drilling to the log line at the failing
     span. Build all three so the jump is one click, not one ticket.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 13 map]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch43 OBSERVE WELL (metrics/logs/traces/alerts/SLOs) ─▶ Ch44 OPERATE     │
  │                                                  AT SCALE (multi/cost)   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Expanded, the day-2 loop these chapters wire up looks like this:

        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                                              │
        │   easypj Pods                                                │
        │   (Django + gunicorn)                                        │
        │      │  emits                                                │
        │      ├──▶ /metrics  ──▶  📊 Prometheus  ──┐                  │
        │      ├──▶ stdout    ──▶  📜 Loki         ──┼─▶ 📈 Grafana    │
        │      └──▶ OTLP spans ─▶  🔗 Jaeger/Tempo ─┘   (dashboards)   │
        │                                  │                           │
        │                                  ▼                           │
        │                          ⏰ Alertmanager                     │
        │                          (SLO burn-rate rules)               │
        │                                  │                           │
        │                                  ▼                           │
        │                          📟 on-call / PagerDuty              │
        │                                  │                           │
        │                                  ▼                           │
