        │                                                              │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [PART 13 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  Implementation thread: instrument easypj with Prometheus metrics + Grafana
  dashboards + alerts on SLOs (latency/error rate), then reason about running
  it across clusters/regions within a budget.

  Concretely, by the end of this part you will have wired easypj so that:

    • The jobpost app exposes a /metrics endpoint (request count, request
      latency histogram, DB query time, 5xx rate) scraped by Prometheus on a
      ServiceMonitor.
    • Grafana shows a "easypj golden-signals" dashboard: traffic, errors,
      latency (p50/p95/p99), and saturation (CPU/memory vs. requests/limits).
    • Container stdout/stderr from every easypj Pod is shipped to a central
      log store, queryable by Pod, namespace, and request ID.
    • An SLO is declared (e.g. "99.9% of jobpost requests succeed in <300ms
      over 30 days") and an alert fires on the ERROR-BUDGET BURN RATE — not on
      every transient blip — so on-call is paged for real degradation only.
    • You can reason about running this same stack across multiple clusters
      and regions, and about where the money goes (compute, storage, egress,
      observability overhead) so the bill stays inside budget.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which pillar do I reach for?
     ┌────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
     │ "Users say easypj is slow."        │ → 📊 metrics: latency p95/p99 │
     │ "ONE user's job post 500'd."       │ → 📜 logs: filter by request  │
     │ "Requests slow but CPU is fine."   │ → 🔗 traces: find the slow hop│
     │ "Will we run out of nodes Friday?" │ → 📊 metrics + Ch44 capacity  │
     │ "Why did last month's bill spike?" │ → Ch44 cost attribution       │
     └────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA  `kubectl top` needs metrics-server installed and gives you ONLY
     the most recent CPU/memory sample — no history, no latency, no error
     rate. It is a flashlight, not a dashboard. The exam may use it; do not
     mistake it for an observability stack.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA  Observability is not free. A naive Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger
     stack can consume more CPU, memory, and storage than the app it watches.
     Cardinality (every unique label combination = a new time-series) is the
     usual culprit. Ch44 treats the observability stack itself as a cost line.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP  In an interview or an incident, name the four GOLDEN SIGNALS
     in order — Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation — then map each to a
     metric on the easypj dashboard. It signals you think in SRE terms, not
     just "is the Pod Running."

  🔑 MUST-REMEMBER  These two chapters are 🏢 beyond-exam. They will NOT be
     graded on the CKA, but they are exactly what separates someone who
     PASSED the exam from someone who can be TRUSTED with production easypj.
     Read them as the bridge from certification to the on-call rotation.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Chapter 43: Observability — Metrics, Logs, Traces, Alerts            🔴 🏢
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  META: 🔴 Hard · ⏱️ ~2.5h · 🏢 Beyond-exam (the SRE toolkit, but failing
        scenarios on the CKA lean on `kubectl logs`/`top`/`describe`, so the
        fundamentals here ARE exam-relevant).

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHY THIS MATTERS                                                           │
  │   You cannot operate what you cannot see. When easypj starts returning     │
  │   500s on /jobs/, or page loads crawl, or a pod silently CrashLoops, the   │
  │   difference between a five-minute fix and a five-hour outage is whether   │
  │   you have METRICS to spot it, LOGS to read it, TRACES to localize it, and │
  │   ALERTS to wake you before the user does. Observability is how you turn   │
  │   "the site feels slow" into "the db query in the JobPost list view jumped │
  │   from 8ms to 900ms at 14:03 when the Skills join lost its index."         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧠 ANALOGY: a car dashboard. METRICS are the gauges (speed, RPM, fuel,
     temperature) — always-on numbers that tell you "how much / how fast / how
     hot." LOGS are the event recorder — "at 14:03 the check-engine light came
     on." TRACES are the trip computer breaking the journey into legs — "you
     spent 40 min on the highway, 5 min at the gas station, 20 min in traffic"
     so you know WHERE the time went. ALERTS are the warning chimes that fire
     when a gauge crosses a line you care about.

  OBJECTIVES
    • Understand the observability stack and the three pillars.
    • Prometheus & PromQL basics — pull model, exporters, ServiceMonitor.
    • Build Grafana dashboards around easypj using RED/USE.
    • Alerting & SLO/SLI/error budgets — alert on symptoms, not causes.
    • Tracing overview with OpenTelemetry — follow a /jobs/ request.

  CKA RELEVANCE
    🎯 The exam will not ask you to write PromQL, but it relies heavily on the
       built-in observability primitives: `kubectl logs` (incl. `--previous`
       and `-f`), `kubectl top pods/nodes` (needs metrics-server), `kubectl
       describe` (Events!), and `kubectl get events`. Knowing the bigger
       picture — what a sidecar log shipper, metrics-server, and a probe each
       do — makes the troubleshooting domain (30% of the exam) far easier.

  SECTION MAP
    43.1 The Three Pillars — metrics vs logs vs traces; what each answers.
    43.2 Prometheus — pull model; exporters; ServiceMonitor; basic PromQL on
         easypj (request rate, error rate, p95 latency).
    43.3 Grafana — dashboards; key easypj panels (RED/USE methods).
    43.4 Alerting & SLOs — Alertmanager; SLI/SLO/error budget; alert on
         symptoms not causes.
    43.5 Tracing — OpenTelemetry; following a /jobs/ request across services.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  43.1  The Three Pillars 🏢
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — Observability: the property of a system that lets you ask
     ARBITRARY questions about its internal state from the OUTSIDE, without
     shipping new code. Monitoring answers known questions ("is CPU high?");
     observability lets you answer unknown ones ("why is THIS user's /jobs/
     request slow, only on Tuesdays, only on node-3?").

  Three signal types — three different questions about easypj in production:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  THE THREE PILLARS — observe easypj in production                          │
  │                                                                            │
  │   📈 METRICS (Prometheus)   what & how much?   rate · p95 latency · err %  │
  │       └─ numeric, time-series, cheap to store, great for trends & alerts   │
  │                                                                            │
  │   📜 LOGS   (Loki / EFK)    what happened?      structured stdout/stderr   │
  │       └─ discrete events, high detail, expensive at scale, great for "why" │
  │                                                                            │
  │   🔗 TRACES (OpenTelemetry) where's the time?   a /jobs/ request, end-end  │
  │       └─ one request stitched across web→db→cache spans, finds bottlenecks │
  │                                                                            │
  │           └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘                         │
  │                              ▼                                             │
  │       🚨 ALERTS (Alertmanager) on SLOs / symptoms ─► error budget          │
  │                                                                            │
  │   📖 RED (Rate / Errors / Duration) for SERVICES                           │
  │   📖 USE (Utilization / Saturation / Errors) for RESOURCES (nodes/disks)   │
  │   ⚠️ alert on SYMPTOMS not causes · watch metric CARDINALITY               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which pillar answers which question?
  ┌────────────────────────────┬───────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Question you're asking      │ Pillar    │ Tool / signal                   │
  ├────────────────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ "Is easypj up & how fast?"  │ Metrics   │ Prometheus rate/latency series  │
  │ "What % of /jobs is failing"│ Metrics   │ error-rate PromQL               │
  │ "WHY did THIS request 500?" │ Logs      │ kubectl logs / Loki query       │
  │ "What did the worker print?"│ Logs      │ stdout/stderr → log shipper     │
  │ "WHERE did the 900ms go?"   │ Traces    │ OTel spans (web→db→cache)       │
  │ "Is the NODE saturated?"    │ Metrics   │ USE: node CPU/mem/disk          │
  │ "Should I get paged?"       │ Alerts    │ SLO burn-rate rule              │
  └────────────────────────────┴───────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT: the pillars are complementary, not redundant. Metrics tell you
     SOMETHING is wrong (error rate up). Traces tell you WHERE (the db span).
     Logs tell you WHY (deadlock / missing index / null author). A mature
     workflow flows alert → metric → trace → log, narrowing each step. Modern
     stacks link them with EXEMPLARS (a metric data-point carries a trace_id)
     so you click a latency spike and jump straight to the slow trace.

  📖 KEY TERM — Pillar economics:
    • Metrics — pre-aggregated numbers; constant cost per series; cheapest;
      you query the SHAPE, not the individual event.
    • Logs — one line per event; cost scales with traffic; pricey but the
      richest "what exactly happened" detail.
    • Traces — usually SAMPLED (e.g. 1%) because tracing every request is
      expensive; you keep enough to find patterns and slow outliers.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  43.2  Prometheus 🏢
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — Prometheus: an open-source, PULL-based metrics system. It
     SCRAPES HTTP endpoints (`/metrics`) on a schedule, stores the numbers in a
     local time-series database (TSDB), and lets you query them with PromQL.
     The pull model means Prometheus decides who to scrape and when — targets
     just expose `/metrics` and stay dumb.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PROMETHEUS PULL MODEL — scraping easypj                                   │
  │                                                                            │
  │   ┌────────────────┐  scrape every 15s   ┌─────────────────────────────┐  │
  │   │  PROMETHEUS    │ ───── GET /metrics ─►│ easypj pod   :8000/metrics  │  │
  │   │  (server+TSDB) │ ◄──── 200 text ──────│  http_requests_total ...    │  │
  │   │                │                      │  http_request_duration_...   │  │
  │   │  service       │ ───── GET /metrics ─►│ kube-state-metrics          │  │
  │   │  discovery ───┐│ ───── GET /metrics ─►│ node-exporter (USE/node)    │  │
  │   │   (k8s API)   ││ ───── GET /metrics ─►│ cAdvisor/kubelet (per-pod)  │  │
  │   └───────┬───────┘└──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘  │
  │           │ targets resolved from ServiceMonitor / Pod annotations         │
  │           ▼                                                                 │
  │   ┌────────────────┐    PromQL     ┌──────────┐   alerts  ┌─────────────┐  │
  │   │  TSDB (15d def)│ ◄──── query ──│ Grafana  │           │Alertmanager │  │
  │   │                │ ───────────── │ Explore  │   rules ─►│ route/dedup │  │
  │   └────────────────┘               └──────────┘           └──────┬──────┘  │
  │                                                       page/Slack ◄┘         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERM — Exporter: a small process that translates some system's stats
     into Prometheus `/metrics` text. node-exporter (node CPU/mem/disk),
     kube-state-metrics (k8s object state: deployments, pods, replicas),
     postgres-exporter (easypj's PostgreSQL), and your app's own client
     library (django-prometheus) all expose `/metrics`.

  📖 KEY TERM — ServiceMonitor: a Prometheus-Operator CRD that declaratively
     tells Prometheus which Services to scrape. Instead of editing Prometheus
     config, you create a ServiceMonitor whose selector matches the easypj
     Service; the Operator regenerates scrape config for you.

  ───────────────  ServiceMonitor for easypj (Prometheus Operator)  ───────────
    apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
    kind: ServiceMonitor
    metadata:
      name: easypj
      namespace: easypj
      labels:
        release: kube-prometheus-stack   # matched by the Prometheus CR
    spec:
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: easypj                     # matches the easypj Service labels
      endpoints:
        - port: web                       # the named port on the Service
          path: /metrics
          interval: 15s
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD — how Prometheus finds targets: with the Operator, the
     Prometheus CR has a `serviceMonitorSelector`. Each matching ServiceMonitor
     is compiled into a scrape job; Prometheus then uses Kubernetes service
     discovery to enumerate the Endpoints behind that Service and scrapes each
     pod IP directly (not the ClusterIP), so you get per-pod series. Pod
     annotations (`prometheus.io/scrape: "true"`) are the older, non-Operator
     way.

  📖 PromQL primer — the four core functions you actually use:
    • A raw COUNTER like http_requests_total only ever increases; you almost
      never graph it raw.
    • rate(counter[5m]) — per-second average increase over a 5-minute window;
      this is how you turn a counter into a "requests per second" line.
    • sum(...) / sum by (label)(...) — aggregate across pods (or group by a
      label like status or path).
    • histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) — estimate the 95th-percentile latency from
      a histogram's bucket counters.

  ───────────────  Basic PromQL on easypj  ────────────────────────────────────
    # Request rate (req/s) across all easypj pods:
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

    # Error rate (fraction of 5xx) — the canonical query:
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

    # p95 request latency (seconds):
    histogram_quantile(0.95,
      sum by (le)(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="easypj"}[5m])))

    # Per-path request rate (group by path label):
    sum by (path)(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

    # Quick, NO-Prometheus alternative for live CPU/mem (needs metrics-server):
    kubectl top pods -n easypj
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  💡 INSIGHT — counters vs gauges vs histograms:
    • COUNTER — monotonic up (requests, errors, bytes). Use rate().
    • GAUGE   — goes up and down (in-flight requests, queue depth, temperature).
      Use it raw or with avg/max.
    • HISTOGRAM — buckets of observations (request durations) plus _sum/_count.
      Feed the `_bucket` series to histogram_quantile() for percentiles.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING — `kubectl top` returns "error: Metrics API not available":
     metrics-server is not installed or not Ready. metrics-server is the
     LIGHTWEIGHT, in-cluster source for `kubectl top` and the HPA — it is NOT
     Prometheus and stores no history. Install it; verify with
     `kubectl get deploy metrics-server -n kube-system`.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  43.3  Grafana 🏢
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — Grafana: the visualization layer. It queries data sources
     (Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo/Jaeger for traces) and
     renders DASHBOARDS — collections of panels — plus its own Explore view and
     alerting. Grafana stores nothing; it asks Prometheus on every refresh.

  Two complementary dashboard recipes — pick by WHAT you're watching:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RED — for request-driven SERVICES (the easypj web tier)                   │
  │    📈 Rate      requests / second                                          │
  │    📈 Errors    % of requests that fail (5xx / total)                      │
  │    📈 Duration  latency distribution (p50 / p95 / p99)                     │
  │                                                                            │
  │  USE — for RESOURCES (nodes, disks, the easypj PostgreSQL)                 │
  │    📈 Utilization   % of resource busy (CPU %, mem %)                      │
  │    📈 Saturation    how much extra work is QUEUED (run-queue, swap, iowait)│
  │    📈 Errors        device/error counts (disk errors, OOMKills)           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  easypj "Service Overview" dashboard (RED)                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Rate (req/s)         │ │ Error % (5xx/total)  │ │ Latency p50/95/99 │  │
  │  │     ╱╲    ╱╲╱        │ │ 0.3% ──── SLO 1% ─── │ │  p99 ╱╲           │  │
  │  │ ___╱  ╲__╱    ╲___   │ │ ▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▃▁▁ (under)   │ │  p95 ___╱╲___     │  │
  │  └──────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Pods Ready (4/4)     │ │ Restarts (last 1h)   │ │ DB conns / pool % │  │
  │  └──────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: don't hand-build node dashboards. The kube-prometheus-stack
     Helm chart ships ready-made Grafana dashboards for nodes, pods,
     namespaces, and the control plane. Import the community "Node Exporter
     Full" (ID 1860) and "Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Namespace (Pods)"
     and you have USE coverage in minutes; spend your effort on the easypj
     RED dashboard, which only you can write.

  💡 INSIGHT: a dashboard without a reference line is just decoration. Draw the
     SLO threshold (e.g. the 1% error line, the 300ms p95 line) directly on the
     panel so a glance tells you "inside budget" vs "burning budget."

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  43.4  Alerting & SLOs 🏢
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERMS — the SLO vocabulary:
    • SLI (Service Level Indicator) — a MEASURED number that reflects user
      experience. e.g. easypj's request-success ratio, or p95 latency.
    • SLO (Service Level Objective) — the TARGET for an SLI over a window.
      e.g. "99.9% of /jobs/ requests succeed over 30 days."
    • SLA (Service Level Agreement) — the CONTRACT with consequences (refunds)
      if the SLO is missed. SLA ≤ SLO (you set the SLO stricter than the SLA).
    • ERROR BUDGET = 1 − SLO. At 99.9% success, the budget is 0.1% — roughly
      43 minutes of "allowed" failure per 30 days. You SPEND it on risk
      (deploys, experiments); when it's exhausted, you freeze risky changes.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ALERTING PIPELINE — symptom in, page out                                  │
  │                                                                            │
  │  Prometheus ── evaluates ALERTING RULES (PromQL + `for:`) ──┐              │
  │     (e.g. error rate > 1% for 5m → fires "EasypjHighErrorRate")           │
  │                                                            ▼              │
  │                                              ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
  │                                              │  ALERTMANAGER            │  │
  │   group similar alerts ◄── route by labels ──┤  dedupe · group · throttle│ │
  │   inhibit (mute B if A firing)               │  silence · inhibit       │  │
  │                                              └────────┬─────────────────┘  │
  │                                receivers ─────────────┼──────► PagerDuty   │
  │                                                       ├──────► Slack       │
  │                                                       └──────► email       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY PRINCIPLE — ALERT ON SYMPTOMS, NOT CAUSES. A symptom is user-visible
     (error rate, latency, budget burn). A cause is an internal condition (CPU
     high, a pod restarted, a disk 80% full). Symptom alerts:
       • map directly to user pain (so every page is worth waking up for),
       • catch UNKNOWN failure modes (you didn't predict the cause but the
         symptom still fires),
       • stay few in number — less alert fatigue.
     Causes belong on DASHBOARDS for diagnosis, not on the pager.

  📖 KEY TERM — Burn-rate alerting: rather than "error rate > 1% for 5m," the
     modern Google-SRE approach alerts on how FAST you are consuming the error
     budget. A burn rate of 1 means you'll exactly exhaust the 30-day budget in
     30 days; a burn rate of 14.4 means you'd burn the whole month's budget in
     ~2 hours — page NOW. Fast-burn (page) + slow-burn (ticket) multi-window
     rules give urgency proportional to severity.

  ───────────────  Prometheus alerting rules for easypj  ──────────────────────
    apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
    kind: PrometheusRule
    metadata:
      name: easypj-rules
      namespace: easypj
      labels:
        release: kube-prometheus-stack
    spec:
      groups:
        - name: easypj.slo
          rules:
            # --- recording rule: pre-compute the error ratio once ---
            - record: easypj:request_error_ratio:rate5m
              expr: |
                sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
                  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))
            # --- symptom alert: high error rate (fast burn) ---
            - alert: EasypjHighErrorRate
              expr: easypj:request_error_ratio:rate5m > 0.01
              for: 5m
              labels: {severity: page}
              annotations:
                summary: "easypj 5xx error rate above 1% for 5m"
                description: "Error ratio is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}"
            # --- symptom alert: slow p95 latency ---
            - alert: EasypjHighLatency
              expr: |
                histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le)(
                  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="easypj"}[5m])
                )) > 0.3
              for: 10m
              labels: {severity: ticket}
              annotations:
                summary: "easypj p95 latency above 300ms"
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  💡 INSIGHT — recording rules vs alerting rules. A RECORDING rule
     pre-computes a frequently-used PromQL expression into a new series (named
     with the `metric:operation:window` convention, e.g.
     easypj:request_error_ratio:rate5m). Dashboards and alerts then reference
     the cheap pre-computed series instead of re-evaluating an expensive query
     every scrape. ALERTING rules evaluate a condition and, when true for the
     `for:` duration, emit an alert to Alertmanager.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  43.5  Tracing 🏢
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  📖 KEY TERM — Distributed tracing: follows a SINGLE request as it fans out
     across services, stitching the work into one TRACE made of SPANS. Each
     span is one unit of work (an HTTP handler, a DB query, a cache lookup)
     with a start time, duration, and parent. A propagated TRACE ID ties them
     together so you see exactly where a slow /jobs/ request spent its time.

  📖 KEY TERM — OpenTelemetry (OTel): the vendor-neutral standard + SDKs for
     emitting metrics, logs, AND traces. You instrument easypj with the OTel
     SDK (or auto-instrumentation), which exports spans to an OTel COLLECTOR;
     the collector processes/batches them and forwards to a backend (Jaeger,
     Tempo, etc.). One standard, swappable backends.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRACE OF A SLOW /jobs/ REQUEST (easypj)        trace_id=ab12…             │
  │                                                                            │
  │  span: GET /jobs/  ████████████████████████████████████████  920ms        │
  │   ├─ middleware/auth        ██                                  30ms       │
  │   ├─ view: JobPost.list     ░░░░████████████████████████████   840ms ⚠️    │
  │   │   ├─ db: SELECT jobpost ░░░░██                              40ms       │
  │   │   └─ db: SELECT skills  ░░░░░░████████████████████████  ◄── 790ms 🔴   │
  │   │         (N+1 join lost its index — the bottleneck)                     │
  │   └─ template render        █                                   20ms       │
  │                                                                            │
  │  ▶ Metrics said "p95 up." The TRACE says WHERE: the skills query.          │
  │  ▶ Logs for that trace_id then say WHY: "Seq Scan on jobpost_skills".      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT: this is the full loop in one picture. The Prometheus p95 ALERT
     fired (symptom). The OTel TRACE localized the 790ms to the skills SELECT
     (where). The LOG for that trace_id revealed the missing index (why). Three
     pillars, one investigation. EXEMPLARS make this clickable: the latency
     histogram bucket carries a trace_id, so you jump from the spike straight
     to the offending trace.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔧 UTH:
    • Target discovery — the Prometheus Operator turns each ServiceMonitor into
      a scrape job, then uses Kubernetes SD to scrape pod IPs directly (one
      series set per pod), not the ClusterIP.
    • Cardinality — total series ≈ (metric names) × (product of label-value
      counts). Each unique label combination is a separate series held in RAM.
      One unbounded label (user_id) multiplies series without limit and OOMs
      the TSDB. relabel_configs can DROP dangerous labels at scrape time.
    • Recording vs alerting rules — recording pre-aggregates hot queries into
      new series for cheap reuse; alerting evaluates a condition + `for:` and
      hands firing alerts to Alertmanager.

  🔬 DEEPER:
    • PromQL recording rules & histogram_quantile — percentiles are ESTIMATES
      interpolated within histogram buckets; the estimate is only as good as
      the bucket boundaries. Choose buckets around your SLO targets (e.g. extra
      buckets near 300ms) or the p95 is meaningless.
    • Exemplars & native histograms — exemplars attach a trace_id to a bucket
      sample (metric↔trace linking); Prometheus "native (sparse) histograms"
      replace fixed buckets with high-resolution, auto-scaling buckets, giving
      accurate quantiles at a fraction of the series count.
    • OTel collector pipelines — receivers → processors (batch, attributes,
      tail-sampling) → exporters; tail-sampling keeps only interesting traces
      (errors, slow outliers) to control cost.
    • SLO burn-rate alerts — multi-window/multi-burn-rate rules (e.g. 14.4×
      over 1h AND 5m → page; 6× over 6h → ticket) give urgency proportional to
      how fast the budget is draining, far better than a static threshold.
    • Remote-write & long-term storage — Prometheus retains ~15 days locally;
      remote_write streams samples to THANOS or MIMIR/CORTEX for cheap,
      long-term, globally-queryable, downsampled storage and multi-cluster
      views.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Three pillars: METRICS (Prometheus — what & how much: rate/latency/errors),
    LOGS (Loki/EFK — what happened), TRACES (OpenTelemetry — where the time
    went across services). Together they feed ALERTS.
  • The pillars are complementary: alert → metric (something's wrong) → trace
    (where) → log (why). Exemplars link a metric spike directly to a trace.
  • Prometheus is PULL-based: it scrapes exporters/ServiceMonitors on a
    schedule into a local TSDB. Core PromQL: rate() turns counters into
    per-second rates; histogram_quantile() estimates p95/p99 latency.
  • A ServiceMonitor (Operator CRD) tells Prometheus which Services to scrape;
    metrics-server is the lightweight, history-less source for `kubectl top`
    and the HPA — not Prometheus.
  • Use RED (Rate/Errors/Duration) for SERVICES and USE (Utilization/
    Saturation/Errors) for RESOURCES/nodes to decide what to dashboard.
  • Alert on SYMPTOMS/SLOs (user-visible: error rate, latency, budget burn),
    NOT raw causes — and watch metric cardinality so Prometheus stays healthy.
  • SLI = measured indicator; SLO = its target; error budget = 1 − SLO, the
    failure you may "spend." Burn-rate alerts page faster when the budget
    drains faster.
  • Recording rules pre-compute hot queries; alerting rules evaluate a
    condition + `for:` and hand firing alerts to Alertmanager (dedupe, group,
    route, silence, inhibit).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • High-cardinality labels (user id, request id, full URL with query string)
    explode Prometheus memory — keep label sets bounded; drop offenders with
    relabeling at scrape time.
  • Alerting on every cause produces alert fatigue; alert on a few meaningful
    SLO/symptom conditions instead.
  • Dashboards without SLOs are pretty but don't tell you if you're OK — define
    objectives and draw the threshold line, not just graphs.
  • histogram_quantile needs sensible bucket boundaries; bad buckets give
    meaningless p95s. Put extra buckets near your latency SLO.
  • `kubectl top` failing usually means metrics-server isn't installed/Ready —
    not a Prometheus problem.
  • rate() on a GAUGE is nonsense — rate() is for monotonic COUNTERS only;
    likewise don't sum() a gauge across pods blindly (sum of percentages).
  • Forgetting the `for:` on an alert makes it flap on every transient spike;
    too long a `for:` delays paging on real outages.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • RED for services, USE for resources — a fast mental template for "what do
    I measure here?"
  • The canonical error-rate query, memorize it:
      rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])
  • Start alerts FROM the SLO (e.g. 99.9% success) and a burn-rate rule, not
    from arbitrary thresholds.
  • For exam troubleshooting, reach for the built-ins first: `kubectl top`,
    `kubectl logs -f --previous`, `kubectl describe` (Events), `kubectl get
    events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` — no Prometheus required.
  • Import community dashboards (Node Exporter Full = 1860) for USE; only
    hand-write the app RED dashboard.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 COMMANDS / QUERIES
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl top nodes                                  # USE: node CPU/mem
  kubectl top pods -n easypj                          # quick, no Prometheus
  kubectl logs -f deploy/easypj -n easypj             # stream logs (the pillar)
  kubectl logs <pod> -n easypj --previous             # logs of last crash
  kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
  kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj                # Events at the bottom

  # PromQL — easypj request rate:
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

  # error rate:
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
    / sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

  # p95 latency:
  histogram_quantile(0.95,
    sum by (le)(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="easypj"}[5m])))

  # per-path rate:
  sum by (path)(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))

  🧪 DRILL

  panel for each (draw the SLO line), and define one SLO-based alert (e.g.
  error rate > 1% for 5m) on it. Bonus: add a recording rule for the error

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 LAB Q&A
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Q1. Name the three pillars and what each answers.
      A. METRICS (what / how much), LOGS (what happened), TRACES (where the
      time went across services) — together feeding ALERTS.

  Q2. Write PromQL for easypj's request rate.
      A. `sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="easypj"}[5m]))` — per-second rate
      averaged over a 5m window, summed across all pods.

  Q3. Compute p95 latency in PromQL.
      A. `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le)(rate(
      http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="easypj"}[5m])))` — interpolated
      from the histogram's `_bucket` series grouped by the `le` label.

  Q4. RED vs USE — when do you use each?
      A. RED (Rate/Errors/Duration) for request-driven SERVICES (the easypj web
      tier); USE (Utilization/Saturation/Errors) for RESOURCES like nodes,
      disks, and the database.

  Q5. What is a ServiceMonitor?
      A. A Prometheus-Operator CRD that tells Prometheus which Services/
      endpoints to scrape — a label selector plus the port/path/interval. The
      Operator compiles it into scrape config; Prometheus then scrapes the
      pod IPs behind that Service.

  Q6. Define SLI, SLO, and error budget.
      A. SLI = a measured indicator (e.g. request-success ratio); SLO = the
      target for it (99.9%); error budget = 1 − SLO, the allowable failure you
      can "spend" on deploys and risk before freezing changes.

  Q7. Why alert on symptoms not causes?
      A. Symptoms (latency/errors/budget burn) map to user impact and catch
      UNKNOWN failure modes; cause-alerts are noisy, cause alert fatigue, and
      miss novel problems. Causes belong on dashboards for diagnosis.

  Q8. Build a useful easypj Grafana panel — what goes on it?
      A. RED signals — request rate, error %, and p95/p99 latency for /jobs/ —
      ideally with the SLO line drawn on the panel so a glance shows in-budget
      vs burning.

  Q9. Trace a slow /jobs/ request across services — tool and idea?
      A. OpenTelemetry traces: a propagated trace_id follows the request
      through web → db → cache as parent/child SPANS, showing per-span time so
      you find the bottleneck (e.g. the 790ms skills SELECT).

  Q10. What is a cardinality risk and how do you avoid it?
       A. Labels with UNBOUNDED values (user id, request id, raw URLs) create
       millions of series and OOM Prometheus. Keep labels low-cardinality, and
       DROP offenders with relabel_configs at scrape time.

  Q11. `kubectl top pods` returns "Metrics API not available" — diagnose.
       A. metrics-server isn't installed or isn't Ready (it's the lightweight,
       history-less source for `kubectl top` and the HPA — not Prometheus).
       Check `kubectl get deploy metrics-server -n kube-system` and install it.

  Q12. Difference between a recording rule and an alerting rule?
       A. A RECORDING rule pre-computes an expensive PromQL expression into a
       new named series (metric:op:window) for cheap reuse by dashboards/alerts.
       An ALERTING rule evaluates a condition that, once true for the `for:`
       duration, fires an alert to Alertmanager.

  Q13. What does Alertmanager add on top of Prometheus alerting rules?
       A. Routing, GROUPING of related alerts, DEDUPLICATION, throttling,
       SILENCES, and INHIBITION (mute downstream alerts when an upstream one is
       firing) — then dispatch to receivers (PagerDuty/Slack/email).

  Q14. What is a burn-rate alert and why is it better than a static threshold?
       A. It alerts on how fast the error budget is being consumed (burn rate
       14.4× burns a month's budget in ~2h → page). Multi-window/multi-burn
       rules give urgency proportional to severity, reducing both flapping and
       slow detection.

  Chapter 44: Multi-Cluster, Capacity & Cost                           🔴 🏢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~1.5h · Beyond-exam (running at scale, on a budget).
        Focus: how one app like easypj lives across many clusters, how you
        plan capacity from requests, and how you keep the bill honest.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  💡 WHY THIS MATTERS
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Real platforms are rarely one cluster. They are FLEETS — many clusters,
  split by environment, region, or tenant — and every one of them carries a
  real monthly bill. The CKA exam tests whether you can operate a single
  cluster correctly; production tests whether you can operate MANY of them
  WELL and AFFORDABLY. The hinge for both scheduling and cost is the same
  humble field you have set since Chapter 1: the resource REQUEST. Get
  requests right and you bin-pack tightly, autoscale cleanly, and stop paying
  for idle nodes. Get them wrong and you either evict your own pods or burn
  money on headroom nobody uses.

  🧠 ANALOGY: A cluster is a shipping container; pods are boxes; requests are
  the box DIMENSIONS written on the side. Capacity planning is deciding how
  many containers to rent and how to stack the boxes. Cost is the rental
  bill. Lie about a box's dimensions and either it doesn't fit (eviction) or
  you ship half-empty containers (wasted spend).

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🎯 OBJECTIVES
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Recognize the common multi-cluster patterns (per-env / per-region /
    per-tenant) and how fleets are managed with GitOps + a control plane.
  • Plan cluster capacity using REQUESTS as the unit, with deliberate
    headroom and bin-packing in mind.
  • Right-size workloads from REAL usage and apply concrete cost levers
    (autoscaling, spot nodes, allocation tooling).
  • Combine the three autoscaling layers — HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler —
    on their different axes without letting them fight.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  📋 CKA RELEVANCE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Multi-cluster fleet management and cost tooling are NOT directly exam-
  graded — this chapter is 🏢 day-2 / beyond. BUT the building blocks are
  pure CKA: resource requests/limits, the scheduler placing pods by request
  against node allocatable, HPA, `kubectl top`, and `kubectl describe node`
  reading. Mastering the cost lens makes those exam mechanics click into
  place, because you finally see WHY requests matter so much.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🗺️  SECTION MAP
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  44.1  Multi-Cluster Patterns 🏢 — per-env / per-region / per-tenant; fleet
        management with GitOps.
  44.2  Capacity Planning 🏢 — requests as the unit; headroom; bin-packing.

        Autoscaler (nodes), used together.

  44.1  MULTI-CLUSTER PATTERNS 🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  One cluster is the exam. Production is a FLEET. The first design decision
  is what each cluster boundary BUYS you, because a boundary is the strongest
  isolation Kubernetes offers — far stronger than a namespace.

  📖 KEY TERM — Fleet: a managed set of clusters treated as one logical
  estate, configured from a single source of truth (Git) rather than by hand,
  cluster by cluster.

  Three dominant patterns (often combined):

  ┌──────────────── MULTI-CLUSTER PATTERNS — WHAT DRIVES THE SPLIT ─────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │  PER-ENVIRONMENT      dev / stage / prod as SEPARATE clusters           │
  │    driver ► blast-radius + independent upgrades                         │
  │    easypj ► break dev freely; prod never feels it                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  PER-REGION           us-east / eu-west / ap-south clusters             │
  │    driver ► latency (locality) + disaster recovery                      │
  │    easypj ► serve job listings near the user; survive a region loss     │
  │                                                                         │
  │  PER-TENANT           one cluster per customer / business unit          │
  │    driver ► hard isolation + compliance + clean cost boundaries         │
  │    easypj ► enterprise customer demands a dedicated control plane       │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — separate CLUSTER vs separate NAMESPACE?
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Need a separate NAMESPACE when ......... soft isolation is enough:      │
   │   shared control plane is fine, you want RBAC/quota/network boundaries  │
   │   within one team's estate, and you accept a shared blast radius.       │
   │ Need a separate CLUSTER when ........... you need a HARD boundary:      │
   │   separate control planes / blast radius, independent upgrades,         │
   │   regulatory isolation, or a clean per-tenant cost & security line.     │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 INSIGHT: a namespace shares one API server, one etcd, one scheduler. A
  noisy or compromised tenant in a namespace can still affect neighbors
  through the shared control plane and shared nodes. A separate cluster gives
  each tenant its own control plane — true blast-radius separation — at the
  cost of more clusters to operate.

  FLEET MANAGEMENT — you do NOT click through 30 clusters by hand. You
  declare desired state in Git and let a control plane reconcile every
  cluster to it.

  ┌──────────────── FLEET = GitOps + A CONTROL PLANE ──────────────────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │      ┌─────────────┐   reconciles    ┌──────────────────────────────┐  │
  │      │  Git repo   │  ─────────────► │  cluster: dev   (easypj v1)   │  │
  │      │ (desired    │                 ├──────────────────────────────┤  │
  │      │  state for  │  ─────────────► │  cluster: stage (easypj v1)   │  │
  │      │  the whole  │                 ├──────────────────────────────┤  │
  │      │  fleet)     │  ─────────────► │  cluster: prod  (easypj v1)   │  │
  │      └─────────────┘                 └──────────────────────────────┘  │
  │             ▲                                                          │
  │             │ Argo CD / Flux / Rancher Fleet pull & apply per cluster  │
  │   Kustomize OVERLAYS hold per-env differences (replicas/requests/env)  │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: tools like Argo CD, Flux, and Rancher Fleet register
  each target cluster, then continuously diff the live state against Git and
  re-apply drift. The SAME base manifests (easypj Deployment, Service,
  Ingress, the JobPost/Author/Location/Skills schema migrations) are shared;
  Kustomize overlays inject per-environment differences — prod gets more
  replicas and bigger requests, dev gets one replica and tiny requests.

  ⚡ SPEED TIP: keep ONE base and per-env Kustomize overlays so the exact
  same easypj base scales from a laptop kind cluster to a 200-node prod
  cluster by changing only the overlay.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  44.2  CAPACITY PLANNING 🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Capacity planning answers one question: how many nodes, of what size, do I
  need to run my workloads — with room to spare? The unit of that math is the
  REQUEST, because the scheduler places pods by their requests against each
  node's ALLOCATABLE capacity. Limits cap a pod; requests RESERVE for it.

  📖 KEY TERM — Allocatable: a node's total capacity minus what is reserved
  for the kubelet, OS, and eviction thresholds. This is the real pool the
  scheduler can hand out as requests.

  📖 KEY TERM — Bin-packing: the scheduler's job of fitting pods (boxes sized
  by their requests) into nodes (bins sized by allocatable) so that as little
  space as possible is wasted.

  ┌──────────────── CAPACITY = Σ REQUESTS + HEADROOM, BIN-PACKED ──────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │   Step 1  Sum the REQUESTS of everything you must run:                   │
  │           Σ(cpu requests)  and  Σ(memory requests)                      │
  │                                                                         │
  │   Step 2  Add HEADROOM for spikes + node failure (e.g. N+1).            │
  │                                                                         │
  │   Step 3  Pick node SIZE/TYPE so requests bin-pack to a sane            │
  │           utilization target (e.g. ~60–75% of allocatable).            │
  │                                                                         │
  │   nodes ≈  ceil( (Σ requests + headroom) / node allocatable )          │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERM — Headroom: spare capacity deliberately reserved so the cluster
  can absorb a traffic spike OR survive losing a node WITHOUT immediately
  producing Pending pods. Headroom feels like waste but is insurance — size
  it on purpose, not by accident.

  Reading a node's current allocation tells you how packed it already is:

  ┌──────────────── kubectl describe node — "Allocated resources" ─────────┐
  │  Allocated resources:                                                   │
  │    (Total limits may be over 100 percent, i.e. overcommitted.)          │
  │    Resource           Requests        Limits                            │
  │    --------           --------        ------                            │
  │    cpu                1450m (72%)     3200m (160%)                       │
  │    memory             2400Mi (60%)    4096Mi (102%)                     │
  │  ◄ Requests % = how full the bin is for SCHEDULING.                     │
  │  ◄ Limits over 100% = overcommit (fine for CPU, dangerous for memory).  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: pods WITHOUT requests are invisible to this math. The scheduler
  treats them as needing ~nothing, so they wreck bin-packing AND cost
  accounting — they pack onto nodes that are "full" of real workloads and
  then fight for the actual CPU/memory at runtime. Always set requests.

  🔧 DEEPER — topology-aware bin-packing: a naive packer minimizes node
  count, but you often want pods SPREAD across zones for availability
  (topologySpreadConstraints) — which trades a little packing efficiency for
  resilience. Karpenter and similar provisioners do "just-in-time"
  node provisioning: they look at the actual shape of Pending pods and launch
  a node sized to fit them, then consolidate (bin-pack onto fewer nodes and
  retire the emptied ones) when usage drops.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  44.3  RIGHT-SIZING & COST 🏢
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Requests are the unit of BOTH scheduling and cost. The whole cost game is
  keeping requests close to real usage and keeping nodes busy.

  ┌──────────── REQUESTS = the unit of BOTH SCHEDULING AND COST ───────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │   requests too HIGH ─► poor bin-packing, idle $$$   (over-provisioned)  │
  │   requests too LOW  ─► evictions, noisy neighbors    (under-provisioned)│
  │                                                                         │
  │   🧭 right-size from REAL usage (kubectl top / VPA recommendations).    │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  RIGHT-SIZING METHOD — compare declared requests against measured usage and
  move requests toward reality:

  ┌──────────────── RIGHT-SIZE easypj-web ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │   $ kubectl top pods -n easypj                                          │
  │     NAME                       CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)               │
  │     easypj-web-7d9c-abcde      120m         180Mi                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │   declared requests:  cpu 500m  ·  memory 512Mi                         │
  │   measured usage:     cpu 120m  ·  memory 180Mi                         │
  │                                                                         │
  │   ► OVER-PROVISIONED: paying for 500m, using 120m.                      │
  │     new requests ≈ usage + buffer:  cpu 200m  ·  memory 256Mi           │
  │     (keep a sane limit; don't pin requests below real steady usage)     │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA — symptoms of OVER-provisioning: low node utilization, requests
  >> usage, idle nodes the Cluster Autoscaler cannot remove (because the
  reserved requests look "used"). You pay for capacity you never touch.

  ⚠️ GOTCHA — symptoms of UNDER-provisioning: OOMKills and evictions, noisy
  neighbors stealing CPU, pods Pending under load. Cheap on paper, expensive
  in incidents.

  COST LEVERS — four big knobs, in order of bang-for-effort:

  ┌──────────────── FOUR COST LEVERS ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. RIGHT-SIZE requests ........ stop reserving capacity you don't use. │
  │  2. AUTOSCALE ................... remove idle nodes (Cluster Autoscaler).│
  │  3. SPOT / PREEMPTIBLE nodes .... much cheaper, but reclaimable anytime. │
  │  4. MEASURE allocation .......... OpenCost / Kubecost map spend to       │
  │                                   namespace / team / workload.          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  📖 KEY TERM — Spot / preemptible nodes: deeply discounted nodes the cloud
  provider can reclaim with little or no notice. Great for interruption-
  tolerant work; dangerous for anything that must stay up.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — can this workload run on SPOT?
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ YES, if .... it tolerates restarts: stateless web (easypj-web replicas │
   │              behind a Service), batch/queue workers, CI runners — with  │
   │              a PodDisruptionBudget + topology spread so losing nodes     │
   │              doesn't take the whole Deployment down.                    │
   │ NO,  if .... it is singleton / stateful / latency-critical: the         │
   │              database, leader-elected controllers — keep these on        │
   │              on-demand nodes; use spot only as overflow.                │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ GOTCHA: spot nodes can vanish with short notice. Protect workloads with
  PDBs and topology spread, and keep critical pods (the easypj PostgreSQL
  database, control-plane add-ons) on on-demand nodes.

  🔧 DEEPER — cost allocation with OpenCost / Kubecost: these tools read pod
  requests/usage and node prices, then ALLOCATE the bill back to namespaces,
  labels, and teams — turning one opaque cloud invoice into "easypj prod web
  costs $X/mo, the database costs $Y/mo." OpenCost is the CNCF open-source
  core; Kubecost is the commercial product built on it. Allocation is what
  makes "right-size" actionable: you can see exactly which workload is
  over-provisioned and what fixing it saves. Karpenter's consolidation is the
  automated complement — it continuously repacks pods onto fewer nodes and
  retires the empties to cut idle spend.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  44.4  AUTOSCALING LAYERS 🧭
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Three autoscalers operate on THREE DIFFERENT AXES. They are not rivals —
  they are layers, used together. Confusing them is the classic mistake.

  ┌──────── THREE AUTOSCALERS — different axes, used together ──────────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │   📈 HPA  ─ more/fewer PODS         (on CPU/mem/custom metrics)          │
  │   📐 VPA  ─ bigger/smaller REQUESTS (right-size one pod)                 │
  │   🖥️ Cluster Autoscaler ─ more/fewer NODES (when pods can't fit)        │
  │                                                                         │
  │   easypj-web: HPA 3→10 on CPU · VPA tunes requests · CA adds nodes if    │
  │   pods go Pending.                                                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │   ⚠️ HPA + VPA on the SAME metric conflict — split their signals.       │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  How they chain together for easypj-web under a traffic surge:

  ┌──────────────── THE THREE LAYERS IN MOTION ────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                         │
  │   load rises ─► CPU per pod climbs                                       │
  │        │                                                                │
  │        ▼                                                                │
  │   📈 HPA: scale replicas 3 → 10 (target CPU on metrics)                  │
  │        │                                                                │
  │        ▼  new pods may not FIT on current nodes                         │
  │   🖥️ Cluster Autoscaler: pods are Pending → ADD a node → pods schedule  │
  │        │                                                                │
  │        ▼  (separately, over time, on steady-state)                      │
  │   📐 VPA recommender: "your requests are 500m but you use 120m" →        │
  │        right-size requests so HPA/CA math is honest                      │
  │                                                                         │
  │   load drops ─► HPA scales back down ─► nodes idle ─►                    │
  │   🖥️ Cluster Autoscaler removes the empty node (saves $$$)              │
  │                                                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️ THE CONFLICT — HPA vs VPA on the SAME signal:
  HPA scales pod COUNT based on (say) CPU utilization against requests. VPA
  CHANGES those requests. If both act on CPU at once, VPA shrinks requests →
  utilization % spikes → HPA adds pods → VPA shrinks again — they oscillate.

  🧭 HOW TO AVOID IT:
  • Use VPA in RECOMMEND-ONLY mode (updateMode: Off) and apply its
    suggestions yourself, while HPA handles live scaling — safest combo.
  • Or split signals: HPA on a CUSTOM metric (e.g. requests-per-second or
    queue depth) while VPA owns CPU/memory requests.
  • Never run VPA in Auto mode AND HPA on the same CPU/memory metric.

  🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING — "HPA won't scale / shows <unknown>":
  • metrics-server not installed/healthy → HPA can't read CPU → targets show
    <unknown>. Check `kubectl top pods` works first.
  • No requests set on the container → HPA has no baseline to compute % →
    set requests.
  • Cluster Autoscaler not adding nodes → check the autoscaler logs and that
    the node group's max size isn't already hit, and that Pending pods are
    actually unschedulable (not blocked by taints/affinity instead).

  🔧 DEEPER — VPA internals: the VPA RECOMMENDER watches historical usage and
  emits target/lowerBound/upperBound request values; the UPDATER and ADMISSION
  CONTROLLER can evict and recreate pods with the new requests (Auto mode).
  Because changing requests requires a pod restart, VPA is disruptive — which
  is exactly why recommend-only mode is so popular alongside HPA.

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🧪 DRILL
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Pull easypj-web's actual usage with `kubectl top`, compare it to its
  requests/limits, set right-sized requests, add an HPA, and reason about
  exactly when the Cluster Autoscaler would add a node (hint: when HPA's new
  pods go Pending for lack of allocatable capacity).

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD / 🔬 DEEPER
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔧 UTH: requests drive BOTH scheduling and cost. The scheduler's filter +
  score phase places a pod only on a node whose ALLOCATABLE minus the sum of
  existing requests can still fit this pod's requests. So inflated requests
  fragment your bins (idle, paid-for capacity) and tiny requests overcommit
  (evictions). Node utilization = Σ requests / allocatable; the cost game is
  pushing that ratio to a healthy target without crossing into eviction
  territory.

  🔬 DEEPER (exam + beyond):
  • Karpenter CONSOLIDATION — continuously repacks pods onto fewer nodes and
    retires emptied nodes; just-in-time provisions a node shaped to the
    Pending pods rather than from a fixed node group.
  • TOPOLOGY-AWARE bin-packing — spread vs pack tradeoff via
    topologySpreadConstraints; resilience costs a little packing efficiency.
  • SPOT / PREEMPTIBLE handling — combine PDBs, spread, and node-termination
    handlers that react to the cloud's interruption notice and drain
    gracefully.
  • VPA RECOMMENDER right-sizing — historical-usage-based request targets,
    used recommend-only beside HPA.
  • Kubecost / OpenCost ALLOCATION — map spend to namespace/label/team to
    make right-sizing actionable.
  • FLEET GitOps — Argo CD / Flux / Rancher Fleet reconcile many clusters
    from one Git source of truth with Kustomize overlays per environment.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • Multi-cluster patterns split by ENVIRONMENT (dev/stage/prod), REGION
    (latency/DR), or TENANT (isolation/compliance); fleets are managed with
    GitOps + a control plane (Argo / Flux / Rancher Fleet) rather than by
    hand.
  • Per-environment (and per-tenant) CLUSTERS give stronger isolation than
    namespaces — separate control planes / blast radius, independent
    upgrades, and clean cost/security boundaries.
  • REQUESTS are the unit of BOTH scheduling and cost. Too high = idle,
    wasted spend (bad bin-packing); too low = evictions and noisy neighbors.
    Right-size from REAL usage.
  • Capacity ≈ Σ requests + deliberate HEADROOM, bin-packed to a sane
    utilization target; pick node size/type to fit.
  • THREE autoscalers on different axes: HPA scales POD COUNT (metrics), VPA
    right-sizes a pod's REQUESTS, Cluster Autoscaler scales NODE COUNT (when
    pods can't fit) — used together, not as rivals.
  • Cost levers: right-size requests, autoscale away idle nodes, use spot/
    preemptible nodes (with PDBs), and measure allocation (OpenCost/Kubecost).

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ⚠️ GOTCHAS
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • Pods WITHOUT requests wreck both scheduling (bin-packing) and cost
    accounting — always set requests.
  • HPA and VPA acting on the SAME metric fight each other (VPA changes
    requests while HPA scales on them) — separate their signals or run VPA in
    recommend-only mode.
  • Spot / preemptible nodes can vanish with short notice; protect workloads
    with PDBs and topology spread, and keep critical pods (database,
    leader-elected controllers) on on-demand nodes.
  • Over-provisioned HEADROOM feels safe but is pure cost — size it
    deliberately, not by accident.
  • Idle nodes full of over-sized REQUESTS can't be removed by the Cluster
    Autoscaler (reserved requests look "used") — right-size first.
  • metrics-server missing/unhealthy or no requests set → HPA shows
    <unknown> and won't scale.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ⚡ SPEED TIPS
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • Compare `kubectl top pods` to the declared requests to spot over/under-
    provisioning INSTANTLY.
  • Let VPA's recommender suggest requests even if you don't auto-apply them.
  • Put per-env differences (replicas / requests) in Kustomize OVERLAYS so
    the same base scales across clusters.
  • Read `kubectl describe node` "Allocated resources" to see how full a bin
    already is before adding workloads.
  • Label nodes by instance-type and zone so you can see spot vs on-demand
    and topology spread at a glance.

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🔑 COMMANDS
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # Actual usage vs declared requests
  kubectl top pods -n easypj
  kubectl get deploy easypj-web \
    -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'

  # Autoscaling state
  kubectl get hpa -n easypj
  kubectl describe hpa easypj-web -n easypj

  # How full is each bin?
  kubectl describe node <n> | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'

  # See node types and zones (spot/on-demand, topology)
  kubectl get nodes -L node.kubernetes.io/instance-type,topology.kubernetes.io/zone

  # Cluster-wide capacity sniff
  kubectl top nodes

  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🧪 LAB Q&A
  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Q1. Name a multi-cluster pattern and its driver.
      A. Per-ENVIRONMENT (dev/stage/prod), per-REGION (latency/DR), or
         per-TENANT (isolation) — chosen for blast-radius, locality, or
         compliance.

  Q2. How do you estimate cluster capacity?
      A. Sum pod REQUESTS (the scheduling unit) + headroom, then size node
         count/type so requests bin-pack to your utilization targets.
         nodes ≈ ceil((Σ requests + headroom) / node allocatable).

  Q3. Right-size easypj-web. What is the method?
      A. Compare `kubectl top` actual usage vs requests/limits (or VPA
         recommendations) and set requests near real usage with sane limits.
         e.g. usage 120m/180Mi against requests 500m/512Mi → drop requests to
         ~200m/256Mi.

  Q4. HPA vs VPA vs Cluster Autoscaler — roles?
      A. HPA = more/fewer PODS (on metrics); VPA = bigger/smaller pod
         REQUESTS; Cluster Autoscaler = more/fewer NODES when pods are
         unschedulable (or nodes idle).

  Q5. Trade-offs of spot/preemptible nodes?
      A. Much cheaper but can be reclaimed at any time; safe only for
         interruption-tolerant workloads with PDBs/spread and an on-demand
         fallback for critical pods.

  Q6. Why do requests drive bin-packing?
      A. The scheduler places pods by their requests against node
         ALLOCATABLE; inflated requests waste capacity, tiny ones overcommit
         and cause evictions.

  Q7. Give two concrete cost levers.
      A. Right-size requests + autoscale to remove idle nodes; use spot nodes
         and internal LBs where appropriate; measure allocation with
         OpenCost/Kubecost.

  Q8. What is headroom and why have it?
      A. Spare capacity reserved for spikes/failover so the cluster can
         absorb load or a node loss without immediate Pending pods — sized
         deliberately, since it is insurance you still pay for.

  Q9. Symptoms of over-provisioning?
      A. Low node utilization, requests >> usage, idle nodes the autoscaler
         can't remove — paying for capacity you don't use.

  Q10. Why might per-environment clusters be preferred over namespaces?
       A. Stronger isolation (separate control planes / blast radius),
          independent upgrades, and clearer cost/security boundaries than
          namespace separation within one shared control plane.

  Q11. HPA shows TARGETS <unknown> and won't scale. Diagnose.
       A. Usually metrics-server is missing/unhealthy (verify `kubectl top
          pods` works) OR the container has no resource requests, so HPA has
          no baseline to compute utilization against — install metrics-server
          and set requests.

  Q12. Why can running VPA in Auto mode alongside HPA on the same CPU metric
       be a problem, and how do you fix it?
       A. VPA changes requests while HPA scales on utilization computed
          against those requests, so they oscillate. Fix it by running VPA in
          recommend-only mode (updateMode: Off) and applying suggestions
          yourself, or by splitting signals (HPA on a custom metric, VPA on
          CPU/memory).

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🖼️  VISUAL SUMMARY — easypj across clusters with the 3 autoscalers
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Git (desired state)  ──►  dev cluster ─ stage cluster ─ prod cluster   │
  │        per-env Kustomize overlays: replicas + requests differ            │
  │                                                                         │
  │   In EACH cluster, easypj-web is governed by three axes:                │
  │     📈 HPA  → pod COUNT      (3→10 on CPU)                               │
  │     📐 VPA  → request SIZE   (right-size from usage)                     │
  │     🖥️ CA  → node COUNT     (add when Pending / remove when idle)       │
  │                                                                         │
  │   REQUESTS tie it together — the unit of scheduling AND cost.           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  .vs-prose — In plain words: one Git repository holds the desired state for
  the whole fleet, and a GitOps control plane reconciles it into each cluster
  (dev, stage, prod), with Kustomize overlays supplying per-environment
  differences such as replica counts and resource requests. Inside every
  cluster the easypj-web workload is shaped on three independent axes: the
  HPA changes how MANY pods run based on metrics, the VPA right-sizes how BIG
  each pod's requests are based on real usage, and the Cluster Autoscaler
  changes how many NODES exist — adding one when HPA's new pods go Pending and
  removing one when nodes fall idle. The single field that links scheduling
  and cost across all of this is the resource REQUEST: set it from measured
  usage, give yourself deliberate headroom, and you run easypj across many
  clusters both reliably and affordably.

  ┌──────────────────────── PART 13 — KEY TAKEAWAYS ────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Three pillars: metrics (Prometheus), logs, traces (OTel) -> alerts.   │
  │    Alert on symptoms/SLOs, not raw causes; RED for services, USE for     │
  │    resources.                                                            │
  │ ✅ Requests are the unit of both scheduling AND cost; right-size from    │
  │    real usage; combine HPA (pods) + VPA (size) + Cluster Autoscaler.     │
  │ 🏢 BEYOND: this is the SRE layer that turns "can operate" into "operate  │
  │    well" — not exam-graded but career-defining.                          │
  │ 🔑 kubectl top · PromQL rate()/histogram_quantile · get hpa             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  [PART 13 VISUAL SUMMARY]: see easypj, alert on it, scale it, afford it.

  [PART 14 INTRO]                                                        🎯
  Knowing Kubernetes is necessary but not sufficient: the CKA is a SPEED +
  ACCURACY test under a 2-hour clock. This part converts knowledge into points.

  Every previous part taught you a domain — Pods, Deployments, Services,
  storage, networking, security, cluster lifecycle, troubleshooting. You can
  now BUILD a Kubernetes platform and host easypj on it. But the exam does not
  reward what you know; it rewards what you can FINISH, CORRECTLY, while a
  countdown timer burns in the corner of the screen. The gap between "I knew
  how to do that" and "I scored those points" is exactly what this part closes.

  💡 The single biggest reason competent engineers fail the CKA is not a
     knowledge gap — it's a TIME gap. They get the right answer to question 12
     at minute 130, when the clock stopped at minute 120. Speed is the skill
     this part trains; accuracy keeps the speed honest.

  🧠 ANALOGY — The exam is a sprint-distance triathlon, not a written test.
     You already swam, biked, and ran in training (Parts 1–13). Now you must
     transition between disciplines without fumbling your gear: alias setup,
     context switching, kubectl explain, imperative-to-YAML, verify, move on.
     Transitions — not raw fitness — decide the podium.

  📖 KEY TERM — Point-per-minute (PPM): the exam is weighted, ~15–20 tasks
     worth 1–13% each, 120 minutes total. Treat every minute as currency and
     spend it on the highest-weight, lowest-effort tasks first. Leaving a 13%
     question untouched to perfect a 2% question is how strong candidates fail.

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  chapter turns everything in Chapters 1–44 into a repeatable, point-maximizing
  exam process — a setup ritual, a 3-pass clock strategy, a domain attack plan,
  and a full 20-task simulator on the easypj/jobpost app you have been building.
