    🔑 APPLY ORDER (dependencies first):
    ┌────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ #  │ Object                   │ Why this order                       │
    ├────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ 1  │ Namespace                │ Everything else lives inside it      │
    │ 2  │ ConfigMap + Secret       │ Pods mount these at startup          │
    │ 3  │ StorageClass + PVC       │ DB needs storage before it boots     │
    │ 4  │ StatefulSet + Service db │ Web waits on the DB being reachable  │
    │ 5  │ Job: db-migrate          │ Schema must exist before web serves  │
    │ 6  │ Deployment + Service web │ The app itself                       │
    │ 7  │ Ingress / Gateway        │ External routing, last              │
    │ 8  │ NetworkPolicy            │ Lock down after wiring works         │
    │ 9  │ RBAC, PDB, HPA           │ Hardening + scaling controls         │
    └────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
    One-liner:  kubectl apply -f manifests/ --recursive   (kustomize honors
    its own ordering; for raw YAML, apply the Namespace and Secrets first.)


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.1  Namespace
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: easypj
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
        environment: production


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.2  ConfigMap (non-secret config)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: easypj-config
      namespace: easypj
    data:
      DEBUG: "False"
      DB_NAME: "easypj"
      DB_USER: "easypj"
      DB_HOST: "easypj-db"
      DB_PORT: "5432"
      ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com,easypj-web,localhost"
      DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.3  Secret (sensitive values — base64 in transit, encrypt at rest)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Secret
    metadata:
      name: easypj-secret
      namespace: easypj
    type: Opaque
    stringData:                       # stringData lets you write plaintext;
      SECRET_KEY: "django-insecure-REPLACE-ME-with-a-real-50-char-key"
      DB_PASSWORD: "REPLACE-ME-strong-db-password"
    ⚠️ GOTCHA: a Secret is only base64-encoded, NOT encrypted, unless you have
       EncryptionConfiguration enabled on the API server. Never commit real
       values to git — use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external secrets store.


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.4  StorageClass + PVC
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
    kind: StorageClass
    metadata:
      name: db-storage
    provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner   # swap for your CSI driver
    volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
    reclaimPolicy: Retain
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      name: db-data
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: db-storage
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
    (When using a StatefulSet, the PVC is usually generated by
     volumeClaimTemplates — see E.5 — so this standalone PVC is for the
     Deployment-style alternative.)


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.5  PostgreSQL StatefulSet + headless Service
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: easypj-db
      namespace: easypj
      labels: { app: easypj-db }
    spec:
      clusterIP: None                 # headless → stable DNS per pod
      selector: { app: easypj-db }
      ports:
        - name: postgres
          port: 5432
          targetPort: 5432
    ---
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: StatefulSet
    metadata:
      name: easypj-db
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      serviceName: easypj-db
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: { app: easypj-db }
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: postgres
              image: postgres:16
              ports:
                - containerPort: 5432
              env:
                - name: POSTGRES_DB
                  valueFrom: { configMapKeyRef: { name: easypj-config, key: DB_NAME } }
                - name: POSTGRES_USER
                  valueFrom: { configMapKeyRef: { name: easypj-config, key: DB_USER } }
                - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
                  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
                - name: PGDATA
                  value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
              volumeMounts:
                - name: db-data
                  mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
              readinessProbe:
                exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "easypj"] }
                initialDelaySeconds: 10
                periodSeconds: 5
              livenessProbe:
                exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "easypj"] }
                initialDelaySeconds: 30
                periodSeconds: 10
      volumeClaimTemplates:
        - metadata: { name: db-data }
          spec:
            accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
            storageClassName: db-storage
            resources: { requests: { storage: 10Gi } }


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.6  easypj (Django) Deployment + Service
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: easypj-web
      namespace: easypj
      labels: { app: easypj-web }
    spec:
      replicas: 3
      selector:
        matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
      strategy:
        type: RollingUpdate
        rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: { app: easypj-web }
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: easypj-sa
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            fsGroup: 1000
          containers:
            - name: easypj
              image: registry.example.com/easypj:5.2.5
              ports:
                - containerPort: 8000
              envFrom:
                - configMapRef: { name: easypj-config }
              env:
                - name: SECRET_KEY
                  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: SECRET_KEY } }
                - name: DB_PASSWORD
                  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "256Mi" }
                limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
              readinessProbe:
                httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8000 }
                initialDelaySeconds: 5
                periodSeconds: 10
              livenessProbe:
                httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 8000 }
                initialDelaySeconds: 15
                periodSeconds: 20
              securityContext:
                allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
                readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
              volumeMounts:
                - name: tmp
                  mountPath: /tmp
          volumes:
            - name: tmp
              emptyDir: {}
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: easypj-web
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      type: ClusterIP                 # NodePort/LoadBalancer if no Ingress
      selector: { app: easypj-web }
      ports:
        - name: http
          port: 80
          targetPort: 8000


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.7  Ingress
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Ingress
    metadata:
      name: easypj-ingress
      namespace: easypj
      annotations:
        nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
        cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
    spec:
      ingressClassName: nginx
      tls:
        - hosts: ["easypj.example.com"]
          secretName: easypj-tls
      rules:
        - host: easypj.example.com
          http:
            paths:
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service: { name: easypj-web, port: { number: 80 } }
              - path: /api
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service: { name: easypj-web, port: { number: 80 } }


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.7b  Gateway API: Gateway + HTTPRoute  (modern alternative to Ingress)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🏢 The Gateway API is the successor to Ingress: role-oriented (infra team
       owns the Gateway, app team owns the HTTPRoute) and far more expressive
       (header/weight-based routing, traffic splitting, cross-namespace refs).

    apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Gateway
    metadata:
      name: easypj-gateway
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      gatewayClassName: nginx          # or istio, envoy-gateway, etc.
      listeners:
        - name: https
          protocol: HTTPS
          port: 443
          tls:
            mode: Terminate
            certificateRefs:
              - name: easypj-tls
          allowedRoutes:
            namespaces: { from: Same }
    ---
    apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: HTTPRoute
    metadata:
      name: easypj-route
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      parentRefs:
        - name: easypj-gateway
      hostnames: ["easypj.example.com"]
      rules:
        - matches:
            - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / }
          backendRefs:
            - name: easypj-web
              port: 80


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.8  NetworkPolicy (default-deny + allow web→db, ingress→web)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: default-deny-all
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
    ---
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: db-restrict
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: easypj-db }
      policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
      ingress:
        - from:
            - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: easypj-web } }
          ports:
            - protocol: TCP
              port: 5432
    ---
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: web-allow
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
      policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
      ingress:
        - {}                          # allow from ingress controller / anywhere
      egress:
        - to:
            - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: easypj-db } }
          ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
        - ports:                      # DNS
            - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
            - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.9  RBAC (ServiceAccount + Role + RoleBinding)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ServiceAccount
    metadata:
      name: easypj-sa
      namespace: easypj
    ---
    apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Role
    metadata:
      name: easypj-role
      namespace: easypj
    rules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
        verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
      - apiGroups: [""]
        resources: ["pods"]
        verbs: ["get", "list"]
    ---
    apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: easypj-rolebinding
      namespace: easypj
    subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: easypj-sa
        namespace: easypj
    roleRef:
      kind: Role
      name: easypj-role
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.10  PodDisruptionBudget
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: policy/v1
    kind: PodDisruptionBudget
    metadata:
      name: easypj-web-pdb
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      minAvailable: 2                 # keep ≥2 of 3 web pods during drains
      selector:
        matchLabels: { app: easypj-web }
    ⚡ SPEED TIP: PDB only protects against VOLUNTARY disruptions (drains,
       upgrades). It does not save you from node hardware failure.


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.11  HorizontalPodAutoscaler
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
    kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
    metadata:
      name: easypj-web-hpa
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      scaleTargetRef:
        apiVersion: apps/v1
        kind: Deployment
        name: easypj-web
      minReplicas: 3
      maxReplicas: 10
      metrics:
        - type: Resource
          resource:
            name: cpu
            target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
        - type: Resource
          resource:
            name: memory
            target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 80 }
    ⚠️ GOTCHA: HPA needs the metrics-server installed AND resource requests set
       on the pods (see E.6) — without requests, utilization is undefined.


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.12  Jobs (db-migrate, collectstatic) + CronJob (db-backup)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: batch/v1
    kind: Job
    metadata:
      name: db-migrate
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 4
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: migrate
              image: registry.example.com/easypj:5.2.5
              command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
              envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: easypj-config } }]
              env:
                - name: DB_PASSWORD
                  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
    ---
    apiVersion: batch/v1
    kind: Job
    metadata:
      name: collectstatic
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: collectstatic
              image: registry.example.com/easypj:5.2.5
              command: ["python", "manage.py", "collectstatic", "--noinput"]
              envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: easypj-config } }]
    ---
    apiVersion: batch/v1
    kind: CronJob
    metadata:
      name: db-backup
      namespace: easypj
    spec:
      schedule: "0 2 * * *"           # 02:00 daily
      concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
      successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
      failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
      jobTemplate:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              restartPolicy: OnFailure
              containers:
                - name: backup
                  image: postgres:16
                  command:
                    - /bin/sh
                    - -c
                    - >
                      pg_dump -h easypj-db -U easypj easypj
                      > /backup/easypj-$(date +%F).sql
                  env:
                    - name: PGPASSWORD
                      valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
                  volumeMounts:
                    - name: backup
                      mountPath: /backup
              volumes:
                - name: backup
                  persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: db-backup-pvc }


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.13  Dockerfile (multi-stage) + .dockerignore
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # ---- Dockerfile -----------------------------------------------------
    # Stage 1: build wheels
    FROM python:3.13-slim AS builder
    WORKDIR /app
    RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        build-essential libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

    # Stage 2: slim runtime
    FROM python:3.13-slim
    WORKDIR /app
    RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        libpq5 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
        && groupadd -g 1000 app && useradd -u 1000 -g app app
    COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels -r requirements.txt
    COPY . .
    USER 1000
    EXPOSE 8000
    CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", \
         "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

    # ---- .dockerignore --------------------------------------------------
    .git
    .gitignore
    __pycache__/
    *.pyc
    *.pyo
    *.sqlite3
    db.sqlite3
    .env
    .venv/
    venv/
    node_modules/
    *.md
    k8s/
    manifests/

    🔧 UNDER-THE-HOOD: multi-stage keeps build tools (build-essential) OUT of
       the final image — only the compiled wheels + libpq5 ship, shrinking the
       image and its attack surface. Running as UID 1000 satisfies the
       runAsNonRoot/readOnlyRootFilesystem securityContext in E.6.


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.14  Helm chart skeleton
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Directory layout:
      easypj/
      ├── Chart.yaml
      ├── values.yaml
      ├── templates/
      │   ├── _helpers.tpl
      │   ├── configmap.yaml
      │   ├── secret.yaml
      │   ├── deployment.yaml
      │   ├── service.yaml
      │   ├── statefulset.yaml
      │   ├── ingress.yaml
      │   ├── hpa.yaml
      │   ├── pdb.yaml
      │   └── NOTES.txt
      └── charts/

    # ---- Chart.yaml -----------------------------------------------------
    apiVersion: v2
    name: easypj
    description: easypj Django job board on Kubernetes
    type: application
    version: 0.1.0           # chart version
    appVersion: "5.2.5"      # Django app version

    # ---- values.yaml ----------------------------------------------------
    replicaCount: 3
    image:
      repository: registry.example.com/easypj
      tag: "5.2.5"
      pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    config:
      debug: "False"
      allowedHosts: "easypj.example.com"
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
    autoscaling:
      enabled: true
      minReplicas: 3
      maxReplicas: 10
      targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70
    ingress:
      enabled: true
      host: easypj.example.com

    # ---- templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt showing templating) ---------
    spec:
      replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
      ...
          containers:
            - name: easypj
              image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
              resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 16 }}

    Install / upgrade:
      helm install easypj ./easypj -n easypj --create-namespace
      helm upgrade easypj ./easypj -n easypj -f values-prod.yaml
      helm rollback easypj 1 -n easypj


    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    E.15  Kustomize base + dev/prod overlays
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Directory layout:
      kustomize/
      ├── base/
      │   ├── kustomization.yaml
      │   ├── namespace.yaml
      │   ├── configmap.yaml
      │   ├── deployment.yaml
      │   ├── service.yaml
      │   └── ingress.yaml
      └── overlays/
          ├── dev/
          │   ├── kustomization.yaml
          │   └── replicas-patch.yaml
          └── prod/
              ├── kustomization.yaml
              └── replicas-patch.yaml

    # ---- base/kustomization.yaml ----------------------------------------
    apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: Kustomization
    namespace: easypj
    commonLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
    resources:
      - namespace.yaml
      - configmap.yaml
      - deployment.yaml
      - service.yaml
      - ingress.yaml

    # ---- overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml --------------------------------
    apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: Kustomization
    resources:
      - ../../base
    patches:
      - path: replicas-patch.yaml
    images:
      - name: registry.example.com/easypj
        newTag: dev
    configMapGenerator:
      - name: easypj-config
        behavior: merge
        literals:
          - DEBUG=True

    # ---- overlays/dev/replicas-patch.yaml -------------------------------
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: easypj-web
    spec:
      replicas: 1

    # ---- overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml -------------------------------
    apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: Kustomization
    resources:
      - ../../base
    patches:
      - path: replicas-patch.yaml      # sets replicas: 3
    images:
      - name: registry.example.com/easypj
        newTag: "5.2.5"

    Build / apply:
      kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/dev
      kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/prod
      kustomize build kustomize/overlays/prod | kubectl apply -f -

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — Helm vs Kustomize:
      • Helm    → packaging/distribution, versioned releases, rollback, values
                  templating with logic. Best for shipping a reusable chart.
      • Kustomize → patch-based, template-free, native to kubectl (-k). Best
                  for env overlays of YAML you already own.
      Many teams use both: Helm to install third-party charts, Kustomize to
      overlay their own app manifests.


    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      • Apply order matters: Namespace → Config/Secret → Storage → DB → migrate
        Job → web → Ingress → policies/hardening.
      • The DB is a StatefulSet with a headless Service and volumeClaimTemplates
        for stable identity + per-pod persistent storage.
      • Web is a Deployment with 3 replicas, requests+limits, probes, a hardened
        securityContext, an HPA (3→10), and a PDB (minAvailable 2).
      • Schema changes run as a one-shot Job (db-migrate), never inline in the
        web container's entrypoint at scale.
      • Default-deny NetworkPolicy + targeted allows is the baseline; RBAC grants
        the app SA only get/list on configmaps, secrets, pods.
      • Package it with Helm (versioned releases) or Kustomize (env overlays) —
        or both.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      • Secrets are base64, not encrypted at rest unless you enable
        EncryptionConfiguration — keep real values out of git.
      • HPA silently does nothing without metrics-server AND resource requests.
      • readOnlyRootFilesystem breaks anything that writes to disk — mount an
        emptyDir at /tmp (and any other writable path the app needs).
      • PDB only guards voluntary disruptions; node failure still kills pods.
      • Ingress needs an ingress controller installed; Gateway needs a
        GatewayClass — neither routes traffic on its own.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      • kubectl apply -k <overlay> applies a whole environment in one shot.
      • kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n easypj  → watch a deploy.
      • kubectl get all,ing,pvc,netpol -n easypj  → one-glance inventory.
      • helm rollback easypj <REVISION>  → instant revert of a bad release.

    🔑 COMMANDS
      kubectl apply -f manifests/ --recursive
      kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/prod
      kubectl create job --from=cronjob/db-backup backup-now -n easypj
      kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web -n easypj
      kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web -n easypj
      kubectl scale deploy/easypj-web --replicas=5 -n easypj
      helm upgrade --install easypj ./easypj -n easypj --create-namespace
      kubectl logs job/db-migrate -n easypj

    🧪 LAB Q&A
      Q1: The web pods are CrashLoopBackOff with "could not connect to server:
          Connection refused". The DB StatefulSet is Running. What's the likely
          cause and fix?
      A1: Web came up before the DB was Ready, or a NetworkPolicy blocks 5432.
          Check: the db-restrict policy must allow ingress FROM app=easypj-web
          on TCP 5432, and web's egress policy must permit it. Add an init
          container or readinessProbe-gated startup; ensure DB_HOST=easypj-db
          matches the headless Service name.

      Q2: You applied the HPA but `kubectl get hpa` shows TARGETS as
          <unknown>/70%. Why?
      A2: metrics-server isn't installed, or the Deployment has no CPU
          resources.requests. HPA computes utilization as usage÷request — with
          no request it cannot compute and reports unknown. Install
          metrics-server and set requests (E.6).

      Q3: During a node drain, all three easypj-web pods got evicted at once and
          the site went down. How do you prevent this?
      A3: The PodDisruptionBudget (E.10) with minAvailable: 2 forces the drain
          to evict at most one web pod at a time, keeping ≥2 serving.

      Q4: A teammate committed the Secret YAML with real values to git. Is the
          base64 encoding protection enough? What should you do?
      A4: No — base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone can decode it. Rotate
          SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD immediately, purge the value from git
          history, and move to Sealed Secrets / SOPS / an external secrets
          store. Enable EncryptionConfiguration for at-rest protection in etcd.

      Q5: You need the same manifests for dev (1 replica, DEBUG=True) and prod
          (3 replicas, DEBUG=False) without duplicating YAML. What tool and
          structure?
      A5: Kustomize (E.15): a shared base/ plus overlays/dev and overlays/prod,
          each with a replicas-patch and a configMapGenerator merge to flip
          DEBUG. Apply with kubectl apply -k overlays/<env>.

      Q6: After deploying, static files (CSS/JS) 404. Migrations ran fine. What
          step did you miss?
      A6: The collectstatic Job (E.12) — Django needs `manage.py collectstatic`
          to gather static assets into STATIC_ROOT before they can be served.
          Run it as a Job (or in the image build) and serve via whitenoise or a
          sidecar/Ingress path.

      Q7: How do you trigger an ad-hoc database backup right now instead of
          waiting for the 02:00 CronJob schedule?
      A7: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/db-backup backup-now -n easypj —
          this clones the CronJob's jobTemplate into an immediate one-off Job.

      Q8: You want to switch from Ingress to the Gateway API. What two objects
          replace the Ingress, and who typically owns each?
      A8: A Gateway (owned by the platform/infra team — defines listeners, TLS,
          the GatewayClass) and an HTTPRoute (owned by the app team — defines
          hostnames, path matches, and backendRefs to easypj-web). See E.7b.

    F.1  Exam Format and Rules
         - Duration: 2 hours
         - Questions: 15-20 performance-based tasks
         - Passing score: 66%
         - Open book: kubernetes.io/docs allowed during exam
         - Environment: Remote proctored, Linux terminal
         - Retake: One free retake if you fail
         - Validity: CKA certification valid for 2 years

         [EXAM ENVIRONMENT DETAILS]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  📺 Your exam has multiple clusters — you MUST switch  │
         │  context for each question. Context command is given.  │
         │                                                        │
         │  ✅ Allowed: kubernetes.io/docs                        │
         │  ✅ Allowed: github.com/kubernetes                     │
         │  ✅ Allowed: kubernetes.io/blog                        │
         │  ✅ Allowed: helm.sh/docs (2025)                       │
         │  ✅ Allowed: gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io (2025)            │
         │  ❌ Not allowed: Any other websites                    │
         │  ❌ Not allowed: ChatGPT, forums, Stack Overflow       │
         │  ❌ Not allowed: Personal notes or bookmarks           │
         │                                                        │
         │  Terminal: Ubuntu Linux                                │
         │  Editor: vim, nano available                           │
         │  Tools: kubectl, etcdctl, kubeadm pre-installed       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ⚠️ GOTCHA: every question starts by telling you which cluster/context
         to use. Run the given `kubectl config use-context ...` line FIRST,
         every single time. Solving the right task on the wrong cluster scores
         zero — and is the single most common avoidable mistake.

    F.2  CKA Exam Domain Weights (2025 syllabus)
         [TABLE: Domain weights]
         | Domain                                  | Weight | Questions |
         | Cluster Architecture, Install & Config   | 25%    | ~4-5      |
         | Workloads & Scheduling                   | 15%    | ~2-3      |
         | Services & Networking                    | 20%    | ~3-4      |
         | Storage                                  | 10%    | ~1-2      |
         | Troubleshooting                          | 30%    | ~5-6      |

         [DOMAIN STUDY PRIORITY — Where to focus]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                        │
         │  🔴 TROUBLESHOOTING (30%)      ←── MOST IMPORTANT     │
         │  ████████████████████████████████                      │
         │                                                        │
         │  🟡 CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE (25%) ←── VERY IMPORTANT     │
         │  ██████████████████████████                            │
         │                                                        │
         │  🟡 NETWORKING (20%)                                   │
         │  ████████████████████                                  │
         │                                                        │
         │  🟢 WORKLOADS (15%)                                    │
         │  ██████████████                                        │
         │                                                        │
         │  🟢 STORAGE (10%)              ←── LEAST BUT DON'T    │
         │  ██████████                        SKIP IT             │
         │                                                        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🔑 Troubleshooting + Cluster Architecture together are 55% of the
         exam. If you are short on study time, drill those two domains until
         they are automatic, then round out Networking and Workloads.

    F.3  Time Management and Exam Strategy
         ✅ Set up the environment in the first 60 seconds:
            alias k=kubectl
            export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
            k run pod1 --image=nginx $do > pod.yaml
         ✅ Bookmark important docs pages (see F.7 for the full list):
            - kubectl Cheat Sheet
            - kubeadm upgrade
            - etcd backup/restore
            - RBAC
            - Network Policies
         ✅ Time budget: ~6 minutes per question
         ✅ Skip hard questions, come back later
         ✅ Verify every change (kubectl get, describe)
         ❌ Don't memorize YAML — use kubectl create --dry-run
         ❌ Don't spend >10 min on one question

         [TIME MANAGEMENT STRATEGY]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  FIRST PASS (0-60 min):                                │
         │  → Do all easy/medium questions first                  │
         │  → Mark hard ones and SKIP (flag button)              │
         │  → Target 60-70% of questions completed               │
         │                                                        │
         │  SECOND PASS (60-100 min):                             │
         │  → Return to flagged questions                         │
         │  → Use remaining time on harder problems              │
         │                                                        │
         │  FINAL PASS (100-120 min):                             │
         │  → Verify all answers — kubectl get to confirm        │
         │  → Check context — are you on the right cluster?     │
         │  → Double-check namespaces                             │
         │                                                        │
         │  ⚡ Speed boosters:                                    │
         │  → Tab completion saves seconds per command            │
         │  → alias k=kubectl saves ~100+ keystrokes             │
         │  → Copy/paste from docs saves writing YAML            │
         │  → --dry-run=client -o yaml is your best friend      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         💡 INSIGHT: each question is worth a fixed percentage shown in its
         header (e.g. "Weightage: 7%"). Spend time proportional to the weight.
         Bank the high-weight, low-effort questions first; never sink 20
         minutes into a 2% question while a 7% question sits unflagged.

    F.4  Practice Lab Recommendations
         1. killer.sh (official CKA simulator — two free sessions ship with
            your exam registration; sessions are deliberately HARDER than the
            real exam, so finishing them is a strong readiness signal)
         2. KodeKloud CKA course labs
         3. Kubernetes the Hard Way (Kelsey Hightower)
         4. Set up a local cluster with kubeadm (vagrant/VMs)
         5. Practice etcd backup/restore at least 5 times
         6. Practice cluster upgrades at least 3 times
         7. Build kubeadm-the-hard-way style multi-node clusters until the
            init/join/CNI sequence is muscle memory

         🧪 LAB: stand up a two-node kubeadm cluster, deploy the easypj /
         jobpost app to it (PostgreSQL StatefulSet + Django Deployment +
         Service + Ingress), then deliberately break it — delete a Secret,
         corrupt a probe, taint the node — and time yourself fixing each.
         This mirrors the exam's "diagnose and repair" troubleshooting style.

    F.5  Exam Day Checklist
         [CHECKLIST: Day-of preparation]
         ✅ Government-issued photo ID ready
         ✅ Webcam working, room clean and clear
         ✅ Stable internet connection (wired preferred)
         ✅ Second monitor disconnected
         ✅ Room must be private — no other people
         ✅ Desk must be clear except computer
         ✅ Know your PSI bridge login credentials
         ✅ Check-in opens 30 minutes before exam
         ✅ Have water in a clear container (allowed)
         ❌ No phones, smart watches, or external devices
         ❌ No headphones or earbuds
         ❌ No writing on walls or desk

         ⚡ SPEED TIP: the moment the terminal opens, paste your setup block
         (alias k=kubectl, the $do export, kubectl completion, vim ~/.vimrc
         with `set ts=2 sw=2 et`). Thirty seconds here saves minutes across
         every YAML question for the next two hours.

    F.6  What Changed in 2025
         The 2025 CKA syllabus modernized the tooling expectations. Be ready
         for these in addition to the classic core:

         [TABLE: 2025 syllabus additions]
         | Area                  | What's now in scope                        |
         | Helm                  | Install/upgrade/rollback releases; inspect  |
         |                       | values; helm.sh/docs is allowed in-exam.    |
         | Kustomize             | bases + overlays; `kubectl apply -k`;       |
         |                       | patches and common labels.                  |
         | CRDs                  | Read/apply CustomResourceDefinitions and    |
         |                       | their custom resources; inspect with        |
         |                       | `kubectl get crd` / `kubectl explain`.      |
         | Gateway API           | GatewayClass / Gateway / HTTPRoute as the   |
         |                       | successor to Ingress; gateway-api.sigs.k8s. |
         |                       | io is allowed in-exam.                       |
         | Dynamic provisioning  | StorageClasses + PVCs that auto-create PVs; |
         |                       | reclaim policies and volume binding modes.  |

         🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: Ingress is still on the exam, but Gateway API is
         now fair game too. Know how a Service is exposed via BOTH an Ingress
         resource and an HTTPRoute, and how to copy each YAML straight from
         the docs rather than authoring from memory.

    F.7  Exam-Day Doc Bookmarks (the exam is OPEN-BOOK)
         Allowed sites: kubernetes.io/docs, helm.sh, gateway-api docs,
         kubernetes.io/blog, github.com/kubernetes. Pre-bookmark the pages
         below. SEARCH the docs, don't scroll; copy the complex YAML straight
         from the page into your file and edit it.

         🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING WORKFLOW (memorize this loop — it solves most of
         the 30% troubleshooting domain):
           1. kubectl get nodes / pods -A   → what's NotReady / not Running?
           2. kubectl describe <obj>        → read Events at the bottom first
           3. kubectl logs <pod> [-p]       → -p for the previous crash
           4. kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
           5. On the node: systemctl status kubelet; journalctl -u kubelet
           6. Fix → re-apply → kubectl get to CONFIRM the fix landed

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
       - 66% to pass, 2 hours, 15-20 hands-on tasks, multiple clusters.
       - Switch context FIRST on every question; wrong cluster = zero credit.
       - Troubleshooting (30%) + Cluster Architecture (25%) = 55% of marks.
       - It's open-book: search the docs, copy YAML, edit. Don't memorize it.
       - 2025 adds Helm, Kustomize, CRDs, Gateway API, dynamic provisioning.
       - One free retake is included — but plan to pass on the first attempt.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
       - Forgetting `use-context` and editing the wrong cluster.
       - Ignoring the namespace; many tasks specify `-n <ns>` and grading
         checks the exact namespace.
       - Hand-typing long YAML instead of copying from the open docs.
       - Sinking >10 minutes into a single low-weight question.
       - Not verifying the fix with `kubectl get`/`describe` before moving on.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
       - alias k=kubectl ; export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml" ; enable
         kubectl completion; set vim to 2-space expandtab.
       - Generate manifests: k run / k create deploy ... $do > f.yaml.
       - Use `kubectl explain <resource>.spec` instead of guessing fields.
       - Flag-and-skip hard questions; finish the cheap points first.

    🔑 COMMANDS
       kubectl config get-contexts
       kubectl config use-context <ctx>
       kubectl run pod1 --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
       kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx $do > deploy.yaml
       kubectl get pods -A -o wide
       kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
       kubectl logs <pod> -p -n <ns>
       kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A
       kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod        # Kustomize
       helm upgrade --install <rel> <chart>     # Helm

    🧪 LAB Q&A
       Q1. A question opens with a context command but you skip it and solve
           the task on your current cluster. What score do you get?
       A1. Zero. Grading runs against the cluster named in the question. Always
           run `kubectl config use-context <ctx>` before touching anything.

       Q2. You need a NetworkPolicy YAML but can't recall the selector syntax.
           What's the fastest legal move in the exam?
       A2. Open kubernetes.io/docs Network Policies page (it's allowed), copy
           the example manifest, and edit the selectors/ports for the task.

       Q3. The exam header says "Weightage: 8%" but the task is fiddly and
           you're 12 minutes in with no progress. What do you do?
       A3. Flag it and move on. Bank the remaining easy points first, then
           return on the second pass — never blow your time budget on one item.

       Q4. A 2025-syllabus question asks you to expose a Service using the
           Gateway API instead of Ingress. Where do you look?
       A4. gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io is allowed in-exam — copy the GatewayClass /
           Gateway / HTTPRoute examples and adapt them to the Service.

       Q5. You restored etcd but the API server still shows old data. First
           check?
       A5. Confirm you pointed the static pod / kube-apiserver at the restored
           data-dir and restarted it; verify with `kubectl get` after the
           kubelet brings the control-plane pods back. Practice this 5+ times.

  Appendix H: CKA Exam Simulator — 20 Performance Tasks
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The full timed simulator (see Ch 45.8) broken out as a standalone, with
    domain distribution, suggested pace, and per-task answer + explanation +
    YAML/diagram. Target: <120 min, self-score, 75%+ = ready.

    META | appendix=H | mode=timed-simulation | tasks=20 | budget=120 min
         | pass=75% | env=2025 syllabus | project=easypj / app=jobpost
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------

    🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS
      The real CKA is 2 hours, ~15–20 weighted performance tasks, on live
      clusters, scored by an automated grader. You don't get partial credit
      for "almost"; the resource either matches the rubric or it doesn't.
      This simulator rehearses the three things that actually fail people:
      (1) running out of TIME, (2) editing the WRONG cluster/namespace, and
      (3) producing YAML that looks right but doesn't apply or doesn't pass.
      Run it once cold to find your weak domain, then again to confirm pace.

    🧭 HOW TO USE THIS SIMULATOR
      1. Set a real 120-minute timer. No pausing, no docs except
         kubernetes.io/docs (mirrors the exam's allowed tab).
      2. Each task names its target context and namespace — switch FIRST,
         every time. Most lost points are "right answer, wrong cluster."
      3. Do the easy/high-weight tasks first; flag and skip hard ones.
      4. Self-score against the rubric checkbox list per task. 1 point each.
      5. 15/20 (75%) within the time box = exam-ready. Below 12/20, drill the
         weak domain (see the per-domain chapter pointers) and rerun.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    📊 DOMAIN DISTRIBUTION (mirrors the 2025 CKA blueprint weighting)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------

      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┬──────┐
      │ Domain                                         │ Weight │ Tasks │ Pts  │
      ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┼──────┤
      │ Cluster Architecture, Installation & Config    │  25%   │  T1–5 │   5  │
      │ Workloads & Scheduling                         │  15%   │ T6–8  │   3  │
      │ Services & Networking                          │  20%   │ T9–12 │   4  │
      │ Storage                                        │  10%   │ T13–14│   2  │
      │ Troubleshooting                                │  30%   │ T15–20│   6  │
      ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┼──────┤
      │ TOTAL                                          │ 100%   │   20  │  20  │
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┴──────┘

      Note Troubleshooting is the single heaviest domain on the real exam
      (~30%). The simulator deliberately back-loads six diagnose-and-fix
      tasks (T15–T20) so you practise debugging under time pressure.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⏱  SUGGESTED PACE (120-minute budget, with built-in buffer)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------

      Phase 0 (00:00–00:03)  Setup: read all 20, flag the 3 hardest, note
                             which need a context switch. Set kubectl aliases.
      Phase 1 (00:03–00:45)  Sweep the "fast wins": T1, T6, T7, T9, T13, T15,
                             T16 — short, high-yield, ~5 min each.
      Phase 2 (00:45–01:35)  Heavier tasks: T2–T5 (control plane), T10–T12,
                             T14, T17–T19. Budget ~8–10 min each; skip-and-flag
                             anything you stall on past +3 min.
      Phase 3 (01:35–01:55)  Return to flagged tasks (T20, etcd, upgrade).
      Phase 4 (01:55–02:00)  VERIFY: re-run `kubectl get` on every object you
                             created; confirm namespace/context on each.

      🧠 ANALOGY: Treat it like an exam invigilator's clock, not a workout —
      banking three 5-minute wins early buys you the calm to think on the
      30%-weighted troubleshooting block later.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔧 PRE-FLIGHT SETUP (do this in the first 60 seconds, every run)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------

      # Aliases that save ~15 min over a 2-hour exam
      alias k=kubectl
      export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"     # generate manifests fast
      export now="--grace-period=0 --force"    # immediate delete (cleanup)
      source <(kubectl completion bash)
      complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k

      # Always know where you are before you touch anything:
      kubectl config get-contexts
      kubectl config current-context

      ⚡ SPEED TIP: vim ~/.vimrc once — `set ts=2 sw=2 et ai nu` — so pasted
      YAML keeps 2-space indent. A single bad tab fails an entire task.

    ==========================================================================
    DOMAIN 1 — CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE, INSTALLATION & CONFIGURATION (T1–T5)
    ==========================================================================

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 1  (1 pt, ~4 min) — RBAC: bind a Role to a ServiceAccount
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Create a ServiceAccount `deploy-bot` in namespace `jobpost`. Create a
      Role `pod-reader` granting get/list/watch on pods, and bind it to that
      ServiceAccount with a RoleBinding `read-pods`.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] SA deploy-bot exists in jobpost
         [ ] Role pod-reader allows get,list,watch on pods (core group "")
         [ ] RoleBinding read-pods links Role -> SA in jobpost

      ✔ Answer (imperative — fastest, fully scorable):
        kubectl create sa deploy-bot -n jobpost
        kubectl create role pod-reader -n jobpost \
            --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
        kubectl create rolebinding read-pods -n jobpost \
            --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=jobpost:deploy-bot

      ✔ Equivalent YAML (kubectl apply -f -):
        apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
        kind: Role
        metadata:
          name: pod-reader
          namespace: jobpost
        rules:
        - apiGroups: [""]
          resources: ["pods"]
          verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
        ---
        apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
        kind: RoleBinding
        metadata:
          name: read-pods
          namespace: jobpost
        roleRef:
          apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
          kind: Role
          name: pod-reader
        subjects:
        - kind: ServiceAccount
          name: deploy-bot
          namespace: jobpost

      💡 Explanation: RBAC is additive and deny-by-default. A Role is
      namespaced; the RoleBinding's roleRef is immutable once created (delete
      and recreate to change it). Verify it actually grants access:
        kubectl auth can-i list pods -n jobpost \
            --as=system:serviceaccount:jobpost:deploy-bot   # -> yes
      See Ch 18 (RBAC).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 2  (1 pt, ~8 min) — Upgrade a control-plane node with kubeadm
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster2   Node: cp-1
      The control plane runs v1.30.x. Upgrade the control-plane node `cp-1`
      and its kubelet/kubectl to v1.31.0. Drain and uncordon as required.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] kubeadm upgraded to 1.31.0 on cp-1
         [ ] `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.0` succeeded
         [ ] kubelet + kubectl on cp-1 are 1.31.0, kubelet restarted
         [ ] node cordoned for the upgrade then uncordoned, Ready

      ✔ Answer (run on cp-1):
        # 1. drain it (from a node that can reach the API)
        kubectl drain cp-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

        # 2. bump the kubeadm binary (Debian/Ubuntu repo)
        apt-mark unhold kubeadm
        apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.31.0-1.1
        apt-mark hold kubeadm
        kubeadm version                       # confirm 1.31.0

        # 3. plan + apply the control-plane upgrade
        kubeadm upgrade plan
        kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.0

        # 4. now the kubelet + kubectl
        apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl
        apt-get install -y kubelet=1.31.0-1.1 kubectl=1.31.0-1.1
        apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
        systemctl daemon-reload
        systemctl restart kubelet

        # 5. bring it back
        kubectl uncordon cp-1
        kubectl get nodes                     # cp-1 Ready, v1.31.0

      💡 Explanation: ORDER matters — kubeadm binary first, then
      `upgrade apply` (which upgrades the static-pod control plane: apiserver,
      controller-manager, scheduler, etcd), THEN kubelet/kubectl. On worker
      nodes you use `kubeadm upgrade node` instead of `upgrade apply`.
      ⚠️ GOTCHA: Never skip a minor version (1.30 -> 1.32 in one hop is
      unsupported). See Ch 6 (kubeadm upgrades).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔴 TASK 3  (1 pt, ~9 min) — etcd snapshot save AND restore
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster2   Node: cp-1
      Take a snapshot of the etcd database to /opt/etcd-backup.db, then
      restore it into a new data dir /var/lib/etcd-restore.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] snapshot saved to /opt/etcd-backup.db
         [ ] snapshot restored to /var/lib/etcd-restore
         [ ] etcd static pod points at the restored dir, cluster healthy

      ✔ Answer (on cp-1, certs from the etcd static-pod manifest):
        export ETCDCTL_API=3
        CACERT=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
        CERT=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt
        KEY=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

        # SAVE
        etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
          --cacert=$CACERT --cert=$CERT --key=$KEY \
          snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db
        etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db

        # RESTORE into a fresh dir
        etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
          --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore

        # point etcd at the restored dir, then let kubelet restart the pod
        # edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
        #   - hostPath volume "etcd-data": path: /var/lib/etcd-restore
        #   (the --data-dir flag stays /var/lib/etcd, the MOUNT moves)

      💡 Explanation: `snapshot restore` writes a brand-new member directory;
      it does NOT touch the running etcd. You activate it by repointing the
      etcd static pod's hostPath volume to the restore dir. Because etcd is a
      static pod, moving its manifest out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests stops
      it and moving it back starts it — handy if the API is unstable.
      ⚠️ Restore times out? Check certs and that you used --data-dir, not the
      live dir. See Ch 7 (etcd backup/restore).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 4  (1 pt, ~6 min) — Static Pod on a specific node
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Node: node01
      Create a static pod named `web-static` running image nginx:1.27 on
      node01 only. It must come up via the kubelet's manifest path.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] manifest placed in node01's static-pod dir
         [ ] pod shows as web-static-node01 in `kubectl get po -A`
         [ ] image is nginx:1.27, Running

      ✔ Answer (on node01):
        # find the path (default below); confirm with:
        #   grep staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
        cat <<'EOF' > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/web-static.yaml
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Pod
        metadata:
          name: web-static
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: web
            image: nginx:1.27
        EOF
        # kubelet auto-creates it within seconds; the API mirror pod is
        # named web-static-node01 and cannot be deleted via kubectl.

      💡 Explanation: Static pods are managed by the kubelet, not the
      scheduler. The mirror pod in the API server is read-only — delete the
      MANIFEST to remove it. The "-node01" suffix is how you tell a static
      pod from a normal one. See Ch 9 (static pods).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 5  (1 pt, ~7 min) — Generate a kubeconfig user via CSR
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1
      A new user `dev-amy` needs cluster access. A CSR named `dev-amy` is
      already submitted. Approve it, then build a kubeconfig context that
      authenticates as dev-amy.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] CSR dev-amy Approved and Issued
         [ ] credential set with the issued client cert + key
         [ ] context dev-amy@cluster works for `kubectl get pods`

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl get csr
        kubectl certificate approve dev-amy
        kubectl get csr dev-amy -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' \
            | base64 -d > dev-amy.crt

        kubectl config set-credentials dev-amy \
            --client-certificate=dev-amy.crt --client-key=dev-amy.key
        kubectl config set-context dev-amy@cluster \
            --cluster=cluster1 --user=dev-amy
        kubectl --context=dev-amy@cluster get pods   # verify

      💡 Explanation: x509 client certs are the simplest CKA auth path. The
      cert's CN becomes the username, the O field becomes the group — those
      drive RBAC. Certs can't be revoked, only expired; that's why production
      uses short-lived tokens. See Ch 17 (authentication, CSR API).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 6  (1 pt, ~5 min) — Deployment + rolling update + rollback
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Create a Deployment `jobpost-api` with 3 replicas of
      easypj/jobpost:1.0. Update it to 1.1, then roll back to 1.0.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] Deployment jobpost-api, 3 replicas, all Ready
         [ ] image updated to 1.1 (rollout recorded)
         [ ] rolled back; image is easypj/jobpost:1.0 again

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl create deployment jobpost-api -n jobpost \
            --image=easypj/jobpost:1.0 --replicas=3
        kubectl set image deploy/jobpost-api jobpost=easypj/jobpost:1.1 \
            -n jobpost
        kubectl rollout status deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost
        kubectl rollout undo deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost
        kubectl rollout history deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost

      💡 Explanation: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets; a rolling update creates
      a NEW ReplicaSet and scales the old one down. `rollout undo` simply
      scales the previous ReplicaSet back up — that's why revision history
      matters. See Ch 11 (Deployments).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 7  (1 pt, ~5 min) — Taints, tolerations & nodeSelector
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1
      Taint node02 with `gpu=true:NoSchedule`. Create a pod `gpu-job`
      (image busybox, sleep 3600) that tolerates it AND is forced onto node02.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] node02 has taint gpu=true:NoSchedule
         [ ] gpu-job tolerates gpu=true:NoSchedule
         [ ] gpu-job is Running on node02

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl taint nodes node02 gpu=true:NoSchedule
        cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Pod
        metadata: { name: gpu-job }
        spec:
          nodeSelector: { kubernetes.io/hostname: node02 }
          tolerations:
          - key: "gpu"
            operator: "Equal"
            value: "true"
            effect: "NoSchedule"
          containers:
          - name: c
            image: busybox
            command: ["sleep", "3600"]
        EOF

      💡 Explanation: A toleration only lets a pod be SCHEDULED onto a tainted
      node — it does not ATTRACT it. To pin the pod you also need nodeSelector
      or affinity. Taint without toleration = repelled; toleration without
      selector = allowed but not required. See Ch 13 (scheduling).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 8  (1 pt, ~6 min) — Resource requests/limits + HPA target
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Edit Deployment `jobpost-api` so each container requests 100m CPU /
      128Mi memory and is limited to 250m / 256Mi. Then create a HPA scaling
      2–6 replicas at 70% CPU.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] requests cpu=100m mem=128Mi set on the container
         [ ] limits cpu=250m mem=256Mi set
         [ ] HPA targets jobpost-api, min=2 max=6, cpu 70%

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl set resources deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost \
            --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi \
            --limits=cpu=250m,memory=256Mi
        kubectl autoscale deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost \
            --min=2 --max=6 --cpu-percent=70

      💡 Explanation: HPA needs metrics-server running and CPU REQUESTS set,
      or it reports <unknown>/70% and never scales. Requests drive scheduling
      and HPA math; limits cap usage (memory limit overrun = OOMKill, CPU
      limit = throttle). See Ch 14 (autoscaling) and Ch 12 (resources).

    DOMAIN 3 — SERVICES & NETWORKING (T9–T12)

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 9  (1 pt, ~4 min) — Expose a Deployment as a Service
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Expose `jobpost-api` on port 80 -> targetPort 8000 as a ClusterIP
      Service named `jobpost-svc`.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] Service jobpost-svc, type ClusterIP
         [ ] port 80, targetPort 8000
         [ ] selector matches jobpost-api pods; Endpoints populated

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl expose deploy/jobpost-api -n jobpost \
            --name=jobpost-svc --port=80 --target-port=8000
        kubectl get endpoints jobpost-svc -n jobpost   # must be non-empty

      💡 Explanation: A Service's selector must match the POD labels (the
      Deployment template labels), not the Deployment name. Empty Endpoints =
      selector mismatch or no Ready pods — the #1 "service doesn't work"
      cause. See Ch 21 (Services).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 10  (1 pt, ~8 min) — Ingress routing two paths
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      An ingress controller is installed. Create an Ingress `jobpost-ing` on
      host easypj.local routing `/api` -> jobpost-svc:80 and `/` ->
      frontend-svc:80.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] Ingress jobpost-ing, host easypj.local
         [ ] /api -> jobpost-svc:80 (Prefix)
         [ ] / -> frontend-svc:80 (Prefix)

      ✔ Answer:
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: Ingress
        metadata:
          name: jobpost-ing
          namespace: jobpost
        spec:
          rules:
          - host: easypj.local
            http:
              paths:
              - path: /api
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service:
                    name: jobpost-svc
                    port: { number: 80 }
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
                backend:
                  service:
                    name: frontend-svc
                    port: { number: 80 }

      💡 Explanation: Order paths most-specific first; many controllers match
      top-down. `pathType: Prefix` is the safe default. The Ingress is inert
      without a controller and an IngressClass — check `kubectl get
      ingressclass`. See Ch 23 (Ingress).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔴 TASK 11  (1 pt, ~9 min) — NetworkPolicy default-deny + allow
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Lock down `jobpost`: deny all ingress by default, but allow pods
      labelled `role=frontend` to reach pods labelled `app=jobpost-api` on
      TCP 8000.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] a default-deny-ingress policy selects all pods
         [ ] an allow policy permits role=frontend -> app=jobpost-api:8000
         [ ] frontend can curl :8000, other pods cannot

      ✔ Answer:
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: NetworkPolicy
        metadata:
          name: default-deny-ingress
          namespace: jobpost
        spec:
          podSelector: {}
          policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
        ---
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: NetworkPolicy
        metadata:
          name: allow-frontend
          namespace: jobpost
        spec:
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: jobpost-api }
          policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
          ingress:
          - from:
            - podSelector:
                matchLabels: { role: frontend }
            ports:
            - protocol: TCP
              port: 8000

      💡 Explanation: NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE allow-lists; the empty
      podSelector `{}` selects every pod, and with no ingress rules that means
      deny-all. The second policy then opens one path. ⚠️ GOTCHA: policies do
      nothing unless the CNI enforces them (Calico/Cilium yes, flannel no).
      See Ch 24 (NetworkPolicy).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 12  (1 pt, ~6 min) — CoreDNS / Service DNS resolution
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1
      DNS lookups for Services in namespace `jobpost` are failing from pods in
      `default`. Diagnose and confirm the correct FQDN that resolves
      jobpost-svc.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] CoreDNS pods Running in kube-system
         [ ] kube-dns Service has a ClusterIP and Endpoints
         [ ] FQDN jobpost-svc.jobpost.svc.cluster.local resolves

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
        kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system
        kubectl run dnstest --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
            nslookup jobpost-svc.jobpost.svc.cluster.local

      💡 Explanation: Cross-namespace lookups need the FULL name
      `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`; a bare `jobpost-svc` only resolves
      inside the SAME namespace via the search domain. If even the FQDN fails,
      check CoreDNS pods and the kube-dns Service Endpoints. See Ch 22 (DNS).

    DOMAIN 4 — STORAGE (T13–T14)
    ==========================================================================

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 13  (1 pt, ~6 min) — PV + PVC + mount into a Pod
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Create a 1Gi hostPath PV `pv-data` (/mnt/data), a matching PVC
      `pvc-data` (1Gi, RWO), and a pod that mounts it at /usr/share/data.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] PV pv-data 1Gi, RWO, hostPath /mnt/data
         [ ] PVC pvc-data Bound to pv-data
         [ ] pod mounts pvc-data at /usr/share/data, Running

      ✔ Answer:
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: PersistentVolume
        metadata: { name: pv-data }
        spec:
          capacity: { storage: 1Gi }
          accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
          hostPath: { path: /mnt/data }
        ---
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
        metadata: { name: pvc-data, namespace: jobpost }
        spec:
          accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
          resources: { requests: { storage: 1Gi } }
        ---
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Pod
        metadata: { name: data-pod, namespace: jobpost }
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: c
            image: nginx:1.27
            volumeMounts:
            - name: d
              mountPath: /usr/share/data
          volumes:
          - name: d
            persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: pvc-data }

      💡 Explanation: A PVC binds to a PV only if capacity, accessModes and
      storageClassName are all compatible. Leaving storageClassName unset on
      both (or "") avoids the default-StorageClass dynamic provisioner. RWO =
      one node at a time. See Ch 26 (volumes) and Ch 27 (PV/PVC).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 14  (1 pt, ~6 min) — StorageClass + dynamic provisioning + expand
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Create a StorageClass `fast` (allowVolumeExpansion). Create a PVC
      `pvc-fast` (2Gi) using it, then expand the PVC to 4Gi.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] SC fast, allowVolumeExpansion: true
         [ ] PVC pvc-fast requests storageClassName fast
         [ ] PVC spec.resources.requests.storage updated to 4Gi

      ✔ Answer:
        apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
        kind: StorageClass
        metadata: { name: fast }
        provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner   # use your cluster's
        allowVolumeExpansion: true
        volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
        ---
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
        metadata: { name: pvc-fast, namespace: jobpost }
        spec:
          accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
          storageClassName: fast
          resources: { requests: { storage: 2Gi } }

        # then expand:
        kubectl patch pvc pvc-fast -n jobpost \
          -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"4Gi"}}}}'

      💡 Explanation: Expansion only works if the StorageClass has
      allowVolumeExpansion: true AND the provisioner supports it. You can only
      grow a PVC, never shrink it. WaitForFirstConsumer defers binding until a
      pod schedules, so the volume lands on the right node. See Ch 28
      (StorageClasses).

    ==========================================================================
    DOMAIN 5 — TROUBLESHOOTING (T15–T20)  ← heaviest, 30%
    ==========================================================================

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 15  (1 pt, ~5 min) — Fix a CrashLoopBackOff pod
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Pod `broken-app` is in CrashLoopBackOff. Diagnose and make it Running.
      (The container command points at a binary that doesn't exist.)

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] root cause identified from logs/describe
         [ ] pod corrected (command/image fixed)
         [ ] broken-app Running, restartCount stable

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl describe pod broken-app -n jobpost   # Last State, Exit Code
        kubectl logs broken-app -n jobpost --previous # crash output
        # fix the bad command, then re-apply (pods are mostly immutable):
        kubectl get pod broken-app -n jobpost -o yaml > fix.yaml
        # edit command/args, then:
        kubectl replace --force -f fix.yaml

      💡 Explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts then exits
      repeatedly. `--previous` shows the dead container's logs (the live one
      may not exist yet). Exit 0 = finished (needs a long-running cmd);
      Exit 1/2 = app error; Exit 127 = command not found; Exit 137 = OOMKill.
      See Ch 43 (app troubleshooting).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 TASK 16  (1 pt, ~5 min) — Recover a NotReady node (kubelet down)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster2   Node: node01
      node01 shows NotReady. SSH in, find why, and bring it Ready.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] kubelet service status checked
         [ ] root cause found (kubelet stopped / misconfig)
         [ ] node01 returns to Ready

      ✔ Answer (on node01):
        systemctl status kubelet
        journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
        systemctl enable --now kubelet
        systemctl restart kubelet
        # back on the control plane:
        kubectl get nodes

      💡 Explanation: NotReady almost always = the kubelet isn't running or
      can't reach the API server. Order of checks: kubelet service ->
      journalctl -> /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml -> /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
      -> container runtime (`crictl ps`). A stopped or crashed kubelet is the
      textbook cause. See Ch 42 (cluster troubleshooting).

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 17  (1 pt, ~7 min) — Pod stuck Pending (scheduling failure)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Pod `big-app` is Pending. Find why and let it schedule. (It requests
      8 CPU, more than any node offers.)

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] Pending cause read from `kubectl describe` Events
         [ ] fix applied (lower request OR add toleration/label as needed)
         [ ] big-app schedules to a node, Running

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl describe pod big-app -n jobpost   # Events: 0/3 nodes available
        # "Insufficient cpu" -> request exceeds capacity. Lower it:
        kubectl get pod big-app -n jobpost -o yaml > big.yaml
        # set resources.requests.cpu to a feasible value (e.g. 500m)
        kubectl replace --force -f big.yaml

      💡 Explanation: Pending = the SCHEDULER couldn't place it. Read the
      Events at the bottom of `describe`: "Insufficient cpu/memory",
      "node(s) had taint", "didn't match nodeSelector/affinity", or "no PV
      available". Each maps to a precise fix. See Ch 42.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟡 TASK 18  (1 pt, ~8 min) — Service has no Endpoints
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      `jobpost-svc` exists but returns no traffic. Diagnose and restore
      connectivity. (The Service selector doesn't match the pod labels.)

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] confirmed Endpoints empty
         [ ] root cause = selector/label mismatch (or no Ready pods)
         [ ] Endpoints populated; curl to ClusterIP succeeds

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl get endpoints jobpost-svc -n jobpost      # <none>
        kubectl get svc jobpost-svc -n jobpost -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
        kubectl get pods -n jobpost --show-labels         # compare labels
        # fix the Service selector to match the pods (or fix pod labels):
        kubectl patch svc jobpost-svc -n jobpost \
          -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"jobpost-api"}}}'
        kubectl get endpoints jobpost-svc -n jobpost      # now populated

      💡 Explanation: A Service with empty Endpoints means kube-proxy has
      nothing to route to. Causes, in order to check: selector ≠ pod labels;
      pods not Ready (failing readiness probe); wrong targetPort. The fix is
      almost always aligning the selector with the pod template labels.
      See Ch 21 (Services) and Ch 42.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔴 TASK 19  (1 pt, ~9 min) — Control-plane component down (API errors)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster2   Node: cp-1
      kubectl commands intermittently fail. The kube-apiserver static pod has
      a bad flag in its manifest. Fix it so the API is healthy.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] identified apiserver static pod / manifest as the fault
         [ ] manifest corrected (bad flag/value/port)
         [ ] API server healthy; `kubectl get nodes` stable

      ✔ Answer (on cp-1):
        # static pods log to the container runtime, not the API:
        crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
        crictl logs <apiserver-container-id>
        # inspect & fix the manifest:
        vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        #   e.g. correct --etcd-servers, --service-cluster-ip-range, a typo'd
        #   flag, or a wrong cert path. Save -> kubelet recreates the pod.
        crictl ps | grep apiserver        # confirm it stays Up
        kubectl get nodes                 # API responsive again

      💡 Explanation: When the API server is down you CAN'T use kubectl —
      drop to `crictl` on the control-plane node and read the static-pod
      manifests under /etc/kubernetes/manifests. The kubelet watches that dir,
      so saving a corrected manifest auto-restarts the component. A crash-loop
      right after editing = your fix has a new typo. See Ch 42.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔴 TASK 20  (1 pt, ~9 min) — Failing readiness/liveness probe
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      Context: cluster1   Namespace: jobpost
      Deployment `probe-app` never becomes Ready and pods restart. The
      liveness probe hits the wrong path/port. Fix the probes.

      ✅ Rubric:
         [ ] root cause = misconfigured probe (path/port/timing)
         [ ] probe corrected (httpGet path/port or thresholds)
         [ ] pods become Ready and stop restarting

      ✔ Answer:
        kubectl describe pod -l app=probe-app -n jobpost
        #  "Liveness probe failed: HTTP 404" or "connection refused"
        kubectl edit deploy probe-app -n jobpost
        # correct the probe, e.g.:
        #   livenessProbe:
        #     httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }
        #     initialDelaySeconds: 10
        #     periodSeconds: 5
        #   readinessProbe:
        #     httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8000 }
        kubectl rollout status deploy/probe-app -n jobpost

      💡 Explanation: A failing LIVENESS probe restarts the container (causes
      restart loops); a failing READINESS probe just keeps the pod out of the
      Service Endpoints (no restart, but no traffic). Symptoms tell you which:
      restarts -> liveness; Ready 0/1 but no restarts -> readiness. Common
      culprits: wrong port/path, initialDelaySeconds too short for a slow app
      (Django migrations!), or probing before the server binds. See Ch 12 and
      Ch 43.
