      <12  / 20    ▓▓▓░░░░░░░   Not yet. Don't book. Work the domain with the
                                most ☐ — usually Troubleshooting or Cluster.

      🔑 MUST-REMEMBER: a task only scores if (a) it's in the RIGHT cluster
      and namespace, and (b) it actually APPLIES and PASSES verification. "I
      typed the right YAML" earns nothing if you never ran kubectl apply.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 EXAM-DAY COMMAND CHEAT (the 12 that win the most points)
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------

      kubectl config use-context <ctx>            # ALWAYS, before every task
      kubectl run pod --image=img $do > p.yaml    # fast manifest skeleton
      kubectl create deploy d --image=img $do      # fast deploy skeleton
      kubectl expose deploy d --port=80 --target-port=8000
      kubectl explain pod.spec.containers --recursive   # field lookup, no web
      kubectl describe <obj> | tail -20            # Events tell the story
      kubectl logs <pod> --previous                # crashed-container logs
      kubectl get ev -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp   # cluster-wide timeline
      kubectl auth can-i <verb> <res> --as=<user>  # verify RBAC
      kubectl get endpoints <svc>                  # is the Service wired up?
      kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
      crictl ps -a / crictl logs <id>              # when the API is down

    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ⚠️ THE FIVE SIMULATOR GOTCHAS THAT COST REAL CANDIDATES POINTS
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
      1. Wrong context/namespace — switch FIRST, verify with get-contexts.
      2. YAML indent drift from pasting — `set ts=2 sw=2 et` saves you.
      3. Editing a running Pod's immutable fields — use `replace --force`.
      4. Forgetting to VERIFY — re-`get` every object in the last 5 minutes.
      5. Sinking 20 min into one hard task — flag, skip, bank the easy points.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      • Generate, don't type: every create/run with $do gives scorable YAML.
      • `kubectl explain --recursive` replaces the docs tab for field names.
      • Bank all 🟢 tasks first; they're the same point value as 🔴 ones.
      • Keep a scratch terminal on the control-plane node for crictl/etcdctl.
      • Re-read the task's exact resource NAMES — the grader matches strings.

    🧪 LAB Q&A — SIMULATOR DEBRIEF
      Q1. You scored 16/20 but two failures were both "right YAML, wrong
          namespace." What single habit fixes the most points fastest?
        A1. Make `kubectl config use-context` + an explicit `-n <ns>` (or
            `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>`) the
            first action of EVERY task. Namespace/context errors are the
            cheapest points to recover.

      Q2. A task says "the resource must be named pv-data" and you created
          "pvdata". It otherwise works. Scored?
        A2. No. The automated grader matches exact names. Always copy the
            literal name from the task text.

      Q3. During T3 your etcd restore "succeeded" but the cluster lost recent
          objects. What did you likely get wrong?
        A3. You restored an OLD snapshot or pointed the static pod at the
            wrong data-dir. Restore writes a fresh member dir; you must
            repoint etcd.yaml's hostPath volume to that dir and confirm the
            pod restarted. A snapshot only contains data up to its save time.

      Q4. T18's Service still has no Endpoints after you fixed the selector.
          Next check?
        A4. Pod readiness. Endpoints only include READY pods — a failing
            readiness probe (or no running pods) keeps Endpoints empty even
            with a correct selector. Then verify targetPort matches the
            container port.

      Q5. You finished all 20 with 25 minutes left. Best use of the time?
        A5. VERIFY, don't tinker. Re-run `kubectl get` on every object you
            created, confirm Ready/Bound/Running states, recheck the exact
            names and namespaces, and re-read each task's rubric line. Most
            recovered points in the buffer come from catching a typo or a
            missed sub-requirement — not from attempting more.

      Q6. T16: node is Ready after `systemctl restart kubelet`, but flips
          back to NotReady minutes later. What now?
        A6. Restart masked a deeper fault. Read `journalctl -u kubelet`:
            common causes are a bad /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, expired
            kubelet client cert, a down container runtime (`crictl ps`), or
            disk/memory pressure taints. Fix the root cause, not the symptom.

      🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
        • The exam rewards SPEED on correct, verified resources — not elegance.
        • Troubleshooting is 30%; T15–T20 are where passes are won or lost.
        • Context + namespace discipline is the highest-leverage exam habit.
        • Generate manifests with --dry-run=client -o yaml; never hand-type.
        • Static-pod / control-plane faults live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests
          and are debugged with crictl when kubectl itself is down.
        • Self-score honestly: 15/20 inside 120 minutes = you're ready.

================================================================================
  Appendix I: Well-Known Labels, Annotations & Taints
================================================================================

  META: reference appendix · difficulty 🟡 · CKA-relevant (scheduling, node
        management, affinity, taints/tolerations) · keep this open during labs.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
  ----------------
    Kubernetes ships a large set of RESERVED keys — labels, annotations and
    taints under the kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ namespaces — that the control
    plane, the kubelet, cloud-provider integrations and the scheduler set and
    consume automatically. You don't invent these; you READ them (for affinity,
    topology spread, nodeSelectors) and occasionally SET them (taints,
    recommended app labels). In the CKA you'll lean on node labels for
    nodeSelector/affinity questions and on the well-known taints for
    troubleshooting "why won't my Pod schedule?". Knowing the exact key spelling
    saves you from typos that silently never match.

    💡 INSIGHT: any key WITHOUT a slash, or whose prefix is NOT a reserved
    Kubernetes namespace, is "user" territory and safe to invent. Keys under
    kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ are reserved — treat them as read-only contracts.

  OBJECTIVES
  ----------
    - Recognise the standard node topology labels and use them in affinity.
    - Apply the recommended app.kubernetes.io/* labels to easypj workloads.
    - Read common annotations the control plane and add-ons set.
    - Decode the built-in taints the node controller and kubelet add, and write
      tolerations against them.

  CKA RELEVANCE
  -------------
    🎯 nodeSelector / nodeAffinity / podAffinity keyed on topology labels.
    🎯 topologySpreadConstraints using topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
    🎯 Tainting/cordoning nodes and tolerating control-plane / NoSchedule taints.
    🎯 Troubleshooting Pending Pods caused by taints or unmatched selectors.

  SECTION MAP
  -----------
    I.1  Well-known NODE labels (identity & topology)
    I.2  Recommended app.kubernetes.io/* labels
    I.3  Common annotations
    I.4  Well-known taints (and the tolerations for them)
    I.5  Quick command reference
    I.6  Reserved-namespace decision guide
    🧪  LAB Q&A

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.1  WELL-KNOWN NODE LABELS (identity & topology)
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The kubelet self-labels its Node object on registration; cloud providers add
    the topology keys. These are the labels you target with nodeSelector and
    affinity.

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
    │ LABEL KEY                                    │ SET BY                    │ EXAMPLE VALUE / MEANING      │
    ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubernetes.io/hostname                       │ kubelet                   │ node-1  (node's hostname)    │
    │ kubernetes.io/os                             │ kubelet                   │ linux | windows              │
    │ kubernetes.io/arch                           │ kubelet                   │ amd64 | arm64                │
    │ topology.kubernetes.io/region                │ cloud provider            │ us-east-1                    │
    │ topology.kubernetes.io/zone                  │ cloud provider            │ us-east-1a                   │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/instance-type             │ cloud provider            │ t3.medium                    │
    │ node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane        │ kubeadm                   │ "" (marks control-plane)     │
    │ node-role.kubernetes.io/worker               │ admin / distro            │ "" (convention, not built-in)│
    │ node.kubernetes.io/windows-build (Windows)   │ kubelet                   │ 10.0.17763                   │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

    📖 KEY TERM — DEPRECATED ALIASES: older clusters used the BETA spellings
    failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone and .../region, and
    beta.kubernetes.io/{os,arch,instance-type}. These still appear on legacy
    nodes; the GA forms above (topology.kubernetes.io/*, kubernetes.io/*,
    node.kubernetes.io/instance-type) are what you should write today.

    USING THEM — spread easypj across zones and pin to linux/amd64:

        apiVersion: apps/v1
        kind: Deployment
        metadata:
          name: easypj
          labels:
            app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
        spec:
          replicas: 3
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
          template:
            metadata:
              labels:
                app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
            spec:
              nodeSelector:
                kubernetes.io/os: linux
                kubernetes.io/arch: amd64
              affinity:
                nodeAffinity:
                  requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                    nodeSelectorTerms:
                    - matchExpressions:
                      - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                        operator: In
                        values: ["us-east-1a","us-east-1b"]
              topologySpreadConstraints:
              - maxSkew: 1
                topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels:
                    app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
              containers:
              - name: web
                image: easypj:latest

    ⚡ SPEED TIP: list a node's labels fast with
        kubectl get nodes --show-labels
        kubectl get node node-1 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | tr ',' '\n'

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.2  RECOMMENDED app.kubernetes.io/* LABELS
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    These are the COMMON application labels Kubernetes recommends so tools
    (kubectl, dashboards, Helm) can group resources consistently. They are NOT
    enforced — but adopting them on the easypj/jobpost stack makes selectors and
    `kubectl get -l` queries clean.

    ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
    │ LABEL KEY                        │ DESCRIBES                    │ easypj EXAMPLE              │
    ├──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
    │ app.kubernetes.io/name           │ application name             │ easypj                     │
    │ app.kubernetes.io/instance       │ unique deployment instance   │ easypj-prod                │
    │ app.kubernetes.io/version        │ app version (semver/image)   │ 5.2.5                      │
    │ app.kubernetes.io/component      │ role within the app          │ web | worker | db          │
    │ app.kubernetes.io/part-of        │ higher-level app it belongs  │ jobpost-platform           │
    │ app.kubernetes.io/managed-by     │ tool managing the resource   │ helm | kubectl | argocd    │
    └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

    APPLIED to the easypj web Deployment and its PostgreSQL StatefulSet:

        # easypj web tier
        labels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
          app.kubernetes.io/instance: easypj-prod
          app.kubernetes.io/version: "5.2.5"
          app.kubernetes.io/component: web
          app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jobpost-platform
          app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: helm
        ---
        # PostgreSQL data tier (same part-of, different component)
        labels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: postgres
          app.kubernetes.io/component: db
          app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jobpost-platform
          app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: helm

    💡 INSIGHT: part-of ties the web tier and the database together as one
    logical platform; component distinguishes their roles. Query the whole stack
    with:  kubectl get all -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jobpost-platform

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.3  COMMON ANNOTATIONS
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Annotations carry NON-identifying metadata — too large or not meant for
    selectors. Many are set by the control plane or add-ons automatically.

    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ANNOTATION KEY                                     │ PURPOSE                                      │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration   │ stores last `kubectl apply` manifest        │
    │ kubernetes.io/change-cause                         │ rollout history note (--record / set)       │
    │ kubernetes.io/description                          │ free-text description of the object         │
    │ deployment.kubernetes.io/revision                  │ Deployment revision number (for rollback)   │
    │ control-plane.alpha.kubernetes.io/leader           │ legacy leader-election holder record        │
    │ scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/critical-pod         │ legacy: mark Pod critical (now PriorityClass)│
    │ kubernetes.io/ingress.class (deprecated)           │ pre-IngressClass Ingress controller select  │
    │ node.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl                       │ kubelet attach/detach reconcile hint        │
    │ volume.kubernetes.io/storage-provisioner           │ CSI provisioner that owns a PVC             │
    │ pv.kubernetes.io/bound-by-controller               │ PV/PVC bound automatically by controller    │
    │ batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index (Indexed) │ completion index of an Indexed Job Pod      │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: `kubectl apply` reads and writes
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration to compute a three-way
    merge — that's why apply behaves differently from create/replace. Inspect it:
        kubectl get deploy easypj -o jsonpath=\
          '{.metadata.annotations.kubectl\.kubernetes\.io/last-applied-configuration}'

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.4  WELL-KNOWN TAINTS (and their tolerations)
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The node controller and kubelet add these taints automatically to signal
    node conditions; the scheduler keeps Pods OFF tainted nodes unless the Pod
    TOLERATES the taint. Effects: NoSchedule (don't place new Pods),
    PreferNoSchedule (soft avoid), NoExecute (evict running Pods that don't
    tolerate).

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
    │ TAINT KEY                                        │ EFFECT     │ ADDED WHEN                        │
    ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
    │ node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane            │ NoSchedule │ kubeadm marks control-plane node  │
    │ node-role.kubernetes.io/master (legacy)          │ NoSchedule │ old control-plane taint name      │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/not-ready                     │ NoExecute  │ Node Ready condition = False      │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/unreachable                   │ NoExecute  │ node controller can't reach kubelet│
    │ node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable                 │ NoSchedule │ node cordoned (kubectl cordon)    │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure               │ NoSchedule │ kubelet sees memory pressure      │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure                 │ NoSchedule │ kubelet sees disk pressure        │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/pid-pressure                  │ NoSchedule │ kubelet sees PID pressure         │
    │ node.kubernetes.io/network-unavailable           │ NoSchedule │ node network not configured (CNI) │
    │ node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized   │ NoSchedule │ cloud node not yet initialised    │
    │ node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/shutdown        │ NoSchedule │ cloud reports instance shut down  │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

    THE not-ready / unreachable FLOW (NoExecute eviction):

        Node goes bad ──► node controller adds NoExecute taint
                          (not-ready or unreachable)
              │
              ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Pod tolerates taint?                        │
        │   yes ──► stays; tolerationSeconds counts   │──► after N s, evicted
        │   no  ──► evicted immediately               │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    📖 KEY TERM — DEFAULT TOLERATIONS: the admission controller auto-adds these
    to EVERY Pod so a brief node blip doesn't cause instant eviction (default
    300s grace):

        tolerations:
        - key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoExecute
          tolerationSeconds: 300
        - key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoExecute
          tolerationSeconds: 300

    TOLERATING the control-plane taint (run a Pod ON the control-plane node):

        tolerations:
        - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule

    A DaemonSet-style "tolerate everything" (system add-ons like CNI/monitoring):

        tolerations:
        - operator: Exists      # bare Exists with no key tolerates ALL taints

    🩺 TROUBLESHOOTING a Pending Pod: if `kubectl describe pod` shows
    "node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane}" the
    only candidate node is the control plane — either add the toleration above,
    untaint it (`kubectl taint nodes node-1 \
    node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane-`), or add a worker.

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.5  QUICK COMMAND REFERENCE
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🔑 COMMANDS

      # LABELS
      kubectl get nodes --show-labels
      kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
      kubectl label node node-1 disktype=ssd            # add custom label
      kubectl label node node-1 disktype-                # remove label
      kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jobpost-platform

      # ANNOTATIONS
      kubectl annotate deploy easypj kubernetes.io/change-cause="image to 5.2.5"
      kubectl annotate deploy easypj kubernetes.io/change-cause-   # remove

      # TAINTS
      kubectl taint nodes node-1 dedicated=easypj:NoSchedule      # add
      kubectl taint nodes node-1 dedicated=easypj:NoSchedule-     # remove
      kubectl describe node node-1 | grep -A2 Taints
      kubectl cordon node-1        # adds node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable
      kubectl uncordon node-1      # removes it
      kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  I.6  RESERVED-NAMESPACE DECISION GUIDE
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — is this key mine to invent?

        Does the key contain a "/" ?
          │
          ├─ NO  ──────────────► free to use (e.g. environment=prod)
          │
          └─ YES ──► is the prefix kubernetes.io or k8s.io (or *.kubernetes.io)?
                       │
                       ├─ YES ──► RESERVED. Read it; only set the documented
                       │           ones (taints, app.kubernetes.io/*). Don't
                       │           invent new keys here.
                       │
                       └─ NO  ──► your own DNS-style prefix — fine
                                  (e.g. easypj.io/tier=web)

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      - kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ prefixes are RESERVED; treat them as contracts.
      - Topology affinity/spread keys: topology.kubernetes.io/{region,zone},
        kubernetes.io/{hostname,os,arch}, node.kubernetes.io/instance-type.
      - app.kubernetes.io/* are RECOMMENDED (not enforced) grouping labels.
      - not-ready & unreachable are NoExecute taints; every Pod gets a default
        300s toleration for them.
      - The control-plane taint (NoSchedule) is why workloads avoid masters.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      - Beta aliases (failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone,
        beta.kubernetes.io/arch) still exist on old nodes — match the spelling
        actually present, prefer the GA form on new manifests.
      - A nodeSelector that names a label NO node carries fails SILENTLY: the Pod
        sits Pending with no error beyond "0/N nodes available".
      - `operator: Exists` with NO key tolerates ALL taints — powerful and easy
        to over-grant; scope it to DaemonSets/system Pods.
      - node-role.kubernetes.io/master is the LEGACY taint; new clusters use
        node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane (some keep both for compatibility).

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      - `-L key` prints a label as its own column — faster than --show-labels for
        spotting zone/instance-type at a glance.
      - Trailing "-" on label/annotation/taint commands REMOVES the key.
      - kubectl cordon == add unschedulable taint; uncordon == remove it.

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  🧪  LAB Q&A
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    🟢 Q1. Which label key selects nodes by availability zone, and what's the
           region equivalent?
       A1. topology.kubernetes.io/zone (zone) and topology.kubernetes.io/region.
           Legacy beta forms: failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/{zone,region}.

    🟢 Q2. Print every node with its zone and instance type in dedicated columns.
       A2. kubectl get nodes \
             -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type

    🟡 Q3. Your easypj Pod is Pending; describe shows "untolerated taint
           {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: NoSchedule}". Give two fixes.
       A3. (a) Add a toleration:
               tolerations:
               - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
                 operator: Exists
                 effect: NoSchedule
           (b) Provide/uncordon a worker node, OR untaint the control plane:
               kubectl taint nodes node-1 \
                 node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane-

    🟡 Q4. Label the easypj web Deployment template with the full recommended
           app.kubernetes.io/* set for version 5.2.5, component web.
       A4. app.kubernetes.io/name: easypj
           app.kubernetes.io/instance: easypj-prod
           app.kubernetes.io/version: "5.2.5"
           app.kubernetes.io/component: web
           app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jobpost-platform
           app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: helm

    🟡 Q5. A node fails. Which taints get added, with what effect, and how long
           before a default Pod is evicted?
       A5. node.kubernetes.io/not-ready (Ready=False) or
           node.kubernetes.io/unreachable (controller can't reach kubelet), both
           NoExecute. Pods carry an auto-added 300s toleration, so eviction
           happens ~5 minutes after the condition, not immediately.

    🔴 Q6. Make a DaemonSet that runs on EVERY node including cordoned,
           pressured and control-plane nodes. What single toleration achieves it?
       A6. A bare Exists toleration with no key, no effect:
               tolerations:
               - operator: Exists
           This tolerates all taints (NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute),
           which is exactly how cluster-critical DaemonSets (CNI, kube-proxy,
           node-exporter) stay scheduled everywhere.

    🔴 Q7. You set nodeSelector: disktype=ssd but the Pod never schedules and
           there's no event error beyond "0/3 nodes available". Diagnose.
       A7. No node carries the label disktype=ssd (unmatched selectors fail
           silently). Verify with `kubectl get nodes -L disktype`; fix by
           labelling a node: `kubectl label node node-2 disktype=ssd`, or correct
           the selector to a label that exists.

================================================================================


==============================================================================
  Appendix J: Gateway API Reference (2025)
==============================================================================
  META  | role-oriented L4/L7 routing API; the successor to Ingress
  ICONS | 🎯 exam  🏢 day-2  🧪 lab  💡 insight  🧠 analogy  📖 term
        | 🔧 under-the-hood  ⚠️ gotcha  ⚡ speed tip  🔑 must-remember
        | 🧭 decision  🩺 troubleshoot  🟢🟡🔴 difficulty

  WHY THIS MATTERS
    Ingress froze years ago: every advanced feature (header routing, traffic
    splitting, gRPC, cross-namespace delegation) was bolted on through
    vendor-specific annotations, so a manifest written for nginx-ingress would
    not run on Traefik or a cloud LB. The Gateway API replaces that mess with a
    portable, role-separated, expressive resource model that went GA (v1.0) in
    Oct 2023 and is the strategic direction for north-south AND (via the GAMMA
    initiative) east-west service-mesh traffic. For the easypj jobpost platform
    it lets the cluster (platform) team own the public listener/TLS while the
    application (jobpost) team owns only its own routes — without sharing one
    brittle Ingress object.

  🎯 CKA RELEVANCE
    Gateway API is now an examinable topic under "Services & Networking." You
    must recognise the resource model (GatewayClass / Gateway / *Route), read
    status CONDITIONS to debug, and translate a simple Ingress into an
    HTTPRoute. You will NOT be asked to install a controller, but you must know
    Gateway API is CRD-based (not built into the API server) and needs a
    controller (Istio, Cilium, NGINX Gateway Fabric, Contour, etc.).

  📖 KEY TERMS
    Gateway API ... a family of CRDs (gateway.networking.k8s.io) for L4/L7
                    routing, designed role-oriented and portable.
    Role-oriented .. each resource maps to a human role (infra provider /
                    cluster operator / application developer).
    North-south .... traffic entering/leaving the cluster (clients -> Services).
    East-west ...... traffic between workloads inside the cluster (GAMMA / mesh).
    Attachment ..... a Route "attaches" to a Gateway via parentRefs; the Gateway
                    "allows" routes via listener allowedRoutes.

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  SECTION MAP
    J.1  The three-tier resource model (who owns what)
    J.2  Resource reference: GatewayClass / Gateway / HTTPRoute / friends
    J.3  Status conditions cheat-sheet (how to debug)
    J.4  Gateway API vs Ingress (side-by-side)
    J.5  Common patterns (path / header / weight / TLS / redirect / rewrite)
    J.6  Cross-namespace routing & ReferenceGrant
    J.7  kubectl commands & glossary
    🔧 DEEPER / Under-the-Hood
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS · ⚠️ GOTCHAS · ⚡ SPEED TIPS · 🔑 COMMANDS · 🧪 LAB Q&A
